text: Both the Vajrayoginī and Jogeśvara temples are believed to be built on a single rock without a proper foundation.
In 2000/2001 CE, the Friends of Sankhu, a local organization, repurposed copper sheets from the Vajrayoginī temple to cover the Jogeśvara temple(B. Shrestha2012, p. 417).
A person named Kulavīrasiṃha had donated the decorative covering during the reign of King Surendra in 1878 CE (NS 998).
The Temple also gets its name from the Caitya known as Jogeśvara Caitya named after Jogadeva Vajrācārya, who founded the town of Sankhu (D. Sharma and T. Shrestha2016, p. 256).
The establishment of this monastery also marks the rise of the Buddhist civilization in Nepālamaṇḍala (Vajrācārya et alNS 1120, p. 10).

An inscription of Aṃśuvarman at Hā̃ḍigāũ, Kathmandu states that the Gũ Vihāra was allocated a grant of 6purāṇas 2paṇas from the state equal to the grants for Paśupati and Cā̃gunārāyaṇa in 608 CE i.e., Mānadeva Era 32 (D. Vajrācārya2030, p. 320-321).
This tiered Temple/Monastery was once constructed in theśikharastyle as well.
An entry of an annal dated the 1st of the dark fortnight of Māgha in 1689 CE (NS 809) refers to it as a two-tier temple (T. Siṃha1136, p. 15, folio 23A).

On the 13th of the bright fortnight of Phālguna in 1689 CE (NS 809), King Bhūpālendra Malla got the two-tiered Temple dismantled and got a door installed for constructing aśikhara-style (granthakūṭa) temple (T. Siṃha1136, p. 15, folio 23A).

A few years later, theśikhara-style Temple constructed at the orders of Bhūpālendra Malla was again rebuilt as a two-tiered Temple and a finial was installed on the 3rd of the bright fortnight of Phālguna in 1727 CE (NS 847) (T. Siṃha1136, p. 28, folio 46A).

Another record shows that the Temple was renovated and aguthiwas formed by donating plots of land by a person named Bhikhvādhana along with his wife Mayajudhaṃ and other family members in 1849 CE (NS 969).
Although the Temple did not collapse in the 2015 earthquakes, it suffered severe damages and stood on wooden supports.
The Department of Archaeology rebuilt both the Vajrayoginī and Jogeśvara Temples at a total cost of NRs. 59.2 million.
The Nārāyaṇa temple at Dhālāchẽ Ṭola, Lalitpur, was originally constructed in the medieval period in the multi-tiered pagoda style.
Although the structure collapsed and deteriorated over time, it was later rebuilt in its present form.
No inscription recording its foundation or date of construction has been found, yet surviving sculptures and wooden elements confirm its late medieval origin.
The image here corresponds to “Vāmana Viṣṇu” (S. Mainālī VS 2070, p. 63).
This conception is supported by inscriptions such as the one from Jayabāgeśvarī (1602 VS/1545–46 CE), which invokes Viṣṇu alongside both goddesses.
By contrast, Sarasvatī’s association with Brahmā is rare in Nepal, though an inscription from Śaṅkhamūla (1731–32 CE/1788 VS) records their names together (R. Vanta VS 2061, 18).
The original images of Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī from this shrine were stolen, and replicas now occupy their places.
The sanctum also houses a damaged image of Garuḍāsana Viṣṇu and a rare sculpture of Garuḍāsana Kṛṣṇa, depicted playing the flute while mounted on Garuḍa.

Local elders recall that prior to the 1934 CE earthquake (1990 VS), the temple retained this form, and that its roof nearly touched that of the neighboring Lokeśvara temple (LAL2180) (local resident, Maharjana, male, age 83).
In 2005 CE (NS 1125), the temple underwent major renovation under the Lalitpur Sub-Metropolitan City.

During this process, replicas of Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī were installed to replace the stolen originals, a task initiated in the 1970s by local residents Hirabahadur Bajrācārya and Candralakṣmī Pradhāna (local resident, Maharjana, male, age 64).

Jayabali Dyaḥ is apīṭha(abode) of Goddess Rudrāyaṇī, one of the Eight Mother Goddesses (aṣṭamātṛkā) whose shrines date back to the foundation of Sankhu in in 1300 BC (Kaligata Era 1801).
[2]The Suntvāḥ Ṭola Sudhara Samiti, a local committee formed for the conservation of the area, renovated the Pīṭha (i.e., Jayabali Dyaḥ) in 2021 CE.
During the renovation, a newtoraṇawas installed while the oldtoraṇathat was in poor condition was kept inside the wall of the Pīṭha.
A stone pillar for offering flames or lighting butter lamps was also installed on the same occasion.
Before the renovation, the Pīṭha used to be under the shed of corrugated tin sheets (Sharma and Shrestha2016, p. 2088).

Footnotes^Regarding the foundation of Sankhu, theMaṇiśaila-Mahāvadāna, a Buddhist scripture, mentions that Jogadeva Vajrācārya founded the town in the shape of aśaṅkha(conch shell) in 1300 BC (Kaligata Era 1801) as per the instruction of Vajrayoginī by assimilating seven villages.
He divided the town into eightṭolas and constructed a palace at the centre, along with the shrines ofaṣṭamātṛkās, ninebāhāḥs, and four gates in four directions (V. Vajrācārya1119, p. 32-33).

They state that it was constructed by Kulānanda Siṃha in 1789 CE (NS 909).

However, an inscription installed in the Sataḥ records that Vīra Siṃha from Sankhu engaged in constructing ahitiand a rest house for pilgrims (dharmaśālā) in 1783 CE (NS 903), and that he also installed a statue of Viṣṇu.
Although the Girīs have stopped receiving donations from the Jośīs since the early 2000s, the offerings are still made.
Ratnarāma Bhāro and his wife Caṃpāvatī Mayī, residents of Sikochẽ, Cāpāgāũ, established the statue of Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa and built this temple in 1681 CE (NS 801).
While the primary deity, a statue of Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa, has unfortunately been stolen, the sanctum still houses other statues, including Yamarāja, Umāmaheśvara, and Nārāyaṇa.
To the north of the temple, a shrine dedicated to Muni Gaṇeśa can be found, with a jaḥdhuṃ water tank installed in front of it.
A Brahmā statue (CHG0160-004) was previously placed atop thejaḥdhuṃbut was later moved to a small iron cage south of the Mūla Gaṇeśa temple after theft attempts.
Ratnarāma Bhāro and his wife Caṃpāvatī Mayī, residents of Sikochẽ, Cāpāgāũ, established the Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa statue and constructed this temple in front of their home in 1681 CE (NS 801).
They also installed statues of Hariśaṅkara to the right of Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa and Bhavānīśaṅkara to the left, following a day-and-night fire oblation.
Unfortunately, all three of these statues have been stolen.
In 2008 CE (VS 2065), the temple underwent renovation, funded by the Chapagaun Village Development Committee (VDC).
The donor couple donated 12 ropanis of land to sustain the temple's operations.
They specified that donations should be made during the annual Vajrabārāhī procession in Caitra and the Yẽnyāḥ (Indra Jātrā) festival.
There are no historical sources to date the initial construction of the Phalcā, but it still has aguthi.
The three-bay Phalcā facing north is currently (August 2022) under construction.
No inscription records the initial construction of the Phalcā.
Possibly, it was built around the same time Pīgaṃdyaḥ was established in 1670 CE (NS 790).
It was dismantled in 2020 CE for reconstruction.
However, due to insufficient fund, the roof of the Phalcā remains to be installed.
Locals say the reconstruction will be completed soon.
Tāpālāchi Phalcā was built around the middle of the Rana period.
Since then, the descendants of its builder have continued the tradition of distributing a ritual drink made of water and sugar (sākhaḥti)that is distributed on the day ofAkṣaya Tṛtīyā.

There is an inscription in Tāpālāchi Phalcā regarding its construction according to which the arcaded platform was built to facilitate rituals in the name of Viṣṇurāja Bharo (Jośi), his brother Mānyaraja, and their descendants.
The Phalcha was constructed in 1911 CE (NS 1031).
The inscription also mentions that land was allocated to a guṭhi to support annual rituals, and it includes the names of the guṭhiyāra.
About 80 years after its construction, Tāpālāchi Phalcā's state has dilapidated.
In 1990 CE (NS 1110), it was rebuilt with a reduced size by the descendants of the original builders, Nārāyaṇarāja and Badrīrāja Jośi.
During this restoration, they replaced the disappeared idol of Viṣṇu with a new one (LAL4055-001).
An unrelated inscription, recovered from a house south of Tāpālāchi, is now preserved in this Phalcā.
This inscription records that a three-bay phalcā was built on the ground floor of the same house in 1850 CE (NS 970).
Since Tāpālāchi Phalcā was built on this day, the Jośī clan also performs an anniversary worship of the idol and receives offerings.

Constructed in a blended architectural style amidst a cluster of Śiva temples in Mṛgasthalī, this Kṛṣṇa temple’s specific year of construction and the patron behind remain veiled in uncertainty due to the absence of historical sources.
Due to the absence of inscriptions at the site, details regarding the temple's establishment remain unclear.
Apparently, it was constructed during the Rāṇā period (1846-1951 CE), akin to most temples within the complex.
The earthquakes of 2015 inflicted severe damage upon the temple, leaving visible cracks on its walls that persist to this day.
Previously, daily rituals were conducted in the mornings and evenings until the 2015 earthquakes.

monument_name: Nārāyaṇa Mandira (believed to built during the Licchavi Period)
text: The old set of the doorframe of the main entrance to the sanctum was used again in the reconstruction.
A person by the name of Cikiti Bhāvo and other members of the community facilitated the construction of the Phalcā in 1795 CE (NS 915).
In 2008 CE (VS 2065), it was reconstructed from its base up.
The Lalitpur Municipality contributed NR 660.000 for the reconstruction.
During the reconstruction, another floor was added.
An inscription inside the Phalcā mentions that the Caitya was there before the Phalcā was built.
After the reconstruction, statues of Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa, Saṅkaṭā, Kṛṣṇa, Rām-Lakṣmaṇa-Śita, and Nārāyaṇa were established in the Phalcā’s northern wall.
The Phalcā was badly damaged in the 2015 CE earthquakes and is since supported by timber braces.
The Temple preserves only one trilingual (Sanskrit, Maithili and Newari) inscription (embedded on its plinth) from 1667 CE (NS 787).
It records a land endowment by King Jagatprakāśa Malla to form aguthifor performing the daily and anniversary rituals at the Temple.
Local elderly residents say that it was a two-storied Temple tiled withjhĩgaṭībricksbefore it collapsed in the 1934 earthquakes.
Previously, the statue also had a flute, and Śrīkṛṣṇa Mahāviṣṇu is also known as Harikṛṣṇa (G. Vajrācārya VS 2033, p.84).
Although Pruscha (1975, p. 62) identifies the temple as a 17th-century structure, there is no historical source that dates its initial construction.
However, a manuscript records King Pratāpa Malla offering acakrato a Viṣṇu temple in 1666 CE, which appears to be this one (G. Vajrācārya VS 2033, p.84).
The temple was renovated by the Kathmandu Valley Preservation Trust in 2004 CE, and despite minor damage caused by the 2015 earthquakes, it still stands strong.
Miśra brahmins conduct daily rituals at the temple, and on Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī, the 8th day of the dark fortnight of Bhādra, a fire oblation is performed.
Additionally, a ceremonial pole (yaḥsĩ) is erected next to the temple on the 12th day of the bright fortnight, marking the beginning of the Yẽnyāḥ festival in Kathmandu.
The Caṇḍī Bhagavatī Mandira was constructed during the reign of King Raṇajita Malla in 1734 CE (see the inscription from NS 854 below).
It is a one-story Temple raised on a high plinth, and hassataḥs constructed to its northern and western sides.
The statue of Gaṇeśa still exists but another image posted on the eastern wall has already been stolen.

It is clear that the Temple was constructed to enshrine Bhagavatī, as an inscription from the Temple records the construction of a Bhagavatī Temple and all the struts of the Temple contain the figures of various forms of Bhagavatī.
Probably, the Temple with the image of Bhagavatī inside the sanctum collapsed at some point in history and was reconstructed in the present form using the old struts.
The presence of modern tiles and the condition of the walls all around the Temple suggest that the monument had undergone multiple renovations.
Unfortunately, nothing is known of the past renovations due to the lack of documentation.
Among the gates constructed during Nepal’s Malla period, this is the most magnificent and renowned.
Built just before the rise of the Śāha dynasty, it also stands as the final royal artistic masterpiece of the Malla era.
Located in Bhaktapur Durbar Square, this gate stands between the Fifty-five Window Palace and the Siṃhadhvākhā Durbar buildings.
Traditionally, gates were built by placing a stone foundation block (īlvahaṃ) on the ground and raising the structure upon it.
According to P. Śreṣṭha (VS 2055, p. 43), these represent Kubera and his consort.
A goldentoraṇaarches above the panels, featuring an exquisitely crafted central figure of Taleju Bhavānī (P. Shrestha, VS 2055, p. 43).
According to local tradition, some Bhaktapur residents believe these gilded patches were added to conceal bullet marks left during the Gorkhali invasion (local resident, Rājopādhyāya, male, age 73).
Its most striking feature is the lavish use of gilded sheets, which adorn not only various divine figures but also architectural elements such as the finial, inscriptions, and roof.
In 1646 CE (NS 766), King Jagajyoti Malla summoned artisans from this clan from Ko Bāhāḥ in Patan to Bhaktapur.

Drawing from these facts, P. Shrestha (VS 2055, p. 36) suggests that the conceptualization and a preliminary model of the Golden Gate were developed under Jagajyoti Malla, while it was Raṇajita Malla who later executed the final construction.
The "Nivā" Śākya clan completed the gate's construction in 1753 CE (NS 874) after three years of work.
The principal artisans involved were Sabhākara, Karaṇākara, and Ratikara, who performed monthly worship of Mañjuśrī throughout the construction period.
Upon completion, they presented ahelepho(a type of metal ornament) to Mañjuśrī as an offering to mark the project's successful conclusion (S. Śākya VS 2078, p. 29).
Both offerings bear the same inscription date: the 10th of the bright fortnight of Kārtika, NS 875 (1754 CE).
P. Shrestha (VS 2055, pp. 44-45) erroneously records the construction year as NS 874.
A golden inscription detailing the gate's construction is affixed to its facade, dating to a period when Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa Śāha was aggressively expanding his territory.
Against this backdrop of territorial conquests, the inscription on the Golden Gate boldly proclaims the extent of Raṇajita Malla's dominion.
Such inscriptions proudly declaring territorial boundaries are not uncommon from the Malla period.

The gate’s inscription declares: "During the reign of Raṇajita Malla, whose rule extended over Nāladuma, Dolakhā, and as far west as the Dūdhakośī River." This is not the sole instance of his political assertions.
As the ceremonial entrance to the political heart of Nepālamaṇḍala, the gate was historically referred to as the Pāla Gate and Nepal Gate in contemporary inscriptions.

Having procured substantial quantities of gold from Tibet, he conducted a grandthāpūjā(establishment ritual) at Taleju Temple to sanctify this acquisition—an event documented in the temple’s ritual records (P. Śreṣṭha VS 2044, p. 16).
Adjacent to the gate’s western side lies another historically significant inscription from 1453 CE (NS 573), dating to Yakṣa Malla’s reign.
This inscription, which details the construction and administration of Bhaktapur’s fortifications, is a critical primary source for studying the Malla-era military defense systems.
P. Shrestha (VS 2055, pp. 44-45) has mistakenly read the year as NS 874.
The golden inscription written about the construction of this door is placed on the facade of the door itself.
Amidst this peak of land expansion politics, the inscription on the Golden Gate expresses the extent of Raṇajita Malla's kingdom.
Such a Malla-era inscription proudly citing the kingdom's boundaries is not considered very rare.

The inscription on the gate states, "While Raṇajita Malla was ruling over Nāladuma, Dolakhā, and as far as the western Dūdhakośī." This is not the only inscription where he has demonstrated his political success.
In the sense of being the gateway to the ruling center of the entire Nepālamaṇḍala, this gate was referred to as Pāla Gate and Nepal Gate in contemporary inscriptions.
He had brought a significant amount of gold into Bhaktapur from Tibet and performed an establishment ritual (thāpūjā) at Taleju to mark the acquisition of gold.
This ritual is also mentioned in the list ofthāpūjās performed at Taleju (P. Śreṣṭha VS 2044, p. 16).
To the west of this gate is another important inscription dating back to 1453 CE (NS 573) during the time of Yakṣa Malla.
This inscription, written about the construction and management of the fort in Bhaktapur, is considered very important for the study of the history of the Malla-era defense system.
The original quadrangularjalaharī, with its shaft representing Śiva, was stolen.
A newśivaliṅgawith a circularjalaharīwas then installed.
The shrine has three inscriptions.
One records its initial construction in 1676 CE (NS 796) during the reign of King Nṛpendra Malla, confirming Kathmandu's influence over Nuwakot.
This inscription also notes that Gopīdeva Bhāro donated land to set up a trust for worship.
Another inscription, dated NS 917 (1797 CE), is no longer readable.
A third inscription on the pedestal of five donor statues names Gopīdeva, the main donor, and other family members, suggesting the statues were installed when the shrine was established in 1676 CE.
The 2015 CE earthquakes severely damaged the shrine, prompting renovation by Bidur Municipality in 2016 CE (VS 2073).
On Śivarātrī, they gather at the shrine to set a bonfire and distributeprasāda.
Certain Śreṣṭhas having family name Mulmī built this Bāhāḥ in NS 835 (1715 CE) and appointed a Vajrācārya family living in the area to maintain and run it.
A statue of Dīpaṅkara Buddha was installed in the Bāhāḥ premises in NS 839 (1719) and its courtyard was paved with the bricks in NS 883 (cf.Pruscha1975, P-188;Locke1985, 87).
Thetoraṇawas removed from the door and was kept inside the sanctum for some time because of security issues.
Aśikharakūṭa caityaanddharmadhātu maṇḍalaare established in the courtyard.
The Bāhāḥ was severely damaged by the 2015 earthquakes hence the Vajrācārya family members, who have been taking care of the Bāhāḥ since its initial establishment, do not live here anymore.
Since it might collapse anytime, they do not enter the sanctum, but worship the deity from outside.
Footnotes^The inscriptions recording these events cannot be found in the Bāhāḥ’s premises anymore.
They must have been lost or moved somewhere else.
Thecaitya-like superstructure and theCaturvyūhaimage reinforce its identification as aCaturvyūha Caitya(H. Śākya NS 1113, pp. 63–64).
Prayagraj Sharma (Sharma 1999, p. 9) suggests that only pedestals were made in stone during the Licchavi period, and the tradition of constructing full stone temples had not yet begun.
In Patan, the construction of stone temples gained momentum after King Siddhinarasiṃha Malla built the renowned Kṛṣṇa Mandira.
According to Pruscha (1975, p. 202), the Dyaḥnani temple was constructed slightly earlier, around 1617 CE (NS 737–38) by Sanjajena Śākya, though no primary source is cited.
The temple features multiple inscriptions, four of which are engraved on its façade, and several others on the middle tier’s stone surfaces.
These inscriptions, though partially damaged and obscured by layers of limewash, include references to construction and ritual provisions.
The only clearly legible inscription dates to 1664 CE (NS 784), documenting the establishment of aguṭhī(ritual trust) during the reign of King Śrīnivāsa Malla (Pruscha 1975, p. 202).

The main annual events include theVarṣavardhana Pūjāheld on the second day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, which involves a fire ritual and concludes with a communal feast hosted by the managing Śākya family.
Some of the lands mentioned in the inscriptions remained under the temple's ownership until the 1990s.

Theprāṇa(spiritual essence) of theBhairavaorMātṛkādeities enshrined outside the settlement is often ritually invoked and installed within the settlement—in temples ordyaḥcheṃ(god-houses)—through tantric consecration.
Architecturally, thepīṭhaconsists of an aniconic stone installation set a few feet below ground level.
The upper part of the principal stone bears a now-damaged sculptedchepū(canopy), while the lower portion remains unshaped and is venerated as the goddess Indrāyaṇī herself.
As of August 2025, several newly installed images of Hindu deities are found around thepīṭha.
Over the twentieth century, however, this open expanse was reduced by the construction of modern facilities such as a police post and a ward office, and the entire precinct was enclosed by walls.
Chronicles suggest the widespread establishment ofAṣṭamātṛkāshrines in the valley’s early urban history.

TheDevamālāvaṃśāvalīrecords that King Ānandadeva developed Bhaktapur into a major city in the year Kaliyuga 4197, founding the eightMātṛkā pīṭhasoutside the city and installing golden images within thedyaḥcheṃ(Devamālāvaṃśāvalī, p. 106).

Similarly, theBhāṣā Vaṃśāvalīstates that King Guṇakāmadeva, when founding Kathmandu in Kaliyuga 3825, established severalpīṭhasaround the city—including the “Luṭi Pīṭha” (Indrāyaṇī) to the north (Bhāṣā Vaṃśāvalī, part II, p. 24).
The earliest direct evidence for the Indrāyaṇī cult comes from an inscription carved on the aniconic stone itself, dated to 1710 CE (NS 831).
This record indicates that the stone was established in that year, though it remains uncertain whether the inscription commemorates a pre-existing cult site or marks the foundation of thepīṭhaitself.
A later inscription dated VS 2038 (1982 CE) documents the renovation of apāṭī(resting platform) at thepīṭhaundertaken by Śrī 3 Māhilī Mahārāṇī Kṛṣṇakumārī.

The inscription does not specify which Rāṇā ruler’s consort she was; while both Jit Śamśer’s and Dev Śamśer’s queens were named Kṛṣṇakumārī (D. Panta VS 2055, pp. 1, 22), neither identification can be confirmed.

The same inscription also records new ritual prescriptions for the observance ofNavarātra,Bālācaturdaśī,Maṅgal Cauthī, andŚivarātri, reflecting the growing influence of late-Vedic Hindu ritualism upon the earlierŚāktacult.
The Dāsa Dhārā (water spout) is situated along the traditional route linking Triśūlī Bazaar to Nuwakot, a passage widely used by people before the construction of a motor road in the area.
This similarity suggests that the Dāsa Dhārā was likely established around the same time as the Baṭāra Bazaar Dhārā, which was built in 1911 CE (VS 1967).
However, there is no inscription to definitively date the initial construction of the Dāsa Dhārā.
Locals speculate that it was built by a "dāsa," meaning a slave, but this seems implausible.
Another water spout from Nuwakot, Tīna Dhārā (NWK0380), was renovated by Colonel Madanamānasiṃha Basneta in 1925 CE (VS 1982).
The traditionalbajraplaster used during the renovation of Tīna Dhārā can also be seen at the Dāsa Dhārā, suggesting the possibility that Dāsa Dhārā was also renovated at the same time.
However, the water is now (as of May 2024 CE) collected in an underground tank behind the spout, leaving the spout itself dry.
With the construction of a motor road, the hiking route connecting Triśūlī and Nuwakot is no longer used, and the spout has remained unused for a long time.
Due to years of neglect, the water spout is currently in a poor state of repair, and no socio-cultural activities associated with it have survived.
Nuwakot—historically within the territory and cultural sphere of the Malla polities—likewise adopted the cult of Taleju Bhavānī, for whom a prominent shrine-house (Taleju Ghara) was established.
In remembrance of this sacred past, the knoll on which the Taleju Ghar stands is still known locally as Ṛṣivanapattana (D. Vajrācārya and Ṭ. Śreṣṭha VS 2032, p. 14).
citations: (D. Vajrācārya and Ṭ. Śreṣṭha VS 2032, p. 14)

text: Prior to the 2015 CE (VS 2072) earthquake, it was a five-storeyed building with a tiled (jhiṅgaṭī) roof surmounted by a metal pinnacle (gajura).
On the fourth floor, a small enclosedbhujākoṭhāwas constructed toward the north-west, while the third floor featured abārdalī(veranda).
The second floor housed the sanctum of Goddess Taleju, access to which was restricted exclusively to the king, royal priest, and designated attendants (D. Vajrācārya and Ṭ. Śreṣṭha VS 2032, p. 7).
citations: (D. Vajrācārya and Ṭ. Śreṣṭha VS 2032, p. 7)

text: According to the ritual specialist (dhāmī) of the Bhairavī temple, the original image of Taleju was cast in copper and crowned with a jewel-studded headdress; following its theft, the remaining feet of the goddess were venerated as her embodied form (P. Śreṣṭha 2024).
The first floor comprised three rooms opening onto a westerndalāna(porch) roofed with tiles and formerly hung with a bell, long since stolen, accessed by a stone staircase from ground level.
No inscriptions survive within the Taleju precinct to attest to the precise date or patron of its foundation.
Nevertheless, documentary evidence confirms that the cult of Taleju shrine was firmly established at Nuwakot by the later medieval period.

In 1638 CE (NS 758), during the removal of thegajurafor the renovation of the Bhairavī temple (NWK0040), offerings of buffaloes, goats, and ducks were dispatched to various deities; among them, Taleju Bhavānī received worship accompanied by the offering of two ducks (D. Vajrācārya and Ṭ. Śreṣṭha VS 2032, p. 77).
citations: (D. Vajrācārya and Ṭ. Śreṣṭha VS 2032, p. 77)

text: In 1776 CE (VS 1833), Dāmodara Pāṇḍe granted fields yielding fortymurīof produce to the Taleju priest Bhājurāma for the performance of daily worship (D. Vajrācārya and Ṭ. Śreṣṭha VS 2032, p. 77).
citations: (D. Vajrācārya and Ṭ. Śreṣṭha VS 2032, p. 77)

text: Later, in 1831 CE (VS 1888), King Rājendrāvikrama Śāha issued an order to protect Ṛṣivana—the site of the Taleju Ghar—recognizing it as a place sanctified by ascetics and integral to the Bhairavī Jātrā.

Following the great earthquake of 1934 CE (VS 1990), the structure lost much of its original fabric during repairs, and further roof maintenance was undertaken around 1970–1971 CE (VS 2027–2028) (V. Śarmā VS 2050, p. 51).

On Saturday, 1973 CE (VS 2030 Śrāvaṇa 6), the image of Taleju was stolen; its feet were broken off and abandoned by the thieves, and despite the presence of nearby government offices and a military barracks, the theft went unnoticed (T. Naḥghaḥbhanī VS 2043, p. 15).
After the image was not recovered, a replacement was installed by the Guthī Saṃsthāna, but this too was later stolen, leaving the goddess’s feet as the sole object of worship (P. Śreṣṭha 2024).
An unverified report suggests fire damage around 1980 CE (VS 2037), though no official confirmation survives (Shakya 2013).
Already structurally weakened, the Taleju Ghar suffered severe cracking during the 2015 CE (VS 2072) earthquake.
Although the eastern roof was damaged, it did not collapse; however, prolonged neglect led to water infiltration, and on 2017 CE (VS 2074 Śrāvaṇa 19) the eastern section collapsed entirely.
In response, the Government of China pledged assistance for the restoration of earthquake-damaged heritage sites at Nuwakot.

A bilateral agreement was signed on 17 June 2019 CE (VS 2076 Āṣāḍha 2) between China’s Agency for International Economic Cooperation and Nepal’s National Reconstruction Authority, assigning conservation responsibility to the Chinese Academy of Cultural Heritage with a completion period of forty-five months.
Progress was delayed by logistical setbacks and the COVID-19 pandemic, but work resumed in September 2024 CE (VS 2081 Bhādra).
A ritual ofkṣamāpūjāwas performed on 2024 CE (VS 2081 Mañsira 27), followed by abhūmipūjāon 2025 CE (VS 2082 Mārgaśirṣa 10) for foundation conservation.
As of February 2026 CE, the original foundation has been retained while all upper storeys have been dismantled for reconstruction.
Owing to structural instability, the deity has been temporarily relocated to a southern shed within the compound, where regular rites continue.

This unique association with Vajrācāryas—unparalleled among other Taleju shrines within and beyond the Kathmandu Valley—exemplifies a notable instance of religious syncretism (D. Vajrācārya and Ṭ. Śreṣṭha VS 2032, p. 7).
citations: (D. Vajrācārya and Ṭ. Śreṣṭha VS 2032, p. 7)

text: On Ghaṭasthāpanā (First of bright fortnight of the month Āśvina), a sacred grass, calledjamara, is traditionally sown in the Daśaĩ chamber on the second floor; since the earthquake, this rite has been conducted in the temporary southern shed.

On the ninth of bright fortnight of the month Āśvina, a buffalo sacrifice is offered to the Goddess Taleju, the animal being led up the stone steps into the first-floordalāna, from where its blood is ritually presented to the deity on the second floor.
Its roof was restored in 1890 CE (NS 1011) by Judha Thāpā and his family.
No historical records have been discovered regarding the temple's construction.
However, Pruscha (1975, p. 246) estimates that it was built in the 19th century.
A bell, installed in 1907 CE (NS 1027), hangs from a bell stand near the temple entrance.

Additionally, an inscription on the eaves board records that Judha Thāpā, his wife Bijayālakṣmī, and their children—residents of Thimi—renovated the temple’s roof and installed brass sheets in 1890 CE (NS 1011).
Further renovations were carried out by locals in 1964 CE (Pruscha, 1975, p. 246) and again in 2004 CE (VS 2061).
This is a newly constructed temple built atop apīṭhaof Bhairava.

Among the limited number of new pagoda-style temples in the valley that feature correct proportions and high-quality carvings, this temple, completed only in VS 2080 (2024 CE), can be counted as a notable example.
This temple was built targeting an abstract Bhairava stone that is about five feet below the road.
The then ward chairman of Ward No. 2 of Tokha Municipality took a vow to build a temple over the stone and constructed the new temple in 2024 CE (VS 2080).

Among the hundreds of newly constructed pagoda temples in the valley, this structure stands as one of the limited examples where architectural harmony is achieved and traditional methods are correctly followed.
Following the temple's construction, a painting of Bhairava’s face was created on the wall facing the main road.
An inscription on a bell dedicated here in 1921 CE (VS 1978) explicitly refers to it as 'Seto Bhairava'.
The culture of displaying Hāthudyaḥ and dispensing rice wine saw hundreds of such installations established in the valley between the 16th and 18th centuries.
The old wooden mask from the past was replaced with a new one in 2022 CE (VS 2078).
An organized group known as the 'Hāsadyaḥ Guthi Khalaḥ' exists to oversee the temple and to manage during festivals (local resident, Śreṣṭha, male, age 75).
Bhīmabhakteśvara Mandira was constructed by Prime Minister Bhīmasena Thāpā and his wife Bhaktakumārī in 1823 CE (VS 1879).
With a gilded finial on top, the temple has aśivaliṅgaestablished inside the sanctum as the main deity.
Thāpā constructed the temple at the Janaralabāga (lit. general’s garden).

He also endowed lands to form aguṭhīfor performing daily and other periodic rituals at the temple, along with feeding mendicants on various occasions and brahmins on the occasion of Bhīmasena Thāpā’s birthday.
More temples in foreign style were built after the construction of Bhīmabhakteśvara (Tiwari2013, p.175).
About a year after its construction, Bhīmasena Thāpā’s younger brother Raṇavīrasiṃha Thāpā offered a bell at the temple.
In 1865 CE (VS 1922), the second wife of Bhīmasena Thāpā endowed 77ropanīs of land from various parts of Nepal for theguṭhīto perform various rituals at the temple.
However, both the sculptural evidence and the historical inscriptions associated with the site refer not to Sarasvatī but to Mañjuśrī.
A renovated inscription of the Mañjuśrī temple at Patan (LAL0108), dated 1724 CE (NS 845),  begins with a hymn in praise of Sarasvatī.
Likewise, a palm-leaf manuscript of 1713 CE (NS 833) refers to the same shrine in Patan as “Sarasvatī Nani” (Rājavaṃśī VS 2042, p. 21).
On the festival of Śrīpañcamī, worship is offered at Svayambhū in the name of both Mañjuśrī and Sarasvatī.
The temple itself is built around a natural cave located within the sanctum (garbhagṛha).
TheSvayambhū Purāṇarecounts that Mañjuśrī, having journeyed to Nepal via Pañcaśīrṣa Mountain, stayed for three nights at Mahāmaṇḍapa (H. Śākya NS 1098, p. 9).
It was not until 1859 CE (NS 979) that a stonetoraṇawas added above the mouth of the cave.
During the same period, a temple structure was constructed enclosing both the cave and thetoraṇawithin a sanctum.
The resulting temple resembles the modest Śiva shrines commonly built during the Rāṇā period.
In 1968–69 (VS 2025), however, an anthropomorphic image of Mañjuśrī was installed in front of the cave.
The construction of the temple over the cave in 1859 CE (NS 979) was undertaken by a Buddhācārya family from Ināco (Indravat Mahāvihāra) in Bhaktapur.

The inscription in the temple records the names of several members of the donor family—Amṛtamuni, Dharmavatī, and Maṇithaku—although the principal patron’s name has been eroded and cannot be read clearly.
A later inscription dated 1883 CE (NS 1003), which records the construction of asataḥat the site, reveals that the principal builders of the temple were Jogamuni and his wife Jñānīthaku.
The same patrons also constructed asataḥadjacent to the temple they had built.
Subsequently, their descendants Caityarāja and Vikuratna renovated the temple in 1944 CE (NS 1064).

Later still, members of the same lineage undertook further restoration in 1949 CE (VS 2006), during which they repaired the temple and the adjacent caitya (BKT0710-009), and also constructed ahiti, a boundary wall, and anothersataḥto the left of the temple.
Lands in Ināco, Bhaktapur, together with properties elsewhere, were endowed asguṭhīfor the maintenance of the shrine.

According to the inscription, the income from these endowments was to support priests, attendants (avāla), and other necessary personnel, who were to reside there and annually celebratevarṣavardhanawith a communal feast on the full moon day of Kārtika (full-moon day of Kārtika).
In later generations, members of the same family relocated from Bhaktapur and settled near the temple, and they continue to conduct the daily worship and care of the shrine.

The Buddhācārya lineage that established the temple continues to observe itsvarṣavardhanaby performing a special ritual including ayajñaon Kārtika Pūrṇimā, followed by a communal feast (one of the family members of the priest, Vajrācārya, male, age 59).

With the presence of an inscription of King Lakṣmīnarasiṃha Malla from of 1641 CE (NS 761), this temple was renovated by Bahādura Śāha, the son of Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa Śāha, and established thenavayoginīdeities inside the sanctum and a sandalwood statue of Śiva-Pārvatī in the window of the first floor.
It is possible that the soldier statues were carved as an expression of military sentiment because Bahādura Śāha built this temple while expanding the borders of Nepal (J. Regmī VS 2033, p. 189).
Five doors are installed on the southern façade of the sanctum, andtoraṇas are placed above all five doors.
Some of the statues in the middle of thetoraṇas have been stolen.
Inside the sanctum, a Tārakeśvara Śivaliṅga is established.
Nine stone statues ofyoginīs are established on the northern wall of the sanctum.
The temple is called Navaoginī (Navayoginī) Mandira, as nineyoginīstatues are installed.

These statues, considered as feminine powers (śakti) of thenavagraha(nine planets), are established in order from west to east as follows: Maṅgalā, Piṅgalā, Dhānyā, Bhramarī, Bhadrikā, Ulkā, Siddhā, Saṅkaṭā, and Vikaṭā (J. Mānandhara VS 2051, p. 20).
No clear historical sources have been found that provide definite information about the construction of this temple.
According to legends, King Mahendra Malla (reign 1560-1574 CE) built this temple.
Thedabūat this location had already been constructed before the temple was built.
King Mahendra Malla built the temple in remembrance of Śiva and Pārvatī coming to watch thepañcakanyās’ dance (V. Pāsā VS 2075, p. 36).
As a commemoration of that event, Lakṣmīnarasiṃha Malla had this temple built (P. Tāmrākāra NS 1122, pp. 45-46).

The earliest historical record in the temple is the stone inscription of 1641 CE (NS 761) attached to the east side of thedabū, which was placed by King Lakṣmīnarasiṃha Malla himself, issuing a royal decree.
The inscription is considered the earliest inscription in the Nepali language found in the Kathmandu valley (G. Vajrācārya VS 2033, p. 56).
It is not possible to say definitively whether there is a connection between the inscription and the temple.
The Mahādeva mentioned in the inscription could be the Tārakeśvara Śivaliṅga inside the sanctum of the temple.
Sundarānanda, an 18th-century Buddhist scholar from Patan, attributes the temple's construction to Bahādura Śāha, Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa Śāha's second son.

At the behest of his nephew, King Raṇabahādura Śāha, Bahādura Śāha installed a sandalwood Ardhanārīśvara (Śivapārvatī) statue in the window, donated a large bell, and established anavagraha(nine planets) temple featuring theaṣṭamātṛkādeities (D. Vajrācārya VS 2019, pp. 146-147).
While the precise construction date is unknown, it likely occurred during Bahādura Śāha's regency (1785-1794 AD) (J. Regmī VS 2033, p. 185).

Alternatively, Bahādura Śāha may have renovated an existing Malla-era Tārakeśvara Mahādeva temple that had fallen into disrepair (S. Khativaḍā VS 2081, p. 168), subsequently adding thenavayoginīstatues to the sanctum and the Śivapārvatī window statue.
In 1975 CE (VS 2031), the government renovated the temple for the coronation of King Vīrendra (J. Regmī VS 2033, p. 189).
The temple sustained multiple cracks in the 2015 earthquakes with its western part severely damaged.
The renovation work of the temple was carried out with the assistance of NRs. 37.1 million received from the Bagmati Provincial government.
The renovation work started in 2022 CE (VS 2079) and was completed in 2024 CE (VS 2081) (temple priest’s mother, Rājopādhyāya, female, age 80).

Despite 176ropanīs and 6ānās of land being designated as a religious endowment in the temple's name (Guṭhī Saṃsthāna VS 2071, p. 36), the Guṭhī Saṃsthāna provides the priest with a daily stipend of only Rs. 30 (temple priest’s mother, Rājopādhyāya, female, age 80).
On this occasion, a fire ritual (homa) is performed, and a goat is sacrificed to Svacchanda Bhairava located outside the temple.

Later, in 1993 CE, Rāma Prasāda Śreṣṭha constructed the present structure (local resident, Śreṣṭha, male, age 61). Śreṣṭha had served aspradhānapañca, a post equivalent to a mayor during the Pañcāyata rule.
None of such activities take place now, as many residents have moved out while the water in the channel is also polluted.
It is said to have been built by a Jośī clan from Bakhuṃ Bāhāḥ, though no documented evidence has so far been found with which one might ascertain the date of its initial construction.
Thephalcāhad one storey before it collapsed during the earthquake of VS 1990 (1934 CE).
Thephalcāwas rebuilt in 2006 CE (VS 2069) under the supervision of the Khapiṃchẽ Youth Club and with financial support of 30 lakh Nepali Rupees provided by the Lalitpur Metropolitan City office.
After the renovation, the Club used thephalcā’s upper floor as its office, however, they had to move out when the residents of Neuta Ṭola claimed the right to the monument.
Three empty niches (gavākṣa) can be seen on its back wall; statues of Gaṇeśa, Umāmaheśvara, and Viṣṇu were kept here before the building collapsed in the earthquake.
It seems that these statues were stolen.
Commanding Colonel Ḍambara Śamśera Thāpā, a close associate of Prime Minister Padma Śamśera, commissioned the construction of this Śiva temple.
The Dharmamukteśvara Mandira (PPK1931), another Śiva temple built in the name of his elder brother Dharma Śamśera Thāpā, is positioned to its east.
Unfortunately, the statues of Durgā in the northwest and Gaṇeśa in the southwest have been stolen.
A stone trident (triśūla) stands erect in the north, while the statue of Kāmadeva, established southwest of the temple, has also been stolen.
There is no inscription that records the establishment of Ḍambarabhakteśvara Mahādeva.

G. Ṭaṇḍana (VS 2053, p.347) notes that the temple was built by Ḍambara Śamśera Thāpā (1883-1970 CE) without specifying the year of construction. Ḍambara Śamśera, the son of Keśarasiṃha Thāpā, was dispatched to Allahabad, India, by Prime Minister Candra Śamśera in 1902 CE (VS 1959) for accounting training (Ḍ. Thāpā VS 2034, p.11).

A childhood friend of Padma Śamśera, the 8th Rāṇā prime minister, Ḍambara Śamśera played a pivotal role in facilitating Padma Śamśera's resignation in 1948 CE, which paved the way for Mohana Śamśera to assume the prime minister’s post (P. Rāṇā VS 2070, p.298).
The temple had fallen into disrepair even before the 2015 earthquakes, which further damaged it.
In 2021 CE (VS 2078), the Pashupati Area Development Trust undertook the renovation of the temple's cracked walls.
The four holy pilgrimage sites of the present-day India—Badrīnātha, Kedāranātha, Jagannātha, and Rameśvaram—are constructed also at the Bhaktapur Durbar Square in the form of separate temples.
A person named Svāmī Vārtta had established a statue of Hariśaṅkara at Paśupati in ŚS 487 (565 CE) (D. VajrācāryaVS 2030, p. 198-203).
Locally known as Lā̃paṃdyaḥ (the deity that blocks the path), the temple collapsed in the 1934 earthquakes and was never rebuilt.
Almost all of theśikharatemples of the Kathmandu valley have porches built over stone pillars that contain akalaśacarved at the bottom.
Like most of the temples at the Bhaktapur Durbar Square, the Hariśaṅkara Mandira, too, lacks inscriptive evidence to date its initial construction.
The art of the pillar and the main statue suggest that this Temple was constructed around the end of the medieval period.
The Department of Archaeology had started reconstructing this Temple before the 2015 earthquakes.
The reconstruction halted due to the earthquakes and was completed only in 2018.
Noguthirelated to this Temple survives now and the daily rituals have also ceased to be performed (local knowledge, local resident, Śarmā, male, age 76).
citations: (local knowledge, local resident, Śarmā, male, age 76)

text: While referred to as a temple, the building retains the essence of asataḥ.
The ground floor features a seven-bayphalcā(rest-house), with the middle bay granting access to the inner sanctum.
The temple's construction, attributed to Bama Bahādura Kũvara in 1851 CE (VS1907), was part of a larger complex on the Bagmati riverbank, featuring multiplesataḥs.
Subsequent generations of his family likely added smaller temples and rest-houses, possibly including this building now known as the Rāma temple.
A large bell hangs in front, one of four originally installed at the clock tower (Ghaṇṭāghara) but relocated after the 1934 CE earthquakes.
These relocated bells now grace the Rāma temple, the Umāmaheśvara temple in Kirtipur, the Siṃhadarabāra (Singhadarbar), and Bhaktapur (S. Śreṣṭha VS 2057, p.51).
Godāvarī Mārbala (named for the Godavari source) adorns the sanctum exterior, bearing an inscription.

Though lacking specific dates, the inscription identifies Prime Minister Bam Bahādura Rāṇā and his lineage, including Teka Bahādura Rāṇā, Yakṣa Vikrama Rāṇā, Bamavīra Vikram Rāṇā, Bhuvana Vikrama Rāṇā, Līlā Vikrama Bahādura Rāṇā, and others.
Prior to the 2015 CE earthquake, the temple endured some deterioration.

Reconstruction efforts, funded by the Asian Development Bank through the Urban Development Ministry's Integrated Development Committee for the Conservation of the Bagmati Civilization, began after the disaster.
While restoration was completed on Kartik 6, 2079 (October 23, 2022 CE), the temple remains closed as of October 2023 CE due to ongoing work.
These activities are currently suspended (as of October 2023 CE).
East of the Bhīmasena temple, a rest house with an open pavilion has been constructed, featuring enshrined statues of Gaṇeśa and Kṛṣṇa.
Two inscriptions are set into the southern temple wall.
The first (DPC0010_I_001) records the temple's construction in 1785 CE (NS 905) by "Māhā" Viṣṇu and his wife Manamayi, residents of Bholāchẽ (text: Bhulāche) Ṭola in Bhaktapur.
The title "māhā" likely indicated a position of authority at the time, as it was historically used to designate soldiers, military personnel, or police officers (cf. Mālī NS 1130, p. 461 s.v.mahāṃ).
The second inscription (DPC0010_I_003) from 1846 CE (ŚS 1768) details a land endowment by Dāpcā resident Lakṣmī, yielding an annual produce of 10murīs for Viśvakarmā worship.
However, no statue of Viśvakarmā is currently (July 2024 CE) present at the temple.
Statues of Gaṇeśa and Kṛṣṇa have been added to the east.
In 1996 CE (VS 2053), the eastern rest house was expanded into a temple with the installation of a Kṛṣṇa statue.
Subsequent renovations included plastering and painting the temple in 1998 CE (VS 2055).
Located northeast of the temple, Pauḍela Pāṭī was constructed in 1829 CE (VS 1751), as indicated by an inscription (DPC0010_I_002) crediting its construction to a Brahmin named Candra and his family.
Local accounts suggest that Pauḍela Pāṭī was built after a Gaṇeśa statue was installed on the eastern side of the nearby Bhairava temple complex.

Candra endowed approximately 12ropanīs of land and established an annual tradition of paying twomurīs of rice from the land's seven-murīyield to an Avāle, a Newar roof tile specialist, for roof maintenance.
Pauḍela Pāṭī is currently (July 2024 CE) undergoing restoration.
Following the theft of the original metal Kṛṣṇa statue in 1970 CE (VS 2027), a replacement was installed for the procession.
As of July 2024 CE, the statue is rotated among the homes of trust members.
The Kṛṣṇa statue enshrined in thepāṭīwas a personal donation from a local Brahmin named Khilarāja, intended for daily worship (local resident, Śreṣṭha, male, age 56).
Instead of akvāḥpāḥchẽ, a small temple is built in the Bāhāḥ’s courtyard (calledkvāḥpāḥdegaḥ), and a statue of Akṣobhya is enshrined inside its sanctum.
A stonetoraṇaon which the images of Five Buddhas (Pañcabuddha) have been carved, is installed above the entrance to the sanctum.
An additional stone statue of Akṣobhya which is slightly bigger than the main one is installed behind the main statue of Akṣobhya in the sanctum.
A Dharmadhātu Maṇḍala has been established right in front of thekvāḥpādegaḥ’sentrance.
The inscription on the Dharmadhātu is broken, thus the date of its establishment can not be ascertained.

No documented evidence has so far traced out to date the initial construction of Vasu Bāhāḥ.Śākya(1994, 110) mentions that leftover bricks after the renovation of Mahābuddha Mandira (LAL2340) in 1938 CE (1058 NS) were used to construct this Bāhāḥ.
Therefore, we can assume that it was built around that time.
However, local residents claim that it was built before the 1934 CE (1990 VS) earthquakes.
Initially built to provide water for the daily worship of Ṣaḍakṣarī Lokeśvara, thishitiwas renovated by Rāṇā Prime Minister Candra Śamśera in 1912 CE (VS 1969).
The west-facinghitihas only one spout installed.
A Bhagīratha statue is installed below the spout, while a statue of Umāmaheśvara with Kumāra is established above the spout.
Ajaḥdhuṃwater tank is also established on the southern wall of thehiti.
Therefore, a cement tank has been built along with thehiti, and modern pipes have been installed to pour water into thehiti.
No historical sources have been found that provide information about the construction of thishiti.
According to locals, thehitiwas built to provide water for the daily worship of Ṣaḍakṣarī Lokeśvara (BDG0040-001) established in the Bāḍegāũ Caitya (caitya’s caretaker, Vajrācārya, male, age 55).
In 1912 CE (VS 1969), Rāṇā Prime Minister Candra Śamśera carried out the renovation of thehiti.
During the expansion of the road in the mid-1960s (VS 2022-23), a part of the western side of thehitiwas used up by the road.
The water from thehitiis used during the daily worship of Ṣaḍakṣarī, the six-syllable Lokeśvara established in the Bāḍegāũ Caitya.
Constructed with stone on three plinth levels, Thāpābhakteśvara features a bell-shaped roof adorned with a metallic finial.
The temple's initial construction details remain elusive, with no historical source on-site providing insights.

The absence of the bell, said to contain an inscription with information on the year and donor of the temple's construction (priest, Ḍhuṅgela, male, age 50), contributes to the confusion surrounding its inception.

Despite this, the temple's architectural style suggests a Rāṇā-period origin, possibly built by an influential Thāpā clan courtier before Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā's rise to power in the 1846 CE court massacre.
Badly damaged in the 2015 earthquakes, the temple underwent reconstruction by the Pashupati Area Development Trust in 2019 CE (VS 2076).
Kvā Bāhāḥ possesses two Āgãchẽs;something rather unusual for monastic buildings.
The Āgãchẽ has statues of Saṅkaṭā and Cakrasaṃvara installed on its ground floor and first floor respectively.
The oldest existing record of this place is an inscription dated 1699 CE (NS 819).
The inscription mentions the construction of a place (pura) dedicated to Cakrasamvara on the building's topmost floor.

R. Vajrācārya(VS 2059, 29) writes that this building was solely worshipped as the Āgãchẽ or Digi of the esoteric deity Cakrasamvara from the late Malla period until more recently; the statue of Saṅkaṭā was introduced only after 1950 CE (NS 1070).

The most senior man amongst them takes the title of Cakreśvara (vernacular: Cakreśvarī); this title gives him the right to perform the compulsory worship (nityapūjā) of the statues of Saṅkaṭā and Cakrasamvara consecrated in the Āgã.

Despite a lack of historical records detailing its construction, a chronicle (preserved in the collection of Bhadrakālī’s priest) suggests that King Guṇakāmadeva transported Lũmadhi Ajimā from Kāmārukāmākṣa to Nepal in 724 CE (VS 781).
The earliest historical record stems from two brothers offering an ornamented arch to the Dyaḥchẽ in 1684 CE (see ’historical events’ below).
A resolution in 1806 CE (NS 926) sought to prevent future disputes.

The Dyaḥchẽ underwent renovations in 2003 CE (VS 2060) but sustained damage in the 2015 CE earthquakes, spurring a collaborative reconstruction effort supported by the Kathmandu Metropolis and local communities.
During the reconstruction, Lũmadhi Ajimā's statue was temporarily placed in Navadurgā Mandia (KAT1370).
Presently (February 2023 CE), the Maharjana family oversees daily rituals.
Notably, a total of 14ropanīs8ānāsof land, endowed in the name of the Dyaḥchẽ, are registered under the ‘state trust’ (rājaguṭhī) at the Guṭhī Saṃsthāna (Guṭhī Saṃsthāna VS 2071, p.31).
This extensive area, located behind the ancient Kathmandu palace, stretched to what is now New Road, Bhūgola Park, and the Nepal Bank Limited building.
These modern landmarks, established after the 1934 earthquakes, were once part of the Bhaṇḍārakhāla complex (G. Vajrācārya VS 2033, p. 125).
The Garuḍa statue positioned before Nārāyaṇa was likely established at the same time (G. Vajrācārya VS 2033, p. 127).
The Buḍhānīlakaṇṭha Jalaśayana image dates back to the seventh century and was commissioned by King Viṣṇugupta.
It is believed that the Nārāyaṇa image King Pratāpa Malla relocated from Jñāneśvara to the Hanumandhoka Palace is, in fact, the Bhumbhukkikā Jalaśayana (G. Vajrācārya VS 2033, p. 125).
This statue is mentioned in an inscription of Aṃśuvarmā's from 608 CE (Mānadeva Era 32), found in Hā̃ḍigāũ (Vajrācārya VS 2030, pp. 320-321).
No historical evidence has been found regarding the construction period of the pond.

However, according toNepālikabhūpavaṃśāvalī(2016, 19.2.168-173), King Pratāpa Malla founded Bhaṇḍārakhāla, built a large pond, and brought the Nārāyaṇa statue from the vicinity of Jñāneśvara and placed it in the middle of the pond.
An inscription dated 1829 CE (NS 939 NS) states that Bhīma Bhāro built the Nṛtyeśvara Temple and that it contained three niches worshipped as Nṛtyeśvara.
Inside the temple, on the right-hand side, is an inscribed stone pillar.
According to a local informant, the temple had a tiled roof and a metal pinnacle before its renovation in VS 1998.
The temple's architecture points to its construction during the later medieval period.
The absence of historical records makes it impossible to pinpoint its construction year and benefactor.
Prior to its collapse in the 1934 CE earthquakes, any alterations to the temple remain shrouded in mystery.
Following the seismic event, reconstruction took place a little less than a decade later, in the early 1940s.
The bricks used for the reconstruction bore the inscription “Śrī 3 Juddha 1998,” attesting to its renewal by Prime Minister Juddha Śamśera in 1941 CE (VS 1998) (KVPT report 2007, p.7).
Photographs captured soon after the earthquakes showcase the temple's severe damage, yet it managed to avoid total collapse.
Pruscha (1975, p.63) briefly mentions a renovation around 1957 CE, a period when many monuments underwent beautification for King Mahendra's coronation (KVPT report 2007, p.7).
In 2007 CE (VS 2064), collaborative efforts from the Department of Archaeology, Kathmandu Metropolis, and the Kathmandu Valley Preservation Trust (KVPT) restored the temple based on archival images.
The funding for this restoration was provided by the US Ambassadors Fund for Cultural Preservation.
After enduring further damage in the 2015 CE earthquakes, the Ambassadors Fund once again contributed to the temple's revival, carried out by the KVPT.
The merchant then used the amount he was supposed to pay as a fine to build this Phalcā in front of the Bhagavatī Mandira (SKH0240) outside Bhaudhvākhā (lit. gate of daughter-in-law) in Sankhu.
The three-bay Phalcā facing east does not have any inscription.
The Phalcā collapsed in the 2015 earthquakes.
In 2020, the Department of Archaeology rebuilt the Phalca and a water tap next to it in cooperation with the Shankharapur Municipality at a cost of NRs. 2.3 million.
Of Jaṅga Bahādura's many queens, the one from Gorakhpur constructed this temple and donated a vast tract of land as a religious endowment.
She built the temple six years after Jaṅga Bahādura's death (J. C. Regmi VS 2033, p. 279-280).
Two inscriptions mention "the queen of Gorakhpur" without revealing her name.
It is unusual that in such a significant religious inscription, the donor's name is not mentioned, only a formal title.
A detailed account of the land allocated for daily worship, annual rituals, cleaning, regular music, and temple maintenance is inscribed on a large stone slab housed in the east wing of thesataḥ.
A bell inscription from a nearby Vaiṣṇava monastery mentions a bell offering in 1860 CE for the liberation of Jaṅga Bahādura's queen, Śubhakumārī, at the Śubhamukteśvara temple.

However, the custom was to establish aśivaliṅgain a person's name with the suffix 'mukteśvara' only after their death, and since the Gopāla temple was built 22 years after the establishment of Śubhamukteśvara, it seems unlikely they refer to the same person.
Regmi (VS 2033, p. 279-280) describes this style as Rajput.
Inside the temple is a small metal statue of Gopāla, which is likely a replacement for a larger stone statue now lost, given the statue's large base (throne).
A traffic police office has been erected on the northern section of the temple's land.
The temple was damaged in the 2015 earthquakes and was restored by the Department of Archaeology in 2021 CE (VS 2078).
The terracotta Temple is built in theśikharakūṭa-style and faces south.
Although no historical sources exist to date the Temple, locals believe it was built during the mediaeval period.
According to Parajuli (1986, p.152), the Temple has two stone lions with inscriptions that were installed in 1690 CE (NS 810) by a man named Rāmabhadra Bhāro.
The stone lions with inscriptions he mentions, however, are not from this Temple, but from Banepa's Bholāchẽ Gaṇeśa Temple (cf. S. Rājavaṃśī VS 2020, p.68 [inscription no. 165]).
The Temple was plastered in bajra mortar (cunāsurkhī) prior to its renovation in 1977 CE (VS 2034) by the Bhaktapur Development Project funded by the Federal Republic of Germany.
This three-bayed Phalcā has a pointed roof and is engaged to a building in the south.
According to a member of the Ṭola Sudhāra Samiti, this latticework was installed to prevent street children and 'strangers' from using it.
The small courtyard of the Bāhāḥ measures 3.6 m x 3.8 m and is surrounded by residential buildings.
The main temple is a single storey structure built on a raised plinth that is 80 cm high.
It is open to the east side, while its rear west wall is attached to the neighbouring building.
This is an independent Bāhāḥ;it was constructed by a member of Hiraṇyavarṇa Mahāvihāra (Kvāḥ Bāhāḥ).
This was installed in 1895 (NS 1015).
No inscription recording the history of the Bāhāḥ could be found.
Standing impressively tall, it stretches to fill almost two-thirds of the open space in front of the building.
Gutschow(2001, p. 639) writes that "the house of the death association was replaced by a monstrous four-storeyed structure in reinforced concrete in 1999.

The two-storeyed house for the performance of music was replaced by an even larger structure in 2004 to accommodate a primary school sponsored by 'Mitra Japan'."Previously (until the 1990s), this monument was a two-storey Phalcā with a tiled roof and 14 bays.

The photo, which Pruscha uses to describe the Dupāt Gaṇeśa, also shows that Kṛṣaka Pustakālaya (the library currently housed in the Pichū Phalcā) was still operating from this building back then (PruschaII, 1975: 188).
However, Dupāt Capāḥ was was dismantled in 2004 and replaced by a four-storey highconcrete structure with seven bays and concrete pillars.
It is now part of a larger building, and the Sanāḥ Guṭhī Chẽ today represents over 450 members of the funeralguthiof Dupāt Ṭola.
The four-storey building has a verandah-like structure extending from all of its three upper floors.
Vajrācārya(VS 2056, 164) has referred to thiscapāḥas Nāṭyeśvara Temple due to the fact that a statue of Nāsaḥdyaḥ has been enshrined on the second floor.
Alongside other deities, newly installed images ofAṣṭamātṛkācan be seen on the outer sides of the concrete pillars of the building.
However, it appears that these images have neither been consecrated nor are they worshipped; they seem to serve more of an aesthetic purpose.
In July 2015, an image of Nāmasaṅgīti Mañjuśrī was installed in a narrow space between the shrine of Gaṇeśa and the main door of the Guṭhī Chẽ.
The original two-storey building had a shrine of Nāsaḥdyaḥ on the upper floor; this was relocated to the second floor after the structure was rebuilt.
Altogether, seven inscriptions have been attached to the wall of the ground floor.
Two of the inscriptions are no longer legible, three of them are partially legible, and two remain in good condition.
The transliteration and interpretation of four of these inscriptions is included below.
Usually, the sanctum (garbhagṛha) of a temple is built on the ground floor.
Its sanctum is on the first floor where a Bhīmasena statue is consecrated as the main deity.
Two divine (Arjuna and Draupadī) and two human (Dhusi Āḥju and Dhusi Ajimā) statues are also installed inside the sanctum.
The Bhīmasena Temple was constructed by a local ruler (mahāpātra) of Kathmandu.
In 1484 CE, the eleventh of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha in NS 604, Ratna Malla, Yakṣa Malla’s son, captured Kathmandu by assassinating all eightmahāpātras(cf.Śreṣṭha2059, 14-17).

Toyūju Thakura, a descendant of one of thosemahāpātraswho used to rule the territory of the lower Kvāḥ Bāhāḥ, constructed the Bhīmasena Temple, consecrated a Bhīmasena statue inside its sanctum, and established aguṭhīin 1564 CE the third of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha in NS 660 (cf.Śreṣṭha2059, 40).
A copperplate inscription detailing this event has been already published.
Note that the chronicles record a different date regarding the construction of the temple.

For example theDevamālā Vaṃśāvalī(2013, 43) andBhāṣā Vamśāvalī(part 2, 2023, 28-2) mention that Toyūkhvāḥ, a Ṭhakurī ruler, constructed the Bhīmasena Mandira and consecrated a Bhīmasena statue inside its sanctum in 1140 CE (NS 260).
However, the abovementioned copperplate inscription, detailing the construction of this temple, nullifies the information recorded in these chronicles.
For this reason, Tuyūkhvāḥ constructed this temple for him and consecrated his statue.
In 1655 CE (NS 775) King Pratāpa Malla had installed the abovementioned Draupadī statue in the sanctum.
The temple was renovated in 1959 CE (VS 2016) with the active participation of the local community and was stewarded by King Mahendra.
There are two inscriptions on the wall of the Bhelāchẽ Phalcā.

The first inscription mentions that a three-bay north-facing phalcāwas commissioned by Guhya Lakṣmī Brāhmaṇī in NS 943 (1823 AD), whilst the second informs readers of the renovation of the phalcāundertaken by the Mahāju family.
The inscription points to the existence of two different phalcā,which seem to have later been joined together to become one.
The Department of Archaeology has undertaken the full reconstruction of the temple since then.
The temple is (re)built on a cruciform platform and itself has a cruciform plan oriented to the four cardinal directions.
Large doors are placed on each side of the building.
There is no inscription or solid evidence indicating when thesataḥwas originally constructed.
However, it is believed that thissataḥ, built near the 17th-centuryBālakumārī Temple, may have been added later, focusing on the temple's purpose.
An old photograph of thesataḥwas published in an inventory by the Department of Archaeology (Department of Archaeology, VS 2060, p. I).
In 2003 CE (VS 2060), the Department of Archaeology, along with the localguṭhī, reconstructed thesataḥ, maintaining its original appearance.
A statue ofĀryanāmasaṃgītiis installed in the southern corner of the ground floor of thesataḥ, and regular recitations of theNāmasaṃgītitext take place in front of the statue.

It remains uncertain whether the Gorakhanātha pādukā shrine was established by the ascetics themselves or if they began using the site because it was adjacent to the foot impression of their spiritual leader.
Historical records are unavailable to determine the initial construction date of the Phalcā.
The dismantling of the upper floor did not affect the use of Pīra Pāṭī by the ascetics.
In 2013 CE (VS 2070), the Hanumandhoka Palace Supervision Office renovated Pīra Pāṭī.
Inside the four bays of Pīra Pāṭī, a separate pādukā of Gorakhanātha has been established.
A smoky fire (dhunī) remains continuously lit in the hollowed space built for fire oblations.

Offerings made by devotees during fire oblations on special occasions serve as a source of income for the religious activities of Pīra Pāṭī, along with contributions from the ascetics from Mṛgasthalī at Paśupati, Kathmandu.
In 1847 CE (VS 1905), Prime Minister Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā initiated the construction of this Śiva temple.
Inside the sanctum, a stoneśivaliṅgais established at the center, representing Jaṅganandabhogeśvara Mahādeva, the temple's principal deity.
Notably, the statues of Sūrya, Gaṇeśa, Durgā, and Viṣṇu, which were once enshrined within the inner sanctum walls, following the Śiva Pāñcāyana concept, have all been stolen, leaving empty niches.
A Bhairava mask is embedded in the southern outer wall, while a statue of Nandī, Śiva's sacred animal mount, is established in front of the western entrance.
Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā initiated the temple's construction in 1847 CE (VS 1904) (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p.  344; Michaels and Tandon 2017, p. 62).

text: It is possible that he built the temple with his wife, Nandakumārī, as the temple's name includes the term "Nanda" attached to Jaṅga Bahādura's name.
Nandakumārī was the sister of Kājī Sanakasiṃha Ṭaṇḍana and married Jaṅga Bahādura in 1839 CE (VS 1896), before he ascended to power and while his finances were in a precarious state.

Prior to becoming the prime minister, Jaṅga Bahādura and Nandakumārī jointly constructed a dome-style temple in Thapathali in 1845 CE (ŚS 1767), naming it Jaṅganandaprakāśeśvara (J. Regmī VS 2033, p.241).
After assuming the role of prime minister, he bestowed the title ofmahārāṇīupon Nandakumārī (B. Bhaṇḍārī VS 2071, p. 132).
She gave birth to two daughters, Badanakumārīdevī (Magaranī Maiyā) and Tārākumārīdevī, and two sons, Jagatajaṅga and Jītajaṅga (P. Rāṇā VS 2059, p. 190).
In 2003 CE (VS 2060), the Pashupati Area Development Trust undertook the renovation of this temple.
According to local residents, this statue was recently installed for devotees to worship while the old one consecrated in the sanctum has been moved to a secret chamber.

The old stone statue of Viṣṇu—flanked by his consort, Lakṣmī and hisvāhana,Garuḍa, and worshipped as Ādinārayaṇa—used to be under an open sky before the present temple structure was constructed by Ratnamāna Śreṣṭha and Īndramāna Śreṣṭha in 1955 CE (NS 1075).
The pillars were offered to the deity by a Śreṣṭha family from Tājāchẽ in Sunṭola in 1976 CE (VS 2033).
Another pillar erected in 1589 CE (NS 709) can be seen in front of the Temple.
The name of the donor is unclear due to the poor condition of the inscription at this pillar which is the earliest inscription related to the temple.
The former statue of Garuḍa on top of this pillar was stolen and was replaced by a new one in 1991 CE by Nārāyaṇabhakta Śreṣṭha.
The main structure of thebāhāḥhas mostly collapsed.
The main structure on the left side of the metal door has been destroyed and is fenced off with CGI sheets.
The building lacks adyaḥchẽ, something which is normally a major feature of suchbāhāḥ.
Local people say that it was probably destroyed during the 1934 earthquake and never reconstructed.
Locke(1985, 152) assumes that thebāhāḥwas abandoned after the earthquake.
Later, Pradhānas, non-Buddhist Newar families from Kathmandu, bought the surrounding lands and constructed houses upon it.
These buildings now surround thebāhāḥarea.
There is no inscription at the site through which one could date the monument.
Opposite the hill, to the west, is a similar elevation on which is built a stone pavilion (baiṭhak,JUM0100).
It had visibly been dismantled and partly (and poorly) re-assembled.
The original structure was built on a square platform with receeding steps leading to a cubical volume.
On the eastern side, the central projection on the cubic volume contains an low relief inscription.
The epigraphy is identical to the one seen on the same mantra inscribed on Dullu's Kīrtikhambā (DLK0260), the Patharnauli reservoir (DLK0160).
Both monuments were built in the 1350's, during the rule of king Pṛthvīmalla (r. 1338-1358) (Andolfatto 2019, p. 96;Pant 2009, 301).
It is likely that the Śrīḍhuskā Stūpa was built around the same period.
Although this one was built by Queen Lalitatripurāsundarī, the tower is referred to as Bhīmasena Stambha, mistakenly crediting Bhīmasena Thāpā for its construction.
Meanwhile, the tower that he had initially constructed was destroyed in the 1833 (VS 1890) earthquakes and was never rebuilt.
In 1824 CE (VS 1881), he first constructed a tower at Bāga Darabāra in the form of a minaret that came to be known as Bhīmasena Stambha (lit. pillar of Bhīmasena) (Tevārī and othersVS 2020, p.17).
A year later in 1825 CE (VS 1882), Queen Lalitatripurāsundarī also built a similar tower.
A gold-plate inscription posted on top of its entrance mentions that she built the tower and offered a finial (N. Yogī VS 2012, p.86).

A record from 1830 CE (VS 1887) gives the height of both towers with the first one built by Bhīmasena Thāpā standing 124 cubits (hāta) tall while the second one built by Queen Lalitatripurasundarī was only 90 cubits tall (G. Vajrācārya VS 2033, p.273).
Within a decade of its construction, the tower constructed by Bhīmasena Thāpā collapsed in the earthquakes of 1833 CE (C. Nepalī VS 2035, p.155).
On the other hand, the tower built by the queen survived the earthquakes but was cracked from top to bottom as seen in a painting byOldfield.

It collapsed in the 1934 earthquakes and was renovated by Prime Minister Juddha Śamśera in 1936 CE (VS 1992) (Tevārī and others VS 2019, p.8-9).
Having remained mostly unused after its renovation in 1936 CE, the Bhīmasena Stambha was leased to a private company to allow public access (KMC staff, Daṃgola, male, age 58).
The tower collapsed again in the 2015 earthquakes.
Instead of rebuilding it, a new tower of concrete was erected next to the old tower, leaving the stump covered with metal sheets.

They are installed to honor the memory of deceased persons, mostly warriors.

An inscription dated 1633 CE (NS 753), preserved at the temple, documents local regulations concerning the maintenance of the adjacent Nāgapokharī (serpent pond) and its associated water channel (kulo).

Although the temple lacks an establishment inscription, its architectural features—such as the two-tiered tiled roofs, plain struts, a stonekalaśa(finial), and the upright image of Nārāyaṇa inside—suggest it was constructed during the late medieval period.
Outside the temple, on a platform at the southwestern corner, the inscription outlines the annual obligation to clean the Nāgapokharī on the 1st day of dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa.
A special annual ritual is held on 12th day of bright fortnight of Bhādra, during which a wooden pole is erected in the southeastern courtyard, and a statue of Yamāḥdyaḥ (Indra) is displayed.
Notably, noguṭhī(ritual endowment trust) supports this festival.
The Sataḥ partly collapsed in the 2015 earthquakes and its superstructure was dismantled shortly thereafter.
There is valuable photographic documentation of the building spanning almost 50 years.

The earliestphototaken by Werner Jacobsen in the 1950s shows the building in its original configuration: ten carved columns rest on a heavy base beam (lākāṃsĩ) with base stones (īlvahaṃ) in the shape of lions below.
Four carvings of Garuḍa can be seen attached to the centers of the capitals and nine carved wooden statues of unidentified deities are installed on the front face of the main beam.
Aguthirelated to the Dhũllā Sataḥ is still in operation.
The members of the Guthi claim that one of their ancestors, Jaya Śaṅkara, built the Sataḥ some 400 years ago (Sharma and Shrestha 2016, p. 304).
This clan was very influential in Sankhu and commissioned the construction of many monuments.
A record book of 1916 CE (VS 1973) states that the Guthi is responsible for taking care of the Dhũllā Sataḥ and should renovate it when required (Sharma and Shrestha 2016, p. 306).
Elders recall a portion of the Sataḥ’s roof collapsing in the 1934 earthquake.
At that time Guthi members managed to renovate the Sataḥ within only a few months.
In those days the Guthi received income from landholdings that made regular repairs and maintenance of the building possible.
However, since this land is no longer under the Guthi's ownership it has been become difficult to raise the necessary funds.

The failure in arranging a regular income for the proper care and timely maintenance of the Sataḥ coupled with most of the Guthi members moving out of Sankhu left this rest house in a state of disrepair.
Around 2010 CE a portion of the roof collapsed and parts of the central window fell off.
It wasn't till mid-2012 CE that the Guthi covered the damaged portion of the roof with corrugated metal sheets, but unfortunately, the windows were never repaired.
Despite the Sataḥ's importance and high artistic value no more efforts went into maintenance and the condition of the Sataḥ deteriorated further, resulting finally in its collapse.
Following the dismantling of the Sataḥ in 2015, the Department of Archaeology initiated the administrative process for the reconstruction of the Sataḥ.
A member of the clan believes it was built by one of his ancestors during King Raṇabahādura Śāha's reign.
The clan renovated it in the 1990s, but the roof collapsed after the 2015 Gorkha earthquakes.
Years of neglect have left the building in ruins.

Santakumārī, the wife of Prime Minister Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā, was responsible for the establishment of this Śiva temple in the year 1865 CE (VS 1922).
Situated on the eastern side of the Bagmati river, opposite the cremation grounds, this temple, constructed from stone, showcases a bell-shaped roof adorned with a metallic finial.
Additionally, a Bhairava mask is embedded in the southern outer wall, and a statue of Nandī, Śiva's sacred animal mount, is established before the western entrance.
The temple's construction is attributed to Santakumārī, the wife of Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā, in the year 1865 CE (VS 1922) (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p. 344).
However, Michaels and Tandon (2017, p.62) suggest an alternative name, Śāntakumārī, and the date of 1848 CE as the temple’s donor and the year of its construction.
This may be due to a possible misspelling of Santakumārī's name and an error in converting the temple's construction year from the Vikrama era to the common era.
It is worth noting that Santakumārī is not recognized as a formally-wedded spouse of Jaṅga Bahādura, according to a list provided by Prof. Śivarāja Paṇḍita (K. Dīkṣita VS 2034, p. 78).
In 1871 CE (VS 1928), Jaṅga Bahādura donated land parcels measuring 12khetas for various rituals to be conducted at the Pandhra Śivālaya complex (K_0331_0025).
It boasts a square layout constructed with stone masonry, and its facades are adorned in white and ochre.
They are replaced annually on the day of ghasthpana.
Two inscriptions on large stone slabs are positioned along the wall of the northern wing of the courtyard.
These inscriptions date back to 1908 CE (ŚS 1965) and 1878 CE (VS 1934) and document donations made to the temple.
The monument is built on a stone platform.
The temple is built on one layer of a low square plinth.
At the first glance, it appears like shrines of Lord Śiva built during the Rāṇā regime.

Although there is no historic source available to confirm the construction of the temple, locals believe that the temple was called Vīra Vināyaka as it was constructed by Rāṇā Prime Minister Vīra Śamśera (1885-1901 CE) (Śreṣṭha, Male, 75 years). the temple suffered damages multiple times due to the flood on Mūkhusi and was slightly tilted.
The 2015 earthquake caused more damages to the temple and was reconstructed by the Department of Archaeology in 2020 CE.
The items required for both occasions are being provided by the Kālamocana Guthi, Kathmandu (Śreṣṭha, Male, 75 years).
A preserved manuscript details the construction of this magnificent five-tiered temple, suggesting it was completed in approximately six months.

Siddhilakṣmī, who stands upon Vetāla and Bhairava, is depicted with nine faces and eighteen arms (Gutschow 2011, p. 484), although D. Śamśera (VS 2036, pp. 121-130) and P. Locana (VS 2080, p. 241) record sixteen arms.
Lampstands (tvāḥdevā) stand beside Siddhilakṣmī, and a large bell, offered seventeen days after the temple's completion, hangs nearby.
A drain, running north from the sanctum to the first platform level, carries away liquids offered to the goddess (Gutschow 2011, p. 484).
