While tradition ascribes this temple's construction to Bhūpatindra Malla, the 19th-centuryDevamālā Vaṃśāvalīembellishes the narrative, claiming that the king built the Bhavānī temple after a dream in which Bhairava of Taumaḍhī instructed him to do so.
The chronicle also incorrectly dates the construction to 1756 CE (NS 876) (Yogi Naraharinatha VS 2013, p. 72).
Strangely, despite the temple's grandeur, no contemporary inscription documenting its construction was discovered for some time.
However, an inscription found in Tuṃthi Cuka, Bhaktapur, has since clarified the matter.
This inscription, now housed in the Bhaktapur Museum, was previously used as part of the steps leading to a military office.
It establishes the Ṅātāpola temple's construction date as the first day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, 1702 CE (NS 822) (P. Shrestha VS 2058, pp. 183-187).

Further supporting this date, a local hymn celebrating the temple's construction includes the phrase “Nase cyāyā dathusa nase taṅāva,” which translates to “adding two in between two [and] eight” (T. Manandhara NS 1111, pp. 19-20).
This phrase appears to be a coded reference to NS 822 (J. Vaidya VS 2061, p. 62).
A manuscript, "Siddhāgni Koṭyāhuti Devala Pratiṣṭhā," chronicles the step-by-step construction of this temple.
It records that construction commenced with a land purification ceremony on the 13th of the dark fortnight of Pauṣa, NS 822.
The temple's construction concluded later that year (1702 CE) with the finial's installation on the 1st of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha.
From the land purification to the finial's placement, the construction spanned approximately six months.
The continuing annual rituals performed on the day the finial was installed further corroborate the completion date.
The aforementioned manuscript details the materials used in the temple's construction: 1,135,350 bricks, 102,035 floor tiles, and 27,084upā(possibly a specialized type of brick).
Eight brick kilns were established outside Bhaktapur to support this project.
The Ṅātāpola's construction became a source of immense pride and prestige for the kingdom of Bhaktapur.
King invited rulers from neighboring kingdoms, including Gorkha, Makawanpur, and Palpa, to witness the temple's progress (P. Shrestha VS 2080, p. 245).
These details have led scholars such as Shukrasagar, Janaklal, Niels Gutschow, and Purushottam Lochan to conclude that the temple was constructed in approximately six months.
The manuscript further suggests that the Ṅātāpola was not a new construction, but rather a reconstruction.
The site was previously occupied by a five-tiered structure of unknown design called “Ṅātāpula,” which was dismantled to make way for the larger temple (J. Vaidya VS 2061, p. 8).
This reconstruction may have been necessitated by damage sustained by the earlier temple in the 1681 earthquake (NS 801) (P. Shrestha VS 2080, p. 241).
Numerous earthquakes have shaken the Kathmandu valley since this magnificent multi-roofed temple was erected in 1702 CE (NS 822).
Unfortunately, no written records document the temple's condition during tremors prior to 1934 CE (VS 1990).
In both the 1934 and 2015 earthquakes, only the uppermost roof sustained damage.
Subsequent renovations followed the earthquakes of 1962 CE (VS 2019), 1999 CE (VS 2056), and the most recent tremor.
The next day, a group of Brahmins, Karmācāryas, and Jośīs continue the tradition of performingthāpūjā, a special worship ceremony, commemorating the establishment of Ṅātāpola at the Taleju temple.
A single hanging bell remains beneath the temple's eaves, and locals believe that its ringing, stirred by the wind, foretells heavy rainfall (P. Shrestha VS 2080, p. 247).

The 1934 earthquake, which damaged the upper roof, inspired a still-popular rhyming proverb: "Ṅātāpola chatā madu, Bhailaḥdyaḥ patā madu." This translates to "One roof of Ṅātāpola [was lost], and the Bhairava temple was completely gone," vividly illustrating the earthquake's impact.
The hymn expresses a poignant longing, lamenting, "I was born a dove, yearning to see Ṅātāpola, but the Khasa sons shot me down" (P. Shrestha VS 2080, pp. 151-152).
However, this tradition seems to have ended during the Malla period, when the image of Bhagīratha was replaced by various other figures.

Tyāṅgā Bhairava’s shrine was constructed immediately south of the Rāmeśvara Śivaliṅga and oriented southward.
The Rāmeśvara shrine itself had brick pillars and a two-tier copper roof, with two Nandī images installed to its west.
Although the flood caused some damage to the roof of the Rāmeśvara shrine, the stone liṅga remains in situ.
No archaeological material clarifies the original establishment of Tyāṅgā Bhairava, but the origin of the Rāmeśvara Śivaliṅga is well attested in Purāṇic literature and local tradition.
Textual sources state that bathing and worshipping the Rāmeśvara Śivaliṅga on the full moon of Caitra Śukla grants merit equivalent to donating one hundred cows and absolves all sins.
Taking a terrifying Bhairava form, Śiva granted Paraśurāma the boon that he would render the earth devoid of Kṣatriyas, which Paraśurāma subsequently accomplished through twenty-one campaigns.
Through bathing and worship, the goddess Prabhādevī emerged from the waters and instructed her that worship of Rāmeśvara would grant radiance and renown as Prabhāvatī.
Because Rāmeśvara marked him with aṭīkāand established him as his guardian and devotee, he came to be known as Tīkā Bhairava.
A householder who kindly hosted him was later blessed with the boon that his house would never catch fire.
A Haḍigāu inscription dated 608 CE (MāSaṃ 32) records that Aṃśuvarman classified major shrines into three categories and allocated state endowments accordingly.
Rāmeśvara was placed in the second category, alongside Haṃsagr̥hadeva and Māneśvara, and received an annual grant of three purāṇa and one paṇa.
Subsequent historical records remain sparse, but chronicles note repeated flood damage due to the shrine’s riverside location.
In 1798 CE (VS 1855), during the reign of King Raṇabahādur Śāha, severe flooding washed away Tyāṅkā Bhairava.
Similar destruction occurred again in 1833 CE (VS 1890).
In 1889 CE (VS 1946), land was granted to thirteen individuals to performbhajanaat the shrine.

Further flood damage occurred in 1981 CE (VS 2038), partially burying the Rāmeśvara liṅga, and again in September 2024 CE (VS 2081 Āśvina 12), when the painted wall and roof of the Tyāṅgā Bhairava shrine were swept away.
As of November 2025, reconstruction aimed at restoring the shrine to its former condition is underway, supported by a grant of NPR 7.5 million from the Bagmati Province government.
Numerous agriculturalguṭhīlands were historically endowed in the name of Tyāṅgā Bhairava.
Records of the Guṭhī Saṃsthāna indicate that 9 ropanī and 12 ānā of land remain allocated for festival worship.

Other lands have been converted toraitānītenure, with the Guṭhī Saṃsthāna providing annual compensation to sustain ritual obligations, including payments for lands originally endowed to feed those who carried thekhaṭaduring the festival procession.
Whereas daily worship was formerly conducted,nitya pūjāis now performed twice weekly, on Tuesdays and Saturdays, supported by income from three ropanī of endowed land.

During the Nepal–Tibet/China War (1791–1792 CE), the Chinese army had advanced as far as the Pā̃camāne Bhaṅjyaṅga, but the Nepali forces, displaying remarkable bravery, succeeded in driving them back.
According to another assumption, the Chinese side claimed victory and that the emperor erected an inscription in the Potālā Palace of Tibet to commemorate it (Bell 1992, pp. 275–278).
On the upper level of the hiti is a west-facing stone inscription.
Pilgrims traveling from Kathmandu to GosāīKuṇḍa traditionally passed along this path, and it appears that the hiti was constructed to provide them with drinking water along the journey.
Beside thehiti, there once stood a pāṭi and a pauvā, but due to neglect and lack of timely restoration, they no longer exist.
The inscription available at thehitihas been badly eroded by sun and rain.
The words water system are still legible, suggesting that it pertains to thehiti, but the worn letters make it difficult to determine whether it records its construction or later renovation.
During the earthquake of 2015 CE (VS 2072), the lower steps of the hiti subsided.
Restoration was carried out in 2022 CE (VS 2079) with the support of the local government.

In 1851 CE (VS 1907), Prime Minister Bama Bahādura Kũvara erected Tīna Devala (KAT2670), a composite structure of three temples surrounded by rest houses on four sides (caugharā sataḥ) near the banks of the Bagmati River.
Subsequently, additional temples, both large and small, as well assataḥs, were added in the vicinity by his relatives and descendants.
According to Bama Bahādura's descendants, his son-in-law Gumānasiṃha Kārkī constructed the Pañcaliṅga Mahādeva temple near the iconic Tīna Devala.

This information is documented in a written record preserved by one of Bama Bahādura's male descendants, aged 57 (however, it lacks specific information regarding the date of the temple's construction).
This departure influenced the construction of several uniquely styled temples.
Notably, Bhairava masks are present on all four sides, a feature added during the latest reconstruction, according to a male clan member, aged 57.
Post the devastating earthquakes of 2015 CE (VS 2072), the temple, alongside other structures around the Tīna Devala complex, underwent reconstruction.

The High-Powered Committee for Integrated Development of the Bagmati Civilization, under the Ministry of Urban Development, received financial assistance from the Asian Development Bank for the reconstruction.
The project reached completion in October 2022 CE.
A testament to architectural brilliance, this grand Taleju Bhavānī temple was commissioned by King Mahendra Malla in 1564 CE (NS 684).
With its double-walled construction, the temple locally known as "Taḥdevala" (the great temple) features three tiers of copper roofing, each adorned with small temple bells.
The eastern bell was installed by Pratāpa Malla in 1654 CE (VS 1710), while Bhāskara Malla donated the other in 1714 CE (VS 1771) (G. Vajrācārya VS 2033, pp. 118-119).
He installed the flanking, non-functional doors beside the main entrance in 1671 CE (VS 1728), and the two gold door leaves of the central door in the same year.
A unique scene in the northwest corner of the temple shows a nude young woman embracing the phallus of akuṃsala(a mythical winged horse) carved on the corner strut (G. Vajrācārya VS 2033, p. 120).
A dream vision, in which Taleju Bhavānī instructed him to build a tall,yantra-shaped temple visible from Bhaktapur, prompted him to begin construction.
The temple's completion is recorded as the 5th of the bright fortnight of Māgha in 1549 CE (NS 669) (Yogī Naraharinātha VS 2013, p. 54).
However, Pruscha (1975, p. 56), without citing a source, gives the construction date as 1576 CE.
This date, along with the chronicle's account, appears inaccurate, as historical evidence places Mahendra Malla's reign between 1562 and 1574 CE (NS 682-694) (Slusser 1982 Vol. 1, appendix III-5).
G. Vajrācārya (VS 2023, p. 30) states the temple was built by Mahendra Malla on the 10th of the dark fortnight of Māgha in 1564 CE (NS 684).
Gutschow (2011, p. 428) and Slusser (1982, p. 191) also concur with the 1564 CE date, which is now considered the most accurate.
In the 1934 earthquakes, the temple's upper story was destroyed.
Later, in 1939 CE (VS 1996), Juddha Śamśera renovated the temple (Yogī Naraharinātha VS 2013, p. 55).
The 2015 earthquakes also damaged the temple.
The Hanumandhoka Palace Museum Development Committee renovated it in 2019 CE (VS 2076) (Hanumandhoka Museum staff, Maharjana, male, age 54).
The easternmost pillar was erected by Pratāpa Malla in 1664 CE (VS 1720).
Its inscription reveals that it bears statues of Pratāpa Malla flanked by his two sons, Nṛpendra and Cakravartīndra.
Pratāpa Malla dedicated this pillar to Taleju in 1642 CE (NS 762) (G. Vajrācārya VS 2033, p. 202).
A third pillar, its base a tortoise, was erected by Pārthivendra Malla in 1682 CE (VS 1738) (G. Vajrācārya VS 2033, p. 115).
An inscription on this pillar identifies the statues as King Pārthivendra, Queen Mother Indramatī, the young Prince Bhūpālendra, Queen Ṛddhilakṣmī, and Queen Rājalakṣmī.
All rituals adhere to the tantric practices of the Śākta sect (G. Vajrācārya VS 2033, p. 117).

Despite the absence of historical records detailing the establishment process of the temple dedicated to Maṅgalāgaurī within the Pashupatinath premises, the temple's sanctum boasts ancient sculptures dating back to the 7th century.
Adjacent to the Vatsalā Mandira (PPK0224) in the Paśupati vicinity stands the Maṅgalāgaurī Mandira, characterized by a brick-built square sanctum topped with copper sheets.
Her right hands grasp a discus, a sword, a bell, and a gesture of granting boons.
Flanking the main deity are four guardian sculptures (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p. 474), while a statue of Yamunā, positioned southwest of Maṅgalāgaurī, holds a mirror in her left hand.
While historical documentation of the temple's construction is lacking, the sculptures within are considered significantly aged.
According to his account, the Maṅgalāgaurī statue was relocated from Devīghāṭa in Nuvākoṭa to the current site around 1950 CE, although concrete evidence for this assertion is limited.
Bangdel (1989, p. 296) identifies it as a 7th-century statue of Yamunā, which was stolen in 1987 CE and subsequently reinstated.

Schroeder (2019, p. 786, Plate no. 245A), on the other hand, designates it as a 7th-century sculpture of Pārvatī, originally placed alongside her consort Śiva until the latter's theft, leading to her placement atop a turtle.
In 2017 CE (VS 2074), due to the temple's deterioration, the Chaudhary Foundation and the Pashupati Area Development Trust collaborated to undertake its reconstruction.
Next to it is a recently built stone platform with concrete mortar.

Later, during the reign of Rāṇā Prime Minister Vīra Śamśera, Kharadāra Bhāgavatabhakta Kājī offered a golden finial to the Temple jointly with his first son Kharadāra Tulasībhakta and the family.

As the Temple was in poor condition, it was renovated in 2001 CE with the fund provided by the Bhaktapur Municipality and donations collected from the locals.

After the construction of the Cilancva Caitya (KIR0001) in NS 635 (1515 CE) by Jagatapāla Varmā ( amahāpātra‘political elite’of Patan), many Buddhist monuments likebāhāḥs andcaityas were built in the eastern quarter of Kirtipur.
Due to the construction of only Buddhist monuments in the area, the eastern quarter of Kirtipur came to be known as 'Devagala'.
After NS 1055 (1935 CE), however, Buddhist monuments too started to appear in the Śivagala.
Previously, people believed that if anyone built a Buddhist monument in Śivagala, he or his clan would die (Ś. ŚreṣṭhaVS 2057, p. 28).
Based on the inscriptive sources recovered so far, thisŚikharakūṭaCaityaat Ichẽ is the third of its kind in Kirtipur.

Udāsī Akhadā was built by Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā for the followers of Guru Nanak.
Standing in between the Vaiṣṇava and Śaivaakhaḍās, the Udāsī Sataḥ was constructed for the provision of food and accommodation of the ascetics of the Udāsī sect.
A small structure with aśivaliṅgainside has been built in the centre of the Akhaḍā.

Within the heritage complex is a two-storied quadrangular building with a sword and a book containing the teachings of the 33 gurus who are considered as the most important ones in the Guru Nanak sect.
The sacred book, known as the 'Guru Granth Sahib,' is written in Gurmukhi script.
It is believed that the past, Maharajas meditated on a quadrangular plinth on the ground floor of this building (Maharaja of the Akhaḍā, male, age 65).
His preaching journey lasted for 23 years, from 1499 to 1522 CE (Singh 2023, p. 573).
However, at least the structure and construction materials of this site do not appear to be from the medieval period.
After staying in Kashi from 1857 to 1860 CE, King Raṇabahādura Śāha returned to Nepal with ascetics from the Nanak sect.
The king provided them with houses, land, and a fixed salary near the Tukucha river, and ensured their comfortable stay, as mentioned by Sundarānanda Bā̃ḍā (D. Vajracarya VS 2019, p. 187).

Later, Jaṅga Bahādura built thesataḥs along with the establishment of religious trusts to facilitate the living conditions of Indian ascetics of this sect during their visit to Nepal in 1875 CE (VS 1931) (N. Yogi VS 1013, p. 80).
The earliest record from the Udāsī Akhaḍā dates back to 1889 CE (VS 1945), which mentions the completion of a well within the premises.
Following the 2015 earthquakes, the Akhaḍā was reconstructed.

The reconstruction was carried out by the High-Powered Committee for Integrated Development of the Bagmati Civilization under the Ministry of Urban Development with the loan assistance of the Asian Development Bank.
Previously, a group of 12 people, including one Maharaja, was employed by the Guthi Sansthan.
DuringŚivarātrī, ascetics who visit Kathmandu stay at this Akhaḍā as well, and the Guthi Corporation provides them with food and sends them off.

According to a local resident, the inscription records the establishment of acaityaby a person named Jayendra Vajra, who then started living there by buying a house.

The history behind the initial construction of the Āgaṃchẽ is unclear.
It suffered heavy damages during the 2015 earthquakes.
The Guṭhī Saṃsthāna and the Department of Archaeology jointly reconsecrated the Āgaṃche bulding in 2019.
The four-storykvāḥpāḥchẽ(Bāhāḥ‘s main building) faces north and has a corrugated metal sheet roof.
The building's second and third floors are currently vacant (as of October 2022).

The Bāhāḥ's esoteric room (āgã) is on the first floor, and the main sanctum is on the ground floor, where a stone statue of Akṣobhya (with a gilded crown on his head and gilded metal outer garment covering his body) is consecrated as the main deity (kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ).
A metaltoraṇawith in inscription from 1899 CE (NS 1020) is placed atop the entrance to the sanctum, and acaitya(see monument objects below) is erected at the Bāhāḥ premises.
There are no historical sources that record the initial construction date of the Bāhāḥ.
According to legend, Emperor Aśoka, the Mauryan king, founded the Bāhāḥ, so it was named Aśokacaitya Mahāvihāra after him.
According to some locals, the Bāhāḥ was constructed by the son of a man named Aśoka and was thus named Aśokacaitya Mahāvihāra (R. Vajrācārya 2018, p.236).
The Bāhāḥ was originally built to the north of where it now stands.
Later, it was moved to its current location (Locke 1985, p.342; R. Vajrācārya 2018, p.236).
However, no record of the relocation exists.
The earliest record from the Bāhāḥ (see 'historical events' below) is the installation of a stone statue of Akṣobhya inside the sanctum in 1814 CE? (NS 934?).
It is unclear, however, whether a new statue was installed to replace the older one or whether the older statue was consecrated inside the new sanctum after the Bāhāḥ was relocated.

According to the copperplate inscriptions at the Bāhāḥ, the residents of the area had hosted the Samyak Mahādāna (grand alms-giving ceremony) three times in the late nineteenth century: in 1861 CE (NS 982), 1872 CE (NS 993) and 1878 CE (NS 999).
The Bāhāḥ was renovated in 1996 CE (VS 2053) but sustained minor damages during the 2015 earthquakes.
The Kathmandu Metropolitan City Office has already set aside funds for the restoration (October 2022).

Local residents report that thephalcāwas dismantled in the early 1970s, supposedly because it was heavily damaged, however, others argue that it was destroyed when the house behind it was reconstructed.
A formerguṭhīmember recalls that the timber columns had decayed due to the dilapidated condition of the roof resulting in the three-bayedphalcā's dismantling in the 1970s.
Theguṭhīseems to have been dissolved after thephalcāwas dismantled.
It was built as a replica of the Indreśvara Mahādeva temple in Panauti, a quaint city around 30 kilometres southeast of Kathmandu.

The origin of Indrapura Temple lies in the mystical transference of Indreśvara Mahādeva from Panauti, achieved through esoteric practices, hence earning its name as Indrapura Mandira (G. Vajrācārya VS 2033, p.76).
Its architectural marvel is embodied in a novel example of tiered construction, showcasing an upper tier fashioned in the likeness of a balconied tower.

While the entrance to the sanctum on the ground floor remains unadorned without an embellished arch (toraṇa), the sanctum's main deity is aśivaliṅga, venerated as Indreśvara Mahādeva. (However, due to the cessation of daily rituals, photographing the sanctum'sśivaliṅgawas not possible.) According to G. Vajrācārya (VS 2033, p.77), a Garuḍa statue was once positioned to the south of the temple; alas, this statue is now absent.
There are no historical records to date the initial construction of the temple.
However, these records remain silent concerning the exact year of the temple's establishment.
The 1934 earthquakes damaged the temple, causing the upper roof to crumble (cf. KVPT Report 2002, p.7).
Subsequent renovations introduced alterations to the temple's structure.
In 2002 CE, the Kathmandu Valley Preservation Trust undertook restorative efforts, returning the temple to its pre-1934 CE configuration (KVPT Report 2002).
Annually, on the 12th day of the bright fortnight of Bhādra, theyaḥsĩis erected at the nearbyyaḥsĩgāḥ—a pit designated for the ceremonial pole's placement.
There is no confirmed date when thehitiwas built but the motifs on the water spouts suggest that they are from the Malla period (report byLalitpur Sub Metropolitan City2007, 15).
The source of water of the hiti was destroyed and concrete buildings were constructed in its surroundings.
Tamkaḥdyaḥ Phalcā, erected in 2005 CE, stands to the west of the Ugracaṇḍī temple, commonly known as Tamkaḥdyaḥ.
Thephalcāwas commissioned by Madana Rāja Tāmrākāra in the memory of his late parents, Aṣṭa Rāja and Candra Kumārī, with the intention to facilitate social, cultural and religious functions.

Althought commonly known as Tamkaḥdyaḥ Phalcā, an inscription embedded in thephalcā's wall mentions its name as Aṣṭa-Candra-Samay Phalcā, incorporationg the first names of the donor's parents and the term for ritual food.
Today it is rare for donors to built such traditionalphalcās.
Originally, the Phalcā had three bays and traditional look, but it was reconstructed in ca. 1998 CE into a concrete structure with a cover of a cement slab on top.
The fourthāṃs (pillars) now erected inside the Phalcā also came from its former structure.
There is no inscription that sheds light on the initial construction of the Phalcā.
Probably a Buddhist family from the area got the Phalcā constructed, as there are three Buddhist statues installed here.
Built in 1657 CE (NS 777) by three brothers: Kāśī Bhāro, Gaṃgārāma Bhāro, and Śiva Bhāro, thisjaḥdhuṃwater tank is now in a state of disrepair and is not in use.
Suchjaḥdhuṃtanks were built by the roadside in the Kathmandu valley and the surrounding areas to facilitate pilgrims, travelers, and farmers in quenching their thirst.

Although the inscription on thejaḥdhuṃrecords its establishment by the three brothers: Kāśī Bhāro, Gaṃgārāma Bhāro, and Śiva Bhāro, it does not mention the establishment of a trust for its maintenance.
During the Pañcāyata rule, in the 1980s, the local village administration carried out some basic repairs of thejaḥdhuṃ(local resident, Śreṣṭha, male, age 58).
Locals have no information about the family that built thisjaḥdhuṃ.
The water tank is now hidden by the wall built below the Vāsyāḥdyaḥ shrine (K. MallaNS 1142, p.6-8).
The simple design of the Phalcā’s pillars suggests that they were installed a little less than a century ago.
Besides that, no other component of the Phalcā supports exposing the antiquity of the Phalcā and there is no inscription that records its initial construction.
In 2017 CE (VS 2074), the same family replaced its traditional tile roof with corrugated metal sheets.
Constructed in 1664 CE (NS 784) by a group led by Bhavānīśaṅkara of Kirtipur, the main statue of this temple was established by Bhavānīdāsa.
An influential government officer from Kirtipur, Bhavānīdāsa Bhāro, was instrumental in building this temple.
Bhavānīśaṅkara, son of Bhavānīdāsa Bhāro, together with other individuals, constructed the temple in 1664 CE (NS 784).

Bhavānīdāsa Bhāro, on the other hand, installed the sculptures of the deities and donated land parcels to set up religious trusts (guthi) to oversee daily and periodic rituals at the temple (D. Vajrācārya, VS 2056, p. 133-134).
A few years after the temple’s construction, Jayarāma, Śivadāsa, and others offered a gilded flag to the temple, while also installing a brass finial.
Another inscription (see ‘historical events’) records the installation of the gilded finial for the deities enshrined in the temple.
The temple underwent renovation in 2003 CE (NS 1123) with government funding and local community involvement.

Following damage sustained in the 2015 CE earthquakes, the temple was reconstructed in 2023 CE (VS 2079) with financial support from the Department of Archaeology and Chandragiri Municipality, alongside the active participation of the Gaṇeśa Bhagavatī Kālikā Rājaguthi, a religious trust associated with the temple.

Subsequently, the local community intervened, preventing Bhairava's return to Nuwakot, and established his presence within the temple, initiating the tradition of the palanquin procession (local resident, Maharjana, male, age 61).
Situated in an alley of the upper old market in Triśulī, this temple was constructed in the Śivālaya architectural style, commonly seen in Kathmandu and its surrounding areas during the Rāṇā period.
In front of the temple stands a bell, donated by the family of Durgādāsa in 1908 CE (VS 1965).
However, the inscription on the bell does not specify whether the temple itself was built in that same year or earlier.
According to local tradition, the temple was built by the Śreṣṭha family, descendants of Durgādāsa, who had relocated from Triśulī.
Over time, the temple has fallen into disrepair, standing as an example of heritage neglect caused by local migration.
A pole is installed in each of them, and changed every year, on the first day of the greatDasaĩ.
The first metre of wall elevation is built with cut stones.
Above it, the walls and domed ceiling are built out of bricks.
At the centre of the temple is a square stand made of bricks, on which is installed a stone disc and a stoneśivaliṅga.
On it is installed, to the right side of the door, an inscribed stele dated of ŚS 1277 (1355 CE) (DLK0340_I).
A modern altar is built to the south-west of the temple.
It contains various little stone artefacts, of which the most noticable is a damaged Buddha statue (DLK0340-002).
Acoording to local informants, the monument was built in the first half of the 19th, by Jang Bahadur Bal Kunwar (Jung Bahadur Rana) (Lecomte-Tilouine 2009), when he was a captain.
Local residents believe that this Phalcā was built by them.
We have no proof of any inscription exists to confirm the Phalcā's construction date.
The Phalcā, damaged in the 2015 earthquake, was dismantled and reconstructed by the metropolitan city office in 2020 CE.
It is located at Pinchẽ tola and is owned and administered by the local community (without aguthi).
Pinchẽ Phalcā houses a statue of Gaṇeśa and has also been furnished with an inscription.
Built on the north-western side of the Jayavāgīśvarī Mandira (PPK1222), the Jaladyaḥ Sataḥ also stands opposite another arcaded rest house known as the Triśūla Sataḥ (PPK1216).
There is no record of the initial construction.
The Pashupati Area Development Trust (PADT) reconstructed theSataḥin 2002 CE (VS 2059).
A local youth club by the name of Jayabāgeśvarī Yūvā Klaba is based here since 2007 CE (VS 2064).
The club also organizes social activities like blood donation, health camps, etc. in the building.
Kuladīpā Bāhāḥ was built by a certain Kuladīpa Vajrācārya in 1941 CE (NS 1061) and is an idenpendentbāhāḥ(not a branch).
In 1978 CE (NS 1098), the responsibility of running thebāhāḥwas handed over to the Sarvahita Guṭhī.
Thebāhāḥwas renovated in 2007 CE (NS 1127).
Recognized as Bamarāmeśvara, thisśivālaya, or the abode of Śiva, was constructed under the patronage of Bama Bahādura Kũvara, the younger brother of Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā, in 1847 CE (VS 1904).
Additionally, a tulasīmaṭha, a special container for cultivating the tulasī plant, and a statue of Kāmadeva are established to the north and southeast of the temple, respectively.
Thisśivālayawas erected by Bama Bahādura Kũvara in 1847 CE (VS 1904) (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p. 349; Michaels and Tandon 2017, p.106).
citations: (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p. 349; Michaels and Tandon 2017, p.106)

text: Born as the second son of Bālanarasiṃha Kũvara and Gaṇeśakumārī (Rakṣakumārī), Bama Bahādura assumed the role of acting prime minister when his elder brother Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā embarked on an extensive Europe tour in 1850 CE (VS 1907) (P. Rāṇā VS 2070, p.53).
He undertook the construction of the temple shortly after Jaṅga Bahādura ascended to power following the court massacre in 1846 CE (VS 1903).
Bama Bahādura had four sons—Bamavīravikrama, Vīravikrama, Yakṣavikrama, and Ṭeka Bahādura (P. Rāṇā VS 2059, p.331).
On the contrary, P. Yādava (VS 2045, genealogy in the appendix) mentions only one name, Rāmavikrama, as the son of Bama Bahādura, who potentially collaborated in the construction of this temple.
Bama Bahādura, usually plagued by persistent symptoms of tuberculosis, succumbed to poor health and passed away in 1857 CE (VS 1914) (P. Rāṇā VS 2059, p.109).
The earthquakes in 2015 caused damage to the temple walls, prompting the Pashupati Area Development Trust to initiate restoration efforts in 2021 CE (VS 2078).
Due to the absence of an inscription documenting the temple's construction at the site, details about the year of its establishment and its benefactor remain elusive.
Nevertheless, the temple's architectural features suggest probable construction during the Rāṇā period (1846-1951 CE).

The shrine was previously managed by a private trust, but its members have relocated abroad, leading to the cessation of all rituals many decades ago, as reported by a local resident, Pauḍela, male, age 45.
The earliest inscription found on the site dates to 1666 CE (NS 786) and records the restoration of the nearby well by Govindarāma Bhāvo, Darasiṃha Bhāvo, and others.
The same inscription mentions the group’s annual pilgrimage to Jawalakhel during theBhotō Jātrā(Jāhvalā Jātrā) to perform worship and communal feasts.
Although the original inscription is now lost, it suggests that the well andphalcā(pavilion) were built around the same time as the Harisiddhi Bhavānī shrine.

Another inscription from 1711 CE (NS 831) records that after theGuṃlā Dharmafestival, residents led bythakāliCandrarāma Bhāvo restored thephalcāhousing Gaṇeśa, assigning its upkeep to Śiva, Siddhirāma, and Darasiṃha.
Later, in 1920 CE (NS 1040), Budhabīr Kālu of Thathukvākva ṭola, together with his family, paved the area in front of the shrine with stone slabs, and in 1926 CE (NS 1045) a bell was donated.
Thephalcāremained in use until 2021 CE (VS 2078), when it was reconstructed as a temple with financial support from the local government, though the original form was not preserved.

In 2025 CE (VS 2081), Lalitpur Metropolitan City funded brick paving around the well, and in 2026 CE (VS 2082), the local community rebuilt a separatephalcāused for devotional singing in front of the temple.
The Laganakhela Phalcā still retains its traditionaljhĩgaṭīroof, but this has been badly damaged and is now (in 2019) covered with a tarpaulin.
The Laganakhela Bhajana Maṇḍala collects rent under the pretext of looking after the phalcā, however, it is obvious that thephalcāhas been neglected and that its roof is in dire need of repair.
There is neither a record of an activeguṭhīnor is there any inscription with which to date the monument.
This three-bayphalcāwas donated by a family of the Avāle caste that lives across the lane.

In addition to the stone icon, a metal image of Caṇḍikā (Bhagavatī) has also been installed; owing to the current phase of reconstruction, this metal icon has been temporarily placed outside the shrine.
Over time, additional anthropomorphic images were incorporated, and eventually a small, single-tiered pagoda temple was constructed over the sacred spot.
This modest structure has recently been dismantled, and reconstruction in a more “authentic” Nepali architectural style began in 2025 (VS 2081) under a plan of Lalitpur Metropolitan City.
As of January 2026, the temple remains under reconstruction.
Adharmastambhaerected in 1951 (VS 2008) by the Vaiṣṇava activist Kaviprasāda, following a week-longsaptāharecitation andkīrtana, also stands within the compound.
Early inscriptions of 1669 CE (NS 789) attest that the shrine was formerly known asConidevaandCauni Mahākāla.
These shrines originally consisted only of aniconic stones, with anthropomorphic icons added gradually over time.
An inscription of 1684 (NS 804) from Kirtipur refers to a similar shrine asIṣṭaconi Mahākāra(Shokoohy, Shokoohy & Shrestha 2014, p. 72).
At the present site, an inscription of 1702 (NS 822) records the nameChoni Mahākāra, while an earlier inscription of 1669 (NS 789) mentionsChonidevain masculine form.
The earliest inscription found here dates to 1669 (NS 789), recording that members of the Bhāvo (Jyāpu/agricultural) community constructed the central stonetoraṇaand certain stone base structures.
Another inscription of 1701 (NS 822) notes that small stonedevala(miniature temples) were erected on the right and left sides of the shrine, again by members of the farming community.
A building directly in front of the temple, named “Cunīdevī Bhāgavata Bhavana,” hosts daily devotional singing (bhajana-kīrtana).
During its renovation, in early 2022 CE, the existing spouts were removed and a new one was installed.
There are two inscriptions at the premises oft hehiti, but both of them are completely eroded.
It is probable that they record the construction of thehitiand/or of the Vajradhātu Caitya (SKH0580), which is located to its east.
Currently, there is noguthiassociated with thehiti, nor there is evidence of any socio-cultural activities taking place at the spout.
Likewise, Lāṃkva Hiti is constructed to the southeast of this Phalcā.
The details of the initial construction of the Phalcā are unclear.

The local oral tradition credits Candra Nārāyaṇa Śreṣṭha, an ancestor of the Śreṣṭha family living in the adjoining building, for commissioning the construction of this Phalcā during the partyless Pañcāyata rule (1961 CE-1990 CE).
After it collapsed in the 2015 earthquakes, Uttama Nārāyaṇa Śreṣṭha, the grandson of Candra Nārāyaṇa, funded the reconstruction of the Phalcā in 2016 CE (local resident, Śreṣṭha, male, age 54).
The traditional architecture of the Phalcā was not adopted in the reconstruction.
According to local residents, the space of the Phalcā was rented out after its reconstruction following the 2015 earthquakes.
Nothing is known about the initial construction of this Phalcā.
Due to the poor condition of the Phalcā, the locals reconstructed it in 2003 CE (local resident, Śreṣṭha, female, age 70).
The 2015 earthquakes damaged the roof of the Phalcā and the Samiti renovated the roof and laid corrugated tin sheets.
Likewise, aguthiof the Śreṣṭha community of Sankhu offers unhusked rice to Vasundhara when the deity’s palanquin arrives here.
Given the estimate period of architectural activity at the site, it is possible to suggest that this fountain was built between the 13th and 15th century.
A person named Bhaṭṭa facilitated the construction of the Phalcā and the associatedhitito allow bypassers to rest and quench their thirst.
According to the inscription, the monuments were once constructed in front of a water hole.
While today, thehitistands right in front of Hitipine Phalcā, an inscription inside reveals that originally, thehitiused to be behind it.
Bothhitiandphalcāwere constructed i 1863 CE (VS 1920).
A person from the Vaidya caste in Thimi had donated a plot of land to Viśvanātha Bhaṭṭa, who then constructed thehitiand Phalcā on the donated land.
[1]He also formed aguthiby donating tworopanīs of land at Sipāḍola, Bhaktapur for the upkeep of the two monuments.
The inscription also instructs the performance of the anniversary ritual of the monuments on the 3rd of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha.
Theguthialong with the rituals has ceased to exist, the donated land is also lost.
In the course of the expansion of the road from Pepsīkolā to Sānothimi, the contractor demolished the Phalcā in 2019 CE.
Madhyapura-Thimi Municipality then started the reconstruction behind thehiti.
Since then, the reconstruction of Hitipine Phalcā has stopped, the complex is left unattended due to its neared completion.
[1]The inscription mentions Bhaṭṭa's genealogy at the beginning.

Situated at Pakanājola in Kathmandu, this Temple of Lord Kṛṣṇa was constructed by a Pā̃ḍe family in the mid-19thcentury on their private courtyard (see the inscription from VS 1909/ŚS1777 [KAT0040_I_001], erected east of the Bhagavatī Temple [KAT0050) on the same courtyard built by the same family).
citations: (see the inscription from VS 1909/ŚS1777 [KAT0040_I_001], erected east of the Bhagavatī Temple [KAT0050)

text: With only one entrance on the southern side, the Kṛṣṇa Temple is built on two plinths.

The above-mentioned inscription installed by Kaptāna (Captain) Udaya Bahādura Pā̃ḍe and his wife Lalitā Devī records the construction of the Temple by his grandfather Raṇajita Pā̃ḍe, grandmother Candraprabhā, father Vīrakeśarī (inscription: Vīrakesara/Vīrakeśari) Pā̃ḍe, uncles Raṇagaṃbhīra (inscription: Raṇagaṃbhira), Dalakeśarī (inscription: Dalakeśari) and Kīrtidhvaja on their private courtyard, and land endowment made by them in order to operate the Temple.
However, it does not mention the date of the construction of the Temple.
The dates (the Vikrama Samvat Era year and Śaka Samvat Era year) of the installation of the inscription do not correspond to each other.
The VS 1909 (1853 CE) corresponds to Śaka Era year 1774 (1853 CE), but not 1777 (1856 CE).
In 1996 CE (VS 2053), Ḍambarajaṅga Pā̃ḍe renovated the Temple together with his wife Ratna Kumārī Pā̃ḍe and the family.
Again in 2007 CE (VS 2064), Ratna Kumārī Pā̃ḍe renovated it in memory of her husband Ḍambarajaṅga Pā̃ḍe and son, Śivajaṅga Pā̃ḍe.
The 2015 earthquakes caused minor damage to the Temple.
No documented evidence exists regarding the original construction of thephalcā.
However, it underwent renovation in 2014 CE by the Lalitpur Municipality in collaboration with the local community.
An additional room has been constructed at the rear of thephalcāspecifically for storing old chariot wheels.
In 1994, the wheels were relocated, and the room was transformed into a gym by a local youth club.
The courtyard can be accessed by entering through the underpass of a residential building.
The maināgamabuilding is completely ruined and only the wall of the principal east façade remains up to the height of the first floor.
Vegetation has grown wild over the collapsed remains of the building.
According to local residents, the shrine was constructed by Harivaṃśa Śarmā, a priest of King Siddhinarasiṃha Malla.
An inscription of 1746 (NS 866, 5th day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha) mentions that Harivaṃśa Śarmā was a well versed pundit (Sharma1977, 133).
Another inscription, which might contain more information regarding the history of the monument, is semi-visible but buried in the ruins of the building.
The main sanctum building has a three-bay ribbon window on the first-floor level and is topped by two floors with a pitched roof covered with traditionaljhĩgaṭītiles.
The other wings of the courtyard building are two-storied and have a flat concrete slab roof.
The staircase is placed on the north-east corner of the courtyard building.

HemarājaŚākya(1995, 16-21), referring to theDevamālāvaṃśāvalī, a chronicle, mentions that in the reigning period of Licchavi King Vṛṣadeva, a merchant called Sundarasārthavāha spending his money renovated the Aśoka Caitya of Pulchok and made this Bahī.
However, the chronicle mentions only the renovation of the Caitya and the establishment of the settlement in Pulchok, but does not describe the Bahī and gives no record of its foundation.
A Licchavi inscription found in this Bahī was removed to the Kvathu Bahī.
Athyāsaphudated NS 373 (1253 CE) gives the first reference to this Bahī.
Anotherthyāsaphuof 1415 CE (NS 535) mentions that Akhayaśrī (Akṣayaśrī) renovated the Bahī (Śākya 1995,62), and afterwards the Bahī got its classical name Akṣeśvara Mahāvihāra.
In 1980, some of the inspired youth from Lalitpur planned its reconstruction.
The king released a fund for its reconstruction and the youths collected some of the donations from locals.
In 1988, the reconstruction work was completed.
A historical photo (published inPruscha 1975, P-64) of the old Bahī complex shows struts with images of eight Bodhisattvas which are missing in the new building.
After the reconstruction, an organization called Akṣeśvara Mahāvihāra Saṃrakṣaṇa Samiti was formed for the management of the Bahī.

text: This shrine probably constitutes the preceding structure of this temple and the contemporary structure was probably constructed around this stone shrine.
Constructed in 1657 CE (NS 777) by King Pratāpa Malla, it used to be one of the tallest structures in the Kathmandu Durbar Square.
The topmost tier is built only on the protruding section, which makes it appear like a balconied tower (pula).
A photo of Kavīndrapura taken before the 1934 earthquakes shows an additional tier on top.
In the chronicles, the king is said to have established a statue of Nāsaḥdyaḥ in a newly-builtphalcāthat he named ‘Madu-nāsālā-deva’ (lit. Nāsaḥdyaḥ of the Maruṭola) (Wright 1877, p.214).
Two large inscriptions at Kavīndrapura reveal that it was built by King Pratāpa Malla in 1657 CE (NS 777).
The inscriptions state that Narasiṃha, the fourth incarnation of Lord Viṣṇu, got infuriated when the king danced in the guise of the deity.
To appease Narasiṃha, Pratāpa Malla built Kavīndrapura and enshrined a statue of Narasiṃha along with various other tantric deities (G. Vajrācārya VS 2033, p.51).
The portion with the date in the inscription has already eroded.
Hence, the date is no longer legible in the inscription.
Although G. Vajrācārya (VS 2033, p.50) mentions the temple of Nāsaḥdyaḥ later came to be known as Kavīndrapura.
However, it is clear from the two inscriptions here that the building was named Kavīndrapura by Pratāpa Malla himself at the time of its construction.
Pratāpa Malla features in many of his inscriptions with the titlekavīndra(lit. king of poets).

He further mentions in the inscription that a statue of Narasiṃha was also established here along with a statue of Nṛtyeśvara, the Sanskrit name of Nāsaḥdyaḥ, as the building was constructed with a special focus on the performance of dances.
Kavīndrapura collapsed in the 1934 earthquakes and was never rebuilt into its original structure.
Only three roofs survive as the top two floors collapsed in the 1934 earthquake.

Recent encroachments have eliminated the arcade and the balcony in the back, a repair scheme undertaken by the Department of Archaeology renewed the roofing and the walls of the side wings in 1986 (Gutschow 2011, p.512).
Gutschow (2011, p.512-513) has published acomparative viewof the original Kavīndrapura built by Pratāpa Malla and the one reconstructed after the 1934 earthquakes.
The Hanumandhoka Durbar Square Conservation Program of the Kathmandu Metropolis renovated Kavīndrapura at a cost of NRs. 1.76 million (J. Sāha VS 2068, online).
Apaintingof Kavīndrapura by Henry A. Oldfield from 1857 CE with shops on its ground floor is evidence that thephalcāon the ground floor was already rented out to shops back then.
Above the door is a stone inscription recording the construction of the temple under the auspices of Pratāp Śāhī and his nephew Māna Śāhī, in ŚS 1504 (1582 CE).
The inscription was consecrated by Ātmanātha and Laṁgarnātha, two Nātha yogis.
Interestingly, the inscription was written by a certain Rāṃa Kṛiṣṇa from Benares (Naraharinath 1956 (VS 2013), 168-169, cited inShrestha 2009, 280).
The temple was renovated in VS 2040 (1984 CE), as is recorded on an inscription engraved in the cement of the southwestern pillar.
This renovation consisted in a complete dismantlement of the temple and reconstruction with cement mortar.
The four front pillars have also been replaced by new ones.
An inscription from VS 2042 (1986 CE) is running on three sides of the base of the sculpture.

Thisśikharastyle Mandira was probably built sometime in the late Malla era, however, no documented evidence can be found with which to prove thisA polished stone slab (śilāphalaka) sits on the southern side of the Mandira.
This was probably made for the purpose of inscribing a record, but nothing has been carved on it.
It seems that the construction work was abruptly stopped for some reason during its final phase.
In 535 CE (Samvat 487), someone named Svāmī Vārtta made a Hariśaṅkara statue in Pashupati (D. VajrācāryaVS 2030, 198-203).
A structure dedicated to Śaṅkarācārya must have existed in some form before Svāmī Rāma Girī built the temple in 1905 CE (VS 1962).
This is evident from the fact that Svāmī Rāma Girī had already offered a bell to Śaṅkarācārya at the site in 1887 CE (VS 1944).
Inside the sanctum, threeśivaliṅgas – Rāmeśvara, Pratāpeśvara, and Mahākāleśvara – are also installed.
In 1349 CE (NS 470), during an invasion, Sultan Shamsuddin from Bengal touched theśivaliṅga, which led to its removal from the main temple due to the perceived desecration.
Currently (July 2023), thisśivaliṅga, revered as Pratāpeśvara, is enshrined in the Śaṅkarācārya Mandira, protected by a metal covering (M. Thāpā VS 2077, p. 140).
Additionally, a geometric figure known as Śrī Yantra, composed of nine concentric triangles, is established within the sanctum.
Statues of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Gaṇeśa, Durgā, Sarasvatī, and Umāmaheśvara accompany the Śrī Yantra (M. Thāpā VS 2077, pp. 140-141).
The temple was constructed by an ascetic named Paramahaṃsa Mahanta Rāma Girī in 1905 CE (VS 1962) (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p. 359).
Since Svāmī Rāma Girī's offering of a bell to Śaṅkarācārya in 1887 CE (VS 1944) is known, it is evident that a structure related to Śaṅkarācārya existed prior to this temple.
Subsequent to the Nepal visit of Jagadguru Śaṅkarācārya from the Śṛṅgerī Maṭha in 1974 CE, the temple underwent renovation (Michaels 2008, p. 31).
Following the damage sustained in the 2015 earthquakes, the temple was reconstructed in 2022 CE (VS 2079).
However, the bell that was originally positioned northeast of the temple remains uninstalled after the reconstruction.
Thejhĩgaṭītiles covering the roof of the temple were replaced by copper sheets in 1997.
The temple did not suffer any damages during the earthquakes of 1934 and 2015.
No documented evidence has so far been located which can inform us the date of the initial construction of the temple.
TheBhāṣā Vamśāvalī(part 2, VS 2023, 3) mentions that Lichhavi King Vīradeva established the temple of Thache Mahālakṣmī to the south of the city when the city of Lalitpur was first founded.
One of the inscriptions on the site mentions that King Śrīnivāsa Malla erected a pillar and offered a golden lion to Mahālakṣmī Mandira in NS 791 (1671 CE).
Nevertheless, it is evident that the temple had not yet been constructed by that date; a shrine of the deity must have been there at that time instead.
Although theDevamālā Vaṃśāvalī(2013, 76-77) records that King Siddhinarasiṃha Malla commissioned the construction of this temple in NS 750-751, this is not supported by archaeological evidence.
An inscription attached to the temple’s wall mentions that Mahālakṣmī Mandira was commissioned by Vīranārāyaṇa Siṃha in NS 821 (1701 CE), a trader (vaiśya) by profession.
Furthermore, the inscription (dated NS 850) mentions that King Viṣṇu Malla endowed land to sponsor a fire ritual (śirāhūti yajna).
Over the years, numerous donors offered various objects and ritual materials to the temple.
Thedyaḥchẽ(main shrine building of the Bāhāḥ) is built on the southern side of the Bāhāḥ’s rectangular courtyard.
Unfortunately, it was rebuilt in 1990s as a modern house.
Statues of Hanumān, Gaṇeśa, and Mahākāla are installed in the niches on the doorway of this house.
Similar to other Bāhāḥs, a Śīkharakūṭa Caitya and Dharmadhātu have been established in the centre of the Bāhāḥ’s courtyard.
A statue of Akṣobhya has been consecrated in the sanctum as thekvāpāḥdyaḥ.
Besides this, a stone Caitya and a small statue of Tārā have also been installed in the sanctum.
The oldest inscription installed in the Bāhāḥ is from 1642 CE (NS 762), however, it does not record the name of the Bāhāḥ.
It mentions that a person called Hākuju established a statue of Śākyamuni Buddhha and installed acaitya.

It may be the case that following the completion of the Bāhāḥ, Hākuju consecrated the statue of Śākyamuni Buddha as the Bāhāḥ’skāvāḥpāḥdyaḥ, which was then replaced by the present-day Akṣobhya statue.
The second inscription on a Dharmadhātu Manaḍala is from 1817 CE and refers to this Bāhāḥ as Harṣakīrti Mahāvihāra.
[1]Hākuju also built a stoneśikhara-styled temple in Siṃhadvāḥ Ṭola, where the Cvaya Bāhāḥ also lies, and concreted a Buddha statue in its sanctum.
King Siddhinarasiṃha and his son, Śrīnivāvā Malla, had joined the consecration ceremony.
In 1684 CE (NS 804), Hākuju’s two sons built anotherśikhara-styled temple in the same Ṭola in the memory of their father (D. VajrācāryaVS 2056, 531-532).
Bhīmarāja Vajrācārya from Kirtipur renovated Cvay Bāhāḥ after the 1934 CE earthquakes (cf.Locke1985, 184).
The façade of the temple suffered some cracks again during the 2015 CE earthquakes, which was later repaired by Rājendra Vajrācārya.
The courtyard of the Bāhāḥ was paved withteliyābricks in 2017 CE with the financial support of the local government.
Although the Bāhāḥ was supposedly built by a Śākya clan member, Hākuju, no Śākya family lives in and around the Bāhāḥ premises.
Cvay Bāhāḥ used to have asaṅghauntil 1956 CE (VS 2015).
The government of Nepal brought thousandsropanīsofguṭhīland from Kirtipur under its possession and established the Tribhuvan University in 1956 CE.

Footnotes^Locke(1985, 184) andŚ. Śreṣṭha(1994, 142) erroneously mention that this inscription on the Dharmadhātu Maṇḍala records the initial construction of Cvay Bāhāḥ in 1641 CE (NS 761), but neither of the mentioned inscriptions attests to this fact.
Although it survived the earthquake of 2015 CE, it was for a while in a deteriorated state and was used by locals for storing straw, firewood, and the tying of livestock.

In 2024 CE (VS 2081), the Godāvari Municipality financed the reconstruction for 6 million nepalese rupees, adding new carved columns, struts, a latticed window, and balustrades, and making it aesthetically larger than its original form: the original structure had plain columns and a terracotta-tiled roof.
There is no inscription regarding Thaiba Tāhāḥ Phalcā's initial construction.
The monument stands in a Śreṣṭha community neighborhood and is believed to have been donated by a local Śreṣṭha who was involved in administration and finance during the Malla or early Śāha period.

However, Iśvara Bahādura Śreṣṭha claims it was built only 90–95 years ago (that is, around the time of the Great Earthquake of 1934 by a man named Kṛṣṇa Bahādura Śreṣṭha (VS 2077, p. 87). However, local residents are reluctant to accept this claim.A raised platform attached to the north of the Phalcā was used for Harisiddhi jala pyākhaḥ every 12 years. According to local residents, this ritual was last performed in 1961 CE (VS 2018). The Phalcā also accommodated musicians during the dance and folk dramas performed on the raised platform (dabalī) during Guṃlā and Indrajātrā (local resident, Śreṣṭha, male, age 69). In the past, ceremonial food (samaybaji) was distributed here during Indrajātrā and Viṣṇudevī jātrā, and images of Kṛṣṇa were displayed during Kṛṣṇaṣtamī (I. Śreṣṭha VS 2077, p. 87). However, these traditions have now come to an end.
A small farm house is built just opposite de rivulet.
The Bistabara village committee has built a stone and cement wall around the monuments.
Suchśikharaswere erected throughout the Karnali Basin from the 13th to the 15th century (Andolfatto 2019).
The rarity of inscriptions onśikharatemples (locally calleddeval) complicates the dating of this type of monuments.
Furthermore, a stone memorial pillar located 5 meters to the north of the Bistabara temples (JUM0453) bears the date of ŚS 1422 (1500 CE).
It is plausible that the pillar and the temples were built around the same time.
It is crowned by a unique Kīrtimukhatoraṇa, which is dated to 900 CE - 1030 CE through radiocarbon dating (Gutschow2011, 222).
A statue of Cakrasamvara (the esoteric deity ‘āgaṃdyaḥ’of the Bāhāḥ and clan deity of the Tāmrākāra caste members living around the courtyard) is consecrated on this floor.
Three pinnacles (gajūra) are erected on the tip of thejhĩgaṭītiled roof.
The shrine building is well documented by Mary Slusser's photographs from the 1960s.
In 1966 CE, the traditional roof cover had been changed to modern pantiles and a part of the roof had partly collapsed.
Makeshift repairs included the addition of sheets of corrugated metal roofing.
In 1987 CE, the roof structure and the balcony window with its thirteenth century roof brackets collapsed completely.
The precious wood carvings were brought to the safe storage and the building, once again, was temporarily covered with a metal roof cover.
It was not until a decade later when Yatkhā Bāhāḥdyaḥchẽwas restored by the Kathmandu Valley Preservation Trust (KVPT) under the banner of the 'Buddhist Kathmandu Campaign'.
KVPT was particularly positioned to implement this project as one of the very few international preservation groups with an established local fund-raising base.
Between 2000 CE and 2002 CE, KVPT meticulously documented the building, planned its restoration, and raised the necessary funds with additional funding provided by the Sumitomo Foundation, Japan.
The restoration was completed in 2003 CE.
Local residents believe that the wife of King Bhāṣkaradeva (r. 1045-1047) built this Bāhāḥ and named it after him (H. Śākya, VS 2035, 22).

Add to this, some popular legends associate the Bāhāḥ with King Bhāṣkara Malla (r. 1700-1719), but this is entirely late because the Bāhāḥ is referred to as Bhāṣkaramalla Vihāra already in the inscription from 1862 CE (NS 982).

The mentioned inscription, which is the oldest so far found in the Bāhāḥ premises records the formation of aguṭhīin order to carry out the regular worship of thekvāpāḥdyaḥ(Locke1985, 293 has discussed this inscription).

A Vajrācārya family from Ituṃ Bāhāḥ used to live on the first floor of Yatkhā Bāhāḥdyaḥchẽbefore its renovation started in 2002 CE and the head of this family used to carry out the daily worship here.
After the family moved out in 2002 CE due to the restoration work, the daily rituals are performed by aguṭhīof the local Tāmrākāras.
Some also believe that the name Pyaṃthāṃ comes fromPyaṃgaḥthāṃ, four pillars, and surmise that there probably was a building that had four pillars.
The open shrine was later converted into a concrete structure with four pillars in 2009 CE.
In November 2021, the Kirtipur Municipality has disbursed NRs. 14,40,000 for the construction of Buṅgadyaḥ temple here, and the works will commence shortly (2021-11-20).
Padmapāṇi Lokeśvara dressed in silverhegā(offered by a person called Jujuharṣa in NS 1016 i.e. 1895 CE) is consecrated in the sanctum as thekvāḥpāḥdyaḥof the Bāhāḥ.
