text: A statue of Dīpaṅkara Buddha can be seen on the Bāhāḥ‘s ground floor while a room on its first floor is allocated to Kumārī.
The Caturbrahma Mahāvihāra was constructed during the reign of King Rāya Malla.
The king had invited Jīvacandra Vajrācārya of the Taḥchẽ Bāhāḥ in Kathmandu to construct the Bāhāḥ and install a Kumārī in Bhaktapur.
A manuscript containing the textPañcarakṣāfrom the collection of the Bāhāḥ, records Jīvacandra arriving in Bhaktapur in NS 611 (1491 CE) (B. Vajrācārya1124, p. 150-151).
The monastery was constructed soon afterward.
In NS 873 (1753 CE), the Bāhāḥ was renovated by Vajrācārya Tavadhika, his wife Cukuti and his family.
They also offered a finial.
In NS 878 (1758 CE), there was a controversy regarding the selection of girls to be inducted as Kumārī.
The Guṭhī and Tahasila Aḍḍā, a government body that looked after theguthis, carried out a complete renovation of all the roofs of the Bāhāḥ in VS 2028 (1971 CE).
A Sarasvatī statue is established inside the Phalcā, from which the Phalcā takes its name.
There is no inscriptive evidence mentioning the donor and pointing to its initial construction.
In 2014 CE (VS 2071), the then Lalitpur Sub-Metropolitan City and Lũnkhusi Ṭol Saṅgha jointly reconstructed the Phalcā.
After the reconstruction, wooden bars were added, allegedly for security purposes.
A statue of Mahākāla was established later by a local community member.
On the day of Śivarātri, a bonfire is lighted in front of its gate.
The earliest historical evidence of thebahīcan be found in an inscription dated NS 538 (1418 CE).
Thebahīwas reconstructed in 2012.
The exterior front façade of the building and the ground floor courtyard elevations are finished indāci apāwhile other elevations are plastered in cement.
Locke(1985, 217) mentions that there was an inscription in Licchavi script on the base of the Buddha image, which now is missing.
The existing statue of Akṣobhya was consecrated by thesaṅgha-members in 1988 after the loss of the previous one.
Today (2019-09), thebahīarea has been encroached upon by private buildings.
In 1970, members of thebahīallowed the Young Men's Buddhist Association (YMBA) to reconstruct and make use of thebahīcomplex.
The YMBA collected donations for its reconstruction, which was completedonly  in 2012.
Pañcarāja Śākya and Caityarāja Śākya (Bhikṣu Anomadasti) donated their private lands to the association.
Since there is no space for anāgama, the shrine was relocated to Dhaugaḥ Bahī.
A gilt copper pinnacle and trident are installed on the top of the śikhara.
The main deity, a Kopeśvara Śivaliṅga is installed in the sanctum's south-east corner and not in the center as it is usually done.
An inscription located inside the sanctum informs that the Daivajña (Jośī) family renovated the temple in 1893 CE (VS 1950).
[1]The Bāhāḥ is the main esoteric building (āgaṃchẽ) of the Śākyas of Asana in Kathmandu.
There is an inscription on either side of the Bāhāḥ’s entrance.
The inscription on the eastern side has already faded and its content is unknown.
The western inscription records the endowment of land by a monk named Dharmacandra in 1704 CE (NS 825).
The octagonalcaitya(aṣṭakoṇākṛta), constructed right in front of the Bāhāḥ, was commissioned by Nhuchemāna and Thīramāna in 1946 CE (NS 1066).
They also installed statues of Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, two of the Buddha’s closest disciples, and bells.
The Bāhāḥ was reconstructed into its present structure in 1987 CE (VS 2044) (R. Tāmrākāra 2070, p.136).
Previously, it was renovated in 1889 CE (NS 1009).
A stone statue of Gaṇeśa is consecrated in the sanctum of the Temple.
The copper Gaṇeśa statue bears an inscription from 1975 CE (VS 2032) recording the name of its donor, a certain Bhajumāna Maharjana and his family members.
One of the brass statues too has a relatively new inscription from 2018 CE (VS 2075) recording the name of its donor Dila Māyā Maharjana.
The remaining one which has no inscription is the oldest among these three and it is carried on the palanquin during the Gaṇeśa procession.
The Temple (faces west) is built on a rectangular base and has aphalcālike structure, for example three sides of the Temple are open and its roof is supported by twenty wooden columns.
The Mandira suffered major damages during the 2015 CE earthquakes.
Therefore, the Chandragiri Municipality started to renovate it in 2019 CE (the work is almost completed, as of July 2021).
citations: (the work is almost completed, as of July 2021)

text: The reconstruction effort has improved the aesthetic features of the Temple such as all of the plain supporting wooden beams have been intricately carved.
There are no historical sources to date the initial construction of the Temple.
It has two inscriptions in its premises; however, they are completely eroded, thus cannot be deciphered.
A local Kapālī family takes care of the Mandira as thedyaḥpāḥlāḥand enjoys the left overs (such asprasādaanddakṣiṇā) offered to the deity by devotees.
An inscription at the Shrine recording an offering ofdalūlamps by Motilāla Ṭhakurī Lavata Malla in 1932 CE (1988 VS).
According to local residents, Motilāla Ṭhakurī Lavata (Malla) constructed the Shrine for Suntvāḥ Gaṇeśa but they do not remember the year of its construction.
We can assume that he constructed it around the same time he offered thedalūlamps.

According to theMaṇiśaila-Mahāvadāna, a Buddhist scripture, Jogadeva Vajrācārya founded the town of Sankhu in 1300 BC (Kaligata Era 1801) in the shape of aśaṅkha(conch shell) as per the instruction of Goddess Vajrayoginī.

He had divided the town into eight city quarters (ṭola)and constructed a palace at the center, along with the shrines of Eight Mother Goddesses (aṣṭamātṛkā), ninebāhāḥs, and four gates in four directions (V. Vajrācārya1119, p. 32-33).
As it is customary to establish a shrine of Gaṇeśa at eachṭola, it is possible that Suntvāḥ Gaṇeśa, too, was in existence as a small shrine since 1300 BC.
The statue was subsequently consecrated by Śāntikara Vajrācārya (an esteemed tantric) of Makhaṃ Bāhāh (KAT1190).
There is no evidence as per inscription to date the initial construction of the Sataḥ.
It was constructed as a residence for the household ascetics (Kapālī-jogīs).
In 2000 CE (VS 2057), Prabhat Red Star Club, a local club based in Nugaḥ, raised funds for its repair and reconstruction.
Amṛta Hiti, locally known as Pvaḥ Hiti, was constructed during the medieval period for the Poḍhe community residing in Imūkhel, Lalitpur.
Generally, statues of Bhagīratha are installed under the water spout(s) of ahiti, however, this is not the case in Amṛta Hiti.
A statue of Śrīdhara Viṣṇu is established on thehiti’s northern wall which S.Khanal(2068, 173) dates to the sixteenth and seventeenth century.
There is no evidence to appoint the initial construction of thehiti.
However, it is probable that it was built sometime during the medieval period (Lalitpur Sub-Metropolitan City2007, 45).
It was renovated by the local community in 1988 CE (VS 2045).

The UN-Habitat and Integrated Urban Development Project assisted to form a local committee in 2008 CE (VS 2065) for the management of water collection from thehitiduring the night and distributing it to the public during the day.
Above the central bay is atoraṇainstalled in 1664 CE (NS 785), featuring figures of Bālakumārī and her consort Bhairava.
Prior to the 2015 earthquakes, the temple's first-floor roof connected to the adjacentsataḥ(THC0060), enabling access between thesataḥand the temple's sanctum.
This unique architectural element was not preserved during the temple's 2022 CE (VS 2079) reconstruction.
The Department of Archaeology, concluding that the temple was damaged in the earthquakes, rebuilt the temple without adopting its original feature.
The traditional tiles on the roofs were also replaced with copper sheets in the reconstruction.
A stone pillar erected in front of the temple bears a statue of peacock, the animal mount of the goddess.
There are no historical records regarding the initial construction of this temple.
The installation of atoraṇaon top of the central bay in 1664 CE (NS 785) indicates that a temple existed at that time in some form.
Another inscription from 1669 CE (NS 790) documents the offering of a goldentoraṇato Bālakumārī, along with the construction of some form of temple.
It is unclear if it was the temple itself or a portion of it that was built on this occasion.

In 1793 CE (NS 913), Jānakīdatta reconstructed the dilapidated temple by increasing its size, with the help of people from Thecva, Kathmandu, and Patan, and with the assistance of the localjyāpucommunity.
On the 14th of the bright fortnight of each month, the Caturdaśī Guthi performs special worship of Bālakumārī, followed by a feast on the floor where the sanctum is.
More than 10ropanis of lands endowed to Bālakumārī land has been converted into tenant land and has been registered with the Guthi Sansthan (Guṭhī Saṃsthāna VS 2071, p. 100).
In her second right hand, she holds a small double-sided drum (ḍamaru) (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p. 473).
There is no inscription specifically documenting the construction of the temple.
Another later chronicle calledDevamālā Vaṃśāvalī(2013, p. 36) states that King Śivadeva established the Vanakālī statue in 388 CE (Kaligata Era 3489).
However, no historical evidence supports the existence of a king named Śivadeva reigning around 388 CE in Nepal.

On the other hand, D. Vajrācārya (VS 2030, pp. 366-367) published an undated Licchavi inscription found in the Vanakālī area, mentioning that King Aṃśuvarmā's wife established a deity, and Amṛtavarmā built a boundary wall around the temple premises.
However, the inscription does not specifically mention the Vanakālī Mandira, as it was recovered from the Rājarājeśvarī Mandira area.
Hence, it cannot be associated with the Vanakālī Mandira (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p. 584).
The pedestal of the Vanakālī statue bears an inscription, but its content is unclear.
The script used in the inscription appears to belong to the later Licchavi period (Vajrācārya 1973, p. 131).
Unfortunately, cleaning and photographing the inscription were not permitted.
In 1958 CE (VS 2015), King Mahendra renovated the temple and erected a boundary wall around its premises.
In 1797 CE (VS 1854), King Raṇabahādura Śāha endowed 33ropanīsof land in Motīṭāra to establish a trust responsible for organizing the temple's anniversary rituals (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p. 585).
Records from the Guṭhī Saṃsthāna indicate that 30ropanīsand one ānā of land are registered in the name of the trust associated with the Vanakālī Mandira (Guṭhī Saṃsthāna VS 2071, p. 32).
The construction of this Śiva temple is traditionally ascribed to Badrīnarasiṃha Rāṇā, the younger brother of Prime Minister Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā.
No inscriptions at the site document the temple's construction.
According to Michaels and Tandon (2017, p.106), it was erected in 1848 CE (VS 1905).
A document (cf.K_0009_0011) from 1850 CE (VS 1907), issued by King Surendra in the name of Badrīnarasiṃha, addresses the establishment of trusts for various temples, including Badrībhakteśvara.
The document attributes the construction of this temple, among others in the vicinity, to Badrīnarasiṃha.
The earthquakes of 2015 caused significant damage to the temple, leaving visible cracks on its walls that persist to this day (October 2023).
However, Jaṅga Bahādura uncovered the conspiracy and had the Indian government imprison Badrīnarasiṃha in Allahabad for two years (Rāja VS 2071, p.1).
Thepīṭhawas established directly upon this rock, and the temple structure was subsequently constructed atop it.
At the highest point stands an aniconic (amūrta) stone revered as Ādikālī, upon which the temple itself has been erected.
Upon the large stone identified with Ādikālī, a metal image of the goddess has been installed.
Near this image an inscription is visible, and beneath it two metal lions have been placed.
On the southern side of the temple are installed an image of Gaṇeśa and a mask-like representation of Bhairava.
The site has long been associated with renouncers such as Aghorīsannyāsīs, who maintain the tradition of installing and worshipping Kālī according to Vedic ritual procedures.

Although records of thekhaṭa-jātrānote that Svāmī Lalitānanda was residing at this site prior to 1968 CE (2025 VS), no definitive historical evidence has yet been found regarding the original establishment of the Ādikālī Pīṭha or its founder.

An official document issued by the Guṭhī Saṃsthāna in 1938 CE (1995 VS) records alālamoharagranting Śrī 108 Lalitānanda Svāmī formal permission to reside at this sacred site (S. Maharjana 2082 VS, 72).

Following his death in 1968 CE (2025 VS), his disciples have continued to inhabit thekuṭī, conducting the daily worship (nityapūjā),ārati, and other ritual activities in accordance with the establishedguru–śiṣyalineage.

A significant transformation occurred in 1984 CE (2040 VS), when representatives of threeguthis based in Banthachā convened and entered into a written agreement to institute an annualkhaṭa-jātrāof Ādikālī.

The temple and its precincts have undergone continuous conservation and development through donations and collective efforts by local residents, individuals, and institutions across different periods.
In 1929 CE (1986 VS), local residents of Baniyā̃ Gāũ, together with Svāmī Lalitānanda, donated a bell to the goddess.

In 1986 CE (2042 VS), Naikap Ward No. 5 and Kāpikā Rānā Magara provided financial assistance for the purchase of images of Gaṇeśa, Ādikālī, and Bhairava, for the construction of a building to house the festival palanquins (khaṭa), and for the management of the annual procession, including the establishment of an endowment fund of NPR 15,000.
Further improvements to the temple and its surroundings were carried out in 1999 CE (2055 VS) with support from various organizations and individuals.
In 2004 CE (2060 VS), the Ādikālī Temple Area Construction and Conservation Committee completed major renovation works through donations collected from multiple locations and patrons.

In the most recent phase, in 2019 CE (2075 VS), additional financial contributions from institutions and individuals enabled the construction of a truss-supported structure with a copper roof, further strengthening and securing the temple complex.
The Mahādeva Sataḥ was erected during the Śāha-Rāṇā era, a time when such edifices along the banks of the Vāgamatī (the river Bagmati) were primarily commissioned by monarchs.
Resembling a residential dwelling, the Sataḥ today (2024 CE) stands in a severely dilapidated state.
Adjacent to the Sataḥ lies the Mahadev temple, its upper section has collapsed and is now sheltered by a temporary metal roof.
It appears that both the temple and the Sataḥ were erected concurrently.
Two Nevārī inscriptions are found within the Sataḥ.
One weathered inscription from 1834 CE (1891 VS) documents the establishment of a Mahāsnāna guṭhī for Śiva during the reign of King Rajendra Vikrama Śāha.
Another inscription records land donations in Bhaktapur by Satrubhañjana, potentially for the Sataḥ or the Śivālaya.
Both inscriptions mention land donations and guṭhī, though it remains unclear which one pertains to the construction of the Sataḥ.
Following the devastating earthquake of 1934 CE (VS 1990), immediate restoration efforts were undertaken the following year (Inventory VS 2039, p. 164).
Despite sustaining damages of the Gorkha earthquakes in 2015, reconstruction has yet to commence.
Degutale, also called Digutale, is the tallest monument building in the Patan Darbār Square.
The temple is built upon the solid masonry core of the ground floor and can be accessed from the first floor.
To reach it, one must climb the flight of stairs attached to the north wall and pass through a stone arch doorway built on the boundary wall.
A three-bayed colonnaded space to the east of the building leads to the open area known as Nāsala Coka.
A unique feature of this building is the slanting and projecting window that engirds the entire building on the third floor.
Above the windows, a flat balcony also encircles the building on the fourth floor.
On this level, one can find a golden door with atoraṇaabove it leading from the western side of the building out to the veranda.
A statue of a hovering Yoga Narendra Malla alongside a serpent, a bird, and his queens has been erected on a tall stone pillar facing the Taleju temple.
This can be found to the west of the building.
It seems that in the Malla period, Ṣaṣṭhīdevī was replaced by Degutale (Vajrācārya2033, 75).
Devamālā Vaṃśāvalī(see inYogī2013, 55) states that Śivasiṃha Malla took the advice of Lambakarṇa Bhatta and established this temple in 1584 (NS 704).
Other chronicles also suggest that Śivasiṃha Malla was the one to establish this temple.
It seems likely, therefore, that the king really was responsible for its construction.
However, the date that it was constructed is therefore unlikely to have been NS 704.
In NS 704, King Purandara Siṃha was ruling over Lalitpur, as mentioned in a colophon ofDurgāsaptasatīdated NS 717.
This source states that Śivasiṃha only began his rule in NS 718 (Śākya2008, 63).
In 1641 (NS 761), Śivasiṃha’s grandson Siddhinarasiṃha Malla reconstructed the temple as a five-storey building.
In 1663 (NS 783) the temple was destroyed by a fire and later reconstructed with four tiers by Śrīnivāsa Malla.
The temple then collapsed in the 1934 earthquake; by 1940 it had been reconstructed in its present form.
As such, the Department of Archaeology, Nepal has been taking care of its repair and maintenance.
Before 1934 earthquake, the temple had three tiers and was constructed in the style of a pagoda.
However, it was levelled by the earthquake and reconstructed in this mixed style.
At the southwest corner of the plinth, one can find a hanging bell that was donated in 2012.
A statue of Nandī (vehicle of Śiva) is in front of the temple, and a trident has been erected close to this icon.
The image of Sūrya (the Sun god) is a recreation of the archaic one, which was stolen some decades ago.
The stone inscription attached above the southern door of the temple mentions that the monument was reconstructed by Viśvambhara Bhāro in NS 796 (CE 1676) during the reign of King Śrīnivāsa Malla.

The inscription further informs readers that the King and his son Yoganarendra Malla were also present at the consecration of the temple, where lands were bestowed and aguṭhīwas established to fund its ritual worship However, these days noguṭhīlands connected to the temple could be traced.
In VS 2058, local people collected donations in order to try to continue the daily and other ritual worships of the temple.
However, the earthquake 2015 further hindered the daily worship.
This Sataḥ is theguthichẽ(association's house) of the Dhālāchẽ Pradhāns’.
Since Pradhāns’ are known as Pãmāe in Newari, this Sataḥ is known as the Pãmāe Guthichẽ.
There is no evidence that underlines the construction date of this Sataḥ.
However, an inscription on the ground floor of the building mentions that a man called Candravīrasiṃha Bhāro from Dhālāchẽ commissioned its construction.
In 1785 CE (NS 905) Macchindrasiṃha Bhāro, the son of Candravīrasiṃha Bhāro, renovated the Sataḥ, which was said to have been in a bad condition at that time.
He also donated threeropaniof land for its upkeep.
Similarly, during the Indrajātrā festival, when celebrated in the Nugaḥ Tola, a feast is to be organised for theguṭhīyārasandsamaybajiis to be donated.
As it is stipulated in the inscription, both these traditions continue to this day.
The rent from the shop is meant to sustain theguthi.
Matsyendra Singh Bharo also had various pious renovation works done in the Bal Kumari Mandira (LAL2000).
An inscription on the wall above the spout, dated 1939 CE (VS 1996), documents its renovation.
Due to its perceived benefits, a staff member was appointed to fetch two buckets of water daily for the palace until 1977 CE (VS 2034), according to a local resident, Ācārya (male, age 45).
There are no written records about the construction of the spout, only the inscription of its 1939 CE renovation.
The Bāniyā family continues to repair and maintain the spout, which remains a vital resource for the community.
Known as Phatyamukteśvara, thisśivālaya(lit. the dwelling of Śiva) was constructed in commemoration of Phatya (var. Fateh/Phateha/Phatte/Phatye) Śamśera Rāṇā by his sons in 1919 CE (VS 1976).
In 1919 CE (VS 1976), two sons of Phatya Śamśera Rāṇā undertook the construction of Phatyamukteśvara in memory of their father.
The bell inscription records the event but does not mention the names of his two sons.
Phatya Śamśera, the seventh among the 17 sons of Dhīra Śamśera, the youngest brother of Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā (Rāja VS 2071, p.86), was a close confidant of Prime Minister Deva Śamśera.
Alarmed by the prime minister’s liberal tendencies, Phatya Śamśera conspired with Candra Śamśera to remove Prime Minister Deva Śamśera from his office in 1901 CE (VS 1958).
He passed away in 1907 CE (Sever 1993, pp.227/467).
Twelve years after his demise, Phatya Śamśera’s two sons erected the temple in his honor.
The earthquakes in 2015 damaged the temple, and it was subsequently restored by the Pashupati Area Development Trust in 2019 CE (VS 2076).
Kāyegu Nani is a large square courtyard surrounded by residential buildings.
At the north-eastern corner of the temple is a shrine of Hāratī Ajimā, built in 1995.
To the west of the temple is a community building (maṅkāḥ chẽ) which, as of 2019, is under construction.
A recently built shrine to the east houses statues of Sarasvatī, Gaṇeśa and Bhairava.
Inside the Cīdhaṃ Nanī is asanāḥ guthi chẽ/capāḥ,and inside the Āgaṃ Nanī one can find ajinālaya caitya.
There is a two-and-a-half storey building called Maṇkaḥ Chen (a communal house for Maṇkaḥ Bhajan Khala) 7 m west of the temple, which is being rebuilt within the RCC system.
According to locals, all photographic evidence of the building has been lost, however the stone inscriptions that tell the story of its existence and lifespan are still safe.
Cīdaṅ Nani contains a 4-storey building called Capā.
This is a communal house for theguthiand for holding feasts.
Towards its north is a building which was rebuilt in VS 2047 in the loadbearing system.
RCC flat slabs have been used to construct its floor and roof.
The top two floors of this building are being rented out, while the lower floors are still used by locals to organise feasts and gatherings.
The main entry is to the west of the street, between rows of residential buildings and with an open space containing a Licchavi-eracaityain front.
A two-storey building covered in traditionaljhingatītiles forms the front façade of the entrance and exhibits three small latticed windows on its first floor.
The sunken courtyard measures 12.8 x 13.5 m (see site plan), and the main Bāhāḥ building is located on the west wing.
The main temple is attached to the courtyard buildings to the south and is open to its back and to the north.
Threecaitya-shaped finials stand on the top of the building.
These pinnacles were donated by Dhana Thakuṃ and her three sons Dhanacā Muni, Rāja Muni and Harṣa Muni in 1850 (Śākya2535, 86).
The courtyard has annex buildings on three sides, with the northern wing left free.
Alongside Co Bāhāḥ and Kipū Bāhāḥ, Si Bāhāḥ was added to the list of majorbāhasof Patan at a later date.
These images were established in 1982.
A book preserved in the Bāhāḥcontains collections of chants and mentions that this building once only had two storeys.
It seems, therefore, that the upper two storeys were added more recently (Śākya2535, 86).
The sanctum of the Bāhāḥ is located on the ground floor of the building.
The original image of Buddha was made of wood, but it was replaced with this stone image in 1678 due to deterioration.
Theāgamagharaof this Bāhāḥ lies to the east of the esoteric shrine, while residential buildings are located to the north.
Inscriptions provide information about the initial construction of the monastic building.
TheNepālikabhūpavaṃśāvalī(19.3.26) mentions that Si Bāhāḥ was built after King Siddhinarasiṃha Malla (r. 1620-1661) passed rules regarding the fifteenvihārasof Patan.
However, the information provided in the chronicle may be incorrect, since this Bāhāḥ is also mentioned in a colophon in thePañcarakṣāmanuscript copied in 1389 (NS 509) (Bendall1883, 191).
The main shrine building faces east and can be seen from the Phalcā.
The lattice work of these windows has partly been replaced by themāneprayer wheel.
The entire courtyard building is furnished with lattice windows on the first floor, and encircled by an overhanging balcony.
The lattice work and small central window of the balcony are interrupted at the southeast corner due to the new RCC building structure.
The balcony has also been damaged at the northwest corner.
The damaged north wing is now protected by two raking shores.
Within this courtyard, one can find aśikharakūṭa caitya, a statue of the donor, adharmadhātu maṇḍalaand avedīarranged on an east-west axis in front of the main shrine building.

In the northern wing of the Bāhāḥ one can find anotherpāsukhājhyāḥon the first floor, with a long wooden stick below it.Śākya(VS 2036, 40) mentions that the stick was used to support an umbrella which was unfurled in honour of Śrīnivāsa Malla when he was invited to thisbāhāḥ.
According to the copper inscription attached to the façade, Jothā Bāhāḥ was established by Yodhā in 1653 CE (NS 773).
Yodhā was the eldest son of Manikaju and the great grandson of Abhayarāja, who also established a shrine of Mahābuddha.
However, the members of the monastery believe that he was a sculptor who spent his earnings to establish this Bāhāḥ.
A water reservoir topped by astūpaand built in ŚS 1276 (1354 CE).
The monument is built in large blocks of hewn stone.
It is comparable to the stūpa engraved on the south side of the Kīrtikhambā stone memorial pillar (DLK0260-001), which was installed in ŚS 1279 (1357 CE).
The lintel of the door is of special importance as it contains the dated inscription of the reservoir's donor.
The inscription indicates that it was built in ŚS 1276 (1354 CE) by Deva Varmā (Andolfatto 2019, p. 96;Pant 2009, 301).
He is known for building another reservoir, also topped by a stūpa, in Kuchi (Achham district).
The text of the inscription also mentions that the reservoir is ornamented with five stūpa ("caityapaṃcakasaṃyuktā").
Their dismantling (if they were ever built) must have happened before the 1950's as the picture of the monument taken in 1954 by Giuseppe Tucci already shows a single stūpa (Tucci 1956, fig. 54).
It is unclear when the previous building was pulled down and rebuilt as a concrete structure, some local residents say the conversion took place in the 1980s.
Such a shrine is referred to asmaśiriin an inscription (KIR0001_I_20201010_06) at the Cilaṃcva Caitya in Kirtipur.
There are many examples of such small Sthānagaṇeśa shrines of stone constructed during the medieval period.
In the case of Sāḥgaḥ Gaṇeśa Phalcā, it can be assumed that it was constructed later, to 'host' the shrine.
There is an inscription dated 1750 CE (NS 870) on the Phalcā but possibly it does not refer to the site itself.

It records one Bhāgīsiṃha Bhāro (Amātya) and his younger brother Siddhisiṃha, both residents of Dathu ṭola in Kirtipur, to have commissioned aphalcāwith ajaḥdhuṃand enshrining statues of Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa and Trivikrama in the name of their father Manoharasiṃha.
It appears the inscription and the statue of Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa were shifted to Sāḥgaḥ Gaṇeśa Phalcā after the Mandaḥ Phalcā collapsed at some urecorded point in time.
Another statue of Trivikrama mentioned in the inscription can no longer be found in the area.
The inscription on the image states that Amṛta Nārāyaṇa and his five brothers had offered a golden image in 1847 CE (NS 967).
The details of theśivālaya's original construction remain unclear due to the absence of historical records.
Damaged in the 2015 earthquakes, the temple underwent renovation by the Pashupati Area Development Trust in 2019 CE (VS 2076).

As of February 2024, daily worship is conducted at the temple by a Brahmin from the Ḍhuṅgela caste, who also serves as the priest for the five nearbyśivālayas built by Dhīra Śamśera and his four wives.
In 1993, thebahīwas reconstructed as a plain RCC building with a flat concrete slab serving as its roof.
It shares this space with aśikharakūṭacaitya;this structure is located in front of the main building.

No documented evidence is available with which one could date the initial construction of thisbahī,though H.Vajrācārya(2000, 109) mentions that the founder of Khvāya Bahī Taḥdhaṅgu and Khvāya Bahī Cidhaṅgu were brothers.
A stone fountain from the 14th-15th centuryThe fountain is built on the eastern fringe of the village of Mānmā, 1 km south and down the hill of Mānmā-Khām̐ḍācakra, the Kalikot district headquarters.
Cement has been applied in areas were the stone facings were damaged.

The semi-circular arches are characteristic of the Rāṇā period, during which the gate was likely reconstructed, as evidenced by a 1970s photograph by Wolfgang Korn showing its Rāṇā-era form with a rounded, lime-plastered top similar to those found in Rāṇā palaces and temples.
A nearbyhiti(water spout) has Lichhavi-eracaityafragments, and a weathered early-medieval inscription was also found within its premises.
The original construction date and founder of this gate are uncertain, but it likely dates back to the medieval period, aligning with the concept of fortified cities and their gates.
According to an inscription attached to the gate, its most recent renovation occurred in 2011 CE (VS 2068).
Three inscriptions have been placed in the Phalcā, though none of them mention its initial construction.
Rather, they provide information about the renovations undertaken in 1698, 1937 and 2002.
The pillar was most likely relocated from a nearby location.
In any case, it is no longer in its original location, and it was leaning against the southernśikharain 2014 CE.
Before its discovery by David C. Andolfatto in 2014 CE, the site had never been studied.
Suchśikharatemples were erected throughout the Karnali Basin from the 13th to the 17th centuries in honour of war heroes (Andolfatto 2019: 105-119).

King Śrīnivāsa Malla rebuilt Mūla Coka in 1666 and it is clear that Taleju Mandira, a  pagoda-style three-tiered temple resting atop the south wing was built as an afterthought, when Mūla Coka and  Sundarī Coka were already established.
During Viṣṇumalla's reign in the 1730s major renovations and the reshaping of the palace building were carried out.
This included the installation of the Golden Door ensemble featuring life-sized statues of Gaṅgā and Yamunā and the donation of a gilt door andtoraṇa.
The 1934 earthquake caused the temple's complete collapse and the ensuing reconstruction efforts resulted in a poor quality reconstruction in which recycled materials were used.
The roofs were rebuilt with inadequate timber and had a much-reduced overhang.
Between 2006 and 2012, the Kathmandu Valley Preservation Trust carried out a comprehensive restoration programme.
Thanks to funding from a number of international organisations, the KVPT was able to restore the temple to its historic configuration.
This included reconstructing the roof in its correct design and providing the temple with a roof cover using handmade terracotta (jhĩgaṭī)tiles.
The top tier of Taleju Mandira South collapsed in the 2015 earthquake and fell on to the roofs below, causing considerable damage to the temple structure and the palace roof.

The reconstruction work done on the temple in 2016 and the recreation of the lost parts of the pinnacle is testament to the project's artistic excellence and clever use of innovative seismic strengthening techniques.
A buffalo is sacrificed and the meat is offered to Kumārī.
Constructed using cut stone blocks and mud masonry, the structure also incorporates reused carved blocks originating from medieval temples.
The inscription is very eroded.
Stone pillars were erected throughout the Karnali Basin from the 13th to the 17th century.
They are installed to honor the memory of deceased persons, mostly warriors.

Given the fact that stūpas are attested in the Karnali region between the mid-14th century and the early 16th century (Andolfatto 2019: 96-99), it is possible to propose that the Tātopānī pillar was erected during this time frame.

Referred to as Candramukteśvara, thisśivālaya(lit. the dwelling of Lord Śiva) was constructed in 1934 CE (VS 1990) in memory of Prime Minister Candra Śamśera Rāṇā, with the hope for his eternal peace.
Outside the temple, a bell from 1934 CE hangs from a bell stand south of the temple, commemorating its construction.
Additionally, a stone trident (triśūla) stands erected to the north of the temple, with a statue of Kāmadeva enshrined to the southeast.
Theśivālayawas established for the eternal peace of Prime Minister Rāṇā Candra Śamśera in 1934 CE (VS 1990) (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p. 347; Michaels and Tandon 2017, p. 106).
citations: (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p. 347; Michaels and Tandon 2017, p. 106)

text: A bell was also installed at the temple the same year (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2056, p. 655).
However, the exact contributors to the temple's establishment and the donation of the bell remain unclear from the bell inscription.
Born on July 8, 1863 CE (Āṣāḍha 26, VS 1920) (P. Rāṇā VS 2080, p. 27), Candra Śamśera was the son of Dhīra Śamśera and Nandakumārī.

Among the 17 sons of Dhīra Śamśera, Candra was the fifth son, who assumed the prime ministerial position in 1901 CE after displacing his elder brother Deva Śamśera by force (Landon 1928, p. 81-82; P. Rāṇā VS 2080, p. 14).
He passed away at the age of 66 years on December 14, 1928, in Singha Durbar (P. Rāja VS 2073, p. 185).
Theśivālayawas built approximately four years after his death.
The four other, smaller temples, are built one meter away from the central temple, facing its south, west, north and east facades.
The four pillars erected around the structure are richly carved by low-relief decorative motifs and representations of mediums (dhāmī) during oracular possessions (Andolfatto 2019).
Furthermore, the construction ofśikharatemples in the Karnali region seems to have stopped before the 16th century, which narrows the dating of this type of plan down to the 14th-15th century.
Furthermore, wooden images are installed on the beams (nināḥ) over each bay.
There used to be a two-storey wooden tower (pula)on top of the sanctum as can be seen in photos taken before the Great Earthquake of 1934.
The tower collapsed in the 1934 earthquake and was never rebuilt.
An inscription, dated 1683 CE (NS 803), posted on the wall of thephalcā records its construction.
It was constructed during the reign of King Jitāmitra Malla by his younger brother Ugra Malla and and son Bhupatindra Malla along with minister Duḥkhi Bhāgirāma (Gutschow2011, p. 645).
Impressed by the construction of the phalcā and its shrines the king enforced a new system regarding irrigation canals to facilitate the farmers of Bhaktapur.
A few bays and thepulaon the eastern section of this phalcā can be seen in a painting byHenry AmbroseOldfieldfrom 1854 CE.
A portion of the 27-bayed section of thephalcācollapsed in the 2015 earthquakes.
It was reconstructed by the Department of Archaeology in 2020 CE.
Noguthirelated to thephalcā exists and the daily worship at the shrines of Bhagavatī andśivaliṅgahas been discontinued.
They were removed in the 1990s by the Municipality stating that they disturbed the ambiance of the palace square (local knowledge, local resident, Śarmā, male, age 69).
citations: (local knowledge, local resident, Śarmā, male, age 69)

text: Before the construction of the Ring Road, this gate likely served as a primary city entrance, granting access to the Paśupati area.
However, over time, this arch may have collapsed and never been rebuilt.
In Newar settlements, it was customary to constructdhvākhāat various points along the boundary walls encircling the city outskirts.
Nevertheless, the exact date of its construction remains unclear, as historical sources do not document this event.

The gate underwent reconstruction by the Kathmandu Municipality's Ward No. 8 office in 1996 CE (VS 2052) (PPK1231_I_001), and the metal arch on top was added during another reconstruction in 2018 CE (VS 2074) (PPK1231_I_002).
After circumambulating the Tāmreśvara Mandira (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p. 532), the palanquin is finally taken to the western gate of the Paśupatinātha Temple, where the procession ends.

The middle jaḥdhuṃ in this case contains an early medieval inscription indicating its installation by Ajasiṃha during the reign of Mahāsāmanta Jaitarāmajīva under King Bhīmadeva in 1260 CE (NS 381) (D. Vajrācārya VS2068, p. 136-137).
The inscription does not mention a dharmaśāla or the phalcā itself, suggesting that the jaḥdhuṃ was installed first, with the phalcā being added several centuries later.
Pharpiṅga Jaḥduṃ Phalcā was renovated in 2013 (2070 VS) by the Department of Archaeology.
Built by Maṇiratna Vajrācārya of Musuṃ Bāhāḥ after having separated from his ownbāhāḥ, Mikhā Bāhāḥ was reconstructed in 2022 CE (VS 2078).
This north-facing bāhāḥ has a four-story main building (dyaḥchẽ).
Around 1988 CE (VS 2045), after the old Akṣobhya statue was stolen, a new statue was installed (bāhāḥmember, Vajrācārya, male, age 50).

Maṇiratna Vajrācārya, a former member of Musuṃ Bāhāḥ (KAT2540), established Mikhā Bāhāḥ as a separate entity, choosing the name Maṇisaṃgha Mahāvihāra, which mirrored the Sanskrit name of his formerbāhāḥ(P. Vajrācārya NS 1144, p. 253).
Among thebāhāḥ's inscriptions, one from 1683 CE (NS 803) records the name as “Mṛkhā Bāhāḥ” (Locke 1985, p. 334).
This inscription is believed to be the copperplate, bearing the name of Pārthivendra Malla, that P. Vajrācārya (2000, p. 107) referenced, but it has unfortunately been lost.
Likewise, the inscription documenting the 1866 CE renovation (Locke 1985, p. 334) is also no longer extant.

A rest house on the eastern side of the Rānīdarabāra Coka in Dolakhā was built by Nalindramuni (Narendramuni) Vajrācārya of Mikhā Bāhāḥ, along with his wife and family members in 1792 CE (NS 913) (D. Vajrācārya and Ṭ. Śreṣṭha VS 2031, pp. 125-126).
citations: (D. Vajrācārya and Ṭ. Śreṣṭha VS 2031, pp. 125-126)

text: Thedharmadhātujinālayacaityain thebāhāḥcourtyard was established in 1918 CE (NS 1038).
Puruṣaratna, abāhāḥmember, and his family, including his brother Sudharatna, built thecaityaand renovated the Aśoka Caitya while also laying traditional floor tiles in the courtyard.
Reconstructed after the 2015 earthquakes with Kathmandu Metropolis funding, thebāhāḥwas inaugurated by Mayor Vidyāsundar Shākya in 2022 CE.
Prior to reconstruction, a painting of thepañcabuddhadeities withyoginīs on either side adorned the first-floor (P. Vajrācārya NS 1144, p. 256).
This painting was not reproduced during the renovation.
The monument is built on a recently made platform constituted of roughly cut stones and cement.
The tower was recently rebuilt, as is indicated by traces of cement between stone blocks.

A stone lion, probably contemporaneous to building activity at the site (13th-15th century) is found lying in the ground north of the temple. it may have been installed on top of a temple's pediment, or in front of a door.
This formerly traditional Sataḥ was demolished and converted into a five-storey concrete building in 2018.
This building has a veneer and molded bricks, and the Sataḥ now constitutes a small part of the ground floor.
After its renovation in 2008, the Sataḥ (which belongs to the  “32 Pāneju Saṃgha”) was leased out to a person from a Vaidya caste under a contract of twenty years.
No inscription could be found to provide any further information about the Sataḥ and its origins.

The ground floor is divided in three rooms, a kitchen (in the veranda space), a room containing thedhunifire with where the temple'smahantperforms rituals and room with beds for the priests in charge of the Jvālā Ghar (DLK0331).
According to local informants the monument was built in 1943 CE (1999 VS).
It is believed that Dolakhā Bhīmasena, a powerful deity, prefers not to be sheltered (D. Vajrācārya and Ṭ Śreṣṭha VS 2059, p. 6).
citations: (D. Vajrācārya and Ṭ Śreṣṭha VS 2059, p. 6)

text: Despite this belief, and although this Bhīmasena is also worshipped as Dolakhā Bhīmasena, a roof has been constructed here.
Aniconic stones representing the lineage deities of various communities are installed around the shrine.
While no inscription documents the shrine's founding, several artifacts suggest the area's antiquity.
A Varāha statue located just west of the shrine is believed to date from the fifth or sixth century (P. Śreṣṭha VS 2080, p. 491).
The proximity of Jagāti, likely an ancient toll collection point for traders (P. Śreṣṭha VS 2080, p. 829), further supports the area's historical significance and Bhīmasena's connection to trade.
The spot where he rested became sacred, and a shrine was erected, known thereafter as Dolakhā Bhīmasena (shrine caretaker, Vādyakāra, male, age 57).
However, no inscriptions predating the Rāṇā period have been discovered at the shrine.
The earliest inscription found here dates to 1855 CE (VS 1912) and records the installation of a statue of Tanasiṃ.
Even today, relatives of those abroad believe that worshipping Bhīmasena will bring swift news of their loved ones' well-being and ensure their safe return (P. Śreṣṭha VS 2080, pp. 821-822).
These twośivālayas are built on the same plinth, suggesting they were built at the same time.
It was recovered during an excavation in the area circa 2019 CE (VS 2076).
The history behind the initial construction of the temple is unclear due to the lack of historical sources.
Michaels and Ṭaṇḍana (2017, p. 70) and Taṇḍaṇa (VS 2053, p. 739) have identified the temple as Prakāśeśvara without mentioning the source for the information.
Usually, the donor of such temples also installed a bell at the site, recording the event.
The family also sets a bonfire every year onŚivarātrī, the 14th of the dark fortnight of Phālguna, and offers food items to locals and visitors as gifts (prasāda) from the deity.
A special worship is performed at the temple premises with fire rituals on the 12th of the bright fortnight of each month.
No reliable information could be garnered regarding the building's history and its date of construction.
However, it is very similar in size and style to a mansion in Phaplu that was built in the first decade of the 20th century.
She married young and established a new household with her husband on the west side of Junbesi.
The Calākhu Dabū is one of the five historic elevated platforms (dabūs) constructed at separate locations of Sankhu.

monument_name: Bhurtī group of three śikharas (13th-15th cent.)
text: It seems that the central temple was rebuilt, as indicated by numbers marked on the stone masonry.
There are no historical sources to date the initial construction of the Phalcā.

The designs of the pillar and the carving of Kṣepu at the center of the two Methas suggest that these parts of the Phalcā date back to the end of the Malla period (ca. the 18th century) when this Phalcā was probably constructed.
Probably, the Phalcā was rebuilt back then.
The Phalcā suffered damages in the 2015 earthquakes.
The Siṃha family funded its reconstruction in 2017 CE.
An inscription installed after the reconstruction mentions that Miśrī Devī, together with her family, rebuilt the Phalcā in memory of her husband Cakramāna Siṃha.
The site comprises a dozen of structures, including fortification walls and buildings of various shapes.
According to Ram Niwas Pandey the fortress was built by the Doṭiyali king Niraṅjanapāla, also known as Niraipāla, of the Rainka dynasty (Pandey 1997: 171).
This king is known from inscriptions dated between 1352 CE and 1362 CE.
He also erectedśikharatemples to the east of the fortified area.
Dilli Raj Sharma reports that the fortress was destroyed in 1685, during a war opposing the kingdom of Doṭi with Kumaon (Sharma 2012: 318-321).
The site had at least two phases of occupations, as indicated by the re-used construction material visible in the quadrangular tower (DDL0180-004).
Most of the buildings have been dismantled, probably to be re-used for construction by nearby inhabitants.
There are no historical records available to date the initial construction of the temple.
It is believed that Manorathasiṃha Māske, who was childless, built the temple and enshrined theśivaliṅga.
Unfortunately, some statues from the upper floor pavilion have been stolen.
The temple was taller in its original form before it was destroyed by the earthquake of 1934 CE (VS 1990).
The height was reduced in the subsequent reconstruction process.
As of December 2022 CE, the temple has been coated with black enamel, and the pillars andtoraṇaat the entrance to the sanctum have been painted with golden enamel.
Theśivaliṅgarepresents Santāneśvara, a form of Śiva believed to bestow the boon of offspring (cf., K. Śreṣṭha VS 2044, p. kha).
The Māske clan still operates aguthi, and they perform anniversary and other rituals at the temple, using a few plots of endowed land as a source of income (see, ‘social religious events’ below).

However, following the decision of the Kathmandu Metropolitan City to displace all street vendors in 2022 CE, certain activities such as cleaning the temple and various annual worship events have been discontinued.
A fire ritual (homa) is performed every day in the Agnimaṭha, as isŚuklayajurvedīyatradition.
The fire for the ritual is produced by rubbing two pieces of wood together, and it is kept aflame for a long time.
If the fire at any of thesemaṭhais extinguished, it must be replenished by fire brought from the Agnimaṭha of Vajrayoginī.
Similarly, the fire of the Vajrayoginī Agnimaṭha may only be replaced by fire from this Agnimaṭha.
The fire ritual at Vijeśvarī Agnimaṭha came to an end around 1966 (Śreṣṭha N.2013, 7).
However, a Vedic fire ritual is still performed daily at the Agnimaṭha of Patan.
Witzel(1992, 779-780) claims that this Agnimatha is the only place across the whole Indian subcontinent where this three thousand year old fire ritual is still observed.
During the daily fire worship, the public make offerings and can observe the ritual through this door.
There are five fire altars (agnikuṇḍas) made from unbaked bricks (kaccī apā) and mud on the ground floor.
The fire burns continuously in this altar.
Kīrtipatākā(verse 23), a long poem composed by Kunu Śarmā in 1652, describes the fire ritual that takes place in this shrine.
An inscription from 1403 (NS 523) provides the earliest recorded mention of the monument.
The latticework at the opening to the north is still intact, while the latticework on the east and west openings has been lost and replaced by metal grill works.
According to an inscription mentioned in an unpublished record by Heimo Rau, the temple was built in 1727 CE.

Lettering in Devanāgarī script has been inscribed on the fringes of two upper floors, and informs readers of the name of the temple (Koṭarākṣa Bhairava) and of its renovation in (1904 CE (NS 1024). On top of the first roof in the sanctum is a stone image of Bhairava.The struts:East, 1st floor: Bhairava, Maheśvarī, Bhairava, Brahmayāṇī; 2nd floor: Brahmayāṇī, Indrayāṇī; 3rd floor: Bhairava, BhairavaSouth, 1st floor: Bhairava, Vaiṣṇavī, Bhairava, Kaumārī; 2nd floor: Varāhī, Vaiṣṇavī; 3rd floor: Bhairava, BhairavaWest, 1st floor: Bhairava, Indrayāṇī, Bhairava, Varrāhī; 2nd floor: Kaumārī, Cāmuṇḍā; 3rd floor: Bhairava, BhairavaNorth, 1st floor: Bhairava, Bhagavatī, Bhairava, Cāmuṇḍa; 2nd floor: Bhagavatī, Maheśvarī; 3rd floor: Bhairava, BhairavaOn thetoraṇaabove the main door, one can find a Bhairava statue (constructed in brass in NS 1033) flanked by Gaṇeśa and Kumāra inālīḍhaandpratyālīḍhapostures on either side. There are carved wooden windows facing in all four directions on the two upper floors, and in three directions on the first floor. Images of various deities have been carved on the struts (ṭũḍālas). Statues of two sitting lions have been placed on both sides of the main entrance, and behind the two lion statues are two brass banners. A bell is hanging to the left of the main entrance, upon which the date of its donation (NS 1033 /1913 CE) is inscribed. Eight auspicious signs (aṣṭamaṅgalas) have been carved on the stone beam that supports the bell. There are images of mice on both sides of the beam and an image of Jvālānhāyakaṃ in the middle. A Kavã and Khyāḥ have recently been added to the walls to the main entrance on the left- and right-hand side respectively. Oil lamps, heightened and supported by a wooden structure, surround the temple in a row. On the western plinth of the temple is an image of Umāmaheśvara. Next to this image are two inscriptions. Aliṅgahas been established on the northern side of the temple.The main sanctum is below ground level, almost 110 cm below the main entry level, and can be accessed via stone steps. A metal stair with a handrail was added recently. The main deity is in its non-iconic form, and sits in a niche framed by a metal repousse. The east wall has a niche with a hole exactly above the shrine (dyaḥpvaḥ), allowing the unhindered circulation of unspecified spirits. The sanctum has stone flooring; the space in front of the main entrance (approx. 470 cm x 235 cm) is stone-paved. There is a stone slab showing a carved human body (in a prostrate form, ormhadanā vanegu) and a circular lotus leaf (padmapatra) in line with the main entrance. All the floors have carved windows on each side.Exactly behind the temple, to the north, is a square sunken pit with a width of 70cm on each side, and a depth of 30cm. This has aliṅga. Almost half of the pit is below the plinth level.
The name derives from the fact that it was constructed for bhajans dedicated to goddess Tripurasundarī.
Because of leakage during the rainy season, the roof has been covered with plastic (2025 CE).
No historical record providing information about the construction of this Sataḥ has been found.
The oldest inscription discovered here is a stone inscription from CE 1742 (NS 862), but it does not appear to be related to the construction of the Sataḥ.
This is confirmed by the carving of Bālakumārī along with the text “Śrī Śrī Śrī Bārakumāli (Bālakumārī)” at the top of the inscription.

The inscription records that a group of residents living around the pond in Codo ṭola of Thimi settlement, where Kvarakhu Bālakumārīdevī is enshrined, collectively built a hiti and aphalcāat the very place of Codo.

In CE 1910 (NS 1030), Cakravira, a resident of Tulāchẽ ṭola in Bhaktapur, together with his wives Cidhi Thakuṃ and Hari Thakuṃ, installed a statue of Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa (BKT0770-002) on the ground-floor wall.
To ensure the daily worship of Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa and the annual ritual, the donor also endowed land as a guṭhi.
In 1976 CE (VS 2033), the Sataḥ was renovated (Bhavana ra Āvāsa tathā Śaharī Vikāsa Vibhāga VS 2048, p. 100).

text: Tripurasundarī Sataḥ was once equipped with a statue of Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa installed in 1910 CE (NS 1030).
The Nāsaṃdyaṃ (BKT0770-005) installed in the Sataḥ is the Nāsaṃdyaṃ of Tulāchẽ ṭola.

The Gaṇeśa (BKT0770-006) installed in theSataḥis the Gaṇeśa of Tulāchẽ ṭola, and as the local Gaṇeśa, it has been customary that before celebrating any life-cycle ritual such as birthdays, the rice-feeding ceremony (pāsni),vratabandha, orBhīmarathārohaṇa,the very first worship must be performed here.
Notoraṇais installed above the doorway leading into the sanctum (garbhagṛha).
In front of the temple stand two images of Nandin, while to the rear are installed a figure of Hanumāna and aśivaliṅga.
No historical records directly documenting the original construction of this temple have yet been identified.
Local tradition holds that the Licchavi king Dharmadeva relocated this cremation ground, and elderly residents continue to refer to the site as Dharmathalī, associating it with the king.

Even today, among the Jyāpu communities of northern Hāḍīgāũ, it remains customary during funeral processions to pause briefly with the deceased to the west of the Dhanvantari site, suggesting that the surrounding area was once amaśānalater moved elsewhere (S. Tivārī 2023, p. 87).

During the reign of King Śivasimha Malla, in 1589 CE (NS 709), the goddess is said to have warned the people of Hāḍīgāũ that she was about to be swept away by the Bagmatī River, but her warning went unheeded.
The residents of Lalitpur retrieved the image from the river and installed it at the place where it was found.
From that time onward, the goddess remained on the banks of the Bagmatī in Lalitpur, having cursed the people of Hāḍīgāũ (Yogī Naraharinātha, VS 2013, p. 73).
Repentant, the inhabitants of Hāḍīgāũ later commissioned a new image of Vārāhī and installed it in their own temple.
The image presently enshrined is therefore a relatively recent one, the earlier image having been stolen several decades ago.
The earliest inscription presently associated with the temple dates to 2010 CE (VS 2067).
It records that Haribhakta Buḍhāthokī offered a bell (ghaṇṭā) to the temple in memory of his late parents, Sanaksiṃha Buḍhāthokī and Bhagavatī Buḍhāthokī.

As the earlier temple structure had fallen into disrepair, a complete reconstruction was undertaken in 2012 CE (VS 2069) through the initiative of the Hāḍīgāũ Sampadā Samāja, with the cooperation of local residents and the Kathmandu Metropolitan City.
The temple is built in thelatina nāgaramode.
This affiliation is probably dur to the magnificient, although damaged movable image of Viṣṇu (001).
The temple is built on the same layout as theśikharain Devala Hāṭa (BTD0030) and may be approximately dated from the 14th-15th century.
Stone pillars were erected throughout the Karnali Basin from the 13th to the 17th century.
They are installed to honor the memory of deceased persons, mostly warriors.
The inscription found on the eastern side of the pillar is lacunary.
One may nevertheless read the date of 1261, which, if in the Śāka era, would correspond to 1339 CE.
This dating is in conformity with other inscribed pillars in the Dullu area (the date was misread inAndolfatto 2019: 108).
The inscribed section of the object is eroded by metal tool sharpening on the left and right sides.
The northwest-southeast orientation of the temple follows that of the hill slope along which it is built.

While the Karnali's oracular practices could be traced from at least the 14th-15th century (Andolfatto 2019: 201-254), the antiquity of the Rugā Maṣṭā Temple is difficult to establish as it was most probably rebuilt over time.
Built during the early Rāṇā period, the rest house has been in ruins for a long time with only the base and a portion of the rear wall remaining.
The surviving portion of the resthouse' wall contains an inscription recording its construction in 1836 CE (NS 955).
It was built by the Aṣṭamī Sevā Samiti, a group of devotees from the Svayambhū area in Kathmandu.
A photo by Richard Darsie from 1965 CE shows thephalcāwith its roof still intact.
It is in poor condition due to the lack of timely renovations (as of April 2022 CE).
Manycaityas of this form, in the Kathmandu Valley, date back to the late medieval period, but there are no historical records to determine when the DevāḥCā Vajradhātu Caitya was constructed.
Unlike many other monastic courtyards, there is no large independent shrine building here.
Instead, the present form of thebāhāḥconsists of a narrow room on the ground floor of a residential house where the principal deity, an image of Akṣobhya, is installed asKvāḥpā Dyaḥ.
Anāgaṃdyaḥis installed there, and rituals associated with theāgaṃare still actively performed (the owner of the house, Śākya, male, age 63).
On the western side of the courtyard, in the ground floor of an east-facing residential building, there is an entrance doorway surmounted by a brasstoraṇa.
Inside the doorway, a stone image of Akṣobhya is installed on a stone pedestal.
According to members of the local Śākyasaṃgha, the image of Akṣobhya installed here asKvāḥpā Dyaḥbelongs to the Rāṇā period.
During that time, Buddharatna Śākya installed the image and added the brasstoraṇaabove the entrance.
This installation took place on the occasion of the marriage of his son Bhairavkara (one of the members of the Śākyasaṃgha, male, age 69).
At Ratnākara Bāhāḥ an inscription recording construction activities dated to 1924–25 (VS 1981) has been discovered.
It therefore appears likely that Ratnākara Śākya and his contemporary Buddharatna Śākya established the twobāhāḥat approximately the same time.
The residential building that contains thebāhāḥon its ground floor originally belonged to a member of the monasticsaṅgha.
As the image of Akṣobhya was regarded as an ancestral installation, the householder who belonged to thesaṅghaactively maintained the daily worship and care of the shrine.
After the building was eventually sold, however, the ritual activities and cultural practices once associated with the site gradually declined.
Until 2002–03 (VS 2059), during the lifetime of Bhairavkara Śākya, the annual worship (varṣavardhana) of the bāhāḥ was performed annually on the day of Śrīpañcamī.
Sitauated in Nālāchāpa, a hilly area on Bhaktapur’s eastern border, this pond is a small, fully stone-built structure that is rare in such hilly terrain.

The pond’s construction date is unclear, but it presumably predates thehitiandsataḥbuilt by Subbā Pṛyavarta, Priyalakṣmī, and Ratnabahādura Thāpā on Akṣaya Tṛtīyā, the 3rd of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha in 1851 CE (VS 1908).
The inscription recording the construction of thehitiandsataḥmandates trust land’s income used for feeding brahmins and distributing sherbet.
Over time, thesataḥcollapsed, thehitidried up, and the pond nearly vanished.
In 2024 CE (VS 2081), Changunarayan Municipality restored the structures, adding a Śiva statue, along with his vehicular mount Nandī, and a Hanumān statue donated by Kedārabahādura Thāpā’s family.
As of May 2025, the traditional water flow system has collapsed, leaving thehitidry.

It is assumed that the term "Gāthā" refers to "cattle shed," and there’s an example from a Malla period inscription where the word "Goṭha" (cattle shed) is inscribed as "Gvāṭha (Malla 2000, p. 97)." Gāthādyaḥ is traditionally worshipped when cows, buffalos, goats, and sheep are pregnant.
An inscription at Gāthādyaḥ Phalcā mentions that it was built by a member of the Jyāpu community, a Harisiddhi resident, in 1780 CE.
The inscription also records the existence of a Gaṇeśa statue from an earlier period.
Gāthādyaḥ Phalcā was built during the reconstruction of the Gaṇeśa temple and the inscription also mentions the establishment of the Yosiṃ guṭhī (Indradhvaja guṭhī).
It seems likely that members of the same community that also celebrates Indrajātrā in Harisiddhi was responsible for building the phalcā.
Although Gāthādyaḥ Phalcā survived the 2015 earthquakes it was in a rather dilapidated state until the Lalitpur Metropolis reconstructed it in 2023 CE (2080 VS).
Ālko Gaṇeśa Mandira was built in 1704 CE and is located in the Ālko Hiti complex (LAL0990) at Ikhāchẽ, Patan.
A stone statue of Nandī is installed in front of the temple and a stone statue of Gaṇeśa is consecrated in its sanctum.
The temple was built by Yaśovanta Siṃha Raghuvaṃśa in 1704 CE (NS 824).
A group of six people donated twenty silver coins namedmahendra mallīin 1755 CE (NS 875).
An individual named Bhavānī Rāotta (Rāuta) Raghuvaṃśa and his wife offered a golden pinnacle to the temple in 1864 CE (NS 984).
The temple was renovated in 2017 CE (VS 2074) with the financial support of thirty lakhs rupees from the Lalitpur Metropolitan City.
Some of the old struts were restored during the renovation.
It has not been formally inaugurated yet (April 2021), although the renovation is already completed.
An inscription dating NS 787 (1667 CE) records Guṇasiṃha Bhāro offering one statue of lion to the goddess while theSaṃkrantiGuthidonating the other one (Vajrācārya2056, p. 145).
There are no historical sources to date the initial construction of the Temple.
However, its art and architecture suggest us that the Temple must have been built during the later medieval period.
The 2015 earthquakes caused considerable damages to the inner part of the Temple.
Therefore, locals together with the Department of Archaeology rebuilt it from the foundation up in its former structure.
The reconstruction began in 2019 CE and completed in 2021 CE.
The worn-out old struts were replaced by new ones.
Large tiles laid on the roof were also replaced by traditionalā̃ypātiles.

text: A pair of lions donated in NS 1028 (1908 CE) stand in front of the Gaṇeśa image and guard the site, whilst and a bell donated in NS 1016 (1896 CE) has been placed on the right corner of the Phalcā.

text: A pair of rats made of metal has been installed in front of the Gaṇeśa shrine (rats are considered to be Gaṇeśa's avatar).

text: The inscription found there informs us that it was renovated during the festivities celebrating King Vīrendra Śāha's 23rd year of his reign with the help of Department of Archaelogy, and the Nepal and German Governments.
This Bāhāḥ is located in Ikāchẽ Ṭola and is a private Bāhāḥ founded in 1678 (NS 798) by Bekhādeva Vajrācārya, a member of the Ikāchẽ Bāhāḥ (LAL0950).
Corrugated zinc sheets cover the roof of the building, which is supported by plain struts, and acaitya-shaped cement pinnacle surmounts it.

The upper storey of the building has a triple opening window in the center which is flanked by two ordinary windows. (Locke1985, 50) mentions that there was a repouseetoraṇadepicting the Buddha, Dharma and Saṅgha above this window.
The sanctum sanctorum of the monastic building is located on the ground floor and houses a statue of Akṣobhya.
A pair of stone lions flank the stairs leading to the sanctum, and a woodentoraṇashowing an image of Akṣobhya and the Five Buddhas has been installed above the entrance.
The Caitya was consecrated before the foundation of the Bāhāḥ and renovated in 1657.
The three-story building, constructed in traditional Newar style, faces north.
Pruscha (1975, p. 259) refers to thedyaḥchẽas "Nyākucā Mahādeva" and notes its renovation in 1951 CE.
While the exact date of its initial construction remains unknown, the woodentoraṇaabove the entrance suggests a medieval origin.

Thedyaḥchẽsuffered minor damage during the 2015 earthquakes but was renovated in 2022 CE through the collective efforts of the local government and community members (temple priest, Maharjan, male, age 65).
On Śivarātrī, the 14th night of the dark fortnight of Phālguna, a bonfire is lit in front of thedyaḥchẽ.
The main sanctum is built on the monastic building of the Subāhāḥ and makes use of the southeastern corner of the ground floor, which is plastered with lime.
Curved bricknāgvaḥand plastering have been used to construct the base of the sanctum's door.
However, this name seems problematic: the stone inscription attached to thedharmadhātumaṇḍalaclearly calls it Puṇyacandra.
Thebāhāḥwas constructed by Puṇyarāja Śākya, who had three daughters but no sons.
After establishing thebāhāḥin NS 1062 (1942) and after the ritual worship of the Dvādaśa Tīrtha and Aṣṭavaitarāga Tīrtha, his wife bore three sons.
RS 50 was expended for the construction of thekvāḥpāḥdyaḥand RS 100 was spent on thedharmadhātumaṇḍala.
The woodentoraṇainstalled above the entrance of thedyaḥchẽshows an image of Akṣobhya.
Underneath it, one can find an inscription.
This Śiva temple and the nearby rest house, built by Śyāmasiṃha Thāpā, received land grants from Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa Śāha to set up a religious trust in 1769 CE (ŚS 1691).
The trust was later retained by Prime Minister Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā in in 1874 CE (VS 1931).
Two Nandī statues are established in front of the temple.
This temple was built by Śyāmasiṃha Thāpā.
It is likely that he built a rest house (pāṭī) before constructing the temple.

The place became famous as Śyāmapāṭī due to the rest house built by Śyāmasiṃha Thāpā, and later, after the construction of the Śiva temple at the same place, it came to be known as Śyāmapāṭī Śiva temple.
The dates of construction of the rest house and the temple are unknown.

The inscription from 1769 CE (ŚS 1691) found attached to the rest house mentions that Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa Śāha had granted land parcels with an annual produce of 40murīs of crop in Nepālavyāsī to set up a religious trust for the Śyāmapāṭī Śiva temple.

Since Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa Śāha is referred to as "Śrī5" in this inscription, it seems that this inscription was installed during the Rāṇā period, retaining the old text. Śāha kings used the "Śrī5" title only after the Rāṇās took “Śrī3” title, which was previously used for the Śāha kings.
This inscription shows that the rest house and the Śiva temple were already built during the time of Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa Śāha.
In 1874 CE (VS 1931), Prime Minister Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā retained the 40murī-land trust that Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa Śāha had granted for the Śyāmapāṭī Śiva temple.
One of Jaṅga Bahādura’s daughters, Badana Kumārī (Magarnī Maiyā̃), was married to Gajarāja, who started tea cultivation in Ilam (B. Bhandari VS 2071, p. 145).
Gajarāja Thāpā's name was also included in the list of those who agreed to the Mulukī Ain (National Code) issued in 1854 CE (VS 1910) (Kānūna Tathā Nyāya Mantrālaya VS 2022, p. 5).

Since it is mentioned as “62sāla” in thelālamohāra, it is possible that the land of Śyāmapāṭī Śiva temple was also confiscated by Raṇa Bahādura Śāha in 1805 CE (VS 1862), and Jaṅga Bahādura may have returned the same land to retain the trust.

In 2022 CE (VS 2078), the Department of Archeology reconstructed the Śiva temple (NMB0010-009) located southeast of the temple and the rest house located south of the temple.Śyāmasiṃha Thāpā built the rest house and the Śiva temple together to provide accommodation for travelers going to Kathmandu from Sindhuli and Ramechhap.
He also endowed land parcels to set up a religious trust for worship and upkeep of these structures.
Paddy used to come from Sindhuli for the temple's worship, and firewood used to come from 300ropanīs of forest named Karṇela Vana (lit. Colonel's Forest) in Ḍā̃ḍāgāũ in Dhulikhel Municipality.
Every year onŚivarātrī, a large lamp is lit and a sacred fire is ignited, and the next day, brahmins are brought in to perform theekādaśarudrī, a recitation dedicated to Rudra or Śiva.
It was a tiered temple of one story, but a pipal tree started growing around the Temple, eventually enveloping it and completely damaging the temple structure.
In 2004, a statue of Amoghasiddhi was installed southwest of the Temple by two local groups named ‘Bhagavāna Buddha Palisthā Samiti’ and ‘Sāymi Dabū’.
No records are available to date the initial construction of the Temple now hidden inside the tree.
Historical chronicles mention King Ānandadeva founding Bhaktapur in 1096 CE (Kaligata Era 4197) and surrounding it with the Aṣṭamātṛkā deitypīṭhas.
However, precise dating of thesepīṭhas' establishment remains uncertain due to the lack of historical sources.
On the last day of Caitra, her chariot is taken to Yaḥsĩkhyaḥ, where the statue is placed at the Pīṭha for worship, accompanied by animal sacrifices and fire oblations.
Bhansāra Mandaḥ Phalcā, constructed during the late Malla period, has been largely neglected and unreconstructed due to ongoing disputes about a possible state-initiated road expansion.

This area is called Bhansāra ṭola because it is centrally located along the route where customs (bhansāra) used to be collected, and the arcaded platforms built on the edge of this settlement seem to have been constructed for this purpose.
Above Maṃgahiti, there are two Mandaḥ phalcās, one of which was reconstructed during the reign of Yoganarendra Malla.
An inscription mentions that the Mandaḥ phalcās of Pulchowk and Kirtipur were built during his time.
This type of phalcā is referred to as Maṇḍapa in the inscription, and it can be assumed that this one was built in the same period.
It is speculated that a goddess (devi) statue should have been installed here, though elderly locals claim that this has never been the case, nor have their ancestors ever mentioned it.
In 1968 CE (VS 2024), the tall and open Phalcā was used as Motī Library to store books, with its columns covered for this purpose.
In 2023 CE (VS 2079), two thefts occurred, and three statues were stolen from a nearby Caitya (CHG0070).
Nāsaḥdyaḥ is represented by three niches made on the eastern wall of the room inside the building.
There used to be a nicely carvedtoraṇaatop the door, but it was stolen sometime in 2006 CE (VS 2063).
A shrine for thehiphaḥdyaḥ(a deity who demands blood sacrifice) is established on the northern side of thedyaḥchẽ.
Thetoraṇaplaced atop this shrine too was stolen sometime ago.

There are some inscriptions in the Nāsaḥ Chẽ premises, but only two of them, recording the tradition of thedāphā bhajanachanting and theatre training, are related to this monument, one from 1769 CE (NS 889) and 1770 CE (NS 890).
Rest of the inscriptions belongs to the Mahālakṣmī Temple.

The space of this moment building is used by the local community to store the buffalo sacrificed in the Mahālakṣmī Pīṭha (located north of Balambu) during the Mahālakṣmī procession which takes place on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Kārtika.
It is kept here until the members of theguṭhīof the Duvāḥ clan living in Balambu come and take it away (Śreṣṭha VS 2074,21).
The Bāhāḥ consists of a small courtyard with a main sanctum building at its center.
Aśikharakūṭa caitya(180cm high), adharmadhātu maṇḍala(55cm high) and a bell can be found in front of the sanctum building, i.e. to its west.
The courtyard is surrounded by tall buildings on all sides.
This building has timber posts at each of its corners and has been built usingdāciapā.
In 2001, Aṣṭarāja Śākya donated funds to replace the old tiled roof with a RCC slab.
He established this Bāhāḥ in 1845 (NS 965) after having consecrated acaitya.
Later, in 1936, Vratarāja Śākya built a temple and enshrined Akṣobhya in the sanctum.
These events are referred to in two inscriptions dated NS 965 and NS 1056.

Inside the complex, there is acaityato the east along with a shrine that houses two Mahākāla statues (TOK0010-009, TOK0010-010), accompanied by two weathered, unreadable inscriptions from the later-Malla period.

While no inscription confirms the temple’s construction date, Pruscha (1975, p. 241) suggests it was built in the 18th century, with lion statues installed in 1603 CE, indicating Gaṇeśa’s presence before then.

Initially a single-story structure, the temple was rebuilt in 2010 CE (VS 2067), with the northern gate restored and inaugurated by Nepali comedians Madan Krishna Shrestha and Hari Bansha Acharya (local resident, Daṃgola, male, age 55).

Historically, Tokha faced water scarcity, addressed by Prime Minister Juddha Śamśera and his wife Padmakumārī Devī, who installed a water spout in 1937 CE (VS 1994), as noted in an inscription on the complex’s wall, though the spout no longer exists.
Acaityawithin the complex was established by Joganārāṃ from Kathmandu’s Thãhiti and was renovated by Jogaratna and his family in 1945 CE (NS 1065).
The statue (which faces) east is constructed out of a single stone.
An inscription below the statue states it was established by Śakhalāla, his wife Āsāmāyā and their two daughters in NS 1077 (1957 CE).
Around the same time, a roof was constructed above the statue and was capped by a metalcaitya(local knowledge, Maharjana, male, 63 years).
Pruscha(1975, 155) has published a photo of this statue before the railing was installed.Śakhalāla’s family members take care of the statue.
No inscription recording the construction of the Temple has been recovered so far.
It was probably constructed during the medieval period.
A handwritten manuscript dated NS 894 (1774 CE) lists 52 shrines of Nṛtyeśvara in Kathmandu.
Locke(1985, 72) assumes that Nani's present shrine was constructed after the 1934 earthquake.
Following the theft of the original statue a few years ago, this new statue is now protected by a metal grill.
The inscription on the pedestal of these images is now illegible.
The earliest inscription mentioning this Nani is dated to NS 796.

text: The Fountain, built around the 13th to 15th centuries, is two kilometres north of Binayak, between Devkotagaon and Champathagaon.
