Behind the Umāmaheśvara shrine, an inscription from the Licchavi period, installed during Aṃśuvarman, is positioned.
The precise date of the Dyaḥchẽ's initial construction remains uncertain, yet its origin likely traces to the medieval era.
Pruscha (K-138, p.50) references a 1639 CE (NS 750) inscription that is no longer present.
A manuscript from 1774 CE (NS 894) enumerates 52 Nāsaḥdyaḥ shrines in Kathmandu, including the one enshrined here (J. B. Mānandhar 1124, p.47-48).
Renovations occurred in 1979 CE (VS 2036) and again in 2006 CE (VS 2062).
In 2022 CE (VS 2078), the Kathmandu metropolis sponsored the reconstruction of the Dyaḥchẽ.
Before its reconstruction, it was a two-story edifice.
The Vatu Ṭola's jyāpus, responsible for Nāsaḥdyaḥ Guthi, also engage in the socio-religious activities of the Navadurgā temple (KAT1370).
During the Yẽnyāḥ festival, a Bhairava mask used to be showcased on the first-floor window of the Dyaḥchẽ, relocating to the second-floor verandah after reconstruction.
On the 5th of the dark fortnight of Caitra, the Sikhrākāras of Te Bāhāḥ perform the annual worship of Mañjuśrī within the ground-floor sanctum through a fire oblation ritual.

Situated at the entrance of a narrow lane leading from Cikamugaḥ Ṭola towards Bhīmasthāna, this small yet artistically refined temple stands as a rare architectural remnant from the mid-seventeenth century CE that has retained its original form even after several major earthquakes.
Above the doorway once stood a finely carved woodentoraṇadating from the time of the temple’s original construction, which, however, was stolen around 1983 CE (VS 2040).
Only onetuṇḍalon the south-western side is missing, replaced by a plain wooden beam supporting the roof.
Within thegarbhagṛha(sanctum) stands the main cult image identified in the temple inscription asBhavānīśaṅkara—a composite image of Śiva and Pārvatī inardhanārīśvaraform.

After the devastating 2015 CE (VS2072) earthquake, hundreds of temples across the valley were either destroyed or reconstructed—many with unnecessary alterations such as replacing the traditional clay-tile (jhigantī) roofing with copper sheets.

According to the inscription preserved inside the sanctum, the temple was commissioned by a certain Harisiṃha, who endowed it with land grants for the performance of daily (nitya) and annual (vārsika) rituals.
The portion of the inscription containing the date is worn away, but Pruscha (1975, p. 77) dated it to 1637 CE (NS 757–758).

The inscription does not mention Harisiṃha’s family name, yet given that the surrounding area has long been inhabited by Māthema, Śreṣṭha, and Jośī families—groups historically close to power—it is plausible that he belonged to one of these influential lineages.
Gaṇeśa Phalcā 1 is located to the east of Bhṛṅgāreśvara Mandira (SUN0100) in Sunaguthi.
The older and traditionaljhĩgaṭītiled structure was dismantled and replaced with a new RCC structure around 1996.
Gaṇeśa Phalcā 1 suffered heavy damages in the 2015 earthquakes.
Two million rupees have been provided by the Government of Nepal to fund its reconstruction, which began in 2019 and is still ongoing at the beginning of 2020.
The Phalcā has been moved two meters back from its original position so that the front face of the Gaṇeśa Temple (SUN0102) may be widened.
The local residents who are taking part in the reconstruction process of thephalcāhave said that they are planning to reconstruct thephalcāas a two-storied building.

The sanctum contains a statue of Mahiṣāsuramardinī with akīrtimukhatoraṇa. 15 additional statues of Mahiṣāsuramardinī are established on the same level, which is another unique feature of this temple.
In addition to the main door to the sanctum, three false doors withtoraṇas are established on the other three sides.
An inscription installed inside the nearby Vatsalā Mandira (BKT0100) records the establishment of Siddhilakṣmī here in this temple.

According to the inscription, King Jitāmitra Malla established Goddess Vatsalā in the Vatsalā temple in 1696 CE (NS 816) while also enshrining Siddhilakṣmī here in the Siddhilakṣmī temple (B. Pauḍela VS 2022, p.50).
The inscription on a stone on the banks of the Vāsukī river in Bhaktapur reveals that the construction of the Siddhilakṣmī temple began in 1693 CE (NS 813).
Later in 1715 CE (NS 835), King Bhūpatindra Malla added a bell at the temple that contained an inscription recording the event (P. Śreṣṭha VS 2079).
Gutschow points out that the temple was probablyt damaged in the 1833 CE or earlier earthquakes and poorly rebuilt.
The southern portion of the upper part of the temple toppled in the devastating earthquake of 1934 CE (VS 1990).
The temple also suffered damages during the 2015 CE earthquakes.
Even though the temple did not collapse, many cracks developed and the temple required extensive shoring.
The Department of Archaeology (DoA) reconstructed the temple in 2019 CE (VS 2076) by dismantling it to the sanctum level.
Constructed in 1207 CE (NS 327), Gaṃ Bāhāḥ contains a statue of Akṣobhya made of fine-quality clay calledgathicāenshrined as itskvaḥpaḥdyaḥ.
The three-storied main building (kvāḥpāḥchẽ) of the Bāhāḥ faces north.
A woodentoraṇawith a statue of Nāmasaṅgīti at the center is installed on top of the entrance to the sanctum.
After the old Toraṇa was stolen, Pūrṇaprabhā Vajrācārya offered a new Toraṇa in the name of her deceased husband Padmaśrī Vajra Vajrācārya in 1998 CE (VS 2055).
The old Toraṇa contained an inscription dated 1968 CE (NS 1088) (Locke1985, p.275).
Originally, the statue ofkvāḥpāḥdyaḥwas made ofgathicā, a fine-quality clay, but rats damaged the statue.
A smallcaityaat the premises was established at the time of the foundation of the Bāhāḥ.
According to the locals, a group of the members of Dhvākhā Bāhāḥ settled here by constructing a newbāhāḥ.
A donation deed in a private collection of Amoghavajra Vajrācārya records the construction of Gaṃ Bāhāḥ in 1207 CE (NS 327).

Ratnadeva Vajrācārya (text: Vajrācāryya Ratnadeva) and Bramha Thakura, a local functionary (pātra), endowed land and garden in the name of Akṣobhya, the main deity, on the full moon day of Vaiśākha in 1207 CE (NS 327) while Gaṃ Bāhāḥ was being constructed.
With the establishment of Akṣobhya, a Caitya, and the esoteric deity (āgaṃdyaḥ), the construction of the Bāhāḥ was completed on the 10thof the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha in 1207 CE (NS 327).
Nothing is known about the two Vajrācāryas from the donation deed.
Locals say that Pātra Bramha Thakura of the Thāymadu Ṭola was the person to hand over the newly-constructed Bāhāḥ and the two Vajrācāryas who received it were from Dhvākhā Bāhāḥ.
In 1892 CE (NS 1012), the temple that houses the small Caitya was renovated.
The main building of the Bāhāḥ was reconstructed in 2012 CE with funds from the Kathmandu Metropolitan City Office and donations from the locals.
There are altogether 27 Vajrācāryas from seven households as members of the Bāhāḥ, who are said to have moved from Sankhu.
The square is surrounded by residential buildings and is home to many temples,phalcās,and stone water spouts, making it a unique public place.
In circa 2000 the upper half of the wooden tympanum was stolen.
Latticed openings have been added to the east and west as later additions.
There is no inscription to provide information about the establishment of the temple.
Galay Hiti is one of the four water spouts constructed at the slope west of the Ĩllā Ṭola, Sankhu.
It is likely that the Galay Hiti, too, had such a miniature shrine with the above-mentioned Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa statue, but the shrine got damaged later and only the statue survived.
There are no historical records to date the initial construction of the Hiti.
Therefore, we can presume that the Hiti was constructed around the same period.
The Hiti’s wall was renovated by applying cement plaster in the 90s (local resident, Mānandhara, male, age 62).
Three otherbāhāḥscan be accessed from the eastern side of the route to Subāhāḥ, and Pilāchẽ Taḥdhaṃ Bāhāḥ can be found in the courtyard to the east of these three monastic buildings.
The courtyard is paved with telia tiles and is surrounded by tall buildings to the south and north.
Pilāchẽ Taḥdhaṃ Bāhāḥ is a monastic building that was privately built and owned by Maharjans.
As such, it lacks any connection to other monastic buildings in Lalitpur.
It is also known as Jñānakīrti Vihāra, as it is said that it was built by Jñānavīra Bhāvo.
This monastic building currently has no members and it bears no connection to the two other Pilāchẽ Bāhāḥs next door.
The main entrance to the monastic building is via a small passage that runs through privately owned Maharjan houses.
This monastic building has no main godhouse (kvāḥpāḥ chẽ), but it does contain a small shrine with a statue of an Aksḥobya Buddha in Bhusparsa Mudrā as its main deity.
In front of the shrine, a stone inscription (LAL2100-001_I_20190204_01) contains a records of the monastic building's history, as well as the Dharmadhātu Jinālaya Caitya and Dharmadhātu Maṇḍala.
The Dharmadhātu Jinālaya Caitya (LAL2100-002) was constructed in NS 1050 (CE1930), six years before the construction of the main god house.

This traditionally built Mandira is located right to the main road leading to the city of Patan.
A four-armed Gaṇeśa statue is consecrated inside the sanctum.
According to the oldest inscription found in the temple dating 1683 CE (803 NS), asuvarṇamukha(gilded face) was fixed to the previously existing statue of Gaṇeśa.
This attests the fact that there was a Gaṇeśa shrine or a temple in situ even before 1683 CE.
This proves that the temple was reconstructed sometime after the late medieval period.
However, there is no record regarding to the frequency and timeline of the reconstruction activities.
Pruscha(1975, 145) mentions that the temple was reconstructed in 1682 CE without giving any reference.
His photographs of the temple, published in 1975 CE, do not show the metal flags and banner (patāḥ) which are part of the temple in the present-day.
Thus, these objects must have been installed after 1975 CE.
In 1938 CE, a person named Gaṅgārāja paved the sanctum (garbhagṛha) with imported tiles.
A wooden structure for lighting up butter lamps was offered to the temple in 2015 CE by Amīramāna Amātya and his wife.
The temple was reconstructed entirely except the ground floor with regular brick and new structural timber.
As a result of this reconstruction activity, all original struts are lost.
While the corner struts were replaced with poorly carved replicas painted in bright colors, all others are simple timber brackets.
The extend of reconstruction of the ground floor is difficult to assess since the exterior walls and plinth are covered with cement terazzo.
This particular one, constructed by Bamabahādura, a brother of Jaṅgabahādura, during his prime ministership, underwent reconstruction in 2023 CE.
In 1851 CE (VS 1907), Bamabahādura Kũvara constructed the Tīna Devala temple (KAT2670) along the bank of the Bagmati, featuring a distinctive architectural style.
Atāmrapatra(copper-plate) of the temple records the concurrent construction of it, forming a perimeter around the temple on all four sides (Darnāl VS 2061, p.37-43).

Bamabahādura Kũvara Rāṇā, a brother of Jaṅgabahādura and son of Bālanarasiṃha Kũvara's youngest wife Mukhenī Gaṇeśakumārī (B. Bhaṇḍārī VS 2071, p.16), designated numerous lands for theguṭhīassociated with these heritage structures, along with other temples anddharmaśālāsthat he had erected.
The Tīna Devala temple was built during Jaṅgabahādura's visit to Europe in 1850 CE (VS 1906-07) (P. Rāja VS 2073, p.71).
Throughout Bamabahādura's reign, he actively contributed to the establishment of religious eminence.
After the 2015 CE earthquake (VS 2072), more than two dozen families permanently resided in the temple complex andsataḥ.
Subsequent to the earthquake, the families were permanently displaced and reconstructed in their original form.
The restoration was facilitated by the Bagmati Civilization Integrated Development Committee under the Ministry of Urban Development, with support from a loan provided by the Asian Development Bank.
The reconstruction of the temple was successfully completed on October 23, 2022.

Additionally, individuals unrelated to the family who find themselves without a residence and need to do death mourning of their deceased family are granted permission to dwell in it (one of the guṭhī members of Bamavīravikaṭeśvara Guṭhī, Rāṇā, male, age 56).

Additionally, on the seventh bright fortnight of Māgha (Acalā), the Tīna Devala's anniversary ritual is observed, marked by a feast and the arrangement of materials in it (S. Adhikārī VS 2064, p.33-34).
After the recent reconstruction, historical materials have been collected and displayed on the upper floor of the western section, signalling intentions to convert it into a museum.
Constructed by Khaḍgikāra Gvārā in the 1940s, Bhajana Phalcā is currently being used for devotional singing dedicated exclusively to Buṅgadyaḥ.
The construction of the Phalcā began in 1943 CE (VS 2000) after its foundation was dug up.
Khaḍgīkāra Gvārā, Tulasimāyā, and the family from the Iti Ṭola constructed the Phalcā.
Khaḍgīkāra built the Phalcā wishing his deceased grandfather Lāju and father Kuberasīṃ the heavenly abode of Sukhāvatī Bhuvana.
The descendants of Khaḍgīkāra Gvārā still carry out the necessary repairs to the Phalcā.
Motilāla Śilpakāra installed metal railings on the Phalcā in 1998 CE (VS 2054).
Thephalcāwas reconstructed in 2011.
The site is mainly constituted of two structures built with reused medieval elements dating from the 14th-15th century.
Ajayamerukoṭa is rich in monuments that were mostly erected during the 14th and 15th centuries.
This political and economical rise is demonstrated in the numerous monuments erected between the second half of the 14th century and throughout the 15th century.

Situated west of Pukhūlāchi Pukhū (SKH0342), Sohra Khuṭṭe Mahādeva Mandira (lit. 16-legged Mahādeva Temple) has no trace of any temple-structures as of March 2022, except a Śivaliṅga enshrined in the middle of the platform on which aphalcā-like structure supported by 16 pillars (with 12 wooden pillars on four cardinal directions and four stone pillars at the centre around the Śivaliṅga) used to stand before it collapsed completely sometime after 1975 CE.
According to local residents, parts of the Temple started to fall apart already from 1975 CE.
After it collapsed, a Śreṣṭha family of the Pukhūsi clan has stored the clay finial of the Temple safely at home.
Some of its wooden pillars were stolen while some were burnt.
Broken pieces of the stone pillars can still be seen on the northern and eastern sides of the Temple platform, and a recently-constructed water spout can be seen attached to its southern plinth.
The Spout was installed in the course of the renovation of Pukhūlāchi Pukhū (SKH0342) by the Shankharapur Municipality in 2021 CE.
There are no records to date the initial construction of the Temple.

No historical records could be traced that confirm the initial construction date of the temple.
Gutschow(2011, 534) assumes that the temple once had three terracotta-tiled roofs but that the structure collapsed on 26 August 1833 when the Kathmandu Valley was hit by a disastrous earthquake.

The outer arcade was reconstructed using new large stone pillars and a heavy timber frame, whilst the upper structure was rebuilt in the shape of a Śikhara temple rather than in its original three-tiered configuration.
The temple suffered only minor damage in the great earthquake of 1934 (Locke1980, 324) but collapsed in the 2015 earthquake.
As of November 2019 it is under reconstruction.
The two Licchavi inscriptions that have been found in the village do not make any mention Karuṇāmaya Mandira.
The first inscription refers to the village as 'Bugāyumīgrāma' (D. Vajrācārya, VS 2030, 290).
The second one has been badly damaged, but appears to speak of someone who will have mercy on living beings (Ibid. 586-87).
Locke(1980, 250) assumes that this inscription refers to Karuṇāmaya (lit. "The one who is full of compassion").

One of the inscriptions placed at the temple of the same deity in Taḥ Bāhāḥ, Patan (LAL0050) mentions that King Śrīnivāsa Malla made many provisions for the cult of the deity in 1673 (Locke1980, 308).
During medieval times, coins bearing Buṅgdyaḥ's name were issued (H. Śākya,VS 2048, 16) and postage stamps are now available with his image.

Tamoṭa(NS 1129, 63), a manuscript preserved in the National Archives of Nepal mentions that Narendradeva brought Buṅgadyaḥ to Nepal 305 years before the beginning of Nepal Saṃvat, which started in 879 CE.
A number of inscriptions were also placed by King Narendradeva I; none of them, however, mentions the deity.
The middle part is composed by a rectangular register, of square section, where a text was probably inscribed.
Stone pillars were erected throughout the Karnali Basin from the 13th to the 17th century.
They are installed to honor the memory of deceased persons, mostly warriors.

The area surrounding the Dharmadhātu Maṇḍala is paved with black flagstones and has been encroached upon by some of the building materials used for the reconstruction of the Karuṇāmaya Mandira.
The Maṇḍala was constructed in 1964.
The inscription does not mention the name of its founder, though locals state that his name was Harṣamuni Śākya.
Thephalcāwas originally built by the Avāles of Lāmanaṃ Guṭhī(theguṭhīof non-meat eaters), the Cidhā Guṭhī and the Cidhā Khalaḥ Guṭhī of Bhindyaḥlāchi area (Tiwari1994, pp. 30 and 60).
Thephalcāwas dismantled and rebuilt in 2018 with support from the Lalitpur municipality.
The Phalcā formerly had three bays, however it was dismantled and incorporated into a five-storey building as a concrete structure in 1993 CE.
No inscription could be found with which to date Chvāsa Phalcā and so the original date of construction remains unknown.
An inscription at the bottom of these struts explains what will happen to evildoers when they arrive in hell (for an edition of these inscriptions, seeGail 1984: 74-76, andGutschow 2019).

Based on the architectural similarities between this temple and the Viśveśvara Temple, it can be hypothesised that Hariśaṅkara Mandira was also built by Siddhinarasiṃha Malla around NS 747 (Śākya2031, 14).

However, theNepālikabhūpavaṃśāvalī(19.3.198) states that in NS 826 (1706 CE) Rudramatī Maiyā, a daughter of king Yoganarendra Malla, built a three-storied temple to the south of the pillar in her father's name.
She established the deity Hariśaṅkara inside the temple.

The Vaṃśāvalī mentions that Rudramatī was the daughter of Yoganarendra Malla, which seems to be incorrect; the inscription of Buṅmatī (dated NS 801) mentions Rudramatī as the daughter of Śrīnivāsa Malla (Vajrācārya2056, 206-207).

Similarly, another inscription of Kṛṣṇa Mandira, Saugala, Lalitpur dated NS 825 suggests that Rudramatī is the dauthter of Śrīnivāsa Malla and the elder sister of Yoganarendra Malla (Vajrācārya2056, 346-348).
The temple collapsed in the April 2015 earthquake, leaving only the plinths intact.
The monument is currently under reconstruction (2019).
For the documentation of it's reconstruction seeGutschow 2019.
In most of the correspondence made during its reconstruction, the Phalcā is referred to as ‘Ḍhalaṃko Pāṭī’.

For this documentation, it is named Dhalāṃkva Dhvākhā Phalcā as the Phalcā is constructed next to the gate known as Dhalāṃkva Dhvākhā (lit. gate below a gutter or channel) in an area east of the Calākhu Ṭola called Dhalāṃkva due to its location below therājakulo(lit. royal channel), Sankhu’s main water channel.
The 2015 earthquakes caused severe damages to the Phalcā and was dismantled to be rebuilt.
Locals say that the Phalcā is being rebuilt in its former structure.
The reconstruction of the Phalcā began in 2022 after the Department of Archaeology disbursed over NRs. 1.9 million.
As of February 2022, the Phalcā was still under reconstruction.
One of the inscriptions at the Phalcā mentions that it was constructed in 1789 CE (NS 909) while also forming aguthifor its upkeep.
Unfortunately, due to the erosion of the text in the Inscription, the name of the donor and other details are unclear.

There were two other inscriptions on the Phalcā, which were unavailable for reading at the time of this fieldwork in February 2022 as they were stored away for protection while the Phalcā is being rebuilt.

Known as Dīrabhakteśvara, thisśivālaya(lit. the abode of Lord Śiva) was built by Ḍirakumārīdevī, the wife of Dhīra Śamśera, in 1865 CE (VS 1922) as a tribute to her, with a bell offered four years later in 1869 CE (VS 1926).
While also referred to as Dhīrabhakteśvara (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p. 770; Michaels and Tandon 2017, p. 106), the inscription on the temple bell confirms its name as Dīrabhakteśvara.
citations: (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p. 770; Michaels and Tandon 2017, p. 106)

text: Outside the temple, a bell from 1869 CE hangs from a bell stand to the south, commemorating its construction.

Additionally, a stone trident (triśūla) stands erected to the north of the temple, with a statue of Kāmadeva enshrined to the northeast.Ḍirakumārīdevī established the temple in 1865 CE (VS 1922) and also installed a bell in 1869 CE (VS 1926) (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2056, p. 561).
The inscription on the bell seems to have been engraved much later than the temple's establishment, referring to it as Dīramukteśvara instead of Dīrabhakteśvara.
Given that Ḍirakumārīdevī commissioned the temple during her lifetime, she likely suffixed her first name "Ḍira" with the term "-bhakteśvara" to name it.
Theseśivālayas, mostly built by royals during the Rāṇā period, were either established in one's name suffixed with "-bhakteśvara" or in memory of a deceased family member suffixed with "-mukteśvara".
It is possible that the person who inscribed the letters on the bell mistakenly engraved the temple's name as Dīramukteśvara.
After the temple's establishment, Dhīra Śamśera donated land parcels for the temple and established a trust to oversee various rituals.
The eaves board is also clad in copper sheets with inscriptions upon them and holds a line of wind chimes.
Three gilt finials shaped likecaityasadorn the top of the building, with a metal banner hanging down from the central one.
The principal deity is a stone statue of Amitābha, installed in the ground floor sanctum.
No historical record concerning the establishment of thebāhāḥcould be found.
At that time, thevaidyaswere granted permission to establish abāhāḥbehind the Mahāvihāra.
The two monuments are built in front of each other, in a plan usually referred to asduidevala(double temple).
The southernśikharawas missing itsāmalakaring and a new one was recently installed.
An inscription dated 1730 CE (NS 850) records the establishment of Bhīmasena by a group led by Manoharasiṃha Bhāro.
Their collective efforts led to the establishment of the Bhīmasena statue.
Thirty-seven years after the establishment of the Bhīmasena statue, in 1756 CE (NS 876), Dhanasiṃ and Māneśvarī of Tekhāco, Bhaktapur, expanded the temple.
They enclosed the sanctum and added aphalcādirectly in front, dedicated to Bhīmasena.
To ensure the temple's continued maintenance, they endowed a four-ropanīplot of land in Banepa.

An inscription from 1586 CE (NS 707) refers to Kirtipur's Bāghabhairava as " Bhīmasena Bhaṭṭāraka," and a Malla-era song describes Bhīmasena as a manifestation of Bhairava, a form of Śiva (S. Śreṣṭha VS 2056, p. 93, K. Tamoṭa NS 1101, p. 218-219).
citations: (S. Śreṣṭha VS 2056, p. 93, K. Tamoṭa NS 1101, p. 218-219)

text: They revere him for promoting business prosperity, protecting husbands abroad, reuniting couples separated by foreign trade, and listening to the sorrows of wives whose husbands are away (Lienhard NS 1110, p. 13).
Numerous Newar folk songs invoke Bhīmasena, expressing the sentiments of wives whose husbands are engaged in trade with Tibet (T. Simha NS 1135, p. 43-50).
Merchant families predominantly established Bhīmasena temples in Nepal.

Following the establishment of the Bhīmasena temple andphalcāin Dāpcā, a remote area outside the Kathmandu valley, a Gaṇeśa shrine, a Nāsaḥdyaḥ (deity of music and charm), and rest houses were added in 1771 CE (NS 891).
A local committee spearheaded the renovation of the temple andphalcāin 2022 CE.
Animal sacrifices are offered to Bhīmasena during this procession.
Although an inscription from 1756 CE (NS 876) instructed the temple's anniversary ritual on the 10th of the dark fortnight of Caitra, this practice has lapsed, and locals are unaware of it.
It is one of the two Śiva temples that Amarakānteśvarī built in the Paśupati area in 1856 CE (VS 1913).
The square superstructure is built in neo-classical architecture but coated with traditionalbajraplaster with a miniature dome in four corners.
The sanctum houses aśivaliṅgaamid statues of four other deities – Gaṇeśa, Durgā, Viṣṇu, and Sūrya – established on four corners of the inner walls as per the Śivapāñcāyana concept.
Amarakānteśvarī is credited for the construction of the temple in 1856 CE (VS 1913) (M. Thapā VS 2077, p.205).
There used to be a bell installed south of the temple in 1856 CE (NS 976).
The inscription on a bell recorded Princess Amarakānteśvarī offering it to the temple through Captain Juddhamānasiṃha Rājabhaṇḍārī (Ṭaṇḍana VS 2056, p.537).
Michaels and Tandon (2017, p.70), on the other hand, mention that she offered the bell through Siddhimānasiṃha Rājbhaṇḍārī.

While the year mentioned on the bell may have prompted them to believe that the temple was built in 1856 CE, a later document from 1915 CE (VS 1972) relating to the settlement of a dispute regarding the operation of the temple cites alālamoharaissued in 1852 CE (VS 1909) in connection with Sureśakānteśvara Mandira (K_0131_0001).
This suggests that the temple was already in existence in 1852 CE.
The exact year of its construction is unclear, as currently (August 2023), there is no other historical source that sheds light on its initial construction.
The temple was badly damaged in the 2015 earthquakes.
It was reconstructed by the Pashupati Area Development Trust in 2018 CE (VS 2075) (guard at Pashupati, Lāmichāne, male, age 48).
The bell, which is the only source of information regarding the temple’s construction, is no longer at the site.
As of August 2023, it is yet to be reinstalled back to its original place even after the completion of the temple’s reconstruction.
Usually, the donor of the bell is also the person to commission the construction of the temple the bell was donated to.
However, all of the daily and periodic rituals have been discontinued since the 2015 earthquakes (guard at Pashupati, Lāmichāne, male, age 48).

text: The single-bay Digichẽ features some beautifully executed decorative plaster work which unfortunately has become damaged in many places.

text: A lack of regular maintenance as well as damage caused by the 2015 earthquake have left the building exposed to the elements.

text: The Digichẽ was restored again some time around 1948 (Weiler2009, 252).
The main shrine building faces north and stands on a double plinth.
The monument appears to have been constructed relatively recently and has an overhanging concrete roof with a bell-shaped pinnacle and astūpaabove it.
The courtyard is surrounded by residential buildings and has a colonnaded structure on the ground floor.
Thisbāhāḥwas established by Devajyoti Vajrācārya in 1889.
After his death, his wives established aguṭhīfor the management of thebāhāḥin 1897.
There are no records to date the initial construction of the Hiti.
It suffered heavy damages during the 2015 earthquakes.
Local youths formed a Non-Governmental Organization by the name of Gāyatrī Fund and raised 1.95 million rupees for the restoration work carried out in 2017.
This residential house was built for the priest of the Nārāyaṇa Mandira (NWK0170) in Brahma Ṭola, Nuvākoṭa.
The three-story, east-facing house, characterized by its terracotta-tiled roof, has been abandoned since the 2015 CE earthquake (VS 2072).
As of April 2024 CE, the house's roof is in a dilapidated state.
There are no historical records detailing the construction of the house.

However, an inscription from 1441 CE (NS 561) in the Nārāyaṇa Mandira (the inscription is on the tripod of a lamp, see D. Vajrācārya and Ṭ. Śreṣṭha VS 2032, second part, pp. 4-5, but the lamp is no longer available at the site) records an offering ofpānasaby Ripu Malla, indicating the temple's long history.
citations: (the inscription is on the tripod of a lamp, see D. Vajrācārya and Ṭ. Śreṣṭha VS 2032, second part, pp. 4-5, but the lamp is no longer available at the site)

text: The house's architectural features, such as windows and doors, suggest it was built during the Rāṇā period, implying it is newer than the temple.
The house was already in disrepair before the 2015 CE earthquakes, which exacerbated the damage, rendering it unsuitable for residence.
After the 2015 CE earthquakes, this practice was moved to a private home in Brahma Ṭola (as communicated by the priest of the Nārāyaṇa temple, from the Pandey caste, male, age 62).
Ram Mandir was built in 1782 by Amar Singh Thapa, a Gorkhali General.
P. L. Śreṣṭha(2064, p.135) assumes that the Temple was constructed by Rājalladevī, the queen of Jayasthiti Malla.
Once he could not reach the Mandira due to a flood on the way.
Lord Śiva then came to his dream and instructed him to build a temple in his locality.
Therefore, he constructed Anantaliṅgeśvara Temple at Khaumā Ṭola and endowed 99ropanīs of land to form aguthi.

The persons who are currently (as of September 2022) looking after the management of the Temple and providing its priest (from the Karmācārya caste) with a monthly salary, claim that they are the descendants of that rich person who constructed the Temple.
Built facing south, this temple has a single-tiered roof made ofjhĩgaṭītiles.
An idol of Gaṇeśa is established on the ground floor.
As the old Gaṇeśa idol was worn out, a new Gaṇeśa idol was made and established alongside it.
No inscription regarding the establishment of this temple has been found.
A stone inscription dated 1732 CE (NS 852) is attached to thephalcālocated to the west of the temple, though it is not directly related to the temple itself.
The inscription states that acaityawas established during the reign of King Jayajaga (Jagajjaya Malla).

It states that thecaityawas constructed by Dvāre Dhanasiṃha, a resident of Dhugāma Ṭola in Gokarṇa, and his wife Rachamani, together with their children Kṛsṇanasiha (Kṛṣṇanarasiṃha), Sumati, and Dhanakṛṣṇa.
Another stone inscription dated 1755 CE (NS 875) is also attached to the samephalcā.
That inscription states that Dhanasiṃha and his wife Rachamani built thephalcātogether.
As the temple had fallen into disrepair, it was reconstructed around 2022 CE (VS 2079) at a cost of 19 lakhs (Guṭhī member of the Kāntibhairava Guṭhī from a Śreṣṭha caste, male, age 55).
To conduct thejātrā, aguṭhīcomprising nine Śreṣṭhaguṭhiyārshas been formed.
Thereafter, the metal idols of Kāntibhairava and Kumārī, kept at the guṭhiyār's house, are also placed on the dabū in front of the Kāntibhairava Dyaḥchẽ.
After thejātrāconcludes, the idol of Pakanāvatī Gaṇeśa is taken out of the ceremonial palanquin and taken to theguṭhiyār'shouse to be kept.
It was probably initially installed above, in a terrasse that had collapse due to road widening.
MUG0050-005 bears a damaged inscription.
Such stone pillars were erected throughout the Karnali Basin from the 13th to the 17th century.
They are installed to honor the memory of deceased persons, mostly warriors.
In this case, the typology of the pillars is similar to pillars from Mugu erected in the 15th century.

The site is important for it still present an untouched alinement of memorial stone pillars (such artefacts are usually moved around, especially because of construction activities and road widenings).
Passing through the small door of a five-storey building, one notices that the door is decorated with a carved frame against a stone wall.
The shrine building has four storeys and is part of the southern wing of the courtyard.
This courtyard is home to avajradhātu caitya, abimba caitya, and adharmadhātu maṇḍala, which are aligned alongvthe building's south-north axis.
The main building has been reconstructed, with the northern façade now clad indāciapā.
Finally, the roof of the building is covered withjhingatītiles and has astūpaas its finial.
According to a local resident, Dinakara Śākya, the founder of thebāhāḥ, was the brother of Padmarāja Śākya, who established Padmavarṇa Vihāra in 1658 CE (Śākya1994, 104).
This connection implies that Hitiphusa Bāhāḥ was likely constructed during the same period.
The Pañcadevala ensemble consists of five dome-style temples that were constructed in 1870 CE by King Surendra Vikrama Śāha (r. 1847-1881 CE) and his family members.
They are situated on a wide platform raised on four levels of plinths, and stone steps are built on the northern and southern sides for access.
The construction of the Pañcadevala ensemble was a collaborative effort involving five donors, as mentioned in G. Ṭaṇḍana (VS 2053, p. 127).

The ensemble was built in 1870 CE (VS 1927) by King Surendra Vikrama Śāha, his second wife Sūryarājyalakṣmī, his third wife Devarājyalakṣmī, his father Rājendra Vikrama Śāha, and his son Trailokya Vikrama Śāha.
Each of the five temples within the ensemble has a separate bell installed with an inscription, marking the year of their construction.

King Surendra offered a bell to the central Surendreśvara temple, Sūryarājyalakṣmī offered a bell to the Sūryarājyeśvara Mandira, Devarājyalakṣmī offered a bell to the Devarājyeśvara Mandira, and Trailokya Vikrama Śāha established aśivaliṅgain honor of his mother Trailokyarājyalakṣmī and also offered a bell to the temple.
He established aśivaliṅgain his name and offered a bell to the Rājendreśvara Mandira (PPK0610-009).
Unfortunately, the 2015 earthquakes caused damage to all five temples, which were already in a poor state of repair.
The central temple of the ensemble is dedicated to Śiva, who is surrounded by these four deities, following the concept of Śivapāñcāyana (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p. 127; M. Thāpā VS 2077, p. 216).
citations: (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p. 127; M. Thāpā VS 2077, p. 216)

text: Additionally, five tridents (triśūla), one of Śiva's implements, are established on the northern side.
However, the statue of Chatracaṇḍeśvara in the middle appears to have been moved to the northwestern corner under a pipal tree (cf. PPK0610-032).
Within the eastern area, there is a four-faced śivaliṅga (PPK0610-029) known as Kalpeśvara, which is believed to date back to the 9th-10th century (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p. 622).
Anotherśivaliṅga(PPK0610-012) from 488 CE (ŚS 410) is established on the western side of the temple and is revered as Śivapūjeśvara (Michaels and Tandon 2017, p. 70).
These rest houses were originally used as the Pañcadevala Pākaśālā, a kitchen that served food to the poor and mendicants since 1919 CE (VS 1976).

However, in 1975 CE (VS 2032), these rest houses were converted into an old-age home (vṛddhāśrama) (M. Thāpā VS 2077, p. 216), in 1975 CE (VS 2032)bthat was managed and run by the Missionaries of Charity of Mother Teresa of Kolkata.
The Pañcadevala temple complex is supported by an endowment of over 192ropanīsof land, which was dedicated for its maintenance and the performance of regular rituals (Guṭhī Saṃsthāna VS 2071, p. 36).
In 1892 CE (VS 1949), the management of the temple was entrusted to the Guṭhī Bandobasta Aḍḍā, a government body responsible for overseeing the administration of socio-religious trusts.
Subsequently, with the establishment of the Guṭhī Saṃsthāna in 1964 CE (VS 2021), this governing body took on the responsibility for all activities related to the temple (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p. 127).
Additionally, anniversary rituals are observed every year on the 8th day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, commemorating the day when the temple was consecrated (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p. 127).
As a result, various heritage structures were added in different periods, and the streetscape came to include numerousdabū,phalcā, temples, andsataḥ.
These features indicate that the structure was originally aphalcā, to which an upper storey was added later, thereby giving it the form of asataḥ.
No inscriptional evidence has been found to clarify the date of the original construction or the identity of the builder.
Local elders recall that the space was once used for communal gatherings, where devotional songs (bhajana) were sung; however, this practice has not resumed since the earthquake of 2015 (VS 2072).
Some recall that thephalchāwas occasionally used for shop-related purposes, and it is also said that about two decades ago a local club made constructive use of the space.
As of January 2026, the identity of the builder, any associatedguṭhī, and the traditionalrīti-thiticonnected with thissataḥ–phalcāhave largely fallen into obscurity.
For the protection of Lalitpur City, the tenMahāvidyāgoddesses were installed in ten different neighborhoods.
The eighth bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha when it falls on a Wednesday, is considered to be Dhūmāvatī's birthday (J. Mānandhara VS 2046, p. 33).
As a deity born from smoke, she is called Dhūmāvatī (M. Miśra NS 1127, p. 43).
As she is a widow goddess, she is also called 'Alakṣmī' (J. Mānandhara VS 2046, p. 32).
Similarly, there is a popular belief that making offerings of dark-colored roses, sweets, samaybaji, black grapes, and coconuts appeases unfavorable planetary influences (M. Miśra NS 1127, p. 41).
Three aniconic stones are installed facing north within the shrine.
No historical evidence has been found indicating when the Dhūmāvatī shrine in Lalitpur was established.

It is likely that Dhūmāvatī was established when Lalitpur was systematically developed, with the tenMahāvidyāgoddesses positioned in various directions for the city's protection, using Kopeśvara Temple (LAL1381) as the central point.
No old inscriptions have been found at the shrine either.
The oldest inscription found at the shrine is from 1984 CE (VS 2041), which records that Tulsī Nārāyaṇa Śreṣṭha of Kobāhāl Tola donated a bell for Dhūmāvatī.
In 2024 CE (VS 2081), the Dhūmāvatī shrine was reconstructed with financial assistance from Lalitpur Metropolitan City and donations collected from devotees.
Identified as one of the ancient statues of Nepal, this Buddha statue with broken limbs was renovated by the Pashupati Area Development Trust (PADT).

Established on the banks of the Bāgamatī river at the Rājarājeśvarī cremation ground facing east, the Buddha statue at the holy Hindu site of Paśupatikṣetra is considered to be a rare one (M. Thāpā VS 2077, p.204).
Standing on a lotus throne, the Buddha makes a boon-granting gesture (varadamudrā) with his right hand while holding the end of his robe (ciivara) over his shoulder with his left hand.
There is no inscription on the statue.
While H. Śākya (NS 1097, p.102) and Singh (1968, p.203) believe the statue to belong to the 5th-6th century, Schick (1997, p.56) thinks it to be a 9th-century sculpture.
The right hand was already broken below the elbow (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p.488).
The PADT later renovated the statue by adding the missing portion of the right arm and feet.
Therefore, a separate shrine with a metal door was built for it.
The statue is not worshipped on a daily basis and there is no community-based trust (guthi) associated with it.
The establishment of a Buddha statue in the holy Hindu site of Paśupati shows the religious tolerance practiced in Nepal.
Local residents of the Ṭola collected donations and constructed the Bhīmasena Shrine in 2000 CE (2056 VS).
The roofs of thephalcāare constructed using traditional bricks (jhiṃgaṭī), while the supporting columns (thāma) exhibit intricate artistic work.
There is no inscriptive evidence detailing the original construction of thephalcā.

However, an inscription (BKT0250_I_002) kept within thepīṭha's sanctum reveals that the local community undertook the restoration of thephalcāafter its destruction in the 1933 CE earthquake (1990 VS), completing the task in 1940 CE (1997 VS).
This implies that thephalcāwas established prior to 1933 CE (1990 VS).
Another Bhagavatī statue (object no.NWK0010-001) in the form of Mahiṣāsuramardinī from Nuwakot dates back to NS 737, corresponding to 1617 CE, and is enshrined at the Bhagavatī Mandira (NWK0010).
Although the statue in the Nuwakot Śobhābhagavatī temple is undated, its origin likely aligns with the period when the statue at the Bhagavatī Mandira was installed.
The sole inscription found in the temple commemorates the installation of a bell by Juktamāna Śreṣṭha from Asvabārī in 1941 CE (VS 1997).
The temple was already in a dilapidated state even before the 2015 CE earthquakes.
Following the earthquakes, the Department of Archaeology undertook the reconstruction of the temple, along with several other temples in Nuwakot (a local resident, Ḍaṃgola, age 38).
Presently (April 2024 CE), the temple lacks any existing trusts (gūṭhī).

Additionally, on the full moon day of Caitra each year, a ceremonial pole is erected at the Buḍhībhairavī Mandira (NWK0300) before the Dhāmī, the oracle medium of Nuwakot, performs rounds in the main settlement, offering cooked rice and unbroken rice grains (akṣatā) to various temples and shrines, including Śobhābhagavatī.
The temple collapsed in the 1934 CE earthquakes and was subsequently rebuilt in a mixed style with a domed top over a traditional tile (jhĩgaṭī) roof.
There is no inscription at the site indicating when the temple was originally constructed.
The only available inscription is that of Rājavīra Jośī (text: Rājavira Josi), who donated a bell to the temple in 1833 CE (NS 953) when it was still a three-tiered temple.
Gutschow (2011, p.460-461) has published a photo of the temple in its original tiered structure taken by Kurt Boeck in 1899 CE.
Another Śiva temple (KAT1280) at the Bheḍāsiṅga Ṭola collapsed in the same earthquakes and was also rebuilt in the same manner.
During the reconstruction, the Gaṇeśa temple (KAT1330-011) on the south-eastern corner of the temple was significantly reduced in size to make it appear like a small shrine.

The Vaṃśeśvara Mahādeva temple was not seriously damaged in the 2015 CE earthquakes, but the Kathmandu Metropolis has prioritized its reconstruction in its original 3-tiered configuration as it is a prominent temple in the heart of the old town, Indrachowk (based on a personal conversation with the chairperson of the local government, Ḍaṃgola, age 53).
No historical record exists regarding the original construction date of thephalcā.
An inscription dated NS 939 (1819 CE) mentions that Thākusiṅ and Toyuṣvā Thakunī, a couple from nearby Valā Ṭola, funded its restoration.
The inscription further states that land was bestowed upon theguṭhīof thephalcā.
Another inscription inside thephalcāstates that the building was restored again in VS 2003 (1946 CE), likely because it had been damaged during the Great Earthquake of 1934.
In 2019, thephalcāwas rebuilt with funds from the Lalitpur Municipality.
An inscription dated NS 939 directs theguṭhīto light three oil-lamps on the day when the chariot of the deity pauses here, indicating thephalcā's connection to the deity's chariot procession.
Thephalcāsandcapāḥswere constructed in these areas to accommodate devotees who traveled from afar and needed places to rest.
Ayuguthi Sataḥ was probably first established in the early 18th century CE, but is said to have originally been built under the order of the sister of a Malla king of Patan.
She commissioned the monument after the death of her brother and founded aguṭhīin his memory.
The historical inscription is said to have been stolen in 2000.
In the 1990s the building was in a dilapidated state and its ruins were removed by bulldozers in 1999.
It was then renovated.
Emergency repairs had already taken place in 1992 under Sr Eduard Sekler and the KVPT had then also indicated the need for further repairs, developing a first plan and outlining the damage in 1994.
A court had ordered the repair of the monument in 1993, though this request was apparently ignored.
The owner filed an appeal against this order in 1996 and the case was delayed for months, while the building continued to fall apart.
The majority of the historical materials became rotten due to monsoon rains, and it took until 1999 for the site to be removed and then rebuilt.
In 2001, it was rebuilt by the KVPT with the support of the DOA.
Some of the historical carved materials were used for this (see KVPT Final Report 2002; a detailed chronology of the restoration can be found on p. 11).

text: While the exact date of the temple's initial construction cannot be determined due to the lack of historical sources, its architecture indicates that it likely originates from the Rāṇā period.
Locals attribute the construction of the temple to a woman named Gaṅgārānī, though there is no inscription to support this claim.

It is believed that Gaṅgārānī was one of the wives of Prime Minister Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā, who is also associated with the establishment of the Gaṅgeśvara Śivālaya (PPK0312) at the Pandhra Śivālaya complex in 1863 CE (VS 1920).
Jaṅga Bahādura married Gaṅgādevī in Benares on his way back from leading a troop to Lucknow to suppress the Sepoy Mutiny of 1857 CE.

An inscription from the temple indicates that an ascetic named Buddha Girī Bābā installed door leaves in the temple in 1848 CE (VS 1905), almost a decade before Jaṅga Bahādura married Gaṅgādevī, thus ruling out the possibility of her founding the temple.

The piece that fell into Viṣṇu's hand was taken toAmarāvatī(Indra's celestial city) for installation, the piece that fell into Indra's hand was taken toPātālaloka(the netherworld) for installation, while the piece that fell into Brahmā's hand was installed on the banks of the Bāgmatī River near the Gokarṇa Pihāmaha Tīrtha, thus establishing Gokarṇeśvara (N. Pouḍela, VS 2020, p. 16).
Built in the Nepalese tiered style, this temple has three roofs.
On the very top of the temple, a golden pinnacle and an umbrella (chatra) have been installed.
On the ground floor, a sanctum sanctorum has been constructed.
A Śivaliṅga made of stone is installed at the center.
The temple, built facing east, has doors on all four sides.
In front of the western door, a Nandi is installed.
This bell was offered by the younger Queen Lalitatripurāsundarī of Raṇabahādura Śāha in 1825 CE (VS 1885).
All around the temple, one can see numerous idols of various gods and goddesses installed.
The main door covered with gold-gilded copper, and many of the idols here were established by Balabhañjana Pāṇḍe.
The idol of Pārvatī installed in the temple's sanctum is considered the power of Gokarṇeśvara Mahādeva, and the craftsmanship of this idol is considered very beautiful.
Although there is evidence that King Jayasthiti  Malla  first restored the temple and brought it to its current form, no facts have been obtained regarding who built the initial temple and when.
In 1392 CE (NS 512), King Jayasthiti Malla restored this temple, appointed a Southern Bhaṭṭa priest to perform worship, and also established a religious endowment.
From that time until now, worship has been continuously performed here through the Southern Bhaṭṭa Brahmaṇa (Ś. Śreṣṭha, VS 2045, p. 24).
Inscriptions are affixed to the wall at the northern corner of the temple.
Among these inscriptions, the one from 1583 CE (ŚS 777) from the reign of Śivasiṃhadeva and Raṇajītasiṃha is the oldest, which mentions that Gopirāma Bhāro installed a golden pinnacle on the temple.
Looking at past history, it appears that the temple's restoration occurred at various times.

According to details mentioned in an inscription dated 1693 CE (NS 813) located on a pāṭī within the Gokarṇeśvara courtyard, 3 ropaṇīs of land were allocated for the restoration of the śivālaya and for applying lime annually (S. Bhaṇḍārī, VS 2068, p. 32).
In 1787 CE (NS 908), Dharmanārāyaṇa constructed a pāṭī and a dharmaśālā on the southern side of the temple for the salvation of ancestors (pitṛ uddāra) and established an endowment (GKN0010_I_002).
That top roof was restored, and during the reign of Raṇabahādur Śāha, in 1830 CE (SS 1759), a brass roof with gold gilding was installed.
Similarly, the main entrance on the east was covered with gold-gilded copper plates by Balabhañjana Pāṇḍe in 1846 CE (VS 1902).
This shows that people from different periods have carried out restoration work on the temple, giving it great importance.
More recently, in 2023 CE (VS 2080), the temple's roofs were reconstructed and all three roofs were covered with gold-gilded copper plates.
Jayasthiti Malla, in 1392 CE (NS 512), appointed a Southern Bhaṭṭa priest to conduct worship at this temple and established an endowment to manage the temple's annual rites.
Continuing this established tradition, Southern Bhaṭṭas remain the main priests, performing all daily and religious rituals here.
The tradition is to perform this rice pudding offering in a very secretive manner, without even keeping an assistant priest (B. Bā̃skoṭā, VS 2063, p. 71).
For special festivals, the endowment organization makes separate arrangements here.

However, it is incorrectly labelled as the Rājendreśvarī Temple in the published inventory of the Kathmandu Valley Development Plan ‘Kāṭhmāḍauṃ Upatyakā Nagara Vikāsa Yojanā’ (Inventory VS 2039, p.162).
Constructed in the style of a common Śivālaya, the temple stands on three levels of square plinths.
The entrance to the sanctum is adorned with atoranafeaturing a Kīrtimukha motif, and beside it, a Bhairava face is installed on the southern facade.
The lack of conclusive evidence makes it challenging to determine the exact date of the temple's construction.

From the confluence of the rivers Vāgamatī and Viṣṇumatī to the confluence of Vāgamatī and Ṭukucā, numerous temples and shrines were established by nobles and royal families from the early Śāha period to the end of the Rāṇā period.
For instance, during the Rāṇā era, Colonel Gupta Bahādura Karkī built a nearbysataḥ.
Similarly, a merchant named Dharmanārāyaṇa and Munsī Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa constructed separatesataḥsnearby.
A photo published in the above-mentioned inventory of the Kathmandu Valley Development Plan displays a two-story and five-bayedsataḥon the backside of the temple (Inventory VS 2039, p.162).
The inventory, without citing any sources, mentions that this two-storysataḥwas built by a certain Ratnavīra.
The context suggests that thesataḥwas constructed as part of the temple, leading us to assume that both structures were built around the same time.
A metal cover used to shield the Śivaliṅga in the sanctum during annual rituals bears an inscription recording its donation by a certain Harṣamāna from Jyābāhāḥ.
Although several temples in Teku were affected by the recent earthquakes (2015 CE), this temple appears to have sustained minimal damage.
It was commissioned in 1724 CE by a certain Gomatī and her three sons in memory of her husband.
In 2003 CE, the three-bayed traditional structure was demolished and reconstructed 15 centimetres wider than the original.
The wooden posts were replaced with concrete columns clad in traditional brick (dāciaḥpā) and the roof was covered with traditional roof tiles (jhĩgaṭī).
In the same year, a small wooden shrine of Kṛṣṇa was installed and a group of senior residents began using the space regularly to chantbhajanas.
During the reconstruction work in 2003, an inscription from the Licchāvi period was found in the surrounding area and placed at the left corner of the Pāṭī.

According to one of the inscriptions, he is even believed to be a form of Bhīmasena.
There is no documented evidence to date the initial construction of the Bāghabhairava Mandira.
The earliest inscription related to this temple was issued in 1514 CE (635 NS), recording its renovation by a powerful elite called ‘Mahāpātra’ of Patan.
In the light of this evidence, the temple must have been constructed before 1514 CE (635 NS).Ś. Śreṣṭha(VS 2057, 39) suggests that King Śivadeva could have built it during his reign.
A statue of Bāghabhairava is consecrated in its sanctum, facing east.

The old structure of the Phalcā was dismantled in 2010 and reconstructed as a two-storey narrow building.
The builders used concrete and replaced all of the original old materials.
To compensate for this, the owner of this plot of land donated 2 feet of their land, thus increasing the breadth of the Phalcā when it was reconstructed.
Jyotirliṅgeśvara Mahādeva is believed to be established at Yoga Tīrtha, the confluence of Ratnāvatī and Nārāyaṇī rivers.
Althoughpurāṇas mention about Jyotirliṅgeśvara Mahādeva, this Temple was constructed only in 1635 CE (NS 755) by Kāśirāma Bhāro, Virāja Bhāro, and Gayārāma Bhāro of Sankhu.
They had also offered a goldenkalaśato the deity after the completion of the Temple.
The Śivaliṅga of Jyotirliṅgeśvara Mahādeva was probably under an open sky before the construction of the Temple.
Jhĩgaṭītiles cover the roof of the building, which is supported by ten struts: six to the east, two to the north and two to the south.
The Sataḥ was built on the initiative of Cakrasiṃha Bābu, one of the grandsons of King Siddhinarasiṃha Malla, in 1700 CE.
The inscription that details the initial construction of the building mentions that a golden pinnacle was fixed on top of the Satah.
Bābu also established aguṭhīfor the management of the Sataḥ, and King Yoganarendra Malla was present at its inaugural ceremony in 1700.

text: The courtyard also has two morephalcā, one of which was destroyed by the 2015 earthquake.
The three-storey building consists of a five-bay Phalcā in the ground floor and two upper floors.
The building is positioned on the elevated ground floor of the adjunct building of Śaṃkhadhara Bahāl (LAL1700).
The building adjacent to the Phalcā is now private property.
Bhajanachẽ (lit. ‘house for [singing] devotional songs’) is a building constructed for performing devotional songs (bhajana) every day.
The two-story building at the Dugāḥ Hiti Ṭola in Sankhu provides space for the locals for daily performance ofbhajanasdedicated to Lord Kṛṣṇa.
Facing west, the building is being used to storebhajana-instruments and items on its upper floor.
Other tools and construction material used in development works at the Ṭola are also stored upstairs.
There are no records to date the construction of Bajanachẽ.
The Department of Archaeology in cooperation with the Shankharapur Municipality reconstructed the building follwing the damages caused by the 2015 earthquakes.

text: Following the chariot procession of Matsyendranātha, a fire sacrifice calledmāṃsāhutiis performed (usually on a Saturday) in the sacrificial pit (yajñakuṇda) in front of the temple.
An inscription installed on its wall attributes its construction to Devīdāsa Bhāro in NS 784 (1664 CE).
According to this inscription, Bhāro established a statue of Mañjuśrī here to wish for the liberation of his late uncle Viśva Bhāro's soul.
Regrettably, the statue had been removed (August 2020).
Aphalcābuilt in front of the temple houses a stone statue of Sarasvatī, the only statue of goddess of wisdom in town.
While a shrine of this Gaṇeśa already existed before, a temple was built by Harinasī and his family from Thaiba later in 1877 CE (NS 997).
They also installed a gilded roof on top.
Over time, the descendants of the donor founded religious trusts by donating land for the performance of daily rituals and musical instruments at the temple.
In 2005 CE (VS 2062), a local committee reconstructed the temple under the supervision of the Department of Archaeology.
The deity is also referred to as “Dey Gaṇeśa,” or, the Gaṇeśa of the town, as he is revered by the whole town (Ī. Śreṣṭha NS 1131, p. 22).
The trust founded by the donor family used to sacrifice a goat during the anniversary ritual.
Vairāgī Mandira is one of the threeakhaḍās of religious renunciates on the banks of the Bagmati river in Thapathali built specially for the Rāmānandī sect of the Vaiṣṇava ascetics.
An ascetic named Rāmānanda established this sect in the 13th or 14th century and is, therefore, widely referred to as the Rāmānandī sect.
Among these, the Śubheśvara temple (KAT2820-009) housing aśivaliṅgaestablished in the name of Śubhakumārī, one of Jaṅga Bahādura’s wives, has already collapsed, leaving only stone remnants.
Details of the temple’s initial construction are unclear due to the lack of historical sources.
The trend of establishing temples of Hindu sects on the banks of the Bagmati river in the Thapathali and Teku area began only during the early Śāha period.
The Vairāgī Mandira was also one among these temples established during that period.
According to a bell at the Śubheśvara temple, it was built in 1860 CE (VS 1917), wishing for eternal peace of one of Jaṅga Bahadura’s queens Śubhakumārī.
A document (K_0583_0058) from 1887 CE (VS 1944) instructs Jayarāmadāsa, the thenmahantaof this temple, to make arrangements for food and accommodation for ascetics staying in theakhaḍā.
An inscription here recounts Prime Minister Juddha Śamśera restoring the temple damaged in the 1934 earthquakes without clearly mentioning if it was a renovation or a reconstruction.
After the temple sustained damages in the 2015 earthquakes, the Department of Archaeology rebuilt the rest houses and the temple in 2023 CE (VS 2080).
In the course of dismantling the temple for reconstruction, bricks with the inscription ‘Śrī3 Candra’ were recovered from the temple’s foundation.
This suggests that the temple was built during the reign of Prime Minister Candra Śamśera (1901-1929 CE).

The Sulima Āgama is the oldest survivingāgamachẽ(esoteric shrine) building in the Kathmandu Valley.
The three-storied building had a tympanum (toraṇa) displaying an image of Nṛtyeśvara above its main door, however this was stolen in 1998.
This building is the onlyāgamabuilding of the Valley known to have a ground floor built from solid dressed sandstone.
These walls were adorned with wall paintings dating from the first construction of the building, however these paintings did not survive the restoration process in 2016.
These fine but heavily damaged paintings depicted nine deities in a row, and were the last examples of such wall paintings from this period in Patan.
The door and windows of the principal façade mostly date back to the 15th century and were restored and conserved.
No inscription could be found to confirm the date of this building's original construction.
Inside the building, there is an inscription which was installed during the reign of King Śrīnivāsa Malla (r. 1661–1685).
However,Burleigh(1976, 39) reads the date of the inscription as NS 701 (1581 CE).
No more information about the inscription could be gathered; only those descending from the aforementioned two lineages are allowed to enter theāgama.
The building had suffered extensive damage following several decades of neglect.
The roof of the building partially collapsed in 2012, leaving the structure exposed to rain.
The 2015 earthquake caused further damage and it was only in in 2016 that the KVPT started the restoration process.
Its original structure is well preserved and an inscription dates the baluster columns back to 1871 CE.
Minor renovations were undertaken in August of 2003 CE (VS 2060-65).

The Pīgaṃdyaḥ Pīṭha was established for protecting the town of Balambu.
Kumāra Śreṣṭha, a resident of Balambu, constructed a wall at the premises and also offered a roof.
The earliest inscription from the area is the record of the installation of two stone figures of lions by theguthis of Bhāro and Bhābos of Balambu.
Due to the poor condition of the inscription, the date cannot be ascertained although the first digit can be read as '8'.
As the inscription mentions the name of the king as Mahīndra Malla, it is certain that the event took place in between his reigning years NS 829 (1709 CE) and NS 835 (1715 CE) (Burleigh 1976, 56).
Interestingly, the inscription records that the lion figures were offered to Cāmuṇḍā, not Mahālakṣmī.
After the statue was stolen, Gurmāṃ Bājyā, a resident of Balambu, offered a new statue in VS 2042 (1985 CE) (local knowledge, local resident, Maharjana, male, age 70).

Reṇukābhakteśvara Śivālaya, one of the nine Śivālayas erected by Kṛṣṇa Bahādura Rāṇa, stands in the Gorakhanātha premises.
Aśivaliṅgais installed in the sanctum, with Pāñcāyaṇa deities positioned at its four corners.
Furthermore, a statue of Kāmadeva is installed in the southeast.
G. Ṭaṇḍana (VS 2053, p. 346) and Michaels and Tandon (2017, p. 62) have marked the temple as a Śivālaya on their maps.
Kṛṣṇa Bahādura Rāṇā, the younger sibling of Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā, is renowned for constructing several temples, with Nau Śivālaya being particularly popular.

The Śivālayas in Gorakhanātha were constructed in the year 1863 CE (1920 VS). (Michaels and Tandon (2017, p. 106). Following the earthquake of 2015 CE (2072 VS), numerous Śivālayas suffered severe damage. The Paśupatī Area Development Trust has undertaken the reconstruction of the dilapidated Śivālayas in 2019 CE (2076 VS). Even though the reconstruction is done, the temple roof doesn’t have its finial. However, the reason for the absence of finial on the temple roof remains unknown to the priests (priest of Nau Śivālaya, Ḍhuṅgela, male, age 55).A Brāhmaṇa belonging to the Davāḍī caste, conducts ritual worship of all Śivālayas in Gorakhanātha. text: Despite its name, which implies the presence of fivecaityas, only three remain today (June 2024 CE).
The current threecaityas, constructed from brick and concrete mortar, each feature an empty niche on their eastern side.
Locals interpret the name "Pā̃camāne" as “five measuring pots,” although historical records confirm their original establishment ascaityas.
The construction of the Nyāgaḥmaṇicaityasis recounted in two versions.
The first attributes their creation to Atiśā Dīpaṅkara Śrījñāna, a Buddhist scholar who traveled from India to Tibet and passed through Nepal in 1041 CE.
According to this account, Atiśā and his 20 followers built fivecaityas—four black and one large white—at the Pā̃camāne mountain pass (Decleer 1996, p. 45).
A map drawn by Chinese official Song Yun (1754–1835 CE) following the Nepal-China war depicts these fivecaityas(Boulnois 1989, p. 100).

Additionally, apaubhāḥpainting from 1802 CE in the National Museum of Delhi and a painting by Margaret Oldfield from 1857 CE both show the fivecaityas(Decleer 1996, p. 53; Oldfield & Oldfield 1975, Plate no. 8).
The second version ties the construction of Nyāgaḥmaṇi to the Sino-Nepal wars of the late 18th century.
Tensions over currency issues and the asylum granted to the Shamarpa Lama led to the first Nepal-Tibet conflict, which ended with the Kerung Treaty of 1789 CE.
However, Tibet’s failure to fully comply with the treaty led to renewed conflict in 1791 CE, with China intervening on Tibet’s behalf.
Chinese forces, advancing through the Pā̃camāne pass, eventually reached Betrāvatī in Nuwakot, where a treaty was signed in 1792 CE (Uprety 1980, pp. 42-43).
The Nyāgaḥmaṇicaityasare said to have been built during this war, commemorating the arrival of the Chinese forces at the pass (Regmi 2007, p. 471).
Oral traditions also suggest that the fivecaityaswere constructed in memory of Chinese emissaries who perished during the conflict (Oldfield & Oldfield 1975, Plate no. 8).

Although oral traditions attribute thecaityas’ construction to the Chinese army, it is likely that Tibetan soldiers in the Chinese forces, who revered Atiśā, undertook the renovation of the Nyāgaḥmaṇicaityas.
At that time, the original structures may have already been in disrepair.
By 1985 CE, fourcaityasmade of bricks, clay, and stone remained (Boulnois 1989, pp. 101-103).
Over time, the Nyāgaḥmaṇicaityasfell into neglect until restoration efforts began, spearheaded by Nirmalaratna Tulādhara.
In 2014 CE (VS 2071), the three remainingcaityaswere renovated, and a statue of Amoghasiddhi was installed in the south.
A Malaysian Rinpoche provided NRs. 25 million for the reconstruction of the two lostcaityas.
This Rinpoche, through meditation, recalled that he had built the Nyāgaḥmaṇicaityasin a past life, leading him to fund the renovation.
Restoration efforts continue under the Pā̃camāne Jīrṇoddhāra Samāja, which has also built a retaining wall to prevent future landslides.

The current structure of the temple, however, dates back to the medieval period, although the exact year of its construction and the donor remain unclear.
According to a chronicle, Pratāpa Malla's son Nṛpendra Malla (r. 1674-1680 CE) built a double-layered temple of Jayavāgīśvarī (D. Lamsāla 2023, p. 94).
It is possible that he constructed a new temple by adding another layer of walls to the existing one.
Interestingly, during the renovation of the temple after the earthquakes in 2015, evidence of the temple's previous construction was observed.
The temple of Jayavāgīśvarī miraculously remained intact after the devastating earthquakes in 1934 (Devamālā Vaṃśāvalī 2013, p. 34).
However, during the earthquakes in 2015, the uppermost tier of the temple was dislocated, and the walls suffered cracks.
In order to reconstruct the temple, it was dismantled, and during this process, the original structure with three finials and a wall mural was recovered (S. Maharjana 2019, p. 3).
These precious elements were preserved and incorporated into the reconstructed temple.
Additionally, aśivaliṅga(PPK1222-008) was discovered during the dismantling and was reestablished at its original location within the temple.
After the completion of the reconstruction work in 2023 CE (VS 2079), the temple was opened to the public once again.
In 2011 CE (VS 2068), the Pashupati Area Development Trust implemented a new regulation that introduced a salary-based appointment system for the priests and established a retirement age for them.
Chamomile flowers, known asdhavaḥsvāṃ, are brought from Bhaktapur and offered to the deity during this occasion.

Furthermore, on every full moon day, a duck is sacrificed at the Navadurgā shrine, which has a trust established by King Raṇabahādura Śāha for its worship.
The Maṇḍapa's name derives from the Newari word “dhvākhāpine” which literally means “outside the door” and indicates that the original Phalcā was constructed just outside a historical city gate.
Originally, the structure was built in the shape of a two-storey south-facing Phalcāand its roof was covered with corrugated metal sheets.
Before the earthquake, the local governmental authority rented the space out as a shop.
The new Maṇḍapa was reconstructed in 2019 at a cost of NRs. 25 lakh (ca. US$ 17,000) with funding from the LUMANTI Support Group for Shelter and local contributions.
The upper part of Dhvākhāpine Maṇḍapa is open on all sides and can be accessed by newly installed stairs at the south.
A new gate has been built right next to the new Maṇḍapa.
This is an unusual construction, since such monuments normally have their storage rooms on the first floor.
With no written records available, the identity of the builder and the construction date remains unknown.
An inscription from CE 1825 (NS 945) mentions the renovation of a structure, possibly a Śivaliṅga, by Tejanarasiṃha, a resident of Phasikeba. Śivaliṅga was initially established by his ancestors.
On the full moon day of Kārtika in 1955 CE (VS 2012), Gopāla Bahādura led an overnight religious song (Harirāma Kīrtana) organized by Kaviprasāda Gautama at the site of the Hanumāna statue.
Following the event, a stone stele was erected with instructions to continue singing religious songs at this location annually.

This three-bayed Phalcā, built in the 16th-17thcentury CE, takes its name because of the main deity and statue of Gaṇeśa (also the neighborhood deity Sthānagaṇeśa) placed inside and its location in Samala Ṭola.
While it is unclear when the Phalcā was first constructed, the original statue of Gaṇeśa and the Toraṇa on top is said to belong to the 16th-17thcentury (Shokoohy et al2014, p.110).
Samala Gaṇeśa Phalcā was rebuilt into a concrete structure of two floors in the mid-1980s.
In 2014 CE (VS 2071), another  floor was added with financial support from the Kirtipur Municipality Office.
The Guitaḥ Gaṇeśa Temple was constructed from the Guṭhī comprising Śākyas and Maharjana caste members of the Ṭola.
There are some other statues established on the plinth of the Temple.
Moreover, there is also a Sarasvatī statue (LAL2030-011) established in 1775 CE (NS 895) by a certain monk īndrajyoti.
We have no historical sources to date the initial construction of the Temple.
In 2008 CE (VS 2065), it was reconstructed with the financial support from the Lalitpur Municipality.
On this day,samaybajiis offered to the deity.

A Buddhist scripture namedMaṇiśailaMahāvadānamentions that in 1300 BC (Kaligata Era 1801), Jogadeva Vajrācārya had founded the town of Sankhu in the shape of aśaṅkha(conch shell) by assimilating seven villages as per the instruction of Vajrayoginī.
He had divided the town into eightṭolas and constructed a palace at the center, along with the shrines ofaṣṭamātṛkā, ninebāhāḥs, and four gates in four directions.
However, there is no historic record of the Temple’s construction.
A person named Jñānavajra Vajrācārya had got the Temple renovated in 1964 CE (VS 2021).
His son commissioned the construction of a new gate to enter the Temple premises in 2013 CE.
She was enshrined in the form of an esotericyantraof stone by offering a human sacrifice during the reign of King Śivadeva in 206-205 BC (Kaligata Era 2895-96).
Two or three years later, Paśupatinātha invited various goddesses, such as Bhadrakālī and Kaṃkeśvarī, from Kathmandu and founded the tradition of worshipping Vatsalā with a human sacrifice.

Later, during the reign of King Viśvagupta in 80 CE (Kaligata Era 3181), special worship was performed to appease Vatsalā to replace the annual human sacrifice with an unblemished black he-goat (Devamālāvaṃśāvalī2013, pp.36-37).

He also established the tradition of feeding a group of virgin boys and girls on the 13th lunar day of Caitra, and lighting an uninterrupted fire (akhaṇḍāgni) at the Mahādeva shrines of the entire city on the 14th of the dark fortnight of Caitra (Piśācacaturdaśī), and the chariot of the goddess to be carried around in a procession (Nepālikabhūpavaṃśāvalī2016, 12.136-137).
Besides these accounts, there is no historical record of the temple’s initial construction.
There is, however, a large stone inscription set on the rear wall of the Pañcagaṇeśa Mandira north of Vatsaleśvarī.
The fully-eroded inscription related to the Vatsalā Mandira probably belongs to the Licchavi period.
Other historical records from the temple document the endowment of over 45ropanīs of land to set up a trust to perform various rituals at the temple in 1675 CE (NS 795) (M. Panta VS 2055, pp.43-44).
Likewise, King Raṇabahādura Śāha offered the horns of a wildarnābuffalo for fermented beer (thvã) to be poured from it on to the stoneyantrarevered as Goddess Vatsalā (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2056, p.290).
Another record relates to the offering of a bell to Vatsalā by Ṭhākuraprasāda Ṭaṇḍana Lāhurī Kṣetrī and his wife in 1911 CE (VS 1968) (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2056, p. 111).
The 1934 earthquakes did not render any damage to the temple (Devamālāvaṃśāvalī2013, p. 37).
In 2017 CE (VS 2074), the Chaudhary Foundation in cooperation with the Pashupati Area Development Trust renovated the temple and furbished it with colors.

TheNepālamāhātmya, a scripture recounting the legends of sacred places and deities of Nepal, states that worshipping and receiving the blessed view (darśana) of Vatsalā, after purifying oneself with a bath in the holy Bagmati river, will grant devotees a place in Kailāśa, the divine abode of Lord Śiva.
On the new moon day of Caitra, Vatsalā is bathed with locally brewed beer made from fermented rice (thvã), which is discharged through the horns of a wild buffalo offered by Raṇabahādura Śāha.
A member of the Dhvaṃ Guthi (lit. jackal trust) then howls like a jackal thrice.
The Dhvaṃ Guthi, as recorded in Guṭhī Saṃsthāna (VS 2071, p.41), possesses over 31ropanīs of land.
The history behind the construction of this Dabū is unclear like the other historicdabūs of Sankhu.
However, ‘NS 797’ is inscribed on a stone, which can be seen on the northern side of the Dabū.
The year corresponds to 1677 CE but it is unclear whether the year refers to the construction of the Dabū or some other event.

There is another inscription on the same side that records the renovation of the Dabū by the Sālkhā Ṭola Sudhāra Samiti, a committee of local residents for the care and welfare of the Ṭola, in 2009 CE.

During reconstruction, the stone lintel was replaced with a RCC beam, which was heavily damaged in the 2015 earthquake.

The main sanctum building is built on the western wing and faces east across a courtyard measuring 12.95 m × 12.95 m.
The building is a three-storey structure with aphucāon top of the ridge of the gale roof.
Two stone lions guard the entrance, and access to the sanctum is restricted by a metal grill-work that has been installed for security.
The coping of this cornice has been constructed in concrete rather than special cornice bricks.
The roof of the building is covered in plain copper sheets, and the eaves are decorated with metal frill work.
Thephucāis built in brick masonry on top of the ridge with bands of decorated carved cornices, and this entire structure is surrounded by wooden latticework.

However, local residents say that Bikhu Siṃha Bhāro (a Śreṣṭha and a resident of Ikhāchẽ Ṭola) constructed thisvihārain NS 757 (1637) during the reign of King Siddhi Narasiṃha Malla and handed over to Dharmacakra Guruju, Dharmadeva Guruju and Lāyaju Śākya.

The Kārañjitaghāṭa Sataḥ, originally erected by the Kārañjita clan alongside a temple, underwent a significant transformation around 1983 CE (2040 VS).
The former two-story Sataḥ was replaced with a single-story concrete structure (attested by a guṭhī member, Kārañjita, male, aged 52).
The Kathmandu Inventory (Inventory VS 2039, p.162/photo) includes a photograph of the original Sataḥ.
A larger inscription placed in the Sataḥ has unfortunately been obscured by a thick layer of ghee, thus rendering it unreadable.
Consequently, the year of construction and the identity of the builder remain uncertain.

During the early Śāha to late Rāṇā period, affluent families undertook the commissioning of sataḥs, caityas, and statues at the convergence of the Bāgamatī and Biṣṇumatī rivers, extending up to the junction of Bāgamatī and Ṭukucā.
The three adjacent sataḥs to this one were built by Colonel Gupta Bahādura Kārkī, Sāhu Dharmanārāyaṇa, and Munsī Lakṣmīnārāyana during the Rāṇā regime.
This implies that this Sataḥ was likely commissioned by a prosperous individual in Kathmandu during the same era.

The inventory published by the Kathmandu Valley Department of Housing and Physical Infrastructure attributes the construction of the Sataḥ to Ratnavīra, although the source of this information is unspecified (Inventory VS 2039, p.162).
Probably, the Sataḥ was built to serve the temple (KAT2613) situated in front of it, suggesting that both structures may have been erected by the same individual.
Presently (2023 CE), the maintenance of the Sataḥ is overseen by the Kārañjita clan from Kathmandu.

The door is built as a tripartite portal.
Gutschow(2011, vol. II, 395) suggests that these struts were probably added at a later date.

Purandara Siṃha, a Mahāpātra of Lalitpur made a donation for the initial construction of this temple in 1566 (see the inscription from NS 686 below) in memory of his father, Viṣṇu Siṃha.

Later, Viṣṇu Siṃha’s three sons Nara Siṃha Deva, Purandara Siṃha Deva and Uddhava Siṃha Deva jointly ruled Lalitpur until 1597, when Śiva Siṃha Deva took Patan back from the local dynasty and restored it to Malla rule (cf. Gurschow 2016, 101).
TheNepālikabhūpavaṃśāvalī(19.2.88) mentions that Purandara Rājavaṃśī built the temple of Nārāyaṇa in front of the palace in Lalitpur during the reigning period of King Mahendra Malla.

An inscription to the left of the main deity is no longer readable, but a jagged-edged knife (kartṛ) and a skull cup (kapālapātra), the implements of Bhairava, can still be seen on its topmost part.
Although there is an inscription at the shrine, it fails to provide any information on the establishment of thepīṭhadue to the erosion of its text.

In contrast, a copper-plate inscription from 1583 CE (NS 703) refers to the main deity as Devāvatāra, which is also a reference to Maitreya Buddha.

Therefore, we can assume that the Maitreya statue was replaced by a statue of Padmapāṇi Lokeśvara sometime after Pruscha but before Locke mapped the site, possibly because the original statue was stolen or damaged.
