The inscription of Aṃśuvarmā, dating back to 608 CE (Māndeva Era 32), includes the first known reference to Māneśvara, the male counterpart of Manamāneśvarī.
Licchavi King Mānadeva (r. 464-505 CE) had previously established Manamāneśvarī as his tutelary deity.
Originally named "Māneśvarī," meaning "the goddess (īśvarī) established by Mānadeva," the epithet "mana" (desire) was added later to signify her power to fulfill desires (Y. Acharya VS 2061, p. 24).
The main deity, Manamāneśvarī, is represented by a copper pot placed on a stone lotus pedestal within a secret chamber on the ground floor (P. Darnāla VS 2078, p. 213).
Although a golden pot was originally used, it was replaced with a copper one after being stolen (Y. Acārya VS 2061, p. 28).

The chamber also houses other deities, including an iconic representation of Manamāneśvarī in the form of an eight-armed Bhagavatī established by King Bhāṣkara Malla in 1702 CE (NS 822) (Y. Acārya VS 2061, p. 28).
As it is also worshipped as Bhairava, animal sacrifices are offered here, while Manamāneśvarī does not accept blood sacrifices.
According to theGopālrājaVaṃśāvalī, King Mānadeva consecrated Manamāneśvarī after establishing the Mānavihāra (Vajrācārya and Malla 1985, folio 21A).

Later chronicles like theBhāṣā Vaṃśāvalīfurther elaborates that he commissioned a golden statue of the goddess and composed a hymn in her honor, installing her in the royal palace itself (N. Pauḍela VS 2020, p. 77-78).
This suggests that Mānadeva's palace was built around the site of the Manamāneśvarī Dyaḥchẽ.
The practice of establishing tutelary deities predated Mānadeva's reign.
His great grandfather, Viśvadeva (also known as Vṛṣadeva), had consecrated "Rājadevī" in the nine-storied palace that he had built (N. Pauḍela VS 2020, p. 74).
However, there's no direct mention of Manamāneśvarī in any of Mandev's inscriptions.
The deity, Śrīdevī, mentioned in the Aṃśuvarmā inscription of 606 CE (Mānadeva Era 30) was possibly a reference to Manamāneśvarī.
Although Manamāneśvarī is missing in Licchavi inscriptions, her male counterpart, Māneśvara, first appears in the Aṃśuvarmā inscription from 608 CE (Mānadeva Era 32).
The inscription records the allotment of financial assistance to various temples and monasteries, including Māneśvara (D. Vajrācārya 2030, pp. 320-321).
This indicates that Māneśvara, having already been established, had also received state recognition during Aṃśuvarmā's reign.
A dateless Licchavi inscription from Naxal Nārāyaṇacaura elevates Māneśvara to the status of a "draṅga" or urban settlement (D. Vajrācārya 2030, p. 565), further solidifying its significance.
King Bhāṣkaradeva (r. 1045-1048 CE) sold his father’s crown and destroyed the golden statue of Māneśvarī, resulting in severe suffering, including blindness (Vajrācārya and Malla 1985, folio 23B).

In the colophon of a manuscript titled "BhāratīyaNāṭyaśāstra" written in 1223 CE (NS 344), King Abhaya Malla is praised as "Śrī Māneśvarīpādapaṅkaja" (a lotus at the feet of Māneśvarī) (Petech 1984, p. 83; M. Panta VS 2070, p. 181).
Nevertheless, Manamāneśvarī, instead of being replaced, continued to be worshipped with equal status as of Taleju (Slusser 1982, p. 319).
In the colophon of theKāmandakīyaNītisāra, a manuscript copied in 1527 CE (NS 647), Manamāneśvarī is mentioned as the tutelary deity of King Sūrya Malla (M. Panta VS 2070, p. 186).
In 1702 CE (NS 822), King Bhāṣkara Malla established an eight-armed statue of Bhagavatī (Y. Acārya VS 2061, p. 28).
On the same date, a strut with a carving of Bhairava trampling on Vetāla was also installed at thedyaḥchẽ.
The name of the strut's donor is not inscribed, but it was possibly King Bhāṣkara Malla himself who established the Bhagavatī statue and also installed the strut.
Although Manamāneśvarī was established during the Lichhavi period, thedyaḥchẽmust have been built only in the later medieval period (P. Darnāla VS 2078, p. 211).
In 1771 AD (VS 1828), Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa Śāha exempted 104ropanīs of land dedicated to Manamāneśvarī frompotātaxes (M. Panta VS 2044, p. 68; Y. Acārya VS 2061, pp. 84-86).

text: In 1799 CE (VS 1721), King Gīrvāṇayuddha granted land with an annual produce of 420murīs to set up a trust to ensure the smooth conduct of worship at Manamāneśvarī (Y. Acārya VS 2061, pp. 87-88).
Deo, conducted excavations in the vacant area north of thedyaḥchẽin 1965 CE.

The excavations yielded artifacts such as Paśupati coins, stone seals with the imprint of a cow and calf from the Aṃśuvarmā period, and earthenware from the pre-Lichhavi period (P. Darnāla VS 2078, pp. 211-212).
In 2001 CE (VS 2058), the Kathmandu Metropolis carried out the renovation of the Manamāneśvarī Dyaḥchẽ (P. Darnāla VS 2078, pp. 211).
During the Lichhavi period, when a great fire ravaged Hā̃ḍīgāũ, the principal priest of Manamāneśvarī moved to Lalitpur and established Agniśālā (LAL0280).
Under his guidance, the Karmācārya family of Hā̃ḍīgāũ was appointed as the temple's priests (Y. Acārya VS 2061, p. 47).
The customary offering of two goats and a duck from Bhaktapur Taleju to Manamāneśvarī in Hā̃ḍīgāũ on the 5th of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha is still observed (V. Śarmā VS 2050, p. 40).
Special fire worship (agnipūjā) was performed twice a month, on the first day of both the bright and dark fortnights (Y. Acharya VS 2061, p. 47).

The worship of Manamāneśvarī would only be performed after offering sacrifices of a buffalo, goose, and goat to the Māneśvara Śivaliṅga, and then having four Karmācārya priests ritually offer pieces of the neck meat as oblations (Y. Acharya VS 2061, pp. 39-40).

Although there was a tradition of performing fire oblation at Manamāneśvarī and Ṭũḍāladevī on every 14th of each lunar fortnight, the ritual is only performed at Ṭũḍāladevī these days (S. Tiwari 2023, p. 91).
There is a stone inscription attached to the northern wall of the temple below the Garuḍa-toraṇaproviding information about its construction.

Rāmacandra Mandira, built in 1864 CE, stands in the centre of a courtyard at Jaisidevala in Kathmandu.
The temple's ground floor walls are built in the style typical of a tiered temple, but it has a bell-shaped masonry upper portion with a small finial.

text: A large inscription on the temple's western wall dates its construction in 1864 CE (VS 1921).

It was built by Ḍiṭṭhā Dharma Siṃha and his younger brother Premanārāyaṇa Siṃha from Jaisīdevala Ṭola, and it included rest houses (caugharā sataḥ) on all four sides of the courtyard, as well as a garden and a pond.

Known as Cakramukteśvara, thisśivālaya, or abode of Śiva, was erected in 1894 CE (VS 1951) as a tribute to Lieutenant Cakra Śamśera, the third son of Prime Minister Vīra Śamśera.
Hanging from a bell-stand south of the temple is a brass bell bearing inscriptions about the temple's construction.
Despite the temple being constructed in 1894 CE (VS 1951) in memory of Lieutenant Cakra Śamśera, the individual responsible for its construction is unclear from the bell inscription.

Cakra Śamśera is the third son of Prime Minister Vīra Śamśera and the first from his second wife Topakumārīdevī, a Newar from Thimi, who held the title ofŚrī3Baḍāmahārānī(the main queen) after Vīra Śamśera became prime minister (Rāja VS 2071, p.22).
Married but passing away at a young age (Rāja VS 2071, p.25), the wish for Cakra Śamśera's eternal peace is evident from the temple's construction.
It is, therefore, confirmed that he had already passed away by 1894 CE, during the lifetime of his father Vīra Śamśera, who himself passed away in 1901 CE (VS 1957) (Rāja VS 2071, p.21).
Damaged in the 2015 earthquakes, the temple underwent restoration by the Pashupati Area Development Trust in 2019 CE (VS 2076).

An inscription dating back to 1745 CE (NS 865) is found on the pedestal of the northern lion statue, constituting the earliest historical record at the Pīṭha site.
Although the exact year of the Pīṭha's establishment remains uncertain, the above-mentioned inscription on the lion statue traces its history back to the medieval period.
Another medieval inscription, dated 1758 CE (NS 878), records the construction ofphalcāwalls in the vicinity, providing evidence of thephalcā's existence in the mid-18th century.
Jogānārāyaṇa Dhānjule rebuilt this temple in 1832 CE (NS 953), and during reconstruction its entire form was altered and rebuilt in a new style.

The inscription is on a large boulder situated on the side of a path 400 meters east of the village of Kālikā Bajār (Kālikoṭ).
The inscription is facing north-west.
The first line, inscribed in Rañjana script, contains the mantra of Avalokiteśvara.
The line below it is written in Nāgarī script and contains the name of the king under which the inscription was carved.
The document is typical of inscriptions from the 1350's, whereOṃ maṇi padme hūṃ, Avalokiteśvara's mantra, is written in Rañjana, followed by a text in Nāgarī.
Similar inscriptions are found on the Patharnauli reservoir in Dullu (DLK0160) and on the Kuchi Bihāra stūpa and reservoir (ACH0010).
The inscription was first mentioned by Yogi Naraharinath (Naraharinath VS 2013 (1956), p. 75) and by Giuseppe Tucci (Tucci 1956, p. 43).
It can be assumed that thephalcāwas constructed for the people who gather here in thehitifor cleaning and doing their laundry.

Although the inscription is lost, we know of one inscription from 1692 CE (NS 812), mentioning that Yasovanta Siṃha constructed it in the name of his late father, Māhākāra Bābu.
The inscription also mentions the donation of a statue of Bhavānīśaṅkāra in 1693 CE (NS 813), a year after constructing thephalcā.
It is probable that this was added during thephalcā’s initial construction.
However, this inscription is now lost.
D. Vajrācārya(VS 2056, 284) has published an inscription which he found in a dilapidatedpāṭībehind the Ālko Gaṇeśa Temple.

It mentions that a person by the name of Bhavānisaṅkara Bābu from Dvaka Ṭola reconstructed the structure, which was almost in a dilapidated condition.
The same donor later established a  statue of Bhavānīśaṅkāra in thephalcāand endowed land for future repairs.
Names of six devotees are carved on the bottom part of the inscription.
It is possible that he is the same person also mentioned in the inscription published by D. Vajrācārya.
If that is so, then it is highly likely that thephalcāwas constructed in 1692 CE (NS 812).
However, since that inscription is lost, a final evidence can not be provided.
Buĩcā Hiti Phalcā was completely reconstructed in 2017 CE (VS 2074), with the financial support from Lalitpur Metropolitan City and the World Bank.
Two old wooden columns from the previous structure were used for the reconstruction.
The statue of Bhavānīśaṅkāra mentioned in the inscription is not in thephalcāin the present-day.
A signboard with thephalcā's name was installed by PURPP/LMC (Pro-Poor Urban Regeneration Pilot Project under the Japan Social Development Fund of the World Bank and the Lalitpur Metropolitan City).

The pole needs to be replaced every few decades, the last time in 1978, when it took three days to carry it from Nālā to Sunāguthil.
A special ritual takes place on Caitra Caturdaśī to mark the beginning of the three-day long festival at Sunāguthi known as Pekhaḥ Jātrā.
Theyaḥsipole is then erected in front of the Bhṛṅgāreśvara Mandira (SUN0100).

King Raṇajīta Malla is believed to have constructed this temple.

Additionally, a bell is installed on both the northern and southern sides of the plinth.

This Caṇḍeśvarī is established as a symbolic representation of the Caṇḍeśvarī in Banepa (J. Rasika VS 2075, p. 90).

After the procession concludes, the statue of Caṇḍeśvarī is placed within the temple premises, where guṭhī worship is performed by various guṭhīs, followed by a feast enjoyed by the locals (J. Rasika VS 2075, p. 331).
The Bālakumārī Mandira in the Devapattana area boasts an intricately adorned arch (toraṇa) that bears the date 1682 CE (NS 802), suggesting its construction during the late-medieval period.

The artistic style of the Durgā and Bālakumārī statues is similar, indicating that the statue of Bālakumārī may have also been established in the 17th century (Ṭanḍana VS 2053, p.477).

The daily and periodic rituals of this Buddhist monastery (bāhāḥ) established in 1876 CE (VS 1933) by Harṣaratna Vajrācārya and his son Tejaratna Vajrācārya were later reinstated by Jyotiratna Vajrācārya.
Instead of akvapāḥchẽ(main monastic building) housing the principal deity (kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ), it features an east-facing, bell-shaped shrine.
Thesecaityaswere installed followingutkrānti, a post-death tantric ritual.
Thebāhāḥwas founded in 1876 CE (VS 1933) by Harṣaratna Vajrācārya and his son, Tejaratna Vajrācārya, with contributions from Harṣaratna's wife, Harṣalakṣmī, and other family members.
It was constructed on two adjacent plots of land.
The other, granted to Bhājuvīra Prajāpatī of Jyāthā Ṭola, Khyāḥ Bāhāḥ in Kathmandu bylālamohara(royal decree), was purchased by Harṣaratna.
Combining these two plots, Harṣaratna built thebāhāḥ.
Following its construction, he installed thetriratna(Akṣobhya, Prajñāpāramitā, and Lokeśvara), acaitya, and images of Meṣasamvara, Vajrapāṇi, Mahāmañjuśrī, and Bhīmasena.
Land was endowed to thebāhāḥas a religious trust to support its annual rituals.
Thebāhāḥlater fell into mismanagement, but daily worship and other religious practices were reinstated by Harṣaratna's grandson, Jyotiratna Vajrācārya in 1913 CE (NS 1033).
Jyotiratna also erected a commemorative stone inscription.
Because of his systematic organization and management, thebāhāḥbecame known as Jyotiyā Bāhāḥ (Jyoti'sbāhāḥ), after him (R. Vajrācārya VS 2075, p. 241).
The then Prime Minister, Manamohana Adhikārī, presented alms to the initiates (P. Vajrācārya NS 1144, p. 35).
Upendra Vikrama Śāha, King Rājendra's second son, is attributed to building the Taleju temple in Sundhara, Kathmandu.
Legend says he used his tantric power to establish Goddess Taleju at his temple, yet no historical proof confirms this.
Accused of plotting against his elder brother (King Surendra) in 1856 CE (VS 1908), he was confined in Allahabad.
Returning in 1858 CE (VS 1910) to Bāga Darbāra, he immersed himself in tantric practices, possibly founding the Taleju temple.

Originally characterized by a three-tiered roof, the temple suffered during the 1934 CE earthquakes, prompting its reconstruction as a simplified one-story structure crowned with a corrugated metal roof.
The tremors of 2015 CE led to further damage, culminating in the demolition of threesatahs(East-, West-, and North-wings) by May 2023 CE.
The temple's revival is manifested through a substantial concrete edifice currently (as of May 2023 CE) taking shape on its northern precincts, shielded by a metal enclosure barring entry.
Caugharā Bāga Guṭhī trust and Upendra Vikrama's descendants oversee the temple's management and reconstruction with Guṭhī Saṃsthāna.
It is not known when the sataḥ was built.
Due to the lack of maintenance the sataḥ collapsed and remained in ruins for many years.
In 2010 CE (2067 VS) reconstruction was initiated with funds from the Embassy of India.
The Sataḥ's reconstruction was completed in 2013 at a total expense of NRs. 5.6 million.
The jaḥdhuṃ next to the sataḥ was built in 1583 CE (NS 703) by Purandarasiṃhadeva, a powerful local functionary.

Patan’s Matsyendranātha Guthi regularly repaired and maintained the jaḥdhuṃ until the responsibility was handed over to the local community in 1975 CE.
A drinking fountain (jaḥrũhiti) is also attached to the building.
Reconstructed in 2017 CE in traditional architecture with some modifications, this rest house also functions as the shrine of the main Gaṇeśa (Sthānagaṇeśa) of the Thāṃ Bāhāḥ Ṭola in Kirtipur.

According to a photograph published in Pruscha (1975, p. 30 [K-73], the Temple's roof was tiled with traditional brick tiles (jhĩgaṭī). Aśivaliṅgacan be seen on the northwest of the Temple.According to an inscription from 1849 CE (VS 1906) at the site, which records an offering made by a certain Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa Śreṣṭha of Kulāṃbhulu, the Temple was built by Māthavarasiṃha Thāpā, who was the head of the government in the mid-1840s. However, it does not state the date when he built it. Pruscha (1975, p.30) incorrectly writes, without citing a source, that it was built by Upendra Vikrama Śāha, younger brother of King Surendra (r. 1847-1881 CE).Meanwhile, an inscription no longer present at the site confirms that it was indeed Māthavarasiṃha Thāpā who established Goddess Bhagavatī here in 1837 CE (VS 1894) and constructed a temple for the deity in 1844 CE (VS 1901). He also installed a golden finial on the temple after the completion of its construction and endowed 75ropanīs of land to form aguṭhīfor carrying out various rituals at the temple (D. BhaṇḍārīVS 2026, p.135). Aguṭhīdocument related to the temple refers to it as Raṇadivyaśvarī (N. ŚreṣṭhaVS 2079, p.288).According to oral tradition, Amarasiṃha Thāpā used to bring the statue of Bhagavatī enshrined in this Temple to all of the battles he fought during his lifetime. He believed that the goddess had granted him victory in battle. As a result, the goddess is also known as Raṇadivyaśvarī, a divinity of war (based on a personal conversation with a member of the Thāpā clan, male, age 52).

Social activities like blood donation programs are also organized here at the Sataḥ.
Constructed during the early Śāha period by a prominent state officer, the Jayarudreśvara Mandira continues to receive visits from his descendants for annual worship.
Inside the sanctum, a stoneśivaliṅgais enshrined as the main deity, referred to as Jayarudreśvara in the temple's inscription.
Jāiphala Adhikārī, a government officer (subbā), commissioned the temple's construction in 1815 CE (VS 1871) (G. Taṇḍana VS 2056, pp. 420-23).
In the accompanying inscription, he traces his genealogy back to his ancestor Bhāradvāja.

The inscription also documents the construction of the Gaurīghāṭa bridge, the establishment of a path near the cremation site, the construction of a rest house, and other infrastructure projects, along with the provision of food for a thousand brahmins.
Additionally, he endowed 48ropanīs of land to establish a trust responsible for temple rituals and maintenance.
Ancient texts refer to such structures asgiridurga, meaning "hill fort" (D. Śarmā VS 2055, pp. 11-13).
Apīṭha(seat) shrine of Bhairava is established inside the fort as the main protective deity and can be considered the primary structure within the fort premises.
A sacrificial pole (object no. NWK0640-001) can be seen erected on a stone-piled platform with a pair of lions (object no. NWK0640-002 and 003) guarding it.
A newly-built temple of Kālikā stands in front of thepīṭha.
The Kālikā shrine (object no. NWK0640-006) in front of thepīṭhawas reconstructed by the Department of Archaeology in 2023 CE (VS 2080) (a local resident, Rijāla, male, age 63).
On the next day, the 1st solar day of Māgha, a Brahmin from the Rijāla caste performs fire rituals here at the fort.
Thispīṭhaof Mahālakṣmī is established in the small Newar settlement called Bālāgāũ in Mātātīrtha located southwest of Kathmandu, functioning as the protector of the area (kṣetrapāla).
Two imposing stone lion statues flank the steps leading to the complex where two inscriptions can be seen.
One, dated 1721 CE (NS 841), chronicles the establishment of thedāphābhajana, a group of devotional singers led by Mānadeva of the Suraṃki dynasty.
It also records the construction of the rectangular stone structure at thepīṭha.
Following the Muslim invasion of Gujarat in India, members of the Suraṃki (Solaṃkī) dynasty sought refuge in Nepal (Ṭ. Śreṣṭha VS 2078, p. 39).
Having established Pharping as their primary center, the people of this dynasty actively participated in governance and eventually ascended to the position of rulers of Pharping.
The colophon of theAgastyaSaṃhitāmanuscript, copied in 1335 CE (NS 455), mentions Jaitasiṃha of the Solaṃkī dynasty as the ruler of Pharping (Regmi 1965, pp. 409-410).
Thehiti(BLG0010) constructed for this shrine was also built by Balabhadra Bhāro of the same dynasty.
Another inscription from 1724 CE (NS 844) mentions Jayakṛṣṇa Bhāro as the leader of the initiative to erect a wall around the premises of the Mahālakṣmī shrine.
While the installation of the lion statues must have been a significant endeavor, no inscription detailing their placement has been discovered.
Following a fire oblation and an animal sacrifice performed by a Vajrācārya priest, the palanquin carrying the statue is paraded around Bālāgāũ on the subsequent day.
Additionally, an animal sacrifice used to be offered by a Vajrācārya priest on this occasion.

The inscriptions at thepīṭhareference the establishment of adaphābhajana, a group of devotional singers, and the Saṅkrānti Guthi, a religious trust dedicated to performing worships on the first solar day (saṅkrānti) of each month.
In the western enclave of the Hanumandhoka Durbar Square, a series of temples and statues were added by the royal family over time.

Historian G. Vajrācārya (VS 2033, p. 38-42) notes that during the Malla period, this section was named "Svakambu." Among this historical landscape stands the Varāha Temple, a concealed structure hidden from the view of the main road.
However, there are no historical records chronicling the initial construction of the temple.
However, the devastating earthquake of 2015 CE (2072 VS) necessitated its reconstruction.
Located in Omabāhāla Ṭola, Paḥkhāḥ Bāhāḥ serves as a branchbāhāḥof Viśvakarmā (Bikamā) Bāhāḥ, which is known to have been established before 1706 CE (NS 826).
The Dyaḥchẽ of this bāhāḥ is constructed as a three-story structure.
An inscription dated 1905 CE (NS 1126) is located on the base of the toraṇa.
After thebāhāḥsustained damage from the earthquake of 2015 CE (VS 2072), the upper floor and roof were renovated with the assistance of the local community.
In addition, a caitya (KAT2170-002) and aDharmadhātujinālayacaitya (KAT2170-003) are established in the courtyard of thebāhāḥ.
An inscription, along with a statue of Padmapāṇi Lokeśvara, can also be seen affixed to the wall of the house situated on the western side of the courtyard.
No direct inscription regarding the establishment of thisbāhāḥhas been found to date.
Locke (1985, p. 358) mentions that there is a copper inscription at the front part of thebāhāḥwhich refers to it as "Khasā Chẽ Bāhāḥ," but he does not clarify the date inscribed on it.
An inscription dated 1706 CE (NS 826) (KAT0760_I_001) related to the reign of King Bhāskara Malla has been found at Bhoṭe Bāhāḥ (KAT0760) in Kathmandu.

According to this inscription, Siddhimuni Vajrācārya of Varṣacandra Mahāvihāra, which is a branch vihāra of Om Bāhāḥ, established Bhoṭe Bāhāḥ and arranged a land trust (kheta guṭhī) for its operation.
Based on this, it becomes clear that thisbāhāḥwas already established before 1706 CE (NS 826).
An inscription dated 1905 CE (NS 1026) is present on the lower part of the artistic woodentoraṇainstalled above the main door of thebāhāḥ.
According to this inscription, it is known that Caityavara Siṃha, the son of Harṣamāna and grandson of Rudramāna Śākya, along with his family, offered the woodentoraṇa.
However, Locke (1985, p. 358) has mentioned the date of thistoraṇaas NS 1024.
However, due to various reasons following the devastating earthquake of 2015 CE (VS 2072), the daily worship has not been conducted regularly at thisbāhāḥ.
King Śrīnivāsamalla is said to have built Taleju Mandira (LAL1270) in 1663,  rebuilt Mūla Coka in 1666 and established the Yantāju shrine at its centre.
The origins and construction records of the palace buildings of the Patan kings were poorly documented up until the beginning of the 17th century.
The Patan palace area's oldest historic record is an inscription on a stone stele at the north end of the Patan Darbar Square dated 570 CE.
During Viṣṇumalla's reign in the 1730s major renovations and the reshaping of the palace building were carried out.
This included the installation of the golden door ensemble in the south wing featuring life-sized statues of Gaṅgā and Yamunā and the donation of a gilt door andtoraṇa.
In the 1850s, a much larger main door was installed under the patronage of Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā.
Copper-plate inscriptions recording various treaties and declarations were attached to the courtyard's walls.
Unfortunately, most of these inscriptions were lost in the recent past (VajrācāryaVS 2056, 313).
The upper floors of the building are used as exhibition galleries of the Patan Museum.
Thistoraṇawas offered to the temple by King Ṛddhinarasiṃha Malla in 1714 (NS 834).
The 1934 earthquake caused the collapse of the east wing and dealt major damage to the north and west wings.
The ensuing reconstruction efforts resulted in a poor quality reconstruction in which recycled materials were used.
The roofs were rebuilt with inadequate timber and had a much-reduced overhang.
Between 2006 and 2012, the Kathmandu Valley Preservation Trust carried out a comprehensive restoration programme.
This included reconstructing the roof in its historic configuration and using traditional handmade terracotta (jhĩgaṭī)tiles.
Today, the palace building serves as an extension to the Patan Museum with galleries exhibiting historic architectural elements, artworks and a tantric shrine room.
This Cāmuṇḍa temple, a Śāktapīṭha, was constructed next to a cremation ground in an area locally known as Sika Bahī.
Gutschow & Shakya(1980, 174) have also included the site in their list of Buddhist monastic buildings even though no monastic buildings remain.
Various deities have been erected on the east wall of the temple.
A Karmācārya priest used to carry out worship ceremonies in the temple, however there is currently no priest installed here.
Legends tell that the Bagmati River used to flow nearby and Cāmuṇḍā Pīṭha was established at its bank next to a cremation ground.
It is rumoured that the smoke of the funeral pyres often enveloped the monastic building, and that this is why the Bahī got this name (Dyaḥpāḥlāḥof the temple, male, age 56).
After the Bagmati changed its course, the cremation ground was moved to its present location (Pickett2005, 251).
A statue of Umāmaheśvara bearing an inscription of the Śaka Era Year 495 (573 CE) bears testament to the fact that this is an ancient religious place (Vajrācārya2030, 211).
There is no record of when and by whom this shrine was established.
This king is best known for establishing Lalitpur, however, the chronicle's claim is not supported by any other historical document.
An inscription dated NS 939 mentions that the temple of the mother goddess was constructed in 1696 CE.
The temple survived the earthquakes of 1934 and 2015 unscathed.
The Viṣṇu temple is a two-tiered structure that originally was a smallśikharā-style building.
The Garuḍa statue in front of the temple (KAT1501-002) was partially buried up to its chest until 1988 CE (VS 2044).
In the same year, the statue was unearthed and repositioned above ground (S. Rājavaṃśī VS 2044, p. 19).

An inscription on the Garuḍa statue's pedestal records the land donation by Uddava Bābu, a resident of Maṃgalā̃chẽ, Bhaktapur, for the observance of Mādhava Bhaṭṭāraka's anniversary ritual in 1583 CE (NS 703).
Curiously, Uddhava, a person of royal status from Nhurachẽ in Maṃgā̃lāchẽ of Bhaktapur, later engaged in acts of charity in Kathmandu (O. Dhaubhaḍela VS 2075, p.45-50).
The inscriptions' mention of King Śivasiṃha and Raṇajitasiṃha confirms their co-reign during that period.
Meanwhile, Koṭiliṅgeśvara's inscription reveals that Raṇajitasiṃha was Śivasiṃha's younger brother (M. Panta VS 2034, p. 89-90).
It remains uncertain whether the temple's construction coincided with the establishment of the Garuḍa statue in front.
Conversely, M. Panta (VS 2074, p.58-61) claims the statue dates back to the 6th century, with its pedestal bearing the inscription of another sculpture attached later.

In 2004 CE (VS 2061), the locals of Makhana Ṭola, the Department of Archaeology, and the Kathmandu Metropolis collaborated to reconstruct the temple into a two-tiered structure (local resident, Śreṣṭha, male, age 63).
The original statue was stolen, and a new one was installed.
While there is no definitive record of the construction of the Kvāṭhaṇḍau Hiti in Bhaktapur’s Kvāṭhaṇḍau Ṭola, the presence of an inscription from 1548 CE (NS 668) suggests that thehitipredates it.
Unlike typicalhitis with a deity statue above the spout, this one has a niche of acaitya, possibly placed there after the deity’s statue installed there was stolen.
On the northern wall above thecaitya, three statues are installed: a central Śiva statue flanked by donor statues.
To the northeast, aśivaliṅga, Nandī, and a stone pillar with the 1548 CE (NS 668) inscription are established.

The only historical record, the 1548 CE (NS 668) stone pillar, notes the installation of statues of Vijyādhari (Vidyādhari) and Gatirāja, devotees of Viṣṇu, likely the male and female figures above the spout.
This indicates thehitipredates 1548 CE.
No records of renovations or other activities exist.
Along the surveyed artefacts are elements of a least oneśikharatemple (BTD0020-001), a stone lion (002) and three inscribed stone memorial pillars (003 and 004).

The dimensions of these objects are as follow:- stone lion, BTD0020-002: 70 x 90 x 25 cm- memorial pillar, BTD0020-003: 109 x 41 x 39 cm- memorial pillar, BTD0020-004: 101 x 34 x 35 cm- memorial pillar, BTD0020-005: 85 x 36 x 35 cmThe pillars are dated but the content of the inscriptions remains mostly unclear, except for pillar 004, where one may read the date of ŚS 1309 (1387 CE).
The structure is built with locally available materials such as stone, earth, and timber, and displays no deliberate ornamental or decorative treatment.
No dedicatory inscription relating to the construction of this Sataḥ has survived.
However, the persistent oral tradition referring to it as Janārdane Pāṭī indicates that it was commissioned by Janārdana Sāpakoṭā.
In 1914 CE (VS 1971), Janārdana, also known as Pṛthvīvilāsa, constructed both a Śivālaya and this Sataḥ at his family’skuladevatāsthāna.
The construction of Janārdane Pāṭī appears to have been intended to facilitate these emerging religious and cultural practices.
On this basis, the Janārdane Pāṭī can be securely dated to a period after 1914 CE (VS 1971).
During the 1980s CE (VS 2040s), the originaljhĩgaṭīroofing was removed and replaced with corrugated metal sheets.
Even prior to the 2015 earthquakes, the structure had already fallen into a dilapidated condition.

Although the earthquake did not cause its collapse, local informants report (2025 CE) that the Sataḥ exhibits multiple structural cracks and widespread detachment of the plaster surface (oral testimony R. Sāpakoṭā).
Materials required for the cremation of the deceased used to be kept on the upper floor of this building.
However they have since been removed, as it was considered inappropriate to store cremation materials above the Nāga.
A legend tells that Vāsukī and Campaka protect the donations made during the Samyak festival.
The story goes that unhusked rice was once offered to many people.
Upon witnessing this, a Vajrācārya living in Ikhāchẽ Ṭola recognised the glory of the serpant couple and organised that two Phalcās for the Nāgas be built in the area (S. Vajrācārya2058, 31).
The legend further tells that one of the descendants of the Vajrācārya, Tuhudeva, funded the construction of Ālko Hiti (LAL0990).

On the day of Samyak (4th day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna), both the snakes are offered onesumari(a kind ofroṭī) and a handful of rice in the hope that they will allow the festival to take place without any problems.
In 2019 (VS 2076), the Lalitpur Ward Office provided 1.4 million rupees for the reconstruction of thephalcā.
The area of Ajayamerukoṭa is rich in monuments that were mostly erected during the 14th and 15th centuries.
This political and economical rise is demonstrated in the numerous monuments erected between the second half of the 14th century and throughout the 15th century.
Other pavilions were built in Ajayamerukoṭa, probably around the same time (DDL0050,DDL0140).
D. R. Sharma estimates that the pavilion was built around the 12th-13th century (Sharma 2012, p. 314-317).

While the monument indeed shares architectural features with construction such as the Baleśvara complex of Champawat (Uttarakhand, India), dated of ca. 1100-1250 by N. Chanchani (Chanchani 2019, p. 164-166) or some of themaṇḍapaof ca. 10th century temples inPadavali/Bateśvara(Madhya Pradesh, India), it also shows variations from these models.
It is more likely that the pavilion was in fact built around the time of the rise of the Doti kingdom, i.e. in the second half of the 14th century.
The artefact does not show any inscription but may be attributed to the 14th-15th century.
It is believed that the Temple is constructed in the shape of the chariot of Bhairava that is pulled during theBiskāḥJātrāin Bhaktapur.
Later, a temple was constructed at the site and was named Indrasiddhi after both Indra and Gaṇeśa.
There is no historical record of the Temple's initial construction.
An inscription from 1649 CE (NS 770) is there on the plinth of the statue of a lion west of the steps leading to the sanctum.
It records the installation of a pair of lions.

A small room at the northeast corner is accessible from both inside and the front, and a single-run stone staircase on the southern wall ascends towards the sanctum where the main statue of Bhīmasena, depicting him killing Duḥśāsana, is installed.
The two lower roofs are covered withjhĩgaṭītiles, while the top roof is covered with brass sheets, a later addition as indicated in a photograph by Bourne & Shepherd, taken around 1870 CE.

Lalitpur houses four main Bhīmasena temples: Juju Bhindyaḥ (the King's Bhīmasena) in Mangalbazar, Puṃ Bhindyaḥ (the artists' Bhīmasena) in Sundhara, Dhvākhā Bhindyaḥ (a Bhīmasena placed near a door) in Chāḥbahāla, and Kumhāḥ Bhindyaḥ (a Bhīmasena established by potters) in Cyāsal.
Although no historical document records the initial construction, the monument was once a rest-house (capāḥotdharmaśālā) known as Balaṣūni Capāḍa.

TheKīrtipatākā(in vers 79-80), a poem composed by Kunu Śarmā in 1652 CE (NS 772), mentions this building and explains that the merchants became prosperous thanks to Bhīmasena, who killed Kīcaka and defeated Kauravas in the Mahābhārata war.
The post colophon ofDānaratnākarareveals that the building initially had only one storey.
In 1627 CE (NS 747), during the reign of King Siddhinarasiṃha Malla, a certain Hari Bhāro renovated thecapāḥas a one-story building.
A stone stele inscription confirms that in 1681 CE (NS 801), King Śrīnivāsa Malla reconstructed it into its present temple form by adding two additional stories. (Regmi1960, 287).
To the south of the entrance, a bell donated in 1697 CE (NS 817) can be found and another bell, donated in 1697 CE (NS 817), hangs to the north of the entrance.
The temple's roofs are supported by struts adorned with images of Bhairava, Gaṇeśa, Bhīmasena, and other gods, donated between 1682-1683 CE (NS 802-803).
In 1701 CE King Yoganarendra Malla replaced the clay statue of Bhīmasena with one made of bronze and initiated the Bhīmasena procession tradition.
Surviving the 1934 CE earthquake, the temple suffered substantial damage during the earthquakes of 2015.
Between 2015 and 2016, a team from the University of Applied Arts, Vienna, meticulously executed the restoration of both the pillar and the lion statue.
Between 2019 and 2022 CE, the upper two tiers of the temple underwent dismantling and reconstruction under the technical guidance of the Kathmandu Valley Preservation Trust.
During this period, a small replica of the Bhīmasena statue was installed on the ground floor to ensure uninterrupted worship.

text: Traditionally, statues of Pañcabuddhas are established in acaitya’sniches.

text: However, statues of Maitreya Buddha, Vajrapāṇi Lokeśvara, Padmapāṇi Lokeśvara, and Mañjuśrī are established in its eastern, southern, western, and northern niches of this Caitya, respectively.

text: Judging from its design and the Buddha statues, it can be assumed that the Caitya was constructed sometime in the 17thCentury.

monument_name: Vajradhātu Caitya (known as Khāsti Caitya, built in  17th cent.)
text: An inscription situated in the Caitya’s premises from 1682 CE (NS 802) mentions the establishment of aguṭhīand associated rituals on the day of the Kojāgrata Pūrṇimā or Katiṃpunhi.

monument_name: Vajradhātu Caitya (known as Khāsti Caitya, built in  17th cent.)
text: On the Kojāgrata Pūrṇimā day, four bamboo poles are erected in the four corners of the Caitya.
The three-bayphalcāis integrated into a four-storey building owned by a Tāmrākāra family.
As of December 2023, the structures situated behind and above thephalcā, along with the building to the south of it, have been abandoned.
However, it appears that it was altered during a reconstruction at some point, as the wooden posts, capitals, and lintels seem relatively modern.
There are no historical records to date the construction of the Pāṭī.
It appears that the construction of this phalcā is attributed to Rakṣakumārī Devi, the mother of Jaṅgabahādura Rāṇa.
Nonetheless, there is a probable connection between this phalcā and the nearby Śivālaya that she erected.
An additional floor has been added above the phalcā, connected by a vertical ladder, with simple windows and a roof covered in zinc sheets.

An inscription on the inner wall of the phalcā reveals that Rakṣakumārīdevī Rāṇā, wife of Bālanarasiṃha Kũvara Varmā Rāṇā, granted 50 ropanīs of land for a three-day donation event to visitors on the day of Śivarātrī in Mṛgasthalī in 1854 CE (VS 1911).

Additionally, 46 ropanīs of land were dedicated for the rituals and donations to Rakṣeśvara and Raṇabāleśvaradevī, along with an extra 22 ropanīs of guthī land for Gorakhnātha’s anniversary ritual and the donation to visitors.

Serving as bhārādāra during the rule of kāji Bhīmasena Thāpā (Ācārya VS 2075, p.142), Bālanarasiṃha's wife, Rakṣākumārī, made this significant donation during her tenure as the wife of an ancient courtier and mother of Jaṅgabahādura.
Notably, she also installed Rakṣeśvara Mahadeva (PPK1937) in front of this Pāṭī in 1843 CE (VS 1765) (Ṭaṇḍana VS 2056, p.493-495).
While the inscription implies Rakṣākumārī's role in facilitating donations for visitors and the inclusion of inscriptions, it does not explicitly mention the construction of the phalcā itself.
Raksha Kumari constructed a Śivālaya and a phalcā, generously donating sufficient land to facilitate daily rituals and festivals on various occasions.

An inscription details the annual traditions during Śivarātrī, involving lighting lamps in all directions of the Śivālaya, observing Mahādipa on the full moon day of Kārtika, performing fire oblations in front of the Śivālaya, and contributing to Brahmaṇa on the tenth dark fortnight of Vaiśākha.
Following the damage and insufficient space caused by the earthquake of 2015 CE (VS 2072), a family that had long resided in a nearby sataḥ relocated to the upper floor of this sataḥ.
However, in 1677 CE (NS 797), it was renovated by six members of Hāthu Guthi.
It used to be a one-storied phalcā withjhĩgaṭī-tile roof that was then converted into a concrete building with one floor in 1969 CE (VS 2026).
In 1999 CE (VS 2055), it was dismantled again and rebuilt as a two-storied building.
An inscription from 1677 CE (NS 797) mentions the tradition of discharging fermented beer (thvã) from a Bhairava mask (hāthuhāyke) to be observed at the Phalcā during theYẽnyāḥfestival.
The entry porch of the complex has four wooden pillars and is suggestive of a colonnadedphalcāwith seating space added at a later date.
The sanctum building faces east and has a central main door with two stone lions guarding the steps that lead up to it.
The three-storied esoteric building faces east and has aphujāabove it.
A brass-clad aedicule has been fixed to the right of the window and a gilded window has been installed to its left.
The building attached to thedyaḥchẽto the north is used by the Sanāḥ Guṭhī, which is also called Rājakarṇikāra (Halvāī) Śaraṇa Guṭhī.
The southern building attached to the sanctum belongs to the Bāhāḥ.
No inscription or any other documented evidence could be found to provide any information about the establishment of the Bāhāḥ.
The king invited these two individuals and offered them land at Hastināgala Ṭola.
They later became integrated into the Buddhist Newar community and established their ownbāhāḥ.
An inscription located inside the building records that the phalcā was commissioned by Śivarāma Mahāna Bhāva of Mikhābāhāḥ in 1712 CE (825 NS), in memory of his late father.
Seven years later, Śivarāma Mahāna Bhāva donated the Bhuyū Cībhāḥ (LAL0821) in remembrance of his mother.
The inscription also mentions that Bhāva donated a statue of Triratna which used to be placed in the phalcā but has disappeared.
The historic phalcā was demolished in 2013 and replaced with a four-storey brick and concrete commercial building.
In the past the members of a guthi founded by the Jyāpu community of Mikhābāhāḥ used to end religious events by resting in the phalcā and eatingsamaybaji.
Today, the same guthi manages the commercial building that replaced the phalcā.
The commercial building provides substantial income to support relious and social programs whereas otherguthisin Patan have become inactive or disappeared altogether due to a lack of income.

As the Rājavaṃśī clan, its original builders, have continuously inhabited the courtyard where the temple stands, the rituals associated with the shrine have been carried out without interruption by the same family lineage.
The courtyard features beautifully carved traditional windows from the family's house, preserved in their original state despite minor damage.
While the exact date of construction for the Kṛṣṇa statue and Hanumān pillar remains uncertain, their intricate carvings suggest they belong to the late Malla period.
Inside the sanctum, Garuḍanārāyaṇa is the main deity, flanked by Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa and Lakṣmī, though the latter two were stolen in the 1970s (Rājavaṃśī clan member, male, age 87).
DuringŚivarātrī, a bonfire is lit, and sweet pudding (haluvā) is distributed as a sacred offering from Śiva.
Toward the end of the 1960s, a flood in the Rudramatī river eroded the nearby fields, causing the wall adjacent to the then-existing Sarasvatī temple to collapse (S. Tivārī 2023, p. 187).
It was only around the 1970s that this statue was installed here (S. Tivārī 2023, p. 99).
The beautiful statue suffered a theft attempt in 1967 CE (VS 2024).
The statue was recovered from the Tribhuvan International Airport and reinstalled here at same location (local resident, Daṃgola, male, age 56).
In 2001 CE (VS 2057), the temple was reconstructed at the leadership of the then-ward chairman, Sukharāma Maharjana.
In 2006 CE (VS 2063), Jānu Gautama built a shrine north of the temple and installed the statues of Gaṇeśa (KAT3081-003), Hanumān (KAT3081-007), and other deities.
Known as Nandabhakteśvara, thisśivālaya, or Lord Śiva's abode, was built in 1865 CE (VS 1922) by Nandakumārī, the wife of Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā, expressing her devotion to Śiva.
The temple, made of stone and built on three plinth levels, features a bell-shaped roof with a metallic finial.
Outside, a bell hangs from a bell stand to the south, likely indicating the temple's construction.
However, the bell's inscription is no longer legible, so its exact content is unknown.
Nandakumārī Rāṇā, wife of Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā, commissioned the temple in 1865 CE (VS 1922) (Michaels and Tandon 2017, p. 106).

Jaṅga Bahādura married Nandakumārī, the younger sister of Sanakasiṃha Thāpā, in 1839 CE (VS 1896), and she bore him two sons, Jagatjaṅga and Jītajaṅga, and a daughter, Tārākumārī (Rāja VS 2073, p. 5).
The temple collapsed in the 2015 earthquakes but was rebuilt by the Pashupati Area Development Trust in 2019 CE (VS 2076).
As the gate is situated at the Samala Ṭola, people also refer to this gate as Samaladhvākhā [seeHerdick(1988, p. 49) andŚ. Śreṣṭha(VS 2057, p. 35)].
A royal order issued by King Śrīnivāsa Malla of Patan in 1673 CE outlines the responsibilities of the citizens to upkeep such fortification walls (Slusser1982, p. 99).
Also, an inscription of King Yakṣa Malla, dated NS 573 (1453 CE), records the role of his subjects in caretaking and renovating fortification walls, trenches outside the walls, and the fort itself.
It also assigns certain punishments to those who cause damages to them (D. VajrācāryaVS 2021, p. 20-33).
Since such walls were no longer needed after the Gorkhali invasion, they were not anymore taken care and renovated (Slusser1982, p. 99).
Unfortunately, the Sīdhvākhyā already lost its former shape to an unnecessary reconstruction in VS 2055 (1998 CE) (Ś. ŚreṣṭhaVS 2057, p. 35).

The gate was reconstructed because it was not wide enough to allow vehicles like taxis, ambulances, fire brigade, etc. to pass into the city at times of emergency (local knowledge, local resident, Maharjana, male, age 69).

text: Pruscha(1975: C/P-279) dates the temple to 1681 and mentions that it was renovated in 1970.
A heavily damaged inscription is attached to the southern wall of the temple.
Taṅgala Ṭola Sudhāra Samiti reconstructed the building in 2003.
Two stone pillars erected on the west side of the main road to Dailekh Bazar.
Eroded inscriptions are present on the east face of the north pillar and on the west face of the south pillar.
Stone pillars were erected throughout the Karnali Basin from the 13th to the 17th century.
They are installed to honor the memory of deceased persons, mostly warriors.

The town of Lubhu is said to have been established by Hariharasiṃha Malla, the king of Patan, with 300 households in 1586 CE (NS 706), wishing for the protection his children (Yogī Devinātha VS 2013, p. 7).
He also established Mahālakṣmī Pīṭha, the seat of the goddess, and initiated the annual procession.

During the reign of King Amara Malla, the son of Ratna Malla, various festivals were organized and villages were upgraded, and one of these villages included Lubhugrāma (D. Laṃsāla (part 2) VS 2023, p. 56).

An inscription from 1549 CE (NS 669) at the Mahālakṣmī temple reveals that Lubhu was also called Suvarṇa Chatra (Śreṣṭha and Jośī NS 1133, p. 77), thereby also giving the town another name, Suvarṇapura.

Six half-sized brass statues grace the sanctum with Mahālakṣmī established in the middle, flanked by Gaṇeśa and Kumāra, on one side while next to them are the statues of Bhairava in the middle, flanked by Gaṇeśa and Kumārī.
The courtyard provides space for fire rituals and worships related to the temple.
Historical records providing definitive information about the temple's initial construction are currently unavailable.
However, the discovery of inscriptions within the temple, spanning from 1549 CE (NS 669) to 1767 CE (NS 887), unequivocally establishes its existence in some form by the mid-16th century.
Pruscha (1975, p. 252) posits that the temple was constructed in the 17th century and subsequently underwent renovations following the earthquakes of 1934.
He further notes the presence of a bell dating back to 1668 CE and a toraṇa from 1749 CE within the temple.
A small metal inscription affixed to the eastern window of the temple offers a glimpse into its past.
Dated 1646 CE (NS 766), it records an offering made to Luṇḍakoṃḍa Bhairava by Nārāyaṇasiṃha Bhāro, Satyarāma Bhāro, Tulasīrāma Bhāro, and other residents of Lubhu.
The inscription's current state of deterioration precludes the identification of the offered item.
The lion statues flanking the main entrance of the temple were installed in 1658 CE (NS 778) (Vajrācārya VS 2056, p. 113).
The trust members prepare for a fire ritual and worship within the temple premises.
The Paṭāṅgīni Deval are located in the centre of Dullu, north-east of the former king's palace (destroyed by Maoists in April 2002,Lecomte-Tilouine 2009).
Twośikharatemples are built in front of each other, in a plan usually referred to asdui deval(double temple).
They are erected on a 340 x 460 cm stone platform.

The Baṭārabajāra Sattala, featuring three bays, was built by members of the Pradhāna Khalaka family, a family influential since the early Śāha reign.

While there are no inscriptions directly associated with the sattala, an inscription dated 1911 CE (VS 1967) on a nearby water spout (NWK0710) indicates that the descendants of the stone spout's builder also constructed the sattala (NWK0710_I_001).
The stone spout was built by the son of Munsī Gaurīdāsa, who settled in Baṭāra from Kathmandu.
It is thus likely that the sattala was built by this family during the early Śāha period.
An inscription from 1739 CE (NS 859) is located on the pedestal of the Buddha statue in the sattala.
After the damages caused by the 2015 Earthquake, the sattala was reconstructed by the Department of Archaeology in 2021 CE (VS 2075).
On the full moon night of Bhādra, ritual food(samayabaji)is displayed in front of the Sattala, organised by Purāno Bajāra Vikāsa Saṃsthā from 2023 CE (VS 2080).
The Umāmaheśvara temple located in the area is aśikhara-style temple and built in stone.
Moreover, smallśikharastructures have been erected at the four corners of the level.
There is a damaged inscription attached to the western wall of the temple.
The inscription records that it was constructed in NS 834 (1714 CE).
The record also mentions that at that time aguṭhīwas also established for the management of the temple.
This three-bay Phalcāhas been built in a traditional Newar style and is attached to S. Avāle's house.
Both couples are the ancestors of S. Avāle; this can be gleaned from the inscription has been placed below the statues.
The monumentcollapsed in the 2015 earthquakes and was reconstructed in 2018.
Adyaḥchẽis a building dedicated to the Eight Mother Godesses (aṣṭamātṛkās) built within the city proper.
The three medieval cities of the Kathmandu Valley were founded under the protection of theaṣṭamātṛkā-pīṭhas (abode).
However, proper statues of these deities are established at thedyaḥchẽwithin the city.
The Mahākālī Dyaḥchẽ is one of such houses of gods, i.e., Mahākālī in this case, within the city while herpīṭha(BKT0017) is established outside of the city (at the northern part of Bhaktapur).
Devotees andbhajanasingers offered worship to the image every day, as it was easily accessible to all.
The deity is summoned through tantric practices at thepīṭhaand she is offered animal sacrifices.
There are not historical sources to date the initial construction of the Dyaḥchẽ.
Therefore, nothing is known about its construction or the sponsor.

Traditionally, the Kakṣapatis are businessmen and the Dyaḥchẽ was probably built by these rich merchants from the high-status sub-caste of Kakṣapati at the middle of the 18th century (Gutschow2011, p. 579).

A chronicle namedDevamālāvaṃśāvalīmentions that King Ānandadeva established Bhaktapur as a large city in Kaligata Samvat 4197 (CE) and formed a protective ringaṣṭamātṛkāpīṭhas around the city periphery and enshrined golden statues of the deities within the city at their respectivedyaḥchẽs (YogīVS 2013, p. 106).

In the course of renovating and reconstructing various monuments of Bhaktapur during the period of 1974 to 1985 CE, the GTZ dismantled thephujāof the Dyaḥchẽ and reconstructed it while also carrying out other minor renovations to the building.
The Mahākālī Dyaḥchẽ is one of the few monuments in Bhaktapur that sustained little damages during the earthquakes of 2015 CE.

Likewise, in another entry in their records, 6ropanīs of land can be seen allocated for ‘Śrī Mahākālīkā Narabali Bhanyā Hāla Mulā Kāṭne Guṭhī’, aguthithat appears to have opted to offer a white radish in place of a human in sacrifice (Guṭhī Saṃsthāna2071, p. 50).
This suggests that a human sacrifice used to be offered to the deity but the tradition was later replaced by chopping a white radish.

Although the records show ample amount of land in the name of the deity, the concerned people say that many plots of lands are no longer in possession of the deity’sguthi(local knowledge, local resident, Kakṣapati, male, age 77).
