text: The Gãdyaḥ Phalcā is located at Pukhusi, Sunaguthi (widely known as Sunakothi) at the junction where a street leading towards Kulimha curves away from the Sunāguthi main road.
No evidence could so far be traced with which to date the initial construction of this Phalcā.
The photo published inPruscha1975 (vol. 1), 99 shows the building's original structure before it was rebuilt in 1995 due to damage suffered by its earlier five-bayed structure.
The reconstruction saw the addition of a blank masonry wall to the rear and eastern sides.
Local residents come here to worship the masks and take part in a procession around Sunaguthi.
Constructed during the late 19th century by a Buddhācārya family, the Āḥjudyaḥ Bāhāḥ Dhvākhā Phalcā was built as a space dedicated to the distribution ofsamaybajiduring theYẽnyāḥfestival.
The creation of thephalcācan be attributed to Nara Buddhācārya (text: Budhācārjye Bhāju Nara) in collaboration with his wife Thakumati and other family members in 1886 CE (NS 1006).
The passage of time and a lack of timely maintenance led to the survival of only the western wall of thephalcā, which bore an inscription.
In 2001 CE, the Bhaktapur Municipality undertook the reconstruction of thephalcā.
This tradition was established by the original donors, and it is in the name of Thakumati.
Constructed by King Bhūpatīndra Malla in 1712 CE (NS 832), this Śiva temple is notably large in scale and architecturally distinctive.
Among the two largest Śiva temples in Khvaṃrha, both featuring a distinct architectural style, the one built by Bhūpatīndra Malla is slightly more expansive.
Later, in 1892 CE (NS 1012), the abbot (mahanta) of the Taumadhi Maṭha added another similar Śiva temple nearby.

Among the many Śiva temples in the Kathmandu Valley built following the Śiva Pāñcāyana tradition, the Taḥdhaṃ Mahādeva temple stands out due to its inclusion of eight additional deities alongside the usual four (Viṣṇu, Durgā, Gaṇeśa, and Sūrya).
Furthermore, while numerous Śiva temples in the valley adhere to this concept, octagonal Śiva temples constructed on multi-tiered stone platforms are exceptionally rare.
A pillar on the upper plinth, featuring a carved figure of Nandī, bears an inscription documenting the temple’s construction by Bhūpatīndra Malla in 1712 CE (NS 832).
Nearly two centuries later, around 180 years after its completion, a second Śiva temple was erected nearby, replicating the same architectural style and form.
Theft became a serious issue in the 1980s, with statues being stolen one after another (local resident, Rāya, male, age 56).
As of March 2025, replicas have been installed in place of the stolen artifacts.
Several medieval inscriptions refer to the locality as 'Cusathuri,' which later evolved into ‚Cīthū‘.
It is noteworthy that the original Gaṇeśa statue and a wooden toraṇa were stolen in the 1960s and subsequently replaced with new ones (Shokoohys and Śreṣṭha2014, p.280-281).
Adjacent to the main shrine, another stone statue of Gaṇeśa is installed in a wall niche.

Although no inscriptions within Cīthū Phalcā provide direct information about its original construction, the earliest known inscription, dated to 1674 CE (NS 794), records only the year and the name “Custhurī,” an earlier form of the quarter's (Ṭola) name.
The stone bearing this inscription closely resembles the stone used for the toraṇa, suggesting that it may document the installation of the toraṇa itself.
Shokoohys and Shrestha (2014, p. 282) similarly associate the inscription with the toraṇa.
During the recent reconstruction of the phalcā, a stone capital bearing an inscription dated to 1697 CE (NS 817) was discovered, indicating the former presence of a bell mounted on a stone frame.
This gable roof was later replaced with a shed roof following the construction of a multi-story ward office building adjacent to the phalcā.
The 2015 earthquakes caused severe damage, leading to Cīthū Phalcā’s complete reconstruction by the Department of Archaeology in 2021.
Additional funding from Kirtipur Municipality supported the installation of carved wooden elements and special bricks used in the cornice.
This ritual involves a five-foot-tall wooden mask of Bhairava, crafted in Bungamati and permanently installed in Cīthū Phalcā.
Situated in a Tamang settlement, known as Kuncipvākal, on the foot of the Shivapuri hill, Kuncipvākal Caitya contains an inscription from 1789 CE in both Tibetan and Newari scripts.
The inscription refers to the place as ‘Kuncepogo’.

Later in 2010 CE, the remnants of what used to be acaityawere renovated to form a complete Caitya with the statues ofpañcabuddha, Padmasambhava, Vajrapāṇi, along with the figures of donors and a stone stele with the carving of the Svayambhū Caitya.
There are no historical sources to date the initial construction of the Caitya.

The above-mentioned inscription installed on the plinth of the Caitya is not related to the Caitya itself; it records the construction of a guesthouse in the village during the reign of King Raṇa Bahādura Śāha.
The inscription informs us that Dorje Lāmā, themukhiyāof the village, along with his wife Karmāvatī, son Śerbā Dorje and other relatives, constructed the guesthouse.
A Lāmā guru used to perform daily and other periodic rituals at the Caitya up until early 2000 CE.
Its L-shaped building was previously made up of two separatephalcā(one facing west, the other south).
These were constructed at different times, and later united during the restoration of the site in 2018.
According to the head of the Phalcā Renovation Committee, the smallerphalcā (which opens up to the south) had two bays, whilst the longer one (facing west) had eight.
These steps were later removed during its renovation in the 1990s.

Thephalcāborders Nārāṃhiṭi or Nāyahiṭi at the west and, partly, the south-west, and is attached to the building that houses the Gajalakṣmī Khānepānī Vyavasthāpan Samiti (English: "Gajalakṣmī Drinking Water Management Committee") at the east.
The western wing is dedicated to Bhimsen and an inscription dated 1750 CE documents its origin.
Dating back to 200 BC, this statue is one of the oldest in the Kathmandu Valley, and is positioned at the bottom of thehiti,next to the spring.
Thephalcācollapsed in the 2015 earthquake and was replaced with a provisional structure, so as to allowbhajananddāpha bhajanto be performed.
Only a few historical fragments were used in its replacement, which was funded by Photo Kathmandu (2015 and 2016 edition), UNESCO and the Kwelachhi Tol Sudhar Samiti¨, Ward No 9/11.
Before the earthquake, the largerphalcāwas called Bhaila Capaḥ of Nhesaḥ Kumhā/Avāḥ.
The smallerphalcāwas looked after and used by theguthiof the Āśālāl Avāle.
Tiwari also refers to it as Nayo Hiti Jadhu (inv. no 34.2b) and reports that there were plans to establish a garden in front of thephalcāin order to prevent garbage dumping and parking (1994:7).
The falca now also has an added on look with the extention to the south side.

Speaking to those concerned with architectural conservation (or a conservation action plan), Tiwari recommends the following in his 1994 report of Cyasa:"Nayo Hiti and Capa ensemble ( 31.2a, 14.la, etc.): Activation of the stone water conduits and clearing of its two reported sources and control of pollution entry locations from the first 'manhole' within settled area, improvement of drainage of pit, repaving ofhiti floor, action of the twin falcas to the west incorporating two basement rooms on either side of the main approach stairway, reconstruction of the corner falca as 'sunning unit', redesign and replacement of the way side seating to the north, relocation of the inscription and sculpture ( 56.6b, 60.6c) in dry positions, closure of east steps to first platform, relocation of 'Buddha image', clearance of encroachment in front upto Awah Guthi Capa, etc." (p. 24).
After the earthquakes of 2015, Nārāṃhiṭī Phalcā was very badly damaged and had to be demolished down to its plinth.
The analysis of the collapse was undertaken in the name of photo.circle, which raised 12,000 US dollars for the reconstruction from donations made to PhotoKathmandu 2015.
A third collection of contemporary photographs was donated by friends of photo.circle.
Since the platform was still in good shape, there was no need for it to be renovated.
However, the remaining 1m-high back wall was dismantled, as was the small part of the 'L' that was still standing but damaged.

These were rebuilt with the use of as much of the old material as was possible. 16 plain columns were found but most were in bad quality; they were found to be too small to support the roof. 6 of the carved columns were salvaged and were in good conditon.

The project proposal therefore planned for them to be reused (dating from the 'original' pati from before that previous reconstruction). 10 carved columns were to be made new, but were based on the design of the salvaged ones.
Similarly, the project foresaw the construction of 19 new capitals to be made (no capitals were used in the last restoration phase, which did not prepare the structre well for earthquakes).
The walls, windows and roof structure were also to be reconstructed from all new materials, including a corrugated roof.
The Kumārī of Patan is traditionally offered a seat here while the chariot of Buṅgadyaḥ is being pulled away from Thati Ṭola to Jawalakhel, and she is requested to observe the procession from there.

During its renovation in VS 2062, the Pāṭī was further elevated (to four storeys) above the road level in order to offer the Kumārī a more appropriate seat from which to observe the procession of Buṅgadyaḥ.
After its collapse in the Great Earthquake of CE 1934, it was rebuilt near its current location in front of the pond (Tapukhu).
In 2005, Kumārī Pāṭī was dismantled and rebuilt once again from the ground up.
The builders used new materials for its construction.

The Patī was moved ca. 3 m further south to make room for the widened road; the height of the plinth and the roof were increased; a large giltgajur(finial) was added; and new staircases (flanked by two stone lions) were built.
No inscription or documented evidence could so far be found regarding the time of the monument's construction and the donors behind it.
Two inscriptions recording the renovation of the Pāṭī in 1935 and 2005 have been incorporated into its wall.
The Pāṭī does not have aguthi.

As of January 2023 CE, thebāhāḥ's condition is lamentable; a section of the second-floor veranda has already collapsed, and at least two intricately carved struts on the first floor have been pilfered.
Thistoraṇa, featuring a central statue of Vajrasattva, was installed in 1633 CE (NS 754).
Unfortunately, the statue of Sarasvatī, positioned to the west of the entrance, has been stolen.
Fivecaityashave been erected on thebāhāḥ-courtyard.
Historical documentation is lacking to accurately date thebāhāḥ's original construction.
Local accounts indicate that thebāhāḥwas established by a member of the Sthāpita caste and later passed into the custody of Makhaṃ Bāhāḥ.
The earliest historical record from this site is an inscription on a strut dating back to 1624 CE (NS 745).
This inscription commemorates the offering of the strut by Devasiṃ and Bhima Bhāro.
The main edifice of thebāhāḥwas already in a state of disrepair when the earthquakes of 2015 CE inflicted further damage, pushing it to the brink of collapse.
Due to the dilapidated condition of the building, most members of Makhaṃ Bāhāḥ have ceased their regular visits for daily observances at this location.

Kālamocanaghāṭa Phalcā East is almost identical to the Kālamocanaghāṭa Phalcā West (KAT2784), with the two buildings sharing many details such as size, carving styles, and building materials, making it appropriate to refer to them as twinphalcās.

There is no inscriptive evidence regarding the construction of thephalcās;however, architectural features, such as the carving style of columns and arches, indicate that construction likely occurred between the Śāha and Rāṇā periods (e.g. mid 19th century).
An inventory from 1982 CE (VS 2039) reports the dilapidated condition of thephalcāsand recommends renovation.
A photograph depicts the poor state of Kālamocanaghāṭa Phalcā East at that time (Inventory VS 2039, p.132).

Despite its critical condition, the renovation was not undertaken, leading homeless families to repurpose the space as residences by closing the bays with brick walls to create rooms according to their needs.

In contrast to the renovation and reconstruction efforts undertaken for numerous monuments along the banks of the Bāgamatī after the earthquake of 2015 CE (VS 2072), these twophalcāshave remained neglected.
Prior to VS 2030, devotional songs and rituals were performed in thesephalcās.
The fountain (001) is surmounted by three partially dismantledstūpas(002, 003 and 004).
An inscribed block of cut stone is found on site.
A copper spout with amakarahead is now replacing the pvc pipe.
The plan suggests that another two smallstūpaswere originally built east and north of the central one.
This monument was built in ŚS 1276 (1354 CE) by Deva Varmā, a ministre of king Pṛthvīmalla (r. 1338-1358) (Andolfatto 2019, p. 96;Pant 2009, 301).
Their construction in Uttarakhanda dates back to the 10th century.

Most Jaḥrũhitis are constructed from stone, but this construction is made from a mixture of materials; while the tank is made from stone, the base and the top have been built using brick andsurkhiplaster.
The roof is covered in cement, which was probably added in 2006.
The Ākha family established the Jaḥrũhiti and continues to service it despite its disuse.
It does not have an inscription but its design indicates that it dates to the Licchavi era.
An inscription next to the well records the establishment of another caitya by a certain Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa in 1819 CE (NS 939).
A damaged inscription on the plinth of the thirdcaityarecords its renovation in 1899 CE (VS 1956).
The building can be accessed through a small door opening on the western boundary wall.
A small secondary entry door on the principal façade (the eastern end of the building) leads to a stairway.
There were two three-foldpasukā jhyāḥon the first and second floor, both of which were salvaged after the earthquake.
This building appears to be a normal residential building, however, this is in fact theāgãchẽof the Jośīs of Bakhumbāhāla and Kisis (Śreṣṭha) of Ombāhāla.
The three-storey building of the Āgamawas heavily damaged in the 2015 earthquake and now only the front wall of the ground floor remains.
The main deity has been relocated to a neighboring house and various small images have been preserved in the Patan Museum.
No historical record confirming the initial construction of the shrine is available.
A Gaṇeśa statue located to the north-west was established in 1434 (NS 558).
This provides grounds to assume that the Āgama may also have been constructed around this time, or may even pre-date the statue.
Architecturally, the temple is a simple square structure with a pyramidal roof, representing a relatively recent reconstruction although thepīṭhaitself may date back to the medieval period.

In the 1960s CE (VS 2020s), the earlier temple, also a one-storeyed brick-and-tile structure, was destroyed when a large tree beside thepīṭhacollapsed upon it, resulting in the tragic death of a young girl inside.
The present temple was rebuilt thereafter through local voluntary labor (śramadāna) and community donations.
Unlike mostŚākta pīṭhas, which are open-air and templeless, Bālakumārī Pīṭha has long been associated with a constructed shrine.
Though temples built atoppīṭhasare attested as early as the medieval period, they were generally open structures without doors.
No inscription precisely dates the original erection of the temple; however, the earliest extant record from the site dates to 1674 CE (NS 795).

The inscription states that “stonedevalas(shrines) were constructed on both sides and completed, and thepātro(ritual stone container) of this stone was dedicated.” It begins with an invocation to theiṣṭadevatāand records the construction of two stone shrines, indicating that the text does not refer to the construction of the temple itself.
Thus, it appears that aŚākyafamily who regardedBāl Kumārīas theiriṣṭadevatāconstructed small stone shrines and offered the stonepātra(SUN0260-004).

Another inscription dated 1871 CE (NS 991) mentions that “a stone was placed in thepīṭha-area.” The use of the termpīṭha-kṣetra(“thepīṭhaprecinct”) rather thanmandira-kṣetra(“temple precinct”) suggests that a substantial temple structure did not yet exist at that time.

In recent decades, however, the formerly openpīṭha-ground has increasingly been encroached upon by concrete buildings,phalchās(resting pavilions), and subsidiary shrines, reducing its earlier openness.

Within the broaderNavarātriobservance, on the day ofSaptamī, offerings of sparrows, pigeons, snakes, and buffalo are made into the fire ritual (havana), followed by the renewal of costumes and masks (local resident, Mahārjana, male, age 69).
The āgãchẽ was reconstructed in 2002 using reinforced cement concrete.
Theāgãchẽwas reconstructed in 2002 (NS 1122) using reinforced cement concrete, though most of the original materials have now been lost.
The shape of thetoraṇahas also been slightly changed, probably during the 2002 reconstruction.
Recently, (perhaps in 2002?) a shrine to Vasundharā Devī was constructed at the northern side of the Bāhāḥ.
Vajracharya(NS 1121, 82-85) does not mention this Bāhāḥ in his introduction to Dau Bāḥāḥ.
This Gaṇeśa, revered as the main Gaṇeśa (Sthānagaṇeśa) of the Olāchi Ṭola, has a history dating back to the late 17th century, with records of atoraṇainstallation in 1672 CE (NS 792).
Historical evidence regarding the construction of this temple is not available.
According to locals, the Gaṇeśa statue in the temple was established by the Mānandharas (K. Malla NS 1142, p. 39).
Pruscha (1975, K-36) states that it was built in the 17th century.
In 1672 CE (NS 792), two individuals, Bhūrāma and Amīra from Kvāṭhado, jointly offered a woodentoraṇato Gaṇeśa.
This inscription on thetoraṇaproves that Gaṇeśa had already been established by the medieval period.
In 2024 CE (VS 2080), the temple was reconstructed with financial assistance from the Kathmandu Metropolitan City and local donors.
The Gaṇeśa installed in the temple is worshipped as the Sthānagaṇeśa (main Gaṇeśa) of the Olāchi Ṭola.
Dozens of late-Malla period inscriptions also use the wordKobāhāto describe the area.
Since 2000 CE, they have also left the area and their duty.
The 2015 earthquakes caused heavy damage including major cracks in the walls.
Local residents completely restored the temple.
The details of the initial construction of this temple are unknown due to the lack of historic sources.
The earliest inscription from the temple is dated NS 797 (1677 CE).
It records the construction of thephalcāwest of the temple by Vāsi, Jevasiṅa, and Heramani, the sons of Prajāpati Padu.
In NS 958 (1838 CE), Maharjana Jyeṣṭha Mahaṃtasiṃ, Jasalakṣmī, Dhanaoṃtasiṃ, Lakṣmisiṃ, and others of Om Bāhāḥ ṭola reconstructed the easternphalcāafter it had collapsed and reduced to rubble.
Bothphalcās were reconstructed with the financial assistance of the Kathmandu Metropolis in 2018 CE.
They have aguthiof six people and take a turn for six months to serve asdyaḥpāḥlāḥ.
The offerings from devotees were not enough for thedyaḥpāḥlāḥs to run the deity'sguthi.
Therefore, the Hanumānaḍhokā Darabāra Kṣetra Saṃrakṣaṇa Kāryakrama under the Kathmandu Metropolis supports theguthiby providing NRs. 160 thousand per year since the fiscal year 2075/076.
The sixdyaḥpāḥlāḥs host theguthitwice a year onMahānavamī, the 9th of the bright fortnight of Āśvina, andPāhāṃcaḥrhay, the 13th of the dark fortnight of Caitra.
However, historical sources reveal that a golden finial was installed on the temple in 1735 CE (NS 855) in the course of a renovation.
The Vajravārāhī temple, located in the Cāpāgāũ jungle south of Lalitpur, is historically referred to as "Vatābu Devala" (NS 998/1878 CE).
The goddess herself is known as " Vatābu Vajravārāhī Devī" (NS 819/1699 CE).

While some Buddhists perceive her as a Ḍākinī arising from a cremation ground (Slusser 1982, p. 325), others identify her as the female energy of the Vajrayāna deity Herukacakrasamvara (B. Pradhan VS 2052, p. 1).
Crows, too, are absent from this grove (V. Karmācārya VS 2075, p. 39).

One belief is that the temple is surrounded by nine cremation grounds and a finial cannot be placed until all nine cremation grounds are used simultaneously for cremation (S. Mānandhara VS 2059, p. 23).

Yet another legend states that during the cremation of a Cāpāgāũ resident, when the corpse was half-burnt and the skull cracked open, a devotee could offer a finial (B. Pradhāna VS 2052, p. 3).*The sanctum entrance is adorned with a metaltoraṇabearing a Vajravārāhī statue.
A madman's attack on the sow led to its divine transformation and the establishment of the Vajravārāhī Pīṭha (S. Mānandhara VS 2059, p. 60).
Locals believe that sprinkling water from the waterhole on damaged crops can improve their yield (V. Karmācārya VS 2075, p. 38).
A buffalo statue is established in front of the temple.
The exact construction date of the temple remains unknown.

However, considering the prominence of Vajrayāna Buddhism in the valley between the 9th and 12th centuries, the establishment of these deities likely falls within this period (B. Pradhan VS 2052, p. 1).
King Śrīnivāsa Malla later constructed a grand temple and commissioned a golden statue of Vajravārāhī.
This statue was ceremonially consecrated by Viśvanātha Upādhyāya on Monday, the 8th of the bright fortnight of Caitra, 1666 CE (NS 786) (Yogī Naraharinātha VS 2013, p. 58).

While theBhāṣāVaṃśāvalīdoesn't explicitly mention Śrīnivāsa Malla's temple construction, it does credit him with the installation of the golden statue following its completion on the 8th of the bright fortnight of Caitra, 1666 CE (NS 786).
According to this chronicle, the statue was consecrated three days later on the 11th of the same month and year, following a procession around Cāpāgāũ (D. Lamsāla VS 2023, p. 66).

In 1706 CE (NS 826), a severe drought prompted Yogamatī (daughter of King Yoganarendra Malla) and King Lokaprakāśa Malla (Yogamatī's son) to perform special prayers at various temples, including Vajravārāhī, to invoke rainfall (D. Lamsāla VS 2023, p. 74).
In 1699 CE (NS 819), Heranī Mayī of Cāpāgāũ donated eightropanīs of land to support the temple.
King Yoganarendra Malla, in 1700 CE (NS 820), offered a stone buffalo statue with a golden parasol after performing a night-long fire sacrifice with music and offerings.
King Viṣṇu Malla of Lalitpur renovated the temple in 1735 CE (NS 855), installing a golden finial, contrary to the popular belief of the temple being finial-less.
Subsequent reconstructions might have led to the removal of the finial, giving rise to various legends.
The temple underwent renovations in 1930 CE (VS 1987) by Jītagovinda (Yogī Naraharinātha VS 2013, p. 58) and in 1959 CE (VS 2015) by King Mahendra.
In 2000 CE (VS 2057), copper sheets were added to the roof.
The 2015 earthquakes caused damage to the eastern wall, which was later repaired with financial assistance of NRs. 2 million from the Department of Archaeology (V. Karmācārya VS 2075, p. 61).
To sustain these practices, land and a flower garden were allocated for offerings.

Records from the Guthi Sansthan, a government body overseeing the management of socio-cultural trusts, indicate a land endowment of tworopanis eightānās for the daily worship of Vajravārāhī (Guṭhī Saṃsthāna VS 2071, p. 46).
However, the temple currently receives no support from the Guthi Sansthan.
Traditionally, musicians would play the shehnai during morning rituals and eveningāratīin the temple courtyard (V. Karmacharya VS 2075, p. 41).
This practice, however, has ceased due to the loss of the allocated land.
In 2023 CE (VS 2079), a week-long fire sacrifice ceremony was held to raise funds for an endowment, enabling the resumption of daily rituals.
A stone inscription dating back to 1699 CE (NS 819) records the endowment of land for both processions, confirming their existence prior to this date.
An alternative legend attributes the divine encounter to King Ari Malla (S. Mānandhara VS 2059, p. 62).
In 1968 CE (VS 2025), the Vajravārāhī statue used for the annual procession was stolen from its shrine (dyaḥchẽ) in Bhansāra Ṭola (V. Karmacharya VS 2075, p. 38).
As no one came forward, the statue remained under the protection of the National Museum from 1972 CE (VS 2029) onwards.
A replacement statue was subsequently created for the procession, but it too was stolen and has never been recovered.
In 2021 CE (VS 2078), the original statue was returned to Cāpāgāũ after completing the necessary legal procedures.
Currently, thedyaḥchẽhouses two Vajravārāhī statues: the original, and the second replacement statue.

Young men from Cāpāgāũ's Deśāra caste approached the girl and tempted her with a choice: "Do you prefer the goddess or bread?" When she expressed her hunger, they offered her bread, seized control of the Vajravārāhī statue, and paraded it around the village in a procession (Pradhan 1981, p. 8).
The festival was suspended for a long time due to the theft of Vajravārāhī’s head sculpture in c. 1985-1986 CE (VS 2042-2043).
In 2022 CE (VS 2079), a new statue was made, and the procession resumed (local resident, Deśāra, male, age 44).* This temple was not originally without a spire.
There is an inscription (CHG0110_I_004) indicating that King Viṣṇu Malla had offered the temple a golden finial during its renovation in 1735 CE (NS 855).
Rāṇā Prime Minister Candra Śamśera commissioned the construction of thisśivālaya, or dwelling of Lord Śiva, in 1903 CE (VS 1960) and subsequently donated a bell to the temple a few months later.
A Nandī figure, the sacred bull of Lord Śiva, is seen in front of the western entrance, while a brass bell from 1903 CE, suspended by a bell-stand south of the temple, commemorates its construction.
Additionally, a statue of Kāmadeva is housed southeast of the temple, with a stone trident (triśūla) erected to the north.

Rāṇā Prime Minister Candra Śamśera, honored with the construction of the temple in 1903 CE (VS 1960) (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p.347), later presented a bell to the temple alongside his wife and sons (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2056, p.620).
Candra Śamśera, who had two formally wedded wives, Lokabhaktarājyalakṣmī and Bālakumārī, as well as a consort named Rojānānī (P. Rāja VS 2070, pp.47-48), had a total of nine sons.
The exact contributors to the bell donation remain unclear.

Given that both this temple and the nearby Candralokaprakāśeśvara Śivālaya (PPK1910) received bell offerings on the same occasion from Candra Śamśera and his first wife Lokabhaktarājyalakṣmī, it is likely that they offered the bell here as well.

Candra Śamśera ascended to the prime ministerial position in 1901 CE after forcibly displacing his elder brother Deva Śamśera (P. Rāṇā VS 2070, p.199), and he initiated the construction of this temple a few years into his tenure.

The descendants of its founder sold the Bāhāḥ to a Maharjan family and it had already been changed into a private residential building when Pruscha (1975, p. 40 [C/K-106]) mapped the site sometime around 1973-1974 CE.
In the courtyard, directly in front of the sanctum door, twocaityas, aśikharakūṭa(object number KAT1060-004) and ajalaharyoparijinālaṅkṛta(object number KAT1060-005) have been erected.

According to R. Vajrācārya (VS 2075, p.247), a Śākya family from Dhavalacaitya Vihāra, one of the branch monasteries of Ituṃ Bāhāḥ, moved to Tamvaḥ Gaḥli and established the Bāhāḥ on the ground floor of their private house.
The above-mentionedjalaharyoparijinālaṅkṛtacaityawas erected in 1876 CE (NS 997) by Śākyabhikṣu Dharmma, Jujuvirasiṃ, and others.
[1]More than a half-century later, in 1929 CE (NS 1050), Sujabhānasiṃ installed the Akṣobhya statue inside the sanctum.
Therefore, it is unclear whether the Bāhā was built concurrently with thecaitya, or whether it was constructed after or before the Akṣobhya statue was installed.
As previously stated, the descendants of the Bāhāḥ’s founder sold the Bāhāḥ building along with the sanctum on the ground floor to a Maharjana family.
Footnotes^Pruscha (1975, p. 40 [C/K-106]) specifies the year as 1877 CE.

Situated at the southern edge of the street that leads to Okubahāl (east) from Tangaḥ and to the west of Cābahā Bahi (a monastic building dating back to the 14th cent. CE), the Cābāhāḥ Phalcā has had a dynamic history of destruction and reconstruction.
An image of Umāmaheśvara was installed in 1680 AD, and thephalcāwas renovated on the same occasion, just 12 years after its initial construction.
It collapsed during the 1934 Great Earthquake, and there is no evidence that it was reconstructed until the late 20th century CE.
In 2002 it was finally reconstructed with the support of URBAN MANAGEMENT AND ECONOMIC DIVERSIFICATION PROJECT (UMEDP), the Kathmandu Valley Preservation Trust (KVPT) and Jyapu Samaj in Lalitpur.
It completely collapsed again during the 2015 earthquakes and in 2019 was once more rebuilt from the plinth up.
Part of the reason that it took so long for thephalcāto be reconstructed was that the residential house attached to the rear of thephalcāalso needed to be rebuilt simultaneously.
Moreover, financial resources were scarce in the wake of the earthquakes.
The reconstruction process saw the reuse of four of the historical columns, though new ones were also introduced.
These newer ones are somewhat too high and of rather low craftsmanship (Malaysian wood was used because the price for Salwood went up dramatically in the wake of the earthquakes).
It is believed that Cābāhāḥ Phalcā was originally commissioned by a Shrestha family living in the adjacent rear house.
An inscription in front of Cābahā Phalcā claims that it was initially constructed in 1668 CE.
After the 1934 earthquake, six of the historic pillars were salvaged and stored, as well as the plinth base stones.
These deities have since been stolen, most probably some time in the 1980s.

The safeguarding of threatened architectural heritage of the Valley was already a prominent issue in the early 2000s, and the reconstruction of this monument was part of a larger project that saw the restoration of 15 monuments deemed to be under threat due to urban encroachment and development.

A contemporary report states that "[t]he reconstruction of thepāṭīto its original state portrays a model attempt to preserve the historic architectural type of rest house, and retains the significance of thepāṭīand its open space for the modern community.

The project also involved the training of Nepalese team in project management, restoration project design, community negotiation, publicity and financial reporting." (Joshi and Ranjitkar Final Report Chabaha Pati 2003, p. 3) The report also stressed that these historic rest houses play a central role in Patan's World Heritage Site.
citations: (Joshi and Ranjitkar Final Report Chabaha Pati 2003, p. 3)

text: Thephalcāis of great importance for the local Tamrakar community, and most of thebhajanamembers that regularly perform in the building come from this community.
The Caturvyūha Caityā in front of thephalcāis an important resource; its inscription mentions the renovation of thephalcā,and an image of the building has been engraved into it.
There is no evidence to appoint the initial construction of thisbāhāḥ.
Cuka Bāhāḥ is also known as Cakravarṇa Mahāvihāra and is believed to be built by King Mānadeva.
TheGopālarājavaṁśāvalī(1985, fol. 21) also mentions that King Manadeva constructed avihāra.
As discussed inPetech1984, 45, a palm-leaf manuscript copied in NS 162 (1042 CE) refers to avihārabuilt by Mānadeva in its colophon, however, the exact location is mentioned.
Similarly, an inscription issued by Aṃśuvarman in Saṃvat 32, too mentions avihārabuilt by Mānadeva.
Moreover, the Narendradeva’s inscription of Yaga Bāhāḥ, Patan mentions Mānadeva’s vihāra.
D. Vajrācārya(VS 2030, 323) cites this as an evidence to believe that Mānadeva’svihārais located in Patan.
King of Patan exiled thesaṅghamembers of thisbāhāḥafter he could not stand them doing a favour to the king of Bhaktapur who constructed abāhāḥin Thimi for them in return (H. Vajrācārya2000, 76).

Thedyaḥchẽhaspāsukāwindows on its first and second floors, and apurais erected above its roof.^All of the necessary rituals of the Bāhāḥ (for examplebare chuigu,ācāḥ luigu,andthapāḥju luigu) is carried out in the Kvā Bāhāḥ.
No documented evidence about the initial construction is present.
In NS 1021 (1901 CE) stones were paved in thegarbhagṛha.
In VS 1987 (1930 CE), a golden parasol (chatra) was donated to the Mandira.
The latest restoration of the temple, after the 2015 earthquake, was done by the Department of Archaeology.
The initial construction of thismandirawas completed on the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha in 1649 CE (NS 769).
On that day, the pinnacle (gajū) was mounted atop of the temple’s roof and a statue of Śākyamuni was consecrated in its sanctum.
A fire sacrifice calledlakṣyāhutiyajña, followed by traditional music and a dance performance, was also performed on that occasion.

The inscription, recording these events, also mentions that the kings of Patan, Siddhi Narasiṃha and Śrīnivāsa Malla, (the father and son duo jointly ruled Lalitpur from NS 769. i.e. 1649 CE; cfD. R. Regmi1966, 274) were present at the opening ceremony of this temple.
citations: (the father and son duo jointly ruled Lalitpur from NS 769. i.e. 1649 CE; cfD. R. Regmi1966, 274)

text: The inscription identifies Hākuju Śākya, a resident of Siṃhadvāḥ, where the temple is located, as the founder of Buddha Mandira.
It informs us that he constructed the temple in the memory of his father and mother.
He also founded Cvay Bāhāḥ (KIR0011), which is located nearby this temple.
Buddha Mandira is entirely stone-constructed.

The contemporary Śākyamuni statue, consecrated in the sanctum (garbhagṛha), was established by Kānchī Vajrācārya, a local community member, after the old one was stolen in 1984 CE (cf.Ś. ŚreṣṭhaVS 2057, 58).
The temple suffered damages in the 2015 CE earthquakes and was reconstructed by the Department of Archaeology in 2019 CE.
Usually, the shrine of the main deity is facing the main entrance, however, in thisbāhāḥ,the three-storey monastic building is located on the south.

The three-storey main monastic building has been reconstructed: one can find evidence of this in thedacīaḥpācladding on the northern (frontal) façade, while the walls of the other three sides have been built using local bricks in cement mortar.
The main façade of the building is furnished with two blind windows with double lotus flowers containing 18 and 21 petals respectively.
The eastern and western walls are attached to the adjacent buildings, though the main building can be circumambulated via a narrow passage.
The Sataḥ built by Siddhimāna Rājabhaṇḍārī in the 1850s CE was reconstructed in 2021 CE (2078 VS).
The south-facing three storied building is covered byjhiṅgaṭītiles.
No statues of deities are installed.
There is no inscriptive evidence that records the construction of this Sataḥ, but it can be estimated to have been around 1850-55CE.
The Sataḥ was built under the initiative of Siddhimāna Rājabhaṇḍārī, a resident of Yaṃgāla, Kathmandu (Patron of the Satprayāsa old age home from Rājabhaṇḍārī caste, female, age 76).
During the rise of Jaṅga Bahādura in 1846 CE, he served as a governor or chief administrative officer of a province or district (subbā).
In 1859 CE, he attained the post ofsardāraand became a treasurer (khajāncī).
In 1864 CE, he was promoted to the position of a colonel and appointed governor of Banke, Bardiya, Kailali, Kanchanpur districts (the Nayā Muluka, ‘New Kingdom’).
He accompanied prime minister Jaṅga Bahādura on his official state visit to Great Britain in 1850 CE (Rana 1974, p.116).
He also built Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa temple (KAT2636), Siddhimukteśvara temple (KAT2637) and Dhaneśvara temple (KAT2638) at Pacalī ghāṭa in 1855 CE (1911 VS) (See,KAT2636_I_20210116).
It is well possible that the Sataḥ was constructed at the same time.

The reconstruction of the Sataḥ was carried out in 2021 CE (2078 VS) by the committee for the Integrated Development of Bagmati Civilization under the Ministry of Urban Development of the Nepal Government, with an assistance from a loan provided by the Asian Development Bank.
On the same day annual ritual worship is performed in Siddhimukteśvara temple, Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa temple and Dhaneśvara temple, all of which were built by Siddhimāna Rājabhaṇḍārī.
Lotuses from Dhũllā Pukhū were customarily offered to Vajrayoginī as part of the daily ritual.
Dhũllā Pukhū is one of the sources of water constructed at the Dhũllā Ṭola in Sankhu.
Government records show that Dhũllā Pukhū was registered as a pond back in 1964 CE (VS 2021) with a local resident named Śerabahādura Śreṣṭha as its patron.
Attempts are being made since 2018 CE to bring the Pukhū back to its original form.
As of January 2022, the Shankharapur Municipality has provided NRs. 3.5 million in two installments to remove clay deposited in the Pukhū and to build an embankment and boundary wall.
After the reconstruction of the Pukhū, locals plan to plant lotuses here that will be used as an offering to Vajrayoginī like in the past.
This temple is one of the earliest Sarasvatī temples (initially constructed before 1314 CE) in the Kathmandu Valley and it lies outside of the medieval settlement in Patan.
[1]This Sarasvatī statue is one of the rear ones found in the Kathmandu Valley with the inscriptions.
There are two inscriptions from two different dates, 1314 CE and 1447 CE, in the temple recording the establishment of the statue.
Therefore, it remains obscure in which date the present-day statue was installed.
The five feet tall statue suggests that this temple was huge in size when it was initially constructed.
It was renovated in 1776 CE, and also in 1937 CE after it collapsed during the 1934 CE earthquakes.
None of the inscriptions record how the temple looked like before it was restored.
Therefore, most of the Sarasvatī shrines in the valley are built in the relatively open spaces.

However, her images from the late Malla period found in the Kathmandu Valley (such as the inscription from VS 1602, i.e. 545 CE found in Jayavageshwori, Kathmandu in which Viṣṇu, Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī are venerated together) suggest that people accepted her as a wife of Viṣṇu.
citations: (such as the inscription from VS 1602, i.e. 545 CE found in Jayavageshwori, Kathmandu in which Viṣṇu, Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī are venerated together)

text: Barring the inscription from VS 1788 (1731 CE) of Sankhamul, Khatmandu (cf.R. VantaVS 2061), no other image or document shows her as the wife of Brahmā.
The shrine is built in theśikharaarchitectural style and is entirely clad in brass sheets.
A brass arch (toraṇa) surrounds it, with a small Gaṇeśa figure installed at the top.
Although there is no inscription indicating when the shrine was originally built, medieval records confirm that each neighborhood in Patan traditionally maintained its own Sthāna Gaṇeśa shrine.
The earliest known inscription here dates to 1931–32 CE (VS 1988) and records the installation of a bell.
During Indrajātrā, a brass image of Gaṇeśa is temporarily installed on the shrine’s platform, and a large offering ofsamaybaji(sacred food) is made.
The sanctum of thebahīis on the first floor of the western building and houses an east-facing statue of Akṣobhya.
As a result, thisbahīwas constructed and the deity accepted the request to live here.
According to thebahīmembers, thisbahīwas established by Dhyānacandra Miśra.
Three merchant brothers from Patan, Dharmaśrī Miśra, Jñānaśrī Miśra and Dhyānacandra Miśra, spent the money they had earned through Tibetean trade to establish threebahīs.
The only inscriptions found in thebahīcomplexstem from the late Malla period.
Thebahīsuffered from multiple earthquakes and has undergone reconstruction multiple times.
Aguṭhīendowed with 45ropanīof land in Bungmati and Sunaguthi was established to run the social and religious activities of thebahī(Locke 1985, 223).
Thesaṅgha-members of thebahītherefore rely on the collection of donations in order to fund these activities.
The Pīṭha is the abode of Goddess Brahmāyaṇī, one of the Eight Mother Goddesses (aṣṭamātṛkā)and is believed to have been established when the town of Sankhu was founded.
Dissimilar to otherpīṭhasin the Kathmandu Valley, Brahmāyaṇī Pīṭha is established within the town.

TheMaṇiśailamahāvadāna, a Buddhist scripture that reports the foundation of Sankhu in 1300 BC (Kaligata Era 1801), also mentions the presence of Śvetabhairava at Brahmāyaṇī Pīṭha (V. Vajrācārya1119, p. 32-33).
Beside this, there are no historical records to date the establishment of the Pīṭha.
The earliest inscription inscribed on the stonetoraṇaplaced above the aniconic stone in 1845 CE (NS 965) records the installation of thetoraṇa.
Two other inscriptions temporarily kept at the Pīṭha belong to other monuments of the Sālkhā Ṭola.
The inscription under thetoraṇarecords the renovation of the Maṇḍapa Phalcā (SKH0140) in 1763 CE (NS 883).
It also mentions a land endowment made for the emancipation of Piunārāyaṇa and his family members of Kathmandu.
In 1734 CE (NS 854), a gilded flag was offered to the deity after a large lamp was lit at the temple.
No records have been found regarding the establishment of this temple.

The earliest record from the temple dates back to 1734 CE (NS 854), when individuals from Jholachẽ, including Śyāma Bhābo, Suryya Bhābo, and Gunadeva Bhābo, lit a large lamp (mahādīpa) at the Gaṇeśa temple and offered a gilded flag.
On the same occasion, aketakīflower was offered to Āryāvalokiteśvara located in Haka Ṭola.
Based on this record, it can be confirmed that the temple was already built before 1734 CE.
In 1971 CE (NS 1091), Nīlakumārī Dhāinī, the granddaughter of Rāmakṛṣṇa Bārāhī from Haka Ṭola, offered a bell to the Gaṇeśa temple.
Around 1993, Urban Development through Local Efforts (UDLE) reconstructed the temple.
Prior to the reconstruction, the road surface had risen, causing the temple to be situated below the road level.
During the reconstruction, the ground level of the temple was raised compared to its previous position (local resident, Maharjan, female, age 46).
The chariot, taken out from Jayavāgeśvarī for the trident festival (Triśūlajātrā) celebrated on the 8th of dark fort night of Āṣāḍha in Deopatan area, is built in front of thissataḥ.
Nepal Army has reconstructed it in 1996 CE (2053 VS).
No deities are installed in the sataḥ.
Apart from this, other chariots are stored in poḍepāṭī of Vajraghara and Vatsaleśvarī (Ṭanḍana VS 2056 p. 508).

According to (Devamālā Vaṃśāvalī VS 2013, p.102), in 1514 CE (NS 634) there was an annual procession of nine young boys and girls (kumārakumārī) in a chariot, which was constructed through a tantric ritual performed by a priest Muni Bandhu Ācārya of Vatsālādevī during the reign of King Amara Malla and manyguṭhīs were granted for performing this ritual.
Although there is lack of detailed evidence regarding the construction of the sataḥ, it can be considered as ancient as the trident festival.
A dilapidated sataḥ was reconstructed by Nepal army in 1996 CE (VS 2053) (a local resident resident, Kapālī, male, age 43).
citations: (a local resident resident, Kapālī, male, age 43)

text: No casualties were found here in earthquake of 2015 CE.
Young boys and girls are selected on the sixth of bright fortnight of Jeṣṭha (Ṭanḍana VS 2053, p. 507).
Recently (May, 2023), the festival is led by a guard (dvāre) of Amālakoṭa court (kacaharī) with support of Bhuvaneśvarī guṭhī endowment (chuṭaguṭhī) and Paśupati area development trust.
With regards to the history of the monument, the lack of a foundation inscription means that we must rely on indications and references made in some literary sources.

TheNepālikabhūpavaṃśāvalī(2016, 13.23-24) mentions that King Vīradeva made a Maṇi-pond, a Maṇi-caitya, a Maṇi-spout, a Maṇi-liṅga, a Maṇi-kumāra, a Maṇi-maṇḍapa and a Maṇi-galabhaṭṭa whilst he was establishing Lalitpur as a city.
However, the entire story of King Vīradeva is not corroborated by any other source material and no inscription found in Nepal mentions his name.
The physical appearance of thecaityasuggests that the monument is not an archaic construction.
It is thus possible that it was reconstructed many times until it got its present shape.
During the reconstruction of the Bahādura Śāha Bhavana, an old remnant of a water drain leading towards thiscaityawas found underneath the entrance of the building.
According to local information, Maṇi Caitya was constructed over these foundations after a pond was filled in (Jośī2065, 15).
Aśikharatemple from the 14th-15th century built on top of a buried fountain.
The temple is built on a small stone platform, atop a fountain.
Eroded inscriptions are also observed on blocks of the pediment.
The sanctum contained a large stoneyoni, on which aśivaliṅgamust have been installed, in 2000.
The pinnacle is constituted of two stone discs (Skt. āmalaka)A stone memorial pillar is installed fifteen meters west of the temple (JUM0070-001).
Suchśikharatemples were built throughout the Karnali Basin from the 13th to the 15th centuries (Andolfatto 2019).
The rarity of inscriptions onśikharatemples (locally known asdevala) complicates the dating of these monuments.
Yet a line of eroded inscription on the pediment (below the riders' carving) appears to bear the date (ŚS) 1408 (1486 CE).
Although the inscription may be much later than the monument itself, it provides a terminus ante quem for the temple's construction.
This specificjaḥdhūṃ, located adjacent to the SapājaḥdhuṃPhalcā, was built with the same purpose in mind, along the road that connects Lele and Patan.
According to local residents, there was once an inscription here, but it has since been buried.
From the late Malla period to the early Śāha period, constructing such structures became a common practice, and thisjaḥdhūṃis part of that tradition.
A local Tamang family has been responsible for filling thejaḥdhūṃwith water since 1983 CE (VS 2040), continuing a long-standing tradition (local resident, Tamang, male, age 43).
In 2001 CE (VS 2075), thejaḥdhūṃwas reconstructed by theṭola sudhāra samiti.

Thephalcā, originally situated closer to the road, was relocated a few meters away and rebuilt in the early 2060s (VS) with assistance from the Lalitpur Sub-Metropolis and the Sapājaḥruṃ neighborhood.
In 2020 CE (VS 2077), aŚreṣṭhafamily installed a stone statue of Gaṇeśa near thephalcā.
The main façade is decorated with latticed woodwork and two small latticed windows have been installed in the eastern and western walls of the temple.
Before thehitiwas completely filled in, some of the statues were removed and relocated to this temple and the nearby Licchavicaitya(BUN0026).
The temple was reconstructed in 2003.
The projecting roof on the northern side was left unfinished during the reconstruction process, meaning that the temple's structure appears unbalanced.
The entry façade has been reconstructed and does not appear to display any significantbahīarchitecture.
A stone aniconic image of Bālakumāri is located in front of the Lokeśvara image and a metal mask of Mahākāla hangs on the wall of a more recently built room.
It contains statues of devotees, aśikharakūṭa caityaanda dharmadhātu maṇḍalalined up centrally in front of the main sanctum building.
This building faces east and has a central door that can be accessed via steps guarded by two stone lions.
The building extends outwards towards the north and south; the northern end is now a residential building while the southern end is used as community space.
The upper floor of the sanctum building has a projecting balcony that faces out towards the courtyard, as well as a central door similar to that on the ground floor.
The two-story building is roofed with traditionaljhĩgaṭītiles.
Aphucāhas been built on top of the ridge of gable roof and is surrounded by lattice windows.
The building has aphucāand has been roofed withjhigaṭītiles.
A few years ago, agumbāwas constructed next to to the esoteric shrine that houses the image of Amoghapāśa Lokeśvara.
These two buildings are now connected.
No inscription or any other document providing information about the establishment of the Bahī could be found.
However, an inscription dated from the Śaka Era 464 (CE 542) discussing the Mū Guitaḥ Bahī was recently found in the Taḥdhã Bahī.
This inscription strongly suggests that the history of these three monasteries stretches back to the Licchavi period.
Referenced in an inscription by King Narendradeva in 679 CE, Gullataṅgagrāma is a village that is now thought of as modern Guitaḥ.
Some years passed and yet anotherbahīseparated from the original one and established itself.

Caityawith a circular base, built by Dhammasiṃha Varuḍākāra and Devarāja in 1727 CE (NS 847)Situated in Okhā Ṭola, Cāpāgāũ, near the main Godāvarī road, thiscaityafeatures a circular base, which deviates from the usual square shape, and has been externally coated with cement plaster.

While it houses the traditionalpañcabuddhastatues in the cardinal directions, iron bars have been installed to protect the Buddha statues after the 2023 CE theft of three statues from BhansāraCaitya(CHG0070) at Bhansāra Ṭola, Cāpāgāũ.
Thecaityawas jointly established by Dhammasiṃha Varuḍākāra and his wife Māratimayi, along with Devarāja and his unnamed wife.

An inscription, installed in aphalcāto the east of thecaitya, records this event along with Devarāja’s donation of land parcels to fund rituals at thecaitya, such as lighting lamps on the full moon day of Āśvina.

A subsequent inscription, added a few days later, documents Dhammasiṃha Varuḍākāra and Māratimayi’s donation of land, a garden, and money, with instructions to revere Bhagavatī and perform worship on the full moon day of Āśvina.
The Hiti’s stone conduits are copper-claddedand gilded.
The Licchavi inscription dated Mānadeva era year 34 (610 CE) and preserved in the Hiti premises suggests that Nugaḥ Ṭola dates back to the Licchavi period.
In his poemKīrtipatākā(verse 57) composed in NS 772 (CE 1652), the court poet Kunu Śarmā compares the flow of this waterspout with the flow coming down from the mythical mount Sumeru.
The Hiti was probably built before the Nepal Calendar Era (nepālasaṃvat) which began in 879 CE.

To make the Nepal Calendar Era a common calendar in the Kathmandu Valley, the date (written down most probably in Mānadeva Calendar Era) inscribed in the inscription recording the Hiti’s initial construction could have been purposely erased (Nepālikabhūpavaṃśāvalī,19.3.171-172).
Based on a fragmented inscription,C.
Kāyastha(1119, 9) argues that the Hiti was built in NS 106 (986 CE).
The one from Saugala built Satigata Hiti (Saugaḥ Hiti) with the help of the king.
The other friend from Navagala got jealous of his friend and thus announced that he, too, will build a Hiti in his Ṭola.
Thus, she granted him a boon for his successes and gave three water conduits.
He then constructed a water channel from Nāykhyaḥ (Nāgakhela) to Nvagala and constructed 5 stone conduits.
He also cladded and gilded the stone conduits, which are known as Sundhārā at present (source: advisor of Sundhārā Ṭola Sudhāra Samiti, Jośī, male, age 78).
The Hiti had five conduits when it was initially constructed: three facing north and two facing east and west.

In NS 821 (1701 CE), the sons (Pratāpasiṃha Bābu, Vīrasiṃha Bābu, Jayabhadrasiṃha Bābu and Ānandasiṃha Bābu) of the daughter of King Siddhinarasiṃha Malla renovated this Hiti and added another one called Byāṃcā Hiti and established a golden statue of Lakṣmī.
Last time in 2012 CE Prabhāta Red Star Club renovated the Hiti with the financial support of Lalitpur Metropolitan.
Constructed in theśikharastyle, the stone shrine features a tower adorned with 21 finials intricately carved into the stone blocks.
These characteristics suggest that the statue originated between the 5th and 7th century, as mentioned by M. Khanāla (VS 2074, p.163).
Unfortunately, there is no recorded historical information about the establishment of the shrine.
However, a stone stele located southeast of the shrine bears an inscription dating back to 1821 CE (VS 1877).
This inscription pertains to the construction of a road by a group of individuals.

monument_name: Gaṇeśa Phalcā at Cvachẽ (built in 1782, rebuilt 2018 CE)
text: Gaṇeśa Phalcāis freestanding, with the exception of its north-eastern corner; this adjoins the neighbouring buildings.

monument_name: Gaṇeśa Phalcā at Cvachẽ (built in 1782, rebuilt 2018 CE)
text: Just in front of Śaṅkha Bāhāḥ, there is acaitya, and two morephalcās(LAL4142 ans LAL4141) were also built by Avāle families from Cvachẽ.

This suggests that this monument was most likely constructed during the reign of King Niraya Pāla, around the same time as the other structures in Ajayamerukoṭa.
Siddhinagara Mahāvihāra (also known as Brahmackra Vihāra) was founded in 1706 CE (NS 826) and is popularly known as 'Bhoṭe Bāhāḥ'.
The (Bhoṭe) Bāhāḥ's roof is covered in brass sheets and topped with a brasskalaśainstalled as a finial.

According to the stone inscription inside the sanctum, Siddhimuni Vajrācārya (text: Vajācājya Siddhimuni), a resident of Varṣacandra Mahāvihāra (a branch monastery of Om Bāhāḥ), built Bhoṭe Bāhāḥ, endowed land, and formed aguthifor its operation and maintenance in 1706 CE (NS 826).
Kājī Tulsīmāna renovated the Bāhāḥ in 1934 CE (VS 1991).
The renovation was modelled after Chusyā Bāhāḥ (R. Vajrācārya VS 2075, p.250).
The Bāhāḥ was renovated again in 2007 CE (VS 2064).
The Vairāgī Akhaḍā was erected by the family of Prime Minister Bhīma Śamśera to offer free lodging and sustenance to ascetics, mainly Rāmānandī sand other VaiṣṇavaVairāgīs.
This religious sect traces its origins to the 13th or 14th century and was founded as a branch of Vaiṣṇava tradition by Rāmānandī, a disciple of Saint Kabīra (Michaels 2004 p. 321).
The building stands south of the Viṣṇu Mandira (PPK0408) in the Paśupati area.
Additionally, aśivaliṅgastands to the southeast of the building.

Although historical records regarding the monastery's construction are scarce, it is widely believed that Prime Minister Bhīma Śamśera's family commissioned its creation to provide accommodation for ascetic monks (M. Thāpā VS 2077, p. 566).
However, the devastating earthquakes in 2015 pushed the structure to the brink of collapse.
Consequently, the statues of various deities and the sacredśāligrāmastone were relocated to another building intended for ascetics, known as the Bhāgavata Sanyāsa Āśrama.
In 2021 CE, the Pashupati Area Development Trust undertook the dismantling of hazardous sections of the building.
Initially, numerousvairāgīascetics found refuge here, with specific mention of Rāma Vairāgī (M. Thāpā VS 2077, p. 566).
During the celebration ofŚivarātri, visiting ascetics were welcomed here and offered complimentary lodging and sustenance.
However, following the dismantling of the monastery, resident ascetics relocated to other hermitages within the Paśupati area.
The Temple is currently (January 2022 CE) a small shrine standing on three steps of large plinths.
According to the locals, there used to be a large temple of Viṣṇuvikrānta here, which collapsed in the earthquakes of 1833 CE (VS 1890) and was never rebuilt.
Unfortunately, it was stolen in 1990 CE.
The statues currently enshrined inside the Temple were recovered from its rubbles after the earthquakes of 1833 CE.
Since the statue of the main deity is already stolen, people are now compelled to worship the statue of Kṛṣṇa (local resident, Śreṣṭha, male, age 69).

Pinchẽ Bāhāḥ, also known as Khũ Bāhāḥ,** is a branch monastery (kacābāhāḥ) of Taḥdhaṃ Bāhāḥ (KAT1420) in the Vaṭu Ṭola, Kathmandu, and it is one of the very few monastic buildings in Kathmandu that has managed to preserve its old structure.
The main building (dyaḥchẽ‘god house’) of thebāhāḥfaces north, with wings extending to the western, northern, and eastern sides.
However, thetoraṇadoes not currently have such an image (as of December 2022 CE).
A Lokeśvara shrine has been built in front of (slightly to the right of) the entrance to thebāhāḥcourtyard.

The stone inscription, which is located to the north of thebāhāḥcourtyard (see, inscription KAT1400_I_001 below) records that Jayalakṣa from Taḥdhaṃ Bāhāḥ founded the Pinchẽ Bāhāḥin 1593 CE (NS 713) during the reign of King Śivasiṃha Malla.
He not only founded thebāhāḥ, but also the statues of Dīpaṅkara, Mañjuśrī, and Halāhala Lokeśvara, as well as acaityain thebāhāḥpremises and a Lokeśvara shrine (see, object no. KAT1400-009 below).

Jayalakṣa, the donor, was also in charge of renovating the Svayambhū Caitya in 1605 CE (NS 725) per King Śivasiṃha Malla's order (cf. S. Rājavaṃśī VS 2078, p.47-48).**This is a reference to a mediaeval practice of detaining people accused of theft here for one night to determine whether or not they actually committed the crime.
The two small blind windows are installed inside the sanctum on the south and west wall.
These timber elements put inside suggest that the temple was reconstructed and those carved elements were somehow saved.

Afterwards, Bālārcanadeva had Balabala’s portion of rice collected from all the farmers and established a rule that people should annually worship the image of Balabala and make offerings of yomaḍhi made from Balabala’s portion of rice on the full moon day of Mārga.
The original stone statue of Balabhadra, dated MS 109 (685 CE), was stolen in 1986.
The new statue was installed in 1988.
A small shrine of standing Gaṇeśa is built attached to the south wall of the temple.
At the North-east corner, there is a smallcaityawith its western half part of the dome destroyed.

Constructed as a replica of Śhobhābhagavatī/Svāhā Bhagavatī (KAT3210) in an area densely populated by the Newars, a non-Newar family of the Khatrī caste formed aguthiin the late 19thcentury to provide income for Thãhiti Bhagavatī Temple.

Before the present Temple structure was constructed in 1989 CE (VS 2046), the Bhagavatī statue was under an open sky (see, for example, a historical photo below, taken in the early 1970s and published inPursha1975, p. 15).

text: The statue of Bhagavatī here at Thãhiti Bhagavatī Temple has many features similar to the statue of Bhagavatī consecrated at Śhobhābhagavatī Temple.
An inscription on the pedestal of the Thãhiti Bhagavatī statue records a person named Siṃharatha and his family members establishing the statue in 1756 CE (NS 876) (Ś. RājavaṃśīVS 2057, p.47).
One morning, he could not cross the flooding river and, therefore established a shrine of the deity in front of his residence.
In another inscription from 1883 CE (NS 1003), the deity is referred to as Śhobhābhagavatī (text: Svabhābhagavati).

The date of its original construction is not documented, however,Gutschow(2011, 360) estimates that the temple was built in the 16th century and increased in size in the 17th century.Śākya and Vaidya(1970, 93-95) refer to an inscription of NS 723 (1603 CE) which was erected during the joint reign of Kings Śivasiṃhadeva and Hariharasiṃha.
It mentioned that a golden urn and a pinnacle were offered to the deity.Śākya & Vaidyaassume that thetemple was built at that time.

However, as there is a tradition of offering a pinnacle even after the restoration or reconstruction of a temple, it cannot be ascertained that the initial construction of the temple took place on this date.

The text at the end of the inscription mentions that the donor family restored the temple and donated a pinnacle; this phrase also indicates that the temple was not built at that time but rather was restored or reconstructed.
An inscription of NS 808 (1688 CE) mentions Princess Kīrtimaṅgalā Thakunī and her husband Amarasiṃha Kumhārāja having funded the installation of a roof for the temple and bestowed land.
The inscription does not mention the number of roofs constructed.
Another inscription mentions that a donor from Patan Gāḥ Bāhāḥ offered a pinnacle to the deity in 1849.
The same pinnacle must have been restored by Deva Śamśera in 1877 when the arcadedsattalstructures were created to form a courtyard (Gutschow 2011, 458).
The temple was badly damaged by the 2015 earthquakes.
It was reconstructed between 2019 and 2021.
At night, fire worships and tantric ritual worships involving sacrifices are performed.
These architectural features evoke temples built in Uttarakhand (India) around the 7th-8th century, and especially Temples 1 and 2 in Jageshwar (seeChanchani 2019, 81-83, fig. 3.7.).
It may thus be suggested that this monument, as well as the four others found at the site, was built between the 8th and 10th century (Andolfatto 2022, 38;Sharma 2012, 284).
The god house was badly damaged by the 2015 earthquake and is now supported by wooden columns.
While the construction of thesataḥis attributed to an army officer named Jayanta Kumedāna, the exact year of its establishment remains unclear.

An inscription on the northern wall of thesataḥcommemorates the construction of a cremation ground (ghāṭa) in front of thesataḥby Śivānanda Vaidya in 1826 CE (NS 946) and credits Jayanta Kumedāna with the construction of thesataḥ.
However, an inventory published by the Kathmandu Upatyakā Nagara Vikāsa Yojanā mistakenly indicates that Jayanta Kumedāna built thesataḥin 1826 CE, the same year the cremation ground was established.
In 1967 CE (VS 2024), thesataḥunderwent renovation, with the upper floor being repurposed for accommodation (Inventory VS 2039, p.88).

In the past, during the occasion ofṚṣiPañcamī, which falls on the 5th of the bright fortnight of Bhādra, women used to perform a holy bath in the Bagmati river and employed thesataḥfor changing and warming themselves by a fire (local resident, Ācārya, male, age 59).
The three-tiered temple in Om Bāhāḥ was built by Rāmakṛṣṇa Bhāro in 1697.
This temple was reconstructed in 2011.
The local Śreṣṭha community handles theguthi.
The water tank built under the "Chandra Loka Water Works" project, initiated by Candra Śamśera in the joint name of himself and his wife, remains in use to this day.
Candra Śamśera constructed a water reserve tank here to supply water to Patan.
The tank was built with brick walls approximately two meters thick, using lime or brick powder mortar.
To the south, a smallphalcā-like structure was built for the caretaker, leading to the surrounding area being named "Pāla," a derivative of the Nepali termpāle, meaning ‘guard’.
Candra Śamśera considered the tank’s construction a significant achievement and installed an inscription to commemorate it.
In 1904 CE (VS 1961), the project was completed under the name "Chandra Loka Water Works" in the joint name of Candra Śamśera and his wife, Candralokabhakta Lakṣmī Devī.
Additional details about the project’s objectives are found not here but in an inscription at the Bagmati Bridge in Thapathali.
Candra Śamśera, who rebuilt the Bagmati Bridge in the modern style, included details in that inscription about the water supply project from Kirtipur to Patan.
The inscription states that, in fulfillment of the resolve of his late wife, Candralokabhakta Lakṣmī Devī, water was brought to Patan through iron pipes from a location 19,900 feet away.
Necessary reservoirs were built along the route, and a 300-foot-long bridge was constructed over the Bagmati to support the pipeline.
The project resulted in 50 public water taps in Patan, with prayers that the merit would grant the late queen salvation and Candra Śamśera a 100-year lifespan.
Thus, this tank was built as part of a major initiative by the Prime Minister and his wife to supply water to Patan.
The monument building can be found on the west side of the courtyard and faces east.
The ground floor of the building has been plastered in cement and painted white.
This floor was recently reconstructed using localdeśī apāon mud mortar (writing in 2019).
The structure is covered with a sloped CGI sheet roof, and is surrounded by tall, five-storey buildings on three sides.
This Bāhāḥ was established by Punaju Śākya of Oku Bāhāḥ in NS 779 (1659 CE), which is why it is also called Pūrṇacandra Vihāra.
Earlier, the god house of the monastic building had three storeys, however it was severely damaged by the 2015 earthquakes.
As a result, the third floor has since been removed, and a roof of corrugated zinc sheets has been installed on top of the second floor.
The structure is built on a double plinth and has a timber lattice that covers the main sanctum.
The current statue was consecrated a few years ago after the loss of the previous one.
Asmall dharmadhātujinālaya caitya(1.3 m high) is also located in front of the temple and was established in 1898.
Thebāhāḥis surrounded by residential buildings on all four sides.
The building at the northern wing is in ruins, though the other buildings are intact.
Thisbāhāḥwas established by Ratnarāja Vajrācārya in 1872.

After the Temple was constructed, the neighbourhood was renamed ‘Jaisideval’.

Gorakhanātha Pīṭha, constructed in 1667 CE (NS 787), stands in Nagaḥcva, just north of Sarasvatī Mandira (KIR0049).

They are one of the castes in the larger Newar community, whose members follow the Kāpālīka and Gorakhanātha religious traditions, and are categorised as water-unacceptable but touchable castes in the a hundred sixtieth Article of theMulukī Ainof 1854 CE (seeKhatiwoda, Simon Cubelic and Axel Michaels, 2021 (forth. coming)).
Since medieval times, this community has been especially devoted to Gorakhanātha as attested from numerous inscriptions found in Kirtipur, Patan, and Banepa (D. KũvaraVS 2062, 193).
There are six inscriptions dating from the medieval times installed by the Kapālī community at thepīṭha.
A large city quarter in Kirtipur is named Gorakhapurī, which has been referred several times in various medieval inscriptions.
A pair of stone feet, representing Gorakhanātha,have been consecrated in the unroofed brickpīṭha.
The upper part of it might have been destroyed and was probably never reconstructed, leaving it in this current state.

An inscription from 1667 CE (NS 787), adjacent to the Gorakhanātha’s feet and Bhairava statue, records the initial construction of thepīṭhaby five members of the Kapālī community from Kirtipur and Balambu.
Another inscription from 1791 CE (NS 911) mentions the renovation of thepīṭhaand addition of a pinnacle by the Kapālī caste members.
An inscription from 1684 CE (NS 804) refers to the deity as Isṭhaconi Mahākāla.
D. Vajrācārya(VS 2056, 510) has identified this as Gorakhanātha Mandira.^This Bhairava has been referred to as Ākāśa Bhairava.
The architecture of the monuments follows the same rules as other śikhara built in west Nepal between the 13th and the 15th century.
Of limited size, they may have been built to honor the memory of ancestors or a lineage.
The religious affiliation of the temples is yet impossible to establish.
According to an inscription the caitya was commissioned by Śivarāma Mahan Bhava in 1705 CE (NS 825).
The inscription is located in the entrance area of the shopping mall built on the foundations of the historic Cībhāḥ Phalcā (LAL4211).
Buṅgadyaḥ was donated in the 1970s by Gopi Maharjan, a member of the Caitya Guṭhī.
A Dharmadhatu has been erected to the east of the monument.
It is likely that the guthi members are descendants of the founder of the caitya.
The guthi owns the commercial building that replaced the historic rest house (LAL4211) and uses income from rent for various social and religious activities.
In 1859 CE (VS 1916), Ḍillīsiṃha Basneta constructed a unique temple that houses three separateśivālayas (lit. Śiva’s abode) within one sanctum.
He later established a trust by donating land parcels in 1868 CE (VS 1925).

A statue of Nandī, the bull mount of Śiva, sits outside the temple to the west.Ḍillīsiṃha Basneta undertook the construction of the temple during the early years of the Rāṇā regime in 1859 CE (VS 1916) (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, pp. 354-355; Michaels and Tandon 2017, p. 70).

text: Concurrently, he established another conjoined temple featuring separateśivālayas named Drihmeśvara, Īśvareśvara, and Śireśvara (PPK0516).

Moreover, he installed a bell (PPK0516-015) to commemorate the construction of both conjoined temples, which now hangs from a bell-stand in front of the other conjoined temple (PPK0516).Ḍillīsiṃha Basneta, appointed as akājī, an officer of ministerial rank, was a trusted appointee of one of Prime Minister Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā (B. Bhaṇḍārī VS 2071, pp. 20-21).

The area known as Ḍillībajāra in Kathmandu was named after Ḍillīsiṃha, who was also among the delegates accompanying Jaṅga Bahādura to England in 1950 CE (P. Rāṇā VS 2059, p. 58). Ḍillīsiṃha’s son, Captain Padmakeśara Basneta, was married to Jaṅga Bahādura’s daughter from Minā Mahārānī, also known as Dākhacoke Mahārānī (P. Rāṇā VS 2059, p. 193).

A few years after the temple’s construction, Ḍillīsiṃha donated land parcels in 1868 CE (VS 1925) to set up a trust that supervised the daily and other periodic rituals at the temple (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, pp. 438).
Despite the establishment of a trust for daily and periodic worship, as of February 2024, only daily rituals are conducted at the temple.
A Brahmin from the Suvedī caste performs the daily rituals here, as well as at the nearby Drihmeśvara, Īśvareśvara, and Śireśvara Śivālaya, the other conjoined temple built by Ḍillīsiṃha.

Despite the few available elements, it is possible to suggest that the temple was built around the second half of the 14th century (nearbyśikharatemples with an almost identical pavilion are dated from 1373 CE (ŚS 1295), seeSharma 2012: p. 303).
The temple enshrines within its sanctorum the original Licchavi-period stone image of Palāñcoka Bhagavatī, believed to have been carried by floodwaters from Kavre.
The present structure was reconstructed in 1997 (VS 2054).
Inside the sanctum, a stone image of the eighteen-armed Mahiṣāsuramardinī is installed as the principal icon.
No definitive historical documentation has been found regarding the original establishment of this temple.
According to local oral tradition, a flood washed away the ancient image of Palāñcoka Bhagavatī from Kavre.
The image was rescued by residents of Gvaḥphaḥ tole and installed in their neighborhood, where she came to be known as Palāñcoka Bhagavatī because of her place of origin.
A temple was subsequently constructed to house the goddess.
Historical sources record that Vijayāsvāminī, the wife of a prominent householder named Samrāṭa, installed Palāñcoka Bhagavatī in Kavre during the reign of King Mānadeva in 503 CE (Śaka Saṃvat 425).

This claim gains some plausibility from historical accounts stating that the Licchavi-period image of Palāñcoka Bhagavatī in Kavre was later replaced with a new image by King Jagajyoti Malla of Bhaktapur (r. 1614–1637 CE), suggesting that the earlier image may indeed have been displaced.
The earliest inscription found at the Palāñcoka Bhagavatī Temple in Gvaḥphaḥ tole dates to 1885 CE (NS 1008).
This inscription was carved on a woodentoraṇainstalled at the temple, although the text has become too worn to yield further details.
The temple underwent a restoration in 1970 CE.
Owing to severe deterioration, it was fully reconstructed in 1997 CE (VS 2054) with financial support from the Kathmandu Metropolitan City and donations collected from devotees.
Prior to reconstruction, the temple was a single-storey structure with a tiled roof.
The rebuilding transformed it into a two-storey temple with brass roofing.
To mark the sacred stone, a small domeddevala(miniature shrine) has been constructed above it.
The façade of this pyramidal section bears eight gilded metal images of the Aṣṭamātṛkās, dated to 1931–32 (VS 1988).
The metal image associated with Bālakumārī is kept in the house of Chibhāḥnanikā Rājabhaṇḍārī, theguthiyār.
Although no inscription survives to date its construction, comparison with other Śākta shrines established during the Malla period suggests that this site likely belongs to the late-Malla era.
Dathu Bāhāḥ is a branch of Rudravarṇa Mahāvihāra, Oku Bāhāḥ (LAL2260) and was built by Kumāraju Śākya in 1678 CE.
Dathu Bāhāḥ faces west and the two-storey monastic building (kvāḥpāḥchẽ) is covered with corrugated pewter sheets (jastāpātā) and the roof is supported by the plain wooden struts.
A Svayambhūcaityaand a well are built in the Bāhāḥ’s premises.

Kumāraju Śākya[3]commissioned the initial construction of this Bāhāḥ on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha (Śrīpañcamī) in 1678 CE (798 NS) during the joint reign of King Śrīnivāsa and Yoganarendra Malla.
[4]During the initial construction, statues of Akṣobhya, Cakrasaṃvara-Vajravārāhī, Gaṇeśa, Mahākāl, and a Svayambhū Caitya were also installed in the Bāhāḥ’s premises.
The first floor of thekvāḥpāḥchẽwas damaged during the 1934 CE earthquakes and was repaired by the Bāhāḥsaṅghamembers.
Thekvāpāḥchẽwas again severely affected by the 2015 CE earthquakes.
[5]The anniversary of the Svayambhū Caitya installed in the Bāhāḥ’s premises takes place on the fifth of the bright fortnight of Māgha (Śrīpañcamī).

The Lichhavi inscription in front of Cvachẽ Phalcā is not related to it.
This inscription with almost half of the text already eroded was recovered in 2004 CE.

Installed during the reign of King Gaṇadeva, it deals with authorizing Kuthera and Śullī, the twoadhikaraṇas (courts) of the Lichhavi period, to execute works performed by the other twoadhikaraṇas called Liṃgvala and Māpcoka (Ś. Rājavaṃśī2061: p. 92).
Lichhavi inscriptions with similar content are found in the neighboring settlements like Caukīṭāra, Balambu, Kisipiḍi, and Satuṃgala (D. VajrācāryaVS 2030: p. 188).
There are twoguthis of the Gopālī community in Thankot. Ānanda Bhairava Guthi is the mainguthiof the Gopālīs of Cvachẽ.

text: Tarpibaḍā Śikhara Temple 2, built around the 13th-15th centuries, is the smaller of twośikharatemples that face each other and are about 20 meters north of a stone fountain (JUM0443).
