Oriented toward thiskuladevatāsthāna, both the Śivālaya and thesataḥwere constructed simultaneously.

Because of the presence of this Phalca, the site is locally designated in Khasa Nepali as apāṭī(rest-house) which explains the name “Kālesāhu Pāṭī.” The plinth (peṭī) is built entirely of stone, above which wooden pillars made of pine are erected.
An inscription preserved on the Sataḥ itself provides detailed information regarding its construction.
According to this record, the monument was built in 1914 CE (VS 1971), during the reign of Candrasamśera, by Pṛthvīvilāsa Sāpakoṭā.
Selecting the site of his lineage deity, he constructed the monument as well as a stone temple dedicated to Naravadeśvara.
Notably, the inscription refers to Kālesāhu Pāṭī not assataḥorsattala, but explicitly as a Pāṭī.
The inscription does not detail after whom the installedliṅgawas named Naravadeśvara.
Alongside the construction of the temple and Kālesāhu Pāṭī, extensive parcels of land in various locations were endowed asguṭhīto support annual rites.
The inscription further details the expenses and ritual materials required for recurring festivals, including anniversary of Kālesāhu Pāṭī (varṣavardhana) and other annual observances.
It also expresses the intention that the bell, temple, and Sataḥ should be renovated when dilapidated, and that surplus funds should be used to purchasevṛttāland in order to augment income.
Pṛthvīvilāsa, described as asāhuof his time, appears to have been a person of considerable means, as evidenced by his ability to commission both thesataḥand the temple.

Architecturally, thesataḥreflects late Rāṇā-period construction techniques, with masonry walls raised using large bricks (mā-appa), whereas the stone temple follows the traditionalśikharākārastyle prevalent from the early medieval period onward.
The most recent major earthquake caused no significant damage to tKālesāhu Pāṭī, apart from minor cracks in a few places.
At present (2025 CE), however, parts of the roof and walls are in a severely dilapidated condition.

The Śrī Vihāvara Ādhārabhūta School, regarded as one of the oldest schools in Kābhre (established in VS 2002), initially conducted classes within Kālesāhu Pāṭī before relocating approximately 200 meters to the east.
Members of his family continue to reside on the upper floor at present (2025 CE), as confirmed by a local resident (Sāpakoṭā, female, aged 63).

Positioned east of the Sātatale Durbar ( (NWK0160) within the Nuwakot Durbar Complex, the Gārada Ghara (term "gārada" originates from the English word "guard", see K. Parājulī & G. Śarmā, VS 2067, p. 319) initially intended as a residence (Nep.ghara) for stationed guards, thus was named as Gārada Ghara. Also serving as a repository for weaponry and supplies utilized by the military (Panta 2012, p. 13), this structure, dating back to the Śāha era, embodies the prevalent Newar architectural style of the 17th century (Nippon Institute of Technology 1985, p. 25). Originally standing at four stories, the uppermost two floors have been disassembled for reconstruction as of March 2024 CE, while the remaining levels exhibit signs of deterioration.The western-facing façade of the building was adorned withjhĩgaṭītiles on its roof before the upper floors were dismantled. The third floor featured a three-bayed window (gāḥjhyāḥ) at its centre, flanked by latticed windows. The now-disassembled second floor also boasted a three-bayed window with smaller openings (trikhājhyāḥ) in the middle, accompanied by latticed windows (tikijhyāḥ) on either side. On the first floor, five latticed windows were interspersed with a wooden string course depicting soldiers carrying arms and banners, including a controversial scene of a soldier inappropriately touching a woman (Gutschow 2011, p. 801). This portrayal on the string course seemingly glorifies the misconduct of victorious Gorkha soldiers towards women from the defeated side. Additionally, the rear of the first floor featured a three-bayed window with shutters, marking the introduction of a triple window with shutters on this level (Gutschow 2011, p. 801). Notably, the ground floor showcases a wooden door embellished with intricate carvings, leading to a lobby with five bays at the rear.While lacking inscriptional evidence for the exact construction date, it is probable that the building was erected after the conquest of Nuwakot by Pṛthvī Nārāyaṇa Śāha in 1744 CE. Stylistic analysis suggests a dating to the late 18th or early 19th century (Gutschow 2011, p. 800). The extent of renovations undergone by the structure remains uncertain, with records indicating governmental occupancy until the late 1970s and subsequent renovation efforts by Bhaktapur carpenters in 1983-84 (Gutschow 2011, p. 801).The devastating 2015 earthquake inflicted severe damage on the Gārada Ghara, resulting in the collapse of half of the uppermost floor and a significant portion of the roof. The Department of Archaeology, acting on behalf of the Nepal Government, engaged the Chinese Academy of Cultural Heritage (CACH) to oversee the restoration of Gārada Ghara and other adjacent monuments. Scaffoldings were erected around these structures, and the roofs were shielded with corrugated metal sheets to safeguard against rain. However, as of March 2024 CE, renovation activities are yet to commence.Given its original purpose as a soldier's residence, the Gārada Ghara does not host any socio-religious activities.

text: Sundarī Coka ("beautiful courtyard") built by King Siddhinarasiṃha Malla in NS 767 (1647 CE) is one of the three royal palaces of Patan Darbar.
Today, the original ivory carvings are kept in the museum and the windows were restored using a composite material resembling the original ivory.
Thevihārawas moved to its present location to make place for the Royal Palace.
The Kathmandu Valley Preservation Trust (KVPT) renovated the palace building between 2006–2017.
For the protection of Lalitpur City, theDaśamahāvidyāhave been established in ten different ṭola.
To the north of the shrine is Triliṅgeśvara Mahādeva, who is her male deity (M. Miśra NS 1127, p. 27).
It is believed that Bhairavī was born at the midnight of bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa  (J. Mānandhara VS 2046, p. 33).

There is a popular belief that if one offers worship on a Friday with black dried grapes, coconut, sweets, and flattened rice, along with yellow and red cloth, the effects of the black magic are removed (M. Miśra NS 1127, p. 29).
This shrine is constructed facing south.
Instead of an idol, only an aniconic stone has been installed in the shrine.
Atoraṇamade of stone has also been offered to Bhairavī.
No historical evidence has been found regarding when the Bhairavī shrine in Lalitpur was established.
The absence of any inscription at the shrine makes it difficult to confirm its historical authenticity.

It is possible that Bhairavī was also established when Lalitpur was developed as a systematic settlement, with Kopeśvara Temple (LAL1381) as the central point, and theDaśamahāvidyāwere installed in various directions for the city's protection.
Later, in 2020 CE (VS 2076), on the initiative of an organization named 'DaśamahāvidyāBhaktibhāva Parivāra', daily worship was restarted by a Rājopādhyāya Brāhmaṇa.
Palṭana Ghara is said to be the first private building in the Kathmandu Valley with glass window panes.
The façade of the building is decorated with a clay relief featuring a line of marching soldiers with guns resting on their shoulders.

The building owes its popular name "platoon house" to this relief and is also known by other names: Māna Mandira (reference to Abhimāna Siṃha Basnyāta, the original owner of the building), Kaptāna Ghara (lit. Captain House) and Tilaṅgā Ghara (Nepali term for soldiers).
The symmetrical façade of the building features a three-bay opening in the center and is flanked by two doors on either side.
The central opening likely once had the same carved wooden arches that survive on the side doors but might have been removed to fit the new doors for the shops.
The relief of marching soldiers covers the entire width of the building.

Following the Gorkhalis' conquest of the Kathmandu Valley, the second Śāha king Pratāpa Siṃha  gave the house and surrounding land to Abhimāna Siṃha Basnyāta as a land grant (sunābirtā) (B. ĀcāryaVS 2060, p. 94-95).
He is said to have begun with the construction of the Palṭana House three days after the ownership of the land was transferred to him in 1777 CE (B. ĀcāryaVS 2060, p. 95).

An inscription (edited and translated inN. Yogī et allVS 2010, p. 4-6), formerly installed at Nārāyaṇa Cuka the courtyard behind Palṭana Ghara, now lost, states that the building was completed on January 10, 1777 CE (Śaka Era 1698).
citations: (edited and translated inN. Yogī et allVS 2010, p. 4-6)

text: The inscription further records the Palṭana Ghara to be "a building with the protection of a line oftilaṅgās(army men) and rich in honor and wealth".
N. Yogī et all(VS 2010, p. ka) mentions that Abhimāna Siṃha had prepared a copy of the Divyopadeśa, a collection of teachings by King Pṛthvī Nārāyaṇa Śāha.
According to another oral tradition in the Basnyāta clan, during the reign of Rāṇā Prime Minister Candra Śamśera, the building was in the name of five descendants of Abhimāna Siṃha.
Today, the building is in the name of eight descendants of a certain Dhokala Siṃha Basneta.
There are no written sources shedding light on the exact process of confiscation and transfer to the new owner (Ś. Aryāla VS 2078,https://www.onlinekhabar.com/2021/07/980408).
The building is currently rented to a number of businesses that use the ground floor for shops and the upstairs for storage.
The Vaidya family who runs the pharmacy claims that their ancestor, the Royal Vaidya (Ayurveda physician) opened the pharmacy at the request of King Pratāpa Siṃha Śāha in 1776 CE.

However, the successful treatment of the King's son Gīrvāṇayuddha pleased the monarch and he rewarded the physician by allocating land at Imāḍola for aguthi. (GorkhāpatraVS 2066, p. 5) Bāsukṛṣṇa Vaidya proudly claims that Kṛṣṇagovinda Vaidya, another ancestor, pronounced Jaṅga Bahādura dead.
Vaidya says that he is running the pharmacy to continue the legacy of his ancestors although the shop is not economically viable anymore. (Gorkhāpatra VS 2066, p. 5).
When the Basnyāta clan tried to sell the building in 1961 CE, the pharmacy's owner filed a complaint with the palace and the sale was averted (N. Basnyat2019, p. 142).
However, its dilapidated condition urgently requires repairs.
The Department of Archaeology has announced the restoration of the building in the near future. (Ś. Aryāla VS 2078,https://www.onlinekhabar.com/2021/07/980408).
The building shares a small space with a single-storey annex structure to its north.
The courtyard measures 7 m × 4.7 m, and has a residential building to the its east and north.
Both of these are built on arcadedphalcāsthat serve as the ground floor.
Small images of different Buddhist deities have been placed on the walls of the southern annex building and western boundary wall.
Jīvanṛsiṃha, a member of the Cikã Bahī and an Āyurvedic doctor (vaidya) by profession, established this Bāhāḥ in 1878 (NS 998).
The lions also sit next to two metal flags that were donated in 1909 (NS 1023).

monument_name: Rāvatakoṭa Pañcadevala (built in the 14th or 15th Cent.)
text: According to the information collected in situ in 2014, this work was done by locals, in reaction to damages done (to the monuments?) by a bulldozer (during road widening?).
Ellderly people from the area claim that the Phalcā must have been constructed by the ancestors of these Jyāpu families.
Inside the Phalcā, there is a collection of wooden structures belonging to the Sanāḥguthi of the Jyāpu clans.
The inscription installed in the Phalcā informs us that its roof was reconstructed by the Sanāḥguthi alongside local residents and the Kathmandu Valley Preservation Trust in 1992.
Nowadays the building is used as a tea shop.
The three stone memorial pillars are found on a stone platform built on the northern side of the path between Rārā lake and Gamgaḍhī.
Stone pillars were erected throughout the Karnali Basin from the 13th to the 17th century.
They are installed to honor the memory of deceased persons, mostly warriors.

Each pillar's upper section is decorated with motifs representing the sun and the moon, referring to the memory of the persons for whom the pillars were erected, and that will last "as long as the sun and the moon exist" (Andolfatto 2019).
The medium section of the pillars contain eroded inscription on the southern faces.
Only the inscription of pillar 3 (MUG0150-003) is partly readable.
It contains the date of 1404 of the Śaka era, which corresponds to 1482 CE.
A stylised double vajra (viśvavajra) is visible on pillar 002,  thus indicating the Buddhist affiliation of the person for which the monument was erected.
Constructed towards the end of the Rāṇā period for religious purposes, Kalmochanaghāta Sataḥ West stands as the last one built among those lining the banks of the Bāgamatī from Ṭeku to Thāpāthali.
There is a photograph taken prior to the construction of the Sataḥ in 1924 CE (1984-84 VS), which can be viewedhere.

The two-storey building, constructed using whitewash and bricks characteristic of the architectural style prevalent during the Rāṇā period, comprises five bays on the ground floor and a room with three windows on the first floor.
An inscription recently installed (February 2024) records the construction of the sataḥ by Durgānātha Miśra in 1945-46 CE (VS 2002).
Another inscription records that the Sataḥ's purpose is to provide care for the terminally ill and to conductkriyāputrīrituals.
The mentioned inscription also indicates that any individual can contribute to the upkeep and maintenance of the Sataḥ for the sake of virtue, given its status as a public site.
Local residents suggest that Miśrabāje, believed to be the builder of the monument, used to reside here.
But the actual constructors were a family living in Asana ṭola (local resident, Śreṣṭha, male, age 77/Maharjana, male, age 56).
citations: (local resident, Śreṣṭha, male, age 77/Maharjana, male, age 56)

text: According to an inventory published in 1982 CE (VS 2039) (Inventory VS 2039, p.133), the upper floor of Kalmochanaghāta Sataḥ West was utilized for devotional songs and dances.
However, this practice was discontinued after 1983 (VS 2040; local resident, Ḍaṅgola, male, aged 73).
The Sataḥ underwent its most recent renovation in 2014 CE (2017 VS), funded through donations.
The stūpa is built next to a shrine topped by a stūpa (JUM0031) on the edge of a hill ridge to the west of Bhaṇḍārībādā.
The stūpa is built on a 300 x 300 cm stone base in the shape of amaṇḍala(a square with a central projection - Skt.bhadra-on each side).
On top of theharmikāare the damaged remains of three steps of decreasing dimensions.
The monument is typologically similar to the stūpa at Kuchi Bihāra (ACH0010, horizontal plinth) and to the one erected on top of the Patharnauli reservoir (DLK0160).
Both monuments were built in 1354 CE (ŚS 1276) by Devavarmā, the Great Minister (mahāmātya) of King Pṛthvīmalla.
It is therefore likely that this stūpa and the shrine built next to it were both built during the 14th century (Andolfatto 2019, pp. 96-97).

monument_name: Licchavi Caitya and statue of Buddha
text: This Caitya was constructed some time in the Licchavi period and stands testament to the antiquity of the Bungamati settlement.

monument_name: Licchavi Caitya and statue of Buddha
text: The Licchavi Caitya is eroded, slightly damaged and missing its finial.

text: Parts of the right hand and leg of the Buddha statue have broken off, most of the nimbus is missing and the damaged head has been patched up with cement mortar.

The principal façade of the structure has a door at its centre; this is flanked by two small blind windows, statues of Maudgalyāyana and Sāriputra and two stone lions (established in VS 2022/1966 CE).
The currenttoraṇais a replacement; the previous one was stolen in the 2000s.
The stolen one is described inLocke(1985, 77) and dated back to NS 808 (1688 CE).
Inside the sanctum of the god house, one can find a north-facing stone statue of Akṣobhya, two stone inscriptions, and the metal cloth of Dīpaṅkara Buddha.
The main god house is attached to residential buildings on its eastern and southern sides.
The courtyard is open to the west and provides access to other residential buildings.
This is a one-storied building with a central five-bayed colonnaded structure.
Two stone inscriptions are attached to the walls of thisdigichẽ.
The eastern building of the courtyard collapsed completely with the 2015 earthquake.
The brick-paved courtyard of thebāhāḥmeasures around 13 m x 13 m and contains a row of different types ofcaityasanddharmadhātumaṇḍala,all of which are lined up in front of the building.
No inscription could be found that mentions the establishment of this Vihāra.
However, according to theNepālikabhūpavaṃśāvalī(19.3.17)  this monastery was established during the reign of King Siddhinarasiṃha Malla.
It is believed that brothers established Jyo Bāhāḥ, Vajrakīrti Mahāvihāra and Om Bāhāḥ.
The Bāhāḥ can be reached by passing through an elongated four-storey building.
This building has a line of eleven vertical windows on its first and second floors and seven central doors with another two doors on either side on its ground floor.
The three-storey monument building is now plastered in cement and has been roofed with corrugated metal sheets.
The principal façade of the building faces west and has a central carved door on its ground floor.
Two small lattice windows can also be found on the first floor near the edge of the building.
The centralpasukājhyāḥseems to have been installed during the renovation of the building.
The projecting balcony on the southern building has created a visual imbalance to the symmetry of the main façade.
Tall buildings surround the courtyard.
Devamuni Śākya ordered the construction of this Bāhāḥ in 1676 (Pruscha1975, P-71;Locke1985, 176).

Constructed during the reign of King Pārthivendra Malla in 1684–85 CE (NS805), this temple ranks among the few monuments in Kathmandu that remained structurally intact following the recent devastating earthquakes.
Many of the religious monuments along this street were constructed by such local aristocratic lineages during the late medieval period.

Only the corner brackets (kuṃsala) and a few upper-tier struts have survived, while 32 historic struts on the first and second roof levels were replaced with plain wooden brackets to support the roof.

The sculpture is remarkable for its detailed pedestal (pādapīṭha) and uniqueprabhā(aureole) carved not as a halo but as a stylizedkadambatree, as explicitly mentioned in the inscription found below the image.
According to oral testimony (Śreṣṭha, male, age 65), the original grand image of Viṣṇu, which matched the scale and style of the pedestal andprabhā, was stolen during the 1960s CE (2020s VS).
The current image, recovered from a police storehouse, was subsequently installed as a replacement.
An inscription carved on the front face of the pedestal records the installation of the Viṣṇu statue in 1684–85 CE (NS 805), during the reign of Pārthivendra Malla.
The lower lines of the inscription are now completely eroded, but it is evident that the same Nayana Bhāro was responsible for constructing the three-tiered shrine itself.

The Bhāros of Cikaṃmugaḥ—associated with the Joshi, Māthema, and Śreṣṭha lineages—were prominentbhāradāras(court officials) during the Malla period, and the builder likely belonged to one of these influential families.
Pruscha (1975, p. 77), however, mistakenly attributed the temple’s construction to the reign of King Bhūpatindra Malla.

While hundreds of temples across the valley were destroyed or heavily restored following the 2015 CE (VS 2072) earthquake—many unnecessarily, with traditionaljhiṅgaṭīroofs replaced by copper sheets—this temple has remained largely untouched, preserving its authentic medieval character.
Elderly residents report that in their lifetime, no active worship has been conducted here under theguthi(endowment) system once associated with the shrine.
Deva Śamśera’s wife Karmakumārīdevī commissioned the construction of Karmabhakteśvara Mandira in 1891 CE (VS 1948).
Unfortunately, the statues of Durgā in the northwestern corner and Viṣṇu in the northeastern corner have been stolen.
Regrettably, thesataḥcollapsed during the 2015 earthquakes, burying the bell under rubble.
In 1891 CE (VS 1948), Karmakumārīdevī consecrated the mainśivaliṅgain her honor (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p.347; Michaels and Tandon 2017, p.106).
citations: (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p.347; Michaels and Tandon 2017, p.106)

text: She was the daughter of King Surendra from one of his consorts (P. Rāja VS 2073, p.108), and she married Deva Śamśera, who later briefly served as the prime minister in 1901 CE.
The couple had two sons, Jaṅga Śamśera and Bhuvana Śamśera (P. Rāṇā VS 2059, p.304).
Additionally, Karmakumārīdevī endowed 44ropanīs of land to ensure the continuity of all rituals (cf.K_0039_0030).
Sadly, Karmakumārīdevī passed away in 1895 CE (VS 1952) while her husband Deva Śamśera held the position of commander-in-chief (P. Rāṇā VS 2059, p.304; P. Rāṇā VS 2070, p.180).
citations: (P. Rāṇā VS 2059, p.304; P. Rāṇā VS 2070, p.180)

text: In memory of his late wife, Deva Śamśera established a water supply system with taps throughout the Cārakose Jhāḍī, the largest and most dense forest of Nepal, stretching from Bhikṣākhorī (currently, Amlekhganj) to Simarā.
The earthquakes of 2015 inflicted damage upon the temple, leading to restoration efforts by the Pashupati Area Development Trust in 2021 CE (VS 2078).
Despite Karmakumārīdevī's donation of 44ropanīs of land to the temple, the performance of daily and other periodic rituals at the temple has now ceased.
The Bhṛṅgāreśvara Mandira is located at the centre of Sunaguthi, an ancient Newar settlement located about 5 kilometres south of Patan Darbar Square.
The Bhṛṅgāreśvara Mandira constitutes the densest and oldest area of monuments in Sunaguthi.
It was built during the Licchavi period and reconstructed in 1553 by Viṣṇu Siṃha.
It is believed that it originally had two tiers (probably gilded, seeD. VajrācāryaVS 2056, 19), but that these collapsed several times during various earthquakes.
It was reconstructed by Viṣṇu Siṃha in 1553 (probably in a pagoda style), collapsed during the 1934 earthquake, and was then rebuilt again, this time in a dome-shape.
Two Licchavi inscriptions can be found on either side of these lions.
A small two-tier temple to Jagannātha has been built at the south-west of the temple complex and is based on a square base of 137cm x 137cm.
A recent stone statue of Hanumān has been established to the west of the main temple.
A statue of Jalaśayana Nārāyaṇa (lying Viṣṇu on water) has recently been installed in the far north-east corner.

The Yaḥsigāḥ (SUN0050, the place where theyaḥsi‘pole’ is erected during Pekhaḥ Jātra) and Halipatāḥ Phalcā (SUN4012, located to the west of Dyaḥ Sataḥ) are peripheral monuments of the larger Bhṛṅgāreśvara Mandira complex.
The termbhṛṅgārarefers to a golden water vessel found by King Vishnu Simgh of Patan in a well, and the name of the village (Sunaguthi, ‘lit. goldguṭhī’) is supposedly derived from this.
Devamālā Vaṃśāvalī(2013, 94) mentions that King Ratna Malla established this village with 300 houses in 1513 and organised an annual procession on the full moon day of Caitra.
During the Licchavi period, Sunaguthi was a separate administrative unit called Bhṛṅgāra Pāñcālī.

However, according to an inscription dated MS 65, the king rewarded the residents of this village for their help in making the statue of Jalaśayana Nārāyaṇa at Buḍhānīlakaṇṭha by granting them a level of autonomy regarding the administration of the area.
Although the date of its initial construction has not been traced out, theGopālarājavaṃśāvalī(fol. 17r), suggests that the Bhṛṅgāreśvara Mandira is older than the Paśupatinātha Temple in Kathmandu.
Adhunifire ritually replaces the extinguished natural flame.
The top of the narrow hill is crowned by a flat area comprising a pillared pavilion (maṇḍapa) containing thedhunifire, built in front of the Śiva Temple.
The temple is built of concrete imitating a brick pattern.
Saṃnyāsi women take care of thedhunifire and Śiva Temple.
It bear an inscribed dated reading:sa 1822.
If this date in the Vikrama Samvat (VS), it corresponds to the year 1765 CE.
Hiraṇyabhakteśvara Mahādeva was established in the year 1858 CE (VS 1915) by Hiraṇyagarbhakumārī, the chief wife of Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā.
It is constructed from stone and features a distinctive bell-shaped roof crowned with a metallic finial.
The primary western entrance bears an inscription beneath itstoraṇa, providing details about the temple's construction.
Hiraṇyagarbhakumārī, also known as Jyeṭhā Mainā Mahārānī, erected thisśivālayain 1858 CE (VS 1915) and named it Hiraṇyabhakteśvara in honor of herself.
She was the daughter of Prāṇa Śāha, whose wife Dīpakumārī Śāhā built a temple named Prāṇamukteśvara (PPK0522) in his name in 1859 CE (VS 1916).
Hiraṇyagarbhakumārī, born in 1826 CE (VS 1883), had two daughters with Jaṅga Bahādura: Lalitarājyalakṣmī and Dīpakumārī, also known as Bāgakī Kānchīmaiyā̃.
Lalitarājyalakṣmī was married to Prince Trailokya and gave birth to Pṛthvī Vikrama Śāha, who eventually became the king (P. Rāja VS 2071, pp. 76-77).

Her attitude changed when, during the marriage ceremony, Jaṅga Bahādura applied vermillion powder to her hair parting, and was later made his principal wife (P. Rāṇā VS 2070, pp.62-63; P. Rāja VS 2071, p.60; B. Bhaṇḍārī VS 2071, pp.133-135).
citations: (P. Rāṇā VS 2070, pp.62-63; P. Rāja VS 2071, p.60; B. Bhaṇḍārī VS 2071, pp.133-135)

text: In 1871 CE (VS 1828), Jaṅga Bahādura conferred upon her the titleŚrī3Baḍāmahārānī, a distinction not bestowed upon his other wives (P. Rāṇā VS 2059, p.152).
In a list of Jaṅga Bahādura's wives compiled by Bhoṭu Dvāre, she is referred to asŚrī5MumāBaḍāmahārānī(K. Dīkṣita VS 2034, p.76).

Tragically, Hiraṇyagarbhakumārī, along with two other wives, Putalī Mahārānī and Miśrī Mahārānī, practiced self-immolation (satī) following Jaṅga Bahādur's death in Pattharaghaṭṭā in 1877 CE (VS 1933) (P. Rāja VS 2071, p.66).

While it is likely that the temple received substantial donations for various rituals during its construction by Rāṇā Prime Minister Jaṅga Bahādura's wife, it is worth noting that presently, none of these rituals, including daily observances, are being carried out.
The pillars have visibly been all gathered together and a thirteenth artefact added to the whole.
Stone pillars were erected throughout the Karnali Basin from the 13th to the 17th century.
They are installed to honor the memory of deceased persons, mostly warriors.
Unfortunately the pillars of Ḍāḍimāḍī have too eroded inscriptions (sometimes totally gone).
Pillar 013 is of special interest since it contains the representation of a stūpa, thus indicating the Buddhist affiliation of the person for whom the pillar was erected.
Local residents still remember the open water channel [deydhaḥ(desadhala)]that used to run through Sunāguthi.
This water was considered to be holy and was offered to the statue of Bālakūmāri located in the temple to the east (SUN0230).
The Capĩgāḥ was filled with rubble, and the current water tank made of brick and cement was constructed in its place.
This Capĩgāḥ stands as an example of tangible and intangible heritage that has been severely affected by modern construction work.
Kvay Bāhāḥ, built NS 1070, is a branch of Cilancva Bāhāḥ (KIR0002).

Locke(1985, 182) andShokoohy(1994, 135) refer to it as "Karṇāṭaka Mahāvihāra," whereasPruscha(1975, 265) andHerdick(1988, 45) designate it as "Karuṇākarama Vihāra" andŚ. Śreṣṭha(VS 2057, 71) identifies it as “Karuṇākara Vihāra”.
This text mentions that a certain Bhāgisiṃha and his family members built thebāhāḥin 1701 CE (NS 821).
Pruscha(1975, 265) mistakenly dated the Bāhāḥ to the nineteenth century, however, the intricately crafted wooden elements in thedyaḥchẽimply an earlier construction date.
The abovementioned scholars suggest that the Śikharakūṭa Caitya constructed in the Bāhāḥ premises bears an inscription dating from 1633 CE (NS 753).
However, thecaityahas no inscription in the present-day (2021).
It is likely that this inscription was relocated at some point.
Shokoohy1994, 138 mentions that the inscription was about the construction of Kvay Bāhāḥ.
However, this claim is not convincing since the Bāhāḥwas constructed sixty-eight years after thecaitya.
Just beyond this entrance, two separate niches built into the right-hand side wall of the hallway house statues of Gaṇeśa and Mahākāla.
A stone statue of Akṣobhya is consecrated as thekvāḥpāḥdyaḥin the sanctum.
Apasukājhyāḥis installed on the first floor of thedyaḥchẽ,where the esoteric deity of thebāhāḥ(āgaṃdyaḥ)is also enshrined.
It is possible that it was removed during renovation; however, there is no documented evidence of such renovation work.
Until 2000 CE, members of a Vajrācāryasaṅgha,residing near thebāhāḥ,took turns performing daily rituals in Kvay Bāhāḥ.
Kvay Bāhāḥ formerly owned plots of land, which were acquired by the government in 1956 CE (VS 2013) for the construction of Tribhuvan University.
Mahālakṣmī Shrine Phalcā is a renovated but closed rest house at the Calākhu Ṭola in Sankhu.
Not much is known about its initial construction due to the lack of historic sources.
In 1976 CE, a primary school was set up in the area that ran its classes at Nhāykaṃ Sataḥ, another rest house at the Calākhu Ṭola.
The 2015 earthquakes incurred severe damages to the Phalcā.
Locals renovated its walls and roof in 2016 CE using modern bricks and concrete with corrugated metal sheets laid on the roof.

Unlike most Newar rest houses—which are typically freestanding or attached to neighboring structures—thisphalcāis partially built below ground level, distinguishing it both architecturally and functionally.
The structure integrates a recently restoredhiti(water spout), reconstructed based on community memory and archaeological findings.

During demolition and reconstruction work, a small underground water stream and a remnant of a wooden water pipe were uncovered, confirming long-standing oral testimony that a hiti once existed within thephalcā(local resident: Śreṣṭha, male, 81).
Responding to this discovery, the original restoration plan was revised to incorporate a functioning hiti within one of the building’s three bays—reduced from an earlier configuration of four.
This upper structure was renovated in 1734 CE (NS 854) and has since been merged into a private residence owned by the Dhvamdaḥ family.
No dedicatory inscription survives to confirm the date of the lowerphalcā’s construction or any subsequent renovation.
However, its use ofsurkīmortar, plain wooden columns, and arched wall niches strongly suggest a construction or major renovation during the Rāṇā period.

From 1990 CE (VS 2047), the phalcā was repurposed as a community library (vācanālaya) operated by the local youth organization Śrī Pragatī Vācanālaya Football Team, which closed off the bays to serve this function.
After the group became inactive in 2006 CE (VS 2063), the structure fell into disuse and remained so for over a decade.
While the building suffered no major damage in the 2015 earthquake (VS 2072), it was eventually reconstructed by the Madhyapur Thimi Municipality in 2024 CE (VS 2080).
As part of this reconstruction, the hiti was formally reinstalled based on the recovered infrastructure and oral tradition.
Noguthiassociation or formal ritual use of the phalcā is currently known.
Guthi Chẽ 1 is the eastern of the two buildings of the Guṭhī Saṃsthāna Patan office located in front of the Matsyendranātha Mandira (LAL0060) at Taḥ Bāhāḥ.
Both buildings seem to have originally been private residences, likely reconstructed after the 1934 earthquakes.
In a sketch by an unknown artist dating from around 1843-1846 CE, the building is depicted as a sataḥ with slanting bay windows on the first floor (Nepālikabhūpavaṃśāvalī2016, p.145).

However, correspondences (K_0355_0066) dating back to 1907 CE (VS 1964) from Patan Potā Tahasila concerning the priestly responsibilities of three major temples at Patan Durbar Square indicate that an office dealing with guthis was already established in Patan before the establishment of the Patan Office of the Guṭhī Saṃsthāna.
It's possible that Patan Potā Tahasila also operated from these two buildings.
Local senior citizens recall that the Guṭhī Office was already situated in these buildings during the Rāṇā period.
The use of these buildings and the courtyard for activities related to Buṅgadyaḥ probably dates back to the medieval period.
The courtyard is used for preparations for the construction of the Buṅgadyaḥ Chariot (LAL0001).
On the northern façade of the building, there is a phalcā-like structure on the ground floor.
The building is also used to store various items related to the Buṅgadyaḥ Chariot.

Guṭhī officials suggest that a guthi associated with Buṅgadyaḥ might have used the building for managing the chariot procession since ancient times and later for running an office related to various guthis during the Śāha/Rāṇā period (Guṭhī Office staff, male, Subedī, age 49).
Before the establishment of the Guṭhī Saṃsthāna in 1964 CE (VS 2021), there were 15 different guthi offices in operation.
The Macchendra Guṭhī Office was one of them (Guṭhī Saṃsthāna Svarṇa Jayantī Samāpana Varṣa 2071 Smārikā, VS 2071, p.6).
citations: (Guṭhī Saṃsthāna Svarṇa Jayantī Samāpana Varṣa 2071 Smārikā, VS 2071, p.6)

text: It operated from this building.
Later, in 1971 CE (VS 2028), the Lalitpur Branch of the Guṭhī Saṃsthāna was also established here.
Currently, it is being reconstructed, and funded by donations from both the Lalitpur Municipality and the local community.
According to the "Nepālikabhūpavaṃśāvalī" (2016, 13.12-27), this pillar was erected where the person named Lalita achieved divine enlightenment.
It features a west-facing shrine attached to asataḥ, built in a simple architectural style typical of the Malla period's mid-era.
Although there are no records regarding the initial construction of the temple, its materials, and carving style suggest it dates back to the Malla period.
The bell-shaped roof, painted with whitewash, became popular during the Rāṇā period, hinting that it may have been replaced during a renovation of the temple in that era.
In 2023 CE (VS 2080), Lalitpur Metropolis allocated funds for the demolition and reconstruction of both the temple and the sataḥ (LAL4189).
As of November 2023, the reconstruction process is currently in progress.

The Thālāchẽ Hiti, located in the northwest corner of Nagpokhari in Bhaktapur’s Thālāchẽ Ṭola, was likely constructed before 1520 CE (NS 640), as an inscription records the installation of a Maṇivināyaka (Gaṇeśa) statue at thehitithat year.
Below the spout, a pair ofyakṣastatues is installed.
No historical evidence details thehiti’s construction.

The earliest inscription, dated 1520 CE (NS 640), states that Śivasiṃha Bhāro installed the Maṇivināyaka statue (BKT0181-006) and built aphalcārest house, wishing for his long life, health, progeny, and wealth.
Another inscription, with a partially eroded date, can be read as starting with “7” and ending with “8,” placing it between 1588 CE (NS 708) and 1678 CE (NS 798).
This inscription records that brothers Gaṃgārāma Bhāro and Purandra Bhāro from Bhaktpur’s Yāchẽ Ṭola installed statues of Śiva, Garuḍanārāyaṇa, and Pāñcāyana.
The Śiva statue may be the Umāmaheśvara statue in thehiticomplex, and the Garuḍanārāyaṇa likely refers to the Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa statue, as the inscription is carved beside it.
No records of renovations or other historical events related to thehitiexist.
Locals later connected a water pipe to restore artificial flow.
The temple area, historically known asNīliśālāduring the Licchavi period, was already a settled locality at that time, as evidenced by inscriptions found in the Naksal region.
A fragmentary inscription of Aṃśuvarmā mentionsNīliśālā(D. Vajrācārya VS 2030, p. 354), while theGopālarājavaṃśāvalīrefers to the same place asNandīśālā(Vajrācārya & Malla 1985, folio 24A).

Later documents preserve its name in various forms—Nanisāla(1526 CE),Nansāra(1839 CE), andNansāla(Vaidya VS 1982, p. 58)—indicating its continuous habitation and linguistic evolution into the modern “Naksal.” Some scholars have suggested that the name derives fromNavasāgara, a queen said to have founded the goddess’s cult (K. Śreṣṭha VS 2044, p. 74).
However, since no inscriptional or historical evidence mentions such a queen, this etymology is considered unreliable.

The oldest inscription in the vicinity, dated 654 CE (NS 78), records that during the reign of King Narendra Deva, a person named Viṣṇudeva built ajah dhuṇ(stone water conduit) for ritual bathing, along with its associated well and water-lifting mechanism.
While no inscription directly records the original foundation of the temple, thevaṃśāvalītradition attributes it to the mythical Queen Navasāgara, wife of King Vikramakeśarī.

According to this account, a craftsman possessed by the god Viśvakarmā presented a fierce image of the goddess to the queen, who enshrined it in the center of Viśālanagara, naming it Navasāgara Bhagavatī (Yogī Naraharinātha VS 2013, p. 87;Nepālikabhūpavaṃśāvalī2016, 6:78–79).
Later, when King Bhoja of Viśālanagara offended the goddess with his arrogance, she is said to have destroyed the city with fire emerging from a well (ibid., 7:5–6).

Subsequently, King Śaṅkaradeva (r. ca. 607 CE) is said to have reinstalled the goddess and instituted her annual chariot festival (rathārohaṇa jātrā) on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Caitra (Yogī Naraharinātha VS 2013, p. 87).
TheGopālarājavaṃśāvalīlikewise records that King Śaṅkaradeva established the goddessManahara Bhaṭārikāat Naksal, likely referring to this same deity (Vajrācārya & Malla 1985, folio 24A).
When his left fingers were also severed, he supposedly created the image of Śobha Bhagavatī with his foot (K. Koirālā VS 2065, p. 91).
In 1782 CE (VS 1839), during the reign of King Raṇabahādura Śāha, the chief mint officer (ṭaksārī) Bhīma Khavāsa carried out a major renovation.

The inscription states that he conducted proper rituals and sacrifices before restoring the structure, using bricks for reconstruction—implying that the earlier temple had been made of other materials.
In 1785 CE (VS 1842), he also built asataḥ(rest house) in front of the temple, under the supervision of Dhanadatta Newar of Asan Tole.
The earthquake of 1934 CE (VS 1990) severely damaged the upper roofs and the finial, as well as the western section of the lower roof.
Prime Minister Juddha Śaṃśera subsequently sponsored the restoration (Yogī Naraharinātha VS 2013, p. 87).
In 2009 CE (VS 2066), the temple was dismantled for complete reconstruction, as the structure had again deteriorated.

The new foundation was laid on 3rd day of Phālguṇa, 2010 CE (VS 2066), and the reconstruction completed on Jyeṣṭha 23, VS 2068 (2011 CE), with the installation of a new gildedgajūr(interview with aDyaḥpāḥlāḥof the temple, Maharjana caste, male, age 54).
The rebuilt temple features copper-sheeted roofs, though earlier it had brass roofing.
Prior to the reconstruction, the western wall was adorned with painted natural scenes and a depiction of the goddess (J. Regmī VS 2033, p. 372), which were not replicated afterward.

The anniversary of the goddess’s establishment is celebrated on tenth day of bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, while on eighth day of bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, local Newars offer water to the goddess praying for agricultural prosperity.

Thus, through its layered architectural evolution, inscriptions, legends, and ritual continuity, the Naksal Bhagavatī temple stands as a vital testimony to the dynamic intersection of Śākta devotion, Licchavi-era settlement, and Newar ritual practice in the sacred landscape of Nepalamaṇḍala.
Built next to the Indrāyaṇī Pīṭha (KIR0007) on the southern side, this three-bay rest house was expanded when being rebuilt in 2021 CE.
A small building of one floor that once stood next to the Phalcā has also been merged with the Phalcā, expanding its width into a seven-bay structure.
Although there is no record of the Phalcā’s initial construction, it appears to have been built after the Pīṭha was established here to facilitate devotees coming for worship.
Since the reconstruction, music is performed here again.

Thedharmaśālāwas constructed during the Rāṇā and Śāha periods, a time when many members of the royal and political elites built religious monuments at the confluence of rivers such as the Viṣṇumatī-Bāgamatī and Ṭukucā-Bāgamatī.
These structures often included temples orsataḥswithghāṭasin front, which were frequently used privately by the builders and their descendants.
Manyghāṭaswere built along the banks of the river Bāgamatī during this period, typically named after their builders.
Candraghāṭa Dharmaśālā follows this tradition, with its name attributed to Candra Śamśera, under whose reign it was likely constructed.
An inscription records that the two-story building, made of brick, measured 266 cubits in length and was supported by 11 columns, extending from Kālamocanaghāṭa to Purohitaghāṭa.

According to the inscription, thedharmaśālāwas built to provide shelter forryots(raitī) from Madheśa, Tarāī, the hills, and also foreigners who came to Kathmandu during the Rāṇā period for work, as they faced hardships due to the lack of adequate housing.
Thedharmaśālāwas officially inaugurated in 1926 CE (VS 1982).

Although the inscription does not explicitly name the ruler or the builder, the phrase “guṭhī rākhī baksekā chau” suggests that Candra Śamśera oversaw its construction, which led to thedharmaśālābeing named Candraghāṭa over time.
The bookImages of a Century(GTZ 1995, p. 87) claims that thedharmaśālāwas built by the government to accommodate lower castes.
However, this account differs from the construction date and purpose described in the inscription.
According to the inventory published by the Kathmandu Upatyakā Nagara Vikāsa Yojanā (Inventory VS 2039, p. 162), thedharmaśālāwas constructed by the Śrī 3 Sarkāra Guṭhī Kharca Aḍḍā.
The inscription confirms that it was a state initiative, with the Guṭhī Kharca Aḍḍā handling the administrative work.
After the establishment of democracy, the building was used by a police unit known asDaṃgā Niyantraṇa Dala(Riot Control).

Following the 2015 CE (2072 VS) earthquake, thedharmaśālāwas reconstructed by the High Powered Committee for Integrated Development of Bagmati Civilization (HPCIDBC) under the Ministry of Urban Development, with funding from the Asian Development Bank.
The reconstruction was completed on October 23, 2022 CE (VS 2079) and on June 4, 2023 CE, the committee formally handed over thedharmaśālāto the Nepal Police.
In contrast to most otherpīṭhas built as open shrines, the Brahmāyaṇī Pīṭha distinguishes itself with a substantial temple structure reminiscent of the Gopuram architecture prevalent in South India.
The precise year of the temple's construction remains unknown due to a lack of historical sources.
According to Pruscha, lion statues at the gate were installed in 1654 CE, and thetoraṇainside was added in 1779 CE.
At present (February 2023), only two inscriptions are found at the site.

One records the establishment of the tutelary deity by a person named Jayadarta in 1773 CE (NS 893), and the other documents the renovation of aphalcā, which collapsed during the 1934 earthquakes, in 1940 CE (VS 1997).

During theDasaĩfestival, a well-fed buffalo (khaḥmyey) is brought to thepīṭhain the evening and sacrificed after worship and fire oblation onMahānavamī, the 9th day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina.
It was originally built as a two-tiered temple and later converted into a hybrid structure with a domed roof.
This painting serves as the sole documentation of the temple’s restorations and reconfigurations over the past 150 years.
No records of its initial construction could be found.
It can be assumed that the temple was severely damaged in the 1934 earthquake and was later rebuilt in its current shape.
The lower roof was preserved but the upper roof was replaced by a plastered brick dome with a gilt copper finial.
Later, the lower roof was rebuilt with a brass sheet cover and decorative eaves.
The original open pillar arcade was closed off with lattice woodwork and a door was installed in the east façade.
The inner cella was partly covered with industrial tiles and a new door and a steel scissor gate have also been installed for security purposes.
The deity found in the ‘nāla’was then established in its current location.
Since the Buddha statue was established in the temple, two families of Śākyas and Tulādhara have taken on responsibility for performing the ritual worships.
Lakṣmīdevī, the wife of Raṇabahādura, oversaw the construction of a sataḥ during the early years of the Śāhā reign in Ṭeku.
This sataḥ, along with Lakṣmīśvara, Purṇeśvara, and Tripureśvara temples, which are dedicated to queens, underwent renovations after a recent earthquake.
Located on the banks of the Bāgamatī river, in Teku and Tripureśvara area, these three Śiva temples are constructed in a three-story pagoda style and are surrounded by sataḥs on all sides.
The three temples share a common architectural style and were constructed with the same purpose in mind: to honor queens by bearing their names.
Nānīsaheba of Raṇabahādura built the Lakṣmīśvara temple in 1813 CE (VS 1870), followed by Lalitatripurāsundarī's construction of the Tripureśvara temple (KAT2760) in 1818 CE (VS 1875).
Purneśvara temple (KAT2740) was constructed in a similar architectural style as the two prior Śiva temples, which were commissioned by queens who did not participate in the practice of Sati.
The sataḥ surrounding these temples was primarily built for the first temple, Lakṣmīśvara.
Lakṣmīśvara temple, among others, is notable for its two-story sataḥ constructed in all four directions, with entrances to the courtyard in the south and east.

An inscription documents the installation of a Śivaliṅga in CE 1813 (VS 1869), followed by the excavation for the construction of a boundary wall in 1813 CE (VS 1870) during the eleventh fortnight of Kārtika (N. Panta VS 2022, p.58).
Within the inscription, a lady referred to as "Śrī Sāhīlā Nānīsāheba" is mentioned among the numerous queens of Raṇabahādura, indicating her position as the third queen in the sequence.
N. Panta (VS 2022, p.56) suggests the possibility that Lakṣmī Devi is the lady mentioned in Bhāsāvaṃśāvalī regarding Raṇabahādura's marriage with a lady from Caukoṭa, Patan.
However, it is clarified in the Sanskrit section ‘Pāṭalīputra’ of the inscription that she is actually from Patna.
Despite Raṇabahādura's assassination in 1806 CE (VS 1863) (B. AcāryaVS 2075, p. 87), most of his queens underwent the satī practice, except Lakṣmīdevi.
Seven years after her husband's death, she initiated the construction of a temple and sataḥ, reflecting her economic and political stature.

Notably, she commissioned Pandit Vāṇī Vilāsa Pā̃ḍe, a renowned scholar, to immortalize her fame through engravings, marking one of the limited five inscriptions authored by Vānī Vilāsa (Vajracārya and Śreṣṭha VS 2037, p.572).
Gutschow (2011, p.7) mistakenly attributed the construction of this temple to Gaṇeśa Datta, the father of Lakṣmīdevi.
The inscription clarifies that Lakṣmīdevī was responsible for erecting the temple and excavating the boundary wall.
She generously allocated over 100 ropanīs of land to the guṭhī for anniversary rituals, temple repairs, and maintenance.
Despite this endowment, the temple currently stands dilapidated, with the guṭhī being poorly managed.
A photograph published by Sanday (1994, p.35-41) illustrates the temple's deteriorated condition, with zinc sheet roofing repairs and multiple families residing within.
In 1982 CE (VS 2039-40), renovations were undertaken on the north and west sections of the sataḥ (Sanday 1994, p.35/local resident, Kũvara, male, age 62).
Following the devastation caused by the earthquake of 2015 CE (VS 2072), both the temple and sataḥ were reconstructed simultaneously.

The reconstruction work, completed with the support of the Ministry of Urban Development of Nepal, the empowered Bagmati Civilization Integrated Development Committee, and loan assistance from the Asian Development Bank, was inaugurated by the then Minister of Urban Development, Ramkumari Jhakri, on January 23, 2022 CE (VS 2078).
While an inscription mandates the observance of religious rituals, they are not practiced.
Additionally, on the occasion of Śivarātrī, a bonfire is lit in front of the sataḥ, and prasāda are distributed there.
Following its reconstruction, the sataḥ remains unoccupied.
Following the reconstruction, Metropolis intends to repurpose the sataḥ for art exhibitions.
The main building (kvāḥpāḥchẽ) of Mū Bāhāḥ is a four-story structure.
Its third floor has been rebuilt in modern architecture.

A woodentoraṇadepicting Nāmasaṅgīti in its centre, offered by Queen Satajīva in memory of her deceased husband King Dhaṃta in 1884 CE to replace the dilapidated one installed previously, stands atop the main entrance to the sanctum on the ground floor, where a statue of Akṣobhya is enshrined as the main deity (kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ) of the Bāhāḥ.
In the courtyard, twocaityashave been built in front of thekvāḥpāḥchẽ.
There are no historical sources to date the Bāhāḥ’s initial construction.
According to legend, Suratavajra, a powerful tantric, built the Bāhāḥ building from a single large tree at the Vaṭu Ṭola.
However, in 1491 CE (NS 611), his son Jīvacandra was invited by Rāya Malla, king of Bhaktapur, to build Caturbramha Mahāvihāra (BKT0400) and install a Kumārī (B. Vajrācārya NS 1124, p.150-151).
This suggests that Suratavajra could have lived during the reign of King Yakṣa Malla (1428 CE-1482 CE), father of Rāya Malla (R. Vajrācārya & V. Vajrācārya NS 1103, p.81).
According toLocke(1985, p.304), an inscription from 1644 CE (NS 764) refers to the Bāhāḥ as ‘Mūra Vihāra’, which is likely the earliest historical reference to Mū Bāhāḥ.
She was previously housed in the esoteric building (āgaṃchẽ) north of thekvāḥpāḥche ̃.
Suratavajra allegedly delegated to the Vajrācāryas of Taḥchẽ Bāhāḥ (KAT0470) the responsibility of selecting the Mū Bāhāḥ Kumārī (S. Vajrācārya NS 1140, p.7 1).
However, the tradition of installing a Kumārī at Mū Bāhāḥ was discontinued after none of the Bāhāḥ members agreed to allow their daughter to be chosen as Kumārī after 1972 CE (Locke 1985, p.30 3).
Although no girl is currently installed as the Kumārī here, her seat is still symbolically worshipped as the deity herself (S. Vajrācārya NS 1140, p.37).
This worship was also impacted by the 2015 earthquakes due to the collapse of the portion of the building that housed her seat.

After having remained neglected inside a dilapidated shrine (temple 'mandira') for years, theśivaliṅgarevered as Cimṭeśvara Mahādeva now has a new concrete temple in addition to a tradition of daily worship that has recently been established here.
This shrine is a modern structure that was constructed in 2012 CE (VS 2069) under the supervision of a Puḍāsainī Brahmin.
The presence of fragments of large-sized traditional bricks (māaḥpā) andjhĩgaṭīroof tiles at the site indicates that there once stood a temple here constructed using these materials.
In 2012 CE (VS 2069), a local brahmin family of the Puḍāsainī clan began living here to serve theśivaliṅga.
After the passing of the initial brahmin, his wife and son have continued the rituals, which are still being carried out regularly as of June 2024 CE.
Located on the Mahāmaṇḍala hillock, north of Nuwakot Palace, the Kālabhairava stone sculpture was established in 1631 CE (NS 752).
The Kālabhairava statue was established on this hillock in accordance with Vajrayāna tantra.
Similarly, Bhairava and Bhairavī, the main deities of Nuwakot, were also manifestations of Vajrayāna tantra (D. Vajrācārya and Ṭ. Śreṣṭha VS 2032, p. 115).
citations: (D. Vajrācārya and Ṭ. Śreṣṭha VS 2032, p. 115)

text: A Licchavi inscription in Gorkha from 698 CE (Mānadeva Erā 122) references the worship of “Vajrabhairava,” a form of Bhairava in the Vajrayāna tradition (D. Vajrācārya VS 2030, pp. 525-526).
The Kālabhairava statue bears an inscription on its pedestal, recording its consecration in 1631 CE (NS 752).
It is one of the few Bhairava statues with dated inscriptions.
The inscription refers to the deity as “Mahābhairava,” while he is locally revered as Kālabhairava.
However, erosion has rendered parts of the inscription unclear.
As of April 2024 CE, the traditional trusts (gūṭhīs) and donor families associated with the statue have ceased to exist.
It is built in a pagoda-style and has three storeys.
The photograph published byPruscha(1975, p. 189) shows an additional pinnacle erected on the roof of the second floor.
No documented evidence is so far traced out which records the date of the temple’s initial construction.
The date inscribed on thetoraṇain Nepāla Calendar Era could be the date of the initial construction.
Pruscha (1975, p. 189) has mentioned that aguṭhīwas established in NS 768 (1648 CE) to sponsor the daily and occasion rituals for this temple.
He also informs us that the struts supporting the roofs were carved in NS 863 (1743 CE).
An inscription from NS 853 (1733 CE) is kept inside the sanctum.
It records about the establishment of aguṭhīthat is responsible to sponsor the rituals for thecaityaerected in front of this Gaṇeśa Mandira.
The Mandira was renovated in VS 2060 (2003 CE) by the Department of Archelogy (source: Local knowledge, a resident of the area, Maharjana, male, age 49).
This temple, originally served by Rājopādhyāya priests, underwent reconstruction in 2023 CE (VS 2080) with the installation of a new Nārāyaṇa statue.
The sanctum enshrines a stone statue of Nārāyaṇa, a replacement in 2023 CE for the original statue that was stolen.
While Pruscha (1975, p. 258) proposed a 20th-century construction date, concrete evidence supporting this claim is lacking.
Photographs from Pruscha's work (1975, p. 258) depict the temple roofed with traditional tiles, indicating renovations following the 1934 earthquakes.
The temple suffered further damage in the 2015 earthquakes but was reconstructed under the local government's initiative.
Although the reconstruction was completed in 2023 CE (VS 2080), the temple remains closed, awaiting its inauguration ceremony.
Local residents attribute this absence to the theft of the original Nārāyaṇa statue (local resident, Maharjan, male, age 56).
Here, in violation of the Archaeological Act, a historicpāṭīhas been removed and modified, and the addition of new concrete structures has caused thepīṭhaprecinct to appear constricted.
Late Medieval inscriptions found here mention the name and eulogy of Caṇḍeśvara Mahādeva alongside Caṇḍeśvarī, indicating that Mahādeva has been established here since that period.
InŚāktatradition, the establishment of a Śivaliṅga in the name of Caṇḍeśvara rather than Bhairava alongside Caṇḍeśvarī in her Cāmuṇḍā form is an unusual and noteworthy practice.
In the year 2006 AD (VS 2063), the tree was removed and a temple was erected over the pedestal that used to be at the base of a former large tree.
Five layers oftoraṇashave been offered in a tiered arrangement oriented toward this stone.
Among these five, thetoraṇaon the third level includestvalaṃthāṃ(the supporting posts of thetoraṇa) and was installed during the decade of 810s NS.
Thetoraṇaabove this level is even more magnificent and was installed during the decade of 800s NS.
A pair of stone lions, installed in 1688 CE (NS 808), flank thistoraṇa.

Although numerous inscriptions in the valley mention the offering of stone items such astoraṇas, lions, and thrones topīṭhas, no inscription has been found that mentions the construction of thepīṭhaitself.
Here too, about half a dozen Late Medieval inscriptions mentioning the addition of various objects to thepīṭhahave been found.

However, in the Devamālā Vaṃśāvalī it is mentioned that during the reign of Ratna Malla, around NS 629-30, a town of 300 houses was built for the protection of the theKuṃkuṃcalled Bhotes (Tibetan groups), and Caṇḍeśvarī was established during this process (N. Yogī VS 2013, p. 96).
However, the discovery of Licchavi inscriptions from the Śivadeva-Aṃśuvarma period in Tokha confirms that the settlement existed at that time (D. Vajrācārya VS 2036, p. 266).

Similarly, the Gopālarājavaṃśāvalī mentions certain events that occurred in Tokha as early as the century of NS 300 (Gopālarājavaṃśāvalī fol. 37). *From this, the description of the Ratna Malla period in the Devamālā Vaṃśāvalī does not appear to be credible.
An inscription has been found mentioning that Padmāvatī, the sister of Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa Śāha, built a phalcā in thepīṭhaarea.
It is interesting and notable that she built a phalcā at the Tokhapīṭha.
Following the recent earthquake, various concrete structures added here have made the open space appear cramped.
While the festival of a settlement's tutelary goddess usually occurs only once a year, an exception is found here and in Sunaguthi, where the custom of celebrating twojātrāsa year exists.

It is a popular belief that this worship is performed with the aim of inspiring procreation by viewing the depictions of erotic art (kāmakalā) in the Caṇḍeśvara temple adjacent to thepīṭha(M. Śreṣṭha VS 2075, p. 87).

Historical Notes:*On the day of fourteenth day of Āśvina, 1254 CE (NS 374), King Jayadeva of Bhvanta (Banepā) captured and took the gold located at Nepīkvāṭha and Tokhākvāṭha, causing this place to rebel.*In the time of 1255 CE (NS 375), while Śrī Abhaya Malladeva was ruling, a massive earthquake occurred, and one-third of the population, including the King, died.

Within the Bālakumārī pīṭha located in Cā Bāhāḥ tole, Lalitpur—generally considered to have been established during the Licchavi period—an installation of Ṣoḍaśī, one of the Daśamahāvidyās, is also enshrined.
Bālakumārī is established at four locations in Lalitpur.
Additional aniconic stones representing Gaṇeśa, Vārāhī, and other Mātṛkās are also installed within thepīṭha.
Full-moon day of Māgha is regarded as her birth anniversary (J. Mānaṅdhara VS 2046, p. 33).
It is believed that worship of Ṣoḍaśī with offerings of bananas, grapes, jujube fruits, sweets, and red cloth alleviates poverty (M. Miśra NS 1127, p. 18).

Although no historical document explicitly records the original foundation of the Bālakumārī Pīṭha, the presence of a Licchavi caitya within it strongly suggests that the pīṭha was already established during the Licchavi period.

Local belief holds that this form of Bālakumārī was once extremely fierce, frightening travelers and causing illness; to pacify her ferocity, a caitya was installed alongside her, which remains visible within the pīṭha.

Upon reaching Sundhārā, soil is said to have fallen from the goddess’s body, prompting them to rest briefly; at that spot, another Bālakumārī pīṭha (LAL4044-003) was established in front of Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa Sataḥ (LAL4044).
When they later halted at Tyāgal, a Bālakumārīdyāḥcheṃ(LAL2140) was founded there as well.
Consequently, a Bālakumārī pīṭha was established at Kwāchẽ, which was later transformed into a tiered-style temple known as the Bālakumārī Temple (LAL2000).

Following their failure to bring the Lalitpur Bālakumārī to Thimi, the tantric practitioners are said to have installed a replica Bālakumārī in Thimi (THI0010) (Local resident from a Śreṣṭha caste, male, age 62).
The cremation ground associated with the pīṭha was later relocated to Kwāchẽ.
The earliest inscription found at the site is a stone inscription dated 1696 CE (NS 817).

It records that Mahān (sipāhī) Bilhāma Bhāro, together with his sons Siddhirāma and Praśurāma (Paraśurāma), his daughter Sarasuti (Sarasvatī), and his grandson Kṛṣṇarāma, performed ayajñaand established Kumārī (Bālakumārī) and Vighneśvara (Gaṇeśa).
Since thepīṭhamust have existed well before this date, this act likely constituted a renovation and ritual reinstallation rather than an original foundation.
In 1717 CE (NS 837), Yajñanārāyaṇa Bhāju, Gaṅgādhara Bhāro, Dhanasiṃ, Cikudhika, and others jointly donated a pair of stone lions to thepīṭha.
In 1897 CE (VS 1953), Mukhiya Puṇyarāja, son of Sidhimāna Śreṣṭha of Cā Bāhāla tole, Lalitpur, together with his family, donated the stone pillar with a peacock and a bell.
In 1925 CE (VS 1981), a brasstoraṇawas installed for the Gaṇeśa shrine within thepīṭha, though the donor’s name recorded in the accompanying inscription has since been erased.

On 10 April 2010 CE (VS 2066 Caitra 10, Tuesday; NS 1130 Chulathva 8), akṣamāpūjāwas performed to commence construction works through which the previously open roadsidepīṭhawas roofed and enclosed on all sides for protection.
After thejātrā, these images are taken to the house of theguthiyāra.

Thisnityapūjāis performed by a Rājopādhyāya Brahmin, with remuneration arranged by an organization known as the “Daśamahāvidyā Bhaktibhāva Parivāra.” Previously, there was no provision for daily worship of Ṣoḍaśī; this practice began only on 8 October 2023 CE (VS 2080 Bhādra 22) (Priest of Pūrṇacaṇḍī Temple from the Rājopādhyāya caste, male, age 74).
Tis rest house was built along with a stone water tank (jaḥdhuṃ) and a well at the premises during the Rāṇā period, commissioned by a Khatrī family.
It seems to have been built next to a small pathway along what once used to be a large stretch of agricultural land, in order to facilitate farmers and passersby to rest and quench their thirst.
In 1888 CE (VS 1945), Narmadādevī and her sons commmissioned the Phalcā along with a water tank (jaḥdhuṃ) and a well as its source of water near their residence.
This is said to have been the request of her husband Pratimāna Khatrī (text: Ṣatri), who passed away before the construction was ended.

An inscription in the Phalcā recording the event of construction also instructs a person named Suratha Daṅgola from Theco to observe the anniversary of the building from the income from the land endowment made by the Khatrī family.
However, when a private trust (guthi) run by the descendants of Pratimāna Khatrī rebuilt thesitein 2022 CE (VS 2079), it was shifted a few meters to the west.
Today, the building is fenced in, as well as the jhadum. the fields have disappeared and the phalca now rests next to a small leisure pavillion, and a badminton court.
Five brothers, including Harikṛṣṇa Bhāro of Dhvakara Ṭola in Sankhu, commissioned the construction of thisśikhara-style temple during the reign of King Bhūpālendra Malla in 1699 CE (NS 819).
They also consecrated statues of Viśveśvara Mahādeva, Mādhava Nārāyaṇa (SKH0020-004), and Hanumān (SKH0020-006) on the same occasion, in memory of their parents Madhusudana and Lakṣmīmayi.
Upon completion the temple, they endowed several plots of land in order to serve as sources of income for conducting the anniversary celebrations and other obligatory and occasional rituals.
The temple was in a dilapidated condition before the 2015 earthquakes: a tree growing from its roof had damaged the walls and dislodged thetoraṇas.
The Department of Archaeology (DoA) reconstructed the Temple in circa 2013 CE.
The 2015 earthquakes caused serious damage to the temple and it was reconstructed once again in 2017 CE by the DoA.

An inscription on the base of theśivaliṅga(SKH0020-003) from 1653 CE (NS 773) records that an individual named Jayanārāyaṇa (text: Jayanārāyana) sponsored the establishment of theśivaliṅgaalong with aphalcāand ahiti(SKH0021).
Thephalcāmentioned in the inscription does not exist anymore.
Despite the sponsors of the temple having donated various plots of land to generate income for the temple's maintenance and ritual activities, the performance of these rituals is declining.
This is due to the temple not directly possessing the donated plots of land, and the members of the relevant guthi having relocated from Sankhu.
The construction of the shrines dedicated to Śiva and other deities near a flowing water source suggests an intention to develop the area as a cremation ground.
The largecaityain the middle of the courtyard of Kvāḥ Nani, also known as Ratnapura Mahāvihāra, was established by a team of eight led by Raṇhuju in 1713 CE (NS 833).
Located at the Kvaylāchi Ṭola of Bāḍegāũ, Kvāḥ Nani, or 'Kvātha Nani' as mentioned in the NS 833 inscription, is believed to have been named so due to its function as a medieval fort for Bāḍegāũ.
To the west of thiscaitya, adharmadhātumaṇḍalaadorned with a vajra has been established, along with four smallercaityas marking the cardinal directions.
Local residents believe that thecaityawas established by King Ratnaketu 2,900 years ago, and hence is named Ratna Caitya(local resident, Vajrācārya, female, age 41).
However, the stone inscription southeast of thecaityacontradicts the belief.
According to the inscription, in 1713 CE (NS 833), a group of eight individuals, led by Raṇhuju, established acaityaat Kvātha Nani (Kvāḥ Nani).
It was decreed that no one should litter or damage thenaniwhere thecaityastood.
The four smallercaityas surrounding the Ratna Caitya were not constructed simultaneously.
In 1917 CE (NS 1038), individuals such as Santa and Herāmuni collectively established one of thecaityas (BDG0050-008) within thebāhāḥcourtyard.
The remaining threecaityas were established in 1982 CE (VS 2039) by Herā, Juju, Puṣpa, Caitya, and Nīlakumārī, symbolizing the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṃgha, respectively.
Every year, on the full moon day of Āśvina, a ritual parasol is offered to the Ratna Caitya.

On the 10th of the dark fortnight of Vaiśākha, the day when wheels are installed on the chariot of the Buṅgadyaḥ, the Vajrācārya members observe their lineage worship (digupūjā) with worship performed at the shrine of their lineage deity (digudyaḥ) established northeast of thenani.
Thisśivālayawas erected in 1858 CE (VS 1915) in honor of Mahārānī Śubhakumārī, the spouse of Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā.
An inscription beneath the western entrance'storaṇaprovides information about the temple's construction.
The southeastern niche once held a statue of Sūrya, adhering to the Śiva Pāñcāyana concept of deity arrangement, but unfortunately, it was stolen, and the niche remains empty as of September 2023.

According to the inscription beneath thetoraṇa, theśivālayawas erected in 1858 CE (VS 1915) in honor of Mahārānī Śubhakumārī (text: Śrubhakumārī), one of the many wives of Rāṇā Prime Minister Jaṅga Bahādura.
P. Rāṇā (VS 2059, p. 196) reports that the marriage between Jaṅga Bahādura and Śubhakumārī was not a formal one, and it is unclear whether she had any children.
The list also identifies her as the daughter of Vīrabahādura Śaha (text: Virabahādura Sāhā) (K. Dīkṣita VS 2034, p. 77).
Since the temple was constructed to honor Rāṇā Prime Minister Jaṅga Bahādura's wife, it likely received substantial donations for various rituals.

The rest house’s name, Dīpaṅkara Jñānamālā (lit. garland of wisdom) Bhajana Sataḥ, comes from its construction as a tribute to Dīpaṅkara, the primordial Buddha enshrined at the Āḥjudyaḥ Bāhāḥ (BKT0210), which stands in front of it at the Kvāṭhaṇḍau Ṭola in Bhaktapur.
The inception of thesataḥdates back to the year 1849 CE (NS 970).
Their devotion extended beyond just thesataḥ's construction; they undertook the restoration of thehitilocated within the premises of the Āḥjudyaḥ Bāhāḥ.
A synergy of communal effort emerged as locals generously contributed both funds and labor to renovate thesataḥin 2008 CE (NS 1128).
Orchestrating these melodious offerings is an organization named ‘Śrī Dīpaṅkara Ārya Nāmasaṃgīti Jñānamāla Bhajana Maṇḍala,’ which was established in 1961 CE (VS 2018).
This dedicated group diligently coordinates the dailybhajanaperformances and the performers are bestowed with light refreshments supported by communal donations.
A stone inscription attests to its original construction in 1775.
Following the 1934 CE earthquake, the roof was replaced with a concrete slab and a brick balustrade featuring ornamental plaster.
Thephalcāwas severely damaged in the 2015 earthquakes.
In ca. 2020, emergency repairs were carried out that included the replacement of the balustrade with an unsightly brick and cement wall and the replacement of two beams with pine timber.
There are no historical sources to date the initial constitution of this Temple, however, its architectural features suggest that it was built in the 18th century.
The Temple was already in a poor state before the 2015 earthquakes, which further damaged it.
Theguthiformed to maintain the Temple rebuilt it in 2017.
Since the original statue of Viṣṇu was stolen sometime in 1985-86 CE a new statue was comissioned.
The present statue is smaller than the original and its shape does not fit the original socle (siṃhāsana) and the ring of fire (jvālāvalī).
There used to be an ‘L’ shapedphalcāto the northeast of the Temple, which collapsed in the 2015 earthquakes and is yet to be reconstructed.
Among the historic monuments at the Calākhu Ṭola, the Nārāyaṇa Mandira is constructed south of the Calākhu Dabū (SKH0152), which is also known as ‘Devī Dabū’, as Devī Pyākhaṃ Dance is exhibited here.
There are no historical sources to date the initial construction of the Temple.
Sharma and Shrestha 2016,p. 283 mention that it was built in 1910 CE (NS 1030).
However, an inscription inside the Temple reveals that it was only renovated and a new statue was added by a person named Budhimāna of the Calākhu Ṭola in that year.
The inscription refers to the Temple as Madhusudana Nārāyaṇa Devala.
Fortunately, the 2015 earthquakes failed to leave any damages on the Temple (local resident, Siṃha, male, 42).
This two-storey building (known as Dyaḥ Sataḥ) is located on the western entrance of Bhṛṅgāreśvara Mandira (SUN0100).
The door divides the ground floor of the building into two colonnaded spaces.
The lintel beams used in this Sataḥ were brought from Bhṛṅgāreśvara Mandira after it collapsed in the 1934 earthquake.
This suggests that the building was rebuilt after the 1934 earthquake.

The front west bay of the Sataḥ is used for storing materials used for Pekhaḥ Jātra, the main festival of Sunāguthi, whilst the eastern bay is located within the Bhṛṅgāreśvara temple complex and is used for singingbhajanas.
A stone statue of Gaṇeśa is consecrated in thegarbhagṛha.
In NS 663 (1543 CE), locals established a Gaṇeśa statue and in NS 777 (1657 CE) they constructed a temple.
In 2009 CE, locals renovated the temple by collecting donations and utilizing financial support provided by the Lalitpur Municipality.
The sizeable bell, also known as Divyaghaṇṭā (literally, divine bell), within the Bhaktapur palace, was established by King Bhupatīndra Malla in honour of Goddess Taleju.
Similarly, in 1737 CE (NS 857), Viṣṇu Malla erected a similar bell (LAL1250) in the Patan palace.

Six decades later, in 1797 CE (VS 1854), King Raṇabahādura positioned the Taḥgaḥ Gaṃ— the bell under discussion—in the Kathmandu Darbar Square, also dedicated to Goddess Taleju (G. Vajrcārya VS 2033, p.60).

The inscriptions do not elucidate the motive behind such installations, but chronicles note that King Viṣṇu Malla set up a bell in front of Mūla Coka in 1737 CE (NS 857), dedicating it to Taleju, aimed at intimidating his adversaries (Nepālikabhūpavaṃśāvali19.3.207).

In a subsequent chronicle known as theDevamālāvaṃśāvalī, it is noted that one of the chains of the bell broke in 1933 CE (VS 1990), leading to the cessation of the tradition of ringing the big bell twice a day.
The tradition was revived a year later following renovations (N. Yogī VS 2013, p.78).
Only in 2009 CE (VS 2066), Bābukṛṣṇa Maharjana, a resident of Kathmandu's Damāī ṭola, was entrusted with the task of ringing the bell 108 times each morning at 9 am.
It was then dismantled and reconstructed, so that its back wall is now attached to an adjacent structure.
Rebuilt in concrete, the new Phalcā is embellished with mouldeddaci-apābricks.
A first floor was added to the building in 2016 so as to provide space for community functions (B. Basukala & Gutschow2018).
According to locals, the statue called Kṛṣṇadyaḥ (statue of Kṛṣṇa and Viṣṇu both made on a single stone slate) and Padmapāṇi Lokeśvara are very old, but the rest were installed more recently.
Financial problems have meant that the construction work has lagged and is not yet finished.
The annex building to the north can be accessed via a small door on the north wall.
A bell donated in NS 778 hangs in front of the sanctum.

Four Bhīmasenas are considered to be the four major Bhīmasena Temples of Lalitpur, namely, Juju Bhindyaḥ (the Kings' Bhīmasena) of Mangalbazar, Puṃ Bhindyaḥ (the artists' Bhīmasena) of Sundhara, Dhvākhā Bhindyaḥ (a Bhīmasena placed nearby a door) of Chāḥ Bāhāḥ and Kumhāḥ Bhindyaḥ (a Bhīmasena established by potters) of Cyāsal.
It is constructed in such a way that the container of thejaḥdhuṃis at the same level as the spout of thehiti.
As Kirtipur is a city founded on top of a hillock, water sources likehitis and wells lack here.
There usually is aguthiformed for filling water in thejaḥdhuṃsand also perform their anniversary rituals.
However, no suchguthirelating to this Jaḥdhuṃ exists at present.
There are no historical sources to date the initial construction of the Jaḥdhuṃ.
A water tap is set up right in front of the Jaḥdhuṃ, and an inscription recording the setting up of the tap is placed next to the Jaḥḍhuṃ.
The inscription records that the installation of the tap was commissioned by Juhāra Kumārī, wife of Dhīra Śamśera, at the request of the subjects of the area.
Therefore, her son Juddha Śamśera accomplished the installation of the tap in VS 1996 (1940 CE).
Users of the Phalcā have built a store-room on its south-eastern side.
Around 2000 CE, the Phalcā was rebuilt with concrete pillars and a flat concrete slab.
Before the reconstruction, it had carved wooden pillars andjhĩgaṭītiled roof.
In 2014, a vehicle driving on the narrow street struck the Phalcā and greatly damaged it.
A brick pillar was added to further support the upper slab.
Its west-facing entrance features steps with platforms for guardian lions, though the lion statues were never installed.
No inscription recording the temple’s construction exists, but two stones—one in the southeast plinth and another above the door—bear the date “Samvat 787,” aligning with Śrīnivāsa Malla’s rule.
Following the construction of the Kṛṣṇa temple in the Patan Durbar Square by Siddhinarasiṃha Malla, many smaller temples, including this one, were built during Śrīnivāsa’s reign.

With the lack of historical sources, the identity of its builder in unknown, but the area was home to affluent communities like Jośī, Pradhāna, and Śreṣṭha castes during the Malla period, suggesting a wealthy patron from the area funded it.
In 2000 CE (VS 2057), Lalitpur Sub-Metropolitan City, locals, and GTZ/Udle jointly rebuilt it over three months.
However, these practices ceased after the 2015 earthquakes, leaving the temple mostly closed (local resident, Jośī, male, age 72).
The building underwent reconstruction in 1995 CE, with no historical materials employed in the process.
The new three-storey concrete building provides two open bays on its ground floor which are still used forbhajanas.

Aguṭhīaffiliated with the local Jyāpu community used to display a mask of Bhairava at thephalcāduring the chariot procession of Buṅgadyaḥ, however, in 1997 the mask was stolen and the tradition came to an end.
No inscription could be found which provides information about the foundation and reconstruction of thecapāḥ.

A photo of thecapāḥ(published inGutschow 2011vol. 2 p. 661) shows that before its reconstruction the two-storey building had 14 bays and paintings of gods on its walls, as well as very rare historical carved struts.
A piece of land owned by the Sanāḥ Guṭhī in Baḥmari of Lalitpur was sold in order to construct the modern building in 1995.
Being the residence of the Rājopādhyāya brahmins who officiate the daily rituals at the shrine of Mādhava Nārāyaṇa, the Building is referred to as Balaṃpū Priest House.
Two of them migrated to Bhaktapur, two other families moved to Kathmandu, and the remaining six had settled in various localities of Patan.

While the 10 families divided among themselves the cities where they would officiate as priests, the head of the two families who moved to Bhaktapur were assigned as priests of Dolakha, Sankhu, and Changu.
The other two again moved from Bhaktapur to Nhāykaṃtalā in Kathmandu with one of them carrying out the priestly functions at Dolakhā while the other serving as the priest of Sankhu.
The history behind the initial construction of the Balaṃpū Priest House is unclear due to the unavailability of inscriptive sources.
However, a manuscript record shows that a Brahmin of Brahmapurī (text: Brahmapuli) in Sankhu went through the initiation ritual in 1682 CE (NS 802) (Regmipart 3, 1966, Thyāsaphū A, p. 19).
This ascertains the fact that the Balaṃpū Priest House was constructed before1682 CE.
In the 2015 earthquakes, the roof of the Priest House collapsed.
Without timely and proper renovation, it is now (December 2021) reduced to rubble after failing to survive years of sun and rain.
The Shankharapur Municipality has commenced the reconstruction of the House.
No religious and cultural activities take place here, as the House was constructed as the residence of the priest of Mādhava Nārāyaṇa.
Recognized as Rakṣāmukteśvara, thisśivālaya(lit. the abode of Śiva) was commissioned by Śoṇajaṅga Rāṇā, the son of Bakhatajaṅga Kũvara Rāṇā, in 1924 CE (VS 1981).
To the west, Nandī, Śiva's sacred mount, guards the entrance, while the statue of Kāmadeva, placed southeast of the temple, has unfortunately been stolen.
Thisśivālayawas erected by Commander Colonel Śoṇajaṅga Rāṇā, son of Bakhatajaṅga Kũvara Rāṇā, in 1924 CE (VS 1981).
G. Ṭaṇḍana (VS 2053, p. 349) mentions his name as Suvarṇajaṅga Rāṇā.
In a record from 1873 CE (VS 1930), he is listed as Suratajaṅga Kũvara Rāṇā and holds the title of colonel (P. Rāṇā VS 2059, p.161).
Bakhatajaṅga Kũvara was the eldest son of Revantasiṃha Kũvara, the younger brother of Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā’s father Bālanarasiṃha Kũvara (B. Bhaṇḍārī VS 2071, p.18).
It seems that Śoṇajaṅga built the temple in memory of a person named “Rakṣā” whose identity is yet to be confirmed.
Of the twin temple, Bakhatamukteśvara, was constructed in memory of Śoṇajaṅga’s father Bakhatajaṅga.

Therefore, it's likely that he built this one in memory of his mother. Śoṇajaṅga is also credited with building three otherśivālayas at the Gorakhanātha complex, namely, Suvarṇaprakāśeśvara, Bahādurajaṅgaprakāśeśvara, and Nīlaprakāśeśvara (PPK1943).
Additionally, he commissioned a rest house (phalcā) in the area and the Tilamukteśvara Śivālaya outside the Kathmandu valley in Ḍoṭī Dipāyala of the far-western region.
