The earthquakes in 2015 caused damage to the temple walls, prompting the Pashupati Area Development Trust to initiate restoration efforts in 2021 CE (VS 2078).Śoṇajaṅga established a trust of IRs. 5,000 for daily and periodic worships, as well as timely cleaning and renovation of the temple.

This Phalcā, located at the Bagmati-Vishnumati confluence in Ṭeku renowned as the Rañjitakāra community's cremation grounds and as pilgrimage site, was rebuilt in 1960 CE (VS 2017), replacing a dilapidated public shelter (sataḥ).
The L-shaped structure has four pillars on the east and three on the south, built with modern cement and brick technology and a semi-circular roof, reminiscent of Rāṇā-era archedphalcās.

An inscription details that the previous dilapidatedsataḥ, used by all castes for death rituals, was replaced by the current Phalcā through public donations totaling NRs. 2,332.68. point given that many riverside shelters The inclusive nature of the Phalca is worthwhile mentioning since many other phalcas neyr the river were privately owned by rather elite families, and thus exclusive.
Original construction date and founder remain unknown.
The Ganedyaḥ Temple of Sunāguthi is attached to the eastern wall of Bhṛṅgāreśvara Mahādeva (SUN0100).
The two-tier temple has been built on a single plinth and stands on four timber columns with one at each corner.
The southern wall of the temple has a Nāsaḥdyaḥ shrine which has been built on a solid masonry base of 180 cm x 54 cm.
According to the inscription from NS 801, the temple was made by Kṛṇasiṃha Bhāro and his followers in 1681 CE.
It was reconstructed in 2012.
Before religious activities such as Bhīmarathārohaṇa, Vratabandha (initiation) etc. begin, people from the Sunaguthi Ṭola first visit this temple to worship their local deity.
The monument is built on an individual stone platform.
Thedyaḥchẽhad its brick stairs replaced with stone stairs in 1915 CE (VS 1972).
Located west of the Hariśaṅkara Mandira (PNG0030) in the Lāchi Ṭola of Pāṅgā, the Viṣṇudevīdyaḥchẽis an east-facing building currently under reconstruction (December 2024 CE).

Before the reconstruction, thedyaḥchẽwas a two-storied building with its southern side of the roof bearing a balconied tower (phucā) crowned with three metallic finials, the central finial adorned with an ornamentation calledābharaṇa.
Currently, windows are being installed on the first floor, with a tripartite window at the centre flanked by latticed windows (tikijhyāḥ).
Owing to the ongoing reconstruction efforts, the statues of Viṣṇudevī and Bālakumārī are temporarily housed in the nearby residence of Nāsaḥdyaḥ, the deity of music and charm.
No historical records have been found regarding the construction of thedyaḥchẽ.
Since the existence of the Viṣṇudevī temple has been traced back to the medieval period, it is likely that thisdyaḥchẽwas also built around the same time.

The earliest historical record from thedyaḥchẽis from 1915 CE (VS 1972), when Bisanārā of the Māhābo Ṭola in Pāṅgā, along with his wife Cidhi and sons Kṛsanbahādura, Jitabahādura, and Lokabahādura, replaced the brick steps leading to the first floor of thedyaḥchẽwith stone steps during the reign of Rāṇā Prime Minister Candra Śamśera.
In 2007 CE (VS 2064), thedyaḥchẽunderwent renovation (D. Maharjan NS 1137, p. 6).
Since November 2024, thedyaḥchẽhas been under reconstruction with financial support from Kirtipur Municipality.
A budget of NRs. 4.5 million has been allocated for this work (Viṣṇudevīdyaḥchẽpriest, Kapālī, male, age 47).
On the 7th of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, special worships are offered to Viṣṇudevī and Bālakumārī before being dethroned from their respective seats and placed on their palanquins.

A bell with an inscription from NS 892, corresponding to 1772 CE, was found on the palanquin used for the procession (D. Maharjan NS 1137, p. 41), suggesting that this festival has been celebrated since the medieval period.

King Pratāpa Malla commissioned the construction of this octagonal temple in 1649 CE (NS 769), with the intention of replicating himself and his deceased wives, by enshrining the statues of Kṛṣṇa along with his consorts Rukmiṇī and Satyabhāmā.
Two stone pillars are positioned in front of the temple, one bearing a fragmented statue on its pinnacle, identified by G. Vajrācārya (VS 2033, p.63) as Hanumān.

An inscription affixed to the outer wall adjacent to the sanctum's entrance commemorates King Pratāpa Malla's patronage of the temple's construction in 1649 CE (NS 769) (cf. Regmi 1966, p.88; Pruscha 1975, p.64).
The act of establishing a deity's statue to mirror oneself is a rarity in history.
The inscription further provides the lineage of his queens and chronicles the king's victorious battles (G. Vajrācārya VS 2033, p.65).
However, in January 2022 CE, a mentally unstable woman dislodged and shattered the inscription.
The Hanumandhoka Palace Supervision Office collected the broken fragments and stored them for preservation (Setopāṭī VS 2078).
Yet, the restoration of the inscription within the temple is pending.
Following the 2015 CE earthquakes, which reduced the temple to ruins, the Department of Archaeology reconstructed it in 2017 CE (VS 2074).
This four bay Phalcā was dismantled and rebuilt ca. 1994 by the German Technical Cooperation (GTZ-udle).
It was renovated by the Dhayiniche͂ family in 1672 CE.
A largely effaced stone inscription stands at the southeast corner of thecaitya.Śākya(1994, 117-18) has identified the date of the inscription as NS 718.
However, the inscription is now mostly illegible and so the date could not be confirmed.
Belonging to the large rock formations in Nālāchāpa of Bhaktapur, this massive rock, known as Vāsukīḍhuṅgā, bears nine inscriptions including one from Kathmandu’s King Pratāpa Malla.
These formations bear inscriptions that mention the names of the kings of Bhaktapur and Kathmandu.

Examining the nine inscriptions found on this particular rock, it seems evident that stones were quarried to create artistic works, fulfilling the desires of King Pratāpa Malla of Kathmandu and King Jitāmitra Malla of Bhaktapur.
Beyond the royal patronage, the inscriptions also indicate that ordinary people were involved in selecting or initiating the selection of stones for religious purposes.
The earliest of these inscriptions dates back to 1636 CE (NS 756).
Another notable inscription from 1658 CE (NS 778) mentions King Pratāpa Malla's decision to select stones from this location to craft sculptures of elephants and lions for installation in Cā̃gu.
Additionally, an inscription bearing the name of Bhaktapur's King Jitāmitra Malla is present.
It is interesting to discover inscriptions of both Kathmandu and Bhaktapur's kings on a single stone.
These inscriptions serve as evidence that stones were extracted from this rock formation to construct statues and monuments in Bhaktapur and its neighboring regions during the late medieval period.

Two inscriptions from the reign of King Viṣṇu Gupta, dated to the Mānadeva Era 64 and 65 (corresponding to 640 and 641 CE), detail the transportation of stone within the valley for sculpting statues (D. Vajrācārya VS 2030, pp. 446-448).

These records indicate that residents of Sunāguthi (a town southwest of Patan) and Dakṣiṇakolīgrāma (southern Kathmandu) were rewarded with the privilege of wearing jewelry for their service in transporting stones for the creation of Buḍhānīlakaṇṭha, the reclining Viṣṇu statue located north of Kathmandu.

Artistic creations crafted from this stone often proudly proclaimed their origin. Śrīnivāsa Malla, the king of Patan, generously provided Koṭakhā stone to Jitāmitra Malla, the king of Bhaktapur, at the latter's request to renovate the Kumārī Coka (Tevārī and others VS 2019, pp. 24-25).
Similarly, in 1691 CE (NS 811), Crown Prince Bhūpatindra Malla utilized Koṭakhā stone to restore a water spout in the Bhaktapur palace (Vaidya & Shrestha 2002, p. 207).
There is speculation that the stone procured by Viṣṇu Gupta for the Buḍhānīlakaṇṭha statue and the Koṭakhā stone originated from the same quarry (D. Vajrācārya VS 2030, p. 446).

The Bhaktapur kings and crown princes' proud proclamation that the stones used in their constructions were sourced from the kingdom of Patan's quarry reveals their sense of accomplishment in acquiring stones from a neighboring state.
It is built on a circular plan with four niches attached to the drum at each of the cardianal directions.
A date (NS 368) has been inscribed on the stone pedestal.
The image of Amitābha that was previously established inside the western niche was stolen in 1984, and a new image of the same deity was installed immediately after this.
This shrine is also known as the Yetāju temple (M. Khanāla VS 2040, p. 92).
Since the tantric goddess Chinnamastā is considered a form of Cāmuṇḍā, the depiction of Cāmuṇḍā (Kālī) on the centraltoraṇais symbolically appropriate (A. Rājopādhyāya VS 2080, p. 175).
After the cremation ground was relocated to Garuḍaghāṭa, north of Cāṅgu, the rear doors were closed (P. Śreṣṭha VS 2073, p. 57).
A sacrificial pit was constructed to the south-east of the temple.
Within the sanctum, the image of Chinnamastā is installed facing north.
To the east of Chinnamastā within the sanctum are installed images of Umāmaheśvara, Sarasvatī, Gaṇeśa, Kumāra, Kaumārī, Brahmāyaṇī, Vaiṣṇavī, and Vārāhī.

Among the Aṣṭamātṛkā, Indrāyaṇī is not installed here; she is believed to reside across the Manoharā River in Kathmandu District, and ritual worship during festivals must therefore be performed at that location (A. Rājopādhyāya VS 2080, p. 174).
A trident (triśūla) is installed in the north-western corner of the sanctum.
According to local belief, life (prāṇa) entered the image during its carving and blood began to flow, causing the work to be abandoned and the sculpture to be installed in its unfinished state.
No historical inscription explicitly records the original installation of Chinnamastā.
Paśupatinātha instructed Nārāyaṇa to worship Bhagavatī (Chinnamastā Devī) in order to destroy the demon.
After destroying the remaining demons, she remained there permanently (V. Dhakāla 2075, pp. 886–888).

The sculptures enshrined within, however, indicate that images had been installed at the site long before the construction of the present temple, and that the temple was built only later to enclose them.
The Umāmaheśvara image is dated to the third century CE (M. Khanāla VS 2040, p. 64).

The Gaṇeśa image depicts the deity holding aladduwrapped by his trunk and bringing it toward his mouth, without the corpulent belly typical of later representations; an inscription in Licchavi script is carved on the image, which is dated to the seventh century CE (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2042, p. 50).
The earliest epigraphic mention of Chinnamastā appears on a gold plate dated NS 515 (1494 CE).

This document records a treaty concluded in NS 515 (1494 CE) among the sons of King Yakṣa Malla—Ratna Malla, Raṇa Malla, Ari Malla, and Jayabhīma Malla—pledging to live in harmony without internal conflict.
Chinnamastā is listed as a witness alongside Cāṅgunārāyaṇa, and is referred to as “Yetā Bhaṭṭārikā” (M. Khanāla VS 2040, pp. 195–197).

The oldest inscription physically preserved at the temple is carved on atoraṇadated NS 799 (1679 CE), recording that Khvār Mānasinh Bhāju, Giridhal Bhāju, and the temple priest Gaṅgārām Bhāro jointly installed a woodentoraṇaabove the rear door of the temple.
During the reign of King Girvāṇayuddha, in NS 936 (1815 CE), Hanumantasinh Amātya, Bhājudhan, Sadāśiva, and Lakṣmīnṛsiṃha together installedbhagiṃand flags on the temple roof.

In NS 977 (1856 CE), Lakṣmīnṛsiṃha Amātya and Mānyalakṣmī Amātya installed a gildedtoraṇafor the image of Chinnamastā within the sanctum and donated ritual vessels as well as sevenropanīof agricultural land to support daily offerings.
In VS 1950 (1893 CE), Captain Caturmānasinh and Sanakmānasinh Amātya of the Bhosi Tol in Kathmandu installed three gildedtoraṇaabove the three northern doors of the temple.
In VS 1960 (1903 CE), Jitgovinda Amātya and Harigovinda Amātya of Daubahā Tol, Lalitpur, donated a gilded gateway to the temple.
In VS 1986 (1929 CE), Rāmdās Amātya and his wife Yogamāyā gilded the copper roof of the temple.
Chinnamastā is worshipped as the royalśaktiof Cāṅgunārāyaṇa (M. Khanāla VS 2040, pp. 192–193).
Photography of the deities installed within the sanctum is strictly prohibited.
Viśvanātha Bābu from Tumbāhāḥ, Patan built this temple in 1655 CE (NS 775).
[1]According to the copperplate inscription in the temple, he had also established aguṭhīto maintain and renovate the temple as well as to perform the rituals (cf.D. VajrācāryaVS 2056, 495).
On the contrary of this inscription,Bernier(1978, 144) erroneously suggests that it was a four-storey temple built in 1673 CE.
The temple was gradually decorated and renovated following its initial construction.
A pair of lions were installed to the left and to the right of the staircase leading to the temple in 1662 CE (NS 782).
A stone entrance to the temple's courtyard was built in 1715 CE (NS 835).
The plinths of the temple were renovated in 1717 CE (NS 839).

The roof of the temple can be seen completely damaged in the 1850s painting of Henry Ambrose Oldfield (see,http://www.bl.uk/onlinegallery/onlineex/apac/other/019wdz000002844u00000000.html; accessed on 21.10.2020).
It is probable that the temple collapsed during the 1833 CE earthquakes and was not renovated until 1850s.
It was again destroyed by the 1934 CE earthquakes but then was immediately renovated by Jagata Bahādura Pradhāna (known as Sipāĩ Bāje) using corrugated pewter sheets for its roof.
During that earthquake, the clock tower of Kathmandu, built by Prime Minister Vīra Śamśera, was also destroyed.
During its renovation, one of its four bell clocks was brought to this temple.
In 1947 CE, the pinnacle, crowning the third floor of the temple, was damaged by a heavy storm.
Since no renovation work took place back then, the temple remained two-storey for the next thirty five years.

In 1982 CE, the thenPradhānapañca(head of the village council) Rudra Bahādura Pradhāna, restored its third-storey and tiled its roof with thejhĩgaṭībricks with the support of the local community (cf.Ś. ŚreṣṭhaVS 2057, 50).
The Kirtipur Metropolitan Office and the local community jointly adorned the temple in 2007 CE by carving its plain pillars and struts.
Neither theguṭhī(established by Viśvanātha who initially built the temple) is active, nor any religious or social events take place in the temple in the present-day.
Jośī(VS 2029, 56) misinforms us that this temple was built by the Pradhānas ofDathutaḥjhyāḥ, Patan.

It is mentioned that when King Ānandadeva constructed the city of Bhaktapur in 1094 CE (Kaligata Saṃvat 4197), he developed the city in ayantra-shaped form(yantraākara) and established theAṣṭamātṛkāin the eight directions, with the Tripurasundarī pīṭha in the center, for the purpose of protection (Devamālā Vaṃśāvalī 2013, p. 104).
In the Bālakumārī pīṭha, instead of an anthropomorphic statue of the goddess, a large stone slab has been established as the deity.
Inside thepīṭha, aniconic stones representing Gaṇeśa, Vārāhī, and other Mātṛkā deities, have also been established.
The oldest inscription found here is dated 1908 CE (NS 1028).
This inscription is located on the pedestal of the two metal lions established as door guardians.

According to the details in the inscription, Bhīma Bahādura Citrakāra of Bhaktapur, along with his family, offered the two metal lions to Goddess Bālakumārī in memory of his father Bhairava Siṃha and grandmother Gaṃgālakṣmī.
Similarly, an inscription on the northern part of the large stone toraṇa featuringChepureveals that the toraṇa was offered by an individual named Kājimāna.
Furthermore, it is known that Kājimāna and his wife Dhanathaku also established the other Mātṛkā deities present in thepīṭha.

Additionally, as thispīṭhasustained damage during the earthquake of 2015 CE (VS 2072), its reconstruction was completed in 2017 CE (VS 2074) through the collaborative efforts of the Puri Foundation and the supporters from Virginia.
Though no original inscriptions exist, Pruscha (1975, p. 245) attributes the temple’s construction to Rudranārāyaṇa Rājalavaṭa in 1841 CE without mentioning the source for this information.
The Department of Archaeology restored its upper tiers in 2005 CE (VS 2062).
This two-tier Hindu temple was probably built in the 15th century.
As stated inBangdel (1989, 246), the original statue of Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa, which was dated to the 15th century, was stolen in 1984 and smuggled to the United States.
The current statue is a replica and was established by local residents.
The carved struts supporting the top floor were replaced by plain ones during its renovation in VS 2065.
Jitāpura Gaṃcā was built in 1758 CE (NS 879) by a group of 38 individuals associated with threeguṭhīs, under the leadership of Siddhisiṃha Bhāvo.
These threeguṭhīsremain responsible for the maintenance and repair of the maṇḍapa.
The structure was erected during the tenure of Candravīra Siṃha Bhāro, who served as thePradhan(chief administrator) of Khokanā.
However, the maṇḍapa sustained severe damage during the 2015 CE (VS 2072) earthquake.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādra in the same year, it was reconstructed in its original form.
The reconstruction was financed by Chinīmayā Maharjan, a Khokanā native who later settled in Dallu, Kathmandu.
She donated NPR 700,000 for the project in memory of her late husband, Aṣṭanārāyaṇa Maharjan, and her deceased parents, with the intention of ensuring that their souls attain a heavenly abode.
Lālabaiṭhaka is probably one of the first ”modern” buildings in Bhaktapur.
Following the overthrow of the Malla dynasty in 1768 by the invading Gorkha King Pritivi Narayan Shah the Bhaktapur Royal Palace fell into disrepair.
At that time the Ranas, the ruling clan of prime ministers of Nepal, established themselves in Bhaktapur.
For their governor’s reception hall a part of the historic Malla-era palace was dismantled and replaced by Lālabaiṭhaka.
This new building exceeded all previously known dimensions and proportions but was constructed employing traditional methods such as hand-made brick laid in mud mortar.

The eastern part of the original Malla-period palace, built in 1697 was reshaped in 1855 by Dhir Samser to demonstrate in built form the advent of the Rana rule and to create a large hall known as Lālabaiṭhaka, complete with a fireplace as a symbol of modernity.
The interior is characterized by two narrow bays that run over the full length of the building.
The inner spine wall is punctuated by a massive wooden door frame located in the central axis of the building.
Little attention was paid to structural consideration and the building has undergone a number of restorations over the past 150 years.
Photos proof that the building retained its original shape until  the devastating earthquake of 1934.
Because of the severe earthquake damage suffered the roof was removed and the upper parapet wall reduced in height by about 100 centimeters.
The reconstructed roof shows a much reduced slope, and less timber was used than would have been traditional standard.
A central dormer replaced the original two.
On the occasion of King Birendra’s coronation in 1975 the lower floor level of the structure was extensively repaired.
The North wall was replaced with machine-made brick (so-called Chinese brick) and the floor covered with terracotta tiles(telia).
The poorly built roof and lack of maintenance caused severe deterioration and can be seen as the main reasons for the poor performance in the 2015 earthquakes.

Therefore, it is likely that the Temple was built in the tiered-style and then reconstructed in the current style after it collapsed at some point in history (it was, probably, destroyed in one of the earthquakes of 1833 CE or 1934 CE).

During special occasions such asjātrāand other festivities, the residents of Sunaguthi are supposed to worship four religious sites in the Sunaguthi area.
This pillar was erected in 1951 (VS 2008) by Guru Kavi Prasada after he organised thesaptāhabhajanain Sunaguthi.
Next to it, a wooden post supports a small bell bearing an inscription from VS 2031 (1974 CE).
A copper plate inscription can be found on the western wall of the shrine and states that the statue was restored in 2001 CE (VS 2058).
The Bāhāḥ building has two floors and faces north.
A carved door has been installed in the ground floor, above which a metaltoraṇafeaturing images of Buddha, Prajñāpāramitā and Lokeśvara is fixed.
Ratnamuni Vajrācārya from Nyākhācuka arranged for this Bāhāḥ to be constructed in 1667 CE.
He also comissioned thecaityain the courtyard and established aguṭhīfor its management.
The statue of thekvāḥpāḥdyaḥwas also stolen in 2009 and was not replaced until some years later.
Thesaṅghaof the Kvā Bāhāḥ funded the daily ritual worship of the Bāhāḥ by providing acommodation for a Śākya family on the first floor of the building.
The entrance features a stonetoraṇadated to 1695 (NS 815), flanked by a pair of stone lions inscribed in 1672 (NS 792).
The earliest inscription on the site dates to 1672 (NS 792), referring to the installation of the lion statues and confirming thepīṭha’s existence by that time.
Later inscriptions indicate the progressive addition of structures and objects.
One long record documents a land grant made during the reign of King Gīrvāṇayuddha for ritual worship in the name of his mother.
Although the 2015 (VS 2072) earthquake damaged portions of the temple atop thepīṭhaand the adjoiningphalcāandsataḥ, the structures did not collapse.
In 2025 (VS 2081), these three components were reconstructed by Tārakeśvara Municipality; the originaljhĩgaṭīroofing was replaced with copper sheeting during this restoration.
According to this chronicle, King Guṇakāmadeva established the Manamayju Pīṭha north of Kathmandu in 3825 of the Kalī era (N. Yogī VS 2013, p. 42).
It also states that King Amara Malla settled a community of 300 households and established thepīṭha—along with initiating ritual dances—in 1483 (NS 603) (N. Yogī VS 2013, p. 96).

TheSvayambhūpurāṇanarrates that at the confluence of the Keshavatī and Vimalāvatī rivers—called Manorathatīrtha—Indra united with a homely young woman named Manamaiju and, instead of taking her to heaven, elevated her to the status of Indrāyaṇī (B. Vajrācārya VS 1128, pp. 38–39).
Maintenance of thepīṭhahas traditionally been overseen by the Maharjan clan, who cultivate the land endowed by King Gīrvāṇayuddha and take turns conducting the daily worship (nityapūjā) andārati.
On the morning of the fourteenth, a ceremonial pole (yaḥsiṃ) is erected before thepīṭha, and the deity from thedyaḥchẽis carried in a palanquin (khaṭa) to the shrine in the evening.

Newars of Kathmandu traditionally visit ninetīrthaover the nine days of the festival, worshipping the associated goddesses; on the sixth, this includes bathing at Manorathatīrtha—the confluence of the Keśāvatī and Vimalāvatī rivers—followed by a visit to the Manamayju Pīṭha (B. Maharjana VS 2080, p. 5).
The Temple is built on a two-levels of the stone plinth and is constructed in stones and bajra mortar.
There are no historical sources to date the initial construction of this Temple.
However, its structural design suggests us that the Temple must have been constructed sometime in the 20thCentury.

D. Vajrācārya(VS 2068, 299) mentions an inscription on an ornament (preserved in the treasure house of the Chā̃gunārāyaṇa Temple in Bhaktapur) from the late medieval period recording an offering of the ornament to please Rāmācandra.
Bangdel(1989, 67) has published a photo of a stolen statue of Rāmacandra (ca. 10thor 11thcentury) from the Paśupatinātha Temple Complex.
Apart from the main Rāma-Sīta-Lakṣmaṇa statue, a statue of Hanumān is also established in the sanctum of this Temple.
King Purandarasiṃha established the Duimāju Shrine in 1588 CE in the name of his deceased daughter-in-law Lalitalakṣmī (see the inscription from NS 709, placed to the west of the shrine).
The inscription refers to Duimāju as Lakṣmī.
In 1688 CE (NS 808), Cikuti Bhāro constructed thephalcāand endowed land to form aguthifor Duimāju.
A record from 1727 CE (NS 847) reveals that a shrine was constructed for Duimāju.
This probably refers to the construction of the stone structure inside thephalcāalong with the finial.

Established by Nānyadeva of the Karṇāṭa lineage in 1097 CE (VS 1154), people of the Tirahuta empire in Simraungadh of southeast Nepal were known as the Ḍoyas in the Kathmandu Valley (P. ŚreṣṭhaVS 2061, p.12).
They appear to have entered the valley in 1111 CE (NS 231) (cf.Gopālarājavaṃśāvalī, folio 36A).
See D. Vajrācārya VS 2021, p.20-31 For more on the Ḍoya invasions on the Kathmandu Valley seeD.
Their invasions also left a religious and cultural influence in the Valley that led to the establishment of Duimāju, their tutelary deity, here.
It is unclear when the shrine of Duimāju was first established in the Kathmandu Valley.
However, the earliest reference to the shrine dates back to 1198 CE (NS 318) (Gopālarājavaṃśāvalī, folio 36A).
The first shrine was established in Bhaktapur during the pre-medieval period.
An inscription from 1482 CE (NS 602) that records the offering of a silver ceremonial bowl to Duimāju by Harṣa Malla elucidates the historicity of the goddess in Bhaktapur (P. ŚreṣṭhaVS 2055, p.3).
The Gopāleśvara temple, the 18th among the 64śivaliṅgas in Nepal, was originally a tiered temple but was reconstructed in the dome style after sustaining damage in the 1934 earthquakes.
Following the 2015 earthquakes, it was reconstructed again, this time adopting its original tiered style.
The place where the Gopāleśvara Śivaliṅga is established is believed to be a holy waterhole (kuṇḍa).
Consequently, the water of thekuṇḍarises and floods the sanctum every year in the month of Śrāvaṇa.
A circular stone symbolizing Guhyeśvarī is established north of the temple.
Statues of Gaṇeśa and Nandī, Śiva’s animal mount, are also established in the temple premises along with parts of stone spouts andśivaliṅga.
Historical records are absent regarding the original construction of this temple.
TheHimavatkhaṇḍa, in its 107th chapter, recounts a tale about the establishment of the Gopāleśvara Śivaliṅga, situating it on Markaṭācala peak.
Innocent demons were also caught in the crossfire.
Therefore, Gopāleśvara is considered to be contemporary to Paśupatinātha (K. Koirālā VS 2052, p. 68).
It is likely that Gopāleśvara was established by the Gopāla dynasty (Ṭ. Śreṣṭha VS 2078, p. 28).
An inscription from to 1432 CE (NS 552) records the Solaṃkī rulers of Pharping describing themselves as 'servants of the feet of Gopāleśvara’ (D. Vajrācārya VS 2068, pp. 283-285).

An inscription from 1716 CE (NS 836) found at Bhairavasthāna in Pharping mentions a land endowment for the worship of Gopāleśvara along with other deities of Pharping (Ṭ. Śreṣṭha VS 2078, pp. 175-176).

Due to the encroachment of the endowed land parcels for the worship of Gopāleśvara and other deities in Pharping, King Gīrvāṇayuddha made new arrangements for the management of the endowment in 1802 CE (VS 1859) (Ṭ. Śreṣṭha VS 2078, p. 28; cf.PRN0010_I_004).
However, no inscription confirming the antiquity of the temple has been found within the temple premises.
Although theDevamālāvaṃśāvalī(VS 2013, p. 65) states that the 1934 earthquakes did not cause any damage to the temple, the earthquake did cause significant damage.
The earthquake left the temple in a dilapidated condition with roofs falling off, necessitating reconstruction.
However, during the reconstruction, the three-tiered temple was reconstructed into a dome-style structure while also reducing the size (Śeṣanārāyaṇa Mandira priest, Rājopādhyāya, male, age 60).
In the late 1950s, it was dismantled again and reconstructed using bajra mortar.
The 1988 earthquake also left the temple in a dilapidated state without any renovation for a long time.
In 2008 CE (VS 2065), the temple was renovated with financial assistance from the Guṭhī Saṃsthāna and community labor (Śeṣanārāyaṇa Mandira priest, Rājopādhyāya, male, age 60).
Prior to the 1934 earthquakes, the tiered temple had a large, shiny finial made ofaṣṭadhātu(eight precious metals).
The 2015 earthquakes, too, damaged the temple and had to be reconstructed.
During this reconstruction, however, the temple’s dome style was replaced with its original tiered style.
The reconstruction that concluded in June 2020 was carried out by the Department of Archaeology at a cost of around NRs. 37.5 million. (Śeṣanārāyaṇa Mandira priest, Rājopādhyāya, male, age 60).
Local residents believe that thehitiwas constructed by Jogadeva Vajrācārya, the founder of the town of Sankhu.

After the statue of Umāmaheśvara was stolen, some time ago, the statue of Vaṭuka Bhairava, who is represented while walking a dog, was relocated from the nearby Mahākāla Shrine to replaced it (based on a personal conversation with a local resident from a Śreṣṭha caste, male, age 67).

text: Temple 1 is a recently reconstructed square room with a central door on each side.
South of this monument is a half-buried square structure (JUM0481), also built with local stones and dry masonry.
Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa Mandira, located at Pacalī Ghāṭa, was built by Siddhimāna Rājabhaṇḍārī in the memory of his deceased father and forefathers in 1855 CE.
He also built Siddhimukteśvara (KAT2637) and Dhaneśvara Mandira (KAT2638).
The temple was consecrated on the full moon day of the bright fortnight of Māgha in 1855 CE (VS 1911).
[1]A stone statue of Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa is installed as the main deity and a statue of Gaṇeśa is installed next to it.
He was asubbāwhen Jaṅga Bahādura seized the power and became the prime minister of the country in 1846 CE.
In 1859 CE, Siddhimāna became a treasurer (khajāñcī) and in 1864 CE, he was promoted as the governor for Banke, Bardiya, Kailali, and Kanchanpur districts, collectively known as the ‘Nayā Muluka’.
He also accompanied Jaṅga Bāhādura during his first official state visit to Great Britain in 1950 CE (Rana1974, 116).
[2]Siddhimāna also established aguṭhīand endowed land to maintain the daily worship in Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa Temple.
However, the endowed plots of land do not exist in the present-day.
Ramacandra Thāpa, who runs a paint shop in Ṭeku, has been painting and repairing the temple from time to time.

text: Located in a small courtyard locally known asJaḥdhuṃchẽgallī Cuka, situated between Josidegāḥ and Lagaṃ Ṭola, this Jaḥdhuṃchẽgallī Bāhāḥ contains a modest shrine that preserves an image of Akṣobhya installed within a small stonedevala.
No written sources providing clear historical information about the establishment of thisbāhāḥhave been discovered.
A single inscription is present at the site, but the portion containing the date and the section describing the specific act commemorated have become worn and illegible.
Both Pruscha (1975, p. 87) and Locke (1985, p. 360) state that an inscription dated to 1679 CE (NS 799) existed here and that it was associated with the construction of thecaitya(KAT2390-002).
It remains uncertain whether they based this conclusion on the same now-damaged inscription or on another inscription that has since disappeared.
Pruscha (1975, p. 87) further reports that the inscription of 1679 CE (NS 799) identified thePūrṇimā Sevāgroup as the builders of thecaitya.
The inscription currently visible at the site, however, does not mention this group; instead, it preserves a list of donors bearing the surname Vajrācārya.
This discrepancy suggests that the inscription consulted by these earlier scholars may have been a different one that has since been lost.
Thedevalhousing the Buddha image was repaired in 1933 (Locke 1985, p. 360).
More recently, in 2024 (VS 2080), oil-fired bricks (teliyā iṃṭatiles) were laid across the courtyard with funding provided by the Kathmandu Metropolitan City (local resident, Śākya, male, age 61).
As apīṭha, the sanctum (garbhagṛha) remains open and has no door; however, a brasstoraṇahas been installed at the shrine.
No historical sources have been identified that record the original establishment of the Naulina Bhadrakālī Pīṭha.
Assuming she was hungry, the farmers offered her their food.

When Tantric specialists were consulted to avert the calamity, they advised that replicas of Bhadrakālī should be installed at intervals of onekośa, beginning from the Bhadrakālī known as Lumari Ajimā (KAT3380), located at the northeastern corner of Tuṇḍikhela and counted among the Aṣṭamātr̥kā (Eight Mother Goddesses)pīṭhasestablished for the protection of Kathmandu.
In accordance with this prescription, the Naulin Bhadrakālīpīṭhawas established at Cunikhel (oral account of a local resident, Śreṣṭha caste, male, age 47).

text: The earliest inscription found at thepīṭhadates to 1653 CE (NS 773).
This stone inscription records that Jasiṃ Siṃha, together with his sons Śivaduti and Rāmasiṃha, donated a bell (ghaṇṭā) to thepīṭha.
Another inscription dated 1685 CE (NS 805) states that Karyān (Kalyāṇa), Śujarām (Sūryarām), Jayakīnh, Bhavānī, and others jointly donated twomoharacoins and tenpāṭhīof rice to Naulin Bhadrakālī.
In 1958 CE (VS 2015), Padam Bahādura, Kīrtī Kumārī (Kīrtikumārī), and others erected a stone pillar in front of thepīṭhain the names of Dilsīṃ (Dilsiṃha) and Viṣṇumāyā.

Thepīṭhasuffered damage during the earthquake of 2015 CE (VS 2072) and was subsequently restored in 2016–2017 CE (VS 2073–2074) under the supervision of the Department of Archaeology (oral account of thedyaḥpāḥlāḥof thepīṭha, Śreṣṭha caste, female, age 64).
Following its collapse in the 2015 earthquakes, the temple remained neglected for almost a decade before its reconstruction 2023 CE (VS 2080).
The sanctum houses a large stone pedestal, upon which a stolen Kṛṣṇa statue has been replaced with a new one.
Although lacking inscriptions, these intricate wooden elements suggest that the temple dates back to the late medieval period.
Despite being a large and artistically significant temple due to its elaborate woodwork, no inscription reveals its builder.
However, the Rājopādhyāya brahmin lineage of Gāḥ Bāhāḥ claims to be its original builders, believing that one of their ancestors erected the shrine.
The temple underwent restoration in the early 1970s (Pruscha 1975, p. 141).
It collapsed in the 2015 earthquakes and remained in ruins for seven years.
The Department of Archaeology completed its reconstruction in 2023 CE (VS 2080).
The reconstruction prioritized the use of original wooden materials, with new replacements only where necessary.
Setopāṭī was built during the late Rāṇā period.
It is a whitewashed building on the site previously occupied by Sohrakhuṭṭe Pāṭī, also known as Mandaḥ Phalcā.
Setopāṭī has not been reconstructed since the earthquake of 2015 CE (2072 BS).
The Sataḥ, featuring sixteen columns and designed in the shape of a maṇḍapa, likely collapsed during the earthquake of 1934 CE (1990 VS).
Upon its reconstruction, it was intended to be rebuilt in a two-storey Rāṇā architectural style.
The building, painted white, became known as Setopāṭī due to its former status as a pāṭī.
Additionally, in the attic, there is an inscription made of bajra plaster.
Since it has not been reconstructed after the 2015 CE earthquake, it currently remains unused, even neglected.
King Narendradeva is said to have built the Akhaṃ Bāḥāḥ in Bhaktapur to house Buṅgadyaḥ, the god of compassion, in case his chariot procession is not completed byDasaĩ.
Inscriptions dating back to NS 757 (1637 CE) have been found at the Akhaṃ Bāḥāḥ.
Originally, a clay statue of Akṣobhya was established, but after it was stolen, a new stone statue was created and enshrined (bāhāḥmember, Vajrācārya, male, age 50).
The courtyard of thebāḥāḥcontains twocaityas: one built by the Rañjitakāras (BKT0490-006) and another by the Citrakāras (BKT0490-007).
No historical evidence has been found regarding the construction of thisbāḥāḥ.
As it is considered the first Buddhist monastery built in Bhaktapur, it is also called the “Ādi Bāhāḥ” (bāhāḥmember, Vajrācārya, male, age 50).
Local legend attributes its construction to Licchavi King Narendradeva for housing Buṅgadyaḥ.
Only inscriptions from the late medieval period have been found at thebāḥāḥ.
The earliest inscription, dated 1637 CE (NS 757), was carved on atoraṇa, but as of April 2025, it is no longer visible.
In 1644 CE (NS 764), Vajrācārya Dhana Bande, Gopisiṃ Bhāro, Jayarāma Bhāro, and others renovated thebāḥāḥ, paving its courtyard with bricks and offering atoraṇato the main deity.
After the renovation, Vajrācāryas from Pasu Bāḥāḥ (BKT0220) performed the consecration rituals.
In 1701 CE (NS 821), a pair of stone lions (BKT0490-004, BKT0490-005) was installed on either side of the staircase leading to the sanctum.
The 1934 earthquakes damaged the deity’s shrine (Locke 1985, p. 434).
Due to financial constraints, it was rebuilt with only two stories and covered with corrugated metal sheets.
The 1988 earthquake caused further damage, leading to the sale ofbāḥāḥ-owned land to fund the reconstruction of a three-story shrine, again covered with metal sheets.
Currently, thebāḥāḥhas 13 Vajrācārya families as its members, some of whom have moved outside Bhaktapur.

Thecaityain the courtyard (BKT0490-006), built by the Rañjitakāras of Bhaktapur’s Golamaḍhī Ṭola, is worshipped annually by the Golamaḍhī Rañjitakāras on the full moon day of Caitra, with the offering of steamed pastry of rice flour (yaḥmari).
The shrine, constructed with bricks, is located north of the Lũ Hiti (PPK1218).
Although there is no specific dating for the construction of the shrine, the statue of the main deity appears to belong to the later medieval period.
An undated inscription on thecaitya's plinth mentions Helamati, Indralakṣmī, Bhājamāsiṃ, and Jyotamāyā as the establishers of thepañcāvaliyukta caitya.
According to Gutschow (1997, p.278), this type ofcaitya, known asjvālāvalī caitya, first emerged in 1831 CE.
Additionally, theśivaliṅgawas established by Jagatabahādura Vaidya in 2003 CE (VS 2059) to commemorate his son Jitendra Vaidya's birthday.
According to the family, one of their ancestors established the statue of Śrīdhara Viṣṇu as the family's private shrine.
Above the gate, one can see adharmacakraand a pair of deer, something usually only found in Mahayana Buddhist monastic buildings andcaityas.
Severely affected by the 2015 earthquake, the temple is now braced on all four sides.
This temple was commissioned by Bhavamāna Siṃha, a merchant from Makhan Ṭola, Kathmandu in 1792.
After the earthquake of 1934, the temple was repaired by a Vaiṣṇava family. (Sanday1994, 43)

Due to its size and its 2,5-storey configuration, thepāṭīshould actually be classified as asataḥ,which means that "it is an integral part of the original endowment [of a temple complex, CB] that made funds available for the annual feasts" (Gutschow2011, 640).
The 13-baypāṭīwas established by two ministers of King Srinivasa Malla in 1678 CE (NS 795) and used to house an Umamahesvara shrine.
Thepāṭīwas constructed by order of the minister Bhagīratha Bhaiyā (also known as Bhāga Kājī).
The building is also known as Tāhāḥ Phale (lit. ‘apāṭīin rectangular shape’) amongst local residents.
Kings from twelve kingdoms were invited to this, as well as to the inaugural ceremony of Bhāidegaḥ (LAL1200) which was also built on Bhagīratha's orders.
The kings were received at the bays of this Pāṭī (cp.VajrācāryaVS 2022, 28), which was built in a Malla style (seeOldfield, 1855:http://www.bl.ukfor the sketch of this Pāṭī).
The inscription installed at thepāṭīinforms us that a statue of Umāmaheśvara was once housed there.

Gutschow(2011, 642) writes that, "the variation of lotus foliage and the petals around the central square opening demonstrates the creativity of the cavers who were not bound by strict rules."Thepāṭīwas given its present shape after the earthquakes of VS 1910.
The top storey and tower collapsed in the Great Earthquake of 1934 CE and were later modified to reflect a contemporary style.
In 1994/95 GTZ/UDLE funded the reconstruction of the building.
It was rebuilt with projecting windows and a pinnacle.
The building is poorly maintained, and this has only become worse after the earthquake of 2015 struck.
New construction work has been carried out in the back yard since 2018.
According to a member of the priest family, the building is earmarked for restoration.
Metal flags have been erected on either side of the door and two brass-clad lion statues guard the temple.
The building behind thephalcāused to be the residence of the Śāha kings' head priest.
Thephalcāwas once free-standing as indicated by the carving details of the corner columns but today it isencroached by residential buildings to the south and west.
It is unclear when the construction of the balcony, replacing thephalca'sroof, was done.
An inscription from 1844 CE (NS 964) with Ardhanāreśvara carved on the upper part records that thephalcāwas built by Rāota Nārāṃ and his wife Bhima Lakṣmī.
Some local people believe that thephalcā’spatron built it with money won when gambling with Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā (local knowledge, local resident, Stāpita, male, age 79).

text: His assassination created political turmoil and eventually led to the rise of Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā and the Rāṇā dynasty which ruled Nepal from 1846 till 1951 CE.
According to a local informant, the Kathmandu Municipality has plans to demolish and rebuild thephalcāin the near future (April 2021).

Since Amoghasiddhi, one of thepañcabuddhas, is also depicted under a serpent hood, signboards with the inscription 'Amoghasiddhi' have started to appear here in recent times, misleading people into believing that the statue is a representation of Amoghasiddhi.
While hundreds of Vajrayāna sculptures have been found in Nepal, there are very few sculptures depicting the events in the life of the Buddha (H. Śākya VS 2026, p. 46).
With the locals' initiation, the broken statue was restored around 1996 CE (VS 2053).
In 2023 CE (VS 2080), a permanent concrete temple was built for the statue.
Bālakumārī Mandira is one of severalpīṭhas(abode of a powerful Mother ‘mātṛkā’Goddess) established to protect the city of Patan.
TheBhāṣā Vamśāvalī(part 2, 2023, 2-3) records that thispīṭhawas built by the Licchavi King Vīradeva, however, there is no documented evidence of a king with that name.
TheDevamālā Vaṃśāvalī(2013, 48) mentions that King Aśoka pleased the Goddess Bālakumārī and conquered Lalitpur in NS 622-641 (1502-1521 CE).
He then built this temple as tribute to the goddesses who blessed him to be victorious over Lalitpur’s Ṭhakurī kings.

The single storey temple was renovated in NS 742 (1622 CE) by Dayāla Bhāro, in NS 817 (1697 CE) Īśvaradāsa Bhāro rebuilt it in a three-storey configuration and in NS 928 (1808 CE) the temple was restored again by Macchindra Bhāro.
The temple was damaged during the NS 953 (1833 CE) earthquakes and repaired.
After it collapsed during the 1934 CE earthquakes Juddha Śamaśera rebuilt it.
In VS 2060 (2004 CE), Sundaralāla Khaḍgī replaced the bricks with copper sheets.
The temple suffered heavily during the 2015 CE earthquakes.
The Lalitpur Metropolitan City Office has already allocated some budget for its renovation, however, the renovation work is yet to be started (as of October 2020).

A Karmācārya caste member performs the daily rituals in the temple and he receives a monthly salary of a thousand and five-hundred rupees from Bālakumārī Mandira Saṃrakṣaṇa Samiti, a non-governmental committee established to preserve and maintain the temple.

A fire ritual,bhairavāgniyajña,followed by a sacrifice of a non-castrated he-goat is performed on the fourteenth lunar day of the dark fortnight of Caitra in the sacrificial pit in front of the temple.
However, the upper tier collapsed during the earthquakes of 2015 CE, reducing the temple to a single-tiered structure.
The metal finial that once adorned the temple was stolen and replaced with a concrete one.

While the exact construction date of the temple is unknown, an inscription on the northern of the two guarding lions by the steps leading to the main entrance dates back to 1696 CE (NS 816), confirming the existence of the temple in the late 17th century.
Another stone inscription from 1763 CE (ŚS 1685) is also present on the temple plinth, but it does not seem to be related to the temple itself.
Instead, it documents Crown Prince Pratāpa Siṃha Śāha forming a trust by donating land parcels to observe the erection of a ceremonial post calledyaḥsĩduring the Indra Jātrā festival.

The devastating earthquakes of 2015 CE caused severe damage to the temple, prompting the Department of Archaeology, acting on behalf of the Nepali Government, to engage the Chinese Academy of Cultural Heritage (CACH) of the Chinese Government to oversee the restoration of the temple and other adjacent monuments.
Scaffoldings have been erected around these structures, and the roofs have been shielded with corrugated metal sheets to protect against rain.
However, as of March 2024 CE, renovation works are yet to begin.
There is no record of the hiti's initial construction, however, a Viṣṇu statue on the eastern wall of the hiti can be dated to the 4th century.
The hiti has undergone many restorations and alterations.
The sourounding area was paved with bricks in 1685 and in 1996 the Lalitpur Sub-Metropolis and the Department of Archeology carried out some repair work.
The shrine of Sage Agastya has been damaged by rising damp and the lime plaster is peeling from its deteriorating walls.
Within the premises, two inscriptions from the early Rāṇā period record the construction of roads and a pāṭī.
The original water spout has since been replaced with a new one due to deterioration.
It is known that this stone spout was constructed to provide drinking water for pilgrims visiting the ghāṭa and the river.
As of June 2025, the site features a newly installed stone spout with a Bhagīratha beneath it and a phalcā.
The ancient water spout was completely destroyed, so it was replaced with a new one during restoration.
An inscription found here refers to the adjacent phalcā as Ḍhikure Pāṭī.

The oldest inscription here dates to 1790 CE (VS 1847) which recordsTilakarāma Kārkī, a resident of Cobhāra, along with his descendants, paved and improved the road from the bank of the Balkhu river to the banks of the Bishnumati river.
The inscription also mentions that thebirtāland was negotiated and converted into adharmaśālāthrough theKausīkhānā.
An additional record was added later in the year 1974 CE (2031 VS) which mentions that the family of Subedāra Gajesī Kārkī from Cobhāra had built the Ḍhikure Pāṭī and restored the hiti.
No inscription has been found regarding the spout's original construction.
However, it can be assumed that the hiti was constructed during the pre-Rāṇā period.
Another inscription from 1837 CE (1896 VS) records that Subedāra Gajesī Kārkī constructed a road from Sundarīghāṭa confluence to Balkhu river confluence.
In 2010 CE, Hari Kaṭuvāla, a resident of Bhājaṃgāla, restored thedhārāpremises by paving and plastering in memory of his wife, Kṛṣṇa Kumārī Katuvāla.
Recently (June 2025), with the support of Kīrtipur Municipality, the 'Pāṭīdhārā Restoration Subcommittee' completed the restoration work of thisdhārāandpāṭī.

During the later medieval period, the family of Lvaṃvā Bhāro from Cāpāgāũ constructed thisjaḥdhuṃwater tank to provide 24-hour water supply to facilitate travelers, while also building aphalcā(rest house) and establishing a deity.
This particularjaḥdhuṃwas built with the same purpose along the main road connecting Cāpāgāũ and Theco.
Records indicate that four statues were established along with thejaḥdhuṃ, and aphalcāwas also built.

According to an inscription that once existed at this site, but has since been lost, four brothers from Cāpāgāũ Capāla Libichẽ, Lvaṃvā Bhāro, Bāsiṃha Bhāro, Pabhārāma Bhāro, and Devarāma Bhāro, constructed aphalcāhere in 1697 CE (NS 818).

They also established four deities, including that of Madhusudana in their father's name, and three other statues in the name of their mothers Sarasvatī Mayī and Maṇikarṇṇa Mayī (D. Vajrācārya VS 2056, p. 298).
Although the inscription mentions the establishment of four statues, no statues can be seen in thephalcāat present.
The four brothers additionally established ajaḥdhuṃin the names of their parents at the same time.
The inscription states that various rituals were to be performed annually for these monuments, and land parcels were also donated as a trust for their maintenance.
Although the inscription mentions the performance of various rituals and the regular filling of water in thejaḥdhuṃ, all of these activities have ceased now.
With the construction of the Kanti Highway connecting the area to Hetauda, the government aimed to widen the road in front of thejaḥdhuṃ.
However, the northern entrance is used to access the main sanctum that is built inside another layer of wall on all four sides.
The presence of Licchavi and pre-medieval inscriptions in the area suggest that it was an old settlement.
A merchant named Jayabhīma from Patan had vowed to build a beautiful temple for Kumbheśvara if his sick wife Anantalakṣmī recovered from the illness.
Unfortunately, his wife passed away but Jayabhīma still built a temple in her memory in NS 512 (1392 CE).
After the completion of the temple, his second wife offered acaturmukhakośa, a four-faced cover, for theśivaliṅgaand also a golden finial on top of the temple after performing alakṣāhutiyajña.
In the course of the construction, statues ofnāga, Gaṇeśa, Śītalā, Nārāyaṇa, etc. were recovered from the water tank north of the temple when it was cleaned.
King Jayasthiti Malla installed the statues in the temple area and commenced a festival to be observed at the water tank on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa.
Jayabhīma had constructed a two-tiered temple.
It was King Yoganarendra Malla who raised it to a five-tiered structure in NS 817 (1697 CE) (Bhāṣā Vamśāvalī, part 2, VS 2023, p. 73;Devamālā VaṃśāvalīVS2013, p. 32).

text: The earthquake in NS 928 (1808 CE) had damaged the temple.
The four brothers of Hanumanta Siṃha, a minister, took permission from the king and renovated the temple in NS 929 (1809 CE) (V. Pauḍyāla2060, p. 186-187).
The temple collapsed in the earthquakes of 1934 CE.
Rāṇā Prime Minister Juddha Śamśera reconstructed the temple from the foundation up (Devamālā VaṃśāvalīVS 2013, p. 32).
The temple suffered damages in the 2015 earthquakes as well.
The topmost tier that collapsed was being installed along with the renovation of other tiers of the temple by the Department of Archaeology while this survey was conducted.
Vaikuṇṭha Bhāro constructed the temple for the Licchavi-era Candanabharāṭeśvara Śivaliṅga and established a trust.
In 1691 CE (NS 811), his grandson Lakṣmīrāja Bhāro reconstructed the temple.
Its first mention was seen in an inscription dated 506 CE (ŚS 428) installed at the Ādinārāyaṇa temple in Thankot, along with other place names (D. Vajrācārya 2030, pp. 91-92).
Meanwhile, an inscription from 1691 CE (NS 811) installed in the temple refers to this place as “Navagvāṭha/Navagvātha.”This two-tiered temple facing east has its roofs laid with copper sheets.
An inscription dated 1691 CE (NS 811) found in the temple refers to thisśivaliṅgaas “Svayambhū Mahādeva” (self-manifested Mahādeva).
Twoyakṣastatues are installed to the west of the temple.
The pair of theyakṣastatues from a ruinedhiti(THK0030-006) located to the southeast of the temple was later installed to the west of the temple.
The main deity, theśivaliṅga, and the temple itself appear to have been established at different times.
The Candanabharāṭeśvara Śivaliṅga installed within the temple is believed to date back to the Licchavi period.

It is said that if one visits this place and performs worship on the 8th of the dark fortnight of Caitra, one's wishes will be fulfilled, and one will earn the equivalent merit of donating one hundred cows (H. Joshi 2058, p. 397).

A stone inscription (THK0030_I_003) dated 1691 CE (NS 811), found within the temple, records thatPātravaṃśaRāutaVaikuṇṭha Bhāro, a resident of Datalhāche in Dhvākhābāhāra, constructed the temple for theśivaliṅgaand established a trust.
However, the inscription does not specify the exact date of construction.
Following the temple's construction, other construction activities intensified in the area.
A weathered stone inscription from 1638 CE (NS 758), located in the Viṣṇu temple southeast of the Candanabharāṭeśvara temple, indicates that three donors jointly arranged a certain worship.
Locals mention that this inscription was originally placed under a large nettle tree near the Candanabharāṭeśvara temple.
It is likely that this inscription records a religious endowment established for the worship of Candanabharāṭeśvara.
Another stone inscription from 1689 CE (NS 808) records a group of locals offering atoraṇato Gaṇeśa.
Over time, the temple built by Vaikuṇṭha Bhāro fell into disrepair and was destroyed.
In 1691 CE (NS 811), Lakṣmīrāja Bhāro, the grandson of Vaikuṇṭha Bhāro, reconstructed the temple.
It is said that Candanabharāṭeśvara Mahādeva appeared to him in a dream, instructing him to rebuild the temple.
After consulting with his mother Lakṣmī and brother Lakṣmīdhara, he obtained permission from King Yoganarendra Malla and reconstructed the temple, offering a golden finial.
Upon completion, Rāmacandra, a brahmin from Bakhanimha Ṭola in Lalitpur, performed a fire ritual.
In the mid-1980s (VS 2042-43), locals collectively renovated the temple (local resident, Maharjan, male, age 57).
As part of the rituals, boiled wheat is also offered to cows.

Standing in between the Lalitamukteśvara Śivālaya (PPK0212) and the Gaṅgāmāī Mandira (PPK0209) at the Āryaghāṭa cremation ground in the Paśupati area, the east-facing temple is built entirely of stone with a bell-shaped roof adorned with a stone finial that resembles akalaśa, a ritual water vase.
A unique feature of this temple is the presence of ancient statues in the sanctum, predating the construction of the temple itself.
Among the multitude of these statues, a stone statue of Virūpākṣa is established as the main deity on the northeastern corner inside the sanctum.
Back in c. 1965 CE (VS 2022), an elderly person of the Kirat community had unearthed this statue.
Those who saw the statue back then reported that one of its hands held an object resembling aśivaliṅga, and the other hand held a rosary (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p. 491).
Virūpākṣa is mentioned as one of the 11 names of Śiva in theViṣṇuPurāṇa(J. Goyandakā VS 2058, p. 17).
Meanwhile, some interpret the statue as the figure of Kirat king Śaṅku (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p. 491).

Another story recounts a sage named Nemuni instructing Virūpākṣa, a Śiva devotee, to take a pilgrimage to sixty-fourśivaliṅgas and bathe in the Bagmati river, which cured him from leprosy or, in another version of the story, atoned for the sin of committing sexual intercourse with his mother (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p. 492).
Some have identified it as the statue of a royal person, while others have called it the statue of Kirat King Yalambara (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p. 484).
The Virūpākṣa statue inside the sanctum and the temple structure were not built at the same time.

Although it is said that this statue was established in the 5th century CE by Queen Bhoginī, the wife of Licchhavi King Mānadeva, in memory of her maternal family's lineage deity (Joshi 1986-1987, p. 3), no historical evidence has been found to support this claim.
The statue of four-armed Śiva (PPK0210-002) was established in 1661 CE (NS 782) during the reign of King Pratāpa Malla.
It appears that the temple was constructed much later after the installation of the Virūpākṣa statue, which probably was under the open sky before the construction of the temple.
The existing structure seems to have been built only in the 19th-20th century (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p. 342).
During the reign of King Mahendra, in 1959 CE (VS 2016), Yogī Naraharinātha conducted research of the temple.
In 2023 CE (VS 2080), the Pashupati Area Development Trust replaced the door leaves of the temple.
According to a local belief, offering libation of water with one's cupped palms to the Virūpākṣa statue prevents him from coming out and cause a great deluge (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p. 492).

Virūpākṣa receives a special offering of a mixture of curd and beaten rice as a concluding ritual on the final day of the pilgrimage to the Bagmati river in the Paśupati area, and during theLiṅgayātrāprocession, where 64śivaliṅgas are worshiped (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, pp. 536-545).
The construction of the Śiva temple in the year 1887 CE (VS 1944) is attributed to Prime Minister Vīra Śamśera.
This temple, named Vīrarājabhakteśvara, is one of the three Śiva temples built by Vīra Śamśera within the Pandhra Śivālaya complex.
Constructed from stone, Vīrarājabhakteśvara showcases a bell-shaped roof crowned with a metallic finial.
Additionally, a statue of Kāmadeva is established on the eastern side of the temple’s plinth.
Prime Minister Vīra Śamśera erected the temple in 1887 CE (VS 1944) (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p. 344; Michaels and Tandon 2017, p. 62).
citations: (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p. 344; Michaels and Tandon 2017, p. 62)

text: He undertook this construction after assuming power by assassinating the incumbent Prime Minister Raṇa Uddīpa Siṃha, who also happened to be his uncle.
The construction of the temple served as his effort to showcase his effectiveness in governance following a tumultuous change in leadership (temple priest, Ghimire, male, age 55).
Vīra Śamśera had also offered a bell after building the temple, but unfortunately, it has already been stolen.

A Brahmin from the Ghimire caste conducts daily rituals at the temple, as well as at two other Śiva temples, Vīramadhuprakāśeśvara (PPK0322) and Vīramāyābhakteśvara (PPK0323), both also established by Vīra Śamśera.
Juddhaśamśera ordered that the gemstone must remain untouched and allowed the construction of thebāhāḥ.
Bābulāla, an associate of Juddhaśamśera, built the Bāhāḥ in 1939 CE (NS 1060/VS 1996) in the memory of his father Siddhilāla.
His descendants also claim involvement in constructing thephalcā.
The constructor of thebāhāḥhas filed a claim of ownership over thephalcā(local resident, Śreṣṭha, male, age 69).
A Kṛṣṇa statue, installed by Kṛṣṇamāna Śreṣṭha in 1991 CE (VS 2048), is enshrined in a niche on the north wall.
The Caitya faces east and a statue of Akṣobhya is installed inside its front niche (gavākṣa), which is adorned with a stonetoraṇaembellished with a statue of Pañcabuddha (Five Buddhas).
The oldest inscription in the Caitya premises is dated 1709 CE (Ns 829).
Another inscription installed in the premises in 1759 CE (NS879) mentions the construction of a staircase to the east of the Caitya (Ś. ŚreṣṭhaVS 2057, 156).
In 1906 CE (VS 1963), a local resident called Harṣa Maharjana and his wife Gukṣmi (Guṇalakṣmī) renovated the Caitya.
The plots of land which were endowed to theguṭhīare not under its possession at the present-day (January 2021).

text: Nāmasaṅgīti Phalcā is located to the west of Sunaguthi main road, to the south of the Dampāchẽ Phalcā (SUN4011).

monument_name: Nāmasaṅgīti Phalcā (second half of 19th cent. CE)
text: Before its reconstruction, the building was of a regular rectangular shape and was furnished with a conventional gable roof with pan-tiles.

monument_name: Nāmasaṅgīti Phalcā (second half of 19th cent. CE)
text: In the reconstruction process, the rear wall of the Phalcā was also removed.
