text: Two were of Mahākāla and Gaṇeśa whilst the final one was unidentified; all of them were stolen in the 1990s.
Thebāhāḥ’s historical buildings have been lost and thekvāḥpāḥchẽwas converted into a Tibetan-stylegompa.
Akṣobhya is consecrated as the main deity of thebāhāḥin the sanctum on the ground floor.
A large statue of Padmasambhava is installed on the first floor.
Thebāhāḥwas originally established by Padma Raja Śākya in NS 778 (1658 CE) (H. Śākya1994, 104).
In NS 838 (1718 CE), Indra Rāja Śākya paved the courtyard withteliyābricks.
In NS 1008 (1888 CE), Narendra Dhana and Ratna Dhana renovated thebāhāḥand walled its compound.
The same donors renovated it again in NS 1064 (1943 CE).
In VS 2040 (1984 CE), thebāhāḥwas reconstructed in the shape of a Tibetangompawith locally raised funds.
It is now known more as a Tibetangompathan a Buddhistbāhāḥafter it was donated to Mahāyāna monks.
Constructed as a residence of thedvāre(a local functionary) of Sankhu, Kvātha Chẽ used to maintain Taleju Kvātha Chẽ (SKH0250), the temple of the tutelary deity of the royal family.
The cities in the medieval Kathmandu Vallely (or Nepālamaṇḍala) were founded as forts with fortification walls all around.
The town of Sankhu was also developed as a fort in the medieval period with fortification walls and ditches constructed for defensive purposes.
This building (i.e., Kvātha Chẽ [lit. ‘fort house]) on the other hand, was not a fort but, as mentioned above, only the residence of thedvāreof the town.
He was a powerful local functionary in the medieval period, used to look after Taleju Kvātha Chẽ and fulfil his religious, cultural, and administrative duties from this building.
[1]An inscription on one of the triangular floor tiles (cikaṃaḥpā) laid on the Kvātha Chẽ premises informs us that the building was constructed by Bhājudeva (text: Bhājudeo) in 1777 CE (NS 897).
Apparently, Bhājudeva was thedvāreof Sankhu at the time he constructed Kvātha Chẽ.
It used to be a three-story building standing on all four sides with a courtyard at the centre.
The building collapsed in the 2015 earthquakes except for the eastern wing.
The Indian Embassy has proposed to rebuild it, but the proposal is still being considered (as of April 2022).
With the change in the administrative system of the country after the fall of the Rāṇā regime in 1951 CE,dvāres were politically marginalized, and subsequently that affected their financial status.
Locke states "that the shrine in its present state is certainly a twentieth century construction." (see Locke 1984, p.154).

Pruscha states that "The monastery was consecrated the year after the great earthquake" (see Pruscha 1975, Vol. II, p. 207.)According toŚākyaVS 2036, p. 51-52: "In 1892 CE, Bekhārāja Vajrācārya invited King Pṛthvī Vīra Vikrama Śāha to his home.

After performing a sacrifice, he donated the funds for the construction of thisbāhāḥand acaityain the courtyard."The main shrine is a hybrid structure with a carved timber enclosure and a roof of lime-plastered brickwork.
A latticed window with a cover of gilded sheets is installed at the center of the first floor.
King Guṇakāmadeva is credited for the establishment of Bhadrakālī in 724 CE (Kaligata Era 3825) (Devamālāvaṃśāvalī, p.66).

Another chronicle in the private collection of the priest of Bhadrakālī narrates the occasion of bringing Bhadrakālī from Kāmārukāmākṣā (Assam, India) to the Kathmandu Valley in the same year, i.e., 724 CE (Kaligata Era 3825), and starting of a palanquin procession of the deity by Lakṣmīkāmadeva, son of King Guṇakāmadeva (J. Vajrācārya NS 1118, p.7).
It is unclear when thedyaḥchẽwas constructed.
J. Vajrācārya (NS 1118, p.12) writes that Goddess Bhadrakālī’s 12-year mask dance commenced in 1485 CE (NS 605) during the reign of King Ratna Malla.
King Raṇabahādura Śāha offered small masks of various deities to be taken around the city during the palanquin procession and also endowed land for it (J. Vajrācārya NS 1118, p.7).

The recent reconstruction of thedyaḥchẽtook place in 2014 CE (VS 2071) with funds provided by the Department of Archaeology, Guṭhī Saṃsthāna, Kathmandu Metropolitan City Office, and donations from locals.
The height of thedyaḥchẽwas increased in the course of the reconstruction (caretaker, Maharjana, male, age 56).
The members of aguthithat carries out the annual procession take a turn for a week to perform daily rituals here at thedyaḥchẽ.
The sanctum of the Hayagrīva Temple is located in the south-west corner of a large rectangular building.
Currently (March 2020), due to the ongoing restoration work the Hayagrīva statue is kept in storage in a building adjacent to the north-east of the temple.
The temple collapsed in the 2015 earthquake.
Its Bhairava statue toppled over but was not seriously damaged.
Restoration efforts are underway and this work is nearing completion (writing in January 2020).
This restoration work is being financed by the Government of Nepal and carried out by the Department of Archaeology.
No records of the initial construction of the temple could be made available.
The earliest record found in the temple is of NS 776 (1656 CE); this date had been engraved at the bottom of one of the struts which used to be part of the lower roof.
However, it is not clear whether the date refers to the original construction or to a restoration effort.

The earlier structure of the temple can be seen in a drawing made by Oldfield in 1857 CE (see:http://www.wikigallery.org/wiki/painting_245294/Dr.-H.A.-Oldfield/Rato-Machhendranath-Temple-at-Bungamati-Newari-Tribe-Village-Nepal-July-1857).
The government allowed workers to fell wood from the forest of Kaṭuvāla Daha to use for its restoration.
The roof was restored by thepānejugroup of Bungmati and others the following year (T. Siṃha and Maharjan2019).
Two Licchavicaityasestablished in Hitigāḥ suggests that it could have been built during that period.
The hiti was renovated in NS 824 and VS 2052.
The water basin below the spouts has filled in with garbage and the lower area of the Hiti is flooded during heavy rains due to the blocked drainage.
The Amoghasiddhi Shrine is damaged by rising damp and exhibiting many dislodged stone components.
Well intentioned repair efforts have resulted in the partial covering of the two Licchavicaityaswith cement mortar.
After the demise of Lieutenant Colonel Dharma Śamśera Thāpā Kṣetrī, his five children erected a Śiva temple in his honor in 1919 CE (VS 1976).
This temple, dedicated to Lieutenant Colonel Dharma Śamśera Thāpā Kṣetrī, was constructed in 1919 CE (VS 1976).
He was the elder brother of Dambara Śamśera Thāpā, the founder of the Dambarabhakteśvara Mandira (PPK1930) (Ḍ. Thāpā VS 2034, p.10).

After Dharma Śamśera's demise, his children Rādhākumārīdevī, Thira Śamśera Thāpā, Nara Śamśera Thāpā, Gaṃbhīra Śamśera Thāpā, and Raudra Śamśera Thāpā established this Śiva temple in their father’s honor.
While G. Ṭaṇḍana (VS 2053, p.347) credits Dambara Śamśera for the temple's construction, the inscription at the temple attributes it to his elder brother’s children.

They also established three additionalśivaliṅgas in the sanctum, namely, Śivamukteśvara in their mother Śivakumārīdevī's name, Śubhamukteśvara in Śubhakumārīdevī's name who probably was their father’s first wife (jeṭhīmumā), and Naramukteśvara in their grandmother Naranandakumārīdevī's name.
The siblings also donated land for daily and periodic worships at the temple.
In 1940 CE (VS 1997), Narendra Śamśera Thāpā Kṣetrī added Rādhāmukteśvara, named after his grandmother Rādhākumārīdevī, resulting in apañcaliṅgaensemble in the sanctum of Dharmamukteśvara.
Narendra Śamśera also donated land for various rituals related to Rādhāmukteśvara.
The temple was in a dilapidated state before the 2015 earthquakes, which led to its destruction.
The Pashupati Area Development Trust reconstructed it in 2021 CE (VS 2078).
It has plain columns and does not contain any statue or inscription.
It is uncertain when the Phalcā was first built.
His principal right arm exhibits the boon-granting gesture (varadamudrā), while the implement carried by his principal left arm is unclear due to erosion.
Despite its importance in the study of Nepalese sculptures, the attempt to restore the statue with concrete has been detrimental.
The shrine also houses a significant Licchavi inscription from 563 CE (ŚS 485), installed during the reign of King Gaṇadeva.
This is the earliest known inscription recovered in Nuwakot.
The upper portion of the inscription features a carving of a conch shell (śaṅkha) and a discus (cakra), which are the implements associated with Nārāyaṇa.
The recovery of a Nārāyaṇa statue and a Licchavi inscription suggests that a proper temple of Nārāyaṇa existed here in the past.
Currently, the inscription lies flat on the ground north of the temple (see below).
Pruscha (1975, p.25) mentions the Dyaḥchẽ being built in the 17th century but does not provide any references.

The earliest epigraphical source in the Dyaḥchẽ is an inscription from 1891 CE (NS 1011) on the first floor below the gilded lattice window, which records the names of those persons who presented the window.
The Dyaḥchẽ was renovated after being severely damaged by the 1934 earthquakes.
During the restoration of the Dyaḥchẽ in 2018 CE, descendants of the person who offered the window, repaired it (see ‘historical events’ below).
Although generally well preserved, it sustained cracks and structural weakening during the 2015 earthquakes but it did not collapse.
Nearly a decade after the earthquake, no initiative for its restoration had been undertaken.
Over time, the structure grew increasingly fragile, and by 2025 it had fully collapsed, resulting in the complete loss of its physical presence.
No inscription has been found at the site, leaving the date and patron of its construction unknown.
Local oral tradition attributes the building of Paṅge Pāṭī to the ancestors of thePāṅge, a well-known merchant clan from Pāũ within Khopāsī (local resident, Khaḍkā, male, age 81).
The construction materials and architectural style suggest that it was built—or perhaps rebuilt—during the later years of the Rana period.
Despite expressions of concern from heritage enthusiasts in other localities, residents living in the immediate vicinity have shown limited interest in advocating for the Paṅge Pāṭī's reconstruction.
The age of this Jaḥrũhitiis unknown; no inscriptions are available to offer an idea of its history.
In the absence of dated inscription it is merely possible to situate these artefacts around the 14th-15th century.
Stone pillars were erected throughout the Karnali Basin from the 13th to the 17th century.
They are installed to honor the memory of deceased persons, mostly warriors, as is illustrated in Kumā (Andolfatto 2019).
This Caitya was commissioned by Harṣamuni Śākya in 1958.
It has been built in a small courtyard surrounded by residential buildings.
Its dome andharmikāhave been fixed in place using cement, and theāmalaka,yaḥsĩanduṣṇīṣa cūḍāmaniwhich are built on top of thetrayodaśabhūmīare made out of brass and have been tied up with iron wires.
A stonepānasa(lamp) has been erected to the west.
No inscription related to the Caitya could be found, its style suggests it was constructed in the 19th or early 20th century.
It is constructed entirely from bricks, plastered withbajramortar, and has three tiers of roof.

Gutschow(2014, 561) mentions that so far seven temples are found in the Kathmandu Valley “that represent a distinct temple type in stone with three tiers of roof.”Aśivaliṅgais consecrated in the sanctum of Ṭaṅkeśvara Mahādeva.
It is believed that Ṭaṅkeśvara Mahādeva was not established and invoked here, but this is his self-manifestation.
There is no evidence to date the initial construction of this temple.

In 1673 CE (NS 793), a devotee constructed the statue of Vyāghriṇī and in 1696 CE (NS 816), during the reign of King Bhūpālendra Malla, a donor named Jayakalyāṇa installed a stone pillar with trident to the north of Ṭaṅkeśvara.
Previously, when the temple had sufficient income generated from its land endowments, twelve people were appointed here for singing devotional songs (bhajana) and seven for playing music.
The originalphalcādating from around the 1920s featured elegant proportions and simple construction thus setting it apart from more elaborately carved and decoratedphalcāsin the cities.
Around 2021, the severely damagedphalcāwas completely rebuilt with new materials.
The formerly simple and slender columns were replaced with heavy and intricately carved columns.
An inscription on the concretephalcā(CHO4100-004) records that once a largerphalcāstood there.
It was replaced in ca. 2001 CE with a roughly built single storey brick and concrete structure.
These fragments seem to predate the primary statue of the shrine and were likely installed here after being found in the vicinity.
While the establishment date of the temple cannot be determined through an inscription, characteristics of a medieval Gaṇeśa statue are evident in the primary deity of the temple.
A small carved window installed on the wall is also closed with metal grillework.
There is also an inscription with a portion damaged due to erosion and breakage of wood.
There is no inscription at the site that records the construction of the Phalcā.
It appears to have been renovated multiple times.
But the details of the renovations are unclear due to the lack of proper sources.
Up until 1987 CE, Rāmaśaraṇa Śreṣṭha from Sankhu used to live here at the Phalcā with the family.
On their way back, the deities are welcomed by the members of the Lasakusa (lit. welcome) Guthi in front of the Mahākāla shrine.
The Phalcā is also used as a space for hosting a feast after the animal sacrifice offered to Mahākāla (D. Sharma and T. Shrestha 2016, p. 290).
The original seven-bayedjhĩgaṭī-tiled Phalcā was replaced by this four-storey structure in 1993.
A Viṣṇu statue and four stone inscriptions are attached to the wall.
One of the inscriptions mentions that the Phalcā was commissioned by a donor from Rupachẽ Nani (the name of the donor could not be deciphered) in 1835.
Moreover, the inscription suggests that the Phalcā was constructed by people from the Jyāpu community.
The upper storeys of the building are being used by the Naka Bahī Maṅkāḥ Khalaḥ (of the Jyāpu community) for various purposes.
It appears to be a three-story residential building with corrugated tin sheets laid on the roof.
The last (third) floor was dismantled and covered with corrugated tin sheets after the second floor was damaged in the 2015 earthquakes.
An inscription from 1682 CE (NS 802) is also installed on the same wall.
They claim to have lived in the Phalcā for many generations and have obtained the building's land ownership certificate.
According to the inscription, in 1682 CE, a certain Kṛṣṇa Mulmī Bhāro of the Cāphare Ṭola in Kirtipur constructed the Phalcā and installed the aforementioned two Viṣṇu statues.
It was most likely built as a one-story Phalcā and later converted to a multi-story structure after being privatized.
This is why Kṛṣṇa Mulmī Bhāro may have constructed the Phalcā so that devotees visiting the water channel could rest.
Adjacent to the pavilion in the northwest direction is a rectangular house-like structure constructed with carved stones.
Within and around this building, stone memorial pillars (khamba) and architectural pillars, potentially originating from a pavilion, are displayed.
It is constructed on a stone platform, with eight pillars supporting a corbelled dome.
In 2011, Prayag Raj Sharma reported that the roof of thebhaithaka(pavilion) had completely collapsed (Sharma 2012, p. 323).
However, the roof was rebuilt prior to the site's survey in 2015.

According to D. R. Sharma, local accounts mention that the nearby Chipur Hati Bhātko Nāulo (DDL0280) was built by a person named Hati Bhāt "during the time of Nāga Malla of Doti state in the 14th century." It is also said that Hati Bhāt's wife constructed another reservoir in the vicinity, but its location is unknown (Sharma 2012, p. 321-323).
Considering the stylistic similarity between the carvings on this monument and those on the Hati Bhātko Nāulo, it is reasonable to assume that they were constructed around the same period.

Furthermore, the 14th and 15th centuries were characterized by significant architectural activity in the region, as evidenced by the numerous monuments erected during that time in the Dadeldhura and Baitadi districts.

During Bhīmasena Thāpā's rule, a person named Hanumantasiṃha Amātya established this Hanumān statue near the Bagmati bridge, on the way from Thapathali to Kupondol and was entrusted with the bridge's maintenance.
For this responsibility, the state granted him land.
An inscription mentions a rest house (sataḥ) that is currently (March 2025) not visible due to the construction of large structures separating the statue and the temple into distinct complexes.
The installation of such Hanumān statues, with similar iconography, was common from the Malla to the Rāṇā periods.

A popular medieval text,Narapatijayacaryā, extolled the benefits of establishing Hanumān statues, claiming they prevent famine, disease, enemy intrusion, lightning strikes, witchcraft, and evil spirits (N. Panta VS 2021, p.28).

During the Śāha-Rāṇā era, numerous such statues were erected in Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava shrines and along riverbanks, leading to many cremation grounds by holy rivers being named “Hanumān Ghāṭa.”This Hanumān statue in Kupondol was established in 1814 CE (VS 1870) by Hanumantasiṃha Amātya, who also established other deities and asataḥwith his brothers Bhājudhana, Sadāśiva, and Lakṣmīnarasiṃha.
They installed the statues of deities like Hanumaṃteśvara Mahādeva, Kṛṣṇa, Gaṇeśa, Bhagavatī, Kaumārī, Naṭyeśvara, Sarasvatī, and others.

His association with the newly built Bagmati bridge led to the state granting him 150ropanīs of land in Kupondol in 1810 CE (VS 1867), followed by an additional 25ropanīs in 1814 CE (VS 1870), on the condition that he maintained the bridge.
This is documented in an inscription near the statue.
The inscription also mentions the allocation of sixropanīs of land for the annual worship of the installed deities.

While a religious trust managed these rituals until about three decades ago, currently (March 2025), the “Hanumān Mandira Saṃrakṣaṇa tathā Vyavasthāpana Samitī”, a committee formed by devotees, oversees the temple, has added religious items, and annually celebrates the Hanumān Jayantī on the full moon day of Caitra (local resident, Rāṇā, male, age 63).
Two statues placed in the upper part of thetoraṇahave been stolen.
The esoteric room (āgaṃ) has been established on the first floor of thebāhāḥ.
On the ground floor of the monastic building (dyaḥchẽ) lies the main sanctum of thebāhāḥ.
Threecaityas are established in thebāhāḥ's courtyard.
Scholars who have researched thebāhāḥmention that it was established in 1621 CE (NS 741) during the reign of King Jagajyoti Malla.

S. Śākya (1120, p.30-31) writes that Devasiṃha Buddhācārya, Jayasiṃha Buddhācārya, Muni Buddhācārya, and Kuśala Buddhācārya jointly founded the bāhāḥ in 1621 CE (NS 741) during the reign of King Jagajyoti Malla.

B. Vajrācārya (1124, p.38) has written that Devasiṃha Buddhācārya, Jayasiṃha Buddhācārya, Melusiṃ Buddhācārya bought a plot of land on the 9th of the dark fortnight of Kārtika in 1621 CE (NS 741) during the reign of King Jagajyoti Malla and established thebāhāḥ.
They claim to possess a palm-leaf document from NS 741 that records the event.
However, the study of the land deed does not prove that the land was purchased for the construction of thebāhāḥin NS 741 as claimed by them.

B. Vajrācārya (1124, p.141, appendix no. 65) has published the original text of the palm-leaf, which only records the purchase of land by Devasiṃha Buddhācārya (text: Budhācāryya Devasiṃha); it does not mention that the land was bought for thebāhāḥor that thebāhāḥwas built on the land.

monument_name: Vināyaka Pañcadevala Śikhara Temple 4 (built between the late 13th and early 14th cent.)
text: Vināyaka Pañcadevala Śikhara Temple 4, built between the late 13th and early 14th centuries, is situated on a large platform that houses four medievalśikharatemples and one more recent shrine.

monument_name: Vināyaka Pañcadevala Śikhara Temple 4 (built between the late 13th and early 14th cent.)
text: In front of each doorjamb, just before the threshold, a column is erected.

monument_name: Vināyaka Pañcadevala Śikhara Temple 4 (built between the late 13th and early 14th cent.)
text: This Temple 4 was most likely built around the same time as its 'twin' to the southeast (ACH0072), i.e. in the late 13th or early 14th century.

monument_name: Tarpibaḍā Śikhara Temple 1 (built around the 13th-15th centuries)
text: Tarpibaḍā Śikhara Temple 1, built around the 13th-15th centuries, is the larger of two śikhara temples that face each other and are located about 20 meters north of a stone fountain (JUM0443).

monument_name: Tarpibaḍā Śikhara Temple 1 (built around the 13th-15th centuries)
text: The Temples and the fountain are built on terraces that are currently planted with apple trees.

monument_name: Tarpibaḍā Śikhara Temple 1 (built around the 13th-15th centuries)
text: From the 13th to the 15th centuries, suchśikharatemples were built throughout the Karnali Basin (Andolfatto 2019).

monument_name: Tarpibaḍā Śikhara Temple 1 (built around the 13th-15th centuries)
text: The rarity of inscriptions onśikharatemples (locally known asdevala) complicates dating of these monuments.

monument_name: Tarpibaḍā Śikhara Temple 1 (built around the 13th-15th centuries)
text: The similarity of the two sites' plans suggests that the Tarpibaḍā Temple1 and 2 were also constructed around the same time.

On the basis of radiocarbon dating, the Dhanaju Caitya Temple, a miniature temple with a caitya in the sanctum, located at the Ituṃ Bāhāḥ Ṭola, was determined to be the earliest extant Temple of the Kathmandu Valley built in the 10th century (cp. Gutschow 2011, p. 219).
The woodentoraṇaplaced atop the sanctum door has been already stolen (only its lower part has survived).
Probably, someone called Dhanaju built and named it after him as ‘Dhanaju Caitya’.
However, there are no historical records of the construction of the Temple andcaitya.
In 1894 (NS 1014), the Temple was renovated and atoraṇawas offered.
Before it was destroyed by earthquakes in 1934 CE, the Temple had two tiers and a circumambulatory path around it.
Thegaḥjhyāḥ(blind window) beneath the roof should have been on the first floor, but it was moved there after the Temple was rebuilt as a single tier following the earthquake.
In 1983 CE, thejhĩgaṭīroof was replaced with corrugated metal sheet (Gutschow 2011, p. 220).
The Temple was recently renovated in 2021 CE (VS 2077).
On the other hand, corner pillars added richness to the structural design.
The wall surfaces were plastered in 1989, whicle three tympana demonstrate an earlier renewal of the temple in 1899 (inscription on the bottom of the tympanum, elevation west).
The former so-called hanging roof (yengaḥpākhā) was replaced by a joist roof (dhalinpākhā), its struts supported by the lower cornice.

On the eastern and southern elevations the aquatic animal is replaced by lotus foliage, but both motif symbolise the abundance of celestial waters. (…) The dating to the 9thor 1th century based on a comparison with the upper decorative panel of the 7th-century frame of Amitābha’s shrine in the eastern wing of the Jokhang in Lhasa (see p. 190) and confirmed by radiocarbon testing.
This evidences that the medieval cities of the valley were fortified starting from the Early Malla Period (cp.D. ŚarmāVS 2055, 23).

In his compositionKīrtipatākā(verse no. 10), Kunu Śarmāmentions such gates, installed in the strategic locations of the boundary walls of the medieval city of Patan, were extremely strong and nicely designed.
An inscription, issued during the reign of Yakṣa Malla, in1453 CE (NS 573) records the role of the citizens to maintain the boundary walls, ditches, and fortresses.
Similarly, the duties of the citizens to take care of such walls are explicitly mentioned in an edict issued by Śrīnivāsa Malla in 1673 CE (cf.Slusser1982, 99).
The Malla Era cities featured walls as tall as ten to thirteen feet, which were destroyed after the invasion of the Kathmandu Valley by Gorakhali King Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa Śāha (cp.Slusser1982, 99-100).
TheGopālarājavaṃśāvalī(fol.38) mentions Kīrtipāla Bhāro being imprisoned at Kirtipur in 1242 CE (NS 362) after the construction of Gundekvātha and Gochekvātha.
Except for its lower part, this gate was renovated around 2000 CE.
In 2010 CE, images of deities were painted on the gate’s retaining walls.
In 2018 CE, the municipality removed the painted plastered layer and preserved the original form of the gate.

There is no evidence regarding to thephalcā's original construction but theKathmandu Nagar Kṣetrako Inventory(VS 2039,185) dates it to the seventeenth century and states that it was constructed in a traditional style with intricately carved wooden elements.
It was reconstructed in its contemporary form in 2007 CE and none of the original elements were preserved.

An inscription embedded in thephalcā's back wall mentions that it was reconstructed with the support of the US Ambassador's Fund for Cultural Preservation (AFCP), Kathmandu Municipality Ward Number12, and the Heritage & Environment Conservation Foundation Nepal.
The reconstruction work started in 2006 CE and was completed in 2007 CEU.
It also mentions that thephalcāwas originally constructed by the Pradhāna clan from Bicche Bāhāḥ.
The Navadurgā Bhajana Maṇḍala tried to use the space for singingbhajana,however refrained due to the 2015 CE earthquakes.
The four other, smaller temples, are built one meter away from the central temple, facing its south, west, north and east facades.
Furthermore, the construction ofśikharatemples in the Karnali region seems to have stopped before the 16th century, which narrows the dating of this type of plan down to the 14th-15th century.
There are no records to date the initial construction of the Temple.
Before its reconstruction in 1996 CE, the Temple’s sanctum was on its first floor, and it (i.e., the first floor) also had a large window ‘taḥpāḥjhyāḥ’.
[2]The reconstruction converted the tiered Temple into a concrete present structure that contains only some features of a tiered architecture.

Footnotes^A building used by the Bhīmasena Bhajana Maṇḍala, a group of hymn singers, stands north of the Temple while Pukhūlāchi Gaṇeśa Mandira (SKH0340) is at its northeast.^Bhīmasena Mandira (LAL1380) of Patan also has a large balconied window on the first floor where the sanctum is also housed.
The Cañcala Gaṇeśa temple is situated between the Lokeśvara Mandira (KAT1250) and the community building (tvāḥchẽ) at the Kilāgala Ṭola.
Due to the temple's proximity to the Pulukisi building, it came to be known as the Cañcala Gaṇeśa Mandira, where ‘Cañcala’ means 'playful nature'.

Although there is no historical record of the temple's initial construction, the earliest historical record dates back to 1924 CE (NS 1045), when Muni Thakuṃ of the Kilāgala Ṭola installed a metaltoraṇaon top of the temple's entrance in the name of her deceased husband Taḥdhi Maharjana.
The temple was rebuilt in 1994 CE (VS 2050) with funds from the ward office and donations from locals.
During the reconstruction, the tile roof was replaced with copper sheets.
In 2011 CE (VS 2067), the residence of the temple's caretaker at Tāhāḥ Nani caught fire, and the Gaṇeśa statue used for the annual procession and his jewellery were destroyed.
A triangular-shaped hole provides an opening between the inside shrine and a shrine on the south side of the building (LAL4126-001).
Kota Pāṭī was restored by the Kathmandu Valley Preservation Trust from 2009 to 2012.
The roof was completely rebuilt with new timber, athough most of the historic columns, capitals and small carved windows in the half-story were reused.
After the earthquake, the remaining bays were converted into small shops, cafes, and an ATM lounge.

Thabũ Phalcā, situated to the west of the street leading from Agnimaṭha to Kumārīpāṭī (LAL0280), appears more like a residential building, lacking carved arcades or other distinctive phalcā features due to the loss of its original structure in the 1980s during reconstruction.
No inscriptions are present at the site that could disclose information about Thabũ Phalcā's construction.
Local residents suggest that it was built by the ancestors of a Śreṣṭha family from Thabũṭola..

D. Vajrācārya(2056, p. 86-87) has published an inscription from Thabũ Phalcā stating that Madhusūdana Deva and Govinda Bhāro renovated it in NS 762 (1642 CE) with the permission of the Śreṣṭha Bhāros of the ṭola.
The inscription is no longer present at the site.
Managed by a private guthi of Śreṣṭhas from Thabũ ṭola, Thabũ Phalcā also has its rent collected by the guthi.
Annually, on the 8th day of the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa,pañjrāṃis offered at this location.
Two weeks later, on the 8th day of the dark fortnight of Bhādra, the guthi members display a statue of Lord Kṛṣṇa outside Thabũ Phalcā in observance of Kṛṣṇajanmāṣṭamī, the birthday of Lord Kṛṣṇa.
Thephalcāappears to have been constructed to provide convenience and shelter for participants in these religious and secular observances.
No written document has yet been found to determine the date or patron of its original construction.
An inscription on the interior wall records that Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa of Vambāhā (Om Bahāḥ), Kāntipura, renovated thephalcāin 1957–58 (VS 2014) in the name of his son.
The same inscription mentions that the structure had sustained damage in the earthquake of 1934 (VS 1990) and was restored only twenty-four years later.
Prior to the major earthquake of 2015 (VS 2072), thephalcāwas already in a dilapidated state; after the earthquake, only the masonry walls remained standing.
In 2023 (VS 2079), the structure was reconstructed under the supervision of Ward No. 12 of the Kathmandu Metropolitan City.
Boys of approximately eleven or twelve years of age are required to remain at the Pacalī Pīṭha for twenty-four hours, where special worship is conducted (R. Maharjana, NS 1137, p. 23).
The domed Śiva temple, constructed in the 20th century, is located on a rocky promontory on the right bank of the Tilā Nadī river in Khalāchaur, south of Michāgāũ.
Built on a platform with three central steps, the temple has a rectangular layout and is constructed using stone and mud masonry.
Within the sanctum, there is an elevated platform housing a damaged temple pinnacle and a stoneśivaliṅgaon ayoni.
Niels Gutschow examined similar dome temples in Far-West Nepal and noted that they were all built between the 1940s and 1980s (Gutschow 1992).
While the exact construction date of this temple is unknown, it is reasonable to suggest that it was built during the latter half of the 20th century.
Facing west, theśikhara-style temple is constructed from brick, with its upper section coated in whitebajra(mixture of lime and brick dust) plaster and topped with a finial.

While specific construction dates and builders remain unknown, the temple likely dates to the late Malla period, similar to otherśikhara-style brick temples from that era, such as the Bhavānīśaṅkara Mandira (THI0030) in Thimi.
It is believed a prosperous individual from Bode commissioned its construction.
The temple is associated with a Śreṣṭha clan, whose ancestors likely built it under a private trust.
Significantly, the temple's hybrid reconstruction incorporates elements from various eras and sources.
Similar doubts about the deity's identity are raised by Śyāmasundara (Ś. Rājavaṃśī NS 1119, p.09).
The presence of existing wooden doors and capitals suggests an original multi-story construction, possibly reconstructed in the domed style after earthquakes in 1833 or 1934 CE (VS 1890 or 1990).
The identity of the builder remains unknown, with Gutschow (2011, 307) suggesting it might have been erected under a local ruler (mahāpātra).
Post the 2015 CE earthquake (VS 2072), the Patan Museum took charge of overseeing the temple's restoration.

Constructed south of the palace building on a square plinth, this Śaiva temple resembles the Paśupatinātha temple of Kathmandu due to its plinth structure, two-tier roof, and three-bay portals on all four sides.
Legend holds King Yakṣa Malla visited Paśupatinātha every day but failed to do so once during the rainy season due to flooding Bāgamatī.
The king got a vision of the deity in his dream, who suggested he build a replica of the Paśupatinātha in front of his palace.
Although the temple is believed to be constructed by Yakṣa Malla, there is no inscriptive evidence that supports the belief.

The oldest inscription found at the temple is dated NS 607 (1487 CE) installed by Kīrtilakṣmī, wife of Yakṣa Malla who did not go through the sati, the tradition of self-immolating the wife/wives of a deceased male.

[3]The inscription records Kīrtilakṣmī installing metal images of lions at the temple and offering various items required for the daily rituals while also donating 12ropanīs of land as a source of income for the temple (B. PauḍelaVS 2022, 15-16).
Yakṣa Malla died on the 11th of the dark fortnight of Māgha in NS 602 (1482 CE) (K. TamoṭaNS 1127, 5).
This inscription installed five years after his death is the first one to mention the term Yakṣeśvara.
Inscriptions reveal that there already was a tradition of naming aśivaliṅga after the main sponsor back in the Lichhavi period.

As there is no source found yet that reveal about the construction of the temple, it is still unclear whether it was Yakṣa Malla who constructed this temple or was it his wife Kīrtilakṣmī who commissioned its construction after the king's death.
The legend suggests that Yakṣa Malla himself built the temple.

However, radiocarbon dating of a sample taken from the jambs of the central door opening turned out a calibration dated 1322-1404 CE, which makes the construction of the temple in the middle rather than the end of the 15th century appear plausible (Gutschow2011, 408).
Another important inscription from the temple dated NS 614 (1494 CE) deals with the formation ofguthis by Rāya Malla and others to carry out daily rituals and other annual worships at the temple.
The Śiva temple must have undergone many renovations over the years, but not much is known about them due to the lack of their documentation.
The woodwork found on the temple date back to the 16th to the 18th century while some were renewed in 1998 CE (Gutschow2011, 408).
Although the inscription dated NS 614 (1494 CE) mentions the varṣavarddhana ritual, this anniversary ritual has stopped long ago.

Footnotes^Other two- or three-tiered temples dating back to the 14th to 19th century with a square base that features three-bay portals on the ground floor are Indreśvara Mandira (1294 CE, Panautī), Jagannātha Mandira (1562 CE, Kathmandu), Cāranārāyaṇa Mandira (1565 CE, Patan), Taleju Mandira (1660s CE, Kathmandu), Paśupatinātha Mandira (1697 CE, Kathmandu), Cā̃gunārāyaṇa Mandira (1708 CE, Bhaktapur), Tripureśvara Mandira (1818 CE, Kathmandu), (Gutschow2011, 401), Vaṃśīnārāyaṇa (Kṛṣṇa) Mandira (Bhaktapur), etc.^B.

Pauḍela(VS 2022: 21) andPruscha(1975: 217) have stated that the river the king failed to cross was Bāgamatī whileSlusser (1982, 229) mentions the name of the river as Manoharā.^Three wives of Yakṣa Malla, Jīvalakṣmī, Sarasvatīdevī, and Jayatana are so far known to have undergone the sati tradition after the king's death (K. TamoṭaNS 1127: 4).
Enshrining a four-faced (caturmukha)śivaliṅgain its sanctum, it is likely that this Śiva temple was constructed in the 18th or 19th century.

Positioned between two streets, to the east of the Jayavāgīśvarī Mandira (PPK1222) across the Ring Road, and north of the Amālakoṭa Kacaharī building, the Laliteśvara Mandira stands on two levels of plinths facing west.
Historical documentation shedding light on the temple's initial construction is not available.
The caturmukha śivaliṅga inside the sanctum is believed to date back to the 18th to 19th century (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p. 622).
Therefore, it is reasonable to assume that the temple itself and the statues of Umāmaheśvara were also built during the same time (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, pp. 453, 625).
An iron water tap, known as Tri-Bhīma Dhārā (PPK1107-006), was installed by Prime Minister Bhīma Śamśera during the reign of King Tribhuvana in 1931 CE (VS 1988).
The temple underwent renovation by the Pashupati Area Development Trust in 2002 CE (VS 2059).
Constructed in an oval shape, thehiticontains one stone spout which faces south.
Inside the niche, atop the spout there used to be a statue of Umāmaheśvara, which was stolen some years ago (according to a resident).
A brick with a date (NS 832, i.e., 1712 CE) was found on the ground of thehitipremises (D. Sharma and T. Shrestha2016, p. 420).
This suggests that the ground of thehitiwas brick-paved during the reign of King Bhāṣkara Malla.** However, the brick is not on the site any longer (as of March 2022 CE).
Thehitiused to contain another inscription installed in 1515 CE (NS 715) during the reign of King Śivasiṃha Malla.
It recorded the installation of a wooden door with carved lion (D. Sharma and T. Shrestha2016, p. 403).
Since there is no wooden door at thehiti, the inscription was most probably brought from somewhere else and later placed at thehiti.

This inscription, too, is not on the site any longer (as of March 2022 CE).**Bhāṣkara Malla and his mother had also rebuilt theśikhara-style Vajrayoginī Mandira (SKH0500) into a tiered structure in the same year.
In 2021, the historic Taṅgaḥ Bāhāḥ building was demolished and replaced with a concrete frame structure.
Its classical name suggests that it was founded by the Licchavi king Bālārcana Deva.
The entrance gateto thebāhāḥcourtyard is built in a neo-classical Rāṇā style.
Thethapāḥjuof the Bāhāḥis supposed to spend his whole life inside the building.
In otherbāhāḥs,thekvāḥpāḥdyaḥis usually placed on the ground floor of the esoteric building.
The southern door of the esoteric building is surmounted by atoraṇashowing Vasundharā.
The Bāhāḥ's classical name is Bālārcanadevasaṃskārita Jyeṣṭhavarṇa Mahāvihāra (i.e. the Jyeṣṭhavarṇa Mahāvihāra founded by Bālārcanadeva).
Thissuggests that it was established by the Licchavi king Bālārcana Deva.
However, further research is needed to establish this monument's historiography.
Thisphalcāwas originally a unique rest house with only one bay, built in 1599 CE (NS 719) by Jikesiṃha Bhābo of Sunāguthi in memory of his deceased father, Hāku Bhābo.
Standing at Cvaylāchi in Thecva, thephalcāwas initially built with only one bay in the west.
A statue of Nārāyaṇa and a stone inscription from 1599 CE (NS 719) are embedded in thephalcā’s wall.
Jikesiṃha Bhābo, a resident of Sunāguthi (text: Śuluṃthigrāma), and his wife built thephalcāin 1599 CE (NS 719) in memory of his deceased father, Hāku Bhābo.
Subsequent renovations added two wooden pillars to the western side for reinforcement.

However, thephalcādeteriorated over time, becoming dilapidated and earning the local name "pulāṃphalcā," meaning "old rest house."In 2023 CE (VS 2080), with financial support from the Godawari Municipality, thephalcāunderwent reconstruction (local resident, Maharjan, male, age 49).
As two additional columns were already present, it was rebuilt as a three-bayed rest house, rendering its old name less fitting.
Originally, thekvāḥpāḥchẽwas built in a traditional Newar style, but it was replaced by a concrete structure after its reconstruction in 2011 CE.
Previously, the main entrance to the sanctum was flanked by various large wall paintings, but only images of Sāriputra and Maudagalyāyana were painted after the above-mentioned reconstruction.
Aśikharakūṭacaityais established at the Bāhāḥ premises.
There are no historical sources to date the initial construction of the Taṃcākone Bāhāḥ.
Its members state that they had originally moved to Bhaktapur from the Taḥchẽ Bāhāḥ (KAT0470), Kathmandu and built a separatebāhāḥhere.
Due to the poor condition of the building, they rebuilt thekvāḥpāḥchẽby collecting donations from thesaṃghamembers.
Every year on the full moon day of Āśvina, achatraused to be offered to the above-mentionedcaityaat the Bāhāḥ premises.
Oneśikharatemples was lost since the construction of the temples.
[1]A stone Dharmadhātu Maṇdala[2]is erected in front of thekvāḥpāḥdyaḥ.
A Śikharakūṭa Caitya, two Dharmadhātu Maṇḍalas, and a statue of Śivapārvatī are established in the Bāhāḥ’s courtyard.

The local residents believe that King of Patan, Siddhinarasiṃha Malla (r. 1620 – 1661) brought the Śilpakāras and Sthāpitas to Patan in order to make them construct temples and statues etc. in his kingdom.
Sometime later, they (Śilpakāras and Sthāpitas) built twoāgamasand started living permanently in Patan.
Locke(1985, 138) has mentioned a copper-plate inscription recording the date of the Bāhāḥ’s initial construction, however, no such inscription is in the Bāhāḥ at present.
The earliest reference to this Bāhāḥ can be found on a palm-leaf manuscript from NS 778 (1658 CE).
Although this Bāhāḥ was initially built by the Śilpakāras, it is also shared by the Sthāpitas.

Footnotes^The Akṣobhya statue is dressed in a metallhegā.^The date NS 795 (1675 CE) is inscribed on the Dharmadhātu (see the object LAL2680-011 below).^The manuscript records the name of a person (Siddhi Bhāro) who is a member of Oṃ (text: Jom) Bāhāḥ (cf.Rājavaṃśī2041, 75).^He receives a monthly enumeration of 3500 rupees.
Locals believe that the Bhvaṃ Bāhāḥ was foundedby someone by spendinghis property that he acquired from his trade in Tibetor Bhoṭa.
Although it is abāhāḥ, nokvāḥpāḥchẽis built here.
ThreeŚikharakūṭa Caityasareerectedin front of theBāhāḥ.
[It is not helpful to talk about things that are not there]No historical sources are available to date the initial construction of thisBāhāḥ.
Thus, it is probable that one of them founded theBāhāḥout of the fortune made from the trade.
Pruscha(1975, p. 76) erroneously mentions that the Bhvaṃ Bāhāḥ was constructed in NS 760 (1640 CE).

The colophons of two manuscripts—VasudharādhāraṇīandĀryamaṇibhadrajambhalahṛdaya—copied in NS 625 (1504 CE) during the joint rule of Ratna Malla and Indra Malla refer to the Bhvanta Vihāra (Panta2037, p. 23).
In NS 760 (1640 CE), Śākyabhikṣu Jayadharma, together with his wife Nugulakṣmī and the family erected the above-mentioned threeCaityasinfront of the Bāhāḥduring the reign of King Pratapa Malla.
Jayadharma also enshrined Varabārāhī and donated land to theBāhāḥin NS 775 (1655 CE).

However, no such rituals take place after the familymoved out (out of what? better "moved away". The door of the sanctum is not locked andis left open.[In some photos the doors are closed, in others they are open - perhaps saying 'unlocked' suffices.]
Even though the Temple looks simple in terms of its architectural design, it was constructed during the late medieval period in 1630 CE, i.e. NS 750 (cf.Ś. ŚreṣṭhaVS 2057, 94).
The Temple, which is around four hundred years old, must have been renovated several times in the due course of time, however there are no sources to trace that history out.
An inscription carved on the lintel of this stone frame from 1630 CE (NS 750) mentions that a certain Ha (?) Bhāro from Kirtipur constructed the Temple.
The stone frame suggests that the Temple was originally constructed in stone.
Nevertheless, in Oldfield’s sketches from 1855 CE, a two-storey building can be seen on this very spot where the Manavināyaka Temple is standing at the present.

Therefore, it is very likely that this Temple was located somewhere else inside the Bāghabhairava Complex before 1855 CE, but no sources are found recording the date when the Temple was relocated to its present spot.
A six-armed stone statue of Gaṇeśa is consecrated inside the sanctum of the Manavināyaka Temple.
Such a motif can not to be found in other regions of the Indian sub-continent (cf.G.Ṭaṇḍana, VS 2042, 59).
An inscription right above the deity’s statue records its establishment by a Hāku Bhāro from Kirtipur in 1503 CE, i. e.
NS 623 (Ś. ŚreṣṭhaVS 2057, 88).
It is clear, from the inscription, that the statue was there 127 years before the present Temple was constructed.
This is the oldest inscription so far found in the territories of Kirtipur.

The Jośī community stands behind the commissioning and constructing of the Joragaṇeśa temple (LAL1750) and Valkhu Phalcā.
An inscription from the time of Yoganarendra Malla records that someone by the name of Keśavarāja Bhāro donated a Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa statue in the month of Āṣāḍha.
He later, in the month of Bhadra, commissioned a maṇḍapa (a 16-bayed phalcā, or sohrakhuṭṭe) in 1700 CE (NS 720) in the memory of his deceased wife Śakuntarāmayī.

The inscription also records that land was granted to support the monument, with the income from the land allocated for the worship of Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa and Valkhu Gaṇeśa, as well as for providing a feast to Brahmins after the worship.

Valkhu Phalcā remained intact in the way it had been built during the Late Malla period, then, in the 1980s-1990s, it was transformed into a concrete structure, following a mutual agreement by the Jośī guṭhī.
This tradition continued until 2014 CE.
According to a guṭhī member, the ritual of lighting a lamp in the Phalcā during the Matsyendranātha (Bungadhyo) festival, as instructed in the inscription, has been discontinued for several decades.
The structure was fully reconstructed in 2019 CE (VS 2076), and within it has been installed a replica of Dakṣiṇakālī that was ritually empowered and brought from the Dakṣiṇakālī Temple.
Architecturally, thedyaḥchẽis a three-storied structure built in a traditional idiom using modern construction methods.
As it is physically connected to an adjoiningsataḥ, the overall ground plan takes the shape of the English letter “L.” Thedyaḥchẽis constructed on a single-tiered stone plinth, oriented eastward.
At the topmost level, the building is crowned with a temple-like pinnacle, and akausī(terrace) has been provided.
At the eastern corner of thekausīof thesataḥ, a smalldevalahas been built, in which a metal replica image of Dakṣiṇakālī is installed.
No historical evidence has been found regarding the initial construction of thedyaḥchẽ.

Reconstruction work began in 1998 CE (VS 2055) with financial support from the Guṭhī Saṃsthāna and was completed in 2019 CE (VS 2076) through the combined efforts of Dakṣiṇakālī Municipality, the Ṭipī Tole Sudhāra Samiti, and local residents.
Although the principal deity of Ṭipī Tole is understood to be Kanakeśvara, it is said that a temple of Kanakeśvara once stood at the Sarasvatī Ḍola of Ṭipī Tole (U. Ācārya, VS 2044, p. 31).
In the past, thecaturmūrtiimage used in processions was kept here, but repeated incidents of theft led to the decision to store the original image securely in the residence of thedyaḥpālāḥ.
An inscription, situated east of theśivaliṅga, is no longer legible.
However, based on the script used in the inscription, it is likely from the later medieval period.
In 1996 CE (VS 2053), the temple's plinths were renovated during the reconstruction of the nearby Triśūla Sataḥ (PPK1216).
The Pashupati Area Development Trust is currently planning to rebuild the temple, as shared by a local resident, Kapālī, a male aged 40.
The local community gathers in front of the temple each year on Śivarātrī, the 14th day of the dark fortnight of Phālguna, to light a bonfire.
With simple pillars and windows, the temple was built in three disproportionate tiers.
According to Pruscha (1975, p. 258), the temple was renovated in 1940 CE (VS 1997), suggesting it may have been damaged in the 1934 earthquakes.
However, in 1986 CE (VS 2043), Govinda Maharjana, the seniormost member (thakali) of Bulu's jyāpu community, installed a physical Bhairava statue.
That same year, the temple was dismantled and rebuilt on a concrete foundation, resulting in a reduced height.
As of October 2024, the temple is undergoing renovation with the financial support of the Bagmati Provincial Government.
The simple columns from the previous construction are being replaced with ornate, carved wooden columns.
The jyāputhakāliestablishes thesukundāin the sanctum.
A religious trust namedKhaḥ Guthiis responsible for matters related to the palanquin.

The first half of the 14th century, and in particular the period of Khaśa Malla emperor Pṛthvī Malla (r. 1338-1358), saw the construction of water architecture in the Dullu region (see for instance the Patharnauli reservoir,DLK0160).
This sculpture was probably installed above the pediment of aśikharatemple, maybe on one of the nearby temples, i.e. from the duidevala (DLK0281) or from the pańcadevala (DLK0280).
The temple appears to have been built only later to alter the openpīṭhainto the temple’s sanctum.
Metal sheets were laid on the roofs during the reconstruction of the temple in 2013 CE (VS 2070).
The original Garuḍa statue on the pillar (PNG0010-004) was damaged and has been relocated within the temple premises.
No historical record sheds light on the temple’s initial construction.

However, considering that the tradition of building temples dedicated to protective deities in the southwestern settlements under the jurisdiction of the Patan kingdom flourished during the 16th and 17th centuries, it can be inferred that this temple was also built during that period.
The erection of the Garuḍa pillar in 1676 CE (NS 796) clearly indicates that thepīṭhaexisted even before that.
The temple was completely dismantled and reconstructed in 2014 CE (VS 2071), as the temple was in poor condition.

During the annual procession of Viṣṇudevī, her statue at thedyaḥchẽis taken to the Viṣṇudevī Pīṭha on the 8th of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa and is taken back to the town deep in the night (D. Maharjana NS 1137, p. 22).
Directly north of thispīṭhais a cremation ground where corpses are cremated using a unique method, different from the common practice of using excessive firewood in other cremation grounds.
In 1911 CE (VS 1968), Līlā Śamśera Rāṇā erected this temple in the name of his deceased father Gehendra Śamśera.
Notably, G. Ṭaṇḍana (VS 2053, p.346) and Michaels and Tandon (2017, p.62) designate the adjacentśivālaya(PPK0336) as Gehendramukteśvara instead of this one.
However, a bell offered to this temple identifies it as Gehendramukteśvara.
A bell is installed south of the temple.
Līlā Śamśera constructed the temple in 1911 CE (VS 1968) in memory of his father Gehendra Śamśera (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p.346; Michaels and Tandon 2017, p.62).

Gehendra Śamśera, born as the first son of Vīra Śamśera in 1871 CE (VS 1928) (D. Panta VS 2055, p.5), was the son of Vīra Śamśera’s formally-wedded wife Munīndra Rājyalakṣmī (P. Rāja VS 2071, p.24).
He managed police and detective departments during the premiership of his father Vīra Śamśera (P. Rāja VS 2073, p.150).
Disheartened by the premier’s behavior, Gehendra turned to alcohol and succumbed to illness in 1907 CE (VS 1964).
Some speculate poisoning, but no investigations were conducted (P. Rāṇā VS 2070, pp.206-207).
Four years after his death, his first son Līlā Śamśera erected thisśivālayain his father’s honor.
In 1675 CE (NS 795), Amara Siṃha Kumhara, son-in-law of King Śrīnivāsa Malla, and his wife Kīrttimaṅgalā, the king’s second daughter, constructed the water spout in memory of their deceased son.
A Bhagiratha statue is installed below this spout.
Alongside thehiti, aphalcā(public shelter) was built, supported by a land endowment of 2.5ropanīs in Pāko and 5ropanīs in Aphala for thehiti’s upkeep.
Though the inscription mentions thephalcā, it no longer exists.
Amara Siṃha and Kīrttimaṅgalā also built the Kṛṣṇa temple (LAL1450) in the Ko Bāhāḥ Ṭola in 1680 CE (NS 800).
In 1698 CE (NS 818), thehiti’s intra-channel system was repaired, and a stone inscription was installed to commemorate the event.
In 1972 CE (VS 2029), locals renovated thehitiand installed an Akṣobhya statue (LAL2421-003).
In 2013 CE (NS 1133), with support from the Urban Environment Management Society (UEMS), a local women’s group built a well south of thehitiand installed a biosand filter for water purification.
In 2014 CE (VS 2081), Lalitpur Municipality funded further repairs, restoring the east-facing spout (LAL2421-004), which had long been damaged.
Thephalcā's was most likely built in 1980 CE.
An inscription from NS 1100 (LAL4310_I_001) records the "restoration" of thephalcāin 1980 which appears unlikely.
It is possible that the inscription actually refers to the reconstruction of the Samay Phalca (LAL4317) that used to be located just to the south.

Could it be that Samay Phalcā was demolished in 1972 CE and subsequently rebuilt in 1980 CE as Nāmasaṅgīti Phalcā, about 10 metres further to the north?Another inscription attests to an extension to the western side of Nāmasaṅgīti Phalcā in 2013.
In 2020, the Nāmasaṅgīti Phalcā was undergoing restoration once again.
A new concrete pitched roof, covered withjhĩgaṭītiles, was added to the flat concrete slab roof, giving the structure a more traditional appearance.
A group known as Nāmasaṅgīti Khalaḥ has been established by residents of Pulchok.
Statues of Umāmaheśvara, Gaṇeśa, Nṛsiḥa, Padmapāṇi, Lokeśvara, Tārā and Nāmasaṅgitī have been installed on the building's northern wall.
Situated in Sītāpokharī Ṭola, Nuwakot, the Bāruda Ghara, meaning “ammunition house,” currently (as of April 2024 CE) lies in ruins.
To the west, aśivaliṅgadedicated to Nātheśvara Mahādeva and a Gaṇeśa statue worshipped as Kāryavināyaka are established.
After the Kapālīs left the area, their cemetery was also destroyed.

Although there is no historical record of the initial construction, locals believe the Bāruda Ghara was built in the late 1740s, during Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa Śāha's rule from Nuwakot. Śāha had already introduced ammunition in his conquests of other kingdoms and needed more to penetrate the fortified town of Nuwakot.

He brought ammunition from Kashi and conquered Nuwakot (D. Vajrācārya and Ṭ. Śreṣṭha VS 2032, p. 66), then likely built the Bāruda Ghara to manufacture ammunition locally to support his planned invasions of the Kathmandu Valley.
citations: (D. Vajrācārya and Ṭ. Śreṣṭha VS 2032, p. 66)

text: Later, during the Rāṇā period, ammunition was manufactured at multiple sites, including Bhaktapur, Thimi, Pulacoka, Ṭhosekhānī, and Nuwakot (B. Paṅgenī VS 2068, pp. 30-31).
In an 1855 CE (VS 1912) communique, Raṇa Uddīpa Siṃha, who later succeeded Jaṅga Bahādura, instructed to care for the Bāruda Ghara (D. Vajrācārya and Ṭ. Śreṣṭha VS 2032, p. 101).

text: However, the manufacturing of ammunition gradually stopped, but a few soldiers were in place here for the building’s care up until 1971 CE (VS 2028), when the district headquarters of Nuwakot was shifted to Bidur.
The Bāruda Ghara fell into complete neglect from then onward and began to collapse due to the poor state of repair.
Tools and utensils were stolen over time.
The building is currently owned by the Nepali Army.
Between 2025-05 and 2025-12, thephalcawas rebuilt from ground-up with new materials.
The whereabouts of the last historic column, one inscription and the Garuḍa statue, which were documented in 2020, are not known.
Following is the description written in 2020 during the first documentation by the DANAM team:Very little of this historic 17th centuryphalcāremains since it was rebuilt with brick and concrete.
Most of the original three-bayphalcāhas been replaced with a brick and concrete structure and only a few historic fragments survive.
The traditional roof was recently replaced with a concrete slab.
B. Basukala & Gutschow(2018) have dated the wooden pillar to ca.1700 CE.
There are five inscriptions in thephalcā- two are embedded in the northern wall and three in the eastern wall.
None of them provides information about thephalcā's initial construction.
One of the inscriptions embedded in the northern wall is dated NS 803 (1683 CE) and names thephalcāas Bāde Phale and the area as Bādephale Ṭola.
The inscription also mentions that a platform paved withteliyābricks was built to serve as a place for the five noble village elders (Pañcasamūha) to hold their meetings.
The second inscription embedded in the northern wall informs that a niche was established and framed with a woodentoraṇain NS 806 (1686 CE).
The three inscriptions embedded in the eastern wall are dated NS 839, VS 1946 and VS 2041; they all relate various restoration works on thephalcā.
This temple, built by the Śreṣṭha clan from the Olā Ṭola in Cāpāgāũ during the medieval period, has seen all its daily rituals and activities cease.
No concrete evidence regarding the construction of this temple has been found.
According to locals, it was built by the Śreṣṭha clan residing in the Olā Ṭola during the medieval period.
After the land endowments were lost, the temple began to be neglected.
In the mid-1990s (VS 2052-2053), the temple was renovated with financial assistance from the Chapagaun Village Development Committee (local resident, Śreṣṭha, male, age 43).
However, due to the loss of the endowed land, it became impossible to pay the priest, and the daily worships were discontinued.
Annually, a fire oblation used to be performed at the temple as part of the anniversary rituals, but these too have ceased.
The earliest historical record of the temple is dated 1668 CE (NS 788) and found on a strut recording the name of a donor, Viṣṇu Māhāta.
It is not clear whether this inscription refers to the initial construction of the temple, or if Viṣṇu Māhāta donated the strut during a renovation.
Two other struts bear the date 1685 CE (NS 805) suggesting that the temple was likely restored on this date.

This Licchavi-era temple of Hariśaṅkara, which houses a statue of Sūrya, the sun deity, with an inscription from 1083 CE (NS 203), stolen.
North of the entrance to the sanctum is a Sūrya statue, while south of it is a stone inscription from 1863 CE (NS 983).
He holds a trident and gestures a boon-granting varada mudrā with his right hands, and a discus (cakra) and a conch shell (śaṅkha) in his left hands.
There is no concrete evidence to determine the exact year of the temple’s construction.
Given that the temple houses a Licchavi-era Hariśaṅkara statue, it is likely that the temple was constructed around the same time.
After the creation of this statue, during the reign of King Guṇadeva in 565 CE (NS 487), Svāmī Vārtta is known to have constructed a Hariśaṅkara statue at Paśupatinātha.
This Hariśaṅkara statue, composed of half Śiva and half Viṣṇu, was established to prevent conflicts among people of different faiths (D. Vajrācārya VS 2030, pp. 198-199).

A new statue of Sūrya has now been installed north of the main entrance to the sanctum, replacing the original one that was stolen on May 16, 1985 (Bangdel 1989, p. 61, plate no. 10) and is yet to be recovered.

The stolen statue also contained an inscription from 1083 CE (NS 203), recording Vāṇadeva, the son of Yaśodeva, establishing the Sūrya statue to fulfill his mother’s vow (Regmi 1966, p. 5; D. Vajrācārya VS 2068, p. 53).

The statue shared similarities with anotherSūrya statuefrom 1065 CE (NS 185) that is currently (September 2024) exhibited at the Patan Museum, but was originally established in Thapāḥ Hiti (LAL2430) before it was stolen.
Therefore, after the creation of the Sūrya statue in Thapāḥ Hiti, it is possible that the same artist created the Sūrya statue in Saugaḥ as well (M. Khanāla VS 2074, p. 101).
In 1863 CE (NS 983), Bhājudhana Bhāro, a resident of the Taṃgaḥ Ṭola, renovated the temple in memory of his late wife, Dhana Thakunī.
In 1952 CE (VS 2009), Govindamāna contributed a Garuḍa statue to the temple.

Following the theft of the Sūrya statue dating back to 1083 CE (NS 203), Īśvaramāna Pradhāna from the Saugaḥ Ṭola established a new statue of Sūrya in memory of his deceased father, Govindamāna Pradhāna.
He also renovated the temple on the occasion.
The exact year this event remains uncertain due to the erosion of the inscription.
In 2003 CE (VS 2060), the locals collectively renovated the temple again.

This renovation was part of a broader initiative to beautify the cultural heritages of the Saugaḥ Ṭola, which was assigned the responsibility of organizing the Matayāḥ procession that year (Hariśaṅkara Guṭhī member, Śreṣṭha, male, age 49).
As the land endowed to the temple's trust gradually diminished, it became difficult to pay the brahmin's salary, and consequently, the daily worship ceased.
Candrabhakteśvara is part of the Nau Śivālaya, erected by Kṛṣṇa Bahādura Rāṇā, the younger sibling of Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā.
Kṛṣṇa Bahādura Rāṇā constructed five Śivālayas at the Gorakhanātha premises and four at the Gaurīghāṭa premises, collectively known as Nau Śivālaya.
Within each Śivālaya, a Śivaliṅga is installed in the sanctum, with Pāñcāyaṇa deities positioned at its four corners.

On the west side of the Śivālaya, there stands a stone figure of Nandī, the sacred animal mount of Lord Śiva, with a trident placed on the north side, and a statue of Kāmadeva is installed in the southeast.
However, G. Ṭaṇḍana (VS 2053, p. 346), and Michaels and Tandon (2017, p .62), have marked Candrabhakteśvara as a Śivālaya on their maps.
The Śivālaya lacks any inscriptive details.
As per the priest, an inscription is present on the bell, and the Śivālaya is named Candrabhakteśvara based on this bell inscription.
During its reconstruction in 2019 CE (VS 2076) by the Paśupatī area development trust, the bell was taken down and has not been rehung since.
According to Michaels and Tandon (2017, p. 106), the construction of the Śivālaya dates back to 1863 CE (1920 VS).
According to an inscription, it was originally dedicated to Lord Bhīmasena and today it is an important space wherebhajanais performed.
Five statues of Viṣṇu, Bhīmasena and Mahākāla are installed on the western wall of thephalcā.
The five-bayeddalāna-esquephalcāoriginally had only one floor, but was later reconstructed as a three-storiedsataḥ.
In 2016, it was rebuilt with the support of the Lalitpur Municipality and the Indian Embassy.
None of the historical wooden elements were used in the reconstruction.
M. Thapa (VS 2077, pp. 488-491) has cataloged 62 principalkuṇḍas in the Paśupati area; however, Tārākuṇḍa's name is conspicuously absent from this list.
There are no inscriptions detailing the construction of thiskuṇḍa, nor are there any associated legends or religious narratives.
In 2000 CE (VS 2056), the water spout was reconstructed by Indu Gautama, wishing for the salvation for her late husband, Rāmacandra Gautama.

According to the priest Krishna Prasad Acarya (interviewed in 1982), ut is likely that the pond was constructed during the time when Jita Jaṅga Bahadura Rāṇā con structed the Tāraprakāśevara in V.S. 1938 (1881 (CE)Tārākuṇḍa does not host any significant socio-cultural activities. Nonetheless, it remains a site of significance for pilgrims who engage in ablutions and worship as part of their journey to the sacred waterholes within the Pashupati area. A Bhaṭṭa Brahmin from the Śaṅkarācārya Āgamaghara in the Pashupati area assumes the role of thetīrthaguru, the guide for the pilgrimage, and is referred to as Nemuni (G. Tandana VS 2053, p. 536). Pilgrims partake in ceremonial bathing and worship rituals at eachkuṇḍabefore proceeding to Sankhu. There, they pay reverence to Nemuni, the statue of Padmapāni (SKH0500-014) within a small shrine. The pilgrimage ofkuṇḍayātrā, once a practiced tradition until a few decades ago, is no longer in practice.
The first floor houses the ritual installation of Taleju, while the second floor is used to store ritual objects associated with her worship.
Below it, on a pedestal, anavagraha maṇḍalais installed and regarded as a symbolic representation of the Navadurgā.
Consequently, during the procession, thekhaḍga—symbolizing theyoni—came to be concealed within bamboo coverings (P. Sapakoṭā, VS 2056, p. 25).
When the Bhaktapur king learned that the people of Tokhā had stolen Taleju Bhavānī’s swords, he came to Tokhā to inspect the procession.
The swords were hidden beneath flowers during thejātrā, leading the king to believe it was merely a floral procession, after which he returned to Bhaktapur (D. Śreṣṭha, VS 2067, p. 40).
Although no inscription records the original establishment of Taleju in Tokhā, a stone inscription dated 477 CE (Śaka 399) elsewhere attests to Tokhā’s existence as a named settlement.

More specifically, an inscription from 597 CE (Śaka 519), dated to the reigns of Śivadeva and Aṁśuvarman, mentions agulma(military post), indicating Tokhā’s early strategic importance (D. Vajrācārya, VS 2030, pp. 266–267).
It records that on the night of 1254 CE (NS 374, Āśvina Kṛṣṇa 14), Jayadeva Pvah of Banepā seized gold from the Tokhā fort (Taleju), provoking a rebellion (Vajrācārya & Malla 1985, fol. 38A).

Another episode notes that in 1340 CE (NS 460), a local Tokhā ruler attempted a revolt with the support of Jogarāja Mūlmī and Gopālacandradeva; Bhaktapur dispatched troops who stormed the Tokhā fort, captured the rebels, and executed Gopālacandradeva within the fort itself (Vajrācārya & Malla 1985, fol. 50A).
In the Late Medieval period, Tokhā Taleju also functioned as a detention facility for prisoners (D. Maharjana, VS 2078, p. 33).
Despite its long history, no commemorative stone inscription is preserved within the Tokhā Taleju Dyaḥchẽitself.
Restoration work was carried out in 1961 CE (VS 2018) under the leadership of Bhailāl Śreṣṭha as a leader (mūlanāike) (M. Śreṣṭha, VS 2075, p. 9).
A major reconstruction was undertaken in 2018 CE (VS 2075) by the Department of Archaeology at a cost of NPR 6.75 million.

In 2022 CE (VS 2079), while excavating foundations for aphalchāslightly in front of the Taleju site, remains of an old wall were discovered, leading to the hypothesis that a former Tokhā palace once stood there.
Its management is overseen by aguthicomposed of thirteen members—twelve from the Śreṣṭha caste and one from the Jyāpu community—with the position ofmūlanāikereserved exclusively for a Śreṣṭha.
The Talejuguthiis responsible for organizing Tokhā’s festivals, religious observances, and cultural affairs, and themūlanāikeis regarded as a key community leader.
On ninth of bright fortnight of Āśvina (Mahānavamī), a buffalo sacrifice is offered to Taleju on behalf of the state.
On the tenth of bright fortnight of Āśvina (Vijayādaśamī), the priest purifies the weapons andjamarawith consecrated water before distributingṭīkā(sacred mark on forehead) andjamaraasprasāda.

A now-missing inscription once recorded on the pedestal of the lions in front of the temple was dated to 1653 CE (NS 773) (N. Śreṣṭha, VS 2065, p. 92), suggesting the structure is more than 370 years old.

The earliest inscription on the temple, dated to 1838 CE (VS 1895), indicates that the structure was built by Balabhañjana Pāṇḍe.

From this inscription, it appears that the temple was constructed at a time when the adjoining road was gradually being developed and widened, a process that later endangered both the temple and its surrounding religious monuments.
The temple’s architectural style corresponds to the modestśivālaya-type shrines commonly built during the late Śāha and early Rāṇā periods.
Constructed withdācchi appā(traditional baked bricks), the temple features doorways on all four sides of thegarbhagṛha(sanctum).
Within the sanctum stands a stoneliṅgaidentified in the inscription as Vāṇeśvara.
The upper section of the temple rises into a domed structure built ofdācchi appāand surmounted by a gilded pinnacle (gaur).
As in other Śaiva temples, an image of Kāmadeva is installed in a subsidiary shrine at the northeastern corner, while a statue of Nandī, the bull vehicle of Śiva, faces the main shrine from the west.
A large inscribed stone slab (śilāpatra) stands to the south of the temple, providing extensive details about its foundation.

The inscription records that Balabhañjana Pāṇḍe, holding the rank ofsardārat the time, not only constructed this temple in 1838 CE (VS 1895) but also added asattal(rest house),phalchā(public shelter),hiti(stone water spout), pond, surrounding wall, gates, and various sculptural embellishments.
The inscription suggests that Balabhañjana attached great importance to this location, as evidenced by the range of religious and civic structures he commissioned.
Balabhañjana was the son of Bhotu Pāṇḍe, who was himself active in the construction of religious structures and the establishment ofguthis(religious endowments) throughout the Kathmandu Valley.
Historical sources indicate that Bhotu Pāṇḍe served as a member of the Nepali delegation negotiating the peace treaty during the Chinese invasion of 1792 CE (VS 1849).
While in captivity, he is said to have vowed to worship and make offerings to the goddess Naradevī upon his release (D. Vajrācārya VS 2037, p. 371).
Upon returning from Tibet (Bhoṭ), he fulfilled this vow by adding a golden roof to the Naradevī temple and endowing it with more than 150ropanīsof land asguthiproperty.
Following his father’s example, Balabhañjana Pāṇḍe likewise established multiple religious structures in the Gokarṇa area and endowed the Vāṇeśvara temple with extensiveguthilands.

The income generated from these endowments was used to sustain daily worship (nityapūjā) and to fund ritual observances throughout the year, with the inscription listing the specific rituals, offerings, and materials required.
The same inscription records the names of Balabhañjana’s parents—his father Bhotu Pāṇḍe and mother Annapūrṇā.
Curiously, however, the sculptural relief beneath the inscription portrays Annapūrṇā alongside a male figure identified not as Bhotu but as Saṭubhañjana.
The inscription also mentions numerous metal ritual objects and ornaments donated to the temple by Balabhañjana and his descendants.

Sixty-eight years after the initial construction, the Pāṇḍe family added a new doorway to the Gokarṇeśvara temple and stipulated that future maintenance of the door be carried out using the funds of the Vāṇeśvara endowment.
Although the temple withstood the earthquake of 2015 CE, it suffered structural damage and was subsequently restored by the Department of Archaeology in 2025 CE.
Many of the ritual observances described in the inscription have since lapsed; however, the daily worship (nityapūjā) and annual commemoration (varṣavardhana) ceremonies continue to this day.

The first one was the temple which he established in his own garden, thejanarala bāg, at the south-eastern periphery of Kathmandu’s core in 1823, and which he named Bhīmabhakteśvara” Mandira (KAT0700) (Gutschow 2011, p.874).
Following that, more temples were built in the hybrid style of Bhīmabhakteśvara, including Kṛṣṇa Mandira.

Raised on (five) stepped plinths, Kṛṣṇa Mandira was, as mentioned above, probably the most ambitious and tallest Temple of the 19th century, but it collapsed in the 1934 earthquakes and is now reduced to the sanctum under a dome with no trace of the earlier building (Gutschow 2011, p.874-875).
Despite being one of the largest temples of the nineteenth century, it is unknown who built Kṛṣṇa Temple.
He writes, it “was most probably established some time in the 1830s, or by Mathbar Siṅgh, who took up residence in his uncle’s place in 1843”.
Pruscha (1975, p.30), on the other hand, assumes that it was built by Upendra Vikrama Śāha, younger brother of King Surendra (r. 1847-1881 CE).
After collapsing in the 1934 earthquakes, the Temple was rebuilt in its current form.
A brahmin from Kālamocana used to come here to perform daily rituals here, but he stopped doing so after 2017 CE (VS 2075) (based on a personal conversation with a local resident, Rāī, male, age 53).

text: The temple is believed to have been constructed around the mid-18th century, possibly before or shortly after the beginning of the Śāha period.
The temple structure has currently (as of April 2024 CE) been dismantled for reconstruction.
The donor statue was previously inside the sanctum but was moved for the reconstruction.
Aphalcā(rest house) once stood south of the pond but was never rebuilt after its collapse at some point in history and has since disappeared.
There is no inscription that records the construction of the temple.
An inscription northwest of the temple has eroded beyond readability, keeping its contents obscure.
The temple'sśivaliṅgaand the statues of Bhairava and Bhairavī appear to date back to the time before or shortly after the start of the Śāha period in 1768 CE.
The temple is currently being reconstructed with funding from the Bidur Municipality.
The temple had plots of land donated in its name.
The Tāmreśvara Mandira, constructed in 1677 CE (NS 798) by Mādheju, the elder brother of the influential courtier Cikutī, is a remarkable two-tiered temple located at Navālī Ṭola.
This event may have been coupled with the foundation of a trust, as Mādheju's descendants were responsible for the temple's worship and renovation until recent times.
Although no other historical sources detail the temple's construction, some scholars like Slusser (1982, plate 340) suggest that it might have been built in the 9th-10th century.
Due to neglect, the temple had fallen into disrepair but underwent restoration in 1990 CE (VS 2047) by the Department of Archaeology, in collaboration with the Pashupati Area Development Trust.
During this renovation, the traditional roofing tiles were replaced with copper sheets (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p.576).
The temple remained unscathed during the 2015 earthquakes.
According to G. Ṭaṇḍana (VS 2053, p.575), there was also a trust established by the Vaidyas from Devapattana responsible for these daily rituals.
The initial construction of the Bhāgeśvara Temple began in 1828 CE (NS 948) under the initiative of a person named Bhājurāma.
He also commissioned the construction of acaugharāsataḥ(rest house with rooms) encircling the Bhāgeśvara Temple on the same date.
Bhājurāma commissioned the construction of the Temple andsataḥto absolve him from the sins committed by his body, speech, and sensory organs.
The construction of the Temple with avānaliṅgaenshrined inside the sanctum was completed in 1831 CE (NS 951).

In 1834 (NS 954), he endowed many plots of land for performing the daily rituals at the Temple, observing its anniversary, performing a fire oblation along with lighting amahādīpaon the day ofŚivarātrī, caretaking thecaugharāsataḥ, and also for offeringpiṇḍa(ritual cooked rice-ball) after his death.
The endowed plots of land were, most probably, fraudulently transferred to individual(s) due course of time.
It was built in 1836 CE (NS 956) under the initiative of a couple: Dhara Bhāro and his wife Chi Thaṃku.

Following the initial construction, the donor couple also established a guṭhī to ensure that the custom of lighting butter lamps in the nearby Ālko Gaṇeśa Mandira (LAL0991) could be practiced on each 13thday of the bright fortnight of the month Bhādra.
They also established a statue of Lakṣṃīnārāyaṇa a few months after they finalised the Sataḥ, exactly on the second day of the dark fortnight of Kārtika.
Around 1987 CE (VS 2044), a kindergarten briefly occupied the Sataḥ for its purpose.
In 2002 CE (VS 2059), the Sataḥ was dismantled and constructed completely anew.
As much as it was possible, historic materials were used during the reconstruction.
Moreove, statues are built there, and displayed on the 13thday on the bright fortnight in Bhādra as the part of a cultural programme.
In 2020 CE (VS 2077), Ālko Sataḥ was used as a quarantine centre for COVID-19 patients.
Facing south, it is a two-tiered Temple with a gilt copper finial (placed during the premiership of Vīra Śamśera in 1832 CE) adorned with an umbrella (chatra).
