There are no historical sources to date the initial construction of the Temple.
King Ānandadeva expanded Bhaktapur into a large city under the protection of theaṣṭamātṛkādeities (Eight Mother Goddesses) in Kaligat Samvat 4197 i.e., 1096 CE (cfDevamālāvaṃśāvalī2013, p. 104).

At the centre of the city founded in the shape of ayantra, a deity named Tripurasundarī was also enshrined at the centre of a designated triangular area marked by three Gaṇeśa shrines called Mulākhu Gaṇeśa, Calākhu Gaṇeśa, and Bālākhu Gaṇeśa (cp.L. Munaṃkarmī2045, p. 26).
However, no archaeological or epigraphic artefact at the Temple proves that it dates back to 1096 CE.
The inscription dated VS 1949 (1892 CE) is the earliest record available at the Temple recording the offering of a gilded finial.
The Temple was reconstructed in 2005 CE (Gutschow2011, p. 367).
Pāhā̃ Bāhāḥ, a branch of Si Bāhāḥ (LAL0690), was founded in 1660 by Knaka, Bhisiṃ and Śākemuni.
The newly built four-storey mainbāhāḥbuilding retains a carved door to the sanctum, the only remaining element from the original structure.
Popularly known as Naḥghaḥ Bāhāḥ for being located at the Naḥghaḥṭola, the earliest historical record from thebāhāḥis a strut inscription of 1630 CE (NS 751).
The place name ‘Naḥghaḥ’ (lit. nine pots) is a reference to the establishment of nine ritual pots (kalaśa) in the area.
The main building of thebāhāḥfacing north has three floors.
Copper sheets are laid on the roof with a gildedkalaśainstalled as its finial.
A window with three openings (gāḥjhyāḥ) is installed on the second floor that houses the esoteric room (āgaṃ) of thebāhāḥ.
A metaltoraṇafrom 1934 CE (NS 1054) is placed on top of the entrance to the sanctum.
Twocaityas as established in the courtyard.
It is unclear when thebāhāḥwas first constructed.
According to a legend, the members of thebāhāḥoriginally came from Simraungaḍha after the southeastern kingdom was destroyed in 1324 CE.
After the Pṛthvī Nārāyaṇa Śāha invasion, they came to the Naḥghaḥ Ṭola and settled here by constructing a monastic building (Locke 1985, p.342).
However, inscriptions at thebāhāḥfrom the pre-invasion period prove the legend to be untrue.
The earliest historical record is a strut inscription from 1630 CE (NS 751) that deals with the offering of the strut by a person named Jayapāla (text: Jayapāra).
Another record is from 1785 CE (NS 805), which relates to the laying of floor tiles (cikaṃaḥpā) at thebāhāḥpremises by Rāmadeva and Dharmarāja of the Naḥghaḥ Bāhāḥ.
The monastic building was reconstructed with thebāhāḥ’s funds and financial assistance received from the Kathmandu Metropolitan City Office.
Constructed southeast of Pīgaṃdyaḥ (KIR0007), the rest house is referred to as Pīgaṃ Phalcā 3 for this documentation since it does not have any specific name.
No inscription records the initial construction of the Phalcā.
It was probably built around the same time Pīgaṃdyaḥ was established in 1670 CE (NS 790).
As the Phalcā in traditional architecture was on the verge of collapse, it was rebuilt into a concrete structure in 1997 CE (VS 2054) (local resident, Maharjana, male, age 54).
Constructed by an ancestor of Arjunanarasiṃha Rāṇā, the exact year of establishment for this Viṣṇu temple remains uncertain.

Despite the absence of inscriptions at the site obscuring the donor's identity and the year of construction, a later marble inscription at the temple attributes its construction to one of Arjunanarasiṃha Rāṇā's ancestors.
Badrīnarasiṃha’s descendants continued this naming tradition, suggesting the possibility of Badrinarasiṃha or one of his descendants being the temple's builder during the Rāṇā period.
The original Bhairava-viṣṇu statue was stolen in 1998 CE (VS 2055) (priest of Nau Śivālaya, Ḍhuṅgela, male, age 55), and a new statue was subsequently installed in the sanctum.
Following the earthquakes in 2015, the temple walls sustained cracks and are currently in a dilapidated state.
G. Ṭaṇḍana (VS 2053, p. 769-770) and Michaels and Tandon (2017, p. 106) have inaccurately identified the temple as Rāmabhakteśvara.
Māhilā Dulahī is credited with the construction of this Śiva temple in 1869 CE (VS 1926).
Located on the eastern bank of the Bagmati river, opposite the cremation grounds, this temple, constructed from stone, showcases a bell-shaped roof adorned with a metallic finial.
The statue of Viṣṇu in the northeastern niche has regrettably been stolen.
Additionally, a Bhairava mask is embedded in the southern outer wall, and a statue of Nandī, Śiva's animal mount, is established in front of the western entrance.
The temple was built by Māhilā Dulahī in 1869 CE (VS 1926) (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p. 344; Michaels and Tandon 2017, p. 62).

A stonepañcamukha śivaliṅgais enshrined at the sanctum, which can be accessed from all four sides but withou any steps constructed in front of the four entrances.
Most of the temples at the Bhaktapur Durbar Square lack inscriptions that shed light on their initial construction.
This temple, too, lacks inscriptive evidence regarding its first construction.
The art and materials used for the pillars and theśivaliṅgasuggest that the temple was probably constructed at the end of the Malla period.
The 2015 earthquake dismantled the upper portion of the temple and the temple stood with supports till 2018 CE.
Bhaktapur Municipality completed the reconstruction of the temple in 2019 CE.
Noguthirelated to this temple exists at present.
Thisśivālaya, which dates back to the year 1864 CE (VS 1921), was erected in honor of Antarī Mahārānī Hemakumārī.
The main western entrance bears an inscription beneath itstoraṇa, providing information about the temple's construction.
Statues of Viṣṇu in the northeast, Durgā in the northwest, and Sūrya in the southeast were also installed, following the Śiva Pāñcāyana concept in deity arrangement.
Unfortunately, these three statues have been stolen, and the niches now remain empty as of September 2023.
A statue of Kāmadeva, the embodiment of love in Eastern mythology, which was placed on the retaining wall east of the temple, has also been stolen.
Thisśivālayawas erected in honor of Antarī Mahārāṇī Hemakumārī, who was one of the formal wives of Rāṇā Prime Minister Jaṅga Bahādura.
She passed away in the year 1961 CE (VS 1918) (P. Rāṇā VS 2059, p. 191) after giving birth to her daughter Rudrakumārīdevī.
However, a list of Jaṅga Bahādura's wives compiled by an individual named Bhoṭu Dvāre mentions Hemakumārī's daughter as Gaurī Maiñā (K. Dīkṣita VS 2034, p. 76).

Notably, Rudrakumārīdevī's son is Jayapṛthvībahādura Siṃha, the king of Bajhāṅa (P. Rāja VS 2071, p. 77), who is renowned for his contributions to the Nepali language, literature, and education sector.

Ten years after the construction of Hemamukteśvara, Jaṅga Bahādura erected another temple named Jaṅge-Hiraṇya-Hema Nārāyaṇa Mandira (KAT2800) at the Kālamocana cremation ground in his name and that of his two wives, Hiraṇyagarbhakumārī and Hemakumārī.
Since this temple was constructed in honor of Rāṇā Prime Minister Jaṅga Bahādura's wife, it likely received substantial donations for various rituals.
Bālakumārī is the main goddess of Sunaguthi.
In 2010 it was reconstructed which saw the roof replaced with copper sheets and the removal of the veranda.

An inscription at the Temple, however, mentions that two brothers from Asan, Rāmaprasāda Śreṣṭha and Lālabahādura Śreṣṭha replaced the upper roof with gilt copper and installed a gilt finial in 1927 CE (VS 1984).
The same year, they covered the wooden door and door leaves with brass sheet, secured the Temple with metal bars and installed a bell on each side of the main door to the sanctum.
A year later, in 1928 CE (VS 1985), they offered an artistictoraṇawith statues of Ṛddhi and Siddhi, Lord Gaṇeśa’s consorts, on its pillars.

They also provided a silver canopy (ilāṃ) on top of the Gaṇeśa statue and installed their on statues in the gesture of reverence (namaskāra), demonstrating their eternal devotion to the deity at the Temple.

According to chronicles, Vanavināyaka was founded by Licchavi King Śivadeva Varmā.
The statue is covered in a mixture of oil and vermillion powder, giving it the local name "Hyāũ Gaṇeśa," meaning "Red Gaṇeśa" (S. Mānandhara VS 2048, p. 35).
No inscriptions at the site indicate when the temple was first constructed.
Chronicles mention that Licchavi King Śivadeva Varmā placed a three-eyed statue of Vanavināyaka after consecrating Vanakālī (PPK2101) (N. Pauḍela VS 2020, p. 82;Nepālikabhūpavaṃśāvalī2016, 12.133).

Although the chronicles date the statue back to the Licchavi period, the current statue appears to be from a much later period, with some suggesting the 15th or 16th century origin (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p. 407; M. Thāpā VS 2077, p. 225), while others believe it is from the 17th century (S. Mānandhara VS 2048, p. 35).

In 2009 CE (VS 2065), the Paśupati Sevā Samāja renovated the temple.
They first come to worship Vanavināyaka before any major worship or rites of passage at home (S. Mānandhara VS 2048, p. 35).
Every year on the 14th of the dark fortnight of Caitra, the Vajreśvarī Guthi offermaraḥjā, a special meal of rice and various dishes, to children behind the temple (S. Mānandhara VS 2048, p. 36).

The name "Vaidya Phalcā" is derived from the Vaidya families who, as per a conversation with the president of Jayavāgīśvarī Ṭola Sudhāra Samiti, Vaidya (male, age 48), were instrumental in its construction, even though there is no specific record documenting it.
Additionally, it is believed that the connected Nāpita Phalcā was built by the Nāpita community.
The office of the Jayavāgīśvarī Ṭola Sudhāra Samiti has been housed in thisphalcāsince 2006 CE.
Around 1992 CE (VS 2049), the Paśupati Development Trust undertook the reconstruction of thephalcā.
Originally open to the public, the space became a haven for garbage and anti-social activities, prompting the initiative to establish the Ṭola Sudhāra Samiti office here.
According to the president of the Samiti, as of July 2023 CE, apart from the activities of the Ṭola Sudhāra Samiti, there are no ongoing socio, religious, or cultural activities in thephalcā.
Originally built by the sister-in-law of national hero Balabhadra Kũvara, this rest house (sataḥ) now (March 2025) features his full-sized statue within its premises.
Located at the Pañcanārī Ghāṭa by the Bagmati river, the Sataḥ has been transformed into a modern three-storey building.
A 1982 inventory photo from the 1970s already documents the Sataḥin poor shape, with a massive brick pillar supporting the façade (Inventory VS 2039, p. 164).
Within the complex are two similarly sized Śiva temples, Dīrghabhakteśvara and Hemamukteśvara, built in 1854 CE (VS 1910) by Dīrghalakṣmī Kũvara, second wife of Balabhadra's brother Vīrabhadra.
She endowed them with over 360ropanīs of land and documented the religious trust’s income and responsibilities in an 1881 inscription.
An inscription installed after the construction highlights her noble birth.
While the Sataḥis not mentioned in the temple's inscription, it likely co-existed due to the tradition of integrating shelters with riverside temples.
Around the late 1980s, the Sataḥ was demolished and rebuilt in concrete.

The original structure hadphalcāson both sides, but the new building only has an integratedphalcāof five bays with unevenly placed columns bearing erotic carvings on its capitals, likely remnants of the original Sataḥ.
One of the earliest examples of this style is the Virāṭeśvara Mahādeva (PPK0730) in Paśupati (S. Parājulī, VS 2080, p. 213).
Although there is a stone inscription at the site, it is completely eroded and no information can be obtained from it.
D. Vajrācārya and Ṭ. Śreṣṭha (VS 2032, p. 114) also refer to Śiva shrines in this region in the context of theSvasthānī, but do not provide specific names.
The fragmentedśivaliṅgahas been restored as much as possible, with its parts joined together.
These artifacts were preserved, and a concrete plinth was constructed, followed by the installation of a zinc roof around 1990 CE (VS 2047) (local resident Śreṣṭha, male, age 81).
On Śivarātrī, locals gather here to light a bonfire.
Apart from special worships performed during Bālā Caturdaśī and other festivals, there are currently (as of June 2024 CE) no other regular socio-religious activities held at this site.

Although the locals claim the temple to be constructed during the Malla period, there is no inscription that records its initial construction.
The temple lost its original three-tiered structure after it collapsed in 1939 CE (VS 1996).
It was never rebuilt (local resident, Rañjita, male, age 66).
Metal railings were installed for the security of the statue but were removed later in 2021 CE.
King Pārthivendra Malla had commissioned the installation of the Trailokyamohana statue at Trailokyamohana Temple at Hanumānaḍhokā in 1681 CE (NS 801).
Bamabahādura Kũvara, a brother of Jaṅgabahādura, constructed a temple in a unique architectural style on the banks of the Bāgamatī known as Tīnadevala (KAT2670).
Atāmrapatra(copper plate) discovered at the site records the simultaneous construction of the Jagannātha temple (KAT2690).
The construction of a boundary wall around Tīnadevala, Jagannātha Mandira, and the garden was also mentioned in thetāmrapatra, indicating the simultaneous construction of this gate.
Located within the Pacalī Bhairava premises, the gate was built to provide convenient access for devotees, musicians, and processions to Tīnadevala.
Facing the Bāgadarbāra erected by Bhimasena Thāpā, two temples in the Rājapūta style grace the surroundings.
Following its 19th-century construction, many temples adopted a similar unique architectural style, characterized by a fusion of European, Mughal, Rājapūta, and Nevāra architectural influences.
It underwent renovation, along with Tīnadevala, and an inscription providing details about the constructor and construction date was added post-reconstruction.
Additionally, three pinnacles were installed above the gate.
The renovation efforts were led by the Bāgamatī Civilization Integrated Development Committee under the Ministry of Urban Development, supported by the Asian Development Bank.
The renovation reached completion on October 23rd, 2022 CE.
The inscriptions recording the temple’s construction documents King Yoganarendra Malla of Patan visiting Lubhu for the inspection of the temple and other monuments.
Situated at the Macāgāḥ Ṭola in Lubhu, this temple dedicated to Sarasvatī, the goddess of wisdom, is entirely built with stone with a bell-shaped roof.
In 1699 CE (NS 819), Pātravaṃśa Hariśaṃkara, along with his mother Rukmanilakṣmī and wife Devīśvarīlakṣmī, from the Tavajhyāra Ṭola, constructed the temple.
The inscription, embedded in the northern wall of the temple, further reveals that the donors invited King Yoganarendra Malla of Patan to inspect the temple and other nearby structures.
It also documents the installation of statues of other deities, including Bhairava and Halāhala Lokeśvara, as well as the construction of two stone platforms providing shade in the vicinity.

The inscription acknowledges the contributions of astrologer Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa, and other individuals such as Guruvācārya Govinda and Sūryarāma, in the successful completion of these constructions.Śrīpañcamī, the 5th of the bright fortnight of Māgha, is believed to be the day when Sarasvatī, the goddess of learning, descends to Earth.
Three out of the four Buddha statues were stolen from thiscaityawithin an interval of two weeks, leaving only the statue of Amoghasiddhi currently intact.
Due to the theft of three of these statues, only the statue of Amoghasiddhi in the northern niche currently (September 2024) survive.
The other three niches are empty after the statues in them were stolen.
Thecaityawas built by Saṃkrabābu Bhāro, a resident of the Bhansāra Ṭola, in 1705 CE (NS 825) during the reign of King Yoganarendra Malla.
He also donated land to set up a trust for carrying out worships at thecaitya.
The stone statue of Ratnasambhava, housed in the southern niche, was stolen on March 1, 2023.
Eleven days later, on March 12, the statues of Akṣobhya and Amitābha were also stolen.
After three sculptures were stolen in a short interval, the remaining sculpture of Amoghasiddhi was secured by installing an iron railing.
Following the theft, police have been stationed regularly at the nearby Bhansāra Phalcā (CHG0060).
The reason as to why this monastic building was named Bhinchẽ Bāhāḥ is disputed, with three main arguments each vying for authority.
The esoteric house of the monastery stands alone, and is not attached to any other building.
This argument is supported by an inscription dated NS 789 in Pinchẽ Bāhāḥ which refers to this Bāhāḥ as Bhinnachẽ.
Proponents of the second argument point out that an image of Viṣṇu image was found whilst digging for the foundations for esoteric shrine of the monastic building was underway.
The main entry of Bhinchẽ Bāhāḥ is to the west and is emphasised by a projectedphalcāattached to a residential building.
An entry door on the wall of the residential building leads to the courtyard.
A tall, three-tier building can be seen when one stands on the central axis of the entrance and the eastern side.
The building is built in such a way that it can be circumambulated.
The rectangular plan of the building has two bays.
The rear bay has a colonnaded structure of three bays built with twin pillars.
A staircase at the northeastern corner of the building leads the visitor upstairs.
A unique feature of this building is its four corner stone pillars on the exterior masonry wall.
The front wall of the ground floor is built in grey stone, whilst the southern wall contains images of Vasundharā, Nāmasaṅgīti and Mahākāla.
A goldencaitya-shaped pinnacle tops the monastic building and a goldentoraṇahas been fixed above a carved window on the second floor showing Vajrasattva sitting at its centre.
A window with a row of five small openings (pāsukājhyāḥ)can be seen on the building's main façade.
A set of copper plate inscriptions, stone inscriptions and metal flags can be found on either side of the door.
The four corners of the esoteric building house images of a leopard (southeast), an elephant (southwest), an immortal man (northwest) and a lion (northeast).
No historical evidence could be found to confirm when exactly this monastic building was constructed.
According to the chronicleNepālikabhūpavaṃśāvalī(12.115), Jayaśrī built this monastery during the reign of King Śaṅkaradeva (son of Vṛṣadeva).
Later, he decided to build a monastic building.
Whilst he was preparing to build thevihāra, he and other Bhikṣus were struggling to work out where it should be constructed when they suddenly saw a peacock land.
They then established an image of Lord Śākyasiṃha at that place.
This legend suggests that this monastic building was established in the Licchavi period.

The earliest mention of this monastic building can be found in a palm-leaf manuscript dated NS 550 (CE 1430) which was found in Hiraṇyavarṇa Mahāvihāra (Śākya1973, 16).Śākya(1980, 13) has surmised that the Busĩchẽ Vihāra mentioned in one of the palm-leaf manuscript dated NS 261 (CE 1141) might be the modern Bhinchẽ Bāhāḥ.
Originally, a woodentoraṇaadorned the sanctum entrance, but during a recent renovation, the oldtoraṇawas preserved on the upper floor and replaced with a new metal one.
Some of the roof struts appear original, though several were stolen in the 1980s and 2010s.
No written records confirm the temple’s exact origins, but its surviving windows, doors, and struts attest to its late Malla-period construction.
It was restored in 1986 CE (VS 2043) and last rebuilt in 2014 CE (VS 2070).

Fortunately, the inscription recording the construction of the temple is still safe and intact.
According to the inscription, Lokeśvara Mandira was constructed in 1684 CE (NS 804) by Guṇajyoti and his family members.
However,Ś. Śreṣṭha(VS 2057, 124) mistakenly reads the date as NS 807 (1687 CE).

Since Śrīnivāsa Malla is mentioned as the reigning king in the inscription, the reading ofŚ. Śreṣṭhais not convincing. Śrīnivāsa handed over the throne to his son in NS 805, i.e. 1685 CE  (D. R. Regmi, 1966, part 3, 24).
It is then clear that the date mentioned in the inscription must be NS 804.
Vajrācārya(VS 2056, 531-532) read the date of the inscription correctly, however, he erroneously mentions that this inscription records the establishment of a Nārāyaṇa Mandira.
Hākuju and Jamunā, parents of Guṇajyoti, are mentioned at the end of the inscription.
It further records that statues of Lokeśvara and Tārā are consecrated in their memory.
Hākuju is the person who constructed the Cvay Bāhāḥ (KIR0011) and Buddha Mandira (KIR0010).
The municipality removed the medieval stones from Lokeśvara Mandira’s plinth and used bricks to renovate it.

Considering that such ritual practices were prevalent in the 17th and 18th centuries, the Cvaylāchi Nāsaḥ Phalcā might have been built durng that time.
In the early 1990s, Cvaylāchi Nāsaḥ Phalcā was demolished and replaced with a concrete structure featuring a sloped, tiled roof.
However, in 2024 CE (VS 2081), Godawari Municipality undertook a restoration project, rebuilding the arcaded platform in what is often referred to as"traditional style".
The original form of thissataḥis documented in an inventory published in 1982 CE (VS 2039) by the Kathmandu Valley Urban Development Plan.
The inventory also notes that the roof was leaking and that the walls were in urgent need of repair, further stating that the building was in residential use at the time.
The upper floor eventually collapsed during the 2015 earthquake, after which a single-storey concrete structure was constructed, incorporating the two remaining original columns.
A family bearing the Nagarkoti surname, who had been residing in the structure for decades, undertook the reconstruction of a single-storey rectangular room at their own expense.
According to local residents—many of whom have lived in the area for generations—both thesataḥand theŚivālayawere likely constructed by the same individual.
As of March 2025 CE, both structures remain within the same compound and continue to be maintained by the resident family, who also perform daily worship.

No inscription identifying the original builder has been found; however, the 1982 inventory records that thesataḥwas constructed in 1816–17 CE (VS 1873) by an individual named Jayadutha (Inventory VS 2039, p. 165).

Given the historical context in which suchsataḥs andŚivālayaswere often established by high-ranking nobles or court officials during the Śāh and early Rāṇā periods—particularly along the banks of the Bagmati River—it is plausible that this structure too was erected by a member of the courtly elite.
It was built by King Jayavishnu Malla and Queen Chandra Lakshmidevi and used for special proclamations by the Malla Kings.
Similar large bells also constructed during the Malla period can be found at Basantapur Darbar Square (Kathmandu) and the Bhaktapur Darbar Square.
This bell hangs on a stone beam supported by two stone pillars that are erected on top of a platform.
To reach the platform, one must enter the inside of the plateau through a narrow door to the east of the building and climb up a ladder with 9 rungs.
The body of the bell holds an inscription informing readers that it was commissioned by King Viṣṇu Malla (1729-1745) and Queen Candralakṣmī Devī.
This inscription does not provide us any information about the intentions behind its construction.
However, a Nepalese chronicle (seeBajracharya and Michaels 2016, 129) states that the King installed this bell to scare his enemies.

Two inscriptions mention "the queen of Gorakhpur" without revealing her name.
It is unusual that in such a significant religious inscription, the donor's name is not mentioned, but only a formal title given.
Jaṅga Bahādura's queen from Gorakhpur also donated land to fund daily and cyclical rituals at the temple, along with the maintenance and timely renovations of the temple and the Sataḥ.

The new building employs a concrete frame construction carried out with little attention to detail but preserves a number of historic windows, a few wooden pillars and is clad with traditionaldaci apabrick.
The original central seven-bayed arcade facing the Bagmati was lost and replaced with poorly executed wooden grill partitions.
The western wing was also rebuilt in 1990 CE as a modern brick and concrete structure and only retains a few historic pillars from the original Sataḥ.
The reconstruction was funded by a Japanese organization and houses printing house of the Nepal Association for the Welfare of the Blind (NAWB).

The style of the Hiti’s Makara motifs belongs to the late medieval period, and differ from the motifs of the Licchavi Period, signalling that they were reconstructed in a later period (S. ParājulīVS 2068, 157).
Another inscription dating 1958 CE (VS 2015) records that King Mahendra renovated the Hiticomplex including its boundary walls.

Commonly known as the 'Pratāpa Malla pillar,' its inscription (as detailed below) refers to it as the 'Pratāpadhvaja' – the Banner of Pratāpa.

This pillar was erected by King Pratāpa Malla in 1670 CE (see ‘historical event’ below), a monarch who demonstrated a proclivity for novelty, evident in his endeavours such as entering the Śāntipura, issuing coins with Arabic/Persian script, featuring an inscription in 15 different scripts, aspiring for the title of Kavīndra (the Lord of Poets), performing a dance as Narasiṃha, constructing the 'Rānīpokharī' pond, and expressing desires of intimate encounters with a significant number of women.
In 1663 CE (NS 784), Pratāpa erected a statue depicting his sons Cakravartendra and Nṛpendra, placed in front of the Teleju temple at Triśūla Coka.
It's noteworthy that G. Vajrācārya (VS 2033, p.70) previously mentioned the presence of a child prince statue between the two queens, though as of August 2023 CE, no such statue is visible.
The inscription on the pillar (1670 CE, NS 790) lists the names of the princes as Cakravartendra, Mahīpatendra, Nṛpendra, and Pārthivendra.
The inscription detailing the pillar's erection reveals Pratāpa Malla's offerings to his tutelary deity Taleju Māju, which included six golden pinnacles and a golden umbrella adorned with amālā.

The inscription further records a land endowment of 4ropanīknown as Dharmasthalī, along with a directive for the pillar's maintenance by anointing it with 3pāthīof oil from the income generated by the endowed land.
Built in the 18th century, this temple was originally assigned to Rājopādhyāya Brahmins as its priests, but no rituals are currently being performed here.
Located in Balima Ṭola of Lalitpur, the east-facing temple is built on a two-tiered stone plinth.
The temple, entirely built with stone, has a bell-shaped roof topped with a stone finial.
A badly eroded stone inscription is affixed to the southern side.
The precise origins of this temple remain unclear, including its founder and date of establishment.
A stone inscription on the temple's southern entrance might have provided clues about its construction, but the inscription has been completely effaced, rendering it indecipherable.
Following the theft of the Nārāyaṇa statue in 2009 CE (VS 2066), a new statue was installed through community fundraising efforts spearheaded by the Misā Pucaḥ, a group of local women from Balima.

Thehiti in front of the famous Ugracaṇḍī temple in Nālā is particularly notable due to inscription evidence indicating that it was constructed during the Licchavi period, with water flowing from it for over a thousand years.
Statues of the Sun, Umāmaheśvara, and Bhagavatī are installed above each spout, inside the Śikhara structure.
Additionally, ajaḥdhuṃis established and connected to the west wall of thehiti, allowing it to be filled naturally by the water flow.

Thehitiwas constructed by Dhruvaśīla and Anaṅgaśīla, residents of Nālāṅga (Nālā), during the reign of Licchavi King Śivadeva I. An inscription from 694 CE (Mānadeva Samvat 118) on a plinth above the stone spout provides evidence of its construction.

Another inscription from 1397 CE (NS 517) records the installation of a sun statue; however, the sun statue is no longer present, and instead, a moon statue has been placed in a niche near the inscription.
The moon statue was stolen during the lockdown in 2020 CE, and a new one was installed in its place (local resident, Śreṣṭha male, age 83).

The earliest documented record pertaining to the temple is an inscription from 1827 CE (NS 947), which chronicles the expansion of the temple during the reign of King Rājendra Vikrama Śāha.
The residents of Navālī Ṭola, including Lachinārā, Āsānārā, and Dhamanārā, dismantled the previous smaller temple of Gaṇeśa and constructed a larger one.
Details regarding the size and structure of the original temple are not specified in the inscription.
The temple was expanded in 1827 CE (NS 947) and in 2000 CE (VS 2057), the Pashupati Area Development Trust undertook renovation efforts for the temple.

No inscription details its original construction date or donor.
In 1907 CE (NS 1027), Baktabārasĩ Guruvācāryya, associated with the palace of Candra Śamśera, renovated thephalcā.
During a period of neglect, statues of Bhīmasena and Sarasvatī were stolen, leaving the niches vacant.
In 2007 CE (VS 2064), thephalcāwas reconstructed with new statues.
As of 2021 CE, no socio-cultural events occur at thephalcā.

Instead, it represents a smaller type of monastic shrine that emerged during the Rāṇā period, when wealthy patrons sometimes established private devotional shrines within the grounds of their residences.

During the Rāṇā period it became customary for affluent householders to install an image of Akṣobhya asKvāḥpā Dyaḥwithin a small shrine resembling adevala, often constructed in the garden or backyard of their residence and functioning as a privatekacābāhāḥ.
The present Gaṃcā Bāhāḥ was also established in this manner during the Rāṇā period.
The principal shrine consists of a bell-shapeddevalaconstructed in the style commonly used for small Śiva temples of that period.
This structure functions as the equivalent of adyaḥchẽand houses an image of Akṣobhya installed asKvāḥpā Dyaḥ.
The image bears striking similarities to the image installed in the nearby Gaṃcānani Bāhāḥ.
Above the doorway of the shrine housing theKvāḥpā Dyaḥthere is a woodentoraṇabearing the inscription “Śrī Ratnapura Mahāvihāra 1981 (VS)” corresponding to 1924–25.
Although the inscription itself does not clearly express the full context of the construction, descendants of the founder preserve oral traditions regarding the establishment of the shrine.

According to them, their ancestor Ratnākara, who had accumulated considerable wealth through the trade of gold during the Rāṇā period, constructed thisbāhāḥbehind his residence and named it after himself (one of the descendants, Śākya, male, age 67; one of the descendants, Śākya, male, age 71).

As of August 2022, items required for rescue operations during natural disasters are stored at the Phalcā from 2012 CE (VS 2069).
Metal bars were installed on the Phalcā in 2016 CE for the security of the items.
Aguthiof the Maharjanas from the Gaḥchẽ Ṭola, Kirtipur offers light on a hanging lampstand (khādalū) here at Dyaḥdhvākhā Phalcā every year during the Indrāyaṇī Jātrā.
A small shrine is built in the south-western corner of the Ghavāḥ Nani.
A Pañcāvalīyukta Caitya, Gaṇeśa, and Mahākāla statue are installed in the Bāhāḥ premises.
Pānda Bāhāḥ was built in NS 997 (1877 CE) by Kiṣṇa (text: Kṛṣṇa) Maharjana and his wife Tuyu (Lakṣmīdevī) living in Lukhusi Ṭola.
They also established the Pañcāvalīyukta Caitya in the Bāhāḥ premises and formed aguṭhīto worship it in NS 1000 (1880 CE).
Originally built by a certain Motirāja in 1674 CE (NS 794) during the reign on King Jitāmitra Malla, this two-floored arcaded platform was reconstructed by the French government in the 1990s CE.
The Phalcā is actually built into asataḥ, that is, an arcaded platform with two floors.
The ground floor has been left open to be used to store the wooden materials used for constructing the Bhadrakālī chariot.
On the northern wall of the ground floor stands a statue of Bhavāniśaṅkara and a stone inscription dating back to 1674 CE (NS 794).
An inscription indicates that Motirāja built this rest house and consecrated a statue of Bhavāniśaṅkara in 1674 CE (NS 794) during the reign of King Jitāmitra Malla.

Intriguingly, a second inscription, dating back to 1428 CE (NS 548) and found on the rest house's first floor, predates the building by over two centuries, mentioning the installation of a wooden pillar.
This suggests a prior structure on the site that likely collapsed over time.
Motirāja may have incorporated remnants of this earlier building into the new construction.
Before the 1934 earthquakes, the rest house also served as a school (S. Lākoju VS 2071, p. 126).
The French government undertook the restoration of Panauti's heritage sites between 1991 and 1998 CE, which included the reconstruction of this rest house as well due to its deteriorating condition.

The Tāhā Phalcā is deeply intertwined with the sociocultural fabric of the Navadurgā mask dance of Bhaktapur, as it was originally constructed as a lodging for the Navadurgā dance troupe during their visits to Panauti.
After the French government reconstructed the Tāhā Phalcā, the first floor has been used as a restaurant.

The Mahāviṣṇu Mandira, a prominent temple in the Hanumānḍhokā area and a rare example in the Kathmandu valley restored to its pre-1934 CE configuration using historical photographs, stands on three tiers of plinths.

This gilded statue, known as Mahāviṣṇu, embodies the visages of his diverse incarnations, including Trailokyamohana, Pañcamukhī-Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa, and Vaikuṇṭha-Viṣṇu (Pruscha 1975, p.54, S. Mainālī VS 187, G. Vajrācārya VS 2033, 78).

Historical photographs indicate that the temple originally possessed three tiers before collapsing during the 1934 CE earthquakes.
Although it was later reconstructed as a two-storied edifice, the gilded statue was relocated to Nāsaḥ Cuka, where it remains as of January 2023 CE.

The initiative to restore the temple to its original design, launched around 2003 CE, was realized through collaboration between the Department of Archaeology and the Kathmandu Valley Preservation Trust.
During this renovation, plain struts were integrated into the temple's structure.

While considerations were made to reintegrate the gilded statue of Mahāviṣṇu from Nāsaḥ Cuka into the temple's sanctum, a decision was ultimately reached to establish a new statue (temple priest, Bhaṭṭa, male, age 54).

Although no historical sources exist to date the initial construction of the Bāhāḥ, the presence of four Licchavi Caityas here suggests that the area was already a Buddhist site during the Licchavi period.

It is octagonal shaped and was constructed by Jitamitra Malla in 1693 CE.
He constructed another one right behind the Siddhilakṣmī Mandira in the same year (Gutschow2014, 33).
His son Bhūpatindra Malla constructed the third one, which is located in the centre of the square, in 1699 CE.
The temple is entirely constructed in stone, except for the pinnacle.
Statues of Mahālakṣmī in the aspect of Mahiṣāsuramardinī (east), Vārāhī (west), Indrāyaṇī (north), and Vaiṣṇavī (south) are established in each of these pavilions.
Statues of aṣṭamātṛkā are established on turrets and installed in all eight directions of the octagonal shaped temple.
Instead of a statue, a stonekalaśaas the representation of the Tantric deity is consecrated inside the sanctum.
The local community also believes that the deity was offered human sacrifice as part of Tantric rites (Gutschow2014, 33).
Devamālāvaṃśāvalī mentions such a rite while consecrating the deity and establishing the shrine in Pashupati (cited fromM. ThāpāVS 2077, 183).
There is a lack of inscriptive evidence to point to its initial construction.
The only inscription found in the temple premises is the one in the bell.
It mentions Bhūpatindra Malla replacing the older bell with a new one.
The older one was offered in 1699 CE (NS 820) and was replaced in 1721 CE (NS 841).
Based on this,Nepālikabhūpavaṃśāvalīmentions that the temple was constructed in 1699 CE (NS 820) and the bell was offered to the temple after the fire sacrifice (Nepālikabhūpavaṃśāvalī19.1-73).
Based on the same,Gutschow(2014, 33) concludes that the temple was built around 1690’s CE.
He has erroneously dated the construction to 1700 CE, instead of 1699 CE.
The anniversary rituals of the temple take place on the same date that the first bell was offered to it.
It adds weight to the assertion that the temple was indeed constructed on that date.
However, it is unusual that a temple of this significance to not have any inscriptions detailing its construction date, priests, and suchlike.
Given that Bhūpatindra Malla had inscriptions installed in other monuments in the square and not this one raises lots of questions.
The upper part of the temple crumbled down in the 1934 CE (VS 1990) earthquake.
The temple might have undergone renovations at other times as well, but the lack of inscriptive evidence makes it difficult to find out about those past activities.
In 1974 CE, the Department of Archaeology with the support of UNESCO and technical support from John Sanday and Wolfgang Korn, renovated the upper part and uprooted a tree growing there.
This renovation activity is captured in a photo taken by Rich Pfau in 1975 CE (psroundsimaging.com/Rich Pfau).
The temple’s structure, except its plinth, crumbled down in the 2015 CE earthquake.
The Municipality formed a users’ committee to oversee the reconstruction work in 2016 CE (VS 2073), and released Rs 1, 28, 62,213 (Bhaktapur Municipality).
The work was completed in 2020 CE (VS 2077).
TheGuṭhī Saṃsthāna(2071,48) records sixropanīof endowed land belonging to the temple.

text: Kanike Devala 2 is the smaller of twośikharatemples built between the 13th and 15th centuries in a hamlet 500 meters south-east of Vināyaka.

In 2014 the pillar was installed on the floor in front of a house.
Stone pillars were erected throughout the Karnali Basin from the 13th to the 17th century.
They are installed to honor the memory of deceased persons, mostly warriors (Andolfatto 2019: 105-119).
The latter one being dated of 1357 CE, it is thus possible to situate the Kolikholā pillar around the same time.
No documented evidence could be uncovered with which to date the initial construction of thisbahī.
An inscription dated NS 643 (1523 CE) at the bottom of Mahākāla statue serves as the oldest record.
The monastic building was reconstructed many times, the last time in 1992.
There are no historical sources to date the initial construction of thephalcā, however, the wood carvings can be dated to the mid/late 17th century.
A residential compound with buildings from different time periods.
Facing east, the Phalcā is a two-storied building kept in traditional architecture.
There is no inscription that records its construction.
Anotherphalcāin the area, Indrāyaṇī Pīṭha Phalcā 1 (BKT4002), was built in 1888 CE (NS 1008).
Probably, this one was also built around the same time.

Launched in the beginning of 1974 CE with the joint funding of the Nepal and German governments, the Bhaktapur Development Project renovated or rebuilt many historic monuments of Bhaktapur including the monuments at the Indrāyaṇī Pīṭha premises.
In this context, the Phalcā was also reconstructed.
The office and the classroom were shifted to its own building in 2017 CE (former project coordinator, Prajāpati, male, age 65).
In the third floor of this building, one can find a balconied set of three windows, flanked by windows on either side.
The date of the establishment of this monastery is unknown.
However, an inscription dating NS 656 (1536 CE) on a begging bowl kept in the Hiraṇyavarṇa Mahāvihāra makes reference to a 'Aṭakī Bāhāra', which might be the same as the presentbāhāḥ.
An inscription installed at the right side of the entrance shows that in 1803 CE (NS 923) a Shrestha family reconstructed the monastery and established aguthi.

Situated to the west of Ipātvāḥ Gaṇeśa Mandira (SH0270) at Ipā Ṭola in Sankhu, the two-storey high and five-bay wide Ipātvāḥ Gaṇeśa Phalcā existed as a concrete structure before its recent reconstruction (2021-2).
Since no inscription records the initial construction of the Phalcā, it is unclear when it was first built.
The previous Phalcā collapsed in the 2015 earthquakes and was reconstructed in neo-traditional style.

A room beneath the Phalcā is currently being used for storing sports and construction materials, this kind of "cellar" is a rather unusual feature of this monument type and can be considered as a "modern contribution".
The procession is managed by the Kṛṣṇa Dyaḥ Guthi from Ipā Ṭola.
A fewropanīs of land were endowed for organizing the procession.
But the tenant of the land stopped paying rent to the Guthi.
Consequently, the Guthi nearly stopped functioning.
A small shop was built on a nearby open space and the rent from the shop was used to carry out the procession.
The Guthi is also responsible for organizing the procession of Goddess Bhagavatī (Shrestha 2012, p. 247).
Six bell stands in wood are installed in front of the monument.
An inscription from 1717 CE (NS 837) suggests additions made by two local brothers, but the exact nature of these additions remains unclear due to the illegibility of the inscription.
The courtyard's brick paving around this time further confirms thecaitya's pre-inscription existence.
Thecaityaunderwent renovation by the Godawari Municipality in 2024 CE.

Situated at Cvaylāchi in Thecva, the Phalcā has only one bay, which is why it is named "Cvaylāchi Chakavaḥ Phalcā," meaning "one-bayed arcaded platform in Cvaylāchi." Until the late 1980s, the Phalcā deteriorated, and in the 1990s, it was rebuilt in concrete, preserving the style of the sloping roof.
In 1725 CE (NS 845), three brothers—Viśvadeva Bhābo, Bhāgīrāma, and Satyadeva—established a religious trust to set up thehāthu hāyketradition.
Cvaylāchi Chakavaḥ Phalcā was built in honor of their father, Phachi Bhābo.

The inscription on Cvaylāchi Chakavaḥ Phalcā mandates the performance of thehāthu hāyketradition during Yẽnyāḥ (Indra Jātrā) and the annual procession of Bālakumārī on the full moon day of Mārgaśirṣa.
It also prescribes the offering of animal sacrifices to Bālakumārī and donations at the nearbycaitya(THC0060).

While the tradition of offering donations at thecaityahas ceased, the core practices of thehāthu hāyketradition endure, even after three centuries of the Phalcā's construction (gūṭhīmember, Maharjana, male, age 82).

As Cvaylāchi Chakavaḥ Phalcā has evolved into a concrete structure, local representatives are now planning to restore it in what is conceived as "traditional architectural form" (ward member, Maharjana, male, age 28).

text: As of February 2022, it was still under construction.
The stone inscription attached to the western platform has been severely damaged.
As of February 2022 CE, thehitiis undergoing reconstruction with funds from the provincial government.
A niche above the spout is vacant and a small serpent figure was added on top of this niche during reconstruction in 2022 CE.
An important statue of Umāmaheśvara is installed inside a niche on the northern wall of the Hiti.
A second Umāmaheśvara statue was stolen in the 1970s but was later recovered and is currently being exhibited at the Patan Museum.
The statues and two inscription prove that Dugāḥ Hiti dates back to the Licchavi period.
The initial construction of Dugāḥ Hiti can be traced back to this period from an inscription installed in 538 CE (ŚS 460) during the reign of King Vāmanadeva.
It is the earliest dated inscription of Sankhu and records King Vāmanadeva installing a statue of the Vāmana incarnation of Viṣṇu and endowing plots of land to establish aguthi.
The Vāmana statue was lost and is now replaced by another statue on the pedestal.
There is a second inscription at the Hiti that mentions the installation of a statue of Sadāśiva, a multi-faced and multi-armed form of Lord Śiva, in 1700 CE (NS 820).
According to the inscription, a family from Dugāḥ Hiti had installed the statue and formed aguthifor performing yearly rituals.
The donor family might have established this Śivaliṅga as Sadāśiva.
A stone statue of Hanumān is placed on top of the stone pillar erected right in front of but far from the Hiphaḥdyaḥ.
There is an inscription on the pedestal of one of the two statues of Hanumān.
It states that thebhābos of Dathu Ṭola established the statues in NS 837 (1717 CE).
Although the inscription does not talk about the Hanumān on the pillar, it is possible that all three statues were installed at the same time.
Noguthioperated by the donors relating to this pillar is in existence.
The garland hence offered is unique, as it is prepared by weaving pieces of reed and of any fruit simultaneously.

monument_name: Bistabara Śikhara Temple 1 (built around the 13th-15th cent.)
text: It's possible that the pillar and the temples were constructed at the same time.
The pillar is of the same type as others erected in the Dailekh district during the 14th century.
The lower part is of quadrangular section, with a central, slightly larger part that would usually contain an inscription.
Stone pillars were erected throughout the Karnali Basin from the 13th to the 17th century.
They are installed to honor the memory of deceased persons, mostly warriors.
No inscription could be found that would indicate the identity of the deceased person or the date of installation.
The phalcā is a recently built copy of an 18th centuryphalcāand stands near to a historiccaitya(KIR0075).
The year of Taḥnani Phalcā's original construction and the name of the sponsor are not known.
Taḥnani Phalcā has been renovated and rebuilt multiple times but little details are known and no photographs from before 2015 CE could be sourced.
In 2006 CE the Kirtipur Municipality provided financial assistance to replace a few of the damaged struts.
In 2019 CE the municipality provided Rs 14,96,000 for the complete reconstruction of thephalcāand the local consumer organization (Upabhokta Samiti) contributed Rs 78,700.
Taḥnani Phalcā was shifted a few feet back and was rebuilt with all new materials.
Only the horse-shaped struts were reused and the two stone statues reinstalled.
The original six wooden columns were shifted to a newly constructed community building on the northern end of the square and reassembled in the ground floor meeting hall.
The rebuilt Phalcā was inaugurated by the Mayor of Kirtipur on June 29, 2021 CE.
There is noguthiassociated with the Phalcā.
Aphalcāwith a square base is generally known as Mandaḥ Phalcā and referred to as amaṇḍapain inscriptions.

An inscription of 1763 CE (NS 883), installed at the Brahmāyaṇī Pīṭha (SKH0123), states that themaṇḍapaof the Sālkhā Ṭola was renovated and land endowment was made to promote the status of Piunārāyaṇa and his family members of Kathmandu.
As this is the onlymaṇḍapathe Sālkhā Ṭola (and the city), it is clear that the renovation refers to this Phalcā.
The inscription has probably been moved to the nearby Brahmāyaṇī Pīṭha after its renovation.
It could well be that the Phalcā came to be known as Rāma Jhopaḍī (lit. Lord Rāma's hut) after the installation of the Vaiṣṇava Statue inside.
In the 2015 earthquakes, the southern base of the Phalcā collapsed.
In 2018, the Department of Archaeology dismantled the Phalcā and rebuilt it in neo-traditional style.
Following the reconstruction, a smalltulasīmaṭhawas established in front of the Phalcā in memory of the late Vīra Kumāra Śreṣṭha.
Two inscriptions  - unrelated to the Phalcā, but significant for the study of Sankhu’s history - are temporarily placed on the plinth of this monument.
D. Vajrācārya(VS 2030, p. 508) has published half of this inscription.
The other half of the inscription was recovered in 2014, when Gāḥ Hiti (SKH0142), placed behind this Phalca, was renovated.

Originally installed in 616 CE (Mānadeva Era 40), the Inscription contains references to a Tṛpura Vihāra and monastic association of the monks of the Mahāsāṅghika (lit. Great Congregation), a Buddhist school of thought (P. ŚreṣṭhaVS 2071, p. 3).

Another inscription, originally installed in 1558 CE (NS 679), records the construction of asataḥat Sālkhā Ṭola and the endowment of many plots of land to feed the Jaṅgama ascetics who come from far ("foreign land") at the Sataḥ (N. YogīVS 2012, p. 61-62).

The three cities of the Kathmandu Valley Kathmandu, Bhaktapur, and Patan is surrounded by the sacred and powerful abodes of the Mother Goddesses (māṭrkāpīṭha), which were built during the post-medieval period.

It is a common tradition amongst the Newars in the Valley to have such Mother Goddesses and Bhairavas, who often reside in their respectivepīṭhaslocated outside of the core city area, invoked to a shrine or temple (calleddyaḥchẽ,‘house of the deity’ in Nevārī) built inside the city.
This Bālakumārī Dyaḥchẽ was also built to evoke the Mother Goddesses Bālakumārī, who resides in herpīṭhalocated north-east of Patan (see LAL2000).
The inscription from NS 986 (1866 CE) installed in the Dyaḥchẽ (see below) records its renovation by Harṣanārāyaṇa.
They even share similar architectural motifs – they are two-tiered, built on a square base, and have three bayed doors in each direction (Gutschow2011, 401).
Statues of Kṛṣṇa and his two wives Rukmiṇī and Satyabhāmā are consecrated in the sanctum.
There is a lack of inscriptive evidence to point to its initial construction.
Many historians believe that it was constructed sometime in the 17thCentury CE.
However, on the back of Oldfield’s sketch, he has dated the monument to 1586 CE (Gutschow2011, 424).
The only dated inscription found in the temple premises is from 1757 CE and records land deed by Jayaprakāśa Malla (ibid).

Pruscha(1975, 216), however, has mentioned that the land was donated by Raṇajīta Malla [Editor’s Note: As of June 2021, we were not able to minutely study the copperplate inscription in-situ due to lockdown.
It will be edited once the present situation eases.]As evident in Oldfield’s sketches from 1853 CE, the temple looks derelict and near a ruinous state.
In 1976 CE, the temple was demolished and reconstructed from the ground up.
Cement was used in its columns, beams, and elsewhere during the reconstruction process (Gutschow2011, 424).
In 1863 CE (NS 983), Govinda Siṃha and his wife Vidyā Lakṣmī established apañcāvaliyukta caityainside the courtyard in memory of their son Jitamāna.
Apancāvaliyukta caityatypically has five layers, consisting of images of lotuses, water, jewels,vajraand fire, and this one does not deviate from this structure.
This shrine has been constructed on a plinth measuring 70 cm high and with a solid brick core.
To the north of this shrine is apañcāvali caityaconstructed on a plinth measuring 150 cm high on a square base of 116 cm.
There is also a newly established shrine for Sarasvatī near this shrine.

Constructed during King Śrīnivāsa Malla’s reign, this water trough (jaḥdhuṃ) in Patan, located along the main road near Taḥdhvākhā, was linked to a vibrant land trust until the 2000s, after which the trust and its traditions faded.

An inscription on thejaḥdhuṃ’s upper section records its inauguration on Akṣaya Tṛtīyā, the 3rd of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha in 1659 CE (NS 779) by Kālirāma Bhāro and his wife Vimalāmayi Bhari of Khalachẽ, with land allocated for maintenance under Vāvusiṃ Bhavo’s care.
Many such community-builtjaḥdhuṃs line Patan’s roads from this period.
The inscription notes the structure was built to please Viṣṇu, though no Viṣṇu statue remains, suggesting one may have existed or a shrine stood nearby.

In 2008 CE (VS 2064), the Amātya and Maharjana families plastered thejaḥdhuṃand added new statues, with a hole in the upper structure for filling water in the trough, preserving some original ornate stonework.
No documented evidence is so far found to date its initial construction.

The inscription from 1716 CE installed inside the Phalcā records its renovation and establishment of a statue of Bhavānīśaṅkara by Vaṃśīdharadeva Śarmā and his wife Lāvatī Brāhmaṇī, the descendants of its founder Jayasiṃhadeva.
However, the Bhavānīśaṅkara statue mentioned in the inscription does not exist in or around the Phalcā at present.
After the Phalcā was renovated, Vaṃśīdharadeva Śarma established aguṭhīto sponsor the celebration of its anniversary rituals, but no suchguṭhīexists anymore.
The Phalcā was completely dismantled and reconstructed in 2003 CE.
During the reconstruction, it was moved few cubic feet back from its original location arguing that it narrowed the street.
It was reconstructed again in 2019 CE with the financial support from the Lalitpur Metropolitan City Office after it was severely damaged during the 2015 earthquakes.
In NS 547 (1427 CE) Rājasiṃha Malla, a major Mahāpātra of Lalitpur, reconstructed this Vihāra together with four other Mahāpātras.
The Vihāra was previously known as Siṃhavarṇa Mahāvihāra; however, once reconstruction had finished it became known as Rājaśrī due to this connection.
This section above the main façade is particularly is impressive; built with traditional timber lathe work, the balcony exhibits features such asdãdikvatā(rod pattern balusters) andphirphircā.
The ground floor had no operable windows, but two small openings have been added at the northwestern corner for ventilation.
Its external wall was constructed in brick masonry and contains small lattice windows in all wings.
Each of the building's four wings are covered with tiled roof.
The brickwork and type of materials used in each wing vary, suggesting multiple phases of reconstruction and renovation works.
The eastern and northern wings were restored between 1990-1993 and the southern and western wings were restored between 1993-1995.
The reconstruction work was undertaken by the Nippon Institute of Technology in Japan and the Department of Archaeology in Nepal.
A copper plate inscription nailed to the front wall of the shrine is dated NS 547 and states that a golden statue of a Bodhisattva was established in the sanctum of the Bahī.
However, the statue was stolen around 1979-80.
A new brass statue of the deity was then commisisoned and installed in its place.
A bell donated in NS 903 (1783 CE) hangs to the left of the entrance.
However, the school moved out after the renovation.
Several ghāṭas line the right bank of the Bāgamatī river, extending from Ṭeku to Tripureśvara, each distinguished by the names of their builders, castes, and shrines.

Yet, in the Inventory of Kathmandu Valley published in VS 2039, an error occurred with Aryāla ghāṭa being mistakenly labelled as Boksina ghāṭa, and the adjacent ghāṭa to the west inaccurately identified as Aryāla ghāṭa (Inventory VS 2039, p.166).
According to the name of the ghāṭa and the information from locals, it can be assumed that this ghāṭa was built during the Rāṇā period by some affluent individual of the Aryāla caste.
The ghāṭa previously served as a residential space (Inventory VS 2039, p.166).

As of January 2024, while still utilized for residential purposes, its outward structure has undergone alterations, with traditional tiles replaced by zinc sheets, and columns covered with a small temporary structure.
Unfortunately, there is no information available about the builder of the small Śikhara shrine and the Hanumāṇa statue.
There is no inscription on Lokeśvara’s statue (KAT2735-002) as well.
However, an inscription found at the site records that a resident of Nakabahī ṭola named Bhājumuni constructed the dharmaśālā possibly a sataḥ or a phalcā in CE 1822 (NS 942).
This inscription on the roadside wall adds to the confusion when trying to identify the specific phalcā/sataḥ mentioned.
According to legend this is one of five stūpas built by Aśoka, the Mauryan king of India, however, there is no evidence that King Aśoka ever visited the Kathmandu Valley.
Today, most of these water bodies have dried up and a school and an army camp have been built upon its land.
A wooden frame (symbolising an umbrella) is installed on the roof, likely as part of a week-long tradition that takes place during the onset of the dry season.
The Stūpa has undergone many restorations and embellishments over time.
The brick retaining wall that now encircles the Stūpa was built some time before 1967, and a steel balustrade with oil lamps was installed around the perimeter in the 1990s.
A brick dome replaced the pyramid roof of the finial and a spire was added to this some time in the middle of the last century.
Since 1995, a total of fourdharmadhātumaṇḍalasanddharmadhātujinālayacaityaswere installed around the Stūpa.
A new entry gate was added, as were walls, fences and two shrines.
Coomaraswamy(1972, 144) states that the four Stūpas of Patan were constructed in an ancient Indian hemispherical style.
Legend tells that King Aśoka visited Nepal during the reign of 14th Kiranti King, King Sthaṃko, and commissioned the construction of fivestūpas.
He became rich and commissioned the fourcaityas (stūpas) on the four sides of Lalitpur in the Kali era 3608-9 on the 5th day of the bright half of Māgha (Devamālā Vaṃśāvalī1956, 71).
The Aśoka Stūpā Sudhāra Samiti, an organisation founded in 1997, manages the the Stūpa.
Kaumārī Pīṭha Phalcā has been constructed on the northern side of the entrance to the Kaumārī Piṭhā premises at the edge of the road.
The phalcā features a south-facing structure with traditional-tiled (jhiṃgiti) roof, five bays, artistic columns (thāma), and two inscriptions on its northern wall.
Constructed on top of a plinth, the phalcā reflects the traditional architectural style.
One of the inscriptions on the phalcā, dating to 1758 CE (NS 878), records the construction of a brick wall in the Dharmśālā (phalcā) by Purṇatāja Vajrācāryā and his family members.
This serves as evidence that the construction of this phalcā took place before the year 1758 CE.

The inscription also records that the anniversary ritual should be conducted at the end of Caitra, and offerings of worship and lights to be made at the piṭha on the third day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina.
The phalcā, which had fallen into disrepair, was reconstructed in 2012 CE (2069 VS) with the support of Bhaktapur Municipality, both financially and technically.
Consequently, the earthquake of 2015 CE (2072 VS) did not cause any damage to the phalcā.
It can be accessed via the entrance of a private building that is located at the southwest corner of the Bhājudhana Bāhāḥ (LAL2350).
Bhīmarāja Śākya, a member of thesaṅghaof Oku Bāhāḥ, established thisbāhāḥ.
Four stone pillars have been erected at each of the four corners above its double-layered lotus petals (which together are 96cm in diameter), supporting a layer of stone that forms a roof.
The courtyard is paved inteliatiles and a plinth surrounds the residential buildings.
The three-storey building on the northern side has a colonnaded three-bayphalcāunderneath it.
No inscription or any other document could be found to confirm the consecration date of thisbāhāḥ.
However, Bhīmarāja, the elder brother of Bhājudhana, established thebāhāḥjust after his younger brother established the Bhājudhana Bāhāḥ in 1909 (Śākya1994, 120).
These were caused by the 2015 earthquake.
The twostūpasare built next to one another.
The monuments are built of carved stone blocks.
The soil below it was collapsing.
A stone fountain (mugrāhā,dhārā) was originally built below thestūpas.
Architecturally, it is a single-storeyed temple constructed in the traditionaltallestyle.
No inscription or written record documenting the construction of the temple has been discovered to date.
Given that this shrine functions as aSthāna-Gaṇeśafor the locality, it is plausible that the Gaṇeśa image was installed already in the medieval period.
It is therefore possible that a simple shrine (devasthala) housing the image existed in the medieval period, over which the present temple structure was erected during the Śāha–Rāṇā period.
The second gate was not reconstructed.
The western entrance is already blocked due to the construction of a house.
No historical sources record the initial construction of this Gate.

A Buddhist scripture namedMaṇiśailamahāvadānamentions: In 1300 BC (Kaligata Era 1801), when Jogadeva Vajrācārya founded the town of Sankhu in the shape of aśaṅkha(conch shell) by assimilating seven villages as per the instruction of Vajrayoginī, he had divided the town into eightṭolas (city quarters) and constructed a palace at the centre, along with the shrines ofaṣṭamātṛkā(Eight Mother Goddesses), ninebāhāḥs, and four gates in four directions (V. Vajrācārya1119, p. 29-33).
As the Sīdhvākhā was one of the four gates, it is clear that it was constructed at the time of the establishment of the town of Sankhu.
The statues installed on the gate were stolen due to the lack of proper care and attention towards the gate.
The statue of Vāsudeva Kamalajā (SKH0010-011) installed at the Jyotirliṅgeśvara Mandira (SKH0010) premises was originally installed at the Sīdhvākhā.
It was shifted to the present location for its safety after the Sīdhvākhā collapsed.

The gate was reconstructed in 1970 CE (Shrestha2012, p. 65), but it collapsed again and was reconstructed by the local body using modern technology with the fund provided by A. W. van dek Hoek from the Netherlands in 1997 CE.
Residents of Sankhu still follow the tradition of offering water to the deities installed on the gate for a year when there is a death in the family.
The Bhaṭṭa family, who has been residing here for generations, claim that a Bhaṭṭa Brāhmaṇa by the name of Dayā Śaṃkara constructed thesataḥalong with twośiivālayasduring the Rāṇā period.
The originalsataḥwas demolished after the 2015 earthquakes.
However, an inventory published in the year 1979 CE (VS 2036) provides a clear depiction of its earlier form (Inventory VS 2039, p. 166)(see photo).
A Śivālaya stands in front of the sataḥ, which was specifically built to accommodate the cultural and religious activities associated with the Śivālaya.
To match the small size of the Śivālaya, the sataḥ was also constructed in a small size.
However, even before VS 2036, these columns were closed off and converted into rooms.
The family had already dismantled and reconstructed the upper floor before the earthquake of 2015 CE.
After the earthquake, they completely demolished the remaining structure and rebuilt it using concrete.
The current concrete structure is the result of this reconstruction.
An inventory published in VS 2036 mentions that this sataḥ was built by Dayā Śaṃkara Bhaṭṭa and that it underwent renovations in VS 2014, 2018, and 2032 (Inventory VS 2039, p.p. 166).

According to Bhāṣā Vaṃśāvalī, a tantric named Lambhakarṇa Bhaṭṭa, who came from southern Maharashtra and resided in Kuleśvara, assisted King Śivasiṃha Malla in capturing Lalitpur and establishing various religious structures.
As a reward, he was grantedgharakheta birtāand a residence in Kāntipura (Bhāṣā Vaṃśāvalī, part II, p. 59).
While the Vaṃśāvalī states that this lineage came from Maharashtra, an inscription in Cāpāgāũ refers to them as Dravida.
Regmi has pointed out that since Brāhmaṇas from the Tamil region of India were called Dravida, Lambhakarṇa Bhaṭṭa may have originated from there (J.C. Regmi, VS 2062, p. 406).
Due to the lack of inscriptions in the sataḥ and temple, determining its historical timeline is difficult.
Such doors were built from the early Śāha period through the Rāṇā period.
If the sataḥ was built alongside the Śivālaya, it should be considered a Śāha-Rāṇā period structure.
Because it was constructed for religious purposes, most records refer to the sataḥ as a dharmaśālā.
However, the descendants of the builder claim that their ancestors have used it as a residence from the very beginning (one of the family members, Bhaṭṭa, male, age 40).
Built in the southeastern corner of the three-way street at the Taṃgaḥṭola, the three-storied Kuṃ Phalcā stands at the crossroads in front of Ibāḥ Bahī (LAL2730).
It is unclear when the Phalcā was first constructed.
Although there is no historical source present at the site, the Tāmrākāra members of the trust (guthi) associated with the Phalcā claim it to date back to the Malla period.
It was damaged in the 2015 earthquakes.
However, the dispute among the members of theguthihas hindered the reconstruction.
The other members moved the court against the transaction and the court is yet to give its final decision regarding the case.
Previously, theguthihad 16 households as members but only three families are currently (October 2021) associated with it.
Theguthiof the Tāmrākāras also owned plots of land and the income from them was used to carry out socio-religious activities at thephalcā.
Theguthino longer owns those plots of land at present.
However, the rituals were discontinued after the 2015 earthquakes.
A member of theguthiruns a shop at the Phalcā and the rent is used for carrying out the activities of theguthi(shop owner, Tāmrākāra, male, age 51).
Kathmandu Nagar Kṣetrako Inventory(VS 2039, 185) mentions that the Sataḥ was constructed by Siddhi Nārāyaṇa and Bhīma Nārāyaṇa.
Both Matū Ajimā Mandira and thesataḥwere renovated in 1965 CE (VS 2022).
Situated in the Digu Ṭola, Thimi, the temple was renovated in 2004 CE (VS 2061) with support from the German donor agency GTZ and contributions from the local residents.
The shrine has a shed roof and appears to have been added later to the main two-tiereddigudyaḥtemple.
Additionally, a metal bell was installed here in 1905 CE (NS 1025) during the reign of King Pṛthvī Vikrama Śaha.
The temple complex houses an inscription from 1586 CE (NS 706), which mentions the use of a platform (dabū) for traditional dance performances (Pant 2019, p. 141).
Historical records indicate that the temple was rebuilt in 1806 CE (NS 926) by Sarjavīra Dvāre and later reconstructed in 1961 CE (NS 1081) by the local community (Pruscha 1975, p. 246).
A woodentoraṇawas added above the entrance to thedigudyaḥshrine in 1978 CE (VS 2034).
In 2016 CE (VS 2072), the facial sculpture of Bhairava was stolen, but a replacement was installed three months later.
This ritual also marks the conclusion of theBiskāḥ Jātrā(Ś. Śreṣṭha VS 2080, pp. 28–29).
The Pāṭī also houses an inscription from the reign of Kathmandu’s King Lakṣmīnarasiṃha Malla.
Originally constructed as an arcaded platform (pāṭī), the addition of a stone finial atop the roof gives it the appearance of a temple.
The finial, flanked by oval stones bearing carvings of a mace (gadā) and fire motifs, is a distinctive feature of the pāṭī.
Notably, a new Bhairava mask (NWK0270-007) was installed in 2013 CE (VS 2070) to replace the previous one, which had worn out and is now safely stored in the Sātatale Durbar.
Two inscriptions are found within the pāṭī; one is located on the northern inner wall, while the other stands against the same wall.
The latter inscription has eroded and is no longer readable.

Although the date of the inscription on the wall is illegible, it dates back to the reign of King Lakṣmīnarasiṃha Malla (r. 1619–1641 CE) and records the installation of three Buddhist deities: Vajrapāṇi, Khaḍgapāṇi, and Mañjuśrī, suggesting it may not be directly related to the Bhīmasena Pāṭī.
After suffering damage during the 2015 earthquakes, the pāṭī was renovated by the local government.
Special worship is offered annually on Bhīmasena Ekādaśī, the 11th day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, when a nearby Śreṣṭha family adorns the statue with silver crowns and jewelry.
Jñāneśvara was a well-established settlement during the Lichhavi period, situated within the vast Viśālanagara region.
This region encompassed a wide area, including Śaṅkhamūla, Devapattana, Paśupatinātha, Guhyeśvarī, Hā̃ḍigāũ, Mālīgāũ, Vāneśvara, Cābahila, and Jñāneśvara itself (S. Amatya VS 2053, p. 18).
An inscription discovered in Jñāneśvara, dating back to 733 CE during King Jayadev II's reign, mentions "Nepālamaṇḍala" (D. Vajracharya 2030, pp. 573-574).
The Jñāneśvara area has yielded ancient artifacts, including a magnificent reclining Viṣṇu statue now housed in Hanumandhoka (G. Vajracharya VS 2033, p. 125).
Constructed on a single-level platform, the temple features a double-tiered copper roof with a gilded finial.
Adharmaśilā(a significant stone slab) covered in metal sheets is installed to the south of the temple.
The Jñāneśvara Śivaliṅga, located within the sanctum of the temple, appears to have been established at a different time than the temple itself.
This self-emergentśivaliṅgacame to be known as Jñāneśvara (V. Dhakāla VS 2075, p. 983).
It is said that a young brahmin named Caraṇa, afflicted with a speech impediment, was cured after sincerely worshipping thisśivaliṅga(V. Dhakāla VS 2075, pp. 984-985).
A shrine has also been built to his name to the east of the temple.
No Licchavi inscriptions mention Jñāneśvara Mahādeva.
King Jagajjaya Malla granted land in 1728 CE (NS 848) for the daily worship of Paśupati, Kirāteśvara, Kileśvara, and Jñāneśvara (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2056, pp. 236-237).
While the Jñāneśvara Śivaliṅga dates back to the Licchavi period, the temple itself was built during the Śāha period.
Before the temple's construction, theśivaliṅgalikely resided in an open space or a small structure.
In 1795 CE (NS 915), royal astrologer (rājadaivajña) Lakṣmaṇa Bhāro, with others, constructed the Jñāneśvara temple and asataḥ(rest house).
This was done to liberate a deceased person, whose name is now illegible due to erosion of the inscription.
Lakṣmaṇa Bhāro's grandson, with his wives, donated a golden finial and trident to the temple in 1851 CE (NS 971).
King Mahendra renovated the temple in 1959 CE (VS 2015), but it suffered damage during the 2015 earthquakes.

text: Other inscriptions on the base of the statue record the construction of walls for the statue's security, installation of metal bars, and construction of concrete roof carried out over the years.
In the vicinity of the monument, there are other contemporary constructions such asDDL0110,DDL0111,DDL0112,DDL0113andDDL0120.
The Ajayamerukoṭa area is renowned for its rich collection of monuments, primarily erected during the 14th and 15th centuries.
This political and economic growth is reflected in the numerous monuments constructed during the second half of the 14th century and throughout the 15th century.
The monument underwent reconstruction by Nepal's Department of Archaeology, as evidenced by the inventory numbers still visible on the structure.
Therefore, it is possible that some elements may have been displaced, lost, or stolen.
Blocks have been carved to replace missing ones.
The nearbyśikhara(DDL0132) contains an inscription dated to 1373 CE (ŚS 1295) (Sharma 2012, p. 303).
This indicates that the monument was most likely built during the same period, specifically during the reign of King Niraya Pāla.
Aphalcāonce adjoined the southern boundary wall, but only its stone plinth remains today (as of July 2024 CE), after falling into ruin around 1973 CE (VS 2030).
No inscription provides details on the builder or date, but the stonework suggests the structures are from the early Śāha or Rāṇā period.
Water still flows from the spout, sourced from springs about 100 meters north and now connected to a modern water tap system (as of July 2024 CE).
Historically, a potter family from Bholakhā distributed jaggery juice here during festivals until 1993 CE (VS 2050).
In 1714 CE (NS 834), during the reign of King Bhūpatīndra Malla, Bīradeva Vajrācārya constructed the Jīsvāṃ Bāhāḥ.
It derives its name from thejīsvāṃ(white jasmine) plant that once stood on the site where the monastery was later constructed.
The monastery faces northward, and its main structure, thekvāḥpāḥchẽ(a traditional multi-tiered main monastic building), remains partially reconstructed as of March 2025.
However, due to ongoing reconstruction, the deity is temporarily housed in the home of abāhāḥmember.
Inside, the main deity is a stone Akṣobhya, installed as thekvāḥpāḥdyaḥ(main consecrated statue).
Long before the construction of thebāhāḥ, a Licchavi-eracaityahad already been established at the site.
By 1690 CE (NS 810), a well had been built nearby.
According to a stone inscription within the monastery, thebāhāḥitself was constructed in 1714 CE (NS 834) during the reign of King Bhūpatīndra Malla.

To ensure the monastery’s sustainability, Bīradeva endowed eightropanīs of land as a religious trust, dedicated to the perpetual worship of Akṣobhya and Dīpaṅkara and the recitation of thePrajñāpāramitā, a revered Buddhist scripture.
There, they constructed a newbāhāḥ, modeled after Cukaḥ Bāhāḥ, and established their community (bāhāḥmember, Vajracharya, male, age 40).
Over time, thebāhāḥfell into disrepair.
Neglect led to the collapse of thekvāḥpāḥchẽ, and the site became overgrown with weeds.
Without a roof, rainwater pooled inside the sanctum, transforming it into a stagnant pond (D. Bajrācārya NS 1124, p. 30).
Efforts to restore the monastery began around 2013 CE (VS 2070) with financial support from the German agency GTZ, which contributed approximately NRs. 800,000.
However, the funds proved insufficient, and reconstruction stalled.
Although four families are formally affiliated with the monastery, only two still reside within its premises, while the others have relocated.
The lion carvings on the stone base suggest that it may have originally been installed inside a Śikhara-style temple.
The Śivālaya was built in his memory, with hopes for his liberation.
In 1911 CE (VS 1968), Candra Śamśera used the water from Silupukhū to establish Nepal’s first hydroelectric power plant.
This water source played a crucial role in that project (B. Paṃgenī VS 2061, pp. 51–64).
Since VS 2038, the Nepal Water Supply Corporation has been collecting water from this source and distributing it throughout Lalitpur district.
According to the Gopālarājavaṃśāvalī, the Licchavi king Haridatta Varmā built Viṣṇu temples on four peaks (Vajrācārya and Malla 1985, folio 20A).
Given that this area has long served as a water source, it is likely that ponds and canals were built here during the Licchavi period.
However, no written records exist to confirm who built the current pond structures or when they were constructed.
It is possible that the ponds were built during the time of Candra Śamśera, when pipelines were laid to direct the water to the hydroelectric power plant.
There is also an inscription mentioning that King Mahendra later repaired these ponds.
In VS 2080, with funding from Dakṣinakālī Municipality, steel bars were installed and new stone slabs were laid on the surface.
The Garuḍanārāyaṇa Sataḥ (see Pruscha 1975, p. 68) is one of two more rectangularsataḥsin the vicinity, this includes the famous and rebuilt Kāṣṭhamaṇḍapa.
Structurally, it is a Sataḥ, althought a two-storied temple was later added to its north parapet wall, including a Lakṣṃīnārāyaṇa statue enshrined in it.
This has made the Sataḥ to be as famous as the Lakṣṃīnārāyaṇa temple (G. Vajrācārya VS 2033, p. 54).
According to G. Vajrācārya (VS 2033, p. 54), a statue of Garuḍanārāyaṇa is located on the top floor of the sataḥ.
The initial construction of the Sataḥ on the first floor’s southern side still retains its windows and struts (ṭũḍāla).

According to oral histories (Locke 1985, p. 417), there used to be a bāhāḥ before the construction of the Kasthamandapa (KAT1970) and the main deity (kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ) was the same Lokeśvara as in the Sataḥ.
When Kasthamandapa was built, the deity was relocated to the Sataḥ.
There is no inscriptive evidence that records the initial construction of this Sataḥ.
Based on its name, the Jośī community of Maru ṭol claims that the Sataḥ was built by Cautāriyā Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa Jośī during the reign of King Bhupālendra Malla.
According to G. Vajrācārya (VS 2033, p.54), the Lakṣmīnārāyaṇ temple attached to the Sataḥ seems to have been added later, and the statue installed in it is only from the 19th century.
Although the sataḥ is in dilapidated condition because of ownership disputes the reconstruction process of this Sataḥ has been stalled (local resident, Jośī, male, age 61).
Remaining nonexistent for an unknown period of time, Deypukhūsi Kuṃ Phalcā was restored prior to the 2015 earthquakes, reviving the stone plinth that had endured through the years.
Among the numerousphalcās built around the pond, this particular one occupies the southeastern corner.
Only the stone plinth had survived until 2013 CE, while thephalcāitself might have vanished at least a century earlier.
Unfortunately, there is no inscription shedding light on the initial construction of thephalcā.

Commencing in November 2013 and in collaboration with UN-Habitat, CIUD, and local communities, a project named "Revitalization of Open Spaces in Kirtipur" oversaw the restoration of Deypukhū, the erection of a boundary wall, and the reconstruction of thisphalcā.
The reconstruction, which was finalized in March 2014, also included the installation of a statue of Lokeśvara within thephalcā(Andersson 2014, report, UIUD).
Inside the sanctum, there is a statue of Hanumān on the western wall, and a square-shaped hollow space designated for fire oblations.
The exact date of the temple's construction is unclear, but its architectural style suggests that it was built during the Rāṇā period.
Theśivaliṅgainside the sanctum was installed around 2022 CE by devotees.
Unfortunately, the temple was already in a dilapidated state when it was further damaged by the earthquakes in 2015.
On the auspicious occasion of Śivarātrī, which falls on the 14th day of the dark fortnight of Phālguna, a bonfire is set up in front of the temple.
Locals report that the area also became to be known as Degaḥ Bahī after the construction of the Buddha Devala.
Local residents claim that the Devala must have been constructed sometime during the Rāṇā period.
The Devala collapsed during the 1934 earthquakes and was reconstructed after four years, in 1938 CE (VS 1995).
Three years later, decorative tiles were added to the exterior walls as well.
During the reign of King Tribhuvana a certain Narasiṃha and his son Jujuratna donated a new roof cover made of copper sheets.

In Newar tantric traditions (particularly in the Shakta tradition), Bhairava or Mātṛkās, who live on the outskirts of the city/village, are invoked to a god house ‘dyaḥchẽ’ built in the centre of the respective city or village and worshipped there.

According to the Devamālāvaṃśāvalī (p. 106), King Ānandadeva developed Bhaktapur as a large city and encircled it by establishing the abodes of the Aṣṭamātṛkās and their respective god-houses inside the settlements in the Kaligata Era 4197.

The first inscription found in the Maheśvarī Pīṭha premises dates from 1746 (NS 866), during the reign of King Raṇajita Malla of Bhaktpur, and it records King Raṇajit and nobles (pañca'lit. five elders') of the A-opa Ṭola composing a drama called 'Rukmiṇīharaṇa' and offering a gilded finial to thepīṭhato please Maheśvarī.
The pīṭha underwent renovation in 1958 CE (VS 2015), during which its floor and walls were tiled with modern tiles.
