This would therefore situate the construction of the Lamjī temples around the 14th-15th century.
When the work was accomplished Govinda Acarya made donations to Narayana Das and settled him in the village.
Sharma therefore suggested that the temple was built at the end of the 13th century, at the time of the Khaśa Malla emperor Jitāri Malla (r. c. 1287-1289 CE).

text: Bhakteśvara Mandira, located at Ṭeku Dobhāna, was built during the early Rāṇā regime, however, there is no evidences to date the initial construction exactly.
Aśivaliṅgais consecrated in the sanctum (garbhagṛha) and the main door is crowned with atoraṇa.
A statue of Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa is established to the east of the main door.

Viṣṇudevī Rājabhaṇḍārī, a fifth-generation daughter-in-law of Siddhimāna Rājabhaṇḍārī who constructed Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa [KAT2636], Siddhimukteśvara [KAT2637] and Dhaneśvara Mandira [KAT2638] in 1855 CE), operates a home for elderly adjacent to this temple and performs the daily worship at the three temples.
A certain Rāmacandra Thāpā, who operates a paint shop in Teku, periodically paints the temple and takes care of repairshe temple.
According to a legend, the Bāhāḥ was originally founded at a place called Tomāco in Kamalapokharī, Bhaktapur.
It was named Tom Bāhāḥ, as it was constructed at the Tomāco Ṭola.
Some claim that it was named Tom Bāhāḥ, as it was constructed at a place with atuṃ(well).
However, the well outside the Bāhāḥ was constructed only in NS 883 (1763 CE) (B. Vajrācārya1124, p. 114) while the Bāhāḥ had already come into existence in NS 690 (1570 CE).
It was probably reconstructed in the present shape after it suffered damages in the 1934 earthquakes.
It was installed during the reign of King Surendra in NS 986 (1866 CE).
It replaced the original statue made of red sandalwood after it was stolen in around 1983 CE.
Not much is known about the founding of the Bāhāḥ due to the lack of inscriptive evidence.
Dated NS 690 (1570 CE), a document containing verses ofvajradhātumaṇḍalarefers to this Bāhāḥ when it writes about a person named Budhācārya Dharmamuni from the Bāhāḥ at the Taulāchẽ Ṭola.
Prajāpati Jagatsiṃha Bhāro offered a goldenkalaśato the roof of the Bāhāḥ’skvāḥpāḥchẽin NS 734 (1613 CE).
At the same time, Jogasiṃha, Viśva, and others offered ornaments to thekvāḥpāḥdyaḥ.
The courtyard of the Bāhāḥ was paved with stones in 1980 CE at the initiation of the Bāhāḥ members.
The main sanctum andāgaṃwere also renovated with financial assistance from the Department of Archaeology, Bhaktapur Municipality, and from the locally collected donations.
Its roof was previously tiled withjhĩgaṭī, but it was replaced with copper sheets in 1982 CE (VS 2038).
There are three pinnacles (gajū) on top of the roof, which were gilded during the temple’s restoration in 1997 CE (VS 2054).
Vagalāmukhī is consecrated in the main sanctum (garbhagṛha) on the first floor.
A small shrine is established around Vagalāmukhī.
A metalmaṇḍala,representing Ānandā Bhairava, is installed in front of the deity.
There is no documented evidence regarding to the initial construction of this temple.
Previously, the deity was consecrated in open-air as there was no temple to house her.
Before the present temple was built, Lakṣmī Nakarmī offered a copper moon and a pair of lions to the deity in 1895 CE (NS 1015).
In 1898 CE (NS 1018), Baktabārasĩ offered a brass flag.
Later, Vyaṣārāja and Kularāja jointly offered a lion pillar to her in 1930 CE (NS 1050).
In 1931 CE (VS 1988), Prime Minister Bhīma Śamśera constructed the present-day temple.
It caught on fire in 2009 CE (VS 2065) due to an electric short-circuit, and was renovated with the generous donations of the local community.
Every year on the last Saturday of the month of Maṅsīra, a sacrifice of buffalo, sheep, goat, duck, and fish (pañcabali) is offered to Vagalāmukhī.
The two-story Dyaḥchẽ facing north has copper sheets laid on the roof with three goldenkalaśas installed as its finial.
Effigies of Maitreya and Lokeśvara are established in the southern corner of the sanctum.

The 2015 earthquakes caused damages to the Dyaḥchẽ and was reconstructed.

Similarly, a special container for growing tulasī plant, referred to as tulasīmaṭha, has been constructed to the southwest.

text: Following the passing of his first wife Lokabhaktalakṣmī on February 11, 1905 (VS 1961) due to tuberculosis (P. Rāṇā VS 2080, p. 64), Candra Śamśera married Bālakumārīdevī in 1906 CE (VS 1963) (P. Rāja VS 2070, p. 15).

Born to Harivikrama Sāha, aṭhakurīfrom Jajarkot (P. Rāṇā VS 2080, p. 65), Bālakumārīdevī was raised in the household of Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā’s daughter Dīpakumārī (Kānchīmaiṃyā) as aḍolā, a girl brought from outside Kathmandu to be groomed by royalty in court etiquette for marriage.
The following day, she was bestowed with the title of “Śrī 3 Baḍāmahārānī”, signifying the principal queen (P. Rāja VS 2061, p. 33).
Born in 1888 CE (VS 1945) (D. Panta VS 2055, p. 14), Bālakumārīdevī bore three sons – Viṣṇu, Śaṅkara, and Madana Śamśera – and a daughter Lakṣmīdevī (P. Rāja VS 2070, p. 48).

Standing south of Thāymadu Sataḥ at the Thaymadu Ṭola, Nhū Bāhāḥ appears to be a residential building, as it has lost its traditional architectures.
The four-story building facing north has corrugated tin sheets laid on the roof.
No historical records are available to date the initial construction of the Bāhāḥ.
The statue spangled with precious gems was stolen from Jhvāḥ Bāhāḥ and the thieves left the statue in a nettle bush at the Thāymadu Ṭola after removing all the gems.
The locals then established him at the Ṭola by constructing a newbāhāḥ.
Being a newly-constructedbāhāḥ, it was locally known as Nhū Bāhāḥ, meaning ‘newbāhāḥ’.
K. Malla(1142, p.26) has mentioned the year of the theft as 1878 CE (NS 998) without mentioning any sources.
However, the name ‘Nhura Bāhā’ had already appeared in an inscription almost a century before that.

The inscription from 1780 CE (NS 900) records the renovation of the Bāhāḥ’s main building (kvāḥpāḥchẽ) by Ghanavīramāna (text: Ghnavilamāna) along with his wife Gunamati, son Vīrasiṃhadeva (text: Virasiṃghadeo), and daughter Pammalakṣmī.

The statue that was stolen from Jhvāḥ Bāhāḥ and discarded at a nettle bush was probably the same wooden statue that was replaced in 1846 CE.
No inscription could be traced to identify the dates and details of any construction or renovation work.

The window frames are damaged and sections of the carved frames are missing.

During thevarṣavarddhana pūjāand other ritual worships, people use the building as a resting place.
On the 8th day of the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, local residents from Sunaguthi offer religious gifts to their Vajrācārya priests at the Phalcā.
A bell donated in 1864 hangs in the northern bay of the Phalcā, suggesting that the Phalcā must have been constructed some time before this date.
The construction of the Śiva temple in 1887 CE (VS 1944) is attributed to Prime Minister Vīra Śamśera.
This temple, known as Vīramadhuprakāśeśvara, is one of the three Śiva temples that Vīra Śamśera built at the Pandhra Śivālaya complex.
Constructed from stone, Vīramadhuprakāśeśvara boasts a bell-shaped roof crowned with a metallic finial.
It is Prime Minister Vīra Śamśera who initiated the construction of this temple in 1887 CE (VS 1944).
He and his wife also offered a bell to the temple in the same year.

A Brahmin belonging to the Ghimire caste conducts daily rituals at the temple, as well as at two other Śiva temples, Vīramāyābhakteśvara (PPK0323) and Vīrarājabhakteśvara (PPK0324), which were also built by Vīra Śamśera.
Apparently erected in the 20th century, the exact origins of this Śiva temple remain elusive due to the absence of historical records.
Regrettably, the statue of Kāmadeva, originally positioned southwest of the temple, has already been stolen.
The absence of inscriptions at the site shrouds the identity of the donor and the year of the temple's construction in mystery.

During the Rāṇā period, it was a usual tradition for royals to constructśivālayas (lit. abode of Śiva), often naming them after a living person suffixed with "bhakteśvara" or in memory of a deceased family member suffixed with "mukteśvara." Although the temple's name, Śrīmānamukteśvara, suggests construction by an individual in memory of a deceased family member, the specific dedication remains unclear.
Despite uncertainties about its origins, the architectural characteristics point to a construction date in the 20th century (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p.347).

The pavilion (baiṭhak) is a unique construction for the whole of the Karnali region.
It is built on a large square platform.
It may be suggested that the construction was used as a meeting pavilion (sabhamaṇḍapa) or even as a pavilion of justice (nyāyamaṇḍapa) (Andolfatto 2019: 92-93).
A stone memorial pillar (JUM0100-001) is erected on the north-eastern side of the pavilion.
There are no inscriptions at the site.
Despite this, it is possible to propose that thebaiṭhakwas erected around the 14th-16th century.

In a dire need for restauration, the pavilion was finally stabilised and restored by the Department of Archaeology in 2015 or 2016, after French-Swiss archaeologist Dominique Baudais provided a detailed documentation of the monument to the institution.

text: TheBhāṣāvaṁśāvalī(part ll, p. 24) mentions the construction of numerouspīṭhas,abodes of the Mother Goddesses,including the‘Luti Pīṭha builtin the northern side of the Kathmandu Valley during the reign of Guṇakāmadeva in the Kaligata Era 3825.
In the history of the Valley, there are two kings named Guṇakāmadeva; one ruled around 987 CE and the other ruled around 1186 CE (cf.Slusser1982, Appendix).

Further, theNepālīkabhūpavaṃśāvalī(13. 252/256) records that Guṇakāmadeva established the city in the Kaligata Era 3824, constructed a cremation ground on the banks of the river Viṣṇumatī, invoked Goddess Manamayaju, and consecrated her in theāgaṃ coka.
Luti Ajimāṃ Temple was entirely reconstructed by the Department of Archaeology in 2017 CE after it was damaged by the 2015 CE earthquakes.
The temple has three stories and two pillars installed in front of it, respectively mounted by a lion (siṃha) and peacock.
A statue of Indrāyaṇī is consecrated inside the sanctum (garbhagṛha).
Statues of rest of theaṣṭamātṛkāsare also established in the temple.
An inventory kept in the Guṭhī Saṃsthāna records several plots of land endowed to the temple, adding up to 39ropanīsand twoānās(cf.Guṭhī Saṃsthāna2071,79).
Known as Bakhatamukteśvara, thisśivālaya(lit. the abode of Śiva) was erected by Śoṇajaṅga Rāṇā in honor of his late father, Bakhatajaṅga Kũvara Rāṇā, in the year 1924 CE (VS 1981).
Commander Colonel Śoṇajaṅga Rāṇā initiated the construction of thisśivālayain memory of his father Bakhatajaṅga Kũvara Rāṇā in 1924 CE (VS 1981).
Bakhatajaṅga Kũvara was the eldest son of Revantasiṃha Kũvara, the younger brother of Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā’s father Bālanarasiṃha Kũvara (B. Bhaṇḍārī VS 2071, p.18).

As Jaṅga Bahādura rose to prominence after the court massacre of 1846 CE (VS 1903), he strategically appointed his trusted brothers and relatives, including Bakhatajaṅga, to key positions to strengthen his control over the state apparatus.
Bakhatajaṅga, bestowed with the title of colonel (P. Rāṇā VS 2059, p.39), led one of the Nepalese army's three companies in the war against Tibet in 1855 CE (P. Rāṇā VS 2059, p.99).

Following Bakhatajaṅga's death, his son Śoṇajaṅga, in addition to the Bakhatamukteśvara temple, commissioned the Rakṣāmukteśvara temple and three otherśivālayas at the Gorakhanātha complex: Suvarṇaprakāśeśvara, Bahādurajaṅgaprakāśeśvara, and Nīlaprakāśeśvara (PPK1943).
He also established a rest house (phalcā) in the area and the Tilamukteśvara Śivālaya outside the Kathmandu valley in Ḍoṭī Dipāyala of the far-western region.

The earthquakes in 2015 caused damage to the temple walls, prompting the Pashupati Area Development Trust to initiate restoration efforts in 2021 CE (VS 2078).Śoṇajaṅga established a trust of IRs. 5,000 for daily and periodic worships, as well as timely cleaning and renovation of the temple.

The Shankhapur Municipality has already decided to reconstruct the Phalcā but the works are yet to be started.
There is no historical source that reveals the details of the Phalcā’s initial construction.

On the eastern façade of a nearby residence, images of Gaṇeśa, Mañjuśrī, and Mahākāla are also installed.
To the north of thecaityalies the Dharmadhātu Maṇḍala, and to the east stands an ancient well, which inscriptions indicate predates thecaitya.
Thecaityawas established in 1821 CE (NS 941) by families residing southeast of the Yaśodharā Mahāvihāra, led by Jagajyoti Vajrācārya and Lakṣmījyoti Vajrācārya.
Inscriptions on thecaitya’s plinth and inside the residence record its construction.

A further inscription inside the house states that after the completion of the house, courtyard, and well, thecaityawas consecrated, and in 1822 CE (NS 942), the Vajrācārya families and local residents jointly performed a city circumambulation (parikramā).
Additional contributions by Puṇyarāja Vajrācārya, his brothers Vajrarāja and Śubharatna, and their mother Sānumāyā led to the establishment of the Dharmadhātu Maṇḍala to the north of thecaitya.
In 1998 CE (NS 1118), the Vajrācārya brothers of Taḥjaḥ Ṭola installed a protective iron railing around thecaitya.

A copper inscription attached to the railing records that the Mahākāla statue on the eastern wall had been stolen twelve years earlier; a new statue was consecrated, and the railing was erected thereafter.
Around 2022 CE (VS 2079), when the house was reconstructed, the well was relocated eastward (local resident, Vajrācārya, male, age 59).
Built during the reign of King Raṇajita Malla, Kuthu Maṭha stands north of Dattātraya Square in Bhaktapur's Kvāthandau Ṭola.
Notably, this is the only monastery where themaṭha's tutelary deity is openly installed (Gutschow 2011, p. 599), though the primary entrance to theśivaliṅgaremains generally closed to public access.
Following Hagmüller’s passing in 2024 CE, Hungerhuber continues to inhabit and maintain themaṭha.

While the exact construction date remains undocumented, a surviving stone inscription from 1748 CE (NS 868) records that Rāma Girī formally donated his residential property, including a house, garden, and land in Kvāthandau Ṭola to Vāṇeśvara Mahādeva consecrated within themaṭha.

Notably, it mentions the installation of a copper plate inscription documenting this endowment during the reign of Raṇajita Malla - though this copper plate appears to remain unpublished in scholarly literature.
Academic consensus, based primarily on this epigraphic evidence, maintains that Rāma Girī founded the monastery around 1748 CE (NS 868).
The inscription's detailed account of property transfer and deity installation strongly supports this interpretation as historically accurate.
The stone inscription records the establishment of a religious trust through the donation of substantial land holdings dedicated to Vāṇeśvara, themaṭha's principal deity.

It notably stipulates specific succession rules: “As long as Rāma Girī's direct descendants exist, no external claims to themaṭha(particularly regarding themahantaposition) shall be recognized; should his lineage cease, authority would transfer to members of Rāma Girī's own sect; in the absence of qualified individuals from his original sect, responsibility would pass to any member of the broader Daśanāmī tradition; and failing all these possibilities, the inscription designates the king as the ultimate guardian of themaṭha."Themahantaof themaṭhais traditionally appointed based on hereditary lineage.
During his initiation, he is said to have resided far from Bhaktapur, possibly at Badrinath Ashram, before returning to establish this monastery (R. Hāḍā VS 2068, p.).
Rāma Girī established a religious trust by dedicating substantial landholdings to fund annual rituals.

A surviving stone inscription records provisions for special worship ceremonies and feasts during festivals, donations to ascetics, wages for workers maintaining themaṭha, including renovation laborers, gardeners supplying ritual flowers, and cleaners of the premises.
During the annualBiskāḥJātrāfestival, after the ceremonial pole was erected at Yaḥsĩkhyaḥ, it was customary for themaṭhato offer a male goat in sacrifice before the Bhairava chariot.
On the 12th of the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, verses dedicated to Rudra (an epithet of Śiva) were recited, followed by fire rituals, before feeding ascetics, monks, and saints.
One male goat each was offered to Bhīmasena and Gaṇeśa at the Dattātraya Square on behalf of themaṭha.
DuringŚivarātrī, the tradition of recitingrudrī, performing fire rituals, and lighting a bonfire in themaṭhacontinues.
On this day,samaybaji(a traditional Newar ritual food platter) and other food items are offered asprasāda(blessed offerings) from the main deity at night.

On that day, firewood collected in theguṭhīchẽfor the cremation process is tallied and stock replenished for the upcoming year.

He passed away in around 1988 CE and his family discontinued running the shop.

The family claims that their ancestors had built this Phalcā.
It was already in a dilapidated condition before the 2015 earthquakes.
The locals used the Phalcā as a space to deposit construction materials.
After the earthquakes damaged the Phalcā, it is currently (January 2022 CE) being reconstructed with the funds of the Shankharapur Municipality.

The Dyaḥchẽ was constructed to keep the statue of Mādhavanārāyaṇa, who is worshipped at the river Śālī (Śālīnadī) throughout the observance of the fasting.
Facing east, the Dyaḥchẽ is a three-story building with the statue of Mādhavanārāyaṇa enshrined on its first floor.
No records about the initial construction of the Dyaḥchẽ are available.
The 2015 earthquakes damaged the Dyaḥchẽ.
The Department of Archaeology started the reconstruction of the Dyaḥchẽ in cooperation with the Shankharapur Municipality that concluded in 2020 CE.
Although the reconstruction is complete, the power supply to the building is yet to be connected.
The priests have, therefore, not moved into the building yet.
The sataḥ was rebuilt in 2003 from the ground-up using mostly new building materials.
The carved columns reused in the reconstruction date from the late Malla period (Bāsukala & Gutschow,2018).
The historic photograph inPruscha’s (1975, 149), taken ca. 1973 already shows a three-storey sataḥ that may well have been built sometime after the 1934 earthquake.
At that time, the building intersected with the eastern lower roof of the Gaṇeśa Temple.
In 2003 (VS 2060), the sataḥ was demolished and replaced with a modern building following traditional design principles.
Kvaylāchi Phalcā is located at the south-western corner of Kvaylāchi, an open square in front of the temple of Mahākāla in Sunāguthi.

The Phalcā was rebuilt between 2018-2019 with the financial support of the Barbara and Wilfried Mohr-Foundation, the South Asia Institute at Heidelberg University's post-earthquake relief fund Nepalhelp and local community donations.
A small opening in this wall overlooks a small pond just behind the building.

This Stūpa (locally known as Tetāthūra) is believed to be built by King Aśoka, however, there is no evidence that King Aśoka ever visited the Kathmandu Valley.
The residents in Patan believe that thesestūpaswere built by King Aśoka.
TheNepālikabhūpavaṃśāvalī(19-20) too records that he constructed severalcaityas and stūpaswhen he visited the Kathmandu Valley during the reign of a Kirā̃tī King Sthuṃko.
However, theDevamālavaṃśāvalīnarrates that thesestūpaswere built in the Kaligata era 3608-9 by a merchant during the reign of King Vīradeva.
Coomaraswamy(1972, 144) mentions that thesestūpasare constructed inḍhisko‘hillock’style of ancient India.
Pruscha(1975, 189), without referring to any source, writes that these niches containing the images of the Dhyānī Buddhas and the wall encircling the Stūpa were built sometime in the 19th century.

Located east of the Rāma Temple (KAT2700), thissataḥis believed to have been constructed with the ease of worship and cultural activities in mind, complementing the nearby Rāma Temple (one of the descendants of the founder of the Tīnadevala [KAT2670], Rāṇā, male, age 56).
The construction of thesataḥ, along with the Rāma Temple, is attributed to Bam Bahadur Rāṇā around 1850-51 CE (VS 1907), according to a descendant of Bam Bahādura Rāṇā clan, male, aged 56.

During Jang Bahadur's visit to Britain in 1850 CE, when he became the acting Prime Minister, Bam Bahādura constructed Tīnadevala (KAT2670), including the foursataḥs(caugharā sataḥ) on the banks of the Vāgamatī.
It is believed that he also added the Rāma Temple to the existing nearby Viṣṇu Temple.

The Dattātraya Mandira at the Tacapāla ṭola of Bhaktapur is said to have been built using timbers from a single tree, similar to the Kāṣṭhamaṇḍapa (KAT1970) in Kathmandu.
The entrance also has a verandah on either side, and there are struts with erotic carvings installed on the temple.
The temple is guarded by two large stone statues of a sturdily-built man (kutuvaḥ) named Jayamala and Patā (Pratāpa) on the steps leading to the ground floor veranda.

Additionally, two pillars with the implements of Viṣṇu on top were erected in 1951 CE, while a third pillar, much taller than the other two, was erected in 1851 CE, with a large gilded statue of Garuḍa.
According to legend, Gosāĩ Gurubakśa Giri, a person who returned from a successful trade mission to Tibet with a lot of gold and cash, built temples at many places on his way back home.
According to a chronicle, King Yakṣa Malla and his son Rāja Malla built the Dattrātraya temple at the Tacapālaṭola(Nepālikabhūpavaṃśāvalī, 19.87).

It appears King Yakṣa Malla and his son Rāja Malla converted thecapāḥinto a temple, possibly before 1467 CE., as Rāja Malla is known to have passed away before 1467 CE (NS 588) (D. Vajrācārya 2019, p.131).
King Viśva Malla later converted the temple into a three-storied structure and named it the Dattātraya Mandira by establishing a statue of Triguṇāṃśanārāyaṇa in it.

He also contributed a lot of land for carrying out the daily rituals here and handed the temple over to the ascetics (saṃnyāsīs) while also building an abode for them (Nepālikabhūpavaṃśāvalī, 19.1.10).

According to theDevamālāvaṃśāvalī, Queen Gaṃgārānī is credited with building a three-storied temple and endowing land to carry out various rituals during the reign of King Śivasiṃha Malla in 1589-1590 CE (NS 709-710) (D. Yogī 2013, p.77).
The temple did not suffer any damage in the 1934 earthquakes (D. Yogī 2013, p.77).
On the occasion, Dattātraya is worshipped with arudrābhiṣeka, a libation of water offered to the deity together with the recitation of therudrīverses.

Since it was not possible to run the daily operations of the Bāhāḥ, itssaṅghamembers, Yogaratna Śākya, Munirāja Śākya, Teja Bahādura Śākya, and others, handed over the Bāhāḥ to a Bhikṣu Saṅgha (an organization of some monks who practice at the Therāvāda school of Buddhism)in VS 2000 (1943 CE).
Later in VS 2007 (1950 CE), it came under the jurisdiction of this organization (Śākya2053, 3).
Contemporary buildings surround the Bāhāḥ in the present-day, and it serves as a learning centre for the Therāvāda Buddhism.
Now, it has been reduced to ruins by the time of this documentation in February 2024 CE.
Jayabahādura Kũvara, the son of Bālārāma Kũvara and Indrakumārī, was responsible for the construction of thesataḥ(G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2056, p. 491).
Meanwhile, B. Bhaṇḍārī (VS 2071, p. 18) has given his father’s name as Balarāma Kũvara.

The western wall of thesataḥhas a large inscription (though not related to thesataḥdirectly) that documents Jayabahādura constructing the Indreśvara Śivālaya (PPK1939) together with his mother Indrakumārī and Jagadīśvara Śivālaya (PPK1938) in 1848 CE (VS 1904).
He also established a trust (gūṭhī) in the name of both temples on the same date.

About seven months later, he installed the inscription after establishing trusts with land endowments to fund the daily and periodic rituals to be performed at these monuments.
There is, however, no mention of thesataḥ's collapse in any sources.
According to the locals, thesataḥwas already in ruins in 2004 CE (VS 2061), with no efforts made to rebuild it even after decades of its collapse.

Before thesataḥ's collapse, it was used as a shelter by homeless people and provided space for the recitation of the Bhagavadgītā, the holy text of the Vaiṣṇava sect, every year for four months starting from Hariśayanī Ekādaśī, the 11th of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, till Haribodhinī Ekādaśī, the 11th of the bright fortnight of Kārtika.
The Dharmadhātujinālaya Caitya, located in a small courtyard in Ipā Ṭola, was commissioned by two couples belonging to the Buddhācārya caste.

An inscription on the Caitya's plinth records that Lokamuni Buddhācārya (text: Buddhācāryye Lokamuni), his wife Dhanamāyā, and Bhaktamuni[1]and his wife Ratnamāyā sponsored the construction of the Caitya.

The inscription states that the two couples had moved to Sankhu from Prasannaśīla Mahāvihāra, also known as Pasu Bāhāḥ (BKT0220) in Bhaktapur and that the Caitya was consecrated on the 5thof the dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa in 1955 CE (NS 1075).
Since the donor family has moved to Kathmandu, the Caitya's anniversary ritual is no longer performed.
A square plinth with a quarter-round profile forms the base of the Caitya and carries the inscription (facing west).
The statue of the esoteric deity (āgãdyaḥ), which used to be located on the first floor, is now stolen.

It is difficult to ascertain which deity was housed as the Bāhā’s principal deity (kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ) because of the theft of thekvāḥpāḥdyaḥ’sicon.
However, the members of thesaṅghamention that the icon of Padmapāṇi Lokeśvara, made with sandalwood, was consecrated as thekvāḥpāḥdyaḥ.
Locke(1985, 112), however, mentions that it is Akṣobhya, and not Padmapāṇi Lokeśvara, established as thekvāḥpāḥdyaḥ, and thatkvāḥpāḥdyaḥ’sicon was mistakenly positioned in the east.
There is no inscriptive evidence about the Bāhāḥ’s construction date and its benefactor.

Anotherphalcāin the area, Indrāyaṇī Pīṭha Phalcā 1 (BKT4002), was built in 1888 CE (NS 1008) and it could be assumed that this one, too, was also built around the same time.

Two inscriptions are preserved on the wall of thehiti—one dated to 1686 CE (NS 807) and another to 1953 CE (VS 2009).
The earlier inscription, from the late Malla period, records that a local resident named Śrī Narasiṃha installed images of Mahādeva (Śiva) and Vaṃśagopāla at the site.
To ensure thehiti’s long-term maintenance, he endowed land in locations such as Bālegrām (present-day Bālagāũ).
Although the inscription details the installation of images and establishment of endowments, it makes no mention of thehiti’s original construction, implying that it predates 1686 CE.
The site is referred to in this record as "Tāhāva Kṣetra." The second inscription, from 1953 CE, uses the name "Tāhākhela" and records a community-led renovation of thehiti.
Descendants of Narabahādura, together with the daughters and sisters of Motilāla, undertook the cleaning of the spring source and installed a new water pipe system to restore thehiti’s function.
Following the installation of piped water to households by the local government, thehiti’s water has been relegated to secondary uses such as washing.
Nevertheless, thehitihas recently undergone renovation with support from the local government.

According to the inscription carved above the stone doorway on the western side of the structure—resembling the entrance style of Śiva-shrines—the well was constructed in 1878 CE (VS 1935) by Bhīmanārāṃ of Vaṭola.
The same inscription also indicates that the area was formerly known as Pañcagāla, a name that has since been replaced by Sañjīvanī Ṭola.
Although wells of this kind were once common across the region, structures built in the temple style with a stone roof and finial are now rare.
Stone pillars were erected throughout the Karnali Basin from the 13th to the 17th century.
They are installed to honor the memory of deceased persons, mostly warriors.
Among the two historical buildings standing as maṭha in Cālakhu, Patan, one was demolished after the earthquake of 2015 CE and has not been rebuilt to this day.
In the courtyards of suchmaṭha, a Śivaliṅga, a supreme deity among ascetics, is often installed.
Calākhu maṭha was likely constructed in a quadrangular shape, similar to Chāybāhāḥ or the Pujārī matḥa.
However, there is no any inscriptive evidence for confirmation.
It was demolished following the 2015 earthquake damaged, and temporary shops have been set up on the ruins.
The northern building has retained its original form.
The ground floor here also has open columns supporting beams where statue of Devī is installed.
One of these columns has a bell offered in 1757 CE (NS 877).
The upper floor of this building features wooden windows, but they are of lower quality compared to those of Bāhālakhu and Chāybāhāḥ.
Between these two buildings, a rectangular platform has been raised, creating an open courtyard where traditional tiles (chikaṃ appā) have been laid.
The courtyard has Śivaliṅga, a statue of Hanumāṇa, and idols of past Mahantas are installed in it.
An inscription of a well near the courtyard records it construction date as 1719 CE (NS 840).
There is no clear evidence regarding the construction of the maṭha or the origins of the Mahanta tradition.
However, an inscription from 1743 CE (NS 864) records that Sundara Purī donated a substantial amount of land to the maṭha to support various socio-cultural activities.
Additionally, Amara Girī donated land in Bāhālakhu to Triliṅgeśvara for annual rituals.
A year after Amara Girī donation, Sundara Purī donated land addressing Guru Dattatreya and his sacred footprints.

The inscription specifies that on the day it was installed the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguṇa—the ascetics of the Daśanāmī order were to be invited for worship with pañcopacāra rituals and a feast.
The Śivaliṅga is referred to in the inscription as Mukteśvara, with instructions for its worship on that day.
Since this is the earliest record relating to the maṭha tradition, some believe Sundara Purī established the maṭha.

However, an earlier inscription from 24 years prior mentions Makranda Puri and his disciple Sundara Purī constructing the Śivaliṅga and the well, suggesting that the Mahanta tradition might predate Sundara Purī.
In 1721 CE (NS 842), Sundara Purī added the stone-carved footprints of Guru Dattatraya.
In 1805 CE (NS 926), on the same eighth bright fortnight of Phālguna, ample amount of land was added in the name of Sundara Purī and Sudāma Purī for alms distribution (sadāvarta).
According to Pande (VS 2059, p. 43), after 62 years Sudama Puri’s son, Pahalamāna Puri who is also grandson of Sundara Purī added more land to the guṭhī established by Sundara Purī.
King Rajendra granted a lālamohara to Pahalamāna Purī to manage the maṭha’s income and its traditions (K_0117_0004).
On days of grand feasts, the Mahanta would be paraded around Patan on an elephant, following the tradition of distributing sadāvarta (Pande VS 2059, p. 47).
To celebrate the maṭha anniversary, the Śivaliṅga was specially worshipped on the day of Sithi Nakha, and feasts and donations were held for Gosāī̃.
Later, saints from Thāpāthalī replaced Daśanāmī ascetics.
There was a tradition of donating goats and sheep for sacrifice from the maṭha for Bhīmsena jātra and the Jalavināyaka deity in Cobhāra.
During Dasaiṃ, a ghaṭṭa would be installed on the day of Mahāṣṭamī, and animal sacrifices were performed.
The public would also gather to receive tīkā from the Mahantas (Pande VS 2059, pp. 46–48).
Occasionally, Rudrī recitations were also organized (Pande VS 2059, p. 47).
Traditionally, Nevāra Rajopādhyāya priests performed these rituals, though they have now been mostly replaced by Nepali Brahmāṇa Upādhyāyas.
Currently, Gokarṇa Purī, residing in the northern building, performs daily morning rituals.
On the first floor, the trust's (guthi) office for Maru Gaṇeśa operates alongside space dedicated to storing various items associated with the deity.

While the precise construction year of the Dyaḥchẽ remains uncertain, inscriptions present within (as detailed in the 'historical events' section below) attribute its creation to Subbā Dharma Nārāyaṇa Mānandhara.
A copperplate inscription on the third floor mentions that the Dyaḥchẽ underwent renovation in 1994 CE (VS 2051), funded by both the Kathmandu Metropolis and contributions from trust members.

The devastating 2015 CE earthquakes inflicted substantial damage upon the Dyaḥchẽ, leading to its reconstruction in 2018 CE (VS 2075), chiefly funded by the Kathmandu Metropolis and the Maru Gaṇeśa trust.

Chāy Bāhāḥ Maṭha is one of the five monastic buildings of ascetics in Patan, managed by the Bhāratī caste group of the Daśanāmī ascetics.Śaṅkarācārya, a renowned ascetic and philosopher, is credited with founding themaṭhatradition in India in the 8th century.
To ensure the continuity of his philosophy, he established fourmaṭhasin different parts of India and appointed four of his foremost disciples as the heads of these institutions.
In Nepal, the Daśanāmī ascetics were warmly received by the state when they arrived to propagate their philosophy, receiving substantial support for constructingmaṭhas.
It was constructed during the reign of King Yakṣa Malla and was later opened to the public after the king’s death in 1486 CE (NS 606) (cf.Amatya1988, p. 1).
It was constructed during the reign of King Yoga Narendra Malla in 1696 CE (NS 816) (Pandey2059, p. 11).
In another publication,Pandey(2059, p. 2) mentions that themaṭhasin Patan were constructed during the reign of King Rājya Prakāśa Malla (r. 1745-1758 CE).
There are no historic sources that precisely date the initial construction of Chāy Bāhāḥ Maṭha.
According to oral tradition, it was constructed by Jayakiśora Bhāratī.
The architecture of themaṭhasuggests that it was built during the Late Malla period.

The earliest historical record from themaṭhais a bell inscription from 1748 CE (NS 868), which mentions that a person named Rāya Bhāratī (text: Rāya Bhārthi) offered two bells to Kāśī Viśveśvara enshrined at themaṭha.
In the same year, Rāya, the son of Jayakiśora Bhāratī, also endowed lands to establish aguthifor the performance of daily and other rituals at themaṭha.
Another ascetic, Hirālāla Bhāratī, formed aguthiin 1907 CE (VS 1964) for performing daily rituals here.
The 1934 earthquakes damaged the north-eastern and eastern sections of themaṭha.
In 1945 CE (VS 2002), Bhāvalāla Bhāratī laid marble tiles on the floor and walls of themaṭha.
The southeastern section of themaṭhawas partially damaged in the 2015 earthquake, and members of themaṭhaundertook renovations to repair the damage.
Although thesemaṭhaswere founded on Śaṅkarācārya’s philosophy, themaṭhasconstructed in the Newar settlements bear a strong influence of Newar culture and language.
The medieval inscriptions at themaṭhaare written in the Newar language.
An inscription from 1748 CE (NS 868) reveals that Sitārāma Bhaṭṭa was the priest of Chāy Bāhāḥ Maṭha at that time.
Themaṭha'sanniversary (varṣavarddhana) is observed on the 6th of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, marked by a fire oblation.
On Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī, the birth anniversary of Lord Kṛṣṇa observed on the 8th of the dark fortnight of Bhādra, fakirs from Kālamocana in Thapathali are invited to themaṭhaand offered food.

A bonfire is set in front of the main shrine on Śivarātrī, the 14th of the dark fortnight of Phālguna, during which legumes are dry-heated and sweet dishes are prepared over the fire to be distributed to the locals.
A water tank was constructed in the northern region of Kathmandu in Chetrapāṭī to meet the city's need for water and also established a Nārāyaṇa temple nearby at Thāymadu ṭola.
The temple has two tiers of copper roof, which replaced theā̃ypātile roof in VS 2048 (1991 CE) in the course of a renovation.
A stone statue of Nārāyaṇa in standing position is installed as the main deity of this temple.
As the previous statue was stolen, locals installed a new one in VS 2049 (1992 CE).
There is a stone pillar with a statue of Garuḍa on top erected in front of the temple.
The Garuḍa figure was dated NS 783 (1663 CE) (Pruscha, K-31).
It was also stolen and was replaced by a new one in VS 2049 (1992 CE).
Although the temple is said to date back to the Licchavi period, no inscription has been recovered to support the claim.
A copperplate inscription, dated NS 916 (1795 CE), at the temple records donation of land by Narasiṃha Bhāro for the anniversary ritual and some utensils for the Dvādaśī Guthi.
The temple also received the protection of metal railings in VS 2049 (1992 CE) when it was renovated.
Notably, the Sarasvatī statue, previously kept outside in the southwest, has been relocated inside for security reasons.
The bell, originally from the Viṣṇudevī Dyaḥchẽ, is currently housed within the sanctum due to ongoing renovations at thedyaḥchẽ.
No records have been found regarding the construction of this temple.
Based on the temple's artwork, it is estimated to have been built during the medieval period (Ṭ. Śreṣṭha and Ḍ Śarmā 2019, p. 138).
In 1669 CE (NS 789), atoraṇawas installed for Akṣobhya residing inside thecaitya’s eastern niche.
Thecaityawas renovated in 1776 CE (NS 896).
Thecaityato the south of the temple (PNG0030-009) was built in 1881 CE (NS 1001).
The temple was damaged in the 2015 earthquakes, and was renovated with a copper roof in 2024 CE (VS 2080) with the help of the Department of Archaeology.
The temple is built on the model of Newar temples with multiple roofs and a peristyle.
It is built with bricks and mud mortar.
Viṣṇu, Narasiṃha Bābu, Nārāyaṇa Bābu and others from Lagana ṭola,Kathmandu constructed thesataḥin Jalavināyaka’s honour, and also endowed land in 1817 CE (NS 937).
It was severely damaged in the Grest Earthquakes of 1934 CE (VS 1990).
Govinda Dāsa Bābu Rājavaṃsi, the descendent of the original builder, reconstrcted it in 1939 CE.
After it was damaged through the 2015 earthquakes, the Department of Archaeology reconstructed it in 2019 CE.
The masonry is entirely new, however, some historic elements such as columns and capitels were reused during the reconstruction.

He wears a crown engraved with depictions of Candra (the moon deity) and Sūrya (the Sun deity), serpent earrings, a garland around his neck, and the Sacred Thread (janai) (S. Mānandhara VS 2047, p. 21).
The base of the seat on which Dakṣiṇāmūrti sits is adorned with 22 small statues of sages (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p. 585; M. Thāpā VS 2077, p. 243).

text: The construction of the Dakṣiṇāmūrti Mandira does not have any historical evidence.

According to a manuscript in the possession of the temple's priest, King Rudra Malla (r. 1295-1326 CE) established Dakṣiṇāmūrti on the full moon day of Āṣāḍha in 1317 CE (NS 437) to alleviate a severe drought and wind that affected his kingdom.
The suggestion to establish Dakṣiṇāmūrti came from his royal priest Deva Śarmā Rājopādhyāya.
The drought and wind subsided after the installation of Dakṣiṇāmūrti.

According toBhāṣā Vaṃśāvalī, a chronicle from the late 18th century, Vimalānanda Svāmī established Dakṣiṇāmūrti during the reign of King Nṛpendra Malla (r. 1674-1680) to protect people from hailstorms (D. Lamsāla VS 2023, p. 93).
The gilded finial atop the temple was donated by Upendra Vikrama Śāha, the second son of King Rājendra Vikrama Śāha.
However, these rituals were discontinued after the finial was stolen (D. Lamsāla VS 2023, p. 93).

In 1884 CE (VS 1941), the temple priest Abhayānanda Rājopādhyāya donated 20 ropanīs of land, which he received as a royal grant three years earlier, to establish a trust for the daily rituals and maintenance of the Dakṣiṇāmūrti Mandira.
The donation was intended for cleaning the temple area and renovating the rest house.
The temple underwent renovation in 1934 following an earthquake that caused some damage.
During this renovation, the traditional roof tiles were replaced with corrugated metal sheets.
Another renovation by the Paṣupatikṣetra Vikāsa Koṣa took place in 1989 CE (VS 2045/46) due to the deteriorating condition of the temple S. Mānandhara VS 2047, p. 24; M. Thāpā VS 2077, p. 243).
Bāgha Dhārā, located on Pragatī Mārga in Bhīmasenagolā Ṭola, Mid-Baneshwor, Kathmandu, is distinctive for its tiger-shaped water spout constructed by Śiva Śaṃkara Koirālā in 1860 CE (VS 1917).
A marble inscription identifies it additionally asMajor Bājeko Dhārā, referring to its builder.
The structure has been maintained over generations by the builder’s descendants.
Kṛṣṇa Prasāda Koirālā undertook repairs in 1914 CE (VS 1971), followed by restorations by Murārī Prasāda and Mādhava Prasāda Koirālā in 1954 CE (VS 2011) and 1990 CE (VS 2047), respectively.
In 2014 CE (VS 2071), pillars and a roof were added.
The water ceased to flow regularly after 2013 CE (VS 2070), now (as of July 2025 CE) appears only seasonally between the months of Śrāvaṇa and Asoja (the rainy season).
Constructed west of Bāghabhairava Mandira (KIR0004), Nāsaḥdyaḥ Capāḥ is a two-floored modern building with its terrace covered by corrugated tin sheets.
It used to be a two-storied building with aphalcāon the ground floor andjhĩgaṭītile roof on top.
It is unclear when the Capāḥ was initially constructed.
It is possible that it was constructed around the same time the temple of Bāghabhairava was constructed forbhajanaperformances.
The photos taken byJohn C. Huntingtonin 1970 CE andNiels Gutschowin 1990 CE suggest that there used to be two rest houses.
Two buildings are clearly visible in the place where Nāsaḥdyaḥ Capāḥ now stands.
The two rest houses were dismantled and rebuilt in 1997 CE (VS 2054) out of the fund collected from a grand fire oblation program.
The northern side of the Capāḥ’s ground floor contains a stone statue of Lord Rāma established in 1961 CE (VS 2018).
On the southern side, one can see a metal statue of Lord Kṛṣṇa, which was established by Śerabahādura Maharjana from Kirtipur.
Although the year of its establishment is not mentioned in the inscription, locals say that it was established c. 1976 CE.
Temple of Bhairava containing a 14th century inscription.
The monument is located on a small hill, south of the Dullu palace (now destroyed).
It is built in bricks and covered by two-storied tile roofs.
Inside the sanctum, a small stepped platform is built along the south-western wall.
The first roof is supported by wooden pillars installed all around the sanctum.
An inscribed stone stele is installed against the wall, on the right side of the door.
It is inscribed in Nāgarī script and dated from ŚS 127(?) (135(?) CE).
The stele's typology and epigraphic features are very similar to those of the stele found a the Bāleśvara Mandira (DLK0340), dated of ŚS 1277 (1355 CE).
The actual monument may have been built in the 19th century, or during the 20th century.
A building of the Nepal Police was recently built in the western side of the hill.
A ping pong table made of cement was built 2 meters west of the Bhairava Temple.
A statue of Unmatta Bhairava is usually established on the southern side of Śiva temples in Nepal.
This statue of Unmatta Bhairava is established in the southern side of Kumbheśvara Mandira.
It was originally tiled withjhĩgaṭībut replaced with copper in 1982 CE (VS 2038).
There are three statues of devotees established in the temple’s plinth, outside the sanctum.
The couple’s statue was placed here in 1723 CE (NS 843).
An inscription from 1392 CE (NS 512) related to the Kumbheśvara Mandira is also installed here.
Right next to the entrance, adjacent to this inscription, there is another smaller pedestal with an inscription on it.
The golden statue mentioned in the inscription is missing and only the pedastal remains in the present-day.
There is no documented evidence to appoint the temple’s initial construction.

However, the anniversary rituals (varṣavarddhana) of both Kumbheśvara Mandira and Unmatta Bhairava are performed on the same day, giving rise to the speculation that it too was established around the same time, 1392 CE (NS 512), as the Kumbheśvara Mandira.
ASaṃkha Bahālhas been built by the Avāles caste, and apañcāvali caityastands in front (to the east) of Cvachẽ Phalcā.
Below it are traces of inscription.
Below is an eroded inscription where one can read 'śake 1330' (1408 CE).
Stone pillars were erected throughout the Karnali Basin from the 13th to the 17th century.
They are installed to honor the memory of deceased persons, mostly warriors.

In this case it is possible to situate the Thokreya stone memorial pillars between the 14th and the 15th century on the basis of their shape and the inscription of 1408 CE on pillar 004 (seeAndolfatto 2019: p. 108).

Twodharmadhātujinālaya caityas, commonly referred to aschaturamukha caitya(i.e acaityawhich has four faces) and adharmadhātu maṇḍalaarelocated on the western side of the main road at Hitipusaḥ Jaḥrũ, Dampāchẽ, Sunāguthi.
On the request of the locals, the Department of Archaeology rebuilt thedyaḥchẽin VS 2044 (1987 CE).
Agandhakuṭī,having the shape of a three-bayedphalcā,is established in its first floor and surrounded by open space in order to facilitate the devotees to circumambulate it.

The stone statue of Akṣobhya, enshrined as thegandhurī devatāin the sanctum inside thegandhakuṭī,got stolen long ago, thus Satya Vajrācārya, a resident of Bhindya Bāhāḥ (LAL1880) installed a new Akṣobhya statue in around 2015-2016 CE (VS 2072-2073) at the same place where the stolen statue was enshrined.
ADharmadhātu Maṇdalaand fourcaityasare installed on thebahī’s courtyard.
Although there are no evidence to appoint the initial construction of thebahī, the presence of twoLicchavi Caityasin the courtyard suggests that it was built during the Licchavi Period.
The Lalitpur Metropolitan Office financed the renovation of the northeast face of thebāhīcourtyard in VS 2071 (2014 CE), and its southeast face is under renovation as of September 202).
An inscription on the lower portion of the plain stone records the establishment of the shrine in 1684 CE (NS 810).
However, the inscription does not mention the name of the donor.
Therefore, the shrine was probably established by the ancestors of the Śreṣṭha clan.
They occasionally renovate the shrine as well.
The shrine was established in 1684 CE (NS 810) by the ancestors of the Śreṣṭha clan, as they come here for the annual worship on Akṣaya Tṛtīyā.
The lower portion of the plain stone has an inscription documenting the establishment of the shrine, but the donor's name is not mentioned.
The Śreṣṭha clan occasionally renovates the shrine.
In 550 CE (ŚS 472), Bhāravi, grandson of Licchavi King Mānadeva, constructed the Satyanārāyaṇa Hiti in Hā̃ḍīgāũ, near the Satyanārāyaṇa Mandira (KAT3080), just north of the main road.
A worn Umāmaheśvara statue (KAT3082-005) on the northern wall, believed to date back to the 7th century (J. Regmi, VS 2057), bears a fragment of Licchavi-eracaitya’s niche.
Themakaraspouts’ distinctive features, like almond-shaped eyes and missing tongues, confirm their Licchavi origin (S. Khanal, VS 2068).

Bhāravi, praised in the inscription as powerful, humble, patient, and generous, built thehitifor public benefit, providing clean, cool water on the 12th of the bright fortnight of Phālguna in 550 CE (ŚS 472).
The inscription, originally at the raised platform in Hā̃ḍīgāũ, was later moved to the National Museum, Chhauni (D. Vajracharya, VS 2030).

Bhāravi is considered the son of Mānadeva’s daughter Vijayavatī, married to Devalābha, though some dispute this, as Mānadeva had other queens (Kṣemasundarī, Guṇavatī) whose daughters are unknown (H. Suvedi, VS 2053).
Twenty years later, in 570 CE (ŚS 492), Bhāravi built the Maṃgaḥ Hiti in the Patan Durbar Square (LAL1360).

Thehitiand temple share a cultural link: temple priests usedhitiwater for daily worship (temple priest, Śreṣṭha, male, age 55), and folklore claims Lord Nārāyaṇa bathed here at midnight (S. Khanal, VS 2068).
Thehiti’s source, Nyālma Pukhū, was disrupted in 1999 CE by a nearby tube well, causing thehitito dry temporarily (S. Tivārī 2023, p. 100).
Here, a three-tiered temple structure has been erected by incorporating thedyahchẽitself into the architectural design.
The tangible image installed on the first floor of the shrine represents the intangible goddess believed to reside outside the settlement—a tradition common to many Newar communities.
The originalmukhākṛtis (metallic face-plaques) of these deities were stolen during the c. 1960s CE (VS 2020s), and the present ones are replicas; only the face ofGaṇeśaremains an original piece.
The building that houses these images was originally a rectangular, east–west oriented two-storeyeddyahchẽṃ.
At the temple’s frontage stand two stone lions dated to 1720 CE (NS 790), flanking a richly ornamented wooden doorway surmounted by atoraṇa.
The presenttoraṇais a modern replica, replacing the original that was stolen during the 1990s CE (VS 2050s).
In earlier times, all three roofs were covered with traditional clay tiles (jhigāṭī), but during post-earthquake restoration works, these were replaced by copper sheets.
No inscription precisely dating the temple’s construction has yet been discovered.
The earliest known inscription from the site dates to 1670 CE (NS 790), recording the dedication of a pair of lion statues in honor of Viṣṇudevī and Indrāyaṇī (D. Vajrācārya VS 2056, p. 167).
This inscription treats Viṣṇudevī and Indrāyaṇī as deities of equal rank.

A comparable transformation is observed in Nuwakot, where the medieval temple of GaṇḍakīBhairava evolved into the Bhairavī Temple during the Śāha period, as Bhairavī(Viṣṇudevī)gained prominence (D. Vajrācārya & T. Śreṣṭha VS 2037, p. 3).
On the third floor, a statue of Vajrasattva is installed in between four small windows.
In front of the Bāhāḥ’s main building, twocaityas–aśoka caityaanddharmadhātujinālaya caitya–have been established.
The Tulādharas who live in the courtyard claim that their ancestors built the Bāhāḥ and handed it over to the Vajrācāryas of Dhvākhā Bāhāḥ.
The earliest record from the Bāhāḥ is an inscription engraved on thetoraṇaabove the entrance to the sanctum in 1651 CE (NS 771).
Other historical events that took place at the Bāhāḥ include the refurbishment of the Bāhāḥ’s main deity (kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ) in 1785 CE (NS 905) and 1811 CE (NS 931).

The inscription from NS 931 (i.e., 1811 CE, see below) records the construction of a balconied pinnacle (phucā) on the Bāhāḥ’s roof and the installation of a Vajrasattva statue there, but no such structure can be seen today.
The Bāhāḥ most likely collapsed at some point in history, and instead of rebuilding the balconied pinnacle, an additional floor was added.
Adharmadhātujinālaya caityawas built at the Bāhāḥ premises in 1885 CE (see the inscription from NS 1005 below).
The 2015 earthquakes exacerbated damage to the Bāhāḥ, which was already in poor condition.
Although local legend attributes the temple’s construction to Gaṃgā Mahārānī, no verifiable historical records confirm this claim.
To provide easier access for devotees, she reportedly established a replica of the deity here with proper rituals (local resident, Śreṣṭha, male, age 67; Pant 2019, p. 141).

text: During renovations, this space was integrated into the temple’s western façade to build aphalcā(resting place) that now adjoins the temple.
After the statue was stolen, a broken stone water spout was repurposed as the base for a new Garuḍa statue (THI0130-002) installed atop it.
The temple was built during the reign of Trailokya Malla and Queen Mother Gaṃgā Rānī (1561-1610 CE) (Pant 2019, p. 141).
While local tradition attributes the temple's construction to Gaṃgā Rānī, no definitive historical records corroborate this claim.
A stone inscription on the western plinth of thecaityain front of the temple notes its establishment by Sunasiṃha Prajāpati.
The inscription's date, however, remains illegible.
According to records in the National Archives, thephalcānear the Nārāyaṇa temple was built in 1726 CE (NS 846) by Jayamohana Duvāra (S. Rājavaṃśī, P. Śreṣṭha VS 2078, p. 198).
A stone pillar erected by Kaviprasāda Gautama in 1949 CE (VS 2006) stands on the site.
In 2004 CE (VS 2061), the temple underwent renovation through a collaborative effort between the German UDLE program (GTZ) and local community members.
They are in the heart of Dullu, north-east of the former king's palace (destroyed by Maoists in April 2002 CE, cf. Lecomte-Tilouine 2009b).

text: Between 2014 CE and 2022 CE, a metal fence was built around the platform.
The statue was one meter away from the 13th-15th century temples (Patangini Devala and Vijayabhagavatī Mandira) when it was surveyed in 2014 CE.
It has been lying outside the temple compound, amidst trash, since the construction of a wall around the monuments.
A partly dismantledśikharatemple from approx. 13th-15th century.
The monument consists in oneśikharatemple erected by the side of the main track in the settlement of Sejuvālagāũ (at a few hundred meters north-west of Samālgāũ).
The south-western side of the monument, where the door was placed, is partly dismantled.
Such temples generally have empty sanctums (which was probably not the case at the time of their consecration).
It is therefore very unlikely that amūrticould have been stolen from this temple.
The current brass made Akṣobhya statue is enshrined recently[1]after the previous one made of stone was stolen from the sanctum in 2012 CE (VS 2069).

Two brothers, Kuladeva and Caityarāja (supported by Kuladeva’s son Mānadeva), had jointly built this Bāhāḥ, installed the aforementioned stone statue of Akṣobhya in the sanctum, and established a Dharmadhātu Manḍala in the Bāhāḥ’s courtyard in 1928 CE (NS 1048).
The Caitya, which has also been erected in the courtyard, is probably older than the Bāhāḥ itself.
The bell offered to the Caitya in 1920 CE (NS 1040) by the same two brothers has evidential value for dating.
One of the fourphalcāsbuilt at Kirtipur's Gutpau Square is the Gutpau Cībhāḥ Phalcā.
The three-bay Phalcā, built in front of the Gutpau Caitya (KIR0021), has a simple design and faces northwest.
There are no sources that indicate when the Phalcā was first built.
Before the 2015 earthquakes, it was already in a deteriorated state, which caused more harm to the Phalcā.
In 2020 CE, the Department of Archaeology rebuilt it.
There is still an activeguthithat is connected to the Phalcā.
On Kati Punhi, the full moon day of Āśvina, the Guthi cleans the Phalcā and applies whitewash to the Gutpau Caitya.
In 2022 CE, only three lions were found in situ.
A small shed built to the north-east of the platform houses a large stoneāmalakaand akalaśa.
Tripurasundarī is situated at the center of Bhaktapur, a city founded in the shape of ayantra.
When Tripurasundarī is added to thegaṇa(group) oftheAṣṭamātṛkā, the eight mother goddesses, they become Navadurgā, the nine forms of Durgā.
Facing north, Vidyāpīṭha Āgaṃchẽ is a four-story building topped with a set of three finials of gilt copper.
Kusumarāma Karmācārya had offered the finials during the reign of King Viśva Malla in NS 674 (1554 CE).
Thetoraṇawith Tripurasundarī as the central deity is dated NS 1032 (1912 CE).
It was initially placed on top of the main entrance of theāgaṃchẽbut was later shifted to the first floor due to the fear of being stolen.
The first floor is theāgaṃof this building where Śiva along with Tripurasundarī are enshrined as the principal deity.
The adjoining building to the west of theāgaṃchẽis the god-house (dyaḥchẽ), where the initiation ritual takes place.
Ahiticonstructed by Viśvarāja in NS 632 (1512 CE) can be seen west of theāgaṃchẽ.
King Ānandadeva is credited to have expanded Bhaktapur into a large city under the protection of the Aṣṭamātṛkā deities in Kaligat Samvat 4197 (1096 CE) (Devamālā Vaṃśāvalī2013, p. 104).
He also constructed a royal palace named Tripura (The Gopālarājavaṃśāvalī, folio 25a).
It is unclear if the king had constructed the palace at the place where Tripurasundarī was enshrined or he also constructed a temple for the deity after building the palace.
The Tripura Palace was constructed east of the current palace building.
Historic sources recording the founding of Tripura Vidyāpīṭha are not available as is the establishment of Tripurasundarī.
The Karmācāryas of the Vidyāpīṭha clan are offereddekhāon a suitable day ahead of Nāga Pañcamī, the day of serpent worship.
A fire oblation takes place on the ground floor of Vidyāpīṭha every year from the 1st till 4th of the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa.
Although there are records of many plots of land donated to the Vidyāpīṭha, it has no source of income at the moment due to the loss of the donated lands.
The Malla kings used to get the priests of Taleju to officiate major fire oblations.
King Bhūpatīndra Malla had employed the Karmācārya priests of Taleju to consecrate the Nyātapola temple.
The king had offered a golden crown to the Karmācāryas on the occasion.
The crown dated NS 822 (1702 CE) is still safe at theāgaṃof Tripura Vidyāpīṭha (J. L. Vaidya2061).

The Dagu Bāhāḥdyaḥchẽ(main monastic building), a five-story structure, faces north, and the sanctum is on the ground floor, where a clay statue of Akṣobhya is consecrated as the Bāhāḥ’s main deity (kvāḥpāḥdyah).
Fivecaityashave been established on the Bāhāḥ premises, inhabited by the caste group of Tulādharas.
They, too, contribute to Bāhāḥ's timely renovations.
An inscription from 1684 CE (NS 804) on acaityais the earliest historical record associated with the Bāhāḥ (cf.Locke 1985, p.300).
Because the Bāhāḥ is currently being renovated (September 2022), the debris has been collected in the courtyard, making it impossible to determine which of the fivecaityasthis inscription belongs to.
In 1899 CE (NS 1019), Cikāji Tulādhara and others established acaityain front of the Bāhāḥ and laid the courtyard withcikaṃaḥpā(see historical events below).
On the same occasion, they also installed the statues of two of the Buddha’s closest disciples Sāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, Sarasvatī, and Gaṇeśa and covered the sanctum door with brass sheets.
A person named Bhāirājā Tulādhara sponsored the renovation of thekvāḥpāḥdyaḥin 1984 CE (NS 1104).
Later, in 1992 CE (NS 1112), he offered atoraṇa.
The two-bay Bhāginanī Phalcā had three-bays until it was dismantled in 2008 and incorporated into a six-storey concrete structure.
The previous inscription was reinstalled in this building.
Athaḥ Bāhāḥ is a branch of Kvāḥ Bāhāḥ and was constructed some time before 1658 CE.
The three-storey building faces east, and two guarding lions flank its entrance.
Metal flags donated in 1935 CE have been erected on both sides of the door.
The oldest inscription found in the Bāhāḥ records the paving ofteliyābricks in its courtyard and is dated NS 862 (1662 CE).
The three medieval cities of the Kathmandu Valley were founded under the protection of theaṣṭamātṛkāpīṭhas.
However, a proper statue of these deities are established at thedyaḥchẽwithin the city.
Thepīṭhaof Indrāyaṇī locally known as Pīgaṃdyaḥ (KIR0007) is established in the western part of Kirtipur outside the city proper.
The Indrāyaṇī Dyaḥchẽ has a woodentoraṇaon top of the main entrance to the two-storey building.
There are no inscriptions to shed light on the construction of the building nor of its sponsor.
A copper-plate inscription dated NS 899 (1778 CE) records the covering of the roof of the palanquin with brass and copper sheets and offering of finials.
The copper-plate is the oldest inscription obtained from the building so far.
The recent reconstruction of thedyaḥchẽtook place in NS 1128 (2008 CE).
A year after, the lion statues, bell andtoraṇawere added.
The metal statue of Indrāyaṇī was stolen back in the early 1970s.
A new statue replaced the stolen one in VS 2032 (1975 CE).
Thekalasacolumns are remarkably delicate and are original to the building.
The building was severely damaged as a result of the 2015 earthquakes and is braced with wooden beams in order to prevent its collapse.
A photograph taken in February 2015 shows the column on the extreme left missing; since then the central column was stolen.
In August 2023, following an order by the Mayor who cited the damagedsataḥas a safety hazard, the Lalitpur Municipal Police demolished thesataḥ.
Neither the date of its initial construction nor of its renovation could be determined.
Since the inner wall of the Phalcā is completely covered by the items displayed there, it was not possible to determine whether any statues or inscriptions are embedded in it.
Located in the Ināy Ṭola, Madhyapur Thimi, the Bhavānīśaṅkara temple is a brick structure built in theśikharastyle, topped with a metallic finial.

The temple, originally built by Indrasiṃha Duvāra in 1648 CE (as recorded in the inscription dated NS 769 on the beam above the temple entrance; see 'Historical Events'), sustained damage during the 2015 CE earthquakes.
It was subsequently restored with financial support from the Madhyapur Thimi Municipality and local community contributions.
Following the reconstruction, the statue of Bhavānīśaṅkara was ceremoniously reinstalled in the sanctum in 2020 CE.
A new idol of Akṣobhya in the east was installed after the previous one was stolen.
Locals believe that Maurya Emperor Aśoka constructed this Caitya and hence call it Aśoka Caitya., which, however, is a generic name for manycaityas.
A pipal tree grows ou of the Caitya in VS 2017 (1960 CE), rendering it on the verge of collapse.
The locals uprooted the pipal tree and renovated the Caitya.
In VS 2036 (1979 CE), cracks appeared on thetrayodaśabhuvanabut the locals restored it too.
The classical name of Konti Bahī is Kāśyapamiśrasaṃskārita Lalitavarṇamahāvihāra, which suggests that a person named Kāśyapa Miśra either established or restored thebahī.
Thebahībuildings were severely damaged in the 2015 earthquake.
The single storey building was constructed after the earlier cracked building at the northern corner was dismanted.
In the first half of 2020, the southern building remained under construction, while the restoration process of the eastern building had not yet begun.
A historical photo of the monument shows that there was once a veranda on the first floor of the buildings.
A historical photo of the building shows atoraṇafixed on the veranda in front of theāgamaroom, however, it is now missing.
Previously, a similar statue made of clay and gold clad was enshrined here, but this was stolen in 2001.
The lower part of this statue of Buddha’s leg broke off during the theft and has been preserved in the sanctum.
TheNepālikabhūpavaṃśāvalī(12.7-37) chronicle mentions the establishment of thebahī.
The King offered him land near the Aśoka Caitya, and he built a monastic building there.
Both of them settled in Patan, where they established two monasteries named Dunta and Lalivana respectively.
The family was reunited, and Sunayaśrī built them a house called Chokā near hisvihāra.
The oldest inscription of the Bahī is dated NS 743.
If one considers the Licchavi Dharmacakra, Aśoka Caitya and the story of the chronicle, it seems likely that the Bahī was established in the Licchavi period.
Majority of the scholars conclude that this Bāhāḥ was constructed by Jagata Varmā, a Mahāpātra of Patan, almost at the same time when he constructed Cilancva Caitya (KIR0001) in 1515 CE.

However, the inscription recording the construction of this Caitya does not explicitly mention Cilancva Bāhāḥ, but refers to this area as 'Padmakāṣṭhagīri which resembles the heaven (padmakāṣṭhagīri bhanne nāmale svargajastai suhāiraheko ṭhāũ).
It indicates that Jagata Pāla could have established a Bāhāḥ called Padmakāṣṭhagīri in the Cilancva premises which was later known as Cilancva Bāhāḥ.
[1]He also renovated Bāghabhairava Mandira (KIR0004) in 1571 CE (NS 635).
Since his wife Rūpalakṣmī (cf.D. VajrācāryaVS 2056, 478) was from Kirtipur (Locke1985, 180), she could have encouraged him to construct and renovate these highly significant monuments.
A pair of lions installed in 1716 CE (NS 836) flanks thedyaḥchẽ’s main entrance.
Twotrikhājhyāḥsare also installed on thedyaḥchẽ’sfirst floor, right above these additional doors.
The woodentoraṇaabove the main entrance was stolen sometime ago, thus thetoraṇa, crowning the eastern door, was shifted here.
Thetoraṇas, kept above its eastern door, were removed during the renovation of thedyaḥchẽbuilding in 2015 CE.
They were completely destroyed during the renovation of the building (cf.Ś. ŚreṣṭhaVS 2057, 67).
The roof of thedyaḥchẽis tiled withjhĩgaṭīand apuracrowned by three pinnacles is installed on its top.
Locke(1985, 180) mentions the beams, which support the aforementioned balcony, bearing the inscriptions from 1629 CE (NS 749) and 1680 CE (NS 800).
They suggest that the Bāhāḥ must have been renovated in those dates.
A local resident named Candramāna Vajrācārya repaired the roof in around 1889 CE after it was destroyed by a wind (Ś. ŚreṣṭhaVS 2057, 68).
The latest renovation of thedyaḥchẽwas carried out by the Department of Archaeology after it was destroyed during the 2015 CE earthquakes.
Because of a dispute that arose amongst thesaṅghamembers in around 1980 CE, the statues were handed over to the Guṭhī Saṃsthāna and National Museum (cf.Ś. ŚreṣṭhaVS 2057, 68-69).

Footnotes^This Bāhāḥ is referred to as ‘Padmakāṣṭhagīri Gũ Vihāra concerted according to the customs’ in the invitation letter sent from Paśupati Bāhāḥ to the member of Cilancva Bāhāḥ in 1574 (NS 694) requesting them to participate to the Samyak festival (cf.VajrācāryaVS 2061, 117).
Since the invitation letter does not refer to the Bāhāḥ as consecrated by Jagatapāla, one may cast doubt on whether he was its initial constructor.
The sanctum houses a statue of Kumāra (Kārtikeya), which M. Khanāla (VS 2074, p. 171) dates to the late 8th century.
This interpretation is supported by both M. Khanāla (VS 2074, p. 171) and Slusser (2005, p. 92).
While precise records of the temple's initial construction are elusive, the sculptural style of the Kumāra statue suggests a late 8th-century origin (M. Khanāla, VS 2074, p. 171).
Although the temple itself lacks inscriptions, a nearby rest house contains two inscribed stones.

One inscription (KAT3070_I_001) from 1700 CE (NS 820) documents an offering of gold ornaments and a crowning jewel (cūḍāmaṇi) to "Khatadeva." Khatadeva appears to refer to Kumāra in local dialect, as he is worshipped on “ṣaṣṭhī,” the 6th lunar day, and “ṣa” is frequently pronounced as “kha”.
Despite the inscription's partial erosion, it clearly mentions an offering of a finial to the thrice-venerated Parameśvarī.
Furthermore, the inscription locates the temple in Vijayapattana, an earlier name for the Hā̃ḍīgāũ area previously referred to as Viśālanagara as well (Pauḍela VS 2020, p. 78).
A second inscription (KAT3070_I_002) dating to 1701 CE (NS 821) records collective renovation efforts by trust members.
The inscription’s damaged state prevents a definitive determination of whether the renovation targeted the temple or the adjacent rest house.
Following the destructive 2015 CE earthquakes, the Department of Archaeology undertook a restoration project in 2023 CE (VS 2080), adhering to the temple's original architectural style.

Due to negligence, Purohitaghāṭa Sataḥ East, formerly erected by a family priest of Rāṇā descendance, remains confined to its ground floor (while sataḥs normally contain at least one additional floor).
Located to the east of three sataḥs built around the Śivālaya (KAT2730) at the center of Purohitaghāṭa, this structure derives its name from its location.
A photograph from 1982 CE (2039 VS) reveals that the ground floor originally featured five central bays with rectangular rooms on the sides.
However, the upper floor of this Sataḥ has collapsed, leaving only the ground floor intact.
While the other twosataḥshave been reconstructed, this one still awaits restoration.
Members of the Satyāla clan, known as the priests of the Rāṇā prime ministers, erected the Śivālaya and other monuments surrounding Purohitaghāṭa Sataḥ East.
Purohita ghāṭa, named after the monuments constructed by a priest (purohita), lies along the Bāgamatī river.
The Satyāla family, exclusive priests of the Rāṇā clan, were permitted to recite the Gāyatrī mantra to selected Rāṇās (P. Rāja, VS 2073, p.36).

Although there is no inscriptive evidence dating the construction of this Sataḥ, an inscription on the bell at the nerby Viṣṇu Mandir (KAT2730_I_002) records an offering made by Kāśirāja Paṇḍita Satyāla, his wife Bhavānīdevī, and son Śivarāja Paṇḍita in 1883 CE (VS 1940).

Another inscription (KAT2730_I_003) dating back to 1916 CE (VS 1973) documents the land allocation for a guṭhī by Kāśirāja and Bhavānīdevī, ordering their son Śivarāja Śarmā (Satyāla) and daughter-in-law regarding their involvement in various religious practices, including daily rituals, musical performances, Sadāvartā donations on Śivarātrī and anniversary rituals.
While the inscription doesn’t explicitly state the construction of the temple, it raises the question of whether the family constructed the temple and Sataḥ simultaneously or earlier.

However, the lālamohara (K_0021_0016) issued by King Surendra in 1874-75 CE (VS 1931), mentions the grant of four ropanīs of land for Purohitaghāṭa Sataḥ East built by Kāśīnātha, thus providing evidence that the Sataḥ existed before that date.

The Kathmandu Inventory, published in 1982 CE (VS 2039), attributed the construction of Purohitaghāṭa Sataḥ East to Śivarāja Śarma (Inventory VS 2039, p.138), based on the inscription from 1913 CE (VS 1973 VS).
However, the inscription itself does not provide clarity on this assertion.
Instead, it identifies Śivarāja as the son of the principal constructor.
Before the 2015 CE (VS 2072) earthquakes, Purohitaghāṭa Sataḥ East and other monuments of the Satyāla family were in a state of disrepair.
Subsequently, the other twosataḥswere reconstructed, leaving this one still in need of restoration.
The Bohorā family, residing in Purohitaghāṭa Sataḥ East for decades, propose that they have occupied it since its construction.
In circa 1998, GTZ/udle supported thephalcā's reconstruction to its original configuration: supported by 12 newly carved pillars, open to all sides and covered with a traditonal tile (jhĩgaṭī) roof.
Thephalcācollapsed in the earthquakes in 2015 and was reconstructed in 2017.

Constructed with a combination of bricks and stones and adorned with traditional plaster (bajra), the temple features a tower (śikhara) crowned by a gilded finial shaped like a ceremonial mirror surrounded by flames (jvalānhāykaṃ).
Unfortunately, a stolen statue of Garuḍa, once positioned on a pillar in front of the temple, is no longer present.
Later, King Jagataprakāśa Malla also visited the temple in 1670 CE (NS 790), as confirmed by a painting preserved in the Victoria and Albert Museum in London.

The painting includes the triad–Jagannātha, Subhadrā, Balabhadra–represented as wooden gods and an inscription that identifies the donor as Jagataprakāśa Malla as well as the ritual the painting celebrates (Gutschow 2000, p.nd / KVPT report).
Influence from the fame of Jagannātha in Puri might have inspired the Malla rulers to build temples of the triad in the valley that continued throughout the Śāha and Rāṇā period.

An inscription found in Nārāyaṇacaura, Naksal from the reign of King Jayadeva the second (713-733 CE) mentions two platforms known asponḍimaṇḍapikāandprekṣaṇamaṇḍapikā(D.VajrācāryaVS 2030, 569 andK. Tamot2013, 20).
Buṅgamatī's Karuṇāmaya Mandira (BUN0001) collapsed in the devastating earthquakes of 2015.
Since the restoration of the temple is likely to last many years, a temporary shrine building has been built on the foundation of thisdabūto house the deity.
This shrine building measures 412 × 412 cm and was built using regular brick in mud mortar.
These have been moved to stand in front of thedabū.
A bell suspended from a stone frame was also moved from its original location to the left of the shrine’s entrance.
Following the 2015 collapse of the Karuṇāmaya Mandira (BUN0001) this temporary shrine was built to house the main deity of Buṅgadyaḥ (BUN0001-008).
Also, two large stone lions (BUN0001-008), two small stone lions (BUN0001-009), and a bell suspended from a stone stand (BUN0001-010) were moved from the temple to the front of this temporary shrine.
No sources can be found with which to date the initial construction of thisdabū.
During the Rāṇā era, the construction of this Śiva temple is apparent, yet its exact origin remains uncertain due to the absence of historical records and the lack of theśivaliṅgain the sanctum.
The absence of inscriptions at the site leaves the donor's identity and the year of the temple's construction shrouded in mystery.
Despite the uncertainty surrounding its origins, the architectural characteristics suggest a construction date during the Rāṇā period (1846-1951 CE).
The temple had already collapsed before the 2015 earthquakes.
The Pashupati Area Development Trust undertook the temple's reconstruction in 2021 CE (VS 2078).
Remarkably, theśivaliṅgainside the sanctum has yet to be restored, even after the temple's reconstruction was completed.
A statue of donors, an image of Padmapāṇi Lokeśvara and a stone inscription are attached to the wall of the Phalcā.
No inscription providing information about the foundation of the Phalcā is available.
However, an inscription attached to the wall informs readers that in 1823 (NS 943) Chatrasiṃ from Iti Ṭola donated 101moharasfor its management.
This Phalcā was renovated in 1960, and it has also been renovated more recently.
These renovations maintained its traditional structure and were funded in by the Lalitpur Metropolitan City.
Lakṣmīśvara Mandira Pujārī Ghara was constructed as the residence of the priest from the Lakṣmīśvara Mandira (KAT2720).
There are no historic records regarding the date of construction of this building.

Located between the temple complexes of Lakṣmīśvara (built in 1812 CE) and Tīna Devala (built in 1850 CE), it is probable that Lakṣmīśvara Mandira Pujārī Ghara was built after Lakṣmīśvara Mandira was completed in 1812 CE (VS 1869) (cf.Tevārī el alVS 2020, 12-15 andPauḍelaVS 2022, 58).
The appointed priests used to live in this building until 1992 CE (VS 2049).
After the caretaker tried to register thie Priest's House as his personal property, the court decided that the caretaker and his family had to leave the building.
Already before the 2015 earthquakes the building was in a deplorable condition since parts of the northern section had collapsed already.
The 2015 CE earthquakes caused further severe damages and the partial collapse of the central part of the building.
In 2020 CE the structure was dismantled and rebuilt from the ground up with funding from the Asian Development Bank (ADB).
As of January 2021 CE, Lakṣmīśvara Mandira Pujārī Ghara is awaiting the completion of the traditional tile roof cover and interior finishes.
Currently, as of December 2023, the phalcā at Candraghāṭa, originally constructed for religious and cultural activities, are occupied by policemen from the Nepal Police Club.
Its design adheres to traditional principles, featuring five front bays with unique half-wall construction in the corner bays.
While the historical date of the phalcā is unknown, in 1926 CE (VS 1982), Candraśamśera constructed a stone-paved ghāṭa from Kālamocana ghāṭa to Purohita ghāṭa, including a dharmaśāla (KAT2745).
This suggests that the construction of the phalcā, along with the ghāṭa and dharmaśālā, aimed to provide accommodation for traditional healers (Ghāṭe Vaidya) and care for the ailing.
Guthi Chẽ 2 stands as the western edifice among the paired structures constituting the Guṭhī Saṃsthāna, prominently situated opposite the Matsyendranātha Mandira (LAL0060) in Taḥ Bāhāḥ.
This particular building serves as the administrative hub for the Patan division of the Guṭhī Saṃsthāna.

Given their lack of distinctive appellations, these structures are conventionally denoted as Guthi Chẽ (building) followed by numerical designations for identification purposes within this documentation.
Both of these Guthi buildings exhibit characteristics reminiscent of private residences, likely reconstructed in the aftermath of the seismic events of 1934 CE.
Adjacent to the building lies a northward courtyard, exclusive in access via this very edifice.
This courtyard finds application in the preparatory phases of constructing the Buṅgadyaḥ Chariot (LAL0001).
Furthermore, the building serves as a repository for an assortment of items linked to the Buṅgadyaḥ Chariot.
The establishment date of the Guṭhī Office's occupancy of this building remains unclear.

Yet, correspondences (K_0355_0066) dating back to the year 1907 CE (VS 1964) from Patan Potā Tahasila pertain to the priestly responsibilities concerning three significant temples at Patan Durbar Square.
This substantiates the existence of an establishment dealing withguthis in Patan prior to the establishment of the Patan Office of the Guṭhī Saṃsthāna at this location.
It is plausible that these two buildings may have also hosted Patan Potā Tahasila.
The historical application of these buildings and the courtyard for tasks related to Buṅgadyaḥ presumably dates back to the medieval era.
In recent years, this area has undergone some modern developments: a public toilet has been constructed, and the site is occasionally used for feasts and communal gatherings.
Another toilet has been added nearby for the convenience of important visitors to the adjacent Bagalāmukhī (Vagalāmukhī) shrine.
As of July 2025 CE, no regular religious rituals are observed at the site.
This shrine bears a brief inscription dated 1751 CE (NS 871), which records that a certain Dhanasiṃha Mulmī constructed both the pathway and thejaḥdhuṃ.
As of July 2025 CE, this shrine is no longer in use.

text: Most probably, it was built for those people using the Dathu Hiti, for instance, to change clothes after taking a bath or to do the laundry.

monument_name: Dathu Hiti Phalcā (c. mid-19th. cent. CE)

text: Dathu Hiti was constructed during the reign of Rāṇā Prime Minister Juddha Śamśera ( between 1932-45; seeLalitpur Sub-Metropolitan City2007, 39).
