monument_name: Dathu Hiti Phalcā (c. mid-19th. cent. CE)
text: In 2017 CE (VS 2074), it was reconstructed from the grounds up with support from the Municipality and the World Bank.
It is attached to the plinth of a residential building.
The owners of the building, a Śreṣṭha family, maintain that the Phalcā was constructed by their ancestors, and they are personally taking care of it.
An inscription, which details the construction of the Phalcā, is attached to the wall of the above-mentioned residential building.
An individual named Gyānasiṃha built the Phalcā in 1693 CE (NS 813).
The donor teamed with another individual named Dharama Bhabo to establish ahāthvaṃguṭhī.
A photograph published by John Hughes in 1976 CE shows corrugated tin sheets instead of thejhĩgaṭītiled roof.
It was reconstructed in 2018 CE by the Śreṣṭha family after it was damaged in the 2015 CE earthquakes.
The roof was tiled withjhĩgaṭībricks in a traditional manner during the reconstruction.

The inscription in the Phalcā tasks the members of Bajrācārya and Bhābo (Jyāpu) community, as part of itsguṭhī, to display an icon of Bhairava, and flow rice beer on the day of the Phalcā’s anniversary rituals.
The Bhairava statue was stolen, and theguṭhīland couldn’t be maintained, and thus the tradition was discontinued (local knowledge, resident of integrated house, Śreṣṭha, male, age 92).
Dhīrjanṛsiṃha Śākya (Gvārā Kampanī), the chief tailor of King Pṛthvī Vīra Vikrama Śāha, constructed the gate to please Candra Śamśera.
The roof is also constructed in brick masonry and covered in lime plaster shaped to resemble three tiers with a pinnacle in the form of astūpa.
Dhīrjanṛsiṃha Śākya (Gvārā Kampanī), a devotee ofCandra Śamśera and the chief of King Pṛthvī Vīra Vikrama Śāha's tailors constructed this gate to please Candra Śamśera.
Thisvihārawas constructed in 1660.
Before it was constructed, this courtyard was used by King Rudradeva (r. 1168-1174) to mete out justice (Śākya 1994, 42).
Known as Dhīrabhakteśvara, this śivālaya, or the abode of Lord Śiva, was constructed by Dhīra Śamśera, the youngest brother of Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā, in 1854 CE (VS 1911) as a tribute to himself.
A year later, in 1855 CE (VS 1912), he offered a bell and established a trust.
While G. Ṭaṇḍana (VS 2053, p. 770) and Michaels and Tandon (2017, p. 106) have identified this temple as Dīrabhakteśeśvara, the inscription on the temple bell confirms its name as Dhīrabhakteśvara.
Outside the temple, a bell from 1856 CE hangs from a bell stand to the south, commemorating its construction.
Additionally, a stone trident (triśūla) stands erected to the north of the temple, with a statue of Kāmadeva enshrined to the northeast.
Dhīra Śamśera Rāṇā established the temple in 1854 CE (VS 1911).
He also set up a trust by donating land parcels along with water and oil mills.
The income from the donations was to be used to carry out daily, annual, and periodic rituals at the temple.
A year later in 1855 CE (VS 1912), King Surendra formalized the donation of 50ropanīs of land for Dhīrabhakteśvara by issuing alālamohara.
The same year, Dhīra Śamśera installed a bell at the temple.
Dhīra Śamśera, the youngest brother of Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā, had 17 sons and had accompanied him on his England tour (P. Rāja VS 2071, p. 80).
He passed away in 1884 CE (VS 1941) after a bone of wild pheasant stuck in his throat (P. Rāṇā VS 2070, p. 121).
Seven of the nine Rāṇā prime ministers within the 65-year period from 1885 to 1951 CE (VS 1942-2007) were the sons and grandsons of Dhīra Śamśera.
After the temple's establishment, Dhīra Śamśera donated land parcels for the temple and established a trust to oversee various rituals and to pay for the services of the cleaners and musicians.
According to a record at the Guṭhī Saṃsthāna, there are 771ropanīs 2ānās of land in the name of Dhīrabhakteśvara Śivālaya (Guṭhī Saṃsthāna VS 2071, p. 34).
Records from the same chronicle also detail minor damage suffered by the shrine during the 1934 CE earthquakes (Devamālāvaṃśāvalī, p.66).

While the chronicle attributes the gilded roof's installation to King Rājendra, an inscription on the eaves facia (mhuraḥpau) states that the family of the late Viṣṇusiṃ Mānandhara undertook this task in his memory in 1847 CE (VS 1904).
In light of the shrine's deteriorating condition, a local trust named Aśoka Vināyaka Guthi reconstructed it in 2012 CE (VS 2069).
It was established in the 16th century by Mulmī Śreṣṭhas.
Thebāhāḥcan be accessed through a narrow alleyway underneath a private building.
The historic shrine building has been destroyed and a three storey RCC-frame structure was constructed in its place.
The building, not yet complete (as of 2018-07), has already started to deteriorate.
A stone threshold at the main door is the only remaining element of the original building.
The north-west corner of the courtyard has been made into an open vegetable garden, while the courtyard is now surrounded by buildings ranging from three to five stories in height.

The image ofkwāpā-dyais a small standing image of the Buddha showing theviśvavyākaraṇa mudrāand facing north."When thebāhāḥbegan to deterioriate, the descendants of its founders managed to gain some financial support from Lalitpur Municipality and in 1995-96 they started to reconstruct the building as a RCC structure.
After three installments, the Municipality cut its funding, arguing that thebāhāḥshould not be reconstructed with concrete.
Since then, the reconstruction process has stopped (2018-07).
A statue of Akṣobhya, the main deity of thebāhāḥ(Vajrācārya 1993, 123) was stolen and later replaced with a statue of Buddha standing in aviṣvavyākaraṇaposition.
Unfortunately, this second image was also stolen around 1981.
An investigation ensued, and the police managed to recover the stolen statue.

However, when people from the Bāhāḥ went to get the statue, the police refused to hand it over to them, stating that they need to be more responsible so as to prevent the statue from being stolen yet again.
The temple itself lacks any ancient inscriptions.

The earliest record, dating as late as 1991 CE (VS 2048), describes the Maṅkaḥ Khalaḥ, a Newar community organization from Hā̃ḍīgāũ’s Dathu Ṭola, constructing a balustrade of 108 lamps around the Dhanagaṇeśa temple.
In 2003 CE (VS 2060), Rameśanātha Pāṇḍe, a former minister, oversaw the temple's renovation, including the installation of a copper roof, a copper finial, a bell (KAT3100-009), and marble flooring.
The people of Cābahila are believed to have stolen the statue and installed it in their own community.
As the statue was dragged during the theft, Newars refer to Candravināyaka as "Lvahaṃsālā Gaṇedyaḥ," meaning "the dragged stone Gaṇeśa" (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p. 485).
Following this theft, the residents of Hā̃ḍīgāũ created a replacement statue, which is now revered as Dhanagaṇeśa.
The people of Hā̃ḍīgāũ attempted to relocate the Candravināyaka statue to their own area but were compelled to abandon it as dawn approached.
A temple was subsequently erected at the statue's abandoned location (Shakya 2006, p. 19).
Due to the absence of a dedicated endowment for the Dhanagaṇeśa procession, the local ward office manages it through a contractual arrangement.
The Nāsaḥdyaḥ Bhajana Phalcā, originally rebuilt in 1876 CE (VS 1932) with donations from locals, was rebuilt again in 2002 CE (VS 2079) and made larger than before.
Since it was built along with the Nāsaḥdyaḥ of this area, it was named the Nāsaḥdyaḥ Bhajana Phalcā.
This south-facing phalcā is built in the maṇḍapa style.
There is no historical inscription about the original construction of the phalcā.
Because the building had become old and damaged, it was completely torn down and rebuilt in 1876 CE (VS 1932) with help from local donations.
When the phalcā became damaged again, it was reconstructed in 2002 CE (VS 2079) with funding from the Madhyapur Thimi Municipality.
During the reconstruction, the south side of the phalcā was expanded, and the Kapilā house in the north was demolished.
After the renovation, the Kapilā families were no longer allowed to live there.
In 1747 CE (NS 767), Mukundasiṃ, Rudrasiṃ, and other members of the Dāphā group jointly offered a toraṇa and a gilded finial to Nāsaḥdyaḥ.
At that time, the Nāsaḥdyaḥ temple had not yet been built, it existed only as a shrine.

It was later, in 1743 CE (NS 873), during the reign of King Raṇajita Malla, that Dhanabilasiṃ (Dhanavīrasiṃ), Bhāgivantasiṃ, and other Dāphā group members built a proper temple for Nāsaḥdyaḥ where Hāku Bande served as the priest.
As the Nāsaḥdyaḥ temple became dilapidated over time, the locals contributed donations to rebuild it in 1853 CE (NS 973).
Later, a peepal tree grew in the temple and caused significant damage.
As a result, the Department of Archaeology reconstructed the temple during the 1990s.
Every year, on the 1st day of Vaiśākha, during the Biskeṭa Jātrā, the chariot of Kvasimāināy Gaṇeśa is placed on the plinth built in front of the Nāsaḥdyaḥ temple.
Savala Bāhāḥ is a monastic building situated in the Guccā Ṭola region of Kathmandu.
The expression ‘saḥvala’later went on to become ‘Savala’, the vernacular name of thebāhāḥ(R. Vajrācārya & V. Vajrācārya 1103, p.5; R. Vajrācārya VS 2075, p.172).

text: The north-facing Bāhāḥ no longer follows traditional architecture and appears to be a private building.
The main building of the Bāhāḥ is a concrete structure of five floors with its finial installed on the terrace.
The fourth and the third floors of the building are currently (December 2022) being used by a family of thebāhāḥ.
The esoteric room (āgaṃ) of the Bāhāḥ is established on the first floor.
The sanctum on the ground floor has a woodentoraṇaon top of its entrance with a statue of Mahāvairocana at the center; it was offered in 1685 CE (NS 805).
There are fivecaityas established at thebāhāḥpremises.
King Pratāpa Malla had established the Karmācāryas here during his reign (1641-1674 CE) (R. Vajrācārya VS 2075, p.175).
While no historical sources record its initial construction, thebāhāḥis claimed to be 2,200 years old (R. Vajrācārya & V. Vajrācārya 1103, p.1).
Legendary tantric Śāśvatavajra Vajrācārya is said to have founded thebāhāḥ.

He is also credited to have established Vajravīra Mahākāla (KAT2870) by the Ṭũḍikhela parade ground in 721 CE (Kaligata Era 3822) and Lũmari Ajimā (KAT2860) in 724 CE (Kaligata Era 3825) (B. Vajrācārya NS 1109, p. 15, 18).

However, Bhattacharya (1968, p.CXVII) places Śāśvatavajra in a much later period, i.e., the 1100s. Śāśvatavajra had initially established thebāhāḥat a place called Ināykhā near the Hyūmata Ṭola but it was later shifted to the present location by Omkāravajra after the ground at Ināykhā sunk in (R. Vajrācārya & V. Vajrācārya 1103, p.17).

The first historical reference of Savala Bāhāḥ was found in a palm leaf document of 1641 CE (NS 805), which records the offering of a palanquin for the esoteric deity (āgaṃdyaḥ) jointly by a person from Khusi Bahī and Hākudeva, thethapāḥjuof Savala Bāhāḥ.
In 2005 CE (VS 2062), the Bāhāḥ was rebuilt with funds from the Kathmandu Metropolis.
Concrete was used in the reconstruction.
Its construction was initiated by Queen Lalitatripurasundarī and supervised by Bhīmasena Thāpā.
The foundation was laid in 1811 CE (VS 1867), and the bridge was inaugurated in 1812 CE (VS 1868).
A stone inscription marked this achievement, noting the bridge's 1253-cubit length and the involvement of a government officer named Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa.
Efforts were made to develop the riverbanks with stone steps and establish settlements near the bridge, with land grants provided for its upkeep.
A land grant of 150ropanīs was made in the name of Hanumantasiṃha Amātya in 1810 CE (VS 1867) for the expansion of settlements in Kupondole and the maintenance of the bridge.
Later in 1814 CE (VS 1870), the king added an additional 25ropanīs of land and mandated that anyone settling on this land must contribute to the upkeep of the bridge.
After enduring 94 years, the bridge suffered damage in the 1902 floods.
Candra Śamśera rebuilt it in 1905 CE (1961 CE) using iron girders from Britain, completing the work in just 131 days.
He also added a lengthy inscription detailing the reconstruction and the Rāṇā dynasty's prowess, even mentioning the engineers involved.
This iron bridge, known as "Red Bridge" due to its color (S. Ulaka VS 2081, p. 1), eventually became congested due to urbanization.
In 1967 CE, the "Red Bridge" was replaced with a two-lane concrete motor bridge built with Indian iron beams.
Another two lanes were added in 1995 CE with Japanese assistance.
According to locals, the ancestors of the Śrṣṭha (Amātya) community built thecaityasand they used to be surrounded by a pond.
The original statue was lost but a new one was installed in 2006.
An inscription records that thecaityaswere renovated in 1614.
After the installation of the new Lokeśvara statue, people started to perform his annual worship on the 5th day of the dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa.
Dharmanārāyaṇa Mānandhara, a powerful merchant from Kathmandu, built this rest house during the Rāṇā period to facilitate his clan members to cremate their deceased family members.
He was supported by his grandsons Gaṇeśadāsa and Ratnadāśa in 1912 CE (VS 1969).
He went on to become an influential figure in the country’s financial sector (B. Paṃgenī VS 2068, p. A-B).
The descendants of the Mānandhara brothers renovated thesataḥand added a restroom in 2002 CE (VS 2059).
In 2014 CE (VS 2071), the walls of thesataḥwere renovated but they were damaged by the 2015 earthquakes.
It was rebuilt by the High-Powered Committee for Integrated Development of the Bagmati Civilization with loan assistance from the Asian Development Bank.
The reconstruction was completed in November 2021.

In the past, the building also served as a space where women could change clothes after a holy bath at the confluence onṚṣiPañcamī, the worship of seven sages (saptaṛṣi) performed on the 5th of the bright fortnight of Bhādra.
According to local residents, the Hiti was neglected and in a state of disrepair for decades.
In 2018 CE, the Shankharapur Municipality renovated it at the initiation of local residents.
As reported in Bangdel (1989, p. 152), the statue was stolen in 1985 CE.
Aphalcā, too, used to stand north of the Hiti, but it collapsed years ago and is yet to be rebuilt.
The courtyard is surrounded by residential buildings and has two narrow exits at the north west and south west corners.
There is a fire pit and another, this time octagonalcaitya, in front of the maincaitya,where oil lamps and prayer wheels are kept.
There is also a yellow painted concrete pillar with no deity (VS 2051).
The four other, smaller temples, are built one meter away from the central temple, facing its south, west, north and east facades.
At the centre of the lintel is a rosette in a inscribed in a medallion.
Furthermore, the construction ofśikharatemples in the Karnali region seems to have stopped before the 16th century, which narrows the dating of this type of plan down to the 14th-15th century.
There arecaityas anddharmadhātumaṇḍalas established in the courtyard of the Bāhāḥ.

This name was first mentioned in a manuscript of the Aparimatayu Dhāraṇī Sūtra, which was copied by ‘Vajrācārya Jīnadeva of Maitripurī Mahāvihāra in the city of Suvarṇapranārī’ in 1659 CE (NS 779) (cf.Locke1985, p.270).

Vākvajra is also credited to have established the Śāntighaṭa Caitya of Śrīghaḥ Bāhāḥ (KAT0280) and later went into meditation in a room at Kvāḥ Bāhāḥ from where he vanished, or is believed to be still in meditation.
There are no records to date the initial construction of the Bāhāḥ.

An inscription on the north-western side of the Bāhāḥ premises records a few events: the hosting of theSamyakMahādānain 1660 CE (NS 780), the establishment of adharmadhātucaityain 1665 CE (NS 785), the consecration of the Dīpaṅkara statue in 1666 CE (NS 786), the consecration of the esoteric deity (āgaṃdyaḥ) and Tārā in 1669 CE (NS 789), and the establishment of avajradhātucaityain 1670 CE (NS 790).
Likewise, another inscription from 1711 CE (NS 831) is carved on the wooden entrance to the Bāhāḥ premises recording the renovation of the door.
The 2015 earthquakes severely damaged the Bāhāḥ.
With the funds from the Kathmandu Metropolitan City Office, Department of Archaeology, and locals, the Bāhāḥ is currently (July 2022) being reconstructed.
There are no sources to date the initial construction of the Temple.
The earliest inscription at the site (set on the northern wall) from 1789 CE (NS 909) records the renovation of thephalcāattached to the Temple.
In 2005 CE, the Temple and the library next to it were renovated (local resident, Mānandhara, male, age 69).
This rest house is constructed next to Svapu Hiti (SKH0640) by the steps that lead to Vajrayoginī Mandira (SKH0500).
The architecture of the Phalcā is different from the traditional style: it is constructed with bricks and clay but has no wooden pillars, beams, or capitals.
The lack of inscriptions makes the history behind its construction unclear.
However, the style of the Phalcā suggests that it was built during the Rāṇā period.
The Phalcā seems to have been constructed to allow devotees visiting the Vajrayoginī temple to rest.
The Hiti next to the Phalcā also appears to have been built for such devotees to quench their thirst.

text: A small shrine dedicated to Gaṇeśa has been built in the southeastern corner inside the phalcā, but the statue, too, is heavily weathered.

monument_name: Thaiba Hāthu Phalcā (late Medieval period; 17th-18th cent.)
text: Although there is no inscriptional evidence regarding its initial construction, it can be assumed that the Phalcā dates back to the Late Medieval period when the Hāthu Jātrā was a popular tradition in the Kathmandu Valley.

monument_name: Thaiba Hāthu Phalcā (late Medieval period; 17th-18th cent.)
text: Historically, this Phalcā was known for organizing the Hāthu, which is why it is referred to as the “HāthuPhalcā.”The Bhairava mask, which used to be displayed during Indrajātrā and otherJātrāsin Thaiba (especially on the full moon night of Kārtika), used to be stored in a nearby house before it was stolen in the 1980s.
The monastery is built on a two-stepped raised plinth.
The west wing was dismantled in the early 1980s and replaced with a single-storey structure that functioned as a primary school (Gutschow 2011, 726).
The school has since moved, and the space left behind on the western side is now used to store musical instruments.
The shrine of kvāpādyaḥ is in the southern wing of the monastic building, and its brass-clad entrance is on the northern side.
Stone inscriptions are attached to the wall on either side of the entrance.
The 2015 earthquake heavily damaged this Bahi and so the local people demolished its upper floor and covered it with temporary CGI sheets.
The monastery has been renovated by INTACH India, and officially inaugurated on 22 March 2024, in the presence of the Indian ambassador.
The old struts and pillars have been replaced by new carvings, the whereabouts of the historic material are unknown as per local residents response.
The former garden, including a small field for begetables and fruit trees has been replaced by a lawn with a festival platform.

text: Thephalcāis connected to a house and has been rebuilt several times, most recently in 1993.

monument_name: Subāhāḥ Hiti Phalcā (c. late 18th cent. CE)
text: This reconstruction saw the columns extended in height by 43 cm and the addition of windows to the dwarf storey above.

monument_name: Subāhāḥ Hiti Phalcā (c. late 18th cent. CE)
text: Inside thephalcā, one can find a Hāratī Ajimā statue dated to the 3rd century, as well as a Gaṇeśa statue (Gaṇeśa being the lineage deity for the Śākyas of Subāhāḥ) and an inscription dated 1025 NS (1905 CE).
Cvachẽ Hiti was constructed by Paduma Bhāro in 1618 CE (NS 738).
Since it was built in Cvachẽ ṭola, it’s called the Cvachẽ Hiti.
Around the hiti, two Śivaliṅga and a statue of Viṣṇu have also been installed.
Since only one lion statue is present instead of a pair, it might have been brought from elsewhere and added to the hiti.
According to the inscription found at the hiti,  Paduma(!) Bhāro constructed the maṃgara(spout of the hiti) on the 6th day of the dark fortnight in the month of Māgh, CE 1618 (NS 738).
This confirms that the hiti was built by Padum Bhāro in  CE 1618 (NS 738).
A modern metal pipe has been installed to supply water.
Architecturally, the temple is built in theśikharastyle and faces west.
Constructed primarily of bricks, it is surmounted by a metal finial (gajūra) in the shape of akalaśa.
East of Maṅgaleśvara lies the Vatsalātemple, also inśikharastyle, where a stonekalaśais installed in thegarbhagṛha.
This deity is locally known asKarma-Vatsalā(P. Śreṣṭha VS 2080, 776).
No authentic inscription records the original foundation of the Maṅgaleśvara temple.
According to local belief, theŚivaliṅgamanifested itself on 14th of dark fortnight of Caitra (H. Jośī VS 2058, 397).

A sage namedMaṅgala Ṛṣiinstalled theliṅgawith proper ritual and performed austerities for a hundred years, abandoning all concern for hunger and thirst until he attained death in meditation at the site.
Although theliṅgaitself is of great antiquity, the superstructure seems to have been built much later.
The earliest inscription discovered within the temple complex dates to 1691 CE (NS 811) and relates to the construction of the adjacent Vatsalā temple.
King Jitāmītra Malla is said to have built this temple for thesiddhipūjāfollowing his composition of theAdhyātma Rāmāyaṇa Nāṭya(P. Śreṣṭha VS 2080, 766).

Another inscription from 1697 CE (NS 817) records that King Bhūpatīndra Malla offered a stone lamp (pānasa) in front of theNāsaḥdyaḥshrine during theghāghara-siddhi-pūjāperformed on the occasion of staging theKolāsuravodhopākhyāna—a drama based on theMahalakṣmī-māhātmya(N. Pauḍela VS 2018, 5).
In 1707 CE (NS 827), Bhūpatīndra Malla dedicated a bell to theNāsaḥdyaḥafter performing the playGaurīvivaḥain Lalitpur with the funds raised from its staging.
Historical records confirm that this drama was performed on 13th of dark fortnight of Phālguṇa in (Nepāla Samvat) 826 (C. Śāha VS 2055, 69).
The inscription engraved on the bell is addressed toNṛtyanātha, suggesting that although offered toNāsaḥdyaḥ, the bell was installed before the Maṅgaleśvara temple.
The smallśikharashrine west of the main temple, though lacking inscriptional evidence, is said to have been commissioned by a sage who died before its completion, leaving it unfinished.
The earthquake of 2015 CE (VS 2072) caused structural cracks in the Maṅgaleśvara temple though it did not collapse.
The Bhaktapur Municipality, in cooperation with the Department of Archaeology, undertook its restoration.
The adjoiningVatsalātemple, already in a dilapidated condition before the earthquake, suffered severe damage and was rebuilt in 2017 CE (VS 2074) (P. Śreṣṭha VS 2080, 765).
TheNāsaḥdyaḥshrine, previously weakened by the earthquake of 1934 CE (VS1990), was also restored only after 2015, though the exact date of its renovation is not known to the present priest.
Witnesses rejoiced, proclaiming victory to Viṣṇu, who thus became known asTilamādhava, “the Lord Manifest from Sesame” (P. Śreṣṭha VS 2080, 1070).
The row of shops situated before the shrine was once part ofNāsaḥdyaḥ’s endowed property, though these holdings have now passed into private ownership.
This west facing Śiva Mandira (built in 1960 CE) is a dome-shaped Hindu Temple.
They represent four elements: earth, water, fire, and air.
Due to the lack of inscriptive records, the four-facedśivaliṅgaof this Temple cannot be preciously dated.
Theśivaliṅgawas under the open sky until the present Temple structure was constructed in 1960 CE.
Dāmodara Śamśera Rāṇā had provided NRs. 15,000 to Phasilāla Maharjana to construct the Temple.
Later in 1997 CE, the Brahmā portion of theśivaliṅgathat was underneath the ground was brought above the ground while renovating the Temple (local knowledge, local resident, Maharjana, male, age 76).

text: There is no evidence to date its initial construction, however, the architectural features suggest that it was built during the second half of the 19th century.
The temple was severely damaged during the 2015 CE earthquakes and was near collapse.
In 2020 CE (VS 2077), the Government of Nepal and the Asian Development Bank invested twentylakhrupees in its reconstruction.
Theśivalingain the sanctum was stolen before 2015.
Following the temple's reconstructionin 2020 CE a newliṅgawas installed.
Duru Bāhāḥ Nani can be accessed from the northwest corner of the Pimbahal area through a narrow alley under the residential buildings or via a narrow path to the west of the Sulima area.
The building has been reconstructed using bricks on mud mortar, and is roofed with corrugated metal sheets.
Twodharmadhātumaṇḍalasand avajradhātucaityaare in line with the front of the main building.
The inscription attached to the wall to the south of the entrance informs that thisvihārawas established by Ratna Vajrācārya in NS 797 (CE 1677).
The courtyard is surrounded by residential buildings and the Bāhāḥ's building.
Thejhĩgaṭītiles of the upper roof were replaced with gilded copper sheets in 1940 and the lower roof was renovated in 1988.
As depicted in the photos (see below), the shrine has suffered severe damage due to a peepal tree (ficus religiosa) that sprouted and grew within its confines.
This statue was erected to facilitate devotees who come to Pīra Pāṭī for fire oblations aimed at appeasing the planet (graha) Śani.
However, a dispute arose regarding this placement, leading to the statue being erected behind the shrine (based on personal communication with one of the ascetics residing in the pāṭī, age 33).
The main temple of thebāhāḥcāis built against the wall of a residential building facing west, and stands on a double plinth with a stone threshold.
Timber lattice work surrounds the sanctum on three sides, whilst its rear wall is shared with the residential building.
Both have been placed on the walls of the other buildings.
Thisbāhāḥwas founded by Munirāja in 1909.
Thecaityawas established prior to this in 1863, most likely by his father Dhanavantasiṃha Vajrācārya.

An inscription from 1680 CE (NS 801) within the shrine documents the construction of the stone shrine subsequent to the installation of a Gaṇeśa statue by Viśvasiṃha Bhāro from the Bāghabhairava temple area.

The twodegudyaḥstones (KIR0083-001 and KIR0083-002), both adorned with the Garuḍa-toraṇa, also hold inscriptions indicating that Mādhasiṅa and Sivarāma established their respective tutelary deities on the same site in 1657 CE (NS 777).
These stones appear to have been placed within an open shrine, with the construction of the stone temple taking place only in 1680 CE.
As of February 2023 CE, the temple is undergoing reconstruction, a recent initiative supported by the Kirtipur Municipality.
The lower portion of the cella has been reconstructed using historic stone and new brick set in cement mortar.
Meanwhile, the upper section has been entirely rebuilt with machine-made brick and substandard soft stone, awaiting the installation of the domed pinnacle.
Three stone statues—the primary Gaṇeśa idol and two inscribeddegudyaḥstones—remain exposed, leaning against a nearby house.
The temple was constructed by Raṇadhvaja Thāpā, the first son of Amara Siṃha Thāpā and his wife Dharmādevī.
The exact year of the temple's construction is unknown.
The stone pillar erected in the courtard features a statue of Raṇadhvaja Thāpā and bears inscriptions on four sides recording various events related to the temple.
The earliest record among them is from VS 1877 (1820 CE), mentioning that the temple was constructed in that year.
Many plots of land were donated to formguthis for performing daily rituals and other worships at the temple.
In VS 1879 (1822 CE), Raṇadhvaja had his family tree (vaṃśavṛkṣa) inscribed on the pillar and installed his statue atop of it.

text: Of note are a few Buddhist deities: a broken Buddha (DLK0200-003), a Saḍakṣarī Lokeśvara (?, (DLK0200-002), and the bust of a potential Avalokiteśvara (DLK0200-007). Another sculpture, also identified as Avalokiteśvara is placed in a niche (DLK0200-005). The face of the figure, seated on a column in a "royal position of ease", has been deliberately damaged. All the Buddhist sculptures show signs of iconoclastic vandalism. The condition of the so-called Avalokiteśvara bust and the Avalokiteśvara seated on the column would therefore tend to identify them as Buddhist figures. The presence of Buddhism in this place is also attested by an inscribed but illegible stele decorated with an incised stūpa at the top (DLK0200-001). A stele of Viṣṇu and Lakṣmī, meanwhile, shows no marks of vandalism (Andolfatto 2019: p. 166). The fact that the Caitya was constructed in the 16th century and the designs on the pillars also date back to the same period leads us to believe that both structures were constructed at the same time.

Jyotirbhakteśvara is one among the various śivālayas (lit. the abode of Śiva) constructed on both sides of the main path at Mṛgasthalī.
Typically, the bell carries an inscription with the donor's name and the installation year, which often coincides with the temple's construction year.
The loss of the bell has obscured details such as the donor's name and the year of construction.

These śivālayas were primarily built during the Rāṇā period by royals, named after a living person suffixed with "bhakteśvara" or in memory of a deceased family member suffixed with "mukteśvara." While the temple's name suggests it was constructed by an individual named Jyoti during the person’s lifetime, the absence of an inscription at the site obscures additional construction details.

Meanwhile, Michaels and Tandon (2017, p.106), without explicitly citing their information source, propose that Jyotirbhakteśvara was constructed in 1848 CE, along with two adjacentśivālayas, Līlābhakteśvara and Badrībhakteśvara.
It is conceivable that these threeśivālayas were commissioned by the same individual, dedicating each to separate individuals.

Concurrently, alālamohara(cf.K_0009_0011) issued in 1950 CE (VS 1907) by King Surendra in the name of Badrīnarasiṃha Kũvara endorses the donation of land parcels in favor of these threeśivālayas in Mṛgasthalī.
This implies that Badrīnarasiṃha, the younger brother of Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā, likely erected these three temples.
The earthquakes of 2015 left the temple in a dilapidated state, and it has remained so since then.
No initiative for its restoration has been undertaken thus far.
Although daily rituals were being performed here, they have ceased following the 2015 earthquakes.

Facing north, on the southern side of Dathu Nani, thedyaḥchẽof Ṣaḍakṣarī Lokeśvara is established.
Thedyaḥchẽwas built to house the statues, ornaments, and other materials related to thejātrāof Ṣaḍakṣarī Lokeśvara, who is established in the Cvaylāchi Ṭole in Bāḍegāũ.
The sanctum is established on the ground floor, resembling the concept of thebāhāḥarchitecture.
Inside the sanctum, a stone statue of Amitābha is established.
To the east of Amitābha, there is a statue of Dīpaṅkara donated by Pūrṇa Śākya, a resident of Pimbāhāḥ Ṭola, Lalitpur, and to the west, there is a statue of Akṣobhya donated by a donor from Thaiba.
In the courtyard in front of thedyaḥchẽ, acaityamade of cement has been established.
No historical records have been found regarding the construction of thisdyaḥchẽ.
The earliest record available in thedyaḥchẽis a stone inscription from 1713 CE (NS 833), recording the bricklaying in the Dathu Nani courtyard.
According to the inscription, Devamuni Bhāro, along with Punarāma, Bāsurāma, Sivaharī, Madhurāma, Harigovinda, and Manhahosiṃ, jointly carried out the work.

The inscription also enforced rules that prohibited bringing cows and bulls in the courtyard, along with other acts like urination and defecation, grinding of wheat, and driving nails on to the ground.
Around 2012 CE, the trustees of the Bāḍegāũ Caitya collectively installed a pair of concrete lions on either side of thedyaḥchẽ's steps and a concretecaityain the courtyard.
Thedyaḥchẽ, which had already deteriorated before the 2015 earthquakes, was rendered uninhabitable due to the earthquakes.
With NRs. 500,000 received from the Godawari Municipality and additional funds contributed by the trustees, the reconstruction began with a concept of developing thedyaḥchẽinto abāhāḥ.

As soon as the ground floor was completed in 2017 CE (VS 2074), Nirakumārī Vajrācārya, a resident of the Naudvã Ṭola, Lalitpur, along with her husband Mānavira Śākya and family members, donated a statue of Amitābha (BDG0030-001) to be enshrined in the sanctum.
She also donated statues of Śākyamuni Buddha, Ṣaḍakṣarī Lokeśvara, and Āryatārā for the establishment in the sanctum.
As of August 2024, the reconstruction is yet to be completed.
Every year, on the day ofJugaḥ, the 14th of the dark fortnight of Bhādra, a palanquin procession of Ṣaḍakṣarī Lokeśvara, established in the Bāḍegāũ Caitya, is organized.
On the day of the procession, the statue, placed on the first floor, is taken out and brought to the second floor of thedyaḥchẽfor worship and various items are offered to the deity in alms.

This connection supports the hypothesis that the Teku Sataḥ was also built by akājīfrom the same Kũvara lineage.
The Teku Sataḥ underwent a renovation in 1971–72 CE (VS 2028) (Inventory VS 2039, p. 165).
This indicates that the building likely served funerary functions: providing shelter for the terminally ill, hostingśrāddharites, and facilitating cremation rituals.
According to oral accounts from the Buḍhāthokī (male, age 56) and Thāpā (male, age 59) families, a Kũvara descendant—who claims relation to the original builder—frequently visits the site.

According to later chronicles, particularly theBhāṣāVaṃśāvalī, this statue was commissioned by Amara Malla during his reign from 1529 to 1560 CE.

The temple enshrines aśivaliṅgawith a fascinating legend behind its establishment.
According to the tale, Lord Śiva himself established theśivaliṅgawhile disguised as a Kirāta (hunter) in the Śleṣamāntaka forest.
There are no historical records available regarding the establishment of the temple.

On a particular day, while assuming the form of a Kirāta, Śiva established theśivaliṅgaon the 14th day of the dark fortnight of Kārtika, which became known as Kirāteśvara Mahādeva (V. Dhakāla 2075, pp. 1042-1043;Devamālā Vaṃśāvalī2013, pp. 30-31; N. Pauḍela VS 2020, p. 46).

text: Another legend recounts that Arjuna, one of the Pāṇḍava brothers from the epic Mahābhārata, sought instruction in archery from Kirāteśvara Mahādeva before the commencement of the great Mahābhārata battle (N. Pauḍela VS 2020, p. 47).

The term Kirāteśvara also indicates the Kirāta community, believed to have ruled the Nepāla valley during the prehistoric Kirāta period, signifying the existence of inhabited areas, including Devapattana, during that time (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p. 14).

The earliest historical record of Kirāteśvara dates back to 1728 CE (NS 848), when King Jagajjaya Malla (r. 1722-1734 CE) of Kathmandu granted land for the establishment of a trust responsible for conducting daily and periodic rituals at various deities in the Paśupati area, including Kirāteśvara Mahādeva (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2056, pp. 236-237).

Over a century later, King Rājendra Vikrama Śāha granted the priestly rights of the temples, including Kirāteśvara, to Ṣaḍānanda Bhaṭṭa, the grandson of Sāmbasadāśiva Bhaṭṭa (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p. 228).

Religious scriptures suggest that worshiping Kirāteśvara on the full moon of Caitra, the 8th day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, and the 14th day of the dark fortnight of Kārtika fulfills one's desires, aids in achieving goals, absolves individuals of their five great sins (pañcamahāpāpa), and grants them a place in Śivaloka, the abode of Lord Śiva (H. Jośī 2058, p. 398).
They worship Śiva as Pāruhāṅga and Pārvatī as Sumnimā (M. Thāpā VS 2077, p. 369).

The present temple structure is built in a mixed style, with stone pillars on the ground floor and entrances carved in the style of tiered temples.

The upper portion of the temple is covered with a brick and plaster dome, and according to Gutschow (2011, p.891), it "was probably a three-tiered temple which collapsed in the 1833 earthquake, to be rebuilt with the original ambulatory and a bulbous dome”.
Raṇabahādura Śāha is said to have built the temple around 1794 CE (cf. Gutschow 2011, p.891), however, no inscription records the event.

C. Nepālī (VS 2020, p.26), on the other hand, mentions Raṇabahādura Śāha building the temple in 1797 CE (VS 1853) without citing specific sources. additionally, an entry in the chronicle published by Hasrat (1970, p.156) records the temple's construction in 1797 CE (NS 917).

Another late 18th-century chronicle (Bhāṣāvaṃśāvalī) nartrates a historical account wherein Raṇabahādura Śāha employed forced labour (jhārā) on his subjects to build the temple at a site of ‘incomparable height’ (cf. J. Regmī VS 2033, p.196).
At the time of its construction it was 125 cubits (hāta) tall (J. Regmī 1972, p.40).

Known as Mālikeśvara, thisśivālaya, or the dwelling place of Śiva, was commissioned by Mālikādevī, the spouse of Dalakeśara Pā̃ḍe, who went into hiding following the infamous Kot massacre of 1846 CE (VS 1903).

Situated on the western side of the main path leading to the Gorakhanātha temple in Mṛgasthalī, this is one of the numerous Śiva temples in the region constructed in the prevalent style during the Rāṇā period.
While the exact year of construction is unclear, Mālikādevī Pā̃ḍe, the builder of the temple, was the wife of the influential courtier Dalakeśara Pā̃ḍe.
He was the maternal uncle of Māthavarasiṃha Thāpā (B. Bhaṇḍārī VS 2069, p.70), the prime minister assassinated by Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā in 1845 CE (Sever 1993, p.48).
Mālikādevī also donated land parcels after the temple's construction.

In 1846 CE (VS 1903), King Rājendra issued alālamohara(K_0008_0040B) approving land parcels donated in the name of Mālikeśvara and Kapileśvara Mandira for performing daily and other rituals of the deities using the rent from the land.
However, G. Taṇḍana (VS 2056, p.487) erroneously mentions that King Surendra issued thelālamohara.
Given that thelālamoharaaddressed to Dalakeśara Pā̃ḍe is related to the temple built by his wife, it is evident that the temple already existed in 1846 CE.
Nine years later, the contents of thelālamoharawere inscribed in a stone inscription placed next to the temple in 1855 CE (VS 1912).
Thebāhāḥcomprises of three buildings: the main god house on the south of the courtyard, anāgaṃchẽto the east and anotherāgaṃchẽto the west.
Thesaṃghamembers installed the present stone Maitreya statue after the original wooden statue was stolen.
These images receive regular renovations, the most recent one in 2012 CE.
A bell placed east of the main entrance was moved to thebāhāḥ‘sāgaṃafter the stone support frame collapsed.
When Śākyas from Kvāḥ Bāhāḥ of Patan moved to Bhaktapur, they became members and today thesaṃghaconsists of both Śākyas and Vajrācāryas.
Thisbāhāḥis referred to as Bhuvanākaravarma Saṃskārita, i.e., consecrated by Bhuvanākaravarma.
Not much is known about Bhuvanākaravarma but he is credited to have built(?) Taḥ Bāhāḥ (LAL0050) of Patan.
No historic sources are available that shed light on the initial construction of Pasu Bāhāḥ.
The earliest record relating to Pasu Bāhāḥ is a loan-deed (tamasuka) issued during the reign of King Jayadharmma Malla in 1407 CE (NS 527).

An early reference to thisbāhāḥis found in a colophon of a manuscript of thePañcarakṣāwhich was copied in 1535 CE (NS 655) for Śākyabhikṣu Jitadeva, his wife Kīrtilakṣmī and his two sons of Paśupati Mahāvihāra (Locke1985, p. 444).
In an invitation to aSamyakfeast in 1574 CE (NS 694), Pasu Bāhāḥ is referred to as Bhuvanākaradharma Saṃskārita Paśupati Vihāra (S. Śākya1118, p. 5).
In 1613 CE (NS 734), Hākudeva, Jivarāja, Mahāpāla, and others had offered atoraṇato the deity of the Pasu Bāhā’sāgaṃ.

The stone pillar with acaityaon top was installed in 1901 CE (NS 1021) and thedharmadhātujinālaya caityain the courtyard was donated by Pūrṇacandra Vajrācārya (text: Varjācāje Punacandra) in 1902 CE (NS 1022) with money he made from the trade in Tibet.
Theāgaṃchẽto the west collapsed in the 2015 earthquakes and was rebuilt from ground-up in 2023.
The shrine was built around 1973; people brought wood from the nearby forest for its construction.
The main shrine building is located to the east of the courtyard.
Thebāhāhhas been reconstructed in RCC and is now a four-storey building.
One traditional building remains and can be found at the south-west corner of the courtyard.
The rest of the buildings are tall RCC buildings.
The courtyard also contains a statue of the consecrator of thebāhāh.
Thisbāhāhwas established by Devasiṃha after he established the Naudvã Bāhāḥ in NS 760 (Locke1985, 105;Śākya1994, 84)He established Jati Bāhāḥ a few days later (Śākya1994, 99).
Nī Bāhāḥ, located in Bhaktapur’s Tekhāco Ṭola, was constructed by Guṇasiṃhadeva, a Śākya from the "Nivā" lineage, 1634 CE (NS 754).
Unlike otherbāhāḥs, Nī Bāhāḥ lacks a traditional monastic building and only features a small temple-like structure instead.
No written sources about the construction of Nī Bāhāḥ have been found, but oral tradition attributes its founding to Guṇasiṃhadeva Nivā Śākya.
Born in 1555 CE (NS 675) in Lalitpur’s Itilhane (Nāgabahāla), Guṇasiṃhadeva was the eldest son of Karmarāja, a member of Kvāḥ Bāhāḥ (Hiraṇyavarṇa Mahāvihāra) (S. Śākya NS 1141, p. 8).
A palm-leaf record from 1594 CE (NS 714) notes his initial residence in Kvāthaṇḍo (S. Śākya NS 1141, p. 11).
Impressed by his craftsmanship—including works in Panauti, Dhulikhel, Sankhu, and Cā̃gu—Queen Gaṃgādevī granted him 28ropanīs of farmland (S. Śākya NS 1141, p. 9).
Later, King Jagajyoti Malla, pleased with his contributions, awarded him half-rights to the Kuthu Bahī (BKT0590) in 1623 CE (NS 743) (S. Śākya NS 1141, p. 13).

P. Śreṣṭha (VS 2080, pp. 1091-1092) claims Guṇasiṃhadeva was summoned to Bhaktapur in 1646 CE (NS 766), but earlier land deeds from 1631 CE (NS 751), 1632 CE (NS 752), and 1634 CE (NS 754) confirm his earlier settlement (B. Vajrācārya VS 1124, pp. 156-157).
Needing abāhāḥfor his descendants’ rituals, Guṇasiṃhadeva sought permission from King Nareśa Malla and built Nī Bāhāḥ in 1634 CE (NS 754), installing acaityaovernight (S. Śākya NS 1141, pp. 14-15).
Guṇasiṃhadeva died in 1646 CE (NS 766), as recorded on a Buddha statue in Kuthu Bahī (S. Śākya NS 1141, p. 14).
His descendants, including his son Guṇākara’s three sons (Sabhākara, Karuṇākara, Ratikara), constructed Bhaktapur’s famous Lũ Dhvākhā (BKT0080) in NS 874 (1753 CE).
The earliest inscription in the courtyard dates back to 1894 CE (NS 1014) on a bell donated by Mahantamuni for thecaitya.
In 1919 CE (NS 1039), Budhācāryye Nānīmāyā offered a pair of bronze lions.
Ratnamāna, with community support, paved the courtyard with floor tiles in 1938 CE (VS 1995) and later restored the shrine in memory of his ancestors in 1954 CE (VS 2011).
Due to the difficulty of traveling there, a statue of Yogāmbara was installed near Siddhapukhū.
The Āratī Guthi ensures continuity.
Previously, Nī Bāhāḥ members performed daily worship at Kuthu Bahī for six months a year, a privilege granted by King Jagajyoti Malla (B. Vajrācārya 1124, p. 64).
The whole building was rebuilt in concrete some time in the 1990s.
The present Temple structure was built only in 2018 CE.

According to the seniormost member (male, age 79) of the Śreṣṭha family whose members live behind (east) the Temple, claim to be the descendants of the person who sponsored its initial construction and are responsible for its maintenance, the old Temple structure was already in a state of disrepair with cracks on the walls and leakages on the roof before it collapsed completely in 1961 CE.

With the collapse of the Temple, its main deity (stone statue of Kalaśanārāyaṇa) remained under the open sky (on adabū-like platform) for almost 55 years before it was reconsecrated in the sanctum of the newly built structure in 2018 CE.
The Śreṣṭha family was motivated to rebuild the Temple from the ground up after seeing other monuments at the Sālkhā Ṭola being reconstructed after the 2015 earthquakes.

As there are no photos available showing the former structure of the Temple, the family got it rebuilt based on their memory of its previous state (source: the above mentioned seniormost member of the Śreṣṭha family).
The upper portion of the Temple before its collapse was similar to the present form except for the small towers that were not there in the past (source: ibid.).
The Bhavānīśaṅkara Mandira constructed in theśikharastyle and entirely in stone by a certain Bhavānīśaṅkara Bhāro in the memory of his parents in NS 797 (1676 CE), is located at Yachu Ṭola, Sundhara.
However, the Statue of Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa is not there anymore and whereabout of that initially consecrated statute is unknown.
Upon the completion of the initial construction of the Temple, a fire oblation (yajña) was performed and a golden pinnacle was offered to it.

Bhavānīśaṅkara Bhāro had endowed a plot of five and a halfropanīs of land and established aguthito operate the Temple and sponsor its anniversary rituals to be held on the 12thof the dark fortnight of Kārtika (cf.C. KāyasthaNS 1135, 56-58).
A copperplate inscription at the temple names this marketplace "Sugatapurabajāra," likely due to the presence of a Theravāda Buddhist monastery named Sugatapura Vihāra in the area.
The original statue was stolen and replaced with a new one gifted by the residents of Guji Bāhāḥ (LAL2490) in Patan.

After the theft, another statue (object no. NWK0600-002) was temporarily enshrined as the main deity until the new statue was established, prompting the temporary statue to be shifted to the eastern side of the sanctum.
Outside the temple, a Dharmadhātujinālaya Caitya (object no. NWK0600-007) is established in the west.

As recorded in the stone inscription embedded to the west of the entrance to the sanctum, Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa Bhāro built the two-tiered temple with a gilded finial in 1821 CE (NS 941) by enshrining a statue of Lokeśvara together with his family members.
As they arrived in Triśūlī, the statue gained so much weight that the thieves were forced to leave it there, where Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa Bhāro then built a temple for it.

In 1894 CE (VS 1951), Subedāra Rāḍhākṛṣṇa Śreṣṭha of Kathmandu's Makhana Ṭola installed a pair of lion statues at the temple; in 1901 CE (VS 1958), Kālīdāsa Śreṣṭha, who had moved to Triśūlī from Ikhāchẽ, Patan, covered the entrance andtoraṇaof the temple with gilded sheets; in 1922 CE (VS 1979), Bṛṣabahādura established the above-mentioned Dharmadhātujinālaya Caitya west of the temple; and in 1982 CE (NS 1102), a local trust named Saṃlhu Guṭhī carried out the renovation of the temple roof that had fallen off using their own funds and donations from the locals (see ‘historical events‘).
There are no historical sources to date the initial construction of this Hiti.
As the above-mentioned Yakṣa statues are believed to be from the Lichhavi period, the Hiti must have been constructed not later than the 9th century.
Bāla Gopāla Ghorī Śreṣṭha of the Ĩllā Ṭola, the Hiti was renovated with the fund provided by the Seva Network Foundation and Nepal Samaj Netherland in 2009 CE.
The renovation was carried out by the Sālkhā Hiti Saṃrakṣaṇa Samiti, a committee of locals formed for the conservation of the Hiti.
Prior to the renovation, the Hiti appeared like a pond as it was waterlogged due to the blockage of its drainage.

Previously, this place was one of the main water-sources for daily usage and worships, but the installation of government water supply in each household resulted in the lack of proper care and maintenance of the Hiti.
Combining elements from both the pagoda andśikharaarchitectural styles, this temple devoted to Lord Śiva was originally named "Bhuvaneśvara," as it was established by Bhuvanalakṣmī.
The temple was built in 1711 CE (NS 831) by Bhuvanalakṣmī.
This indicates that it followed theśikharaarchitectural style (cf. G. Vajrācārya VS 2033, p.40).

There are also indications that the temple might have had multiple levels initially, and some of the wooden components used in the temple might have been repurposed from its original construction (KVPT report 2005, p.3).
A painting from 1852 CE by Henry Oldfield depicts the temple in its present form.
The mix of architectural styles might have emerged during the temple's reconstruction following its collapse during the earthquakes of 1833 CE.
Notably, the temple suffered complete collapse during both the earthquakes of 1934 CE and 2015 CE.
Between these two major seismic events, the Kathmandu Valley Preservation Trust (KVPT) undertook a restoration of the temple in 2006 CE (VS 2063).

Following its collapse in 2015 CE, the KVPT, in collaboration with the Department of Archaeology, reconstructed the Kāgeśvara temple in 2018 CE (VS 2074) with funding from the US Ambassadors Fund for Cultural Preservation.
Two raw bricks have been established as Vajrayoginī, the lineage deity of the Rājabhaṇḍārīs who migrated from Sankhu.
Located in a narrow alley within the Cikaṃmugaḥ Ṭola in Kathmandu, the Vajrayoginī shrine is established on the ground floor of a three-story building facing west.
Inside the sanctum, there is no statue of a main deity; only two raw bricks are established as Vajrayoginī, who is adorned with atoraṇaand an oblong banner (patāḥ).
No records have been found regarding the establishment of this shrine.
According to Pruscha (1975, K-230), this shrine was built in the 19th century.
The earliest inscription found in the shrine is from 1893 CE (VS 1949), recording an offering of a bell to the goddess.
The shrine was renovated after being damaged by the 1934 earthquakes (Pruscha 1975, K-230).
In 1938 CE (VS 1995),SubbāTulasīdāsa Rājabhaṇḍārī,KharadāraMohanadāsa Rājabhaṇḍārī, and others had marble installed on the walls and floor of the sanctum.
In 1998 CE (VS 2055), Heramba Bahādura Rājabhaṇḍārī and his family renovated the Vajrayoginī shrine, adding a new door, in memory of his parents, Dhīrja Bahādura and mother Cinīyālakṣmī Rājabhaṇḍārī.

In 2004 CE (VS 2061), the oldtoraṇaabove the sanctum entrance was stolen and replaced by Acyutānanda Prasāda Rājabhaṇḍārī and Keśava Prasāda Rājabhaṇḍārī in honor of their father, Kṛṣṇa Rājabhaṇḍārī, mother Satyamāyā Rājabhaṇḍārī, and elder brother Dāmodara Prasāda Rājabhaṇḍārī.
While the 2015 earthquakes damaged the building housing the shrine, it remains unrepaired.
Thus, both the Vajrayoginī shrine in Kathmandu and the original temple in Sankhu are venerated by the Rājabhaṇḍārīs who relocated.

Regarding the foundation of Sankhu, a Buddhist scripture calledMaṇiśailamahāvadānacredits a priest named Jogadeva Vajrācārya for establishing the town in 1300 BC (Kaligata Era 1801) in the shape of a conch shell (śaṅkha) as per the instruction of Goddess Vajrayoginī.

He is said to have constructed a palace at the centre along with the shrines ofaṣṭamātṛkās(Eight Mother Goddesses), ninebāhāḥs, and four gates in four cardinal directions while dividing the Town into eightṭolas with a Gaṇeśa shrine at each respectiveṭola(V. Vajrācārya1119, p. 32-33).
As Dugāḥ Hiti is one of the eightṭolas of Sankhu, it is possible that Dugāḥ Hiti Gaṇeśa also came into existence in some form at around 1300 BC.
In 1851 CE (1907 VS), Prime Minister Bama Bahādura Kũvara undertook the construction of Tīnadevala (KAT2670), situated along the banks of the Bagmati River, surrounded bysataḥs.
Subsequently, within the outer area of the courtyard, various smaller shrines and temples were added by his relatives and descendants.
One such addition was the Indrabhakteśvara Mandira (KAT2650), constructed by the youngest wife of Prime Minister Bama Bahādura Kũvara.
Adjacent to it is the Lakṣmīnārāyana Mandira, believed to have been built by one of Bama Bahādura’s three wives.
Lakṣmīnārāyana Mandira is elevated on three levels of square plinths, constructed with locally sourced stone.
A bell is installed within one of the plinths, and the shrine's four walls are adorned with traditional plaster (bajra).
Although a photograph from Pruscha (1975, p. 92) shows a stone statue of Garuḍa near the east-facing entrance, as of July 2023 CE, both the pillar and the Garuḍa statue are missing.
The temple, having suffered damage during the 2015 CE earthquake (2072 VS), is currently in a dilapidated state, worsened by a leaning tree against its structure.
The original statue of Lakṣmīnārāyana has been stolen, leaving only the stone pedestal inside the sanctum.
The temple's constructor also built asataḥto facilitate daily worship and other religious activities.
Reconstruction efforts commenced post the 2015 CE earthquake, and the Bagmati Civilization Integrated Development Committee has allocated funds (as of 2023 CE) to reconstruct it.
Presently (July 2023 CE), the temple, devoid of its original statue and fallen into disrepair, no longer functions as a venue for religious activities.

Interestingly, a bell originally belonging to the nearby Indrabhakteśvara temple (KAT2650) has been relocated and placed on the plinth of this temple, bearing an inscription indicating its dedication to Indrabhakteśvara Mahādeva in 1864/1865 CE (1921 VS).
Below it one can guess the presence of an eroded inscription in Nāgarī script.
The lower register contains at least five lines of eroded Nāgarī inscription.
Stone memorial pillars were erected throughout the Karnali Basin from the 13th to the 17th centuries.
They were erected to honour war heroes (Andolfatto 2019).
Locals refers to this raised platform with the Sarasvatī Shrine as ‘Sarasvatīsthāna’ or ‘Sarasvatī Thāy’ (inscription from NS 1113 &Y. Vajrācārya and others, p. 132).
citations: (inscription from NS 1113 &Y. Vajrācārya and others, p. 132)

text: The statue of Bhagīratha, which is usually found below ahiti, was probably relocated here.
A statue of Akṣobhya in thebhūmisparśa-mudrāis enshrined as thekvāḥpāḥdyaḥ(main deity) at the sanctum, and acaityais installed on the wall to the right of Akṣobhya.
The lower part of the palm contains an inscription, but it is illegible due to the loss of most of the text.
There are no historical sources to date the initial construction of the Bāhāḥ.

TheMaṇiśailamahāvadāna, a Buddhist scripture mentions: In 1300 BC (Kaligata Era 1801), when Jogadeva Vajrācārya founded the town of Sankhu in the shape of aśaṅkha(conch shell) by assimilating seven villages as per the instruction of Vajrayoginī, he had divided the town into eight quarters (ṭola) and constructed a palace at the centre, along with the shrines ofasṭamātṛkās(Eight Mother Goddesses), ninebāhāḥs, and four gates in the four cardinal directions (V. Vajrācārya1119, p. 32).
Yogī2012, p. 62 refers to such inscription asdātṛhastābhilekha(lit. the inscription on the donor’s palm).
There is a similar palm inscription at Sālkhā Sataḥ (SKH0121) in Sankhu.
D. Sharma and T. Shrestha2016 p. 198 have stated that such inscriptions are installed in memory of women who undergo the self-immolation rite calledsatībased on the practices in India.
This does not apply to the case of these palm inscriptions from Sankhu.

monument_name: Bhurtī Śikhara Temples with Pavilion (ca. 14th-15th cent.)
text: There are nevertheless structural differences between the Bhurtī and Ajayamerukoṭa monuments: in Bhurtī the pavilion was built as a planned constituent of the temples, while in Ajayamerukoṭa the pavilion appears as an independant structure.

monument_name: Bhurtī Śikhara Temples with Pavilion (ca. 14th-15th cent.)
text: Given the fact that the Ajayamerukoṭa monuments are dated from 1373 CE (ŚS 1295), the Bhurtī monuments must post-date it and can therefore be dated around the end of the 14th century and the 15th century (Andolfatto 2019: 88).
An inscription in the Phalcā records that it was constructed by Mohanavīrasiṃha Tulādhara, a resident of Asana Ṭola in Kathmandu, together with his family in 1959 CE (NS 1079).
The inscription also mentions that anyone has the right to renovate the Phalcā in the case it collapses or gets damaged.
The Svayambhū Vyavasthāpana ra Saṃrakṣaṇa Mahāsamiti, the body that manages the Svayambhunath area, began reconstructing the dilapidated Phalcā right before the 2015 earthquakes.
By the time of the 2015 earthquakes, the brick walls were already completed.
The walls built with newdāciaḥpāandmāaḥpābricks laid in cement mortar suffered no damages.
After a break of about a year due to the earthquakes, the reconstruction concluded in around October 2016 CE.
Statues and inscriptions found unattended around the Śāntipura area are posted on the rear wall of the Phalcā.

One of the inscriptions dating 1800 CE (NS 920) records Harinārāyaṇa Rañjitakāra of Bākunani at Mañjuśrī Ṭola in Patan donating land for performing anniversary rituals of a certain religious monument.
Another inscription, dated 1798 CE (VS 1855), notes Kājī Bandhu Rāṇā and Kajinī Jayakumārī of Gorakhā (?) constructing a stonecaityaat the Svayambhunath area.
The Phalcā appears to have been built to allow devotees who come for worship at the Śāntipura to rest.
The entrance is clearly marked by a decorative gateway between two residential buildings.
The mainśikharatemple is built on a frontal courtyard measuring 10 m × 10 m.
The courtyard is now surrounded by tall residential buildings; these were constructed at a later date.
The temple structure is constructed in terracotta bricks with thousands of images of Buddha attached to them.
Four turrets have been erected on the first floor of the temple.
Aāgamahouse for the goddess Vidyādharī has been constructed to the east of the temple.
Originally, this was the house of Abhayarāja, the man who built the Mahābuddha Temple.
She appeared to Abhayarāja in a dream, ordering him to construct the Mahābuddha temple in the courtyard of his house.
The ground floor of theāgamabuilding contains a place for chantingbhajana.
King Amara Malla appointed the man who constructed this temple, Abhayarāja, as the Head (nāikyā)Ḍiṭṭhāof manufacturing coins.
He returned to Kathmandu Valley in 1565 (NS 685) and started constructing this temple after hearing a voice in the sky: “O Abhayarāja, Mahābauddha is pleased with your devotion.
Return to your house and build a temple.

Buddhaju also passed away after completing the second floor, and his son Jīvarāja and grandson Jayamuni completed the construction in 1601 (NS 721).Śākya(1988, 10-11) writes that King Śivasiṃha Malla was invited to the opening ceremony of the temple in 1601.

However,Gutschow(1997, 308 and 2011, 516) records two different dates: he argues that the temple was completed in 1602 and was consecrated in April 1610 on the auspicious day ofakṣaya tṛṭīyāby King Śivasiṃha.

Gutschow also notes that the chronicles consistently replace the termbodhiwithbauddha;“the village is called not Bodh Gayā but Bauddha Gayā; the temple in Nepal is not the Bodhi temple but the Mahābauddha temple, which is consecrated to the Great Buddha” (Gutschow1997, 308).
He further adds that the temple was partially renovated in 1776 (ibid. 308).
The four upper storeys collapsed during the earthquake in January 1934.
Dissimilar to most of thebāhāḥsin the Kathmandu Valley, Sunanda Vihāra has nokvāḥpāḥchẽ(main monastic building to house the principal deity of abāhāḥ).
Instead, a small shrine which faces west has been built in one side of the garden and a stone statue of Akṣobhya has been consecrated in its sanctum as the Bāhāḥ’s principal deity (kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ).
The shrine is constructed out of bricks and plastered with bajra mortar.
A statue of the serpent king (nāgarāja) is established in the shrine’s northern direction.
Similarly, a Dharmadhātujinālaya CaityaandDharmadhātu Maṇḍalaare also established in the Bāhāḥpremises.
There are no historical sources to date the initial construction of the Bāhāḥ.
A certain Dharmasiṃha from Ārako Vihāra is mentioned in aKāraṇḍavyūhamanuscript from 1624 CE (NS 744) preserved in the Asiatic Society (Shāstri2005, 28-29).
This gives us clear hint that the Bāhāḥ was constructed before that date.
Pruscha1975, p. 208 (P-102) mentions that it has been thought to be built by one of the students of Śūnyaśrī, the founder of the Yampi Vihāra.
In 1969 CE (VS 2026), the ruined Bāhāḥ was reconstructed by a person called Ratnajyoti Vajrācārya.
During the reconstruction, the Bāhāḥ’s older architectural plans were not followed, and only the above mentioned (modern) shrine as the Bāhāḥ’skvāḥpāḥdegaḥwas constructed.
Additionally, a parasol (chatra) is offered to theDharmadhātujinālaya Caitya(see object numberLAL1000-006 below) on the full moon day of Āśvina after performing its anniversary rituals.
Kanakāsundarī Temple, one kilometre east of Hatsinja village and near Sahubada settlement, is built on the south-eastern end of a rocky hill dominating Sahubada village.
Following the collapse of the Khaśa Malla polity, Sinja remained an important centre of power under the Kalyāl dynasty (Pant 2009and Andolfatto 2019).
The central Temple, built in the centre of a quadrangular compound, is dedicated to the goddess Kanakāsundarī.
It is a square stone construction with mud mortar and wooden chaining.
One version of her legend, collected in Sinja in 2018 CE, goes as follows:"Long ago the king had a servant in charge of the kitchens.
A temple was built to put an end to it.
Originally built as a one-tiered structure, Umāmaheśvara Mandira was later rebuilt into a dome-style temple by the Department of Archaeology.
A stonetoraṇacontaining a depiction of Chepu on its middle is installed atop the door to the sanctum that houses a stone statue of Umāmaheśvara.
There are no records to date the initial construction of the Temple.
Locals informed us (on 25 March 2022) that it used to be a tiered temple with traditional tile (jhĩgaṭī) roof before it collapsed in 1969 CE (2026 VS).
They could not rebuild it in its traditional style due to the lack of funds, thus they raised four wooden pillars in four corners and built the wall without a roof.
The Temple collapsed again in the 2015 earthquakes, and then the Department of Archaeology rebuilt it in the dome style in 2021 CE.
An inscription attached to the western wall of the temple mentions that the temple was made in NS 819 (1699 CE).
The inscription further mentions that on the date the pinnacle was fixed and aguṭhīwas also established.
Pruscha mentions the temple was made in 1683 CE (NS 803), but does not provide any source of information.
According to him, the temple was rebuilt after the great earthquake of 1934 (Pruscha1975, 182).
The temple was badly damaged in the 2015 earthquake.
In 2019, the Department of Archeology has started to reconstruct the temple after dismantling the damaged structure.
In 1851 CE (1907 VS), Prime Minister Bama Bahādura Kũvara initiated the construction of Tīnadevala (KAT2670) along the banks of the Bagmati River, surrounded bysataḥs.

Local tradition holds that thesataḥwas built at the spot where Candra Śamśera received the Vajrayāna initiation.

An inscription atop his painting bears Candra Śamśera's name along with the year 1964, indicating that the portrayal of the longest-serving Rāṇā prime minister was completed in 1907 CE, which corresponds to VS 1964.

While oral history among the locals recounts thesataḥ's construction at the place of Candra Śamśera's initiation, an inscription within thesataḥproves that the rest house existed as early as 1875 CE (NS 995).
The inscription records an instance of endowment by Siṃhanarasiṃha Buddhācārya and his family from Prasannaśīla Mahāvihāra in the name of Nāmasaṅgīti, a Buddhist deity, in 1875 CE (NS 995).
It is unclear what the endowment was but it probably was thesataḥ's construction.
Considering Candra Śamśera's birth in 1863 CE (Sever2014, p.237), it becomes evident that thesataḥwas already established when he was 12 years old.
Thus, it is implausible that thesataḥwas erected post his initiation.
Furthermore, if we place the initiation event in 1907 CE, the year his painting was finished, Candra Śamśera would have been 44 years old at the time.
The 1875 CE (NS 995) inscription by donor Siṃharanasiṃha also instructed the installation of a Nāmasaṅgīti statue in thesataḥ, funded by rent from his ancestral house at Bikumāḥchẽ Ṭola.

In the year 1907 (1851 AD), Bama Bahādura Kuvãra, the brother of Jaṅga Bahādura, undertook the construction of an impressive temple on the banks of the Bagmati River, known as the Tīna Devala (KAT2670).
The construction project also encompassed the Jagannātha Temple (KAT2690), as mentioned in the copperplate inscription discovered on-site.
Simultaneously, a protective boundary wall was erected around the Tīna Devala, Jagannātha Temple, and Garden to safeguard these monuments.

The copperplate inscription instructed thegūṭhī(trust) to undertake repairs, if necessary, to the boundary wall of the Caugharā Sataḥ surrounding the Tīna Devala Temple complex (Darnāl VS 2061, p.43).

The boundary wall features a sizable entrance on the northwestern side of the Tīna Devala for access to the temple complex, and a second entrance constructed along the Bagmati riverside, facing south.
During the earthquake of 2015 CE, the Tīna Devala, along with other surrounding heritage sites, sustained damage, leaving the protective boundary wall in a precarious state (see a photohere).

The Urban Development Ministry, with the authority to oversee such matters, secured financial support for the reconstruction of the Tīna Devala and Caugharā Sataḥ, including this wall, from the Asian Development Bank through the Integrated Development Committee for the Conservation of the Bagmati Civilization.
The reconstruction efforts were successfully completed on Kartik 6, 2079 (October 23rd, 2022).

The temple features a unique hybrid style; its largeśikharatower is supported by the maincella,whilst its circumambulatory path has been constructed using carved timber columns and cross beams and is covered by a tile skirting roof.
According to a report by the Nepal Department of Archaeology, the temple was established in 1887 CE (VS 1944) by the stepmother (kānchī āmā) of Deva Śamśera.
A document dated 1894 (VS 1951) which is preserved in the Guṭhī Saṁsthāna archives refers to this temple and itsguṭhīlands.
The temple suffered severe damage during the 2015 earthquakes.
The brick walls at the four corners of thecellapartly collapsed due to a combination of poor maintenance and ineffective repairs made in the past.
It was discovered that the timber framework of the interior bearing structure had mostly rotted away and was not properly repaired in a restoration effort around 2007.

A detailed damage assessment carried out by national and international structural experts under the aegis of UNESCO revealed that 90 percent of the temple's timber structure was in urgent need of replacement.

The complex structural build-up of timber frames integrated in the brickśikharatower would have madein siturepairs extremely difficult and rendered the building at a high risk of collape in the future.
It was therefore decided that repairs should be made by dismantling the temple and rebuilding it from the ground up.
Reconstruction works commenced in July 2019 and were completed in 2021.
