They begin the worship in Sunāguthi and then proceed to Thecva.
Upon reaching Thecva, the Navadurgā dance troupe is positioned in the east of the Mandaḥ Phalcā, where a goat sacrifice is offered to them.
[1]Although the temple of Taleju, the tutelary deity of the royal families of the Kathmandu Valley, is invariably constructed next to the palace, it is not so in the case of Sankhu.

Although there are no written records to date the initial construction of the Kvāṭha Chẽ, locals presume that it was built during the reign of King Sūrya Malla (1524 -1529 CE) of Kathmandu (cf.T. NaḥghaḥbhanīVS 2043, p. 2).
According to the local residents, the Kvātha Chẽ used to be a three-tier temple ofjhĩgaṭītile roof before it collapsed by the 1934 earthquakes.
Footnotes^The Building also functioned as a fort during the medieval period.
At the highest point of Dhulikhel, a temple has been built where Bhagavatī is enshrined, and special processions are held here duringViśkāḥ Jātrāand Daśaiṃ.
At the centre of Cochẽ, a Bhagavatī temple has been constructed.
Built in a three-storeyed style, the temple faces east.
At the temple’s peak, a gilded gold metal pinnacle has been installed, with a metal serpent placed on each of the four corners.
The temple is constructed upon three plinths.
Inside the sanctum sanctorum, a black stone idol is established as Bhagavatī.
In front of the temple, to the east, stands a stone pillar on top of which an idol of a lion has been installed.
On the southern staircase, a small shrine has been built, and an abstract stone is installed there as Mahākāla.
In the southern courtyard, a caitya, two bells, and idol of Sarasvatī and Gaṇeśa are established.
According to the temple priest, after the temple was rebuilt, simple struts were installed, but in the past, the struts here were artistic, featuring the figures of various gods and goddesses.
When the Śrīkhaṇḍapura people returned with their gold and silver ornaments, the girl had already reached Dhulikhel and been established as Bhagavatī.
Realizing this, the Śrīkhaṇḍapura people believed Bhagavatī had broken her promise, so they cut off the nose and established the nose in the middle part of that area and built a temple.
For this reason, it is said that the Bhagavatī idol here has no nose (H. Śreṣṭha VS 2043 p. 29).
No definite evidence has been found concerning the original construction of this temple.
Observing the installed idol of Bhagavatī, it can be assumed that it existed from the Malla period.
Pruscha (1975, p. 249) mentions that it was restored in 1934 CE.
According to the temple priest, some inscriptions are preserved on the second floor of the temple (a priest of the mandira, Karmācārya, male, age 65).
The temple was rebuilt in 1960 CE (VS 2017) (local resident, Śreṣṭha, male, age 75).

Furthermore, according to the inscription on thetoraṇaplaced at the main entrance, during the reign of King Rājendra Vikrama Śāha and Kājī Bakhata Siṅaga, the Paṃcadeśaora group of Dhulikhel installed the toraṇa in 1820 CE (NS 940).
One of the bells in the temple courtyard dates to 1921 CE (NS 1041) and another to 2025 CE (NS 1145).
As this procession was established by Bāla Narasiṃha Kũvara, it is also called the Bāla Narasiṃha Jātrā (H. Śreṣṭha VS 2043 p. 42).
According to an inscription, the temple originally had two tiers.
However, following its collapse in the 1934 earthquake, it was reconstructed with only a single roof.
In 2017 CE, it underwent another reconstruction, reverting to its original two-tiered structure.
Thephalcāextends outwards from the façade of a traditional building which is also connected to the temple.
A historical photo of the building shows avimāna jhyāḥon the first floor above thephalcā.
On the full moon day of Maṅsira, aguṭhīrelated to the Gaṇeśa temple and run by the Śreṣṭha community organises a secret fire ritual on the ground floor of the building.
It can be assumed that the predecessors of theseguṭhīmembers constructed or commissioned both the building and thephalcā.
An illegible, effaced stone inscription is attached to the wall of thephalcā.
Thephalcāis currently under reconstruction.
However, at the end of the fiscal year VS 2074-75 the progress of the reconstruction work was deemed unsatisfactory and the funds were cut off.
A new fund has been provided from the budget of the fiscal year VS 2075-76.
During Indrajātrā,yaḥsĩand some other small wooden poles are erected in front of thephalcā.
The Harisiddhi Temple is one of Dhulikhel’s important temple, and its pinnacle was installed during the reign of King Surendra Śāha and Prime Minister Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā.
The temple is a three tiered structure built in the traditional Nepali pagoda style, with all three roofs covered in brass.
A metal pinnacle plated with gold is installed on the peak, above which figures of an umbrella and serpents (nāga) are visible.
Inside the sanctum sanctorum, three metal idols of the goddesses are established, each holding a khaḍga (sword) and adorned with silver ornaments.
Although no direct inscription confirms the temple’s foundation date, Pruscha (1975, p. 249) notes that it was built in the 19th century.
The oldest object in the temple is a bell dated 1834 CE (NS 955).
An oral tradition holds that this temple was constructed jointly by the local Mākaju and Byāñju communities.

An inscription found on the temple’s pinnacle states that it was established in 1871 CE (VS 1928) by Hiraṇyagarbhā Kumārī Devī the Queen of Prime Minister Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā during the reign of King Surendra Śāha.
The historic Juddhadhārā, located to the south, was installed in 1939 CE (VS 1996) at the initiative of Śrīnatha Byāñju.
On the wall near the Juddadhārā, an inscription from 1679 CE (NS 799) records the establishment of Śrī Ananta Nārāyaṇa.
In the course of establishing a private cremation site (ghāṭa) for his clan at Cupiṃghāṭa, Hṛdayaratna Gvaṃgaḥ of Bhaktapur built this temple and established various statues in the temple complex.

Situated on the western bank of the Hanumante river at Cupiṃghāṭa in Bhaktapur, this Śiva temple stands in the northern of the two major temple complexes in the area built by two separate caste groups.
While this temple complex was established by the Gvaṅgaḥ clan from Bhaktapur, the southern complex built around the Harṣamukteśvara Śivālaya (BKT0460) was established by a Dhaubhaḍela family.
Thisśivālayaresembles most of the Śiva temples built during the Śāha-Rāṇā period.
Such Śiva temples, with roofs shaped like domes or bells, were built in large numbers during the 19th century.
Here, too, the roof is built in a dome style, with a stone finial.
At the four corners of the dome, small turrets with a finial are erected.
However, the statue of Kamadeva was stolen, leaving the niche currently (January 2025) empty.
A stone inscription placed on the temple's plinth records the temple’s construction but has been somewhat damaged, obscuring some of the details including the year.
Pruscha (1975, p. 230) reports the existence of an inscription from 1865 CE, which corresponds to VS 1922.
The temple's architecture and the artifacts found here seem to originate around the same period, suggesting that Pruscha likely read the date from this inscription.

The inscription records that Hṛdayaratna Gvaṃgaḥ and his wife, Manitha[kuṃ], established Hṛdayeśvara Mahādeva in the temple, along with various other deities, including Hṛdayavināyaka, Hṛdayeśvarī, Hṛdayanārāyaṇa, Garuḍeśvara, Trailokeśvara, Umāmaheśvara, Viśveśvara, Gaṇeśa, Hanumān, Kāmadeva, Durlabheśvara, Umeśvara, Maṇikeśvara, Vaṭuka, Joginī, Kṣetrapāla, Brahmāyaṇī, Mohinī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Mahālakṣmī.
Hṛdayaratna also built anāgaṃchẽdirectly in front of the temple.
The inscription's mention of the installation of various mother goddesses strongly suggests that the Gvaṃgaḥ family also commissioned theāgaṃchẽ.
The inscription's references to the establishment of Hṛdayanārāyaṇa and Garuḍeśvara indicate that the Gvaṃgaḥs were responsible for both the Nārāyaṇa temple and the Garuḍa pillar.
Clearly, Hṛdayaratna and Manithakuṃ established a significant number of deities across a large area of Cupiṃghāṭa.
Ample land parcels were endowed for their worship and upkeep.
A royal decree (lālamohara) issued in 1826 CE (VS 1883) by Regent Lalitatripurāsundarī assigned responsibility for worship at the Taleju temple in Bhaktapur to members of the Gvaṃgaḥ clan.
This demonstrates the considerable influence the Gvaṃgaḥs held at the court during that period (P. Shrestha VS 2080, p. 593).
Some members of the clan continue to use the Rathore surname (D. Shrestha VS 2076, pp. 543-544).
The 2015 earthquake inflicted substantial damage on the temple, leaving cracks throughout its structure.
Tragically, it finally succumbed to the damage and collapsed completely on the day ofŚivarātrīlater that year.
The Department of Archeology completed the temple's reconstruction in 2023 CE (VS 2080).
The recent reconstruction, however, replaced the bell-shaped dome with a dome and reduced the finial's height.
There are no records to date the initial construction of the Jaḥdhuṃhiti.
Before the Shankharapur Municipality renovated the Jaḥdhuṃhiti in 2021 CE, a stone ceremonial mirror (jvalānhāykaṃ) and a broken piece of a finial were also set on the wall behind it.
After the renovation, the Licchavi Caityas have now been installed separately.

Their position has also been changed: the Caitya (SKH0155-004) previously set on the southern side of the Jaḥdhuṃhiti is now installed on the northern side while the Caitya with empty niches (SKH0155-003) is now shifted to the southern side.
In the course of the Jaḥdhuṃhiti’s renovation, the stonejvalānhāykaṃhas now been installed on top of the Licchavi Caitya with empty niches (SKH0155-003).
A plastic faucet was installed on the back of the Jaḥdhuṃhiti.
After the renovation, a small stone spout has now been installed on the back.

A Girī family residing in thesataḥhas partially repaired the earthquake-damaged building and continues daily worship, but other religious and cultural activities have ceased (family member, Girī, male, age 63).
After a JICA-supported bridge construction, theghāṭaand four statues were moved 12 meters west (local resident, Śreṣṭha, male, age 68).
The Śiva enshrined here is referred to as Milaneśvara in the inscription.
Topabahādura Khatrī of this lineage added various structures and established a religious trust.
It also housesśivaliṅgaand Nandī statue, along with later (1972-73) installations of Gaṇeśa, Śiva, Viṣṇu, Sarasvatī, and Lokeśvara statues.
A significant square-base Licchavi-eraśivaliṅga, found at the Bagmati-Vishnumati confluence, was established here in 1986 CE (VS 2043) by the Rāja Tīrtha Parivāra, a local club.
Theghāṭaandsataḥ's original construction is attributed to ancestors of Topabahādura Khatrī, a Panchyat-era zonal commissioner.
He also added deities and established a religious trust for rituals and festivals.
A lengthy inscription by him details his religious sentiments, contributions, and establishment of various deities along with an innovative religious trust (pitṛ guṭhī) dedicated to his ancestors.

The inscription stipulates weekly worship of deities in Sanepa and at theghāṭa, monthly worship and devotional singing at theghāṭa, and an annual Rāma Navamī exhibition of historical books and images in thesataḥ.
His achievements as the head of a local committee are also listed in the inscription.
The Sākyas living in the courtyard claim that their ancestors built the Caitya, however, there are no records available to verify the claim.
The temple underwent its most recent renovation in 2018 CE (VS 2074), after sustaining damage during the 2015 earthquake, with the involvement of the municipality and local community.

Earlier photographs from the early 1970s (Pruscha 1975, p. 241) show a similar, simple structure with square windows on the upper floor and a roof covered with modern tiles, suggesting prior renovations before the 1970s.
Determining the temple’s original construction period is challenging due to the lack of inscriptions and surviving ornate wooden elements from that time.
However, numerous instances of Bheemsen statues being installed in Newar settlements from the late medieval to the early Śāha period suggest this statue belongs to that era.
Pruscha (1975, p. 241) also dates the temple to the 18th century, mentioning renovations in 1934, 1967/68, and 1970-71, though without citing sources.
The temple's location near the main trade route from Nuwakot to Tibet suggests it was built for travelers entering and exiting the valley to offer prayers.

An inscription from 1586 CE (NS 707) refers to Bāghabhairava of Kirtipur as “Bhīmasena Bhaṭṭāraka,” and a Malla-era song mentions Bhīmasena revealing the form of Bhairava Śiva (S. Śreṣṭha VS 2056, p. 93; K. Tamoṭa NS 1101, pp. 218-219).

text: Numerous Newar folk songs are dedicated to Bhīmasena, expressing the longing and youth's thirst of wives whose husbands are trading in Tibet (T. Siṃha NS 1135, pp. 43-50).
Therefore, most Bhīmasena temples in Nepal were built by merchant families, and a Bhīmasena statue is considered essential in every commercial settlement or locality.
Tokha, known for its molasses trade, likely had this temple built by a prosperous merchant family.
[1]The temple is stone-built and stands on a two-layered plinth.
The present stone statue of Bhavānīśaṅkara, consecrated inside the sanctum, was installed in 1984 CE after the old one was stolen (cf.Ś. ŚreṣṭhaVS 2057,43).
An inscription records that Siddhirāma Bhāro and his wife Gaṃgāmayi, residents of Kirtipur, built this temple and consecrated a stone statue of Bhavānīśaṅkara inside its sanctum in 1718 CE (NS 838).
A statue of this couple is installed in front of the temple.
The inscription further mentions that they also established aguṭhīhaving endowed fiveropanīsof land in order to maintain the temple and carry out the daily rituals.
The Department of Archaeology cleaned and repaired the Bāghabhairava Temple complex in around 2007 CE including the Bhavānīśaṅkara Mandira.
Footnotes^The door in the north façade has an inscription recording the initial construction of the Temple.
The second inscription found inside the sanctum is not related to this Temple.
Elements of medieval monuments are also found erected as if they were memorial pillars.
The pillars were all decorated and inscribed.
They are nevertheless too eroded to provide information on the dates and contexts of installation.
Stone pillars were erected throughout the Karnali Basin from the 13th to the 17th century.
They are installed to honor the memory of deceased persons, mostly warriors.
According to local informants the stūpa (007) was dismantled by Maoists during the Civil War.
The monument has been rebuilt since then.
The Śrīḍhuskā Stūpa (JUM0110) bears an inscription readingOṃ maṇi padme hūṃ, Avalokiteśvara's mantra, in Rañjana script.
The epigraphy is identical to the one seen on the same mantra inscribed on Dullu's Kīrtikhambā (DLK0260), the Patharnauli reservoir (DLK0160).
Both monuments were built in the 1350's, during the rule of king Pṛthvīmalla (r. 1338-1358) (Andolfatto 2019, p. 96;Pant 2009, 301).
It is thus likely that the Śrīḍhuskā Stūpa, as well as the stūpa in Koṭgāũ were built around the same period.
The temples were restored by the Department of Archaeology at an unknown date, presumably in the early 2010s.
The discovered artefacts were all placed in a storeroom (BTD0030-008) built between two tempels and even including the smallśikharaBTD0030-001.
After 2015 the storeroom was dismantled.
These images were worshipped until some of them were stolen (at a yet unknown date) (Dulal 2005: 30).
Except for the easternmost temple (BTD0030-001), all temples are built by pairs, with a common platform (except for BTD0030-004 and 005).

Their individual dimensions are as follow:- BTD0030-001: 154 x 110 cm- BTD0030-002: 244 x 228 cm (without platform)- BTD0030-003: 240 x 212 cm (without platform)- BTD0030-004: 432 x 290 cm (with platform)- BTD0030-005: 430 x 285 cm (with platform)- BTD0030-006: 258 x 198 cm (without platform)- BTD0030-007: 248 x 190 cm (without platform)- BTD0030-008 (storeroom, dismantled after 2015): 400 x 450 cmBesides the śikhara tempels the site also comprises stone sculptures, all pertaining to Hinduism, and more specifically to Shaivism with one Gaṇeśa (BTD0030-009), Durgā Mahiṣāsuramardini (BTD0030-010), Brahmā (BTD0030-011), Nandi (BTD0030-012) and Umā Maheśvara (BTD0030-014).
Finally, their is also the undated inscribed base of a stone sculpture (BTD0030-013).
D. R. Sharma estimated that the paleography of the inscription indicates that it was executed during the 13th century (Sharma 2012: 349).
Given the fact that these temples were erected during the second half of the 14th century, it is likely that the monuments in Devala Hāṭa are also dating from this (post-Khaśa Malla) period.
Adorning the main entrance of thegandhakuṭīis atoraṇa, presented in NS 808 (1688 CE), embellished with images of twenty-two Bodhisattvas.

A monastery for the monks, who follow thesthavīradoctrine of the Buddhism, was built by the monk Jñānapūrṇika to the north of thebahī’s courtyard in VS 2028 (1971 CE) which was used as a public toilet before.
Jñānapūrṇika also also renovated thedyaḥchẽin VS 2033 (1976 CE).
The oldest inscription within thebahīpremises, dating 1675 CE (NS 795), records an offering of a gold pinnacle, accompanied by a day and night sacrifice.
Thebahīwas renovated in 1682 CE (NS 802).
These Śreṣṭhas have established aguṭhīto sponsor this program.
Around 150 years back, Caityarāja Śākya a member of the saṅgha of Cikaṃ Bahī built a house in the Nani’s courtyard and started living there.
In earlier times, there was no physical infrastructure built in Om Bāhāḥ Nani, which is located in Om Bāhāḥ.
Around 150 years back, Caityarāja Śākya a member of thesaṅghaof Cikaṃ Bahī (LAL1620) built a house in the Nani’s courtyard and started living there.
He also established a Śikharakūṭa Caitya in the courtyard, which faces east.
The inscription recording the establishment of thiscaityais completely rubbed off.
A Dharmādhātu Manḍala established in NS 1073 (1953 CE) and a pair of Mañjuśrī’s feet can be seen next to the Caitya.

The Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa Temple, situated south of the Rāmaparivāra Mandira in Mṛgasthalī of the Paśupati area, was constructed in 1935 CE (VS 1992) by Dilakumārī, the wife of Rāṇā Prime Minister Bhīma Śamśera.
This dome-style temple is built with meticulously polished stones.

Although there is no separate inscription specifically mentioning the temple's construction, G. Ṭaṇḍana (VS 2053, p. 498) states that Bhīma Śamśera built the Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa Mandira in 1935 CE (VS 1992) and placed a Garuḍa statue in front of it.

However, the bell inscription (PPK0426-003), installed north of the entrance gate, reveals that Dilakumārī, Bhīma Śamśera's wife, offered the bell to the main deity in 1935 CE (VS 1992) along with her daughter Divyalakṣmī.
Another bell (PPK0426-004), installed south of the entrance, was offered by Dilakumārī's daughter, Divyalakṣmī.
Since bells are typically installed during the construction of a temple, it can be inferred that Dilakumārī herself built the temple in 1935 CE.
Bhīma Śamśera, on the other hand, became the prime minister after the death of Candra Śamśera in 1929 CE (VS 1986) and passed away in September 1932 (VS 1989) (P. Rāja VS 2070, p.10).
Therefore, the bell inscription suggests that the temple was constructed by Dilakumārī and not by her husband, Bhīma Śamśera (M. Thāpā VS 2077, p. 324).
Dilakumārī, also known as Sītā Mahārānī, was the final wife of Bhīma Śamśera and belonged to the Tamang community (P. Rāja VS 2070, p. 16).
The brick gate in front of the temple suffered some damage during the 2015 earthquakes.
As of May 2024 CE, the temple is undergoing reconstruction, with only two plinth levels and the base of the main structure rebuilt so far.
At the heart of the sanctum, aśivaliṅgarevered as Raṇabhuvaneśvara is consecrated.
Adjacent to the west of the temple is a raised platform (maṭha) housing thetulasīplant and a bell endowed by Raṇodyota Śāha and his wife (details below).
Originally, the temple featured a two-tiered structure withjhĩgaṭītiles and a finial of gilt copper before it collapsed.
The temple’s history is chronicled in a stone stele inscription dated 1828 CE (VS 1885), positioned south of the temple.

According to the inscription, Raṇodyota Śāha erected the temple in 1824 CE (ŚS 1746) with a golden finial, having discovered avāṇaliṅga(naturally-formedśivaliṅga) on the banks of the Narmada river, and he and his wife, Bhuvanakumārīdevī, donated land to support daily and periodic rituals.
The temple was named after them, and the temple previously featured rest houses also built by Raṇodyota Śāha (no longer, as of May 2024 CE, seen on the site).

text: In 1825 CE (ŚS 1747), a year after construction, the couple donated the aforementioned bell to the temple, as recorded on the bell’s inscription.
Raṇodyota Śāha was born in 1794 CE (ŚS 1716) as the first son of King Raṇabahādura Śāha (M. Panta VS 2041, p. 30).
In 1799 CE (VS 1855), Raṇabahādura issued a copperplate inscription, declaring Gīrvāṇayuddha the king and Raṇodyota Śāha the maincautariyā(the principal officer of the state).
Raṇabahādura then abdicated and became an ascetic (C. Nepālī VS 2020, p. 33).
Raṇodyota Śāha’s name last appeared in a government document in 1836 CE (VS 1893) (cf. Y. Naraharinātha VS 2013, p. 145).
The temple had already collapsed before the 2015 CE earthquakes due to its poor state of repair.
A trident installed inside the sanctum is currently being stored safely by Lalitajaṅga Śāha, a descendant of Raṇodyota Śāha.
In 2023 CE (VS 2080), the plinths of the temple were rebuilt with funds from the Department of Archaeology.
Efforts are being made to arrange funds for rebuilding the temple as well.

Its ground floor is adorned with three bays, simple columns, and a central fire altar (yagyasālā), while main facade on the upper floor has three windows.
Within the Sataḥ are three inscriptions, the oldest dating back to 1862 CE (NS 982).
This inscription commemorates the installation of a Gaṇeśa statue in front of the Sataḥ by Kīrtimāna Siṃha.
It also mentions the allocation of land for the repair and maintenance of the Sataḥ, along with provisions for performing anniversary rituals.
Another inscription of uncertain date records Kīrtimāna Siṃha's establishment of a religious endowment by offering Lord Gaṇeśa's vehicle (vāhāna).
Despite the claim in the inventory (VS 2039, p.163) suggesting that the Sataḥ was built in 1904 CE (NS 1024), this assertion appears inconsistent with the 1862 CE (NS 982) inscription.
Surviving the 2015 earthquake (VS 2072), the Sataḥ required extensive reconstruction due to severe wall cracks.

The Ministry of Urban Development's Bagmati Civilization Integrated Development Committee, with support from the Asian Development Bank, completed the reconstruction on November 29, 2021, with the exterior walls now adorned with white cement plaster.
During the fourth bright fortnight of Āśvina, the clan conducts an anniversary ritual, offering fire oblations at the Sataḥ's phalcā.
Historically, the monument served as a venue for devotional songs, communal gatherings and changing clothes after a sacred bath in the Bāgamatī river, and bonfires during Ṛṣi Pañcamī and Navarātrī.
Erected by Babara Śamśera in 1933 CE (VS 1990), thisśivālaya(lit. the abode of Lord Śiva) is dedicated to his deceased son Bāla Śamśera.
Additionally, a brass bell from 1933 CE hangs on a bell-stand south of the temple, commemorating its construction.
Furthermore, a statue of Kāmadeva is enshrined southeast of the temple, with a stone trident (triśūla) erected to the north.
Babara Śamśera commissioned the temple in 1933 CE (VS 1990) in memory of his deceased son Bāla Śamśera, also presenting a bell on the occasion.
He served as the last Rāṇā army chief (cīphasāheba) (P. Rāja VS 2070, p.50).

During the First World War that commenced in 1914 CE, Candra Śamśera deployed 16,544 soldiers in support of the British army, including two contingents led by Babara Śamśera and three led by his other son, Keśara Śamśera (B. Śarmā VS 2033, p.359).
Babara Śamśera also constructed a water spout (dhārā) in Pokhara in 1921 CE in memory of his late son Bāla Śamśera, which is still known as Bāla Dhāra (Landon 1928, p.197).

Following the declaration of democracy in 1951 CE (VS 2007), Mohana Śamśera assumed the role of prime minister in the interim government, while Babara Śamśera held the position of defense minister (P. Rāja VS 2073, p.313).
It was completely destroyed in the 2015 earthquakes.
Prior to this, the Phalcāhad already been reconstructed once in 1993 by GTZ/udle.
When the NHDP team visited it in October 2019 the Phalcā was still under reconstruction.
According to the president of the Sthānīya Upabhoktā Samiti (Local Consumer’s Committee), the committee that collected these donations added an extra 10% to the total amount.
The Phalcā is being rebuilt in its original form, and historical photos show that the structure once had ajhigaṭī-tiled roof and adhaḥmāin front of it.
Based on this cultural event, however, it can be assumed that the Phalcā was built by the community's ancestors.
Locals celebrate the Śivaratri fireworks in front of the Phalcā every year.

It is the biggestcaityain this area and exhibits a style typical of the 16th century (Gutschow(2011, vol 1: 152).H. Śākya(1993, 82) describes it as a Vajradhātucaitya. The caitya is built with small traditionalmā apābricks which attests to its antiquity. The four corners, the frames around the niches and the finial are all made of stone. Statues of Akṣobhya, Ratnasaṃbhava, Amitābha and Amoghasiddhi are installed in the eastern, southern, western and northern niches of thecaityarespectively. In addition, a statue of Akṣobhya is attached to the eastern plinth and an inscription has been placed on the south-eastern corner of thecaitya. The inscription mentions that thecaityawas renovated by five Śākyas in 1749 CE. A historical photo from 2000 (published inBuṅgamatīko Sā̃skṛtika Sampadāharū,p. 50) shows that thecaityawas in a dilapidated condition. However, it was renovated in 2002. A Śākya family residing in the vicinity south of thecaityatakes care of it and performs all annual rituals.

monument_name: Nhū Bāhāḥ at Dhalāyacā (16th cent. CE)
text: According toLocke(1985, 162), there used to be a badly damaged inscription of King Jayaratna Malla dated NS 639.
The Śiva temple known as Candrabhakteśvara was built in 1865 CE (VS 1922) by Candrakumārīdevī, the wife of Dhīra Śamśera, as an expression of her devotion to the deity.
Constructed in a style similar to other temples in the area, it features a stone structure with a single plinth level and a bell-shaped roof topped with a metallic finial.
Outside, a bell dating from 1869 CE (VS 1926) hangs from a bell stand to the south, while a Nandī figure guards the western entrance.
Additionally, a small shrine housing anotherśivaliṅgastands northeast of the temple with a statue of Kāmadeva established next to it.

Dhīra Śamśera established Dhīrabhakteśvara (PPK1966) in 1854 CE (VS 1911) in Mṛgasthalī, and in 1865 CE (VS 1922), four similarśivālayas, including Candrabhakteśvara, were built by four of his wives, each dedicated to one of them.
Candrakumārīdevī commissioned this temple.

The temples had separate inscriptions with instructions for rituals on designated days, later amalgamated into one large inscription (PPK1966_I_001), revealing the construction by his four wives in 1865 CE.
The bell donated by Eastern Commanding General Dhīra Śamśera four years after the temple's establishment was dedicated to his wife Candrakumārīdevī, who had passed away by then.
The bell inscription refers to the temple as Candramukteśvara, likely due to her passing, but the main inscription identifies it as Candrabhakteśvara, the appropriate name.
Candrakumārīdevī, the mother of Dhīra Śamśera’s first son Vīra Śamśera (P. Rāja, VS 2073, p. 99), passed away before the bell installation, possibly leading to the name discrepancy.
The temple was damaged in the 2015 earthquakes and was renovated by the Pashupati Area Development Trust in 2019 CE (VS 2076) (priest, Ḍhuṅgela, male, age 50).
The building has balconies that face south and west, and a door on the first floor links theguṭhī-house to the neighbouring house.
The main temple deity is Ākāśa Bhairava, though he is also referred to as Kāla Bhairava in an inscription of NS 802.
In 1678 CE (NS 798), the renowned Viśveśvara temple in Kashi fell victim to Aurangzeb's actions, robbing pilgrims of a major sacred site.
Responding to this loss, Bhagīratha Bhaiyā, a trusted minister under King Śrīnivāsa Malla, erected a grand Viśveśvara temple in Patan, providing solace to devotees.
In Kathmandu, a smaller temple, Viśveśvara, was established in the Hanumandhoka palace vicinity, later known as Kāśīnātha Mandira.
The temple did not collapse in the 2015 CE earthquakes, however, recognizing its deteriorating condition, the Department of Archaeology initiated reconstruction in 2022 CE.
As of April 2023 CE, the temple remains under construction and is locked behind a fence.

Prime Minister Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā built this arcaded platform forvairāgīascetics as anakhaḍāaround the time when he also built the Jaṅge Hiraṇya Hema Nārāyaṇa temple (KAT2800) at the cremation ground of Kālamocāna Ghāṭa.

Standing on the banks of the Bagmati river in Thapathali amongst threeakhaḍās of religious renunciates of the Rāmānandī sect, this Vairāgī Sataḥ is a two-storied building with a 17-bayedphalcāon the ground floor, the bays opening up to the river.
Jaṅga Bahādura built the grand temple along with Sataḥs with numerous rooms in 1875 CE (VS 1931).
His intention was to provide facilities to these ascetics, both from Nepal and India, who had come for pilgrimage (N. Yogī VS 2013, p. 80).
Following the 2015 earthquakes, the Sataḥ was deemed unsafe to live in due to the damage and was completely demolished.

The reconstruction was carried out by the High-Powered Committee for Integrated Development of the Bagmati Civilization under the Ministry of Urban Development with the loan assistance of the Asian Development Bank.
The eastern section of the monument has so far been rebuilt.
This hereditary position, granted by the Guthi Corporation, has been passed down through generations.
Previously, the Guthi Corporation had a staff of 12 people to serve these saints, but now it has been reduced to three, including the abbot.

Built next to a large shady platform (cautārā) north of Asvabārī in Nuwakot, the shrine’s main statue depicts a four-armed Nārāyaṇa (an epithet of Viṣṇu) seated cross-legged on his mount Garuḍa (object no. NWK0350-001).
Additionally, a new śivaliṅga (object no. NWK0350-005) has also been added to the assortment of the three statues from various periods under the shade of the same big tree.
On Śivarātrī, locals light a bonfire and occasionally organize special pujas if sponsored.
Kvathu Bāhāḥ is said to have been built by a member of the Tulādhara caste during the medieval period, on the site of a formeraśokavṛkṣa(saracaasoca), popularly known as ashoka tree.

While considered abāhāḥ, it lacks a traditional monastic building (kvāḥpāḥchẽ) and occupies only a single west-facing room on the ground floor of the building commonly known as the "Ghaḍī Ghara" (Clock Tower).
The room above thebāhāḥbelongs to the Vāyudevatā Guthi, a religious trust, with which thebāhāḥhas no affiliation.
Aside from the rooms occupied by the Vāyudevatā Guthi and thebāhāḥitself, the remaining rooms in the Ghaḍī Ghara are used as residences or rented out as shops.
Acaityaand a fire altar (yajñakuṇḍa) are situated in front of the Amitābha statue.
Historical evidence regarding thebāhāḥ’s construction is scarce.
The name "Asana" is believed to derive from "Aśokamaṇḍapa," the name of the platform erected where the ashoka tree stood (B. Pradhāna VS 2064, p. 172).
Thebāhāḥ’s construction is estimated to date back to the 16th century (Pruscha 1975, K-44).
Sometime around 2018 CE (VS 2075), a stone inscription at Kvathu Nani was broken during a dispute concerning the Ghaḍī Ghara.
The fragments of this inscription, which likely contained information about the construction of either the Ghaḍī Ghara or thebāhāḥ, have since been stolen.
The building currently known as the Ghaḍī Ghara originated as a commercial structure during the medieval period.
It only acquired the name "Ghaḍī Ghara" after a clock was installed on its north-facing façade, making it visible from the Asana market.
Local tradition suggests that a Tulādhara merchant who traded with Tibet during the medieval era built thisbāhāḥwithin a section of the Ghaḍī Ghara.
He then entrusted its management to the Vajrācārya priests of Taḥchẽ Bāhāḥ, establishing a land endowment to support its rituals (descendant ofbāhāḥ's donor, Tuladhar, female, age 56).
The Vāyudevatā Guthi (religious trust) is believed to date back to the reign of Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa Śāha.

Following his conquest of Kathmandu, his son, Bahādura Śāha, took possession of the building and established the trust to conduct rituals for the peace of those who died or were killed within the palace.
Worship items were traditionally prepared and carried from this building to Hanumandhoka (S. Shrestha VS 2075).
The 1934 earthquakes damaged both the Ghaḍī Ghara and thebāhāḥwithin it (Locke 1985, p. 300).
Subsequent renovations were carried out by residents of the Ghaḍī Ghara and shopkeepers who rented space there (descendant of thebāhāḥ's donor, Tulādhara, female, age 56).
The 2015 earthquakes further damaged the building.
The Guthi Corporation, responsible for the Ghaḍī Ghara's maintenance and rent collection, obtained approval to demolish the structure and replace it with a commercial complex.
Despite a legal challenge brought by local residents and heritage activists, the court ruled in favor of the Guthi Corporation.
Upon thebāhāḥ's construction, the Vajrācāryas of Taḥchẽ Bāhāḥ were tasked with performing daily rituals and other religious observances.
Although a three-member Tulādhara trust was established to manage thepañcadāna, two members have since withdrawn.
In the past, Vajrācāryas from Taḥchẽ Bāhāḥ would preside over a fire ritual on this occasion, followed by a grandpañcadānaceremony.
With two members gone, the remaining woman continues the trust's work alone, though the fire ritual is no longer performed.
It can be accessed via a narrow alley that runs under a residential building on the way to Cyāsal from Bhelāchẽ.
A stone image of Akṣobhya can be found inside the sanctum - this small image is a replacement of the previous one, which was stolen in the 1960s.
According to local informants, this particular image was installed around 40 years ago.
The building is a simple one-storey structure, and its back wall shares the courtyard's boundary wall.
The building is raised above the level of the courtyard in that it sits on a stone plinth of 1.8 m x 2.4 m.
The roof has astūpafinial that has been built with bricks on cement mortar.
The western residential building in front of thevihārahas some remaining traditional wall paintings on the first floor level, though these are rapidly deteriorating.
No inscription could be found to provide information about the establishment of thisvihāra.
However,Gellner(1987, 405) mentions that the nearby Bhaiṣajya Vihāra was established by Jīvanṛsiṃha in 1878 (NS 998).
He claims that his eldest son established this Kularatna Vihāra some years later.
Thisphalcāwas dismantled by the locals in June 2024, after it was certain to be demolished as part of the road expansion drive.
Before its dismantling, the east-facing structure had a zinc sheet roof.
No historical records detailing thephalcā's construction have been found, but its architecture suggests it was likely built during the late medieval or early Śāha period.
Consequently, the members associated with the Śvetavārāhī trust jointly dismantled thephalcāin Asar 2024 (June 2024).
Plans are underway to construct a newphalcāon the adjacent vacant land to the west.
Following the worship, the chariot circumambulates Bāḍegāũ, and the idol is then ceremonially reinstalled in thephalcā.
After thephalcā's demolition, the statue of Śvetavārāhī has been temporarily moved to the nearby Ṣaḍakṣari Lokeśvara Dyaḥchẽ (BDG0030).
Although the pillar is inscribed, the (devanāgarī) text is currently not readable.
He provided a reading of the inscription where the date of installation of the pillar is ŚS 1037 (1115 CE).
Stone pillars were erected throughout the Karnali Basin from the 13th to the 17th century.
They are installed to honor the memory of deceased persons, mostly warriors.
Within this locality stands an east-facingjaḥdhuṃconstructed of stone.
Two inscriptions are affixed to thejaḥdhuṃ.
The first, located to the south of the finial, is heavily eroded and thus illegible, though it plausibly recorded the construction of thejaḥdhuṃitself.

The second, on the northern side, dates to 1808 CE (NS 928) and documents a land endowment of oneropānīto theguṭhīfor the performance of thevarṣavardhana-pūjā(annual worship) of thejaḥdhuṃon the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa.
It is currently (writing in early 2019) being rebuilt.
The courtyard is surrounded by residential houses, though none of these buildings display any of the original characteristics of a traditional Newar house.
The main shrine building is a two-bay structure, and its main entrance is guarded by a pair of guardian animals.
In 2019, construction work was ongoing above this layer.
A single flight of RCC stairs on the outer northern side of the building leads up to the first floor.
A plan proposed by the municipality shows that an internal staircase will be installed here to allow access to the upper floor.
It was severely destroyed by the 2015 earthquake and is now under reconstruction.
A copper plate inscription attached to the outer wall of thedyaḥchẽinforms the reader that this Bāhāḥ was established by Amṛtavajra Śākya in NS 763 (1643 CE).
The buildingwas reconstructed in 1956.
Thesaṅghamembers told us that the lands endowed upon the Bāhāḥ no longer belong to them, and so they are struggling to fund these religious activities.
Constructed by Rāṇā Prime Minister Bama Bahādura Kũvara's daughter and son-in-law, the Guṇabhuvaneśvara Mandira underwent reconstruction following the devastating earthquakes of 2015.

In 1851 CE (VS 1907), Prime Minister Bama Bahādura Kũvara built the Tīna Devala (KAT2670), a composite structure housing three temples, surrounded by rest houses on all four sides (caugharāsataḥ), located near the banks of the Bagmati River.
Subsequently, additional temples, both large and small, as well assataḥs, were added to the temple complex by his relatives and descendants.
The Guṇabhuvaneśvara Mandira was among these temples, founded by Bama Bahādura's daughter, Bhuvaneśvarī, and her husband, Gumānasiṃha Kārkī, in the southeast.
The couple also constructed asataḥto the north of the temple.

An inscription installed at the temple documents the establishment of a trust, which endowed land parcels at various locations in Bhaktapur to facilitate the performance of annual rituals and timely renovations of both the temple and thesataḥin 1867 CE (VS 1924) (P. Darnāla VS 2061, pp.54-52).
In 1868 CE (VS 1925), the donor couple also presented a bell to the temple.
However, the exact year of the temple's construction remains uncertain.
The temple had already fallen into disrepair when the devastating earthquakes of 2015 struck the nation.
Following these events, the Guṇabhuvaneśvara temple, along with other nearby monuments, underwent reconstruction.

The High-Powered Committee for Integrated Development of the Bagmati Civilization, an organization operating under the Ministry of Urban Development, received financial assistance from the Asian Development Bank to carry out the reconstruction.
These reconstruction efforts were officially completed in October 2022.
While an inscription at the temple outlines various daily and periodic rituals to be performed, most of them have ceased to be observed.
The privatization of the endowed land parcels has affected the temple's revenue, leading to the discontinuation of these rituals (Bama Bahādura’s descendant, male, age 57).
This Phalcā was reconstructed by using the original stone plinth that had physically remained after the Phalcā built on it earlier had been removed.
Some of them have been erased, with the exception of the remaining plinth, while others have undergone reconstruction.
Local elders cannot recall the presence of thebuilding's previous structure; their memory is limited to the plinth.
In 2021 CE (VS 2078), the Kirtipur Municipality constructed a three-bayed rest houseon the very site of the plinth.
Initially, the plan was for just two bays, but an additional bay was added to adhere to traditionalphalcāarchitecture of uneven numbers (former ward president, Maharjana, male, aged 64).
It is possible that one of their ancestors may have played a role in the construction of the building, but this historical connection was lost when the structure collapsed.

monument_name: Taṅgaḥ Buinā Ganedyaḥ Bhajana Phalcā (built in 1916 CE)
text: One of the common features of the Gaṇeśa temples in Patan is the prevalence of aphalcādedicated for singing hymns and devotional songs (bhajana), often constructed in close proximity to the temple dedicated to the same deity.

monument_name: Taṅgaḥ Buinā Ganedyaḥ Bhajana Phalcā (built in 1916 CE)
text: Taṅgaḥ Buinā Ganedyaḥ Bhajana Phalcā is also built right in front of the Buinā Ganedyaḥ (LAL0279).

monument_name: Taṅgaḥ Buinā Ganedyaḥ Bhajana Phalcā (built in 1916 CE)
text: The inscription installed in this Phalcā records that Viṣṇunātha Bhāro (Jośī), a descendant of theguṭhīclan members, constructed this Phalcā in the honour of their clan deity (iṣṭadevatā) Buinā Ganedyaḥ on the fourth day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha in 1916 CE (NS 1036), incidentally on his birthday.

monument_name: Taṅgaḥ Buinā Ganedyaḥ Bhajana Phalcā (built in 1916 CE)
text: It was reconstructed after the 2015 CE earthquakes by the collective initiative of the Taṅgaḥ Ṭola Sudhāra Samiti and the Jośī Guṭhī.
The temple located at the crossroads of Mahapal had three roofs until the earthquake of 1934, but now only one, which is made of gold-coated copper, is left.
This temple stands on four carved columns (each 18cm x 18cm), and its hinter wall is attached to an adjacent building.
The circumambulatory plinth has been encroached upon by the buildings on the west and north sides.
The four-waydhalipāhkāsloped roof is supported by carved struts, and has also been encroached upon by the adjacent building at the northwest corner.

At the puttee under the temple’s brass pinnacle, one can read the following text:śrī 3 māhārājā yuddha samsera jaṅgabāhādura rāṇā(thrice venerable great king Yuddha Śamśera Jaṅgabahādura Rāṇā), which suggests that the temple was reconstructed under Juddha Śamśera's reign, after the 1934 earthquake.
The brass-clad door of the temple has small windows on either side and is topped with a recently donatedtoraṇacontaining an image of Gaṇesa.
No inscription or any other document detailing the establishment of this temple has been discovered amd there is no record of aguṭhīassociated with the temple.
The chariot remains in front of the Phalcā for four days before finally being dismantled.
There is a stone inscription embedded in the south wall of Jāvalākhela Phalcā, however it is illegible.
This presumption is supported by the fact that the building has been divided by a brick wall and two, rather than one, columns are placed at its center.
The eastern half has large edge stones while the western half has been built with a new timber edge.
According to local informants, Jāvalākhela Phalcā was rebuilt from the ground up not long before the 2015 earthquakes struck.
For this reason, this monastic building is also calledikulioryakuli, meaning ‘north-west direction’.
Residential buildings surround the three-storey monastic building.
Both of these statues were established in 1885 CE.
The façade of the first storey contains a latticed window flanked by two inscriptions and two smaller latticed windows, whilst the second storey has a large plain window.
However, the building is currently under reconstruction.
Adharmadhātu maṇḍalaand aśikharakūṭa caityahave been erected in the courtyard.
In the 2015 earthquakes, a building standing to the right of thebāhāḥcollapsed and fell down, destroying two storeys of thebāhāḥ.
This building was completely removed after the earthquake and is now under construction.
The Lalitpur Municipality has provided 2.5 million rupees for its reconstruction.

A photograph of thebāhāḥcomplex taken circa 1974 (published inPruscha1975 C/P-47) shows that the ground floor of thebāhāḥ(as previously reconstructed) is similar to its current structure, with the exception thatdāci apā(bricks) were used instead ofmā apā(bricks) and the white plastered cornice was replaced with decorative bricks.
The height of the first floor has been increased considerably (by approx. 50 cm) and the three old latticed windows were replaced with new ones of different sizes and proportions.
A new carved brick cornice was added above them, matching the design of the ground floor cornice.

Located south of the Indrāyaṇī Pīṭha (BKT0050) at the Khaumā Ṭola in Bhaktapur, this rfive-bayed est house is one of the monuments that were rebuilt in the context of the Bhaktapur Development Project.
It does not contain any statue or inscription, therefore dating its initial construction is problematic.
Anotherphalcā(BKT4002) to its east has similar features and was constructed in 1888 CE (NS 1008).
This allows us to allege that both Phalcās were constructed at around the same time in the late 19th century.
At the beginning of 1974 CE, the Bhaktapur Development Project was launched with the joint funding of the Nepal and German governments.
The project renovated or rebuilt many historic monuments of Bhaktapur including the monuments at the Indrāyaṇī Pīṭha premises.
This rest house was also reconstructed as part of the project.

Cīdhaṃ Bāhāḥ is located at Vatu Ṭola in Kathmandu and was constructed in 1539 CE (NS 660) by Śākyabhikṣu Toyū Āḥju, along with his brothers Śākyabhikṣu Rūparāja, Śākyabhikṣu Maṇirāja, and Śākyabhikṣu Jakarāja, who were residents of Taḥdhaṃ Bāhāḥ (KAT1420) [see, inscription number KAT1410_I_001 below].

Tuyū Āḥju is said to have made a fortune from his trade missions to Tibet and used the wealth to host the grand alms-giving ceremony (Samyak Mahādāna) and established a statue of Dīpaṅkara in 1545 CE (NS 665) during the reign of King Narendra Malla.

The main building (dyaḥchẽ‘God-house’) of Cīdhaṃ Bāhāḥ is a concrete structure of eight floors, with the three lower floors belonging to the monastery and the remaining upper floors being used privately by a member of thebāhāḥ.
Thebāhāḥcollapsed in 1918 CE (NS 1038) and was rebuilt a year later.
Currently (December 2022 CE), thebāhāḥdoes not follow the traditional architecture.
Thebāhāḥwas originally a three-storied building that was dismantled and reconstructed into an eight-storied concrete structure in 2008 CE (VS 2065).
At present, two families reside in thebāhāḥpremises, as the other two families have sold their ancestral property and moved out.

As part of the annualbahīdyaḥ bvayguexhibition, which begins from the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, the statues of Dīpaṅkara established by Tuyū Āḥju and a wooden statue of him are exhibited for three days.
The Samyak Mahādāna ceremony was an important event that used to take place annually at Cīdhaṃ Bāhāḥ, Ituṃ Bāhāḥ, and Lagaṃ Bāhāḥ in the Kathmandu Valley before the Gorkha conquest in 1768 CE.

monument_name: Lāykū Hiti (renovated in 1691 CE by Bhūpatīndra Malla)
text: Situated in front of the palace building of Bhaktapur, the Lāykū Hiti has only one spout that faces west.

monument_name: Lāykū Hiti (renovated in 1691 CE by Bhūpatīndra Malla)
text: There are no historical sources to date the initial construction of the Hiti.

monument_name: Lāykū Hiti (renovated in 1691 CE by Bhūpatīndra Malla)
text: It was probably built at the time the Yakṣeśvara Mandira (BKT0090) was constructed (Vaidya & Shrestha2002, p. 100).

monument_name: Lāykū Hiti (renovated in 1691 CE by Bhūpatīndra Malla)
text: In NS 811 (1691 CE), Bhūpatīndra Malla had replaced the old spout with a new one made out of the stones brought from a place called Koṭakhā.

monument_name: Lāykū Hiti (renovated in 1691 CE by Bhūpatīndra Malla)
text: Bhūpatīndra Malla had renovated the Hiti during this period.

monument_name: Lāykū Hiti (renovated in 1691 CE by Bhūpatīndra Malla)
text: On the same day, he had also constructed ahitialong with aphalcāin Thimi following the instruction of his father (Pauḍel2023, p. 24).

monument_name: Lāykū Hiti (renovated in 1691 CE by Bhūpatīndra Malla)
text: It appears that the Lāykū Hiti was constructed to serve water to various deities in the palace area.
The two Ponds on either side of the Bhaudhvākhā are considered to be a representation ofkalaśaalthough there is nokalaśaestablished here.
At the time of welcoming a new bride through the Bhaudhvākhā, the two Ponds are considered as akalaśaestablished on either side of the Gate and, hence, bless the newly-wedded couple with good luck.
Unfortunately, once the Rājakulo was damaged, the Ponds also started to dry out and were reduced to a muddy space.
Group of four damaged stone statues kept at a Śiva temple.
The statues are all damaged.

They may have been damaged during violent events such as one of the battles between the Doṭeli king Hariśāhī II (17th-18th century) and the Mughals or the Kumaonis (events briefly mentioned inPandey 1997: 179-180).
The taking of the kingdom of Doṭi around 1790, under general Amar Singh Thapa, of which Dadeldhura was a part during the 18th century, may be another moment where the statues would have been damaged.
Jalavināyaka Sataḥ North is one of the threesataḥbuilt around the Jalavināyaka Mandira, which is one of the four major Gaṇeśa temples in the Kathmandu Valley.
In 1877 CE, Deva Śaṃśera Rāṇā renovated the Jalavināyaka Mandira and constructredsataḥsaround it, giving the temple its distintive square shape (Gutschow2011, 458).
The building is poorly maintained but was whitewashed in November 2020 CE.
Thebaithakis used as a store for building materials.
The current Āryatārā statue is a replacement for the one that was stolen.
Statues of the Buddha’s most trusted disciples, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, which were placed on either side of the main entrance, were stolen years ago.
In the courtyard, sixcaityashave been established.
The Bahī collapsed during the 1934 earthquakes and remained in ruins for many years.
In the late 1970s, one floor was added to the previous structure of the Bahī.
There are no historical sources available to date the Bahī's initial construction.
The earliest historical record relating to the Bahī is an inscription at the Vijayeśvarī Temple (KAT3200) from 1685 CE (NS 805).
The inscription records a certain Jinideva of Atalakhu (text: Italaṃṣu) Mahāvihāra, i.e., Arkhu Bahī, offering various ornaments and a gilded window to Goddess Vijayeśvarī.
About the dating of the Bahī,Locke(1985, p.389) writes: “Though this is certainly an old foundation there are no legible dated inscriptions from the early Malla period.

An inscription at Bilāsa Bahi from the time of Pārthivendra Malla (N.S. 800-807) records a donation made by Bhikṣu Śrī Jinadeva residing a Italampu Mahāvihāra in Yatakhā Tole in Śrī Yaṃbu in the city of Kāntipur.
An inscription from the time of Pārthivendra Malla (N.S. 807-21) repairs were made to the caitya and to the shrine of ‘Śrī Śrī Śrī Gandhurijū’.
In N.S. 812 further donations were made (mostly illegible).
Recorded data refer to Italampu Kṛta Mahāvihāra, the Pārāvata was added to the name after the Vajracaryas from Itum̃ Bāhā (Pārāvata Mahāvihāra) came here”.
Pruscha (1975, p. 43 [C/K-116)] describes the Bahī as follows: “Much of the shrine in this specious courtyard has been destroyed.
In 1907 CE (1962 VS), the Sataḥ was constructed by the five sons of Bhāgavatabhakta Māhemā to fulfill his wish for the building.
According to L. Śākya (NS 1122, p.28), the name of the place reverts to Kājī Bhāgavatabhakta Māthemā building it.
Though the Sataḥ bears the resemblance from buildings of Malla era, it possesses a unique architectural style.
Kājī Bhāgavatbhakta had made a commitment to establish the Rādhākṛṣṇa temple (KAT2710) along with this Sataḥ.
Before his demise, he had allocated 20murīs paddy, 1murī10pāṭhī(9 ropanī-s, 12ānā) of land for the annual conduct of rituals of both Sataḥ and Temple.
To fulfill his wish, Bhāgavatbhakta Māthemā's five sons finalised the construction of the buildings.
An inscription attached to a wall in the Sataḥ records that in the event of reconstruction, any descendant of Sardāra Haribhakta Māthema is entrusted with the responsibility of rebuilding it.
To prevent the loss or sale of lands an inscription containing the list of land allocated for the Sataḥ was made and placed on the wall of the Sataḥ in 1951 CE (2008 VS).
The terracotta tiles (jhiṃgaṭī) from the roof were replaced by iron roofing sheets.
After the earthquake of 2015 CE (2072 VS) the Sataḥ had been heavily damaged, leading to the evacuation of the residence.

Subsequently it was reconstructed with the assistance of the Integrated Development of the Bagmati Civilization, a project under Nepal Government's Ministry of Urban Development, in collaboration with a loan from the Asian Development Bank.
The new Sataḥ was inaugurated in October 2022 CE (2079 VS).
On the day of Bālā Caturdaśī the Jyāpu community from Naradevi would come together to construct a wooden bridge (Bātcālã) in front of the sataḥ by the Bagmati river, only to be later dismantled.
Even, the terrace of the sataḥ was used as a room by replacing the terracotta tiles (jhiṃgaṭī) from the roof with iron roofing sheets.
After the earthquake of 2015 CE (2072 VS), the sataḥ suffered a severe damage, leading to the evacuation of the residence inside, and it was subsequently reconstructed.

The reconstruction of the sataḥ was carried out with the assistance of the Integrated Development of the Bagmati Civilization, a project under Nepal Government's Ministry of Urban Development, in collaboration with a loan from the Asian Development Bank.
The sataḥ was inaugurated in October 2022 CE (2079 VS) after completing its reconstruction.

On the day of Bālā Caturdaśī, there was a tradition where the Jyāpu community from Naradevi would come together to construct Bātcālã (a wooden bridge) at the front of the sataḥ on the Bagmati River, and later they would dismantle the temporary bridge.
Most of the monuments are built on the right bank of the Chaurī Gāḍ river, a tributary of the Mahakali (or Sharda) river, which forms the western border between India and Nepal.
Other contemporary constructions in the vicinity include (DDL0110,DDL0111,DDL0112,DDL0113andDDL0120).
The Ajayamerukoṭa area is known for its abundance of monuments, primarily constructed during the 14th and 15th centuries.
The political and economic rise of the region is evidenced by the numerous monuments constructed during the latter half of the 14th century and throughout the 15th century.
All three structures are erected on a shared stone platform.
The monument has undergone reconstruction by Nepal's Department of Archaeology, as indicated by visible inventory numbers present throughout the structure.
Therefore, it is possible that some elements may have been displaced, lost, or stolen.
Blocks have been carved to replace missing ones.
Two inscriptions are engraved on the left side of the door.
One of these inscriptions is dated to 1373 (ŚS 1295) and mentions King Niraya Pāla (Sharma 2012, p. 303).
There is nohitiwithin the settlement of Kirtipur, as the city is founded atop a hillock.
The water of thishitiused to fill up the tank, which was buried by Kirtipur Municipality to build its office building over it.
No inscription has been found so far that records the construction of thishiti.
It was renovated by Kirtipur Municipality in 2019.
The statues of Bhagīratha, Viṣṇu, and the figures of serpents were added during this renovation.

Serving as a place for distributing alms or food (sadābarta) to ascetics, Sarāvata Sataḥ still contains artistic wooden components from its initial construction.
Constructed in the ‘L’ shape, the two-story Sataḥ contains an intricately-carvedsãjhyāḥon both façades.
These wooden components are from the time the Sataḥ was initially constructed in 1716 CE (NS 836).
An inscription at the Sataḥ records its construction and endowment of some 30ropanīs of land to form aguthiin 1716 CE (NS 836).
The donors Harikṛṣṇa, Jayasaṃkara, Ratnasiṃha, Jayalatna, and Saṃkaradeva got the Sataḥ constructed in the name of Kṛṣṇasaṃkala Bhāro, Viṣṇusaṃkara, and his wife Maheśvarī Mayī.

A record from 1819 CE (VS 1876) shows that a person named Bhājurāma Nevāra of Sankhu had also started a similar tradition of distributingsadābartaby getting asataḥconstructed at the Vajrayoginī premises during the reign of King Gīrvāṇayuddha (D. Sharma and T. Shrestha2016, p. 474).
Sharma and T. Shrestha2016, p. 303 have erroneously pointed out that the inscription belongs to Sarāvata Sataḥ.
Some Śreṣṭha families of Sankhu are associated with the Guthi that they claim has been in operation since its inception in the 18thcentury (guṭhīmember, Śreṣṭha, male, age 69).
After the 2015 earthquakes damaged the Sataḥ, it was renovated by a local NGO named ‘Friends of Sankhu’ in 2016 CE (D. Sharma and T. Shrestha2016, p. 302).

The Guthi had continued to distribute rice, black lentil, spices, fruits, etc. assadābartato ascetics and mendicants on the new moon and full moon days and worship the deities at the Sataḥ daily up until the 2015 earthquakes.

In 1652 CE (NS 772), Viṣṇurāja Bhāro, a resident of Cāpāgāũ Bhansāra Ṭola, along with his wives, renovated this temple.
Aśivaliṅgahas been established north of the temple with a stone pillar erected next to it.
No historical evidence regarding the establishment of this temple has been found.
However, an inscription from 1652 CE (NS 772) documents Viṣṇurāja Bhāro, a resident of Cāpāgāũ Bhansāra Ṭola, renovating the temple along with his wives Maṃgarārakṣmī and Caṇḍikārakṣmī.
A statue of Kṛṣṇa was also established in the nearby Kṛṣṇa temple on the same occasion.
This attests the existence of the temple before 1652 CE.
In 1949 CE (VS 2006), Kaviprasāda Gautama and his followers arrived in Cāpāgāũ and erected a stone pillar to promote Vaishnavism.
The Nārāyaṇa statue within the temple was stolen in the 1980s, prompting the local community to replace it with a new one (temple priest, Rājopādhyāya, male, age 77).
Around 1998 CE (VS 2055), a vehicle struck the lower roof of the temple, causing damage.
The temple was subsequently renovated with the collaborative efforts of the Department of Archaeology and local volunteers (temple priest, Rājopādhyāya, male, age 77).

Listed as the 62nd among Nepal's 64 majorśivaliṅgas (Michaels 1994, p. 278), the Bhadreśvara Śivaliṅga was established in 533 CE (Shaka Era 455) by Dhruvasaṅgha, a governmental official who held the significant posts ofvārttaandpratihāra.
Established at the Bhasmeśvara Ghāṭa by the Bagmati river south of the Paśupatinātha Mandira, the Bhadreśvara Śivaliṅga is colloquially addressed as Bhasmeśvara.
Four otherśivaliṅgas are also established here with Bhadreśvara Śivaliṅga at the center.

Vārtta Pratihāra Dhruvasaṅgha established the Bhadreśvara Śivaliṅga on the 10th of the bright fortnight of Caitra in 533 CE (Śaka Era 455), along with four otherśivaliṅgas revered as Nātheśvara, Sthiteśvara, Ravīśvara, and Śubheśvara.
He also endowed plots of land to fund regular worship of theseśivaliṅgas (D. Vajrācārya 2030, pp. 155-157; G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2056, p. 13).
citations: (D. Vajrācārya 2030, pp. 155-157; G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2056, p. 13)

text: Meanwhile, a person holding the position ofpratihārahad the responsibility of presenting people before the king or allowing them entry to the royal court (J. Regmī VS 2026, p. 402).

The inscription recording the establishment of theśivaliṅgas specifically mentions that they were established “in the area of Lord Paśupati” (S.bhagavataḥpaśupateḥkṣetre), making it as the first historical mention of the term "Paśupatikṣetra" (the area of Paśupati) (Slusser 1982, p. 227; Michaels 2008, p. 41).

During the cremation of a body at the Bhasmeśvara Ghāṭa, it's believed that the ashes and smoke that ascend, upon contact with the Bhadreśvara Śivaliṅga, absolve the departed's sins, leading them towards liberation (M. Thāpā VS 2077, p. 505).
It is built adjacent to a Rānā erasataḥwhich was constructed under Deva Śamśera Rānā in 1877 CE (Gutschow2011, 458).
Following his demise in 2020 CE, the place has been locked and remains unused.
There is a lack of evidence to point to the initial construction of the structure.

An inscription in the Jalavināyaka Mandira from 1755 CE (NS 876) mentions an individual named Matsyendra Siṃha Bhāro built aphalcāin front of the Jalavināyaka Temple and installed a statue of Halāhala Lokeśvara.
This inscription might be referring to this structure.
It is then probable that one of the statues corresponds with the one that was established by Matsyendra Siṃha Bhāro in 1755 CE.
However, it remains unclear that this structure is the one that Bhāro built when he established the Halāhala Lokeśvara, since the inscription does not evince this claim.
It only mentions aphalcāconstructed in front of the temple without specifying its position.
In total, there are nine Hindu and Buddhist statues installed in niches inside thephalcā.
It is possible that all these statues were collected and established inside thephalcāat the same time.
This shrine of Sarasvatī, the goddess of wisdom, stands next to the Mahākāla statue that bears an inscription from 1589 CE (NS 709).
However, the inscription erroneously mentions the year as NS 7009.
A small stone pillar that local residents worship as Bhairava is erected to the west.
However, no inscription is carved on the statue.
The pedestal of the statue is carved with a row of donor figures, beneath which lies an inscription.
This inscription, erroneously dated "Saṃvat7009," can be accurately dated to NS 709 (1589 CE) based on the mention of King Śivasiṃhadeva (r. 1578-1619 CE) and his brother, Raṇajitasiṃha.
While some names like Hāku, Lavasiṃha, and Gunasiṃha are legible, the inscription remains largely indecipherable.
It is plausible that these individuals collectively commissioned the creation of this Mahākāla statue, along with the accompanying sculpture of Sarasvatī.
While the site was previously open, a protective wall has now (January 2025) been erected to safeguard the temple and its statues.
The temple was damaged during the 2015 earthquake and reconstructed in 2018 with the financial support of Lalitpur Municipality.
No sources could be found to date the initial construction of the temple.

Some informants further recall that, after the 1934 earthquake, the fivebahāḥwere removed during the reconstruction programme initiated by Juddha Śaṃśera (R. Bajrācārya NS 1136, pp. 258–259), although corroborating evidence for this claim is lacking.
Following the 1934 earthquake, residential houses in the vicinity were demolished and the area was transformed into an open space.
As a result, thedevala, which once stood adjacent to the builder’s house, now finds itself in an exposed and largely unattended condition.
Architecturally, the shrine is a stone structure constructed in a pyramidal (śikhara) form, a type commonly found in small Hindu and Buddhist shrines across the Kathmandu Valley.
In Patan, the courtyard containing a Mañjuśrī temple is called “Sarasvatī Nani,” while the Sarasvatī installed at Mañjeśvarī Ṭola is known as Mañjeśvarī Sarasvatī.
There is no definitive historical record regarding the initial construction of the shrine.
Its strategic location on the trade route to Tibet suggests that the Bhīmasena statue may have been established to allow traders and merchants to pay their homage during their travels.

An inscription located south of the statue, now unreadable due to erosion, may or may not be related to the shrine; it was previously discarded at the Svayambhū Caitya (NWK0320) and was later moved here by locals for protection.
A bell donated by Kṛṣṇaprasāda in 1931 CE (VS 1988) is still present at the shrine.

Bangdel (1982, p. 194) suggests that this statue dates back to the 3rd-4th century, while G. Ṭaṇḍana (VS 2053, p. 624) places its origin in the 2nd-3rd century.
The exact year of construction for the water spout is unknown due to the absence of inscriptions.
However, the artifacts found on the premises suggest that it was built during the early Licchavi period (S. Parājulī VS 2068, p. 148).
An inscription from 679 CE (Mānadeva Era 103) discovered at Vajraghara records Licchavi King Narendradeva constructing several water spouts in the Paśupati area (D. Vajrācārya VS 2030, p. 503).
It is likely that the Varuṇa Dhārā was one of the spouts built by King Narendradeva.
The spout underwent renovations in 1914 CE (VS 1971) by Candra Śamśera and again in 1989 CE (VS 2046) under the reign of King Virendra.
The most recent renovation took place in 2002 CE (VS 2059) by the Pashupati Area Development Trust.
During the 1989 CE renovation, efforts were made to locate the intra-canal system that supplied water to the spout in order to ensure uninterrupted flow.
However, recent construction activities have caused damage to the underground canal system, resulting in the spout drying up (as reported by a male local resident named Śreṣṭha, age 69).

text: G. Taṇḍana (VS 2053,  pp.24-27) mentions the presence of 86 natural water holes in the Paśupati area, one of which is called Varuṇa Kuṇḍa, situated beneath the southern wall of thehitigāḥ.
The Kṛṣṇa Mandira, constructed in 1956 CE (VS 2013), is one among them.

The monastic courtyard belongs to the Śākya Saṅgha and is counted among the principalbāhāḥassociated with the collective organization (bareguthi) of the Śākya community of Kāntipura (R. Vajrācārya NS 1138, p. 238).
However, R. Vajrācārya (NS 1138, p. 238) and Locke (1985, p. 367) identify it asDharmadhātu Mahāvihāra (Svaḥbāhāḥ).
Thedyaḥchẽ(main shrine building) of thebāhāḥstands on the southern side of the courtyard, facing north.
Prior to the most recent major earthquake, thebāhāḥretained its traditional architectural form.
After the earthquake, however, the structure was reconstructed largely in reinforced concrete.
An attempt was made to preserve a traditional appearance in the façade, but the upper storeys remain under construction as of January 2026.
Earlier photographs published by Locke (1985, p. 77) and Pruscha (1975, p. 80) allow a reconstruction of its earlier form.
Earlier photographs do not show a toraṇa above the entrance, whereas a brasstoraṇahas now been installed.
The earlier façade hadtrikhā jhyāḥwindows, but these have since been replaced bypasukā jhyāḥwindows.
On the roof of the shrine building, instead of the traditionalphūcā(spouts used for draining rainwater), abhaupvaḥ‚ more typical of residential houses‚ had been constructed (seephotos).
In the present reconstruction, additional storeys have been added, and the building now rises to four storeys.
Within the sanctum (garbhagṛha) a stone image ofAkṣobhyais installed in the form ofKvāhpā Dyaḥ.
In front of the shrine building stands a small caitya.
Photographs from around 1970 CE show that the roof of the pagoda shrine containing the caitya was originally covered with traditionaljhiṅgaṭītiles.
In photographs from around 1985, however, the roof appears to have been repaired in a dome-like form, indicating that restoration work took place at the bāhāḥ during that period.
No historical inscription has so far been discovered within thebāhāḥ, making it difficult to determine its precise date of foundation.

Although the precise antiquity of thiscaityacannot be firmly established, the presence of nearby Buddhist sculptures indicates that the area had already become a Buddhist sacred site by the tenth century.
Following the earthquake, thedyaḥchẽwas reconstructed, and the pagoda shrine housing the Aśoka Caitya was rebuilt at the same time.
During this phase of reconstruction, traditional tiles were laid throughout the courtyard.
Owing to financial constraints, however, the upper storeys of the shrine building remain incomplete.
Thebāhāḥis associated with a Śākya community organization, but most of its members have relocated elsewhere.
Situated on the banks of the Bagmati River in Ṭeku, Kathmandu, these shrines dedicated to Śiva and Viṣṇu were erected by a family of the Satyāla caste.
The shrines, collectively known as Purohita Ghāṭa Śivālaya, derive their name from the Purohita Ghāṭa, a cremation ground established by priests (referred to aspurohitasin Nepali).
The Satyāla family's priestly role was confined to the Rāṇā lineage, and they were granted the privilege of reciting the Gāyatrī Mantra to the Rāṇās (P. Rāja, VS 2073, p.36).
Additionally, the octagonal shrine (KAT2730-011) suffered tilting during the 1934 CE earthquakes.
The community commonly refers to this ensemble of Śiva and Viṣṇu temples as the 'Satyāla Mandira,' acknowledging the role of the Satyāla priests in their construction.
Unfortunately, there exists no distinct inscription documenting the construction of these temples.

However, a bell situated within the Viṣṇu Mandira (KAT2730-012) bears an inscription commemorating Kāśīrāja Panḍita Satyāla and his family's contribution of the bell to the Dvārikānātha Mandira, where they enshrined a statue of Viṣṇu.
Given that the bell inscription dates to 1883 CE (VS 1940), it is plausible that the temples were also erected during the same period.
Gutschow (2011, p.887) supports this hypothesis, suggesting 1883 CE as the construction year based on the bell inscription.

Subsequently, in 1916 CE (VS 1973), Kāśīrāja and his family endowed plots of land to establish a trust (guthi) responsible for conducting daily and anniversary rituals, playing musical instruments during these rituals, and providing alms to mendicants on Śivarātrī, the 14th day of the dark fortnight of Phālguna.
Besides the carvings on the spout that appear to date back to the 18th-19th century, there are no other means to trace the period thehitiwas initially constructed.
It was renovated c. 1978 CE by a German project.
In the 90s, a pipe was installed on the spout to allow tap water to flow from it.
Noguthiassociated with thehiticurrently survives.
Four architectural remains are erected on the side of the path, south of the Śambhunātha Mandira (KLK0130).
It was completely covered with inscriptions that are now too eroded to allow any reading.
In mid-1986 CE (VS 2043 Jyeṣṭha), the mainśivaliṅgawas stolen, but thieves were unable to transport it in a vehicle and abandoned it near a river in a secluded place.
It was handed over to the locals in mid-1991 CE (VS 2048) and was reinstated in the temple following a grand procession (K. Mitra VS 2070, p. 8).
Statues of Durgā and Akṣobhya Buddha are also established in the inner walls of the sanctum.
These statues were previously established outside the temple but were shifted inside the sanctum due to the fear of theft (K. Mitra VS 2070, p. 8).
Followers of Tibetan Buddhism believe that Padmasambhava meditated on the Kabilāsa hill in 749 CE before heading to Tibet (M. Tamang n.d., pp. 5-6).
On the western side of the temple, there is a stone inscription of King Pārthivendra Malla along with a rest house.
The Kabilāsa hill is also popular for a Nāsaḥdyaḥ shrine established a few meters below the peak on the southern side.
Known as the Kabilāsa Nāsaḥdyaḥ among the Newars of the Kathmandu Valley, this deity of charm and grace is locally worshipped as Nāṭyeśvarī (K. Mitra VS 2070, p. 11).
All other Nāsaḥdyaḥs are believed to have been established by drawing essence from the Kabilāsa Nāsaḥdyaḥ.
After the old lion statue was stolen, it was replaced with a new one.
There are a couple of versions of the legend regarding the establishment of this Nāsaḥdyaḥ.
Angered by this, Nāsaḥdyaḥ left Bhaktapur and came to the Kabilāsa mountain, where he attained a divine perfection (K. Mitra VS 2070, pp. 12-13).
There is no historical record of the establishment of Kapileśvara Mahādeva.
As the poison appeared to destroy the entire creation of the universe, Lord Śiva consumed thekālakūṭapoison for the welfare of the world and the protection of the universe.
Kapilamuni established aśivaliṅgaon the hill and began living there by raising cows.

With villagers from the surrounding areas also coming to the hill to worship theśivaliṅga, it gradually became a popular religious site and, over time, came to be known as Kapileśvara Mahādeva (K. Mitra VS 2070, pp. 5-6).
According to the historical records available so far, the word "Kabilāsa" first appears in an inscription on a traditional lamp from 1441 CE (NS 561).
It was offered by King Ripu Malla at the Nārāyaṇa Mandira (NWK0170) in the Nuwakot palace complex.
The lamp inscription states, "the city of Nuwakot along with Kabilāsa, located in the hilly region in the north" (D. Vajrācārya and Ṭ. Śreṣṭha VS 2032, pp. 4-5).

text: The earliest inscription found at the temple is from 1685 CE (NS 805) installed by King Pārthivendra Malla, expressing his sincere devotion towards Śiva in verses that he composed himself (Yogī Naraharinātha VS 2022, p. 306).
Thejalaharībase of theśivaliṅgainside the sanctum is inscribed with the date, 14th of the dark fortnight of Phālguna in NS 805, which corresponds to 1730 CE (Yogī Naraharinātha VS 2022, p. 307).
This inscription was, however, not seen in thejalaharīduring this documentation.
As chips have come off from the earlier inscription from 1685 CE, the donor of the Kapileśvara Mahādeva cannot be deciphered.
Possibly, Pārthivendra Malla himself established theśivaliṅgarevered as Kapileśvara that year.
In 1923 CE (VS 1979), Motīmāna Nyāsi Śreṣṭha, son of Lakṣmīdevī of Dhuṃllā Ṭola in Sankhu, offered a narrow oblong banner (patāḥ) of silver to Kapileśvara.
In 1944 CE (VS 2001), Colonel Yajña Śamśera, grandson of Dhīra Śamśera and son of Bhīma Śamśera, offered a bell to Sarasvatī, the goddess of wisdom, near Kabilāsa Nāsaḥdyaḥ together with his family.
The temple collapsed in the 2015 CE earthquakes, injuring some people.
It was rebuilt with funds from the National Reconstruction Authority and the cooperation of local people.
Before the earthquake, the temple had a stone roof, but after reconstruction, it was replaced with a copper roof.
All the Nāsaḥdyaḥ shrines established in the Kathmandu Valley were originally brought from the Kabilāsa Nāsaḥdyaḥ by drawing essence from it.
In the evening, a bonfire (dhunī) is lit in the courtyard that ends with the offering of various food items, considered as sacred gifts (prasāda) from Śiva, to devotees.
There was a land endowment to light a large lamp (mahādīpa) in honor of Śiva on the occasion.
After the endowed land was converted into a leaseholder land, the tradition of lighting themahādīpahas ceased.
Originating in the 19th century CE, in 2019 Nāga Bāhāḥ Phalcā was rebuilt in "traditional" style from the ground up.
In 1980 (VS 2037), it was rebuilt in a two-storey configuration, albeit with no attention paid to maintaining a "traditional" appearance.
It was built with regular brick in cement mortar, cement plaster, wood and steel shutters, plain windows and a corrugated metal roof cover.
In 2019, Nāga Bāhāḥ Phalcā was dismantled and rebuilt again from ground up.
According to a community member this was justified in order to make the Phalcā resistent against future earthquake damage.
A Buddha statue is installed in a niche in the north wall and a Gaṇeśa shrine is attached to the southern side of Nāga Bāhāḥ Phalcā.
It was originally a two-storey building owned by a Jośī Guṭhī.
In the 1970s this building was sold to a Mānandhara from Kathmandu who rented out the western part to set up a shop.
An inscription dated 1842 CE (NS 962) informs us that somebody by the name of Daivajña Nārāyaṇa (Jośī) built this Sataḥ with the help of Kājī Śamaśera Jaṅga Pāṇḍe.
Originally, this building was partly connected to another building at its rear and the western sides.
The Sataḥ does not exist any more, the site has been destroyed by means of privatisation.
The members of Ituṃ Bāhāḥ are said to have moved here from Sankhu and thus revere the Svayambhū Caitya established inside Jogeśvara Mandira/Gũ Bāhāḥ (SKH0510) as theirdigudyaḥ.
In the Nani courtyard, 15caityashave been erected.
The Nani's first historical record is an inscription from 1641 CE (NS 762) recording the installation of a pair of lions in front of the main entrance to thedyaḥchẽ.
Another inscription from 1654 CE (NS 774) states that three people, including Narasiṃhadeva, built a structure fordigudyaḥ.
This suggests thatdigudyaḥwas originally an open shrine, and thedyaḥchẽwas constructed only in 1654 CE.
The Nani'sdyaḥchẽwas rebuilt in 2021 CE (VS 2077) with funds provided by the Hanumandhoka Palace Area Conservation Program.
Its earliest date is the fourteenth century when Madana Ram consecrated an image of Dipankara, and his wife consecrated a golden image of Aryatara here.

The monastery is also linked with the bathing ceremony of the Red Machchendranath of Patan.”* Ananiis a large courtyard enclosed on all four sides by private buildings but may also include a monastery on one side.** The elders of the Iṭuṃ Bāhāḥ had renovated this Caitya in 1668 CE.

It is an L-shaped building with a room on the eastern side with a door that gives access to the upper floor.
It used to be a three-story building.

Therefore, the second floor was dismantled and covered with corrugated tin sheets, which enabled the use of the first floor.
The first floor also houses a figure of Hāthudyaḥ that was recovered from a private house that collapsed in the 2015 earthquakes.
After the relocation of the school, the Phalcā now accommodates ‘Śrī Gaṇeśa Dhũllā Bhajana Maṇḍala’, a localbhajanaensemble.
The Phalcā was also used for political meetings during the partyless Pañcāyata rule (1961 CE-1990 CE) (local resident, Śreṣṭha, male, age 66).
No inscription recording the initial construction of this Phalcā has been recovered so far.
