Indrāyaṇī Pīṭha Hiti was built in 1657 and is the main source of water needed for social and religious activities at the adjacent Indrāyaṇī Pīṭha.
A miniatureshikhara-styledshrine is constructed atop of the spout.
A statue of Viṣṇu is established inside the niche of the shrine.
A Śivaliṅga is established on the north-eastern corner of the Hiti premises.
Ritterspach mentions that the Hiti was constructed by King Jagata Prākāśa Malla in 1657 CE i.e. NS 777 (cf.S. KhanālaVS 2068, 254).
It was renovated during the reign of King Mahendra Śāha (ibid).

The details of the carved pillars, as well as the capitals with dragon motifs, the cornice and the layout of the sanctum with a narrow ambulatory path all suggest that the temple was constructed in the late 17th century.
All of the roofs and the third level of the temple collapsed in the 1934 earthquake.
The temple was restored by Patan Conservation and Development Programme in 1995.
The Programme based their restoration of the upper two levels on a comparative analysis of contemporary temples in Patan.
The original statue was lost a few years ago; this new one was established by Śobhā Ḍaṅgola in 2009.

From the 13th to the 16th centuries, such stone memorial pillars were erected throughout the Karnali Basin.
They are erected to honour the memory of deceased people, most of whom were warriors (Andolfatto 2019).
In Bistabara, there are no inscriptions on the pillars (or any discernible ones).
Their typology, as well as the nearby presence of a pillar dated 1500 CE, suggests that they were built between the 13th and 16th centuries.

Constructed during the reign of King Yoganarendra Malla in the style of the Maṇimaṇḍapa Phalcās (LAL1361/LAL1362) that he renovated, this rest house underwent conversion into a concrete structure in the early 1980s.
It underwent another round of reconstruction, again in concrete, following the 2015 earthquakes.

Situated east of the main road, opposite the Dhaḥmā Phalcā (LAL4306) in Pulcoka, this rest house is referred to as Mandaḥ Phalcā due to its square architecture, which likely featured 16 pillars when originally built in the early 18th century.
An inscription from 1704 CE (NS 824) details the construction of the Mandaḥ Phalcā (text:maṇḍapa), including ajaḥdhuṃwater tank by Visarāma Bhābo and his family.
Thephalcāwas consecrated on the 1st of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, the same day the statue of Buṅgadyaḥ is placed on the chariot in Pulcoka.
Five years later on the same day, the donor family established a trust for various activities related to Buṅgadyaḥ.

The backside of thedalūlampstand bears an inscription from 1709 CE (NS 829) documenting the establishment of a trust (guthi) with cash donations for the worship of Buṅgadyaḥ and the distribution ofsamaybaji.
They also exhibit the lampstand with the inscription on this occasion.
Although the inscription mentions the establishment of ajaḥdhuṃtank, there is currently no trace of it at the site.

Thejaḥdhuṃwas not reconstructed after thephalcā's 1980 CE (VS 2037) reconstruction, and the stone water container of thejaḥdhuṃwas relocated to the nearby Lāchi Ṭola, while the stone blocks in excellent condition were repurposed for renovating the nearby Pulcoka Lohãhiti (LAL0570) (descendant of thephalca’s main donor, Maharjana-Śreṣṭha, female, age 72).

Notably,phalcās were erected at sites where the Buṅgadyaḥ Chariot (LAL0001) traditionally made stops during its annual procession, serving as spaces for devotees to light butter lamps in honor of the deity.

However, the chariot is rested in front of the Mandaḥ Phalcā for three days once during the 12-year procession when the chariot is constructed in Bungamati instead of Pulcoka (Bārāhī Guthi member, Bārāhī, male, age 67).
Hence, thephalcāseems to have been constructed specifically for distributingsamaybajion the day the chariot stops in front of it.
In 1970 CE (VS 2027), the donor family dismantled the old structure for reconstruction, as it was already in poor repair.

Elderly locals from Pulcoka recall government bodies seizing the columns and other materials of thephalcāstored by the roadside in 1972 CE (VS 2029) under the pretext of clearing the area, as then King Virendra was due to pass by (descendant of thephalca’s main donor, Maharjana-Śreṣṭha, female, age 72).

Later in 1980 CE (VS 2037), a concrete square building of two floors was erected in place of the Mandaḥ Phalcā, with the upper floor utilized for the operation of a public library named “Pūcva Pustakālaya.” The new concrete structure with an open ground floor sustained damage in the 2015 earthquakes.
It was once again dismantled and rebuilt as a concrete structure in 2020 CE (VS 2077) by the donor family with financial assistance from an NGO named Prārambha.

Notably, an inscription installed after the recent reconstruction erroneously mentions that thephalcāwas originally built in 1709 CE (NS 829), the year the donor family set up a trust in the name of thephalcābuilt five years previously.
On regular days, individuals gather within the confines of thephalcā, indulging in tea from a nearby establishment, while its northeastern corner is presently leased to another shop.

Located at the southeast corner of the Patan Darbar Square, adjacent to the Sundarī Coka (LAL1220), the white stucco Court Building (Nep. Adālata Bhavana), along with the Kota Pāṭī (LAL4126), marks the southern edge of the Patan Darbar.
There are no records to date the initial construction of the Building.
However, its European architecture suggests that the Building was probably built by Prime Minister Bhīmasena Thāpā around 1820 CE (cp.Gutschow2011, p.318).
The original three-story structure suffered severe damages in the 1934 earthquakes and was later restored in a two-story configuration.
The Building acquired its current name after municipal courts were housed there.
More recently, the Building housed a local branch of the post office.
In 2008, the Department of Archaeology initiated the repair of the roof and since then the building has remained vacant (as of July 2022).
In 2022, it was announced that the Court Building will undergo a complete restoration with funding from the Republic of India and implemented by INTACH.
Although widely referred to as the Court Building for housing the Patan District Court for decades, it actually was a Kota Ghara (lit. ‘building used for storing weapons’) during the Śāha period.
Patan Middle School operated from this Building in 1924 CE (VS 1981) (I VajrācāryaVS 2076).
Following the damages caused by the earthquakes in 1934 CE, the school was shifted to another building in Lagankhel.
Currently (as of April 2024 CE), only the eastern spout (object no. NWK0370-001) is flowing, while the western spout (object no. NWK0370-002) has dried up.
The central spout (object no. NWK0370-003) dried up long ago and was removed to build a concrete water tank.
Aśivaliṅgais established to the north of the spouts.
There are no historical records that shed light on the initial construction of these water spouts.
Locals believe the spouts have existed since the medieval period, before Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa Śāha conquered Nuwakot in 1744 CE (VS 1801).
Currently, a new structure is being constructed to the east of the only functioning spout, aiming to decorate the area with flowers, funded by the Kathmandu Lions Club.
Writing of Ikhāchẽ Ṭola in hisKīrtipatākā(verse 34) in NS 772 (1652 CE), Kunu Śarmā, the court poet of King Śrīnivāsa Malla, mentions thishitiby referring to a stone spout at the north of theṭola.
Statues of Buddhist and Hindu deities including Licchavi caityas, Buddha statues from the Licchavi period, and the Śikharakūṭa temple of Nārāyaṇa have been erected in and around the Hiti precinct.

This Hiti was established by Tuhūdeva Vajrācārya together with his wives Indralakṣmī and Jayalakṣmī, son Phyakudeva and daughter Śuṃdaralakṣmī on Thursday 8th of the bright fortnight of NS 535 (1415 CE).
Since it was the dry season, the Hiti was constructed after the performance of a Tantric ritual.
It seems that the Licchavi Caitya was established here even before the establishment of the Hiti.
Similarly, the inscription from 533 BCE (1413 CE), which was erected in the Hiti area suggests that cultural activities took place here even before the watering site was constructed.
Some locals tell the following legend about the establishment of the Hiti.
A copperplate inscription describing the establishment of the Hiti contains a regulation that instructs readers how to perform the anniversary worship of the Hiti.
Mahālakṣmī Phalcā is a rare case of a Phalcā built along a trade route and equipped with a well, several shrines, and a water spout.
The structure has been altered from its original configuration, and the upper story and roof were rebuilt during the 20th century.
For ease of access modern stone steps have been added on three sides of the building.
Referred to as the Jośī Āgaṃchẽ, this three-level building is nestled amidst private homes in the Maru ṭola, to the west of Māju Degaḥ (KAT1910).
This building serves as the residence of the secretive clan deity (known asāgaṃdyaḥ) belonging to the Dvaja Jośī clan located in Maru ṭola, Kathmandu.

Only those who have received tantric initiation (dīkṣā) are granted permission to enter the central esoteric room (āgaṃ), a stringent practice that safeguards the secrets of the clan deity and its ritual practices.
Each Newar clan possesses an esoteric clan deity (āgaṃdyaḥ), who is allocated a dedicated sacred space within a private residence or a separate divine abode.
Constructed with traditional architectural elements, the Āgaṃchẽ faces east and showcases copper sheets enveloping its three tiers, crowned by a bell-shaped finial at its pinnacle.
The third tier has slanting latticed windows with carved struts in between, positioned on the building's second floor.
The structures on either side (north and south) of the main building, adorned with veneer bricks (dāciaḥpā) on their facades, are also linked to the Āgaṃchẽ.
The upper level of the northern building is utilized for Āgaṃchẽ-related feasts and accommodates the trust's office (guthi).
Due to a lack of inscriptive evidence, the historical origins of the Āgaṃchẽ remain uncertain.
An inscription on the eaves fascia (mhuraḥpau) documents the replacement of the roof with copper sheets by certain members of the Dhvaja Jośī clan in 2006 CE (VS 2063).
The southern building attached to the tiered structure suffered collapse during the 2015 CE earthquakes, resulting in partial damage to the primary Āgaṃchẽ building.
The collapsed section was reconstructed in 2019 CE (VS 2076), alongside renovations to the main building.
Additional wooden supports were subsequently added to the main structure.
With approximately 100 members in theguthi, responsibilities for daily rituals at the Āgaṃchẽ are rotated among them.

Some, however, such as Bangdel (VS 2039 [1982], p. 67), consider the small Varāha image from Siddhipokharī in Bhaktapur—dated to the 4th–5th centuries CE—to be the oldest.

Excavations carried out in the mid-1960s (VS 2022–23) uncovered Licchavi-periodterracottafigures, clay moulds, and fragments ofpāthī(measuring bowls), indicating sustained human activity at the site since at least the 4th century CE (T. Miśra VS 2029 [1972], p. 41).

TheGopālarājavaṃśāvalīrecords that King Bhūmigupta installed an image of Dharaṇī-Varāha Viṣṇu, which, according to Slusser and Bajrācārya (2005, p. 45), may refer to this very Dhūmavarāhī image.

A Licchavi inscription from the reign of King Narendra Deva mentions aVarāha-yātrāheld on the auspicious 11th day of bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha (D. Vajrācārya VS 2030 [1973], p. 488), possibly referring to the same cultic festival associated with this image.
During the medieval period, numerousiṣṭadevatāsbelonging to variouskhalakas(Newar lineages) were installed around the main Varāha shrine.
In 1950 CE (VS 2006), the Vaiṣṇava reformer Kaviprasād organized ayajñabefore the image, accompanied bybhajanandkīrtana.
Disturbed by the ongoing practice of animal sacrifice by local Newars, he inscribed a stone slab declaring the site to be aViṣṇu-kṣetrawhere violence (hiṃsā) should be avoided.
With the growing renown of the deity, a management committee was established, and devotees increasingly began to offer various ritual items.
Silver ornaments have been added to the Licchavi image, and it has also become customary for couples to solemnize their marriages before the deity.

The once-spacious sixteen-ropanīmeadow has gradually diminished, as new structures—such as a school, a concretebhajana bhavana, toilets, and an additional modern shrine—have been constructed within the precincts (Rijāla, temple priest, male, age 62).
Facing west, the shrine preserves its original carved wooden doorway from the early construction phase, flanked on both sides by a pair of stone lions.
Of theṭuṇḍalastruts supporting the temple, twelve belong to the original period, while others—stolen in the past—have been replaced with newer replicas.
The pedestal bears an inscription whose date has eroded, but on palaeographic grounds, Regmi (1966, p. 2) assigns it to the 10th century.
The inscription refers to the deity as Mañjunātha.
In his right hand he appears to hold a fruit, while the object in his left hand is difficult to identify due to damage.
The image was stolen in the later years of the Panchayat era but was fortunately recovered; after its return, the local community organized a grandjātrāto reinstall it.
The rear portion of theparvāḥhad been broken during the theft.
A pre-theft photograph clearly showing the intact image was published by Slusser and Vajrācārya (2005, p. 110, Fig. 3).
Given the 10th-century date of the inscribed image, it is likely that a shrine of some form stood here during that time.
This suggests that the old image was preserved in the sanctum when a new temple was constructed during the early modern period.

The year of the construction of thisbāhāḥis unknown.
A new monastery was constructed there and was named Mañjuśrīnaka Mahāvihāra after the deity (B. ŚākyaN.S. 1129, 3).
During the reign of King Yakṣa Malla, two brothers Jayateja Pāla and Anantateja Pāla had offered a golden statue of Akṣobhya to this Bāhāḥ.
In NS 631 (1511 CE), Śākyabhikṣu Rūpateja Pāla, together with his family, installed a golden finial andpañcadhvajā(a set of five flags) on the Bāhāḥ's roof.

Again, during the reign of King Śivasiṃha Malla in NS 706 (1585 CE), Śākyabhikṣu Samalasiṃha of thisbāhāḥand Tāmrākāra (text: Tāmrākāla) Abhayasiṃha Bhāro jointly organizedsamyakmahādānaceremony out of the income from their trade in Tibet.

The bell inscription reveals that the temple was established by General Lalita Śamśera Rāṇā in 1903 CE (VS 1959).
He was the son of Dhīra Śamśera, the younger brother of Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā (Rāja VS 2071 p.75).
The temple was badly damaged in the 2015 earthquakes, and the Pashupati Area Development Trust renovated it in 2019 CE (VS 2076).

text: Bālākhu Gaṇeśa Phalcā appears to be constructed to facilitate worship of Bālākhu Gaṇeśa, who is revered by local residents as a deity who assists in recovering lost or misplaced items.
The Bāhāḥ can be accessed through an underpass underneath a residential building from the western Cidhaṃ Bāhāḥ (LAL2070).
This Bāhāḥ has been built on the eastern wing and faces west.
Three plain windows were installed on its first floor, and a secret room was located on this level.
However, the first and second floors collapsed during the 2015 earthquake.
Although the ground floor was badly damaged, the sanctum of the Bāhāḥ has remained safe.
The main door is well carved and once was surmounted by a ṭoraṇathãheld up by stone lions, however theṭoraṇawas removed after the earthquake.
The back wall (to the east) has been heavily damaged and parts of it have collapsed.
The courtyard is still filled with debris from the collapsed building materials.
The original statue was stolen some time between 1983-1985.
After the 2015 earthquakes, however, the metal garment of the deity disappeared.
Before the earthquake, there was also a woodentoraṇadated NS 1004 with an image of Akṣobhya in the middle, Prajñāpāramitā on the right and Ṣaḍakṣarī Lokeśvara on the left (Locke1985,87).
After the earthquake, broken pieces of thetoraṇawere found scattered around, but the piece containing the date could not be located.
Images of Hanumān and Mahākāla also survived the earthquake; they are now placed to the north and the south of the entrance.

However, the Śivaliṅga consecrated in the sanctum of the Temple appears to be very old, for example its round structuredjalaharī, colour and quality of the stone, and the style of its construction are similar to theśivaliṅgas from the Licchavi period.
There are half a dozen Licchavi inscriptions in the Balambu area, suggesting that the area was already a well-developed settlement during the Licchavi period.
In 2002 CE, the Temple was renovated at the initiation of the locals, as it was on the verge of collapse.
The 2015 earthquakes appear to have not rendered any damages to the Temple.

In the course of constructing a new building of Bhāstipura Jñānamālā Bhajana, a local group of hymnists, in 2018 CE, this Temple also received minor renovations and coats of paint (local knowledge, local resident, Śreṣṭha, male, age 78).

text: Neither someone performs any daily rituals at this Temple nor is there anyguthirelated to it.
Rāṇā Prime Minister Vīra Śamśera constructed this temple in 1888 CE (VS 1945), likely in honor of his uncle Jagatjaṅga, the son of Jaṅga Bahādura.
Vīra Śamśera, who reigned from 1885 to 1901 CE, built four Śiva temples collectively known as Cāra Śivālaya to the south of the Rājarājeśvarī Mandira.
To the west of the temple, a figure of Nandī, the sacred animal mount of Lord Śiva, is placed, while Śiva's trident (triśūla) is erected on the northern side.
There are no historical records documenting the construction of the temple.
However, an inscription on the bell, which was offered by Vīra Śamśera in 1888 CE, is accepted as the year of the temple's construction (Taṇḍaṇa, VS 2056, p. 353).
It is likely that Vīra Śamśera built the temple as a tribute to his cousin Jagatjaṅga, the son of his uncle Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā.
Vīra Śamśera was raised by Jaṅga Bahādura at his Thapathali Palace (P. Rāja VS 2073, p. 99).
Vīra Śamśera was also responsible for orchestrating the assassination of Prime Minister Raṇa Uddīpa Siṃha on November 22, 1885 CE (VS 1942) (B. Ācārya VS 2055, p. 173).

As a result of the assassination, Jagatjaṅga was also beheaded and later cremated with a brahmin performing the cremation rites on the banks of the Bagmati river three days later (P. Rāṇā VS 2070, p. 145; P. Rāja VS 2073, p. 104).

According to theGopālarājavaṃśāvalī, Licchavi king Haridattavarmā established four Nārāyaṇa shrines at the four cardinal peaks (Vajrācārya and Malla 1985, folio 20A).
However, no inscriptions directly attest to the construction date of the current pond structure.
An inscription on-site also records that King Mahendra later repaired the pond.
Moved by her devotion, Nārāyaṇa created the pond, from which Vāsukī and his consort also emerged.
Since then, ritual offerings at the shrine have used water from this pond, with a Rājopādhyāya priest continuing the tradition (J. Mānandhara VS 2060, p. 71).

There, the water is poured into the deity’s mouth, and it is believed that after 200–300 pots, the water reaches and fills the mouth of the image—signifying divine satisfaction and, eventually, rainfall (J. Mānandhara VS 2060, p. 66).
While Kamalādī Gaṇeśa Mandira in Kamalādī, Kathmandu is the main temple of this deity, this building is his residence where various items needed for his annual procession are also stored.
Other details of thedyaḥchẽ’s interiors are unclear, as the building was not accessible for this documentation.
There are no historical records of thedyaḥchẽ’s initial construction.
The religious trust of the Maharjanas associated with the Kamalādī Gaṇeśa built a temple for the deity in 1750 CE (NS 870) (Purscha 1975, p. 99).
Kamalādī Gaṇeśa, however, may have been established long before that as a small shrine.
The Kamalādī Gaṇeśa Dyaḥchẽ was probably built around the same time the main shrine of the deity was established.

The traditional architecture of thedyaḥchẽwas not adopted while the building was reconstructed into a modern building in 1993 CE (VS 2050) after it fell into poor state of repair (guthimember, Maharjana, male, age 60).
The Kamalādī Gaṇeśa Jamaḥmi Guthi, a religious trust managed by them, oversees all socio-cultural activities related to the deity.
On the 14th of the dark fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, special worship is offered to Nāsaḥdyaḥ, the deity of music and charm, residing within thedyaḥchẽ.
This is followed by a festive meal enjoyed by the trust members (guthimember, Maharjana, male, age 60).

monument_name: Gaṇeśa Bhajana Phalcā (originally built in 1505 CE)
text: It was constructed especially for chanting and singing hymns and devotional songs (bhajana) dedicated to Gaṇeśa who is the area deity (sthānagaṇeśa) of the locality (albeit, no deity is enshrined inside the Phalcā).

monument_name: Gaṇeśa Bhajana Phalcā (originally built in 1505 CE)
text: The Phalcā was constructed in 1505 CE (NS 625) on the plots of land endowed by three persons from the Su Bāhāḥ Ṭola—Jivarāma Bhābo, Hṛdāma Bhābo, and Jayarāma Bhābo.

monument_name: Gaṇeśa Bhajana Phalcā (originally built in 1505 CE)
text: The initial construction of the Phalcā took place when a person named Jyoti was thethakāli(seniormost member of theguthi)of a group that used to conductaṣṭamīvrata, a ritual fasting observed on the 8th lunar day.

monument_name: Gaṇeśa Bhajana Phalcā (originally built in 1505 CE)
text: Although it is aphalcāat present, its inscription refers to the building as acapāḥ.

monument_name: Gaṇeśa Bhajana Phalcā (originally built in 1505 CE)
text: In 1626 CE (NS 746), Śivarāma Bhāro commissioned the renovation of thecapāḥand also formed aguthiby a land donation.

monument_name: Gaṇeśa Bhajana Phalcā (originally built in 1505 CE)
text: The Phalcā was renovated again in 1713 CE, i.e., NS 833 (recorded on the inscription issued in NS 833, see the historical events below).

monument_name: Gaṇeśa Bhajana Phalcā (originally built in 1505 CE)
text: This inscription refers to the building as aphalcā.

monument_name: Gaṇeśa Bhajana Phalcā (originally built in 1505 CE)
text: Thecapāḥwas probably converted into aphalcāduring the said renovation.

monument_name: Gaṇeśa Bhajana Phalcā (originally built in 1505 CE)
text: The Phalcā went through another cycle of renovation in VS 2054 (1997 CE).

monument_name: Gaṇeśa Bhajana Phalcā (originally built in 1505 CE)
text: The members of theguthisleep at thePhalcafor the security of the Gaṇeśa repoussé on this day.
This east-facing traditional phalcā has an artistic column with five bays and a roof constructed using traditional bricks.
No deities and inscriptions are installed inside it.
The phalcā is built upon a plinth and includes a lattice window in the middle of its western wall.
There is no inscription recording the initial phase of construction.

However, a similar phalcā (BKT4015), located at the entrance, bears an inscription dating back to 1758 CE (NS 878), which records the construction of a brick wall in Dharmśālā (phalcā) by Purṇatāja Vajrācāryā and his family members.
The phalcā was renovated by Bhaktapur Development Project in 1977 CE (2034 VS) (a local resident, Dyolā, male, 49).

The phalcā was completely damaged in the earthquake of 2015 CE (2072 VS), it was reconstructed in 2018 CE (2075 VS) with the financial support of Bhaktapur municipality and contributions of the locals.
In 2019, it was almost entirely demolished and reconstructed using new materials (for the carved pillars, beams, etc.).
It had been in a dilapidated state since the 2015 earthquakes and had suffered major water damage.
Atoraṇaalso covered by brass sheets is placed on top of the entrance, and a stone pillar erected in VS 2011 (1954 CE) with a statue of a mole on its top stands in front of the Temple.
The shrine with two aniconic stones received minor renovations in NS 741 (1621 CE).
A Temple was constructed only during the joint rule of King Siddhinarasiṃha and Śrīnivāsa Malla in NS 773 (1653 CE).
The Temple received a golden finial hooded by a parasol in NS 818 (1698 CE).
Historical records show that a golden crown was also offered to the deity in NS 825 (1705 CE), but it is not seen at present.
The Temple went through a renovation in NS 857 (1737 CE) and a complete reconstruction took place in VS 2058 (2001 CE).

Aguthiat Pinchẽ Ṭola associated with this Temple carries out the exhibition of a metal-sheet image of Gaṇeśa every year during the Indrajātrā (Yẽnyāḥ)festival in front of the main statues in the sanctum.

monument_name: Nārāyaṇa Mandira at Cāka Bāhāḥ (ca. 1699 CE)
text: In addition to this main statue, there is also a smaller and partially damaged image of Viṣṇu in the sanctum.

monument_name: Nārāyaṇa Mandira at Cāka Bāhāḥ (ca. 1699 CE)
text: An oil-lamp balustrade with 108 lamps surrounds the temple, while a bell donated on the same date hangs on a beam besides the lower plinth at its southwest corner.

monument_name: Nārāyaṇa Mandira at Cāka Bāhāḥ (ca. 1699 CE)
text: A pillar with an image showing Garuḍa sitting and praying to Śrīdhara Viṣṇu was also erected in 2012.

monument_name: Nārāyaṇa Mandira at Cāka Bāhāḥ (ca. 1699 CE)
text: No inscription mentioning the exact date of the establishment of the temple could be found.

monument_name: Nārāyaṇa Mandira at Cāka Bāhāḥ (ca. 1699 CE)
text: However, an astrologer called Śivanārāyaṇa installed a stone inscription dated NS 819 inside the temple.

monument_name: Nārāyaṇa Mandira at Cāka Bāhāḥ (ca. 1699 CE)
text: This stone records the names of his predecessors, and provides grounds to hypothesise that either he or one of them established the temple.

monument_name: Nārāyaṇa Mandira at Cāka Bāhāḥ (ca. 1699 CE)
text: Inside the sanctum, another broken inscription dated NS 754 informs readers of the renovation of aphalcā, which suggests that this inscription was brought here from somewhere else.
To the east of the Hiṭī, there is a Jaḥdhuṃhiti and the base of a Śivaliṅga, while to the west lies a damagedphalcā(rest house), with only the foundation remaining as of April 2024 CE.
There is no inscriptional evidence about the construction of the Hiṭī.

According to local mythology, during the Licchavi period, Bhṛkuṭī, who married King Songtsen Gampo (c.605–650 CE), travelled to Tibet along this route and would bathe at this water spout upon returning home.
The shape of the stones and the structure of the Hiṭī suggest it was built during the late Malla period.
As of April 2024 CE, an external pipe is connected to the stone water conduit for daily use, but no running water was observed during our documentation.
It is believed to have been erected in the 19th century, potentially when the path from the Ārya Ghāṭa cremation ground to the Guhyeśvarī temple was paved with stone slabs.
No inscriptions at the site provide clues about the temple's original construction.
The path from the Ārya Ghāṭa cremation ground to the Guhyeśvarī temple was paved by Sardāra Rāmakṛṣṇa Kũvara in 1868 CE (NS 988).
He also renovated the Ārya Ghāṭa at that time (DevamālāVaṃśāvalīVS 2013, p. 98-99).
It is possible that the statue was erected during this period.

Rāmakṛṣṇa Kũvara was the great grandfather of Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā, who later renovated the stone-paved path and constructed the Viśvarūpa Mandira (PPK2007) in 1863 CE (VS 1920) (DevamālāVaṃśāvalīVS 2013, p. 98-99).
Established by King Mānadeva in the 5th century, the statue of Viṣṇuvikrānta currently remains neglected in the open.

While the statue was once part of a grand temple, it has now (February 2024) been placed inside a concrete west-facing niche just below a narrow path around the makeshift huts built west of the southeastern entrance to the Paśupati area.
In the 1970s, the statue used to be in the open fields (D. Vajrācārya VS 2030, p. 35; S. Jośī VS 2073, p. 66).
citations: (D. Vajrācārya VS 2030, p. 35; S. Jośī VS 2073, p. 66)

text: King Mānadeva established two similar statues of Viṣṇuvikrānta on the same day in 468 CE (ŚS 389) in memory of his mother Rājyavatī with a similar inscription on their pedestal.
The other statue was established in Lazimpat, Kathmandu.
King Mānadeva established two similar statues in two locations on the same day in the name of his mother, who does not feature in any other installations after these two.
This suggests that he established these statues after the death of his mother (D. Vajrācārya VS 2030, p. 38).
Although the inscription of the statue mentions the construction of a grand temple, it no longer survives in the vicinity.
The Pashupati Area Development Trust plans to clear the settlement in the area before reestablishing the statue amid a proper surrounding (S. Devakoṭā VS 2080, p. 1).
Special worship with fire oblation used to be organized occasionally in front of the statue in the past.
In 1693 CE (NS 813), a group led by Guṇarāja Bhābo built a temple for Bhairava, the protector of Sānāgāũ, a village locally known as Thasi.
He is referred to as Mahākāla Bhairava in the inscriptions.
The deities on the wooden toraṇa offered to Bhairava have been stolen.
There are no historical records of the establishment of Bhairava in Sānāgāũ.
It is likely that an open shrine was built for Bhairava as a protective deity at the beginning of the settlement in Sānāgāũ, but it is unclear when a temple was built for him.
However, in 1626 CE (NS 746), a group led by Budha Baṃde and Kṛṣṇa Siṃha Bhāro laid traditional tiles on the roof.
Later, in 1693 CE (NS 813), a group led by Guṇarāja Bhābo built a proper temple for Bhairava and offered a pair of flags as well.
In 1699 CE (NS 819), during the reign of King Yoganarendra Malla, Suṣudeva Bhābo, Karirāma Bhābo, Jagadeva Bhābo, and others jointly offered a pair of stone lions to the temple.
In 1849 CE (NS 969), Indralachami, along with her sons Dhanabṛdhi, Vīramuni, and Dharmmavīra, offered utensils and agricultural tools to the temple.
In 1888 CE (NS 1008), Munirāja Bhāro, along with his wife Dhijalakṣmī, son Byakhā, and other family members, offered a brasstoraṇato the temple.
After thistoraṇawas stolen, a new one was offered by Hareśa Maharjana and Tīrthamāyā Maharjana in 2021 CE(VS 2078).

Kālamocanaghāṭa Phalcā West is almost identical to the Kālamocanaghāṭa Phalcā East (KAT2783), with the two buildings sharing many details such as size, carving styles, and building materials, making it appropriate to refer to them as twinphalcās.

There is no inscriptive evidence regarding the construction of thephalcās;however, architectural features, such as the carving style of columns and arches, indicate that construction likely occurred between the Śāha and Rāṇā periods (e.g. mid 19th century).
An inventory from 1982 CE (VS 2039) reports the dilapidated condition of thephalcāsand recommends renovation.
A photograph depicts the poor state of the Kālamocanaghāṭa Phalcā West at that time (Inventory VS 2039, p.134).

Despite its critical condition, the renovation was not undertaken, leading homeless families to repurpose the space as residences by closing the bays with brick walls to create rooms according to their needs.

In contrast to the renovation and reconstruction efforts undertaken for numerous monuments along the banks of the Bāgamatī after the earthquake of 2015 CE (VS 2072), these twophalcāshave remained neglected.
Prior to VS 2030, devotional songs and rituals were performed in thesephalcās.
Located east of Māheśvarī Pīṭha (BKT0300) in Bhaktapur, this arcaded rest house is a more recent construction on the Pīṭha premises.
The five-bay Phalcā facing west is built in traditional architecture style but using concrete and bricks.
A local committee named as ‘Māheśvarī Pīṭha Saṃrakṣaṇa tathā Vikāsa Samiti’ was formed in 2000 CE (VS 2057) for the conservation of the Pīṭha premises.
The committee had the Phalcā constructed in 2004 CE (VS 2061).
It was never rebuilt.
Later in 2004 CE, a new Phalcā was built a few meters northeast of the spot where the lost Phalcā once stood.

During theBiskāḥJātrāfestival of Bhaktapur, the statue of Goddess Māheśvarī enshrined in her home (dyaḥchẽ) at the Inācva Ṭola is brought to her seat, this Pīṭha, for overnight worship, including animal sacrifice and fire oblation.
Theguthi(ritual association) responsible for thisdyaḥcheṃ(god-house) consists of seven members from the Jyāpu community.
This triadic iconography of Gaṇeśa and Bhairava, which emerged in Patan during the late medieval period, exemplifies a local adaptation of tantric visual conventions (M. Ācārya VS 2079, pp. 100–108).
Beside the main mask, a smaller one is also installed, both regarded as manifestations of Kwayna Gaṇeśa.
The principal brass mask is placed on a brass throne (siṃhāsana), donated by anAmātyaof Patan in (1861 CE) VS 1918.
The present concrete building of thedyaḥcheṃ, surmounted by a dome (fūchāorpur), was constructed only in 1981–82 CE (VS 2038).
The temple’s construction became possible through extensive voluntary labor (śramadāna) contributed by the local residents (currentāḥju, Mahārjan, male, age 85).
Seven senior Jyāpu members from Naḥ Ṭola, Chāḥ Bahāḥ, and Chobhar formed the hereditaryguthiof Kwayna Gaṇeśa.
Before the establishment of thedyaḥcheṃin 1983 CE (VS 2040), the brass mask of Kwayna Gaṇeśa (LAL2970-001) was kept in theāḥju’s private residence.
Because this system of private guardianship became increasingly complex and impractical, the presentdyaḥcheṃwas constructed through collective community effort.
Over time, additional buildings were added, and the site has evolved into a large compound now used for weddings and other social or ritual gatherings.
According to long-established custom, the residents of Patan must worship this Gaṇeśa after any auspicious communal meal (bhĩ bhway).
The obligation applies after ritual feasts following life-cycle ceremonies, annualguthifeasts, musical processions, or any form of celebratory gathering.

After the conclusion of theBuṅgadyah Jātrā, theguthiyārmembers of the festival procession carry the mask to Tamkhaḥ Dyaḥ (LAL0600) for ceremonial worship and later return it to its place in this shrine.
The Bāhāḥ can be accessed via a newly constructed gate with two openings.
The main three-storey shrine building (thedyaḥchẽ)is facing east.

The front façade of the building is plastered withlivã(grey sandy clay + cow dung + rice husk) and white-washed with lime, but the ground floor plaster has already deteriorated due to damp rising from the ground.
The end walls of the buildings (kilāsa) have pilasters of the same height with decorative floral design on the floor cornice levels.
The upper floor can be accessed via the annex building to the north through a single door (see map).
The gable roof of the building is covered with small tiles.
The southern end wall has been reconstructed but is still in a critical condition due to damage suffered by the earthquake and rain.
This building has similar architecture to thedyaḥchẽbuilding but is more decorated.
The inside bay of the building is colonnaded on the ground floor to the south, and the floors are separated from one another by well-carved wooden cornices which cannot be found in thedyaḥchẽ.
All of the openings of this building are rectangular in shape.
Thedigichẽcan be accessed via an annex building to the right on the west side.
This annex building has a main carved door frame with plain lintel ends on its ground floor.
The annex building's walls are of exposed brick, and the western end wall collapsed due to an earthquake.

The monument borrows a spatial organisation similar to that of the Dullu water tank erected by the minister Devavarmā in 1354, during the rule of the Khaśa Malla emperor Pṛthvī Malla and the water tanks visible in Ajayamerukot.
The latter were most probably built during the second half of the 14th century.

Given the historical context of the place, with the nearbyśikharatemples (BTD0030) dating from approx. 14th-15th century, it is most likely that this monument is contemporaneous to the construction of the temples.

Thus, in this perspective the monument would have been erected during the reign of a king of Doti, such as Nirai Pāla (r. c. 1362-1383) or Nāga Malla (also Nāga Pāla, r. c. 1383-1411) (about the Doteli kings seePandey 1997: 171-173 andOjha 1988).
It is unclear when the Hiti first came into existence due to the lack of an inscriptive evidence.

With the permission of the Vajrayoginī Sevā Samiti-a local organization formed for the conservation of the area, the , family of Kṛṣṇa Kumārī Śreṣṭha belonging to a clan named Baḥsimākva Khalaḥ had commissioned the reconstruction of the Hiti in 1996 CE.
Although the Hiti was dismantled down to the foundation and rebuilt on the occasion, the inscription that records the event mentions it to be only a renovation.
Noguthirelated to this Hiti survives at present.
Therefore, anyguthirelated to the Hiti probably ceased to function at least seven or eight decades ago if it ever existed.
Thisśivaliṅgahails from the Licchavi period and holds a unique place in history due to its inscription that reveals the existence of King Rāmadeva, a previously unknown figure in Nepalese history.
Notably, the tip of thejalaharīfaces north while an inscription from the era of King Rāmadeva is found on its western side.
According to the inscription, in 546 CE (Śaka Era 467), a woman named Mānamatī donated land to establish a trust in the name of Nātheśvara.
However, it remains unclear from the inscription whether she solely founded the trust or also established the Nātheśvara Śivaliṅga.

This inscription holds significant historical value, as it not only introduced King Rāmadeva into the Licchavi lineage but also illuminated the rising influence of a courtier named Kramalīna during that period (D. Vajrācārya VS 2030, p. 176).

This Phalcā, constructed on the banks of the river Bāgamatī, has most probably been built for the convenience of those people participating in death anniversary rituals (śrāddha) since it stands in front of three funerary platforms right by the ghats, facing east.
This exceptionally long building incorporates two phalcās under one roof – the left one, towards the South, contains of seven bays, the right one, towards North, has five bays.
Many steps (ghāṭa) have been built along the river bank of the Bāgamatī river at Paśupatikṣetra.
To facilitate the participation during funerals, and other rituals conducted along the river banks, there has been an ongoing construction ofphalcāsandsataḥs.
Rājarājeśvarīghāṭa phalcā has been constructed for such reasons.
The walls are constructed using traditional bricks (dāci appā).
There is no inscriptive evidence that records the initial construction of the Phalcā.

During the early Śāha and Rāna periods, extending up to the later half, the practice of building such a Phalcā along the riverbanks was undertaken either from the royal palace, for high-status individuals or members of noble families.

In the past, on the occasion of Ṛṣi Pañcamī, people bathing in the river during the night, would use the Phalcā as a place for changing clothes and starting fires (report by a clan member, Kārkī, male, age 69).
Before it was dismantled around 1986, the Phalcā had a gable roof with tiles.
This roof was then replaced by a concrete slab supported by three RCC columns during its reconstruction.
Adjacent to the temple's southern side, a bell, installed in the year 1886 CE (VS 1943), hangs on a bell-stand.
Additionally, a faded inscription west of the temple suggests an antiquity predating the temple's construction.

Known colloquially as Salyānī Mahārānī (translated as the queen of Salyāna, a district in West Nepal), Toraṇadivyeśvarīdevī commissioned the construction of Narendreśvara Mandira in memory of her late husband, Narendra Bahādura Śāha, in the year 1881 CE (VS 1938) (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p.351; Michaels and Tandon 2017, p.106).
citations: (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p.351; Michaels and Tandon 2017, p.106)

text: King of Salyāna, he ascended the throne in 1848 CE (VS 1905) following the demise of his father, Teja Bahādura Śāha (R. Gautama VS 2042, p.59).

Post the temple's completion, Toraṇadivyeśvarīdevī, in the same year, donated land for the perpetual observance of rituals at this temple, as well as at the Gorakhanātha and Dhīramukteśvara temples (cf.K_0040_0020).
Furthermore, in 1886 CE (VS 1943), she facilitated the installation of a bell at the temple.
Later, the earthquakes of 2015 inflicted damage upon the temple, necessitating restoration efforts by the Pashupati Area Development Trust in 2021 CE (VS 2078).
A small stonenandīis installed in typical fahion to the west of the temple.
Further west, a brick-paved square measuring 90 x 90 cm is used for the sacred fire (hom).
According to the priest, the large stone platform to the south of the temple, was the sacred place where rituals for the temple's consecration were held.
A Licchavi inscription which dates back toSamvat435 and makes reference to King Vasantadeva (r. 506-532) is attached to the western plinth of the temple (VajracharyaVS 2030: 112).
In 1994 CE, the temple was restored through the combined effort of local stakeholders and the Urban Development through Locat Efforts Project (UDLE).
In 2022, the Lalitpur Municipality replaced the brick with stone paving.

monument_name: Ṭīkā Bhairava at Bhelachẽ (c. mid-16th cent. CE)
text: According toPruscha(1975, 176) this temple was built in 1541 but no inscription could be found  to provide evidence of this date.
In 2023, it was dismantled and was, at the moment of the most recent documentation, in March 2024, in the process of being rebuilt.
The date of the Sataḥ's initial construction is not known, It is believed to be associated with an individual, a man named Lalita.
The first Lalita is connected to the establishment of Lalitpur as a city.
A grass-cutter by profession, this man lived in Lalitavana during the reign of King Vīradeva in the Kaligata Era of 3400 (299 CE).
When the King found out about this magical event, he named the grass-cutter Lalita and established a city in his name, following all Vedic rites and rituals in the process.
The King commissioned this Sataḥ be built alongside the city, and so it was named Lalītāpurī Sataḥ.

A well-known folk tale recounts the following story: a man was sentenced to death and left in the Sataḥ to be devoured by the demon: But the demon spared him when he found him chanting the Nāmasaṅgīti hymns (S. JośīNS 1116, 35-36).
Having remained buried for many years, Mahādeva Hiti (also known as Sikhucā Hiti) was excavated in 2009 CE (VS 2066) and brought it into the present state.

According to an inscription (SKH0020_I_001)preserved at Mahādeva Mandira (SKH0020),a certain Jayanārāyaṇa (text: Jayanārāyana) who enshrined aśivaliṅga(seeSKH0020-003) at the premises of Mahādeva Mandira (SKH0020) constructed the Hiti in 1653 CE (NS 773).
He had also constructed aphalcā, but it is no longer in existence.
Therefore, local youths unearthed it by excavating the site on the occasion of the Sankhu Festival held in 2009 CE (VS 2066).
Bālākhu Hiti, located to the south of Bālākhu Gaṇeśa (BKT0130) in Bālākhu Ṭola, Bhaktapur, is a Late Medieval monument whose precise date of construction remains uncertain.
Although no inscription directly associated with its foundation has survived, stylistic analysis suggests its origin in this period.
On the northern plinth rests a damaged sculpture identifiable as Umā-Maheśvara, based on the surviving elements of its pedestal.
The northern wall contains several vacant niches from which images have been stolen.
Affixed to the western wall of the Hiti is a stone inscription dated 1678 CE (NS 798).
Although situated within the Hiti complex, the inscription is unrelated to it.
Instead, it records the construction of theThaṇthu Palaceby King Jitāmitra Malla.
The inscription states that the palace was built in honor of the king’s tutelary deity and stipulates that it must never be damaged.
Should any destruction occur, it would be the duty of the reigning monarch to restore it.

The inscription also names Jitāmitra’s brother, Ugra Malla, and his son, Bhūpatīndra Malla, and records that the palace complex was to be known as “Thaṇthu Rājakula,” while its outer courtyard was designated “Siddhicuka.”A few years later, an earthquake destroyed theThaṇthu Palace.
On its southern foundations, King Bhūpatīndra Malla erected theNyaynyāpāḥ Jhyāḥ(Fifty-Five Window) Palace.

During the Rana period, the eastern section of theThaṇthucomplex was remodeled in European style, featuring lime-washed walls, large windows, and a corrugated metal roof (B. Kāyastha VS 2078, pp. 18–19).
Despite these later alterations, the palace garden and the Hiti remained intact (B. Pauḍela VS 2065, p. 54).
In subsequent years, the eastern portion of the palace compound housed first the office of the magistrate and later that of the Bhaktapur Municipality (B. Pauḍela VS 2065, p. 54).
Today, however, theThaṇthu Palacebuilt by Jitāmitra Malla has completely vanished (Vaidya & Shrestha 2002, p. 27).

While the temple's benefactor and the year of its construction remain shrouded in uncertainty, the Śiva temple currently languishes in a state of disrepair, with the mainśivaliṅgain the sanctum having been displaced from its original position.
Regrettably, the statues in the other niches, including those of Gaṇeśa, Durgā, and Viṣṇu, as per the Śivapāñcāyana concept, have been stolen.
Additionally, the statue's pedestal holds a Licchavi inscription, buried underground as of August 2023.
While only two letters of the inscription have been deciphered, D. Vajrācārya (VS 2030, p.581) has dated it to the Mānadeva period based on the script.
The statue likely suffered a similar fate around the same time (V. Pauḍela VS 2060, p. 32).
The terracotta figures ofnāgakanyās, the serpent maidens, flanking the entrances were replaced with new ones after the 2015 earthquakes.
The Phalcā was dismantled and rebuilt around 1995, incorporating four baluster columns which had been salvaged from an unknown location and shortened.
Maṇikula Phalcā was commissioned by the Śākya of Maṇikūṭavihāra, which was established in 1865 as a branch of Cikã Bahī (LAL1620).
The three-bayed Phalcā´s ground shape is trapezial due to its location between the Gaṇeśa temple in the east and another building to the west.
Pillar 001 is located in the locality of Pipal Sāre, in front of the Pipal Sāre School, and pillar 002 is installed on the side of a nearby small path.
Both sides are ornamented by carvings but only the northeastern side contains an inscription.
This would date the inscription from 1318-1320.

They are installed to honor the memory of deceased persons, mostly warriors.

text: The temple, built during the medieval period, houses some of the oldest statues in Kirtipur.
A statue of Gaṇeśa, facing east, is consecrated in the sanctum.
The statue is severely damaged, and only certain features such as its big rotund belly and snake garland are visible.
An inscription from 1704 CE (NS 824) briefly mentions a group of five Bhāro caste members from Kirtipur who constructed it.
However, it is not clear from the inscription whether the temple was constructed over the aexisting older statues or they were collected from the Bāghabairava temple complex and consecrated here.
Further, the mentioned group of five Bhāros installed a gilt pinnacle with a parasol, and performed a fire sacrifice calledsahasrāhuti yajñaupon the completion of the construction of the temple.
The temple must have been renovated several times in the past.

The mismatch in the height, inclination, and breadth of the temple’s two roofs, usage of plain struts, and lack of the golden pinnacle and parasol mentioned in the inscription are all indicative of earlier renovations.
But there is no inscriptive evidence to pinpoint the exact dates of such renovation works.
In 1989 CE, the temple’s roofs which were in derelict condition and its cracked walls were renovated (Ś. Śreṣṭha1994, 84).
It was also renovated in 2003 CE (NS 1123) with the financial support from G.E.
In 1637, King Siddhinarasiṃha Malla built this pillar in collaboration with the Kṛṣṇa Temple (LAL1340).
However, it collapsed in the 2015 earthquakes and has not been rebuilt.

However, at some point the mask disappeared (date unknown: according to local information, the mask was displayed in the Phalcā before it was stolen in the night during Indrajātra) and so this tradition came to an end.

The shrine is established near the confluence (dobhāna) of the Uddhāravatī and Pūrnāvatī streams, close to a cremation ground (śmaśānaghāṭa).
At thepīṭha, the principal image of the goddess Kālī is installed facing east.
She is identified as a deity of the southernāmnāya(K. Koirālā, VS 2065, p. 60).
To the south of the main image are installed the Aṣṭamātṛkās—Brahmāyaṇī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, and Indrāyaṇī—together with Gaṇeśa.

As the settlement below became insecure, contemporary tantric practitioners are believed to have compelled the goddess, through the power of mantras, to relocate with her attendant deities to a dwelling place at the river confluence and cremation ground below Pharping.
Remains found on the hill are said to corroborate this relocation of thepīṭha(Ṭ. Śreṣṭha, VS 2078, p. 70).
According to theDevamālā Vaṃśāvalī(Y. Naraharinātha, VS 2013, p. 62), only thepīṭhaoriginally existed here.
The goddess is said to have appeared in the dream of King Pratāpa Malla and instructed him to create and install her image.
The first image commissioned by the king was fierce and unmanifest, prompting the goddess to reappear in his dream and direct that it be installed within the palace instead.
With the assistance of his guru Lambakarṇa Bhaṭṭa, Pratāpa Malla then installed a second image at thepīṭha.

TheBhāṣā Vaṃśāvalīprovides further detail, stating that Pratāpa Malla completed the consecration rites by performingmahāpūjā,sahasrabalī, andnarabalī, and formally installed the image on the day of Vaiśākha Śukla Tṛtīyā (D. Laṃsāla, VS 2023, pp. 82–83).
The earliest known inscription related to Dakṣiṇakālī dates to NS 360 (VS 1297) and is found on the crown of the image used in the Hariśaṅkara Jātrā.
Local belief maintains that Dakṣiṇakālī was also known as Kankeśvarī, theśaktiof Kanakeśvara Śiva (K. Koirālā, VS 2065, p. 66), suggesting that the goddess may earlier have been known by this name.

After the unification of Nepal, the Śāha kings instituted the worship and festivals of Dakṣiṇakālī of Pharping, located closer to the Valley, in place of the Kālīkā of Gorkhā (Ṭ. Śreṣṭha, VS 2078, p. 72).

King Girvāṇayuddha Vikrama Śāha endowed 504murī(approximately 126ropanī) of land in 1799 CE (VS 1856) asguṭhīfor the performance of daily worship andmahāpūjā(thāpūjā) (Ṭ. Śreṣṭha, VS 2078, pp. 182–183).
Offerings,guṭhīarrangements, and inscriptions donated over different periods by kings, nobles, local officials, and lay patrons testify to the historical prosperity of the Dakṣiṇakālī temple.

During the reign of Girvāṇayuddha Vikrama Śāha, aguṭhīof 504murīof land was formally established in 1799 CE (VS 1856) for the goddess’s daily worship andmahāpūjā(D. Vajrācārya & Ṭ. Śreṣṭha, VS 2078, pp. 301–303; K. Koirālā, VS 2065, p. 66).

text: In 1802 CE (VS 1859), a donor named Lakṣmī offered anagarāand established aguṭhīto ensure its use during daily worship.

An inscription preserved in the collection of Gaṇeślāl Mānandhara of Pharping records that in 1848 CE (VS 1905), Surendra Vikrama Śāha donated a silver crown and ornaments and established akheṭaguṭhīfor the goddess.
In the same year, Bhavanakumārī, the wife of Kāji Amṛtasiṃha Thāpā, offered a gildedkikiṃpā, a crown, and 108tolāof silver.
In 1849 CE (VS 1906), General Amarasiṃha Thāpā is likewise recorded as having made offerings to Dakṣiṇakālī.
Around 1884 CE (VS 1941), the younger queen of Jītejaṅga Bahādur Rāṇā performedpañcabalīworship and offered garments to the goddess.

In 1900 CE (VS 1957), Vīra Śamśer Rāṇā constructed apāṭīand dedicated it to the deity, and in 1917 CE (VS 1974), Pṛthvī Vīra Vikrama Śāha and the junior queen donated the bell located on the right side of the shrine.

In 1922 CE (VS 1979), Chibdhoja Śāha, the eldest son of Raṇśer Śāha and grandson of Prāṇa Śāha, offered a gildedcaduvāadorned with four nāgas and tassels, and endowed akheṭaguṭhīfor the annualVarṣabandhanarite performed on Jyeṣṭha Śukla Daśamī.

An inscription behind the temple records that in 1960 CE (VS 2017), on the occasion of King Mahendra Vīra Vikrama Śāha’s birthday, the embankments, walls, and surroundingpāṭī–sattalastructures were restored.
More recently, in 2016 CE (VS 2073), Dal Bahādur Deuwā and his family of Dhangadhī constructed and dedicated the temple’s entrance gateway, as recorded on an inscription affixed to the gateway wall.
Dakṣiṇakālī is worshipped as a goddess who grants royal power and victory over enemies.
The Maharjans are responsible for animal sacrifice, managing ritual vessels and ornaments, registering donated goods with the Guṭhī Saṃsthān, and safeguarding them.
For the security of the shrine, four Maharjans and four Poḍes are customarily assigned (Ṭ. Śreṣṭha, VS 2078, p. 101).
Major ritual observances includemahāpūjā(thāpūjā) performed annually on Vaiśākha Kṛṣṇa Trayodaśī and Bhādra Kṛṣṇa Aṣṭamī (K. Koirālā, VS 2065, p. 66).

Among the four annual Navarātrīs, Baḍā Daśaiṃ (ninth of bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina) and Cāite Daśaiṃ (ninth of bright fortnight of the month of Caitra) are observed here as major festivals of Bhagavatī, marked by worship and animal sacrifice (K. Koirālā, VS 2065, p. 66).
The Sarasvatī Sataḥ, a two-storied public rest house constructed in 1839 CE (ŚS 1761), was commissioned by Vīrabhadra Kũvara, with the approval of King Rājendra Vikrama Śāha.
Situated to the west of the Maṅgalāgaurī Mandirā (PPK0232) in the Paśupati area, the building with corrugated metal roof faces north.
It might be that it was brought from another location and placed there during the plinth renovation.

A large inscription is installed on the western inner wall of the ground floor, detailing the construction of the Sataḥ and documenting numerous deeds of Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā’s ancestors in the Paśupati area.
The inscription begins with the laying of stone slabs on the path from the Paśupati temple to Guhyeśvarī by Rāmakṛṣṇa Kũvara and his younger brother Jayakṛṣṇa Kũvara in 1772 CE (ŚS 1694).
It also records the construction of a bridge at the Ārya Ghāṭa cremation site by Candravīra Kũvara (son of Jayakṛṣṇa) and Raṇajita Kũvara (son of Rāmakṛṣṇa) in 1796 CE (ŚS 1718).

He also built a bridge over the Bagmati river near the Vatsalā temple (PPK0224) and established avāṇaliṅga(naturally-formedśivaliṅga) to the east of the bridge in 1839 CE (ŚS 1761), naming it "Vīrabhadreśvara" after himself.
Vīrabhadra Kũvara's sons Vīrabahādura, Jaṅgadhvaja, and Hemabahādura Kũvara endowed a trust with land parcels in 1845 CE (ŚS 1767) to fund needed renovations of the monuments built by their father.
The large inscription, which records these constructions and donations, was installed on the ground floor of the Sataḥ in 1884 CE (VS 1941).
It was established by Kīrtisiṃha Malla the son of Siddhinarasiṃha Malla.
Two false doors can be found to the north and the west, while the southern wall carries an inscription instead.
The temple may have collapsed in the 1934 earthquake and subsequently rebuilt in the present style.
There are debates concerning thebāhāḥ'sinitial construction date.

The earliest sources related to thebāhāḥare two stone inscriptions issued during the reign of King Pratāpa Malla (r. 1641-74): a well-preserved inscription from NS 788 (1668 CE) and a damaged inscription, most probably issued before NS 788 (1668 CE).
The physical and palaeographical features of these inscriptions suggest that they were issued by the same person a few years apart.

The NS 788 (1668 CE) inscription records the consecration of Guṇākara Mahāvihāra (Chusyā Bāhāḥ) ‘guṇākara mahāvihāra pratiṣṭhā saṃpūrṇa yāṅana’ and the installation of Harāhara Lokeśvara, sponsored by a person named Guṇajyoti (text: Guṇajoti) Vajrācārya together with his family members from Dhvākhā Bāhāḥ, while the damaged inscription mentions the completion of thebāhāḥ‘thva vihara dayakā’.

A third inscription also installed by Guṇajyoti inside the sanctum of thebāhāḥin NS 769 (1649 CE) records the renovation of a rest-house (capāḥ) constructed by his father Jñānajyoti (text: Jñānajoti) in honour of their clan deity, Maricī Devī.
Chusyā Bāhāḥ is not mentioned in this inscription.
If the expansive Mahāvihāra had existed here during this time, it would have been probably mentioned in the inscription which records the family tree of Guṇajyoti and the renovation of thecapāḥ.
Thus, it is likely that the damaged inscription was issued after NS 769 (1649 CE).
We can then conclude that thebāhāḥmust have been constructed sometime after NS 769 (1649 CE), and was consecrated (probably after its renovation) in NS 788 (1668 CE).
One could also argue that Guṇajyoti converted thecapāḥbuilt by his father into abāhāḥand named it Guṇākara Mahāvihāra (Chusyā Bāhāḥ) after him.
Chusyā Bāhāḥ'ssaṅghamembers believe that Guṇajyoti constructed thebāhāḥwith income generated from his trade in Tibet.
There is an inscription at the bāhā dated N.S. 788 which says that the construction of the bāhāḥ was completed in N.S. 769 and at the time an image of Harihara Lokeśvara was installed in the shrine.

In N.S. 788 the King of Kathmandu, Pratāp Malla was invited by Guṇajyoti to the ceremony marking the official opening of the bāhā. …  It seems clear that the bāhā was renovated in N. S. 769, and the occasion marked by the donation of an image of Harihara Lokeśvara some years later.
Pratāp Malla was invited to the consecration ceremony of this image.

It is impossible to say whether Chusyā Bāhāḥ had long been a branch of Dhwākā Bāhā and was renovated at this time, or whether it was a separate foundation that had been abandoned by its original inhabitants, fallen into disrepair and then taken over and renovated by the people of Dhwākā Bāhā as a branch of their bāhā.”The epigraphic evidence does not support Locke’s interpretation.
First, the NS 788 inscription does not say that the construction of thebāhāḥwas completed in NS 769.
As mentioned above, it simply records that the consecration of Guṇākara Mahāvihāra was completed.

Second, the inscription does not mention that King Pratāpa Malla was invited by Guṇajyoti to the consecration ceremony of Harāhara[1]Lokeśvara, it merely mentions that the events recorded in the inscription took place in the kingdom ruled (‘lit. concurred,vijayarājye’) by King Pratāpa Malla.
It is a common feature to mention the reigning king in the inscriptions.
Furthermore, other inscriptions and objects installed in thebāhāḥare dated after Guṇajyoti’s NS 788 inscription.
For example, thetoraṇacrowning the main entrance dates from 1673 CE (NS 793),[2]and the one above thekvāḥpāḥdyaḥ’sdoor is from 1676 CE (NS 796).

[3]APrajñāpāramitāmanuscript copied in NS 798 (1678 CE) during the reign of King Bhūpatīndra Malla of Bhaktapur is kept in thebāhāḥ, which is recited during the Guṃlā ‘Kārtika’ month (cf.A. Vajrācārya, VS 2071, 31).

In 1699 CE (NS 819), Parikhadeva installed his own statue, flanked by his two wives, Vidhyādharī and Dhavati, in front of the principal deity of the bāhāḥ (kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ), making himself the Vajrasattva.
Akṣobhya was consecrated in the sanctum as thebāhāḥ’sprincipal deity (kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ).
They were destroyed during a botched maintenance effort two decades ago which was carried out without any archaeological investigation.

Between 1996 CE and 2003 CE, thebāhāḥwas restored with technical support from the Kathmandu Valley Preservation Trust and funding provided by the International Union for the Conservation of Nature and the German Foreign Office.
The courtyard building is relatively intact, preserved with all its original doors, windows, and four exceptionally artistic tympanums, two of them bearing dates (CE 1673 and CE 1676).

Unfortunately, many of its roof struts have been lost and many of the stone sculptures displayed in the courtyard are severely damaged and have been patched with an unknown material, possibly a cement compound.

Historic photographs (Pruscha, ca. 1973, Locke, ca. 1984, Klimek, 2003) reveal a number of changes: the donor figure and his two wives, previously free-standing, received a new enclosure; two small stonecaityasnow flank the donor figures; a historic pillar with a lion was added, and the Lokeśvara statue was moved and enclosed in a small stone shrine.
The two main stone inscriptions flanking the door of thekvāpaḥdyaḥcannot be seen in Pruscha's photograph.

A miniature stone temple (Mañjuśrīdegaḥ KAT0160-016), which used to stand in front of the main gate, was moved to thebāhāḥ'scourtyard in 1970 CE (NS 1090) during the widening of the road from Jamal to Jyāthā.
Since many of them have moved away, the responsibility for the daily rituals now rests on others who live nearby.
Kuci Bihāra, built in 1354 CE and located in the village of Kuci, is a rectangular stone reservoir with three small arched passages leading inside the reservoir's small room.
Other two arches are on the south-east and north-west sides of the building.
An inscription in Nāgarī script is found above the lintel of the north-eastern door.
Some restoration work done around 2017 CE resulted in the misplacement of a stone block containing the end of the inscription, which is now up-side-down on the north-western side of the building.
The inscription records a dedication in the year ŚS 1276 (1354CE) by Devavarmā, the Great Minister (mahāmātya) of King Pṛthvīmalla.
Devavarmā is the same individual who constructed a large reservoir in Dullu the same year.
The monument and its inscription were first mentioned by Yogi Naraharinath in 1956 CE (Naraharinath 1956: 45), and Prayag Raj Sharma in 1972 CE (Sharma 1972: 28).
A new fountain was installed to the north-east of this mediaeval monument in 2017 CE.
The Satyanārāyaṇa temple lies to the south of the path reached after descending a flight of stairs to the east of the raised platform bearing the Aṃśuvarmā inscription in Hãḍīgāũ.
The lower right hand displays the boon-granting gesture (varadamudrā) while holding a lotus seed (padmavīja).
Regmī (VS 2030, p. 130) suggests this statue might depict Vedavyāsa instead of Viṣṇu.
Anuparama Gupta, a prominent figure in the Licchavi administration, erected this column in honor of Dvaipāyana Vyāsa.
A human-like Garuḍa statues are customarily erected in front of Viṣṇu statues in Nepal.
These statues often resemble the face of the devotee sponsoring the statue (G. Vajrācārya VS 2033, p. 127).
Possibly, Anuparama Gupta established this statue to reflect his own likeness (Slusser 2005, p. 43).
No explicit records have been found regarding the construction of this temple or the installation of the Viṣṇu statue within.
Anuparama Gupta, a powerful figure during the Licchavi period, erected a Garuḍa column in front of the temple and inscribed verses dedicated to Dvaipāyana Vyāsa.
This inscription, with its mature writing style and philosophical content, is considered of high quality.

While the inscription lacks a specific date or the name of the reigning king, based on its script, it is attributed to the reign of Vasantadeva, who succeeded Mānadeva (D. Vajrācārya VS 2030, pp. 158).

As Anuparama Gupta's wife, Ābhirī Gominī, installed the Anuparameśvara Śivaliṅga at Paśupati in 540 CE (ŚS 462) (D. Vajrācārya VS 2030, pp. 170-171), it can be inferred that Anuparama Gupta died around that time.
Therefore, the Garuḍa column in front of the Satyanārāyaṇa temple must predate 540 CE.

Although some scholars (Slusser 1982, Vol. 2, plate 381) suggest that Anuparama Gupta himself installed the Viṣṇu statue around the mid-6th century CE, a definitive conclusion cannot be reached without more concrete evidence.

While no king named Jīva Gupta is found in Nepali history, it was Jiṣṇu Gupta, a powerful figure who issued his own coins, was referred to as Jīva Gupta in the chronicle (J. Regmī VS 2053, p. 153, 167).
Anuparama Gupta, who erected a stone pillar with a eulogy to Dvaipāyana Vyāsa in front of the temple, was Jiṣṇu Gupta's great-grandfather.
After consolidating his power, Jiṣṇu Gupta possibly renovated the temple and gilded its roof.
The oldest inscription found within the temple's sanctum dates to 1545 CE (NS 665).
This inscription records the installation of an Umāmaheśvara statue by Kesarāma, Jayakīta Bhāro, Bhārasiṃṅa Bhāro, and others during the reign of King Narendra Malla.

The inscription on thejaḥdhuṃstates that Priyavarmana installed the water tank at Andigrāma on the 5th of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha in 750 CE (Mānadeva Era 174) (D. Vajrācārya VS 2053, p. 600-iii).
The inscription confirms that the current name of Hā̃ḍīgāũ originated from Andigrāma.

In 2021 CE, Durham University in the UK, in partnership with the Department of Archaeology, conducted a Ground Penetrating Radar (GPR) survey primarily focusing on the western and southern areas within the temple courtyard.
These remains could be the scattered remnants of walls collapsed in an earthquake.

Positioned to the east of the Jagadīśvara Mandira (PPK1938) on the eastern side of the primary path leading to the Gorakhanātha temple, thisśivālaya, or the abode of Śiva, is built from stone on two plinth levels, crowned with a bell-shaped roof but its metallic finial has already been stolen.

text: The donor of the temple is a subject of confusion, with G. Ṭaṇḍana (VS 2053, p.349) claiming joint construction by Jayakṛṣṇa Kũvara and Khaḍga Bahādura Kũvara, while Michaels and Tandon (2017, p.106) attribute it solely to Jayakṛṣṇa Kũvara, the younger brother of Rāmakṛṣṇa Kũvara.
Both brothers were tasked with building an ammunition building in the midwestern district of Pyūṭhāna, where Jayakṛṣṇa passed away in 1788 CE (VS 1845) (B. Bhaṇḍārī VS 2071, p.17).
Given Jayakṛṣṇa's demise 60 years prior to the temple's construction, it is likely that Khaḍga Bahādura Kũvara commissioned the temple's construction.
A decade after the construction of Indreśvara temple, Khaḍga Bahādura offered a bell to the temple along with another Śiva temple, Jagadīśvara, in 1858 CE (VS 1915).
He seems to have offered one bell for two temples.
The 2015 earthquakes left cracks on the temple walls that were restored by the Pashupati Area Development Trust in 2021 CE (VS 2078).
In addition, a metaltoraṇais installed right above it.

The originalsataḥwas built by Viṣṇu Siṃha In 1813 CE (VS 1870).
Details are recorded in the inventory published by Kāṭhamādauṃ Upatyakā Nagara Vikāsa Yoganā (VS 2039, p. 166).

According to an inscription dated 1957-58 CE (VS 2013), now lost, thesataḥstands out as an important site among the extensiveghāṭassituated between the confluences of the Viṣṇumatī and Ṭukucā rivers with the Bagmati.
Locals also mentioned that there used to be an inscription and two statues at the site, however, the current residents claim ignorance about their whereabouts (resident, Kũvara, female, age 63).

Historical records, such as the Bhāṣā Vaṃśāvalī, note that during the reign of King Bhupālendra Malla of Kantipura in 1716 CE (NS 836), many people afflicted by a pandemic sought their final refuge at Pacalī Ghāṭa and Viṣṇumatī Ghāṭa (Bhāṣā Vamśāvalī, part 2, 102-103).
On Ṛṣipañcamī, women used to bath here, change their clothes in thesataḥ, and light a bonfire.
It is located inside an L-shaped courtyard which can be accessed through a narrow underpass by a six storied building.
The main monument building is a small structure attached to a residential building to the west.
The main sanctum is constructed from timber and exhibits intricately carved door jambs and atoraṇa thā(the place fortoraṇa).
Behind the monument, there is a four-storey residential building with a projecting carved open window at the center flanked by two vertical lattice windows on either sides on the first floor.
Bhājudhana Śākya was a member of thesaṅghaof Oku Bāhāḥ and he established thisbāhāḥwith help of his elder brother Bhīmarāja and other family members.
He established thisvihārausing the money he earned from his business.
In NS 1027 (1907 CE), Bhājudhana established adharmadhātujinālaya caityain the courtyard.

Four Bhīmasenas are considered to be the major Bhīmasena Temples of Lalitpur, namely, Juju Bhindyaḥ of Mangalbazar (the King's Bhīmasena), Puṃ Bhindyaḥ of Sundhara (the artists' Bhīmasena), Kumhāḥ Bhindyaḥ of Cyāsal (a Bhīmasena established by potters), and Chāya Bāhāḥ Bhindyaḥ of Chāḥbāhāla.

This temple is known by various names; some refer to it as Dhvākhā Bhindya due to its proximity to the gate of Chāya Bāhāḥ, whilst others know it as Dyaḥ Bhindyaḥ due to the fact that it was established by Dyaḥ Brahmū (Devabrāhmaṇa) Gayo Juju.
According to popular belief, Tantric Gayo Juju (Yogendrānanda Rājopadhyāya) of Sulim Ṭola donated funds for the initial construction of this temple.
It is said that after Gayo Juju established Caṇḍeśvarī Mandira (LAL0770) in Pimbahal Ṭola, Bhīmasena was established in Chāḥbahāla to guard her.
The inscription placed inside the sanctum claims that a group of nine people fixed threetoraṇasabove the three holes of the sanctum in the year NS 845 (1725 CE).
The temple was renovated in 1931 and reconstructed in 2001.
It was last organised here in VS 2075; the next ceremony will therefore be held in VS 2085.
The Gaṇeśa Temple, located in the Ikhālakhu Ṭola of Patan, is a south-facingśikhara-style temple and is built in stone.
Placed in the western niche are two stone inscriptions.
Built into the the four sides of the temple are four small niches with a female deity and akīrtimukhatoraṇa.

The vase of plenty (kalaśa) with the emerging gem on an amalaka ring is in turn supported by a bell-shaped base with amalaka ring” (Gutschow2011 vol. II: 552)The inscription attached to the temple informs that the temple was constructed in 1726 by Balabhadra Bhāro.
It collapsed during the earthquake of 1934 and was renovated in 1942.
Gaṅgādevī, one of the spouses of Rāṇā Prime Minister Jaṅga Bahādura, commissioned the construction of this Śiva temple in 1863 CE (VS 1920).
Notably, the primary western entrance houses an inscription beneath itstoraṇa, offering insights into the temple's construction.
Regrettably, the statues of Sūrya, Gaṇeśa, Durgā, and Viṣṇu enshrined within the inner sanctum walls, following the Śiva Pāñcāyana concept, have all been stolen.
Prime Minister Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā's wife Gaṅgādevī undertook the construction of the temple in 1863 CE (VS 1920), naming it in honor of herself.

She hailed from Cuttack, India, and entered into a formal marriage with Jaṅga Bahādura during his brief stay in Benares while returning from leading a troop to Lucknow to suppress the Sepoy Mutiny of 1857 CE.
He brought her to Kathmandu, bestowing upon her the title of Mahārānī (P. Rāṇā VS 2059, p. 118).
It remains uncertain whether she had any children, but historical records indicate her passing in 1864 CE (VS 1921) (P. Rāṇā VS 2059, p.190).
Remarkably, she passed away just a year after establishing the temple named in her honor.
No inscription nor religious markers could be found at the site.
The sanctums are currently empty and the top slabs of some of theśikharaswere moved, probably intentionnaly.
Despite these lacunae, it is possible to estimate that the monuments were erected around the 14th-15th century.
Furthermore, the construction ofśikharatemples in the Karnali region seems to have stopped before the 16th century, which narrows the dating of this type of plan down to the 14th-15th century.
The influence of Nepali over the years has led to the term Bhelu being replaced by Dhāmī, a Nepali term for an oracle medium, and his residence as Dhāmī Ghara.
The balconied tower (phucā) atop the roof signifies the presence of a divinity within the building.
The initial construction of this architecturally grand building was completed only during the early Śāha period.
The earliest record, one of the copper-plate inscriptions from the Bhairavī temple (NWK0040), mentioning the term "Bheru or Bhelu" dates back to 1643 CE (NS 763).

The inscription from the Pratap Malla era does not clarify whether a residence for Bhelu was already established here, but it does confirm the existence of the Bhelu tradition at the time (D. Vajrācārya and Ṭ. Śreṣṭha VS 2032, second part, p. 8).
citations: (D. Vajrācārya and Ṭ. Śreṣṭha VS 2032, second part, p. 8)

text: Meanwhile, another inscription from 1792 CE (NS 913) found at the Bhairavī temple reports the construction of a house by the then Bhelu Kṛṣṇa and Bhulu Sūryalakṣmī.
The inscription further instructs their eldest son and daughter-in-law, who are the inheritors of the Bhelu and Bhulu titles, to "reside in this house and maintain it".
This suggests that the inscription refers to the construction of the Dhāmī Ghara (D. Vajrācārya and Ṭ. Śreṣṭha VS 2032, second part, pp. 36-37).
