text: Despite having a history of over two centuries, the building's lack of documentation leaves its renovation history unknown.

In 1988-89 CE (VS 2044/45), the building was rebuilt from the ground up with new bricks while reusing the historic doors and windows under the supervision of the Department of Archaeology (K. Joshi VS 2050, p. 16).

The roof tower of the building collapsed in the 2015 CE earthquakes and was rebuilt with new materials, and thejhĩgaṭīcover of the entire roof was renewed by the Department of Archaeology in 2023 CE (VS 2080).
However, this tradition, along with the changing social environment, is no longer practiced as of April 2024 CE.

The presence of Licchavi artifacts in the area suggests that the confluence of the Triśūlī and Tādī rivers was already a holy site during the Licchavi period (R. Kũvara & B. Jñavālī VS 2067, p. 25).
In 1752 CE (ŚS 1674), Bhānu Aryāla, the royal astrologer of the Gorkha King Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa Śāha, constructed the temple.
He is known to have accompanied the king to Benares and suggested the conquest of the valley then known as the Nepal valley (B. Ācārya VS 2061, pp. 95, 124, 125, 547).
A Sanskrit inscription embedded in the southern wall of the temple records its construction by Aryāla.

After Aryāla built this temple on the side that then fell under the Gorkha kingdom, Raṇadyota Śāha later built Raṇabhuvaneśvara Mandira (NWK0610), and Kharidāra Muktinātha Pauḍela established Dharmamukteśvara in the vicinity.
Currently (as of June 2024 CE), the temple is a concrete structure with corrugated metal sheets on its roof, crowned with a finial.
The present structure doesn’t appear to date back to 1752 CE, suggesting the temple must have undergone reconstruction(s) in the past.

According to Nirañjanamāna Siṃha Basnyāta, a descendants of Abhimāna Siṃha, the Gaṇeśa shrine was established by Abhimāna Siṃha at the time when he commissioned the construction of the Palṭana Ghara (N. Basnyat2019, p. 141).

An inscription at Palṭana Ghara designates the area as "the place where Lord Gaṇeśa resides merrily by eliminating obstacles," yet it omits any reference to the establishment of a Gaṇeśa statue (B. BasnyātaVS 2010, p. 6).

Local accounts suggest that the shrine initially existed as a smallphalcā-like building with a traditional tile roof but underwent a transformation into a brick and concrete structure during the 1980s.
According to the locals, this figure contains an inscription.
Unfortunately, the inscription is no longer visible.
After the relocation of the school, thesataḥnow accommodates ‘Śrī Gaṇeśa Dhũllā Bhajana Maṇḍala’, a localbhajanaensemble.
There is no inscription that records the construction of this Shrine.

A Buddhist scripture namedMaṇiśailaMahāvadānamentions: In 1300 BC (Kaligata Era 1801), when Jogadeva Vajrācārya founded the town of Sankhu in the shape of aśaṅkha(conch shell) by assimilating seven villages as per the instruction of Vajrayoginī, he had divided the town into eightṭolas and constructed a palace at the centre, along with the shrines ofaṣṭamātṛkā(Eight Mother Goddesses), ninebāhāḥs, and four gates at four cardinal directions (V. Vajrācārya1119, p. 29-33).
With two Licchavicaityas established at its premises, the earliest historical reference to Dhvākhā Bāhāḥ is found in a palm-leaf document from 1580 CE (NS 701).
The statues installed on one of the twocaityasare said to belong to the 7thcentury (Kramrisch1964, p.27-29).
It contained Buddhist verses inscribed in the script used during the reign of King Narendradeva (r. 643-679 CE).
The inscription is no longer available at the site.
No historical records are available to date the initial construction of the Bāhāḥ.
Hence, this monastic building was called Dhvākhā Bāhāḥ (R. Vajrācārya & V. Vajrācārya1103, p.79).

Likewise, it is also said that a large gate was constructed to enter the Bāhāḥ premises to welcome King Pratāpa Malla, who was due to attend theSamyakMahādānaceremony hosted by Jñānajyoti Vajrācārya in 1656 CE (NS 777).
However, as mentioned above, the name Dhvākhā Bāhāḥ was already in use in a palm-leaf document from 1580 CE (NS 701), proving the statement to be false.

Regarding the Sanskrit name of the Bāhāḥ, it is said that it was constructed with the gold accumulated from the trade in Tibet and was, therefore, named Hiraṇyākara Mahāvihāra, as ‘hiraṇya’is a Sanskrit term to mean ‘gold’.
Before the reconstruction in 2005 CE (VS 2062), the Bāhāḥ used to be a three-story building with corrugated metal sheets laid on the roof without a finial.
The Bāhāḥ was reconstructed with the financial help from the Kathmandu Metropolitan City Office bearing a major portion of expenses.
A finial was also installed after the reconstruction.
There are altogether sixty-five Vajrācārya members at the Bāhāḥ, who are said to have moved from Sankhu.
The neoclassical arcadedsataḥwas built by Deva Śamśera Rānā in 1877 CE.
It is one of the threesataḥsbuilt around the Jalavināyaka Mandira giving the temple complex its distinctive square-shape (Gutschow2011, 458).
Thesataḥreplaces an earlier structure that is documented in Henry Ambrose Oldfield’s watercolor from 1854 CE.
But there is a dearth of concrete evidence about its initial construction.

An inscription in the Jalavināyaka Mandira from 1787 CE (NS 907) mentions an individual named Matsyendra Siṃha Bhāro from Aki Bāhāḥ built asataḥto please Jalavināyaka and installed statues of Umāmaheśvara and Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa.
It also records his donation of fourropaniland and a field.
As the inscription is plastered on a reconstructed wall, it is not clear to which which structures it refers to.

The identification is made more difficult because of the lack of aguṭhīassociated with Aki Bāhāḥ, and none of the existingsataḥshas any statues of deities such as Umāmaheśvara or Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa established inside.
It is possible that the inscription relates to the older existing structures as seen in Oldfield’s sketches.
The main monument in Ikhā Bāhāḥ Nani is a shrine of the esoteric deity (āgãchẽ) ithat lies to the south of residential buildings sorrounding th courtyard of the Bāhāḥ.
This shrine has been reconstructed as a RCC structure, and the only remaining original elements are the main door and two blind windows on either side (with akalaśa) on the ground floor.
Thegod-house(āgãchẽ) is also a residential building and contains an image of Bhagavatī in the first floor.
The building was renovated in 2019 and has four storeys.
A shrine with seven aniconic stones and an image of Kumārī in the middle is also in the vicinity of the building.
John Locke comments on the site: “The present shrine of Ikhā Bāhāḥ is simply a room on the ground floor of a very ordinary building of two storeys.
The Present shrine dates from a renovation after the earthquake of A. D. 1934.
According to an inscription at the site the courtyard was paved in N. S. 770 by one Svakarjū Vajrācārya.” (Locke1985, 241).
Although local tradition credits its construction to Gaṃgā Mahārānī, there are no definitive historical records to verify this claim.
Since 1964 CE (VS 2021), the ground floors of some surrounding buildings have been repurposed for use by a school.
Notably, the upper floor of the Taleju temple stores historical weaponry from past eras (Ś. Śreṣṭha VS 2080, p. 14).
According to popular legend, Gaṃgā Mahārānī—originally from Thimi—probably selected this site to establish her royal seat, including the palace and the Taleju courtyard.
Oral traditions mention a grand seven-story palace that once stood here but was reportedly destroyed in the earthquakes of 1833 (Ś. Śreṣṭha VS 2080, p. 10).
An inscription from 1827 CE (NS 947) can be found on a Nārāyaṇa statue near the entrance to the Taleju courtyard, though most of the text is now illegible.
Additionally, a bell offered to the deity in 1848 CE (VS 1905) hangs from a bell-stand within the courtyard.
The school was originally established in 1964 CE (VS 2021) as the “Thimi Adult Coaching Class” in Siddhikālī Dyaḥchẽ, the god-house dedicated to Siddhikālī.
It was relocated to the palace complex in 1965 CE (VS 2022) (Ś. Śreṣṭha VS 2080, p. 33; Pant 2019, p. 122).
Later, in 1968 CE (VS 2025), the “Janapremi Secondary School”—previously operating from a private residence in Nigū Pukhū—was also moved to the Taleju courtyard.

In 2009 CE (VS 2066), the deteriorating main structure of the Taleju temple was restored through the efforts of the school’s teachers and with support from the Department of Archaeology (Ś. Śreṣṭha VS 2080, p. 33).
This is followed bycyākū bhvay(an eight-piece feast), reserved for specific caste groups such as the Pradhāna, Kāyaṣṭha, and Biśakhala from the palace area (Ś. Śreṣṭha VS 2080, p. 28).
A Śākya from Kvāḥ Bāhāḥ used the tree trunk to carve a statue of Mañjuśrī and constructed the temple where the tree once stood.
The original wooden statue was stolen around five decades ago.
Twośikharakuṭa caityashave been built in the courtyard, one in front of the temple (east) and the other one to the north of the temple.
A shrine to Śākyamuni Buddha has been erected to the south of the temple.
Three inscriptions are attached to the southern, western and northern walls.
The oldest inscription attests to the temple's renovation in 1724 CE.
Two inscriptions,  dated NS 845 and 857, mention to first invoke Mañjunātha before praying to Sarasvatī.
A document concerning land transfers, dated NS 833 (1713 CE), mentions Sarasvatī Nani (S.RājavaṃśīVS 2042, 21).
The temple was renovated in 2002.

In the southwest corner of this courtyard, a small wooden shrine (devala) built into a wall enshrines an image of Bhīmasena, from which the courtyard derives its name—Bhindyaḥcuka(lit. “the courtyard of Bhīma”).
Gutschow (1997, p. 215) classifies it within theŚikharkūṭastyle, a form that emerged in the late medieval period and continued to be constructed through the Rana period.
Architecturally, the caitya rests on a single square base constructed entirely of stone.
During theāratiritual instituted by King Śrīnivāsa Malla, devotees continue to chant “Viriñcinārāyaṇa namo namaḥ” while offering light toBuṅgadyaḥ(J. Mānandhara VS 2046, p. 116).
Hence, the installation ofGaruḍamay symbolize this shared identity ofPadmapāṇias bothLokeshvaraandNārāyaṇa.
Judging by the style of the stone carvings used in thecaitya, it appears to have been built in the early Śāha period; however, in the absence of an inscription, this cannot be stated with certainty.

Theharmikāof the caitya is adorned with a gilded metal plate (pātā) bearing an inscription that reads: “This caitya was established by the family of Kulanārā (Kula Nārāyaṇa) Citrākāra in 1899 CE (VS 1956).” The inscription, however, is ambiguous as to whether it commemorates the construction of the entire monument or merely the upper gilded portion.
Later, in 1935 CE (NS 1055), Kṛṣṇabahādur Citrākāra carried out the gilding of the upperharmikā.
This independentbāhāḥwas established by Kṛṣṇavīra Prajāpati (Tuisiṃ Āḥju) and is sometimes also referred to as anani.
The original Akṣobhya was stolen and replaced with a new one.

Hona Bāhāḥ is nestled between residential buildings on the west and east, two doors lead to a small courtyard to its south and the main facade faces an rectangular courtyard with a row of residential buildings.
A smallpañcāvalicaityawas established in front of the main sanctum in 1895 CE (NS 1015).
There are no records when thebāhāḥwas built, however, it is likely that it was established at the same time as thecaitya.
Hona Bāhāḥ was reconstructed with different bricks and types of mortar: the sanctum was rebuilt indacīapāusing cement mortar while the other walls consist ofmāapā,dacīapāanddesiapāin mud mortar.
The origins of Keśavanārāyaṇa Coka are shrouded in mystery but it is believed that the palace building replaced an earlier monastery.

The monastery was relocated to Hakha Bāhāḥ (LAL0390) and this move is still commemorated every year when an image of Akṣobhya Buddha is placed in a copper pot of water in front of the palace's golden door.
The courtyard building was probably established by Siddhinarasiṃha Malla as Caukoṭa in 1627, reshaped in 1674 and rebuilt again in 1734 by Vishnu Malla as a fort with four towers.
The three-story building has undergone many renovations and alterations over the past centuries with the upper story and roofs rebuilt after the 1934 earthquake and again in the late 1980s and 1990s.
Today, only two of the towers remain, both rebuilt after they were seriously damaged in the 1934 earthquake.
The east-wing collapsed in 1934 and was haphazardly rebuilt with recycled materials.
It was again rebuilt in the early 1990s as a partly modern building in a hybrid style employing both Malla and Rana era design elements.
The golden door is surmounted with a gilttoraṇawhichwas offered by Jaṅga Bahādura in 1854.
A statue of Śani is installed on top of the west wing roof.
Following the end of Malla rule in 1768, the building was used for various administrative purposes and in the 1950s was adapted to house a school.
From 1984-1997 the palace was renovated from ground up and converted into the Patan Museum with funds provided by the Austrian and Nepali Governments.
In 1994, the north-east wing was restored in-situ and today it houses temporary exhibition galleries and guest studios.
It was left in a derelict and ruinuous state after its collapdse in 1987 CE.
After the local level election in 2017 CE, reconstruction and renovation of historical and heritage structures have increased.
Lalitpur Municipality allocated Ten Lakh rupees to reconstruct Ilachen Phalca in 2019 CE.
There is no inscriptive evidence that points to its initial construction.
Of two inscriptions in the Phalcā, the oldest one from 1743 CE (NS 863) mentions renovation by an individual named Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa Amātya.

With the inscription being placed in the niche (gavākṣa) where a statue of Gaṇeśa has been consecrated, it might well be that the renovation was carried out only on thegavākṣa- but likewise it could also have been the entire Phalcā.
In medieval times, there are numerous examples of these families actively engaging in the construction of temples and arcaded platforms.
The renoation acivities mentioned from 1743 CE indicate that Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa Amātya clan might be descendent of the person who funded the construction of the Phalcā.
There is another inscription from 1779 CE (Ns 899) in second niche (gavākṣa)on the Phalcā, mentioning the consecration of a statue in thatgavākṣa.
The name of the deity is not mentioned in the inscription.
After its reconstruction, local community members have added a notice board on the eastern wall and use it as a communal information centre.
This three-bayedphalcāwasdonated in 1665 and isowned by the Maharjans of the Karuṇāmaya Guṭhī.
Cvalcā Phalcā was dismantled in 1995 and reconstructed with funds from GTZ/udle.
The new structure included a new inscription and incorporated its 19th-century columns and capitals.
It was demolished and reconstructed once again in 2019 due to substantial damage from the 2015 earthquakes.
This confluence is regarded as sacred and is traditionally called Śacītīrtha (S. Tāmrākāra VS 2066, p. 16).
Toranas were once installed above all four doorways, though those above the northern main door and the eastern entrance are now missing.
Other aniconic stones representing Mātṛkās, Bhairava, and two fragmentary images are also installed.
Only a person endowed with thirty-two auspicious marks is believed to perceive the water as flowing milk (Toffin 2021, p. 92).
According to local tradition, the temple—originally apīṭha—was constructed without formal foundations, followingtāntrikaprinciples and under the protective power of Vāsukī Nāga.

The southeastern area of the temple is used for the funerary rites of the Newar community of Panauti, while the eastern area is designated for the Dyaḥlā (Podes), followed by the Khadgīs, and further east for the Kapālīs (S. Lākoju VS 2071, p. 119).

No early documentation records its original establishment, but an image bearing an inscription dated 1631 CE (NS 751) installed before the temple demonstrates that thepīṭhaexisted in the early medieval period.
According to this inscription, Rāmeśvara of Kvāchẽ Ṭola, Panauti, dedicated images of his parents (PNT0050-008) at the site.
A weathered stone inscription in early-medieval Nepal script inside thegarbhagṛhafurther supports the antiquity of thepīṭha.

The transformation of the open-air shrine into a built temple occurred in 1716 CE (NS 836), when Viśvalakṣmīdevī, mother of King Raṇajita Malla and queen of King Bhūpatīndra Malla of Bhaktapur, commissioned the construction of the present structure with its gilt finial.
She endowed the temple with twentyropanīsof land to support ritual activities, including obligatory worship at the Brahmāyaṇī and Indreśvara temples on nineth of bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha.
The sacrificial goat offered during the ritual was to be distributed asprasādato the king, the princes, and the queen mother.
Five years later, in 1721 CE (NS 841), Viśvalakṣmīdevī, together with King Raṇajita Malla, endowed an additional fourteenropanīsof land.
Later, in 1830 CE (NS 950), five brothers—Dhana, Hāku, Kṛṣṇa, Siri, and Sukula—installed three toranas inside the temple.
Over time, the structure deteriorated, and the lowest roof collapsed completely.
A major renovation was completed in late September 1982, funded 25% by the Government of Nepal and 75% by the Government of France (Pradhan 1984, pp. 2–3).

After crossing the bridge, she is taken into the temple, where a buffalo sacrifice and atāntrikafire ritual are performed. 14th of bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha is regarded as the main day of the festival, when devotees visit the temple to offer worship and animal sacrifices.
Yatkhā Bāhāḥ (KAT1050) is encircled by private residential buildings.
Dhanasiṃ Bāhāḥ is actually a private shrine, built on the ground floor passage of one of these private houses, located in the southeast corner of the courtyard.
This is probably a rarebāhāḥwhere itskvāḥpāḥdyaḥ(main deity) has been consecrated on the passage of a private house.
A stone slab inscription is embedded on the wall to the west and a Licchavi-style stonecaityais installed in the centre of the shrine room.
The inscription records that a merchant named Dhanasiṃha Tāmrākāra established thisbāhāḥin 1862 CE (NS 982) in his own house and he offered this house to the Svayaṃbhū Caitya and Vajrayogīnī.
He also donated some cash to aguṭhīassociated with the Svayaṃbhū Caitya (cf.H. ŚākyaNS 1099, 32-33 andLocke1985, 295).
Its Sanskrit name, Samantabhadra Vihāra, comes from the name of the main deity, Samantabhadra, consecrated in the sanctum.
According toH. Śākya(NS 1099, 39-40), Dhanasiṃha, founder of thisbāhāḥhad performed a fire sacrifice,daśāṃśahoma, andpañcopacārapūjāin the Svayambhū Caitya in 1862 CE (NS 982).
Moreover, he invited the Kumārī of Kathmandu to his private house and venerated her by celebrating a procession,mahāsindūrajātrāin 1863 CE (NS 983).
Dhanasiṃ, who had generously contributed to the renovation of the Svayaṃbhū Caitya, died before the repairs were completed.
Thus, his son, Harṣaratna Tāmrākāra, completed this task and the consecration ceremonies were performed in NS 987, i.e. 1867 CE (cf.Locke1985, 295).
Until 2000 CE, the descendants of Dhanasiṃha used to perform the daily rituals.
After they moved elsewhere from this house, this tradition has come to an end.
Thisbāhāḥ, documented in historical records since 1576 CE (NS 696), was renovated by Daṇḍapāṇi Vajrācārya in 1688 CE (NS 808).
The traditional multi-tiered main structure (kvāḥpāḥchẽ) of thebāhāḥfaces west and is a three-story building roofed with traditional tiles.
As of March 2025, thebāhāḥis undergoing reconstruction, and its finial remains to be installed.
Due to ongoing reconstruction, thetoraṇahas been temporarily placed inside the sanctum, which enshrines thebāhāḥ’s principal deity (kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ), a stone statue of Akṣobhya.
The Padmasambhava statue was discovered in a field north of thekvāḥpāḥchẽaround 1950 CE (VS 2007) (bāhāḥmember, Vajrācārya, male, age 73).
No historical records have been found regarding the construction of thisbāhāḥ.
The earliest known reference to thebāhāḥcomes from a copper plate inscription dated 1576 CE (NS 696).
The inscription documents an invitation sent by Jitāja Bhāro, a Tulādhara from Asana, Kathmandu, to the Dipaṅkara Buddha statue of Thimi’s Digu Bāhāḥ.
However, the inscription does not clarify whether both of thebāhāḥ’s two Dipaṅkara statues were invited or just one.
Among the two Dipaṅkara statues, the taller one was installed in 1564 CE (NS 684), and the shorter one in 1569 CE (NS 689) (B. Vajrācārya 1124, p. 85).
Unfortunately, this copper plate inscription was not located during the fieldwork, and current members of thebāhāḥhave also stated that they are unaware of its existence.
In 1688 CE (NS 808), during the reign of King Jitāmitra Malla, Daṇḍapāṇi Vajrācārya undertook a major renovation of thekvāḥpāḥchẽ.
His contributions included installing a gilded parasol on the finial and erecting a pillar bearing his own statue.
His wife Ratnamaṇi, son Manamohanasiṃ Vajrācārya, and other family members also supported the renovation efforts.
In 1687 CE (NS 807), he was listed among those entrusted with collecting taxes from Thimi to fund the wedding of Prince Bhūpatīndra Malla, the king’s son (C. Vajrācārya VS 2053, p. 437).
Furthermore, a 1706 CE (NS 826) palm-leaf document recording a land sale in Thimi mentions a Vajrācārya named Daṇḍapāṇi as a witness (Ś. Rājavaṃśī VS 2040, p. 13), likely the same individual.
Later, in 1738 CE (NS 858), Rachamāvati—along with her son Tadhika, daughter-in-law Ranhāvati, and other family members—donated a woodentoraṇato adorn the entrance of the sanctum.
Thebāhāḥsuffered significant damage in the 2015 earthquakes, and reconstruction efforts are currently underway.

Some displaced members remained in Thimi despite facing discrimination, while others relocated to Suntāgāṃ near Kathmandu's Naradevī area (Locke 1985, p. 460; B. Vajrācārya 1124, p. 86; D. Vajrācārya NS 1124, p. 15).

A local women’s group recites the Nāmasaṅgīti verses on auspicious days and the holy month of Guṃlā here at the Phalcā constructed during the Śāha period.
As the Phalcā is constructed next to the Dabū, it is named Dabū Phalcā.
A Licchavicaityais established west of the Phalcā.
The statues of Buddhas on the niche on all four sides of the Caitya appear to have been installed later.
There is a badly-damaged inscription here that probably records the initial construction of the Phalcā.
But as many letters of the inscription are unreadable, it is unclear when the Phalcā was constructed.
The script and language of the inscription suggest that the Phalcā was constructed during the Śāha period.
There is a mention of ‘deceased’ in the inscription, which suggests that Putalināni, Bhājudeva, Jayalachimi, Lādhāmuni, and Gyānavira constructed the Phalcā in memory of a deceased family member.
The chariot festival of Buṅgadyaḥ could not take place in the usual manner in 2020 CE due to the Covid-19 pandemic.
The statue of Buṅgadyaḥ was supposed to be accessioned to the chariot on April 24, 2020, but the chariot was not constructed due to the pandemic.

The committee handed over the responsibility to a group of local women named Śrī Karuṇāmaya Misā Pucaḥ after the statue of Buṅgadyaḥ was taken from the Phalcā to be accessioned to the chariot in 2020 CE.
The group also installed a statue of Nāmasaṅgīti at the Phalcā in 2020 CE.
Peering through the empty niche, one can discern a portion of anothercaitya, revealing that the current structure was built over an older one.
Although thetoraṇawas once covered with a brass sheet, the brass cover has been stolen.
Previously housed in the Bhairava shrine southwest of thecaitya, the statue was relocated to the Ṣaḍakṣarī Lokeśvara shrine for security.
To shield Ṣaḍakṣarī Lokeśvara from the elements, artistic wooden pillars and a roof have been erected.
No historical records shed light on the establishment of thiscaityaand the Ṣaḍakṣarī Lokeśvara, apart from some local legends and references in later chronicles.
Locals claim that the statue of Ṣaḍakṣarī Lokeśvara is older than thecaitya, which was established during the Licchavi period.
According to historical accounts, Licchavi King Vṛṣadeva constructed a statue featuringpañcabuddhanear Godāvarī and established the country of Bandegāũ.
Subsequently, the four statues of Simbu (Svayambhū), Khāsti (Bauddha), Dhando (Chabahil), and Bandegāũ (Bāḍegāũ) gained prominence (N. Pauḍela VS 2020, p. 56).
While the chronicle mentions Vṛṣadeva building a statue, the reference to the fourcaityas suggests he actually built acaitya.
However, in contemporary understanding, the Namarā (Namobuddha) Caitya is often considered the fourthcaityain the group, replacing the Dhando Caitya.

TheDevamālāvaṃśāvalīstates that King Vṛṣadeva constructed a temple (caitya) withpañcabuddhanear Godāvarī in 286 BCE (Kali Samvat 2815) and founded a city with seven hundred houses (Yogī Naraharinātha VS 2013, pp. 101-102).
Among Newar Buddhists, there's a prevalent belief that Vṛṣadeva built the Bāḍegāũ Caitya.

The story posits that after relinquishing the throne to his younger brother Bālārcanadeva, Vṛṣadeva visited the holy confluence of Godāvarī, established acaityaat his resting place, named it Bandhagrāma, and settled the area (A. Vajrācārya NS 1099, p. 87).

An inscription from 733 CE (Mānadeva Samvat 157) found at Paśupatinātha refers to Vṛṣadeva as “sugataśāsanapakṣapātī,” meaning, "a follower of Buddhism," suggesting the possibility of his involvement in building the Bāḍegāũ Caitya (D. Vajrācārya VS 2030, p. 549).
While it is said that thecaityawas established during the Licchavi period, thecaityaand the Ṣaḍakṣarī Lokeśvara statue do not seem to be that old.
Only inscriptions from the late medieval period have been found in thecaityacourtyard.
Among the inscriptions found in thecaitya, the earliest one is from 1679 CE (NS 799), during the reign of Śrīnivāsa Malla.
This inscription states thatPramānaViśvambhara Bhāro of Cākra Bāhāra, Lalitpur, had donated one and a halfropanīs of land to set up a trust for performing daily worship at the Bāḍegāũ Caitya.
Of the income from this land, 20pāthīs of the harvest were allocated for the priest and 10pāthīs for the deity's worship.

In 1684 CE (NS 805), Jayadeva Vajrācārya, Dharaṃsiṅa Vajrācārya, Gopirāma Bhābo, and other members of the “Purṇimā Sevā Guthi” jointly established a pair of stone lions on either side of Ṣaḍakṣarī Lokeśvara.

Another inscription from 1709 CE (NS 829) mentions that Devamuni of Bāḍegāũ had donated one-third of a plot of land located in Dhvapagāma to set up a trust to fund a fire oblation in front of thecaityaon the full moon day of Māgha, along with a sacrifice of a duck to Gaṇeśa, and to perform asinhaḥpūjā(a worship involving vermillion powder) at the shrine of the esoteric deity.
Likewise, in 1941 CE (NS 1061), Bhimarāja Daṃgu covered thedharmadhātumaṇḍalain front of the Ṣaḍakṣarī Lokeśvara with copper sheets.
Around 1975 CE (VS 2032), thecaityaclad in metal sheets was covered to build a largercaityathat now exists (caretaker of thecaitya, Vajrācārya, male, age 88).
Currently (August 2024), with the financial assistance of the Godawari Municipality, the old zinc truss is being removed and a new truss is being installed, adopting traditional style.
Meanwhile, onJugaḥ, the 13th of the dark fortnight of Bhādra, a palanquin procession of Ṣaḍakṣarī Lokeśvara established in thecaityais taken out.
There, various items are offered in alms (pañcadāna) to Amitābha, the caretaker, and other members of the caretakers.

The Bālāgāũ Hiti was established in 1720 CE (NS 841) by a donor named Balabhadra Bhāro.
The statue of Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa bears an inscription, crediting Balabhadra Bhāro of the Solaṅkī (text: Suraṃki) dynasty constructing a stone water spout south of his hometown.

Members of the Solaṅkī dynasty first appeared in the Nepalese history in a manuscript copied in 1335 CE (NS 455), which confirms Jaitasiṃha, who ruled Pharpiṅa as an independent state, to belong the Solaṅkī dynasty (Regmi 1965, Vol 1, pp. 409-410).
They were originally from Gujarat, India and entered Nepal in search of a safe haven after Muslim invasions in India (Ṭ. Śreṣṭha VS 2078, p. 39).

It is yet impossible to say if this was their original orientation nor if they were originally installed in this place or moved around by farmers.
Memorial stone pillars were erected throughout the Karnali Basin from the 13th to the 17th century.
They are installed to honor the memory of deceased persons, mostly warriors (Andolfatto 2019: 105-119).

This Sataḥ, constructed to facilitate socio-religious activities at Māheśvarī Pīṭha, hosts various religious and cultural functions throughout the year.
However, the Sataḥ was dismantled in 2004 CE (VS 2069) and subsequently reconstructed in its present form.
Inside the Sataḥ are two inscriptions.
The first inscription from 1743 CE (NS 863) records the renovation of the Sataḥ's roof and the endowment of land for observing its anniversary ritual.
The other inscription from 1746 CE (NS 866) contains the offering of a golden pinnacle to the temple on the premises and the construction of the Phalcā during the reign of King Raṇajita Malla.

One of the two inscriptions seems to have been relocated to its current position from anotherphalcāwithin the premise of Māheśvarī Pīṭha.
It is unclear which of the two inscriptions was relocated, and locals have stated that these inscriptions have been in their current location for as long as they can remember.
Among the two inscriptions, the one dated to 1743 CE likely belonged to the three-bay phalcā.

There is no surviving inscription within thehiticomplex that provides information about its construction.
The site has long been associated with the Jāmanaḥ lineage of Thimi, and it is widely believed that an ancestor from this lineage built both thehitiand the adjacentphalchā.
It was built in Nepal Era 1025 (1905 CE) by Kanhasiṃ Jāma Śreṣṭha and his wife Nānīthakum, members of the same lineage.
In 2022 CE (VS 2078), the municipality allocated a budget for the simultaneous reconstruction of thephalchās,hiti, pond, and surrounding structures.

A co-financing solution was found in order to restore the building: In 2017, Lalitpur Metropolitan City provided 12 lākh rupees, the descendants of the founder donated some funds and locals contributed by running charity works.

In 1688 CE (NS 808), King Jitāmitra Malla commissioned the construction of theLāykū Lũ Hiti—also known asSunadhārāorThaṃthu Sunadhārā—within the northeastern courtyard of the Bhaktapur palace complex, an area known asLũhiti Cuka(Sunadhārā Coka).

The Hiti acquired the epithetThaṃthu Sunadhārābecause its surfaces were adorned with giltrepousséplates (L. Munaṃkarmī VS 2050, p. 22), while the goat-shaped design of its spout led locals to refer to it asDugucā Hiti(S. Jośī VS 2073, p. 331).
The construction of the Hiti continues a long-standing tradition ofsunadhārāsin Bhaktapur.

As early as the twelfth century, King Ānandadeva (r. 1147–1166 CE) had constructed a palace equipped with a nearbysunadhārā, although this earlier structure no longer survives (Vajrācārya & Malla 1985, folio 25A).
Later, in 1440 CE (NS 560), King Yakṣa Malla (r. 1428–1482 CE) erected theLũ Hiti(BKT0421) inTaumāḍhiṬola, which remains extant (Vajrācārya & Malla 1985, pp. 294–297; cf. BKT0421_I_001).

An inscription dated to the 3rd day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, 1688 CE (NS 808), records that King Jitāmitra Malla built this courtyard, its Hiti, pond, arched windows, and gilt images for his tutelary deity, Taleju Bhavānī.

The inscription also notes his construction of additional palace courtyards—Tuthacuka,Lakṣmīvilāsa Chowk,Dumāju Chowk, andKisigara Chowk(the elephant stable)—and stipulates that water used for Taleju’s daily worship must be drawn exclusively from this Hiti (L. Munaṃkarmī VS 2025, p. 45).
At the Hiti’s consecration, a pair of white geese were released intoNāga Pukhu.

Local tradition holds that the birds swam through the spout’s channel to the source pond,Mahādeva Pokharī, occasionally reappearing for two generations before disappearing altogether (L. Munaṃkarmī VS 2025, p. 46).
The Hiti was supplied by Jitāmitra’s royal canal (rajakulo), constructed a decade earlier in 1678 CE (NS 798).
This canal diverted water fromMahādeva Pokharīand other springs on Mahādeva Mountain, channeling it via Kharipāṭī to Bhaktapur’sBā̃sabārī, where a reservoir was built for purification purposes.
From there, water was distributed tohitisand agricultural fields throughout Bhaktapur, significantly improving irrigation and productivity (L. Munaṃkarmī VS 2050, pp. 19–20).
In 1683 CE (NS 803), a stone inscription was installed to regulate disputes concerning the canal (B. Pauḍela VS 2065, pp. 67–68); it is now preserved atLaykū Phalcā(BKT0094).

A few months after completing the Hiti, on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, 1688 CE (NS 808), Jitāmitra Malla endowed tenropānīsof farmland asguṭhīfor the Hiti’s maintenance and for the ritual worship of Taleju.
The endowment’s income was to support the annualVarṣavardhanapūjāperformed onAkṣaya Tṛtīyā(the 3rd day of the bright fortnight ofBaiśākha) and other festivals.
Witnesses were Ugra Malla (Jitāmitra’s brother), Bhūpatīndra Malla (his son), and Prime Minister Bhagirāma (Rāṣṭriya Abhilekhālaya VS 2080, pp. 64–66).
The Hiti remained functional until 1973 CE (VS 2030), when water still flowed abundantly and Taleju’s priests performed daily ablutions there.
With the gradual deterioration of the canal, however, the water supply ceased, and numerous decorative elements of the Hiti were stolen (Kashajoo VS 2071, p. 55).

As the ritual regulations required that water for Taleju’s worship come exclusively from the Hiti, a member of the Suvāla caste was assigned the arduous task of fetching water daily from the still-functioning segment of the canal—an effort that required over two hours each way (B. Pauḍela VS 2065, pp. 65–66).
When the canal finally failed, water was temporarily procured fromMahālakṣmī HitiinThālāchẽ(S. Khanāla VS 2068, p. 89).
Subsequently, piped water was introduced, which continues to be used as of July 2025 CE.
In 1933 CE (VS 1989), Prime Minister Juddha Śamśera erected an inscription in Bhaktapur during the establishment of new waterworks, recalling both the ancient canal and its subsequent repairs.
This inscription remains affixed atLālabaiṭhaka(BKT0082) (B. Pauḍela VS 2065, pp. 70–71).
In 1863 CE (VS 1920), Rāṇā Prime Minister Jaṅga Bahādura initiated the installation of the Viśvarūpa statue, symbolizing Viṣṇu in his the universal form, at Mṛgasthalī.
Elegantly raised on three tiers of plinths, this temple holds the distinction of being Nepal's largest dome-style temple (J. Regmī VS 2033, p. 253).
Constructed of bricks, the two-story temple features a metallic finial adorning its dome.
The temple faces west and is equipped with entrances on all four sides, with the western doorway granting access to the sanctum.
A geometrical figure called the Śrī Yantra, comprising nine concentric triangles, is positioned in front of the temple and is the object of worship alongside Viśvarūpa (M. Thāpā VS 2077, p. 338).
However, it's worth noting that the statue's portrayal at this temple doesn't precisely align with the Mahābhārata account (M. Thāpā VS 2077, p. 337).
A bell, presented in 1868 CE (VS 1924), hangs from the bell frame in front of the temple.
While there are no inscriptions within the temple complex documenting its construction, the Bhairava stone was already established here before the temple's construction.
Prime Minister Jaṅga Bahādura encountered it during his expedition to Tibet in 1855 CE (VS 1912) and pledged to bring it to Kathmandu for worship should he triumph in the war.
Following his victory, he fulfilled this vow, transporting the stone to Mṛgasthalī with considerable effort and constructing a temple there (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p. 594; M. Thāpā VS 2077, p. 338).

text: TheDevamālāvaṃśāvalī(2013, p.78-79), a later chronicle, recounts Prime Minister Jaṅga Bahādura's performance of a tantric fire ritual involving 10 million oblations (koṭihoma) at the Bhairava stone's location and the installation of the Viśvarūpa statue in 1863 CE (VS 1920), aiming for the welfare of all citizens.

Upon discovering the neglected Viśvarūpa statue commissioned by King Pratāpa Malla in 1657 CE (NS 777) within the Hanumānḍhokā Palace, Jaṅga Bahādura had it relocated to Mṛgasthalī, where he constructed a temple for its housing (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p.594).
Before being established at Mṛgasthalī, the Viśvarūpa statue underwent renovation by two brothers, Harṣadhana and Dhuṃdhana, hailing from Ilā Nani in Patan.
Recognizing their expertise in crafting metal statues, they were conferred with the clan name of Mahādyaḥ Khalaḥ (the clan of Mahādeva) (D. Śākya VS 2047, p. 'jha').

The architectural design of the Viśvarūpa temple blends Anglo-Indian elements with Newar wood carving, reminiscent of temples established by Bhīmasena Thāpā and Māthavarasiṃha (Gutschow 2011, p. 877).
Prime Minister Jaṅga Bahādura, along with his brother Kṛṣṇa Bahādura Rāṇā, donated a total of 305ropanīsof land for the temple's maintenance, with Jaṅga Bahādura contributing 255 ropanīs.
These land plots generated revenue used to fund daily and periodic temple rituals and compensate individuals rendering services to the temple (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p. 595).
Four years later, Jaṅga Bahādura presented a bell to the temple in 1868 CE (VS 1924).
Interestingly, the bell inscription refers to the primary deity as Kāmakāmeśvarī instead of Viśvarūpa (M. Thāpā VS 2077, p. 338).
In the aftermath of the 2015 earthquakes, half of the temple's dome collapsed, with the structure barely standing.
Subsequently, overnight rainfall on August 20, 2015, caused the temple to collapse on the morning of August 21st.
Several years later, in early June 2022 CE (VS 2079), the Minister for Culture, Tourism, and Civil Aviation laid the foundation stone for the temple's reconstruction.
The government allocated a budget of NRs. 450 thousand for the temple's reconstruction, along with the rest houses on the premises.
As of June 2023, the reconstruction of the temple is ongoing.

It's worth noting that Buddhists revere the Viśvarūpa statue as Heruka (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p. 594), while Tibetans worship it as Che-mchog, the Supreme Sovereign Heruka, and some Bhutanese venerate it as the Thousand-Armed Avalokiteśvara (Sahasrabhuja Lokeśvara) (Dowman 1981, p. 271).
Khaḍapu, a Newar settlement situated between Panautī and Banepā, is home to the Śvetabhairava Mandira, established as a Bhairavapīṭha(abode) on the edge of the settlement.
The inscriptions on the temple premises mention Bhairava, Gaṇeśa, Bālakumārī, and the Aṣṭamātṛkā shrine, leading locals to believe that these deities were once established within the premises.

However, a copperkalaḥ(worship vessel) donated to Śvetabhairava in 1825 CE (NS 945) suggests that the temple existed long before this date, though this cannot be confirmed without further inscriptions.
The upper roof of the temple was covered with gilded metal sheets in 1920 CE (VS 1973), and the middle floor’s roof was similarly covered between 1923-28 CE (VS 1980-85).
The temple's interior walls were adorned with tiles by a Śreṣṭha family in 1943 CE (VS 1999).
According to local accounts, these tiles were installed after the temple was destroyed and rebuilt following the 1934 CE (VS 1990) earthquake (local resident, Śreṣṭha, male, age 69).

On the fifth bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, an anniversary ritual (varṣavardhana) is held at the temple, including a pair of goat sacrifices and the hanging of a flag on the temple's pinnacle (P. Karmācārya VS 2067, p. 47).
The one-storied rectangular building facing west has metal sheets laid on the roof that contains a row of five finials.
There are two inscriptions inside the temple, but both are in poor condition.
A few letters that can be read in one of them state something was done at the temple, as ‘the temple constructed by Mahanta Siṃ was in poor condition’.
The script of the inscription appears to belong to the 17th-18th century.
Possibly, a person named Mahanta Siṃha constructed this temple sometime in the 17th-18th century.
Pruscha (1975, p.26) mentions that thetoraṇas on top of the three doors were installed in 1880 CE.
The recent renovation of the temple took place in 1983 CE (VS 2040).

They are installed to honor the memory of deceased persons, mostly warriors (Andolfatto 2019).
Kisi Phalcā is a ground floor Phalcā with three bays located within the Byanjankar Capāḥ building.
It was dismantled some time around 1997 with the support of the German Technological Cooperation (GTZ-udle).
The Capāḥ is used by the Ṭola Sudhāra Samiti and severalguthis, whereas the first floor is used by the Byanjankar Sīguthi.
The sanctum's main deity seat remains empty, as the original statue of Nārāyaṇa, another name for Viṣṇu, was stolen long ago.
Locals later established a new statue, but it too was stolen.
Currently (March 2024 CE), a small brass statue of Nārāyaṇa is enshrined on the northern side of the sanctum instead of his main seat.

Notably, the northern plinth of the temple features five horse statues, suggesting that the entire temple was constructed in the form of a chariot (M. Thāpā VS 2077, p. 271).
Currently, as of April 2023, the sanctum of this shrine remains empty after the statue was stolen.
No historical records exist regarding the initial construction of the Sūrya Mandira.

However, it is speculated that the temple was built around 1604 CE (NS 724), as two similar temples flanking the steps leading to the Lũ Hiti were constructed in the same year, and these temples share a close resemblance in style (M. Thāpā VS 2077, p.271).
This temple of Kobāhāḥ Ṭola was constructed in an imitation of the famous Kṛṣṇa temple of Mangalbazar.
However, after the temple collapsed in the earthquakes of 1934 it was rebuilt in a mixture ofśikharaand domed styles.

Aśivaliṅgawith a gem was installed under the dome.

This suggests the possibility that it was installed as a symbol of an aniconic feminine deity.

Based solely on the name 'Rāmeśvara', they erroneously dated its establishment to 545 CE, attributing it to the Licchavi King Rāmadeva.
The only knownśivaliṅgabearing the inscription of Licchavi King Rāmadeva (see Nātheśvara;PPK0328) is located on the way to Mṛgasthalī.
An inscription of Aṃśuvarmā dated 608 CE (Mānadeva Era 32) records state-allocated funds for various temples in the valley, including 'Rāmeśvara', which received 3purāṇas and 1paṇa.
However, Dhanavajra (VS 2030, p. 324) also acknowledged the uncertainty surrounding the location of this Rāmeśvara Śivaliṅga, stating that "nothing was known" about it.
In contrast, M. Panta (VS 2037, pp. 10-18) suggested its location in Lele, Lalitpur.
In 2022 CE (VS 2079), the ward office cleared the bushes and opened up the area (local resident, Rājabhaṇḍārī, male, age 72).

It was rebuilt in 2002 and has three bays in front and one bay on each side.
These statues were shown publicly for the first time during the Lalitpur Festival in 2018 but by June 2023, the statues have been removed and thephalcāis used for storing building materials.
The Jeṭhā Gaṇeśa Temple was constructed and the finial with achatrawas installed in 1646 CE (NS 766) when Mādhavasiṃha Prajāpati from the Ghaṭakhā Ṭola was thethakāliof the area.

Adjacent to thecaitya, a two-storied temple has been erected above the ancient Mahākāla stone, enshrining a newly installed anthropomorphic image of the deity.
The historical significance of this location became evident following the discovery of an Aṃśuvarmā-period inscription in 1989 CE  (VS 2046), which was later studied by Ś.
Rājavaṃśī (VS 2052, p. ñ).
The inscription, now securely reinstalled on the site, is dated to 614 CE (Saṃvat 536) and attests to the existence of a substantial Licchavi-era monastery namedRājavihāra.
The prefix “rāja-” in its title, according to the inscription, signifies that the monastery was commissioned by King Aṃśuvarmā himself (Ś. Rājavaṃśī VS 2047, p. 22).
Rājavaṃśī (VS 2056, pp. 160–162) further suggests that thisvihāramay have been located near theKailāsakuṭa Bhavana, the principal palace of Aṃśuvarmā’s reign.

The inscription also reveals that this was a large royal monastery accommodating monks from all four directions, reflecting the cosmopolitan character of Buddhist monasticism during the Licchavi period.
TheGopālarājavaṃśāvalī(folio 22) likewise records that Aṃśuvarmā established a monastery calledRājavihāra.

The Hāḍigāũ inscription of Aṃśuvarmā’s year 32 further states that threepurāṇaand twopaṇawere to be allocated annually to thisvihāra, offering insight into its institutional and economic stature (D. Vajrācārya VS 2030, p. 320).

Another Licchavi inscription from Patan, dated to Saṃvat 603, also mentionsRājavihāraand indicates that the monastery was accompanied by a drainage or water channel (kuloorḍhala), providing evidence of its architectural infrastructure (D. Vajrācārya VS 2036, p. 498).
The rediscovery of the buried inscription in 1989 CE (VS 2046) brought to light these long-forgotten historical details.

In continuation of this local tradition, a new anthropomorphic image of Mahākāla was consecrated at the site in 2016 CE, replacing the earlier aniconic stone, and a two-storied temple was constructed above it.

Among the numerousphalcās built around the pond, this particular one occupies the northeastern corner.
According to aninscriptionpresently located in the nearby Nārāyaṇa Mandira (KIR0005), Mādhava Siṃha Kājī and his wife Padminī (text: Padumini) built the Deypukhūsi Phalcā in 1607 CE (NS 727).
The donor couple donated tworopanis of land for the lamp-burning ceremony at thephalcāduring theYẽnyāḥfestival.
In 1987 CE (VS 2044), a structure was erected on the platform of thephalcā.
Decades later, through an agreement with the builder, thephalcāunderwent restoration in 2021 CE (VS 2078), supported by the local community and Kirtipur Municipality.
As part of this reconstruction effort, a statue of Tārā was installed in thephalcā.
Originally established as an openpīṭha, a small temple structure was constructed around it at a later date.
Within the sanctum, an aniconic stone is worshipped as Pāsikva Ajimā, and a stonetoraṇahas been installed above it.
Alongside her, additional aniconic stones representing other Mātr̥kās, as well as Gaṇeśa, Kumāra, and Bhairava, are also installed.
The precise date of the pīṭha’s original establishment is unknown.

According to tradition, when King Guṇakāmadeva founded Kathmandu in a sword-shaped layout in 724 CE (Kali year 3825), following the command of Mahālakṣmī, he installed Mātr̥kā goddesses around the city for its protection; Pāsikva Ajimā is counted among these protective deities.
Local legend recounts that the site was once agricultural land and that the goddess appeared there in the form of a hen; if anyone approached her, she would vanish (D. Ja.Ba.Rā. VS 2036, p. 98).

During the reign of King Girvāṇayuddha Vikrama Śāha, in 1816 CE (NS 936), when the Svayaṃbhū Caitya was renovated, invitations were sent to the Aṣṭamātr̥kās of Kathmandu according to custom, and Pāsikva Ajimā was included among those formally invited (H. Śākya NS 1098, p. 282).
The earliest inscription discovered at the site dates to 1861 CE (NS 981).

This stone inscription records that Biṃnasiṃ (Bīranarasiṃha), a resident of Jamala Bahā Tole in Kathmandu, together with his wife Dhirjalakṣmī and other family members, commissioned twelve copper images for the performance of the goddess’s processionjātrā.

Although some scholars have identified Pāsikva Ajimā as Brahmāyaṇī (e.g., D. Ja.Ba.Rā. VS 2036, p. 98; B. Juju and S. Śreṣṭha NS 1105, p. 38), the inscription’s explicit reference to the deity as “Māheśvarī,” together with the iconography of Nandin on thetoraṇa, clearly indicates that the goddess is Rudrāyaṇī (Māheśvarī), not Brahmāyaṇī.

Further renovations were undertaken in 2012 CE (VS 2069), when the cement roof was replaced with a brass roof, and a gilded finial was installed at a cost of NPR 500,000 (S. Mānandhara NS 1142, p. 80).

Traditionally, on the eighth of bright fortnight of Bhādra, marking the commencement of Indrajātrā, special worship was conducted at thepīṭhas of the Mātr̥kās established for the protection of Kathmandu, including Pāsikva Ajimā, with offerings of various foods, fruits, andsayaṃbaji, accompanied bybhajana-kīrtana.
However, owing to the absence of a stable source of income, this particular observance has now ceased (S. Mānandhara NS 1142, p. 75).

Numerous renovations and reconstructions have resulted in the loss of many of the temple's original elements.
Unfortunately, the absence of historical records leaves the temple's original construction date cloaked in uncertainty.
