This inscription, found among four rock formations in Nālāchāpa of Bhaktapur, was carved on a rock chosen in particular by King Bhupatindra Malla in 1715 CE (NS 835) for an unnamed construction project.

Two inscriptions of King Viṣṇu Gupta, dated Mānadeva Era 64 and 65 (corresponding to 640 and 641 CE), deal with the transportation of stone in the valley for carving statues (D. Vajrācārya VS 2030, pp. 446-448).

These inscriptions declare that the people of Sunaguthi (a town south of Patan) and Dakṣiṇakolīgrāma were granted permission to wear jewelry as a reward for transporting stones for carving Buḍhānīlakaṇṭha, the statue of reclining Viṣṇu situated north of Kathmandu.

Inscriptions on such artistic creations carved on stone from this place proudly mention "made from Koṭakhā stone." Śrīnivāsa Malla, the king of Patan, made "Koṭakhā stone" available to Jitāmitra Malla for renovating the Kumārī Coka in the latter's kingdom of Bhaktapur following Jitāmitra's request (Tevārī and others VS 2019, pp. 24-25).
Likewise, in 1691 CE (NS 811), Crown Prince Bhūpatindra Malla renovated a water spout in the Bhaktapur palace using stone from Koṭakhā (Vaidya & Shrestha 2002, p. 207).
The stone brought by Viṣṇu Gupta for the Buḍhānīlakaṇṭha statue and the "Koṭakhā stone" are speculated to belong to the same quarry (D. Vajrācārya VS 2030, p. 446).
Inscriptions mentioning the kings of Bhaktapur and Kathmandu have been found on four massive rock formations at Nālāchāpa.
This formation of stone with the inscription stands embedded in the edge of a private field.

The inscription from 1715 CE (NS 835) declares that this particular rock has been selected by Bhūpatindra Malla for building a stone temple in the name of his father and that works had already begun for the same.
Another inscription almost identical to this one has been found about 100 meters north of this rock.
These inscriptions show that the rulers used to mark rocks from this area by inscribing a royal declaration, ordering people to not use the rocks for other purposes.
Due to its historical significance, the Changunarayan Municipality has installed zinc sheets as a cover to prevent weathering.
The Vīranārāyaṇa temple is a dedicatory temple commissioned by the 11th Prime Minister Bir Shumsher Jung Bahadur Rana.

The Temple is situated at the central courtyard in the inner sanctum of the Tīnadhārā Pākaśālā, a residential building built by the same prime minister to provide accommodation for the students of Sanskrit.
Although established in reverence and worship of Lord Vishnu, the temple, however, as suggested by the prefix ‘Vīra’ is taken after the patron of the temple, Bir Shumsher.
The earliest known example of this kind of dedicatory temple in Kathmandu valley is that of Bhimbhaktesvara temple established by Bhimsen Thapa.
The general established the temple in his own name (Bhim) as a devotee (bhakta) of Lord Siva.
In Nepal, the temple construction takes the form of identity markers.

Temple construction as an ambitious undertaking is understood to have mnemonic function used by the patrons to forge associations of the king and the deity, in praise and devotion of the deity for the support of his rulership, in public memory.

Perhaps, to distinguish themselves from their predecessor and to commence their own reign with a mark of devotion as represented in their distinct temple style architecture, the new class of rulers, the Ranas, Kunwars, Pandes and Thapa initiated new temple building activities in Kathmandu.

The largest assemblage of consecutive bell-shaped top temples can be found high above the river in Deopatan, where elven temples are built in a row on a terrace high above the river which were established within only six years, between 1858 and 1864, in close similarity to one another.
The pioneering example of this architectural style is the Bhimbhaktesvara Temple, built in 1822 by General Bhimsen Thapa himself, and named in his honour.
The construction of the Bhimbhaktesvara Temple reflects the introduction of building traditions from Lucknow, India.
The most elaborate, in design and engineering, is the construction of lotus-shaped top as observed in the Vīranārāyaṇa temple.
Beginning with the Bhimbhaktesvara temple of 1822, all of the domes were characterised by a pseudo-vault constructed from corbelled bricks, necessitating a supporting timber framework.
The Vīranārāyaṇa temple is guarded by Lord Vishnu’s mount the Garuda, which is situated on top of a tall tower, whose back bears untranslated inscription.
The resulting conflation of these two interests are well reflected in the diverse temple architecture styles built during their time.

The use of white plaster on temple walls and on residential palaces, dome top, Mughal style windows are a result of those acquired skills that proliferated and dominated the building history of the Ranas.
Understanding the Guthi system is essential for appreciating the cultural fabric of Nepal, which is defined by a collective commitment to preserving its heritage.
Guthi is a social system of the Newar people in Nepal that supports the socio-economic status of their community.
Guthi includes trusts to which lands are donated, a deed considered worthy of religious merit, which are used to generate revenue.
These revenues are allocated for various projects including restoration of temples, patis (rest houses), maths (priest houses) and Hitis or Dhunge dhara.
A Guthi is established with the purpose of looking after the cultural heritage of the community past their construction.
The Guthi established by Bhīma Śamśera for Tīnadhārā Pākaśālā and Vīranārāyaṇa manages the property and the encapsulated temple.

While the exact date of the construction is yet to be determined, it can be cautiously concluded that the temple was built well before the first known directive sent out by the Guthi in 1945 VS, which details account of deposition made by a patron named Jujuvīra before the Guthi Administration Office regarding the operations of two specific Guthi organisations: Tīnadhārā Pāthaśālā Guṭhī and Vīranārāyaṇa Guṭhī.
Regular contributions to the Guthi allowed for the management of the two properties over the years.
This inference is well supported by the earliest instructions from the royal authority commanding overseeing various tasks for the welfare of the two guthis.
Prime Minister Bir Shumsher established the Tīnadhārā Pākaśālā to provide residential service for the learners of Sanskrit.

His orthodox Hindu background could help us understand his initial intention behind the establishment, however, his dedication to oversee the welfare of the institution can be discerned from the various legal orders and documents issued by the prime minister to manage the place through Guthis.

There are also executive orders signed by the prime minister providing funds for feeding 108 Brahmins of Tīnadhārā Pāthaśālā (VS 1947), as there are documents instructing the whitewashing of the building of the pākaśālā.

Guthi as a social system and institution is a great initiative from community members that acknowledges the role of tangible heritage in community making, and therefore involves the community in ensuring the longevity of its tangible cultural heritage.
The Kalmochana guthi, the guardian body of the temple, oversees the functioning and well-being of the temple, executing its operations.
A designated priest, appointed and salaried by the guthi, is responsible for the worship in the temple that takes place in the morning and evening.

The guthi generates its income in the same manner as it has since its inception, through revenue earned from the proceeds of cultivated land leased to farmers in whose name the land has been registered.

Nevertheless, after democracy became the form of government, a legal court verdict issued in 1958 AD mandated the admission of students enthusiastic about Sanskrit, irrespective of their caste in the Hindu caste system.
The Kutujhvaḥ Śikharakūṭa Caitya is constructed around the middle of an elongated courtyard at Kutujhvaḥ, the southern end of Kirtipur.
This area is mentioned as 'Kothujhora' in the later medieval inscriptions.

After the construction of the Cilancva Caitya (KIR0001) in NS 635 (1515 CE) by Jagatapāla Varmā, amahāpātraof Patan, many Buddhist monuments likebāhāḥs andcaityas were constructed in the eastern quarter of Kirtipur.
Due to the construction of only Buddhist monuments in the area, the eastern quarter of Kirtipur came to be known as 'Devagala'.
After NS 1055 (1935 CE), however, Buddhist monuments also started to appear in Śivagala.
Previously, people believed that if anyone built a Buddhist monument in Śivagala, he or his clan member would die (Ś. ŚreṣṭhaVS 2057, p. 28).
Unfortunately, there is no inscription around this Caitya.

D. Vajrācārya(VS 2056, p. 488) has published an inscription (seeKIR0026_I_001), dated NS 746 (1626 CE), from Khāḥsibajāra, Kirtipur that talks about the construction of acaityaand renovation of some structure that is unclear due to the loss of text.
T. Śreṣṭha andḌ. Śarmā(2019, p. 108) claim that this inscription belongs to the Kutujhvaḥ Śikharakūṭa Caitya.
Shokoohy and others(2014, p. 247) also opine that this inscription originally belonged to the Kutujhvaḥ Śikharakūṭa Caitya, but disappeared at some point of time from there.
The inscription can still be seen posted on the plinth of a Śiva temple in Khāḥsibajāra.
It is not certain whether this inscription indeed belongs to the Kutujhvaḥ Caitya.
The Bālakumārī Hiti, built to supply water for the daily worship of Bālakumārī Devī, is located west of the Bālakumārī Temple (LAL2000) in Lalitpur.
On the southern wall of the hiti, ajaḥdhuṃ(water tank) is installed, its spout adorned with a figure of Gaṅgā holding two pots, and a statue of Nārāyaṇa placed beneath.
No record survives concerning the hiti’s original construction.
As it was intended to serve the worship of Bālakumārī Devī, the hiti was likely built around the same time as the Bālakumārī Temple.

Later genealogical accounts mention a Bālakumārī Pīṭha, claiming that King Aśoka Malla established both the temple and the hiti in 1521 CE (NS 641) after propitiating the goddess and defeating the Vaiśyas of Lalitpur (Yogī Naraharinātha, V.S. 2013, p. 48; Lalitpur Sub-Metropolitan City, 2007, p. 84; S. Khānāla, V.S. 2068, p. 251).
citations: (Yogī Naraharinātha, V.S. 2013, p. 48; Lalitpur Sub-Metropolitan City, 2007, p. 84; S. Khānāla, V.S. 2068, p. 251)

text: After the water source failed and the hiti remained dry for about twenty to twenty-five years, Queen Gambhīrakumārīdevī—wife of Rana Prime Minister Juddha Śamaśera—funded its restoration in 1946 CE (V.S. 2003).
The work included not only repairs to the hiti’s structure but also the restoration of its water source and supply channels.

Marker stones were embedded along the route to locate future blockages, one placed on the main road from Guita ṭola’s Guita Bahi to Bh̃uḍe Gaṇeśasthana, another twenty-five feet north, and drainage channels (maṃgāla) installed at intervals of one hundred feet.
The hiti underwent another restoration in 1991 CE (V.S. 2048) under the Lalitpur Sub-Metropolitan City (2007, p. 84).
Despite multiple restoration efforts, the water supply has not been reestablished.
Despite its modest size and the absence of sculptural embellishment, this Jaḥdhuṃ was once marked by an inscription of considerable historical importance.
Dated to 1317 CE (NS 437), the epigraph is among the few surviving records from the early medieval period and provides valuable insight into the political context of its time.
The inscription records that the Jaḥdhuṃ was commissioned by a royal physician (rājavaidya) on behalf of a patron.
The text expresses the donor’s aspiration for the liberation of his ancestors, indicating that the fountain was constructed as a pious offering for their spiritual benefit.
D. Vajrācārya (VS 2068, pp. 145–46) has published a transcript and facsimile of the inscription; however, contrary to his account, the epigraph is no longer extant at the site.
Jaḥdhuṃswere typically installed in locations where drinking water was in high demand—along travel routes, in areas of public congregation during festivals or processions, and near sacred sites.
The temple is built on the model of Newar temples with multiple roofs and a peristyle.
It is built with bricks and mud mortar.
Thisbāhāḥwas founded by a member of Lagaṃ Bāhāḥ in Lagana ṭola, Kathmandu.
Thekvāḥpāḥchẽof thebāhāḥis a three-story building that faces east.
The recent reconstruction of thebāhāḥreplaced its tin roof with copper sheets with a set of three finials on top.
There is a legend on the establishment of thebāhāḥ.
The man asked the visitor for constructing a separatebāhāḥto perform thebarechuiguritual to his son, stating that his elder brother had insulted him for being poor.
They found an open space with aśivaliṅgainstalled by the Karmacāryas to be suitable for the purpose.
A newbāhāḥwas established there after it was agreed to let theśivaliṅgaremain there.
No one knew the name of the passerby who constructed thebāhāḥ.
However, they sold their houses and moved out of the area a few years ago.
According to the locals, Rāma Āḥju of thebāhāḥhad hosted aSamyakMahādānaceremony while his younger brother Lakṣmaṇa Āḥju formed the Śrāddha Guthi.
[1]Lakṣmaṇa Āḥju is known to have passed away on the 12th of the bright fortnight of Bhādra in NS 888 (1768 CE).
Theguthiyāras of Lakṣmaṇa Āḥju Guthi claim to possess a historical record of the incident.

During the reign of King Pṛṭhvī Vīra Vikrama Śāha in NS 1027 (1907 CE), Lālabahādura, together with his wife Sirāmāyā and son Puṇamāna, laid stones at thebāhāḥcourtyard in memory of his deceased father Dhanarāja.
Later in NS 1090 (1970 CE), theśikharakūṭacaityawas renovated and the statue of Gaṇeśa and Mahākāla were also installed.
The name of the donor is not known due to the erosion of the text in the inscription.
The 2015 earthquakes damaged thebāhāḥ.
Thekvāḥpāḥchẽwas rebuilt with a fund of NRs. 9 million provided by the Kathmandu Metropolis and a donation of NRs. 1.9 million collected from the locals.
Thekvāḥpāḥchẽwas dismantled in 2018 CE and the reconstruction was completed in 2020 CE.
The annualbahīdyaḥbvayguexhibition is held from the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa till the 3rd of the dark fortnight of Bhādra every year at the ground floor of theguthichẽsouth of thebāhāḥ.
During the exhibition, the statues of Dīpaṅkara Buddha installed by Rāma Āḥju and Sukhāvatī Lokeśvara installed by Lakṣmaṇa Āḥju are put on display.
[1]Theguthiformed by Lakṣmaṇa Āḥju also performs the anniversary rituals of the Licchavicaitya(KAT0890-005) at Kva Hiti on the full moon day of Āśvina every year.
Acaityais consecrated inside it, which is the only heritage property in the Nani.
There is no evidence to appoint the initial construction of thiscaitya.
In an inscription inside the sanctum from 1853 CE (NS 973), it is mentioned that thecaityawas renovated.
In the inscription, thecaityais referred to as Vajradhātu Caitya.
BothPruscha(1975, 44) andLocke(1985, 290) mention that the temple was constructed in a traditional way and tiled withjhĩgaṭībricks.
However, the temple's entire structure transformed into a cemented construction when it was renovated in 1987 CE.
There is no inscription that sheds light on the construction of the temple.
It is said that the temple was constructed by the ancestors of a Śreṣṭha family from Taḥ Nani, Satuṅgala.
People from the area believe that even major earthquakes failed to damage the temple, as it is small in structure but well-constructed.
Fourguthiyāras of the Śreṣṭha clan are responsible for the procession.
Buĩcā Hiti, believed to be built during the premiership of Juddha Śamśera Rāṇā, is one of three hitis located at the bottom of the Imūdvã hillock in Lalitpur.
It is believed that thehitiwas built during the reign of Prime Minister Juddha Śamśera Rāṇā [r. 1932-1945] (Lalitpur Sub-Metropolitan City2007, 39).
Aphalcānext to thehitiwas reconstructed in 1844 CE (NS 964) from the ground up.
Thephalcāwas built to serve those coming to collect water, take a shower, or do laundry.
A minor renovation of the Buĩcā Hiti took place in 2017 CE (VS 2074) when thehitisandphalcāsin the Ālko quarter were renovated with funding from the World Bank and the Lalitpur Municipality.
However, little attention was paid to its authenticity and the use of appropriate material during the renovation process.
Despite its historical significance, details about the construction of thesataḥremain unclear.
The architectural style, reminiscent of the Rana period (post-1846 CE), aligns with the broader constructions in Gaurīghāṭa from that era.
A bell, placed in front of thesataḥ, bears a votive inscription recording its donation by Mukhyānī Viṣṇubhakta Kumārī, the senior wife of Colonel Dalabhajana Thāpā, in 1888 CE (VS 1944).
Renovated in 2013 (VS 2017) by the Paśupati Area Development Trust, thesataḥwithstood the earthquakes of 2015 CE.
For the protection of Lalitpur city, tenDaśamahāvidyāshrines were established in different neighborhoods (ṭola).

It is, however, plausible that the shrine was established when Lalitpur was developed into a planned settlement, as part of a larger network of tenMahāvidyāshrines installed in different directions for the city’s protection, with the Kopeśvara temple (LAL1381) serving as the central point.
In its earliest form, the site consisted of an aniconic stone installed in an open pit.

On Pauṣa śukla 6 of NS 1047 (1927 CE), Bāghanasiṃha (Bāghanarasiṃha Śākya) of the Gautamagotra, a Śākya layman residing in the southwest corner of Hiranyavarṇa Mahāvihāra, Kwāḥ Bahāḥ, organized asamyakdāna(great almsgiving ceremony), inviting King Tribhuvan to the event (H. Śākya VS 2036, p. 57).
The remaining funds from this ceremony were first used for the renovation of Naḥ Bahī.

Surplus funds were then employed to construct anāgamahouse for the Thyakakhalak(ritual association) at Nyākhācuk, and the remaining balance was subsequently dedicated to the construction of the Bhvaneśvarī shrine (Local resident from a Vajrācārya caste, male, age 82).
In NS 1049 (1929 CE), Bāghanasiṃha undertook a major renovation of the dilapidated Lokākīrti Mahāvihāra at Naḥ Bahī.
As part of this project, he built a three-tiered stone staircase in front of thebahīand erected the Bhvaneśvarī shrine.
He also performed asahasrāhuti yajña(fire offering with a thousand oblations) to consecrate the site.

His wife Hel Thakuṃ, his sons Bāhadursiṃha and Lakṣmīnārasiṃha, his nephew Kubersiṃha, and his grandsons Harṣanārasiṃha, Byasanārasiṃha, Harṣamānasiṃha, Ratnanārasiṃha, and Samyakanārasiṃha, along with other family members, actively supported these undertakings (cf. (LAL0880_I_20181126_09_5).The shrine, oriented toward the north, is characterized by a single-tiered brass roof surmounted by a metalgaur(pinnacle), from which a metalpatāḥ(banner) descends to the lower edge of the roof. Above the entrance, a metaltoraṇafeatures a four-armed image of Bhvaneśvarī: her right hands hold anaṅkuśa(goad) and display thevaradamudrā(boon-bestowing gesture), while her left hands hold apāśa(noose) and display theabhayamudrā(gesture of fearlessness). Within thegarbhagṛha(sanctum), an unshaped stone set in a pit is venerated as the goddess, and a metaltoraṇawith a canopy (chepū) has been installed above it. The inner and outer walls are lined with marble, and adabū(raised platform for ritual performances) is located to the southeast of the shrine.Bhvaneśvarī herself is described in textual sources as a goddess radiant like thousands of rising suns, possessing three eyes, wearing a moon-adorned crown and a garland of severed heads (muṇḍamālā), and identified with Bhvaneśvara, the divine male (N. Pokharela 2019, p. 53). Her birthday is celebrated on 12th bright fortnight of Bhādra (J. Mānandhara VS 2046, p. 33). A popular belief holds that offerings made to her on Fridays or Saturdays—consisting of grapes, bananas, flowers, and red or yellow cloth—can cure afflictions caused by malevolent winds (pretvāyu) (M. Miśra NS 1127, p. 22).For many decades, Kapālījugisresided at the shrine as hereditary priests, performing daily worship and collecting offerings. When they eventually abandoned their custodial role, the regular rituals ceased. In VS 2081 (2025 CE), daily worship (nityapūjā) was revived through the initiative of the Daśamahāvidyā Bhaktibhāva Parivār organization, which appointed a Rājopādhyāya Brāhmaṇa priest and continues to provide his remuneration.The Bhvaneśvarī shrine remains embedded in the ritual life of Lalitpur. Every year on Kāyāṣṭamī (8th of bright fortnight of Bhādra), worship of the tenMahāvidyāgoddesses takes place across the city, with the responsibility for organizing the rituals rotating among the neighborhoods hosting these shrines. During the Naḥ Bahī celebration, the Mahārjan community receives the offerings, which are then distributed asprasādato Naḥ Bahī, Mikhābahāḥ, Chāybahāḥ, and Taḥnani neighborhoods. Additionally, the final dance of theGhaṃpyākhaṃperformance during the Daśaĩ (Daśain) festival is staged annually on thedabūsoutheast of the shrine. Known asBelākhaḥ Huikegu, it is performed on 11th of bright fortnight of Āśvina. In the past, ducks, chickens, and goats were sacrificed at the shrine on Mahāṣṭamī (8th of bright fortnight of Āśvina), though the practice of animal sacrifice has now been discontinued.
In the basin's northwest corner, a small stone water reservoir is constructed.
Steps are built on the SE and NW sides.
When the site was documented in April 2022 CE, there was no water coming out of the Fountain.
The original purpose of this element is unknown, but itsmakara-like shape is likely what drew the fountain's builders to incorporate it into the masonry.
Above the main water spout is a stone slab with an inscription recording the name of the Fountain, Mahendra Dhārā, and the date of its construction VS 2020 (1964 CE).

A stone inscription embedded in its wall records that Amātya Rāma Bhāro, Govindarāja Bhāro and others jointly commissioned and engaged in the construction of thephalcāin order to sing devotional songs and hymns (bhajana) to Triliṅgeśvara Mahādeva.
The first digit of the date recorded in the inscription is not clearly readable but most likely refers to 1761 CE (NS 881).
In 1892 (VS 1949), Amātya Kṛṣṇagovinda, his wife Mānakumārī and two sons commissioned the repair of thephalcā.
In 2009 CE (VS 2065), local community members and the Lalitpur Sub-metropolitan City jointly reconstructed it.
Two additional spouts made of pvc pipes have been added to the fountain.
The sanctum contains a 107 cm high stone inscription.
However, hardly any part of the deteriorated inscription can be deciphered.
It is likely that this inscription is his source for this.
Locally, this monastic building is considered the god-house (dyaḥchẽ) where the Dīpaṅkara of Pasu Bāhāḥ is enshrined and not as a properbāhāḥ.
Two inscriptions at Āḥjudyaḥ Bāhāḥ refer to the Dīpaṅkara as Ajājudeva’ (lit. ancestral deity).
No historical source reveals the initial construction of thebāhāḥ.
The earliest mention of thebāhāḥappears in a loan deed (tamasuka) of 1392 CE (NS 512) during the reign of King Jayasthiti Malla (S. Śākya1120, p.17-18).
Acaitya(BKT0210-019) at thebāhāḥwas built in 1630 CE (NS 750).
Thedyaḥchẽof thebāhāḥwas reconstructed in 1923 CE (VS 1980).
The statue of Dīpaṅkara was shifted from the first floor to the ground floor in the course of the reconstruction.

In 1859 CE (VS 1916), Ḍillīsiṃha Basneta erected a conjoined temple that housed three separateśivālayas (lit. Śiva’s abode) and later established a trust by donating land parcels in 1868 CE (VS 1925).

Outside the temple, amaṇḍalaand a relief of Viṣṇu’s feet (viṣṇupādukā) can be seen in the front while other deities are also established at the temple premises, including a fewśivaliṅgas and a statue of Umāmaheśvara on the eastern side.
The site where this conjoined temple now stands was once home to the Bhadreśvara Śivaliṅga established in the Licchavi period.
The statue of Umāmaheśvara (PPK0516-012) in front of the temple is believed to date back to the 12-13th century (M. Thāpā VS 2077, p. 193).

During the early years of the Rāṇā regime, Ḍillīsiṃha Basneta built the temple in 1859 CE (VS 1916) (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, pp. 354-355; Michaels and Tandon 2017, p. 70). Ḍillīsiṃha also established another conjoined temple with separateśivālayas named Padmeśvara, Raṇadīpeśvara, and Maheśvara (PPK0519) in it at the same time.
citations: (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, pp. 354-355; Michaels and Tandon 2017, p. 70)

text: He installed a bell to commemorate the construction of both conjoined temples that now hangs by a bell-stand in front of the temple.Ḍillīsiṃha Basneta, appointed to the post of akājī, an officer of ministerial rank, was one of Prime Minister Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā’s trusted appointees (B. Bhaṇḍārī VS 2071, pp. 20-21).
The area known as Ḍillībajāra in Kathmandu was named after Ḍillīsiṃha, who was also one of the delegates who visited England with Jaṅga Bahādura in 1950 CE (P. Rāṇā VS 2059, p. 58).
Jaṅga Bahādura’s daughter from Minā Mahārānī, also known as Dākhacoke Mahārānī, was married to Ḍillīsiṃha’s son Captain Padmakeśara Basneta (P. Rāṇā VS 2059, p. 193).

A few years after the construction of the temple, Ḍillīsiṃha donated land parcels to form a trust in 1868 CE (VS 1925) that oversaw the performance of daily and other periodic rituals at the temple (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, pp. 438).
Although Ḍillīsiṃha had established a trust for performing daily and periodic worship, as of February 2024, only daily rituals are performed here.
There are three layers built above the doors resembling the tiled roofs of a pagoda-style temple and a stone pinnacle crowning them.
The inscription attached to the base of the temple records that it was built in 1658 CE (778 NS) by two brothers, Hari and Śivarāma Bhāro, both residents of Sataḥkvaḥ Ṭola, Kirtipur.
The two brothers also endowed eightropanīsof land to the temple (cf.Ś. ŚreṣṭhaVS 2057, 100).
Despite the fact that this temple was built in the late seventeenth century,Hutt(1994, 211) dates this Śrīdharaviṣṇu statue to tenth century.
It once disappeared (probably stolen) from the sanctum, however, was found and re-enshrined in its original place.
After this incident, an iron gate was installed to its main door.
The inscription also records the establishment of a Vaṃśagopāla statue, which is not in the temple premises in the present-day.
Around 2007 CE, the temple was cleaned and slightly repaired by the Department of the Archaeology (local knowledge, local resident, Maharjana, age 48).
The temple has a privateguṭhīestablished by the Śreṣṭha clans from Sataḥkvaḥ Ṭola.
Early in the morning of that day, the metal statue used to be carried to the Vāgamatī (Bagmati) River and consecrated with holy water.
The Aśoka Stūpa North is one of 5stūpasbelieved to have been built by King Aśoka in the 3rd century BCE, although, there is no evidence that King Aśoka ever visited the Kathmandu Valley.
Over time dramatic changes took place: a historic photograph from the 1920s depicts the earthen mound covered by grass and a steppedharmikā, most likely built of brick and whitewashed with lime.

The central wooden pillar extends from theharmikāwith the finial missing, which would indicate that thestūpawas under restoration at that time. 50 years later, in ca. 1973, the photograph from Pruscha's inventory, shows the earthen mound covered with white-washed plaster and a completely rebuiltharmikāand finial.
While a legend credits a cowherder (gvāḥor Gopālī) woman for the construction of this temple, an inscription here confirms that the Brahmāyaṇī temple already existed in the 17th century.
A more recent statue, discovered by a local during a firewood expedition in the nearby jungle, is also enshrined here.
No concrete historical records exist regarding the construction of the temple; however, inscriptions verify that it was already built during the medieval period.
According to legend, the temple was constructed by a cowherdess.
Due to a feud among three cowherdess sisters, one established a Gaṇeśa shrine known as Gvāḥdyaḥ, another built the Brahmāyaṇī temple, and the third established a Gaṇeśa shrine at Gvāḥnani.
Another version of the legend states that the elder cowherdess sister established Brahmāyaṇī in Kvaylāchi, while the younger sister established Bālakumārī in Cvaylāchi.
In 1636 CE (NS 756), a group led by Kulasiṃha constructed a dance platform in Thecva.
As the inscription is set in the temple wall, the platform mentioned here probably refers to the one in front of the temple.
In 1702 CE (NS 823), the seniors of Thecva, Bhārasiṃha Bhābo and Sūrya Bhābo, established a Gaṇeśa statue (THC0030-002).
In 1717 CE (NS 837), a guild dedicated to chanting Buddhist hymns in Thecva paved the open space in front of the Brahmāyaṇī temple with floor tiles.
In the same year, Gumīsiṃha Bhābo, Dātemha Bhābo, Indrasiṃ Bhābo, and others collectively donated three woodentoraṇas for Brahmāyaṇī.
In 1901 CE (NS 1021), the old wooden pillar in front of the Brahmāyaṇī temple was replaced with a stone pillar.
As the 2015 Nepal earthquakes damaged the temple, the Department of Archaeology decided to rebuild the temple.
In 2017 CE (VS 2073), the temple was dismantled and the Brahmāyaṇī statue was temporarily relocated to thesataḥwest of the temple.
However, the statue was stolen on January 3, 2018 while it was placed in thesataḥ(local resident, Maharjana, male, age 38).
This was not the first incident of theft; the Brahmāyaṇī statue had been stolen twice before.
Unfortunately, none of the stolen statues have been recovered.
Consequently, the locals collectively installed a new statue on each occasion.
This is the fourth Brahmāyaṇī statue to be installed in the temple.
Following the completion of the temple’s reconstruction, the Brahmāyaṇī statue was re-enshrined back to her usual seat after the installation of finial (local resident, Maharjana, male, age 38).
Three religious trusts in Thecva—Mū Guthi, Kvanā Guthi, and Nhesaḥ Guthi—are responsible for the worship, rituals, and festivals at the Brahmāyaṇī temple.
The Mū Guthi and Nhesaḥ Guthi are managed by the Maharjanas, while the Kvanā Guthi is managed by the Mālīs.
On this day, the Kvanā Guthi offerspañcabali, the sacrifice of five animals.
The Yajñeśvara Mahādeva temple, established in 1864 CE (VS 1921), is dedicated to Yajñeśvaradevī, one of the wives of Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā.
Constructed from stone, it contains a distinctive bell-shaped roof capped with a metallic finial.
Notably, the primary western entrance features an inscription beneath itstoraṇathat provides valuable insights into the temple's construction.
The three other statues of Gaṇeśa in the southwest, Durgā in the northwest, and Viṣṇu in the northeast have been stolen.
The statue of Kāmadeva, the deity of love in Eastern mythology, which was installed on the retaining wall further east of the temple, has also been stolen.
The temple was constructed in honor of Yajñeśvarīdevī, the wife of Prime Minister Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā, and thus, it acquired the name Yajñeśvara.
She is mentioned as the elder sister of Sūryapratāpa Śāha (K. Dīkṣita VS 2034, p. 77).
Very little is know about the history and the original date of construction.

Judging from the carving style of doors and windows and by comparison of other structures this is most likely the oldest residential building in Junbesi and might originate from the mid to late 19th century.
It is unclear when thisphalcāwas originally constructed.
The earliest visual record of thephalcādates back to 1844 CE in a drawing by Rājamānasiṃha Citrakāra.
By 1972 CE, during a visit by King Vīrendra with a foreign dignitary to Godāvarī, the deteriorated state of thephalcāled to its dismantling.
Subsequently, thephalcāwas reconstructed in 1980 CE approximately 10 meters to the north and is now known as Nāmasaṅgīti Phalcā (LAL4310).
In the mid-2000s, the local community embarked on the reconstruction of thephalcāat its original site.

A proper name for thephalcāwas required by the court, leading to the selection of Samay Phalcā, inspired by the tradition of distributingsamaybajiat the site in the past, as mentioned by a member of the reconstruction committee, Maharjana, aged 52.
Eventually, the district court ruled in favor of rebuilding thephalcā, citing evidence from photographs taken in the 1960s and 1970s.
The first elected local body following the promulgation of Nepal's new constitution allocated a budget for the reconstruction.
Nearly 5 decades after thephalcāwas dismantled, the foundation-laying ceremony was scheduled for August 19, 2021.
However, the Patan High Court issued an interim order halting construction work pending the hearing of a writ petition against the reconstruction the day before.
On September 8, 2021, the court dismissed the interim order, clearing the path for construction to commence, as stated by a member of the reconstruction committee, Maharjana, aged 52.
Wooden struts and stone statues, previously stored at a nearby police station, were utilized for the reconstruction.
These items were reportedly retrieved from thephalcāduring its dismantling, although their original connection to Samay Phalcā remains uncertain.
The reconstruction project concluded with a total expenditure of NRs. 3.5 million (D. Nyaupāne VS 2078, ekantipur) and thephalcāwas inaugurated on March 19, 2022.
Aguthiof the Malekūs, a subcaste of the Śreṣṭhas, residing near the Aśoka Stupa (LAL0610), traditionally commemorated the anniversary of thephalcā.
Additionally, thejyāpu(Maharjans) of Pulchowk are affiliated with thisguthi.
The Malekūs established a separateguthidedicated to offering cooked rice (bhujā) to Buṅgadyaḥ.
The monument is a free-standing two-storied construction built in the fashion of Kathmandu valley, with brick walls and Newar style carved pillars and windows.
To the right of the door is an inscribed stone slab inserted in the masonry.
The inscription contains the monument's date of construction, 'śake 1741' (1819 CE).
To the north is a room where computers have been installed but solely used due to maintenance issues and lack of electricity.
Shelves and tables have been installed to showcase various types of objects, mainly everyday objects related to agricultural work.
According to the inscription situated next to the entrance door, the monument was built in 1819 (ŚS 1741, VS 1876), during the reign of King Rājendra Śāha (r. 1816-1846).
The monument's was built as apauvā, a place for distributing water to travellers, which also provided them with a place to rest.
In 2011 Bishwo K. C. Pokharel noted that the building was in a poor state of conservation and that the upper floor was used as restrooms (Pokharel 2011 [VS 2068], pp. 145-146).
After the reconstruction following its collapse, this rest house is currently being used by an organization that manages theMatayāḥprocession.
There is no inscription at the site that reveals the history of the Sataḥ.
It remained in a state of disrepair for a long period.
Before its collapse, the tile roof was replaced with corrugated tin sheets.
The Sataḥ was reconstructed in 2014 CE at a total cost of NRs. 4 million (president of Nyakūjātrā Matayāḥ Central Management Committee, Śākya, male, age 69).
Donations were collected from the locals as well to meet the shortfall.
The Nyakūjātrā Matayāḥ Central Management Committee, the organization that manages the annualMatayāḥprocession in Patan, took over the Sataḥ from the day the reconstruction was completed.
A contract was signed between the representatives of the Building Department of the Ministry of Urban Development and the committee that allowed the use of the Sataḥ by the latter.
During the reign of Candraśamśera, Pṛthvīvilāsa Sāpakoṭā, who was then known as Kālesāhu, constructed thisŚivālayatogether with asataḥat his lineage deity shrine.
During the latter half of the Rāṇā period, a local merchant (sāhu) built this temple at his ownKuladevatāthāna(Shrine of the Lineage Deity).
The temple faces south, and on the edges of its doorway a toraṇa carved with the figure of a chepu has been installed.
The upper part of the temple is raised in the bell style, and a stone pinnacle is installed at the apex.
The other deities belonging to theŚiva Pañcāyanahave been established in the four corners in accordance with scriptural standards.
Later, during the Śāha and Rāṇā period, hundreds ofŚivālayasof this type were built.
A distinct wave of installing suchŚivālayasspread through Āryaghaṭa and Mṛgasthalī of Paśupati.
This particularŚivālayawas established in the latter part of the Rāṇa period, during the reigns of Candraśamśera and Tribhuvana.
Thesataḥassociated with thisŚivālayawas built at the same time.
An inscription carved on thatsataḥrecords details of the construction.
According to the inscription dated 1914 CE (VS 1971), the then merchant Pṛthvīvilāsa Sāpakoṭā built these structures and endowed ample land asguṭhī.
The inscription also specifies the rituals to be performed during various festivals using the income from the land, as well as the quantity of materials to be used.
It further records the intent that surplus savings from the harvest should be used to purchasevirtā(a type of tax-exempt land grant).
In the inscription, the installedliṅgais named Naravadeśvara.
The inscription does not clarify after whom the builder named theliṅga.
It is also not certain from the record whether he added a shrine over a pre-existingliṅgaor installed a newliṅgaand gave it this name.
The shrine does not appear to have suffered significant damage during the recent great earthquake.
At present (2025 CE), cracks have begun to appear in various parts of the shrine, and grass can be seen growing on the upper part.
The shrine was painted in the month of Jyeṣṭha of VS 2082 (local resident, Sāpakoṭā, male, age 68).
All festival-related cultural practices mentioned in the inscription have already disappeared.
Only the daily worship specified in the inscription continues through theguṭhīsystem.

OnŚivarātri, instead of activities being conducted through theguṭhīsystem established by the founder, local people gather spontaneously at the shrine according to their own interest and devotion, light a fire, and cook and distribute Blessed Offering.

On the day ofKulapūjā, cleaning and painting work is carried out at theŚivālayabuilt by Pṛthvīvilāsa of this same lineage, and worship is performed by all the families who have gathered for theKulapūjā. (Source: Priest of the temple, Gautama, male, age 69).
The current stone pinnacle of the temple was installed after the previous golden one was stolen.
A Śivaliṅga is consecrated in the sanctum, and there is also an additional Śivaliṅga inside the sanctum area, itsjalaharīfaces east.
The inscription installed to the north of the sanctum entrance informs us that it was constructed by Kaṃpālidāsa (Kapiladāsa) and his wife Māneśvarī in 1690 CE (NS 810).
The inscription does not mention the caste of Kaṃpālidāsa, but local residents believe that he was from a Pradhāna caste.
His family also constructed the Bicche Phalcā (KAT0941) which is adjacent to the temple.
Kaṃpilādāsa’s family endowed land to the temple and established aguṭhīto finance the daily, annual, occasional, and other rituals.
A fire oblation is performed on the day of Śrīpañcamī (Sarasvatīpūjā) in the adjacent Bicche Phalcā (KAT0941).

Within the palace courtyards, Buddhist monasteries (such asbāhāḥandbahī), and ascetics' abodes (maṭha) in the Kathmandu Valley, constructions of a temple orcaityain the middle and residential structures surrounding it were part of the cultural development.
Along the banks of the Bagmati River, from Vishnumati (Viṣṇumatī) to Bagmati (Vāgamtī), various temples enclosed by rest-houses from all four directions (caugharāsataḥ) were sequentially constructed.
Inside the temple, a large-sized Śivaliṅga has been installed.
The construction of this temple was initiated by King Rājendra in 1823 CE (VS 1879) for the salvation (nirvāṇa/mokṣa) of the consorts of King Raṇabahādura (see, bell inscription KAT2740_I_001 below).
Moreover, a stone inscription kept inside the sanctum, is coated with oily and other substances, completely covering the text inscribed on it.
After being destroyed by the earthquake of 1934 CE (VS 1990), the temple underwent reconstruction eleven years later (Amatya 1994, p.38).
The information released by King Rajendra in 1826-27 (VS 1883) is found related to this temple.
It can be estimated from this information that the construction was likely completed around the same time (E_2775_0039/K_0020_0026).

In the aftermath of the earthquake in 1934 CE, this temple, Vaṃśeśvara Temple (KAT1330), and Naudegaḥ (KAT1280), which were three-tiered pagoda-style structures, were reconstructed in the present dome-style.
Located just outside the Byāsī Gate on the northern periphery of Bhaktapur, this stone spout (hiti) was constructed in 1643 CE (NS 763) by Jāminī Mayī, a resident of Tupulāchi.

The Byāsī Gate itself was part of a broader network of city gates built for Bhaktapur’s defense, and thehitisituated immediately beyond it is locally known as theByāsī Dhvākhā Pine Hiti—the drinking fountain outside the Byāsī Gate.
An inscription from the time of thehiti’s construction records that Jāminī Mayī not only commissioned the water fountain but also installed the sacred images of Umāmaheśvara and Viśveśvara Mahādeva.
The text issues a warning that any act of desecration or damage would invite the wrath of Umāmaheśvara, Viśveśvara, and Cāmuṇḍādevī.
No efforts have been undertaken by the municipality, ward office, or other responsible institutions to restore or maintain the site.
Locally known asPigaṇcuka(Pīṭhachoka, “courtyard of thepīṭha”), it consists of a rectangular structure erected over amorphous stones set a few feet below ground level.
No early textual or inscriptional evidence documenting the shrine’s origin has been found.
No early inscriptions survive at the shrine.
The earliest epigraphic evidence, dated 1840–41 CE (NS 960), records the offering of a bell.

The present square-shaped shrine was reconstructed in 1940–41 CE (VS 1997), most likely following the destruction of an earlier structure in the 1934 CE (VS 1990) earthquake, as noted in the accompanying inscription.
On Vijayādaśamī (the final day of Daśaĩ festival), theguṭhi-members gather for a communal feast, while onSamaybaji Punhi, they offerpañcākūand partake insamaybajiin accordance with tradition.
Land has been endowed in the name of Mahālakṣmī to support these annual observances (one of theguṭhīmembers, Śākya, male, age 69).
A trident (triśūla) has been installed alongside the pinnacle and resembles the weapon of Lord Śiva.
At the bottom of each of the struts, one can find inscriptions that act as the captions of each specific image.
This temple was constructed by King Siddhinarasiṃha Malla in 1627 CE.
Vajrācārya(VS 2056, 69) surmises that this was the first temple the King had built.
The stone inscription placed at the plinth of the temple informs its readers that the King also made a golden spout to the west of the temple.
The upper roof of the temple collapsed in 1989 and was renovated by UNESCO in 1990.
The temple was severely damaged during the 2015 earthquake.
It was recently (2019) renovated by the KVPT.
Amakaramotif is carved on the conduit of thehitiand a statue of Vidhyādhara and Umāmaheśvara are respectively installed below and above the conduit.
Add to this, statues of Bhagīratha, Gaṇeśa, Candra, Lakṣmī, and alike, as well as aśivaliṅgaare also established in thehitipremises.
There are no evidences to date the initial construction of thehiti.
The iconographic program of the statues found in thehitipremises suggest that it could have been built sometime during the Late Malla Period (1482-1768 CE).
The stone inscription (from NS 942, i.e. 1822) installed in thehitipremises records the a pavement of the road above thehitiand of the yard in front of the Bhīmasena Mandira.
The Tīna Dhārā water spout, meaning "three spouts," is believed to have been constructed during the medieval period.
However, there is no clear historical record of when the spouts were first built.
However, there is a fourth spout on the eastern side of the compound, which locals believe was added during the Rāṇā period (a local resident, Ācārya, male, age 42).
Twośivaliṅgashave also been established within the Tīna Dhārā compound.

The spouts have undergone renovations twice: once in 1925 CE (VS 1982) by Colonel Madanamānasiṃha Basneta during the time of Prime Minister Candra Śamśera, and again in 2021 CE (VS 2078) by the joint efforts of the Jabara Jaṃga Gaṇa of the Nepalese Army and the local body.

According to a stone inscription, now stored inside a nearby house’s potato storage facility, thesattalawas constructed by Kājī Phaudavīra Rānā, son of Kājī Bandhu Rānā of Gorkhā, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, a Monday, in 1815 CE (VS 1872).

His grandfather, Jayarāma Rānā, participated in the Bhāradārī Assembly (D. Vajrācārya and Ṭ. Śreṣṭha VS 2037, p. 376), and his father, Bandhu Rānā, was a trusted associate of King Raṇabahādura Śāha, serving as Kājī alongside Dāmodara Pā̃ḍe (D. Vajrācārya VS 2019, p. 161).

Rāṇā Prime Minister Vīra Śamśera is believed to have constructed this temple in 1888 CE (VS 1945), likely dedicated to his uncle Jaṅga Bahādura.
Vīra Śamśera, who reigned from 1885 to 1901 CE, built four Śiva temples collectively known as Cāra Śivālaya, located south of the Rājarājeśvarī Mandira.
To the west of the temple, a figure of Nandī, Lord Śiva's animal mount, is placed, while a trident (triśūla) is erected on the northern side.
The bell that was originally installed on the southwestern side has been stolen.
There is no specific inscription documenting the construction of the temple.
It is speculated that the stolen bell may have contained an inscription related to the temple's construction.
Taṇḍaṇa (VS 2056, p. 353) mentions that the temple was built by Vīra Śamśera in 1888 CE (VS 1945).
It is likely that Vīra Śamśera erected the temple in memory of his uncle Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā, who had raised him at the Thapathali Palace (P. Rāja VS 2073, p. 99).
Vīra Śamśera, the son of Jaṅga Bahādura's younger brother Dhīra Śamśera, was the mastermind behind the assassination of Prime Minister Raṇa Uddīpa Siṃha in 1885 CE (VS 1942).
It is possible that Vīra Śamśera constructed the temple as an act of repentance for the assassination of his cousin, who was the son of the uncle who had raised him.
Since 1962 CE (VS 2019), an annual fire ritual (agnihotra) has been conducted in the building located behind the Jaṅgamukteśvara Mandira.

It does not have a separate monastic building (dyaḥchẽ).
Thetoraṇa, however, is now stored inside the sanctum to prevent further damage due to its poor condition.
At the Bāhāḥ premises, aśikharakūṭa caityahas been established.
By referring to an inscription on the pedestal of the Buddha statue in the sanctum, Pruscha (1975, 32 [K-80]) writes that the statue “was consecrated by Shakyabhikshu Cakrapati deba in 1754”.
However, Locke (1985, p. 348), citing the same inscription, mentions that the image was consecrated in NS 865, which corresponds to 1745 CE.
Because this inscription is no longer on the site (as of November 2022), it is unclear whether Locke misread the date or Pruscha converted it incorrectly to Common Era.
We also do not know if the pedestal of the statue with the inscription was stolen or replaced after Locke and Pruscha assessed the site.
