Despite the uncertainty surrounding its origins, the architectural characteristics suggest a construction date during the Rāṇā period (1846-1951 CE).
The Bāhāḥ is named after the name of its consecrator.
With the exception of the god house, all of the other buildings surrounding the courtyard are residential houses.
The main monastic building was heavily damaged by the earthquake and was dismantled by the residents of the Bāhāḥ.
The building is now under construction, and this work has so far reached the cornice level above the main door.
The reconstruction work has slightly changed the plan of the building by enabling access to the backyard through a narrow opening on the wall at the northern side.
The back side of the monastic building collapsed as a result of the 2015 earthquake, and although the front facade survived, it suffered severe cracking.
Before the earthquake, the three-storey Bāhāḥ had a tiled roof and acaitya-shaped pinnacle made of cement.
The metal pinnacle of the Bāhāḥ was stolen, and so Deep Man Shakya made this new,caitya-shaped one in its place.
A nearby Phalcācontained images of Mahākāla and Gaṇeśa, however it too collapsed as a result of the 2015 earthquake.
Lalitpur Municipality has donated 800,000.00 Nepalese Rupees (8 lakh) for the reconstruction of the Bāhāḥ.
In the first half of 2019, work on the ground floor was completed, and an image of Akṣobhya was installed.
The Bāhāḥ is being rebuilt in its original structure, though the roof of the ground floor is covered with corrugated metal sheets.
The reconstruction process came to a halt in the summer of 2019 as the next installment of the funding was not yet released.
The sataḥ was built in 1883 by a Satyal family and features unique and high-quality woodwork including an unusually shaped five-bay window on the first floor and oval windows on the ground floor.
The sataḥ was badly damaged during the 2015 earthquakes and was consequently rebuilt under a project financed by the Asia Development Bank (ADB).
The building's roof and its first floor collapsed completely in the 2015 earthquakes.
The Sataḥ was built in 1883 by a Satyal family who were residents of Kathmandu (Gutschow2011, 916).
The sattal at Purohitghat was one of the smaller endowments, but probably the most fascinating one.
Thisśivālaya, or the dwelling of Lord Śiva, was erected by Mohana Śamśera in 1933 CE (VS 1990) in honor of his father’s maternal uncle’s son, Ḍillī Śamśera Thāpa.
Additionally, a brass bell, hung by a bell-stand south of the temple, commemorates the temple's construction.
Mohana Śamśera, also known as the last Rāṇā prime minister, commissioned the temple's construction in 1933 CE (VS 1990) and donated the bell along with his family.

He dedicated the temple to the memory of Ḍillī Śamśera Thāpā, the eldest son of Candra Śamśera’s maternal uncle, Keśarasiṃha Thāpā. Ḍillī Śamśera Thāpā was one of 45 individuals who accompanied Candra Śamśera on his official visit to England in 1908 CE.
He passed away in 1928 CE (VS 1985).
The monument is located on a small hill, south of the Dullu palace (now destroyed).
It is built in bricks and covered by a two-storied tile roof.
Inside the sanctum, a small stepped platform is built along the north-western wall.
This statue is installed inside the temple.
The latter sculptures are placed inside a hypaethral concrete shrine of Kālikā built directly north-east of the temple.
The first roof is supported by wooden pillars installed all around the sanctum.
The actual monument may have been built in the 19th century, or during the 20th century.
A building of the Nepal Police was recently built in the western side of the hill.
A ping pong table made of cement was built 2 meters west of the Bhairava Temple.

Situated at Pakanājola in Kathmandu, this Temple of Goddess Bhagavatī was constructed by a Pā̃ḍe family in the mid-19thcentury on their private courtyard (see the inscription from VS 1909/ŚS1777 below).
With only one entrance on the southern side, the Temple is built on two plinths.
Statues of theaṣṭamātṛkāgroup along with Gaṇeśa and Mahākāla are also installed on the inner walls of the Temple.

An inscription east of the Bhagavatī Temple installed in VS 1909/ŚS 1777 by Kaptāna (Captain) Udaya Bahādura Pā̃ḍe and his wife Lalitā Devī records the construction of the Temple by his grandfather Raṇajita Pā̃ḍe, grandmother Candraprabhā, father Vīrakeśarī (inscription: Vīrakesara/Vīrakeśari) Pā̃ḍe, uncles Raṇagaṃbhīra (inscription: Raṇagaṃbhira), Dalakeśarī (inscription: Dalakeśari) and Kīrtidhvaja on their private courtyard, and land endowment made by them in order to operate the Temple.
However, it does not mention the date of the construction of the Temple.
The dates (the Vikrama Samvat Era year and Śaka Samvat Era year) of the installation of the inscription do not correspond to each other.
The VS 1909 (1853 CE) corresponds to Śaka Era year 1774 (1853 CE), but not 1777 (1856 CE).
A bell in front of the Temple was offered by General Jaya Bahādura Kũvara Rāṇā in 1850 CE (VS 1905).
It is likely that the bell was offered upon the construction of the Temple.
However,Pruscha(1975, p. 11) dates the Temple to VS 1905, i.e., 1848 CE, but without citing any sources.
In 1996 CE (VS 2053), Ḍambarajaṅga Pā̃ḍe renovated the Temple together with his wife Ratna Kumārī Pā̃ḍe and the family.
The 2015 earthquakes caused minor damage to it.
A shrine known as Nīla Vṛṣiratna (Dvahaḥ Āju) houses an ox that, at irregular intervals (most recently in VS 2062 /2008 CE) is the starting point of a religious pilgrimage (Dīpaṅkara Yātrā).
The building's design is reminiscent of the "Rana style" that developed in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
Originally, the building would probably have been built with regular bricks (ma apa) and decorated with white-washed plaster pilasters on the four corners.
In 2007, thevihārawas rebuilt with funding from the Lalitpur Municipality.
The removal of deteriorated facade bricks and their replacement with high qualitydaci apabricks was a major change.
Aśikharakūṭa caitya, adharmadhātu maṇḍalaand avajradhātu caityaare lined up on the axis of the building.
The classical name of the Bāhāḥ,Bhuvanākaravarmasaṃskārita Dharmakīrti Mahāvihāra, suggests that an individual named Bhuvanākara Varma established the monastery.
Locke(1980, 253) claims that the Bāhāḥ was established at least 100 years before the temple was constructed.
A historical photo (seePruscha2015, vol. II, p. 132) shows the single roof covered withjhĩgaṭītiles which were later replaced with copper sheets.
No inscriptions or documents related to the establishment of this Bāhāḥ could be found.
Local people mention that Taḥ Bāhāḥ was constructed so as to establish the Red Matsyendranātha in Lalitpur.
It is believed that the Akṣobhya statue was brought from Bhelakhu Bāhāḥ (LAL0230), and that a new image of Akṣobhya was installed there.
It was constructed in NS 931 (1811 CE) by a Mānāndhara family.
Constructed solely out of stone, the Caitya is erected on two layers of square plinths.
There used to be a stone statue of Padmapāṇi Lokeśvara at the northeast corner of the Caitya, which was relocated here from the nearbyphalcā(KIR4027) in ruins some six decades ago.

After thephalcāwas renovated by the municipality in 2020 CE, the statue of Lokeśvara was again shifted to its original place, i.e. to thephalcā. Śākya and Maharjana families from the area carry out minor repairs on the Caitya.
After the construction of the Cilancva Caitya (KIR0001) in NS 635 (1515 CE) by Jagatapāla Varmā, many Buddhist monuments likebāhāḥs andcaityas were built in the eastern quarter of Kirtipur.
Due to the construction of only Buddhist monuments in the area, the eastern quarter came to be known as 'Devagala'.
After NS 1055 (1935 CE), however, Buddhist monuments too started to appear in the Śivagala.
Previously, people believed that if anyone built a Buddhist monument in the Śivagala, he or his clan member(s) would die (Ś. ŚreṣṭhaVS 2057, p. 28).
The inscription related to this Caitya is installed in the above mentioned nearbyphalcā.
The inscription states that the Caitya was constructed by Dhana Mānandhara and his wife Tuyudhari in NS 931 (1811 CE).
It also prescribes that the anniversary of the Caitya should be conducted on the day of Kati Punhi, lamps should be lit andsamaybajion the same evening should be offered and distributed.
The three bays of the temple were originally accessible, however, they were sealed off in 2012 CE with iron bars and a channel gate.
Threetoraṇascrown these three bays, the centraltoraṇadating back to the late medieval period (1482-1768/69 CE).
The flankingtoraṇaswere stolen in 2000s and later replaced with new ones.
There is a big bell in front of the temple, which was installed in 1891 CE.

An inscription found in the temple dating 1744 CE (865 NS) records a person named ??kṛṣṇa Bhāro (two characters of his first name are illegible in the inscription) who gilded the Gaṇeśa statue and offered a golden pinnacle to the temple.
During the late medieval period, it was a common practice to offer golden pinnacles following the construction or the renovation of the temples.
It is not clear, however, that the pinnacle offered by ?? Kṛṣṇa Bhāro was after the construction or the renovation of the temple.
Moreover, the inscription refers to this temple as Calapota Gaṇeśa.
Thus, it is clear that this name was widely in use from around 1744 CE indicating that this temple was already in existence even before that time.
The inscription further records that ?? Kṛṣṇa Bhāro had also endowed threeropanīsof land to sustain the annual rituals of the temple.
Bhajana(hymns) singing takes place in thephalcā, constructed in the eastern part of the temple, every morning and evening.
Originally intended for planting the sacredtulasīplant, the Maṭha now sits in a state of disrepair, devoid of any greenery.

According to a now-lost inscription discovered on the site (refer to D. Vajrācārya and Ṭ. Śreṣṭha VS 2032, second part, p. 9, inscription no. 9), during the reign of Pratāpa Malla, a Brahmin constructed the Maṭha and allocated lands for its upkeep.
citations: (refer to D. Vajrācārya and Ṭ. Śreṣṭha VS 2032, second part, p. 9, inscription no. 9)

text: As of April 2024 CE, the Maṭha sees no rituals or worship, its significance seemingly faded with time.
Ikhālakhu Phalcā has recently been rebuilt using 'traditional' materials: wood and bricks.
The iron railings have been removed.
The construction was of cement (e.g., plinth) and plain wodden pillars and beams.
The local Śreṣṭha community (known as Sāhukhalaḥ, the trader clan) built this Phalcā.
It is therefore possible that the Phalcā was built at this time.
A statue of Viṣṇu is placed to commemorate a man's death, whilst one of Lakṣmī is erected to commemorate a woman.
Many of the installed statues have been taken, and an iron railing has been fixed around the bays to protect them.
Thehiticame to be known as Gũ Bāhāḥ Hiti, as it was established to provide water for the daily rituals at Gũ Bāhāḥ, which is the old name of Jogeśvara Mandira (SKH0510).
Ajaḥdhuṃis installed on either side of the hiti.
Thishitiwas established in 1168 CE (NS 288) during the reign of King Rudradeva.
It was commissioned by an individual in memory of his deceased mother, father, and son.
Unfortunately, the sponsor’s name is unclear due to the breakage of the inscription that records this event.

Additionally, there is a broken piece of another conduit west of thehiti, with an inscription indicating that it was constructed by a person, along with his wife Bhuvaneśvarī and son Raṇavīrasiṃ, in 1705 CE (NS 825).
This Phalcā was established by either the Nijānanda or the Kṛṣṇa Praṇāmī sect of the Vaiṣṇava denomination of Hinduism.
The president of the Bungmati branch of the sect Jñānabhakta collected donations from the locals to construct the Phalcā in 1995.
After its construction, Kṛṣṇabhajanaswere performed regularly in the Phalcā.
In 1997, an organisation named Nijānanda Bhajana Maṇḍala was formed to organise chants on the first floor of the building.
However, this also came to an end with the 2015 earthquakes.
The Phalcā was badly damaged and was not rebuilt until 2019, where the Centre for Integrated Urban Development (CIUD) rebuilt the structure from scratch in 2019 using all new materials.
The complex was first constructed by King Jayaprakāśa Malla, the last ruler of Kathmandu, who built 21 stone spouts (hitis).
In 1798 CE (VS 1855), King Raṇabahādura Śāha added an additional spout, increasing the total to twenty-two, after which the site became known as Bāisadhārā.

Within the garden precinct, several shrines and images have been established, including those of Gaṇeśa (BLJ0010-001), Garuḍa Nārāyaṇa (BLJ0010-009), Umāmaheśvara (BLJ0010-015), Bhagīratha (BLJ0010-016), Mahālakṣmī (BLJ0010-022), and Sūrya (BLJ0010-028), alongside a Śītalādevī temple and an image of Jalaśayana Nārāyaṇa.

In modern times, the flow of water into the spouts has been disrupted due to the construction of a reservoir by the Kathmandu Valley Water Supply Corporation, which diverted the natural source (P. Jośī 2022, p. 203).
In 1961 CE (VS 2018), Minister of Agriculture Sūryabahādura Thāpā initiated the transformation of the site into a landscaped public space named Mahendra Udyāna (Mahendra Park).
Completed in 2021 VS (1964 CE), it was formally designated as the Bāisadhārā Udyāna (Garden of the Twenty-Two Spouts).
Aśikharakūṭacaityais established at the center of the Courtyard.
The 2015 earthquakes badly damaged the houses of this Courtyard.
Some of the houses are yet to be renovated and are on the verge of collapse.
Many residents of the Mū Cuka have already moved out, and they gather here only on special occasions like annual worship andguthis (local knowledge, local resident, Vajrācārya, male, age 53).
citations: (local knowledge, local resident, Vajrācārya, male, age 53)

text: There are no inscriptions in this Courtyard.
Most of the residents who know about the history of the Mū Cuka have already moved out.

The historic Suntvāḥ Sataḥ, the largest rest house at Suntvāḥ (Sun Ṭola), was destroyed in 1988 and rebuilt as a 2 1/2-story tall modern brick and concrete structure covered by a corrugated metal roof.
In February 2022, the Sataḥ was dismantled for reconstruction.
The current reconstruction effort envisions a traditional design even though no historic materials of the Sataḥ seem to have survived the 1988 destruction.
The history of the Sataḥ is not documented, however, local residents believe that the original Sataḥ was built around the time the annual procession of Vajrayoginī first commenced.

According to theMaṇiśailaMahāvadāna,a Buddhist scripture, Jogadeva Vajrācārya organized a procession of Vajrayoginī together with a goldencaityaand statues of Siṃhinī and Vyāghrinī in 1317 BCE (Kaligata Era 1818) (V. VajrācāryaNS 1119, p. 34).
A group of local mucicians, the Suntvāḥ Bhajana Maṇḍala, used to perform devotional songs every morning in the upper floor of the Sataḥ until it was dismantled.
The pedestal of Nandī, thevāhanaof Lord Śiva, contains two inscriptions.
They record the establishment of a non-expendable fund of 50moharas for worshipping Sumeśvara Mahādeva on the day ofŚivarātrīand offering animal sacrifice at Suntvāḥ Gaṇeśa Shrine.
The year of the donation and the names of the donors are illegible.
A marble inscription at the Sataḥ deals with the renovation of the Mahādeva Shrine funded by Lakṣṃībhakta Śreṣṭha and his family in memory of his parents.
However, the upper floor was demolished after the 2015 earthquake (2072 VS) due to safety concerns.
Though there is no inscription detailing the construction date of Tyāgaḥ Sataḥ, the carved columns (thāmā) suggest it dates back to the early Śāhā or Rāṇā period.
The two-storey building faces east, and anaṣṭakoṇoparipadma caityastands in front of its sanctum.
The principal façade of the monument building has a carved wooden door at its centre flanked by two small lattice windows.
The literal meaning of Naḥ Bāhāḥ is ‘a new monastic building’.
Recently, the monastic building located at the north-east corner of this small monastic building was known as Naḥ Bāhāḥ.
No sources could be found with which to date the initial construction of thisbāhāḥcā.
Pruscha 1975(1975, C/P-53) dates this monument to the 17th century and mentions that it was renovated by aguṭhīin 1933, though he does not provide evidence to support this claim.
A palm-leaf manuscript dated NS 688 (1548 CE) makes mention of a monastic building named Naka Bāhāra.

This specific rock, bearing six separate inscriptions containing royal directives, confirms that rocks were procured from this site during the medieval period for crafting various stone artifacts and objects of worship.
Four natural rock formations in Nālāchāpa, a village northeast of Bhaktapur, bear inscriptions referencing Malla kings.
Six inscriptions found here corroborate this, naming kings Jagajyoti Malla, Jitāmitra Malla, and Bhupatīndra Malla.
These inscriptions imply a specific purpose for the stone selection.

The earliest inscription, dating back to 1625 CE (NS 745), reveal that during the reign of King Jagajyoti Malla, stone carvers named Manajurāma, Rāyarāma, and Vā(su)ki worked on artistic projects at this site (J. Maharjana NS 1135, p. 29).
Regardless, this discovery confirms that stones from this site were integral to the construction of statues and monuments in Bhaktapur during the later-medieval period.

Two inscriptions from the reign of King Viṣṇu Gupta, dated to the Mānadeva Era 64 and 65 (corresponding to 640 and 641 CE), detail the transportation of stone within the valley for sculpting statues (D. Vajrācārya VS 2030, pp. 446-448).

These records indicate that residents of Sunāguthi (a town southwest of Patan) and Dakṣiṇakolīgrāma were rewarded with the privilege of wearing jewelry for their service in transporting stones for the creation of Buḍhānīlakaṇṭha, the reclining Viṣṇu statue located north of Kathmandu.

Artistic creations crafted from this stone often proudly proclaimed their origin. Śrīnivāsa Malla, the king of Patan, generously provided Koṭakhā stone to Jitāmitra Malla, the king of Bhaktapur, at the latter's request to renovate the Kumārī Coka (Tevārī and others VS 2019, pp. 24-25).
Similarly, in 1691 CE (NS 811), Crown Prince Bhūpatindra Malla utilized Koṭakhā stone to restore a water spout in the Bhaktapur palace (Vaidya & Shrestha 2002, p. 207).
There is speculation that the stone procured by Viṣṇu Gupta for the Buḍhānīlakaṇṭha statue and the Koṭakhā stone originated from the same quarry (D. Vajrācārya VS 2030, p. 446).
Intriguingly, four massive rock formations at Nālāchāpa bear inscriptions referencing both Bhaktapur and Kathmandu kings.
While the inscribed rock formations from Nālāchāpa may be slightly less refined than those from Koṭakhā, their extensive use in sculpting Bhaktapur's stone artifacts is evident.
An inscription on one of these stones reveals that Jitāmitra Malla initiated stonework for a grand fire sacrifice in 1693 CE (NS 813).
P. Śreṣṭha (VS 2078, p. 1) suggests that this marked the beginning of stone selection for the construction of the Vatsalā temple in the same year.
Bhupatindra Malla, Jitāmitra's son, continued this tradition, as evidenced by a 1715 CE (NS 835) inscription.
Collectively, these inscriptions confirm the quarry's essential role in producing the numerous artifacts that symbolize Bhaktapur's prosperity during the medieval period.
The family of the house that the Phalcāis attached to were also the ones who commissioned it.
A descendant of the donors transformed one bay of the Phalcāinto a small shop and built rooms on the first floor; in doing so, they removed its tiled roof.
Coomaraswamy(1972, 144) notes that the fourstūpasof Patan, still intact, were constructed in an ancient Indian hemispherical style.
According to legend, during the reign of the 14th Kiranti King, King Sthaṃko, King Aśoka visited Nepal and commissioned the construction of these fourstūpas.
He purportedly financed the construction of the four caityas on the four sides of Lalitpur in the Kali era 3608-9, on the 5th day of the bright half of Māgha (Devamālā Vaṃśāvalī1956, 71).
Although (Pruscha1975, 144) asserts that these statues were established in 1455 CE, no inscription verifying this date was found within thestūpaarea.
An inscription dated to 1561 CE (NS 681) mentions the renovation of thestūpa(D. VajracharyaVS 2056, 21), yet this inscription is now lost.
Subsequent renovations occurred in 1959 (Pruscha1975, 144), and following the earthquakes of 2015, the Department of Archaeology undertook further restoration efforts.
Over time, the finial has undergone frequent changes, and approximately 15 years ago, a cast concrete balustrade supporting oil lamps and prayer wheels was added.
Due to the inactivity of the concerned trust and the ongoing debate about road expansion, this temple dedicated to Hariśaṃkara stands in a dilapidated state by the roadside, awaiting reconstruction.
Located at the Bhansāra Ṭola in Cāpāgāũ, this brick temple is built on a two-tiered plinth facing west.
Inside the sanctum, only the pedestal of the main deity remains, as the Hariśaṃkara statue was stolen in the 1980s (local resident, Śreṣṭha, male, age 73).
Without any efforts for restoration, the dilapidated temple’s condition deteriorates day by day.
The area from the platform to the tower is overgrown with weeds and looks unsightly, while the western part of the domed roof has already collapsed.
Despite this, no significant efforts for repair or reconstruction have been seen.
There are no historical records in the temple that reveal its construction details.
One of the ancestors that of the Kāyastha clan was probably responsible for the construction of the temple.

monument_name: Devala Divyapura, śikhara temple 2 (from approx. 8th-10th century)
text: These architectural features evoke temples built in Uttarakhand (India) around the 7th-8th century, and especially Temples 1 and 2 in Jageshwar (seeChanchani 2019, 81-83, fig. 3.7.).

monument_name: Devala Divyapura, śikhara temple 2 (from approx. 8th-10th century)
text: It may thus be suggested that this monument, as well as the four others found at the site, was built between the 8th and 10th century (Andolfatto 2022, 38;Sharma 2012, 284).
In 1918 CE (NS 1038), Rājamānasiṃha and his wife Āsāthakuṃ renovated this caitya and donated land and cash to fund various activities at the monument.
There are no historical records revealing the exact construction period or the donor of the caitya.
In 1918 CE (NS 1038), Rājamānasiṃha (text: Lājamāṃsi) and his wife Āsāthakuṃ of Koṣāchẽ Nani in Thecva undertook restoration work on the caitya.
They also established a land endowment and a non-expendable fund of Rs. 200 to support its upkeep.
The income generated from the land endowment and interest from the fund was designated for the regular maintenance of the caitya.
The endowment also stipulated that lamps should be lit at the caitya on the full moon day of Āśvina.
A stone statue of Sṛṣṭikānta Lokeśvara is consecrated inside the Dyaḥchẽ’s sanctum, however,Pruscha1975, p 190 [P-218]  has identified it as Padmapāṇi Lokeśvara.
Thesaṅghamembers of Hyana Bāhāḥ opine that Nīlakaṇṭha Lokeśvara should have been consecrated instead of Sṛṣṭikānta Lokeśvara.
Based on the above-mentioned facts, thesaṅghamembers of the Hyana Bāhāḥ consecrated a wooden statue of Nīlakaṇṭha Lokeśvara in front of Sṛṣṭikānta Lokeśvara in 2019 CE (VS 2076).
There are no historical sources to date the initial construction of this monument, however, Lokeśvara is mentioned in several chronicles (vaṃśāvalī).
Thedyaḥchẽwas renovated in 1730 CE (cf.Pruscha1975, p. 190).
In 2019 CE (VS 2075), it was reconstructed from the ground up with the financial support from the Lalitpur Municipality.
To manage and preserve this vital resource, a stone structure in the shape of aśikhara(temple spire) was built directly over the spring—a relatively rare architectural solution in the region.

Locally, this well is known asNhūvapi, meaning “new well.” The termvāpi, found in an inscription at the site, derives from Sanskrit and refers to a spring, pond, or any natural water-collecting place.
The nameNhūvapiimplies that a more modest or informal water source likely existed here before the construction of the current structure.
The well is accessed through a doorway, and an image of Viṣṇu is installed at its upper part.
Although thephalcāwas dismantled around the mid-2000s (circa VS 2060), remnants such as roof tiles and carved stones still lie scattered near the site.
Over time, the well became overgrown and neglected, but it was eventually restored through an initiative led by Ward No. 7 of Dhulikhel Municipality.
An inscription placed on the upper part of the structure provides details about its founding.
It records that the well was constructed in 1928 CE (VS 1985), during the reign of King Tribhuvana and the premiership of Candra Śamśera.
The project was commissioned by Viṣṇulāla Mākaḥju, his wife Vālamāyā, and his brother Kṛṣṇalāla.
The inscription expresses the family's wishes for the prosperity of their descendants and the enduring continuity of their lineage.
This practice continued until the early 1990s (around VS 2050) but has since ceased.
Pruscha(2015, 135) assumes that thiscaityawas constructed in the 18th century.
A stone inscription to the south of the caitya is illegible.
Only two historical buildings remain, all others were constructed in 2018.
Within this sacred precinct, alongside the principalpīṭhaof Bhadrakālī, several tutelary deities of the Newar community are also established.
The original entrance had deteriorated over time and was replaced with a cement gateway in 1981 CE (VS 2038).
An inscription dated 1578 CE (NS 698) records that these lions were installed by Vīrabhadra Bhāro during the reign of Nṛpendra MallaŚ.
RājavaṃśīVS 2078 p. 93, S. Amātya VS 2053, p. 7).
A popular legend recounts that ajyāpuonce encountered a crying girl in a field and offered her his bread.
According to chronicle, after establishing the city of Kāntipura, King Guṇakāmadeva installed Bhadrakālī on the eastern side of the settlement as a protective deity (D. Lamsāla, VS 2023, p. 24).
The earliest attested ritual tradition associated with the site is the Bhadrakālī dance, believed to have begun in 1485 CE (NS 605) during the reign of King Ratna Malla.

The oldest extant inscription discovered here dates to the reign of Nṛpendra Malla (1674–1680 CE) and is carved on a stone pillar in front of the shrine, recording that Vīrabhadra Bhāro installed the stone lions in 1578 CE (NS 698) (Ś. Rājavaṃśī VS 2078 p. 93).
From the late 17th century onward, the site underwent several phases of renovation.
An inscription from 1672 CE (NS 792) attests that during the reign of Pratāpa Malla, Rāma Daivajña and Mohan Bhāro restored thecaṭhāra(resting pavilion).
Further repairs occurred under Nṛpendra Malla in 1678 CE (NS 798) and 1680 CE (NS 800), and under Pārthivendra Malla in 1686 CE (NS 806) and again in 1747 CE (NS 867).

During the rule of the last Malla king, Jayaprakāśa Malla, his minister Amātya Jorāvara Siṃha constructed adharmasālāat Lūrmaḍhi and endowed a trust (guṭhī) to maintain nightlydīpamālāillumination at the shrine.
The gilttoraṇawith the Aṣṭamātṛkā and serpent motifs was offered by General Bama Bahādura Kũvara in 1852 CE (VS 1908).
In 1870 CE (VS 1927), Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa Taṇḍukāra of Kathmandu, his wife Dharmalakṣmī, and their relatives restored thehiti,sat:and bells of thepīṭha.

Another inscription (KAT3380_I_011) records that Indra Bahādura Taṇḍukāra of Putalisadak bequeathed his house on the condition that annual rites—śrāddhaandpiṇḍa—be performed in his name using the interest from donated funds managed by the Taṇḍukāraguṭhīof Khĩcā Pokharī (KAT3380_I_016).

Since 2024 CE (VS 2081), Kathmandu Metropolitan City and the Bagmati Province Department of Heritage and Tourism have been undertaking the reconstruction of the surroundingsattalaand boundary structures.

This rite is performed annually on the fourteenth day of dark fortnight of Kārttika (Piśāca Caturdaśī) at the fire-pit (homa-kuṇḍa) in front of the shrine and includes the offering of a buffalo head (V. Vajrācārya NS 1107, p. 3).
Every twelve years, the Bhadrakālī dance is performed, featuring the Aṣṭamātṛkā retinues, a tradition said to originate in 1485 CE (NS 605) (S. Amātya VS 2053, p. 8).
At the onset ofDaśaĩ, the image of the goddess is ceremonially brought from thedyaḥchẽin Saṅkaṭā and installed at thepīṭha.
A Digi Chẽ is a multiple-storey building in abāhāḥthat often houses an esoteric deity and has long halls for hosting feasts.
This Digi Chẽ is also used for organizing feasts related to Taḥ Bāhāḥ’s (LAL0050)guthis,usually hosted by members of the monastic association (saṃgha).
The building has three stories and is attached to the esoteric shrine (āgaṃ) of Taḥ Bāhāḥ (LAL0050), which towers above the eastern entrance to the courtyard.
According to the locals, the Digi Chẽ used to be a traditional two-story building with ajhĩgaṭītile roof.
About 30-40 years ago (ca. 1980/1990 CE, exact date not recorded), thesaṃghamembers of Taḥ Bāhāḥ reconstructed the building as a concrete structure.
Locals say that Bhājurāma Bhāro got this Phalcā constructed on the ground floor of his residence.
He also commissioned the construction of the Bhāgeśvara Mandira (SKH0013) and Śiva Mandira Sataḥ (SKH0014).
Hence, he got aphalcāconstructed on the ground floor of his own house.
As the building was old and on the verge of collapse, it was rebuilt along with the Phalcā in 2010 CE.
Old pillars of the Phalcā were reused in the reconstruction.
There is a three-story building on top of the Phalcā.
The ground floor of the building attached to the Phalcā has now been rented out.
A raised square platform for thetulasīplant (tulasī-maṭha) is established in front of the temple, along with a stone pillar.
No historical records are available to date the temple’s construction.
According to locals, the temple was built during the medieval period.
The temple was damaged in the 2015 CE earthquakes and reconstructed in 2023 CE (VS 2080) by the Department of Archaeology.
Notably, it withstood the 2015 earthquakes without significant damage.
As a result, even after nearly a decade since the earthquake, no restoration effort could be initiated.
No inscription has been found on the monument, and therefore its date of construction remains unknown.
Local belief maintains that Ācāḥju Phalcā was built by an ancestor of this lineage, and its name derives from this association.

A large stretch of land surrounding the monument also belongs to the Ācāḥju lineage, suggesting that the arcaded platform was likely to be constructed along the edge of their agricultural fields to provide shelter during sudden rainfall and storms.

Interest in the reconstruction of Ācāḥju Phalcā has been expressed by heritage enthusiasts from outside the locality; however, the residents living around the site have shown little initiative toward its restoration.
The lack of local engagement in reconstruction appears to stem from this broader mindset.

Although the water spout itself is now (as of June 2023) in a state of disrepair and no longer functional, the presence of a rare statue of Sūrya, the sun deity, on the premises adds significant historical value to the site.
According to Bangdel (1995, p. 101), the Sūrya statue dates back to the 12th century, while G. Ṭaṇḍana (VS 2053, p. 652) places its origin in the 12th-13th century.
There are no inscriptions documenting the construction of the Aruṇa Dhārā, and it remains unclear how the water spout acquired its name.

An inscription from 679 CE (Mānadeva Era 103) found at Vajraghara mentions Licchavi King Narendradeva constructing several water spouts in the Paśupati area and entrusting the monks of the Śiva Vihāra with their upkeep (D. Vajrācārya VS 2030, p. 503).
It remains unclear whether the Aruṇa Dhārā was one of the spouts built by King Narendradeva.
Viṣṇumukteśvara Mahādeva temple, founded in 1858 CE (VS 1915), is dedicated to Viṣṇukumārī, one of Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā's wives.
The temple is constructed using stone and showcases a unique bell-shaped roof topped with a metallic pinnacle.
The primary western entrance is adorned with an inscription below itstoraṇa, offering insights into the temple's construction.
Statues of Durgā in the northwest and Viṣṇu in the northeast have, unfortunately, been stolen.
Further east, on the retaining wall, a statue of Kāmadeva, the deity of love in Eastern mythology, is installed.
The temple was constructed in honor of Viṣṇukumārī, the wife of Prime Minister Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā, and hence received the name Viṣṇumukteśvara.

Viṣṇukumārī, the daughter of Cautariyā Raṇaśera Śāha, gave birth to her son Padmajaṅga Rāṇā, who authored the bookLife of Maharaja Sir Jung Bahadur of Nepal(B. Bhaṇḍārī VS 2071, p. 135; P. Rāja VS 2071, p. 77).
citations: (B. Bhaṇḍārī VS 2071, p. 135; P. Rāja VS 2071, p. 77)

text: While she is recognized as a formally-wedded wife of Jaṅga Bahādura, specific details regarding her birth and death years remain unclear (P. Rāṇā VS 2059, p. 192).
Despite being built in honor of Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā's wife, Viṣṇumukteśvara temple currently does not observe any periodic rituals, including daily ceremonies.
It has been heavily reconstructed and was converted to a four-storey residential building after the 2015 earthquakes.
The original architecture of the building has been completely destroyed, so that only traces of the brass-clad door, two blind windows and some layers of cornices remain today (in 2019).
The main building is raised on a plinth which is 60 cm high.
The courtyard is surrounded by residential buildings on three of the four cardinal directions, with the eastern side as the exception.
The Bāhāḥ is a privatevihāraconstructed by a Joshi family; it is not a branch of any largerbāhāḥ.
Accoding toPruscha(1975, 133), thisvihārawas constructed in the 16th century.
According toLocke(1985, 140) two metal flags used to flank the door and atoraṇawas installed above the main entrance.
However, it seems that thetoraṇawas removed by the residing family of thevihārasome time around 2008.
The building was severely damaged and was no longer safe to live in.
Therefore the owner demolished the building and reconstructed it in a modern style.
After the reconstruction the family sold the building.
Local people say that the family also sold the ground floor of the building where thekvāpādyaḥof thevihārais enshrined.
The bell was donated in VS 1959.
This front part is structurally disconnected from the main part of the building.
The architectural features of the monument evoke temples built in Uttarakhand (India) around the 7th-8th century, and especially Temples 1 and 2 in Jageshwar (seeChanchani 2019, 81-83, fig. 3.7.).
It may thus be suggested that this monument, as well as the four others found at the site, was built between the 8th and 10th century (Andolfatto 2022, 38;Sharma 2012, 284).
Below the spout stands an image of Bhagīratha, and another Bhagīratha sculpture is positioned on the northern wall—possibly relocated from anotherhitiorjaḥdhūṇin the vicinity.
Although no inscription directly related to its construction has been discovered, local tradition holds that the Hiti dates back to the Malla period.
The only extant epigraphical record at the site is a stone inscription dated 1817 CE (NS 938).
It records that Vidyānanda Śarmā established aphalcāalong with images of Umā-Maheśvara and Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa at Corcā Hiti.

While the pavilion and the Umā-Maheśvara image have not survived, the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa sculpture mentioned in the inscription likely corresponds to the image (BKT0820-007) still visible on the Hiti’s northern wall.
Water continued to flow abundantly from the spout until around 1978 CE (VS 2035), after which increasing urbanization caused the spring to dry up.
In 1995–1996 CE (VS 2052–2053), local residents attempted to restore the Hiti and revive the flow (local resident, Gorkhālī caste, male, age 66), but the source had already been blocked.
There are no historical records to date its construction.
Thehitihas one water spout, which is shrouded by bushes and has no running water (as of 2022 CE), due to the lack of regular maintenance.
According to locals, water used to flow from thehitiup until early 2000 CE (local resident, Khaḍgī, male, age 49).
The construction of many houses in the area has probably disturbed the natural flowing of the water.
The courtyard space is occupied by building materials, fallen objects and abandoned materials.
The space urgently needs cleaning and restoration as its exposure to rain and sun has caused the materials to decay.

A fallen object almost covers the deity (although this is a replacement for the orignial one, which was stolen) and the main door is locked - it seems, therefore, that daily rituals no longer take place here.
This Bāhāḥ is basically a courtyard with a monastic building on its eastern side.
The main building has two storeys and is in a dilapidated condition.
Local people informed us that the roof of the Bāhāḥ collapsed in the 2015 earthquake.
The sanctum of the Bāhāḥ once contained a stone image of Akṣobhya, which has apparently been stolen.
A new cement statue of Akṣobhya has been enshrined to replace it.
Vajrācārya(1993, 136) mentiones that the sanctum also contained a smallcaityaas well as images of Mañjuśrī, Gaṇeśa and Mahākāla and two stone inscriptions.

It is claimed that this Bāhāḥ is a branch of Śrīvatsa Mahāvihāra standing nearby, and that Dhīrjapati Vajrācārya from Yaśodhara Mahāvihāra Saṅgha renovated this Bāhāḥ when it was in a state of neglect.

After the earthquake, the daily and annual rituals of the Bāhāḥ came to an end.Śākya(1993, 137) mentions  an inscription dated NS 980 in the sanctum, which makes it clear that this Bāhāḥ was already in existence at that period.
The upper floor features an artistic traditional nevārī window (sãjhyāḥ), while the facade is constructed withdāciappā.
The sataḥ consists of two distinct sections, the inner part is said to have collapsed 20 years ago and was recently (July 2024) reconstructed in an L-shape.
There are no inscriptions detailing the construction of the sataḥ.
The Pyākurela family maintains the sataḥ and believes their ancestor Harinātha Pyākurela built it (local resident, Pyākurela, male, age 81).
Along the route from Sindhulī to Dapcā, and from Syāmapāṭī to Kathmandu, many sataḥ were constructed as resting places for traveling merchants.
This sataḥ was likely built for the same purpose.
However, over time, it has fallen into disrepair as it no longer serves this original function.
The construction of private residences in front of the sataḥ has further diminished its artistic and cultural value.
In contrast to otherbāhāḥs where some rooms or houses are used for residential purposes, Hakha Bāhāḥ utilizes the entire building.
This three-tier building has copper roofs and threecaitya-shaped pinnacles.
Praying wheels have also been installed at both sides of the channel gate.
At each of the four corners of the courtyard there are doors that lead to the upper floor of the building.
The inscriptions refer to thisbāhāḥas Lakṣmīkalyāṇavarmasaṃskārita Ratnākaramahāvihāra, implying its likely establishment by a person named Lakṣmīkalyāṇavarman.

According to theNepālikabhūpavaṃśāvalī13.275 and 19.3.10-11, thisbāhāḥ, originally located where Patan Durbar Square now stands, was moved to its current site by Siddhinarasiṃha Malla during the expansion of his palace.

While there is no available source material specifying the establishment period, a palmleaf deed dated NS 269 mentions "Hatako Vihāra," an earlier name for thisbāhāḥ, indicating its existence as far back as the 12th century.

The statue of Hanumān, a god depicted in a monkey-like form, is believed to have been established by King Raṇajita Malla.
Hanumān is depicted seated on his left knee, with his right hand in the boon-granting gesture (varada mudrā) and his left hand in a protective gesture (abhaya mudrā).
To protect the statue from the weather, a tin roof has been installed over it.
This statue is believed to date back to the 18th-19th century of the Vikrama era (Ṭaṇḍana VS 2056, p. 469).
Unfortunately, there is no historical source available to determine the exact date of the shrine's initial construction.
However, the priest of the shrine claims that the statue was established by King Raṇajīta Malla, who reigned from 1722 to 1769 CE.
The installation of the tin roof over the statue took place in 2019 CE (VS 2076), with the previous small parasol being replaced through the assistance of devotees (priest, Ācārya, male, age 56).
Among the Mātṛkā goddesses installed at various locations for the protection of Kathmandu, Porpā Ajimā occupies a significant place.
Since the goddess was installed in the forest of the Porpā demon, she came to be known as Porpā Ajimā (local resident, Mānāndhara caste, male, age 72).
In earlier times, criminals sentenced to death were executed in the forest where Porpā Ajimā is now installed.
After attainingsiddhithere, she became renowned as Porpā Ajimā (P. Tāmrākāra, NS 1124 [2004–2005 CE], p. 45).
Within the Ranībārī forest, thepīṭhaof Porpā Ajimā is established in an open clearing.
Inside, an aniconic stone representing Porpā Ajimā (Cāmuṇḍā) is installed facing south-east, surmounted by a stonetoraṇa.
Additional stones symbolizing other Mātṛkās are present, along with several recently installed images.
No inscription relating to the original establishment of Porpā Ajimā has so far been discovered.
The forest was subsequently protected and organized by the wife of Pracaṇḍaśamśer, who had a surrounding wall constructed for its preservation.
Pracaṇḍaśamśer was the eldest son of Fatyāśamśer, himself the seventh son of Dhīraśamśer (P. Yādava, VS 2045 [1988–1989 CE], genealogy appendix).
The earliest inscription found within the vicinity ofpīṭhadates to 1980 CE (VS 2037).

This record states that Pañcamāyā Khaḍge of Mahārājagañja constructed thephalcāto the north of the Porpā Ajimā Pīṭha in memory of her deceased father-in-law Śermāna Khaḍge, mother-in-law Ratnamāyā, husband Surjamāna Khaḍge, son Rāmeśvara, and other departed family members.
Rumal Stone Fountain in Lamji, built between 14th and 16th centuries, is accessible via a motorable path that departs from the Dullu's central area.
On both sides of the fountain, a larger platform made of stone and cement has been added.
The central panel has been partially dismantled and reconstructed with small carved stones.

Given that a similar fountain was built in Dullu in 1568 CE (DLK0370) and that it is located near the Lamji Pañcadevala (DLK0320), which is likely to date from the 13th-15th century, it is possible to speculate that this Fountain was constructed between the 14th and 16th centuries, corresponding to the late period of the Khaśa Malla regime (12th-14th century) and the period of the succeeding Rāskoṭi dynasty.
There are no historical sources to date the initial construction of this Temple.

However,Ś. Śreṣṭha(VS 2057, 45), without refereeing to any sources, mentions that it was constructed by Hastikā (one of the nannies of King Raṇabahādura Śāha) in 1803 CE during the renovation of the Bāghabhairava Temple (KIR0004).

According to the elders of this area, the octagonal gilded pinnacle was established by a certain Jītavīra (who was supposedly a government employee), a resident of the Tuṃjhvaḥ Ṭola (Kirtipur) when he renovated the Temple in 1932 CE (VS 1988) by the order of Prime Minister Juddha Śamśera (r. 1 September 1932 - 29 November 1945).
The inscription inscribed on the pinnacle records this information.
It was probably during this renovation the temple’s structure was changed from a tiered style to a domed style.
From his time onwards, several damaged temples were reconstructed in the domed shape.
The present look of the Nārāyaṇa Mandira dates back to 1952 CE (VS 2009).
Around the same time, aguṭhīwas established to look after the Temple and conduct the daily rituals here (Ś. Śṛeṣṭha,1994, 87).
A statue of Śrīdharaviṣṇu standing on thesamapādaposture is consecrated inside its sanctum.
Beside these, a statue of a donor couple in greeting posture (namaskāramudrā) is also erected inside the sanctum.
The descendants of Jītavīra who had renovated the Temple in 1932 CE used to clean the Temple premises, paint the Temple and perform its anniversary rituals.
They had also endowed some plots of land for this purpose.
Rānīpokharī, situated at the heart of Kathmandu, is a man-made pond constructed by King Pratāpa Malla in 1669 CE (NS 790) on the full moon day of the bright fortnight of Kārtika.
The pond, built in memory of his beloved son Cakravartendra Malla, lies on the eastern boundary of thehistoric city and holds both religious and aesthetic significance.
Prior to its construction, the site was referred to asMasāḥkhyaorMasāncaura(“cremation ground”) (G. Ṭaṇḍana, VS 2077, p. 315).
Originally erected in the śikhara style, the temple enshrined the central deity of the pond.
From the elephant’s trunk hangs a grotesque human figure with long hair, locally believed to represent a son of Pratāpa Malla by a concubine (G. Ṭaṇḍana, VS 2077, p. 315).

According to traditional belief, its waters were brought from sacred pilgrimage sites across Nepal and India, and bathing in them was thought to absolve sins and grant the merit of visiting those sites.

According to R. Tivārī (VS 2040, p. 23), three inscriptions once recorded the same text: one on the eastern wall of Vīra Hospital, another on the wall of the Nācaghara at Jamal, and a third within Seto Durbar.
As of July 2025, only the Jamal inscription survives, though its lower portion containing the date remains buried.

Composed in the Nepali language, it records full-moon day of the bright fortnight of Kārtika, in the [Saṃvat] year 1592, while its parallel Newar version mentions ful-moon day of bright fortnight of Āśvina, in NS 790.
Additional inscriptions, carved in two lines on each side of the elephant sculpture at the northern edge of the pond, also remain (Vajrācārya and Panta, VS 2018, p. 26).
The inscriptions note that Pratāpa Malla dedicated the pond in memory of Cakravartendra Malla, for whom he had even issued coins.
The prince’s premature death in 1669 CE (VS 1726) deeply grieved the king, leading him to construct the pond as an act of mourning and spiritual redemption.
Later, Queen Bhuvanalakṣmī, consort of Bhūpālendra Malla, completed the consecration rituals, after which the site came to be known as Rānīpokharī, the “Queen’s Pond” (R. Tivārī, VS 2040, p. 24).
The original śikhara-style Bālagopāleśvara Temple was destroyed in the 1934 CE (VS 1990) earthquake.
It was rebuilt under Juddha Śaṃśera Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā in a markedly different form: a two-tiered square structure crowned with a dome.
Based on its material and form, scholars hypothesize that the original deity may have been Bālagopāla rather than a Śivaliṅga (G. Ṭaṇḍana, VS 2077, p. 314).
Rānīpokharī and its central temple again suffered severe damage in the 2015 CE (VS 2072) earthquake.
Reconstruction was initially undertaken by the Kathmandu Metropolitan City in 2016 CE (VS 2073), but its use of concrete and modern materials drew criticism from locals and archaeologists.
In 2017 CE (VS 2074), the city even proposed developing the pond as a recreational site with concrete embankments, provoking further opposition.
Responding to public pressure, the project was transferred to the National Reconstruction Authority in 2019 CE (VS 2076).

Employing traditional Malla-period style, and materials, the Authority completed reconstruction in 2020 CE (VS 2077), and the restored pond and temple were inaugurated by President Bidya Devi Bhandari (Vidyā Devī Bhaṇḍārī).
In earlier years, the pond also served as a site for Chaṭha festival celebrations, though such permission is no longer granted.
Since 2014 CE (VS 2071), the Kathmandu Metropolitan City has opened the pond daily from 7 a.m. to 4 p.m. for public access, particularly for morning walks.
In 1995, this five-bayedphalcāwas dismantled and rebuilt with pillars and a slab made of concrete (Basukala & Gutschow2018).
In 2019, the local community reconstructed thephalcāin its traditional configuration based on design suggestions by Rohit Ranjitkar and Rupesh Shrestha.
The new building accommodates the youth club, a site for devotional singing(bhajana)and a community area on the first floor.
The Jelā̃ Jaḥdhuṃ was constructed in the Jelā̃ ṭola in 1673 CE (NS 793) by two brothers, Śivakṛṣṇa Bhāro and Bhima Bhāro.
Situated in the Jelā̃ ṭolā of Bhaktapur, this Jaḥdhuṃ faces south and is constructed using brick and stone.
At the center of theJaḥdhuṃ, there is an inscription detailing its construction.
Below the inscription, a spout (ṭuṭī) has been built for water to flow out.
This Jaḥdhuṃ was established on Thursday, the ninth dark fortnight of Āṣāḍha, in 1673 CE (NS 793).
Two brothers, Śivakṛṣṇa Bhāro and Bhīma Bhāro, residents of Khaṇḍachuka in Bhaktapur’s Yaṃparācha ṭolā, jointly built the structure in devotion to their tutelary deity.
In this inscription, theJaḥdhuṃis referred to asJarahdhārā, meaning a water source or spout, and the address of individuals who established theJaḥdhuṃas ‘Yaṃparācha ṭolā’.
Bhaktapur Municipality restored the Jaḥdhuṃ around 2021 CE (VS 2078) (local resident from a Śreṣṭha caste, male, age 78).

text: This temple dedicated to Candrabhairava, who is worshiped as the guardian deity of Cāpāgāũ, received a pair of lions in 1669 CE (NS 789).
No historical sources are available that shed light on the initial construction of the temple.
A pair of lions were installed in front of the sanctum in 1669 CE (NS 789) (D. Vajrācārya VS 2056, p. 157; S. Mānandhara VS 2059, p. 77).
citations: (D. Vajrācārya VS 2056, p. 157; S. Mānandhara VS 2059, p. 77)

text: This proves that the temple was already built before 1669 CE.
As of October 2024, the inscription carved on the pedestal of the lions has been destroyed.
Apart from the lion's inscription, no other medieval inscription has been found in the temple.
In 1952 CE (VS 2008), Jītabahādura Kusle (text: Jitabahādura Kusala), the grandson of Bakhabira and the son of Māhilā, donated a bell for Candrabhairava.
In 2012 CE (VS 2069), the locals collectively managed the finances and reconstructed the temple.
Since the temple had two tiers of roofs before the 1934 earthquakes, it was reconstructed as a two-tiered structure.
However, the eastern and western sides of the temple were open in the previous construction, but were walled in the reconstruction.
Originally, a Maharjan from Kvaylāchi installed a Buddha statue inthe Phalcā and afterwards it turned into a Bāhāḥ.
Acaitya-shaped finial tops thejhĩgaṭī-tiled roof of the building.
The ground floor of the building is in the structure of aphalcā.
After the reconstruction of the Bāhāḥ in 2011, a new woodentoraṇawith the images of the Five Buddhas has been installed.
A pair of lion statues established in NS 1058 flank the passage, which leads to the sanctum sanctorum.
According to  local residents, a Maharjan from Kvaylāchi established it and appointed a Vajrācārya of Bāliphala area as the priest.
No documented evidence is so far traced to date the initial construction of this Bāhāḥ.
However, the name of this monument has been mentioned in an inscription dated NS 832 (Śākya and Vaidya1970, 203).
There are no records to date its initial construction.
Following the devastation caused by the 2015 earthquakes, a vehicle knocked the Shrine down in the course of transferring the rubbles from the area.
The owner of the vehicle got the Shrine reconstructed soon after the incident.
A one-storey square concrete building was constructed in 1973 CE (VS 2030) where the ruins of the Phalcā remained.
The building was used as the office by a local organization called Kirtipur Vācanālaya for decades.
Kirtipur Municipality allocated a budget of NRs 2,364,000 in 2020 CE (VS 2076) to rebuild the Phalcā that once stood here.
[1]The building was dismantled and the newly constructed Phalcā was inaugurated by the local representatives in the same year.
A stone statue of Padmapāṇi Lokeśvara is installed on the rear wall of the Phalcā.
The statue, which was originally recovered from the Phalcā itself, was previously installed on a nearbycaitya(KIR0073) some six decades ago while the Phalcā remained in ruins.
The statue was reinstalled in the Phalcā after its reconstruction (local knowledge, local resident, Maharjana, male, age 83).

text: An inscription placed on the eastern wall of the Phalcā deals with the construction of the nearbycaitya.
There is noguthirelated to this Phalcā in existence today.
As the Phalcā was in ruins since at least seven decades ago, anyguthirelated to the Phalcā may also have ceased to exist around the same time.

Two metal banners (patāḥ) hang from the finial to the bottom tier, and atoraṇawith the statues of the Aṣṭamātṛkā deities is located above the Kalaśa, known as Asaṃghaḥ (lit. water pot of Asana, R. Jośī VS 2072, p.88), which has a carved silver cover and is the main deity of the temple.

text: Locally known as Asaṃmaru Ajimā, the goddess Annapūrṇā is also called Bhumpā (Tib. བུམ་པ།, Wylie.bum pa) by Tibetans and worshipped as Lakṣmī, the goddess of wealth, and Vasundharā, the goddess of prosperity (M. Tulādhara VS 2071, p.16).

The exact date of the temple's construction is unknown due to a lack of historical sources, but the earliest inscription dates back to 1704 CE (NS 824), which records a dispute over ownership of lands belonging to the deity.

Situated at the Bhelāchẽ Square, this narrow Phalcā was donated by the family of the striking pink house that the Phalcā is embedded into.
Once decorated with tiles, Bhelāchẽ Phalcā was reconstructed as a concrete Phalcā with a terrace on top.
The house itself has suffered major cracks due to the earthquake and has been declared unlivable, which puts the Phalcā in danger too.
According to Mr Tandukar (2018 CE), it was built to provide a cool place for those passing by to rest temporarily and take shelter from the heat.
This half of the Phalcāwas lost when the second house was rebuilt some years ago.
The space previously occupied by this half of the Bhelāchẽ Phalcā is still there, but the owner chose not to rebuild it.
The owner informed researchers that Bhelāchẽ Phalcā was previously in a terrible condition and was on the verge of collapse.
It was for this reason that it was dismantled and rebuilt in the present structure around 20 years ago.
He was worried that the Phalcā was tilting forwards, and feared it would have brought the whole house down with it if it collapsed.
The house is built in mud-mortar with one concrete floor on the fourth storey.
He believes that this was one of the main reasons the house sustained so much damage during the 2015 earthquakes.
There are no historical sources to date the initial construction of the Temple.
It seems the Temple collapsed at some point in history and was renovated into the present structure.
The senior citizens of the area mention that the Temple was renovated into the present state after it collapsed in the 1934 earthquakes.

The earliest inscription found at the Temple premises is dated NS 789 (1669 CE), which records the installation of a statue of Nārāyaṇa and construction of a stone plinth around the Temple by a donor named Nātijuti Bhāro.
There is another inscription inside the Temple that belongs to a nearbyhiti(THK0021).
It records the installation of statues of Nārāyaṇa, Umāmaheśvara, and Sarasvatī at thehitiby Kṛṣṇānandana and his wife, residents of Thankot, in NS 853 (1733 CE).

Rest houses are built around the temple with the one in the south has now (July 2024 CE) been converted into a cooperative office.Śiva’s animal mount, Nandī (object no.NWK0760-004), is established on the western plinth of the temple, while an aniconic stone (object no.NWK0760-002) placed near the entrance is revered as Gaṇeśa.
The two inscriptions within the temple complex are currently illegible.
One inscription (NWK0760_I_001) has completely eroded, while the other (NWK0760_I_002) bears some visible characters but their meaning remains undecipherable.

According to information gleaned from another inscription (NWK0760_I_004) in the temple complex, it is understood that the temple was constructed by Kularāja Pãḍe, along with his wives Śivakumārī Pãḍe and Lālakumārī Pãḍe in 1795 CE (VS 1852).
The temple and the surrounding rest houses were in a dilapidated state and there was a risk of collapse.

Consequently, in 2012 CE (VS 2068), a joint effort by the descendants of Kularāja Pā̃ḍe and the Kulabhakteśvara Saṃrakṣaṇa Samiti, a local committee formed for the conservation of the temple, led to the reconstruction of the temple and the rest houses.
Additionally, the 2015 CE earthquakes caused further damage to the temple.
With the assistance of the Pãḍe family and locals, the temple was renovated in 2018 CE (VS 2075) (Kulabhakteśvara Saṃrakṣaṇa Samiti chairman, Pãḍe, male, age 56).
The main deity, revered as Dharmamukteśvara, is aśivaliṅgaestablished at the centre of the sanctum.
A stone stele inscription embedded in the east wall records the temple's history.
The Dharmamukteśvara temple was built by Kharidāra Muktinātha Pauḍela in the name of his father Dharmadatta Pauḍela.
The inscription further informs us that in 1885 CE (VS 1942), Dharmadatta was gravely ill and was taken to the Āryaghāṭa cremation ground at Paśupati during his final days.
There, he vowed to establish aśivaliṅgaat Phirkyāpa on the banks of the Trishuli River in Devīghāṭa.
His son Muktinātha fulfilled his father's wish by building the temple in his father's name and establishing a trust by donating land parcels in 1887 CE (VS 1943).
A pipal tree grew near the temple, causing damage.
The mainśivaliṅgawas stolen, leaving behind its base (jalaharī).
A new four-facedśivaliṅgawithjalaharī(object no. NWK0620-002) was brought from Lalitpur and enshrined west of the originaljalaharīthat survived the theft.
Local resident Lalitajaṅga Śāha found a stone shaft of the right size on the riverbanks and consecrated it in place of the stolenśivaliṅga.
The temple was in poor condition, so it was rebuilt by theTriveṇī Mahilā Samūha, a group of local women, in 2003 CE (VS 2060).
Although Muktinātha Pauḍela had donated land for various rituals and the priest's salary, none of the periodic and daily rituals take place here currently (as of May 2024 CE).
An inscription near the Nandī sculpture commemorates the temple's construction in 1813 CE (VS 1869) by Lakṣmīdevī, the third concubine of King Raṇabahādura Śāha.
Hailing from the Garmiñā village in Patna, India (cf. Vajracārya and Śreṣṭha VS 2037, p.572), Lakṣmīdevī, also known as Sāĩlī Nānīsāheba, undertook the construction alongside thecaugharā sataḥ.

The temple was originally built by Bhagīratha Bhaiyā (also called Bhāga Kājī or Bhāicā Jyāpu) in 1678 CE (NS 798).
In 1669, Aurangzeb destroyedthe Viśveśvara temple of Varanasi (Regmi1966, appendix III, p. 80,).
Bhagīratha Bhaiyā and his younger brother Bhāgī Bhāro therefore decided to construct this Viśveśvara Temple on the 5th day of the bright half of the Māgha of NS 798 (1678 CE).
An inscription on the temple (VajrācāryaVS 2056, 199) mentions that they also established aguṭhīto oversee the daily and other ritual worships.

TheNepālikabhūpavaṃśāvalī(19.3.164) states that they also built the Lamupāṭī (longpāṭī,tāhāḥ phale). 12 kings were invited to the consecration ceremony of the temple in thispāṭī(organised on the 8th day of the dark half of Vaiśākha, NS 798) (VajrācāryaVS 2022, 28).
On the 5th day of the bright half of the Māgha of NS 804, he accused Bhagīratha of not showing appropriate respect to the queen.

This historic water trough (jaḥdhuṃ), dating back to the early Malla period during King Abhaya Malla’s reign (1216–1255 CE), has been relocated from Kamalpokhari in Imadol to the grounds of the Imadol Police Station.
About a decade ago, it was moved here through local efforts for safety and preservation.
To the south of thejaḥdhuṃlies the office building of Mahalaxmi Municipality Ward No. 1.

According to Dhanavajra Vajrācārya (VS 2068, p. 128), thisjaḥdhuṃdates to the reign of King Abhaya Malla (1216–1255 CE), son of Ari Malla, who ascended the throne at age 34 after his father’s death (D. Vajrācārya VS 2066, p. 66).
Thejaḥdhuṃbears an inscription from 1233 CE (NS 353), though as of June 2025, the inscription has worn away and is no longer legible.
According to the details recorded, thejaḥdhuṃwas renovated because the source of a well in a place called “Sūtigala” had been damaged (D. Vajrācārya VS 2068, p. 128).
The inscription does not mention the name of the renovator.
Another similarjaḥdhuṃis also present at this location, but it bears no inscription.
On the southern wall, several inscriptions record restoration works carried out by various individuals and organizations.
No record within the site indicates when or by whom thehitiwas originally constructed.
The earliest known inscription, dating to 1914 CE (NS 1034), mentions restoration by Candra Śamaśera Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā.
Another inscription records renovations by King Mahendra in 1960 CE (VS 2017).

Later marble inscriptions show that thehitiunderwent multiple restorations: in 2001 CE (VS 2057) by the Nepal Water Supply Corporation in collaboration with the Śaleṣanāntaka Samāja; in 2004 CE (VS 2061) by the Mirmire Youth Club; and in 2010 CE (VS 2067) by the Sināmaṃgala Foreign Employment Entrepreneurs’ Group.
Situated in a densely built urban area and with its water supply long inactive, the hiti has seen a decline in community engagement.
Despite several restoration efforts, it currently lacks regular maintenance or associated cultural activities.

The Bālamukteśvara Temple was built by Rāṇā Prime Minister Vīra Śamśera in 1888 CE (VS 1945).
During his reign from 1885 to 1901 CE, Vīra Śamśera constructed a group of four Śiva temples known as Cāra Śivālaya to the south of the Rājarājeśvarī Mandira.
No inscription recording the temple's construction exists, although there used to be a bell south of the temple, which was unfortunately stolen.
It is likely that the bell bore an inscription similar to the one found in the Jagadmukteśvara Mandira (PPK0840) of the Cāra Śivālaya complex.
According to Taṇḍaṇa (VS 2056, p.353), Vīra Śamśera built the temple in 1888 CE (VS 1945) and likely dedicated it to his grandfather, Bālanarasiṃha Kũvara, who lived from 1781 to 1841 CE.

Although the exact date of construction and the identity of the benefactor of this unnamed Śiva temple remain uncertain, architectural and contextual evidence suggests it was built during the Rāṇā period (1846–1951 CE).
Built of brick and set on a two-tiered plinth, the temple features a bell-shaped roof crowned with a metal finial.
An inscription on the northern plinth, though heavily worn and largely illegible, indicates the donation of land parcels in 1920 CE (NS 1040), likely to establish a trust for the temple’s upkeep.
This same trust also manages the neighboring Bhairava Viṣṇu temple, which is believed to have been constructed by an ancestor of Arjunanarasiṃha Rāṇā.
Given the connection, it is plausible that the same individual was also responsible for the construction of this Śiva temple.
Despite its distinct identity, the temple has been misidentified in the past asKṛṣṇabhakteśvaraby G. Ṭaṇḍana (VS 2053, pp. 769–770) and Michaels and Tandon (2017, p. 106).

There are fourphalcāsaround the Pīṭha constructed in different time periods.

Although no records detail its original construction, the Yakṣiṇī sculptures have been dated to the 13th–14th century CE (Schroeder 2019, p. 79), indicating that thehitiwas likely built in the early medieval period.
In 1677 CE (NS 797), during the reign of King Śrīnivas Malla, Minister Bhagīratha Bhaiyā initiated extensive renovations of Kvachu Hiti.
His efforts also included paving stone roads, repairing gateways in Pharping, and installing a stone entrance at the nearby Śikharanārāyaṇa (Śeṣanārāyaṇa) temple (PRN0010).
As part of thehitirestoration, he ensured that water from the spring was divided equally between the two spouts and issued regulations to maintain the water infrastructure.
The eastern spout was damaged at one point (Schroeder 2019, p. 79), but it was later repaired by local resident Bālākṛṣṇa Śreṣṭha, who hired artisans from Bhīnchebāhā in Lalitpur at his own expense.
In 2023 CE (VS 2080), Dakṣiṇakālī Municipality carried out further repairs of thehiticomplex.
During this renovation, local residents also installed images of various deities on the western wall.
Water flowed regularly through thehitiuntil around 1990 CE (VS 2047), but unplanned urban development led to the drying of the spring.

Ratnavajra Vajrācārya, a tantric priest, had constructed the Jhvāḥ Bāhāḥ.
He had originally built it at an open courtyard east of the present monastic building.
With his tantric powers, Ratnavajra caused a downpour of precious gems to build the Bāhāḥ.
He also hung a bunch of gems at thekvāḥpāḥchẽand constructed acaityastudded with jewels.
He also built theāgaṃfacing south in front of thekvāḥpāḥchẽ.
The site where the Bāhāḥ’s originalkvāḥpāḥchẽstood now has houses built on it, leaving no trace of the previous construction.

There is a court case going on regarding theāgaṃbuilding.
The present building of the Bāhāḥ was constructed by Kusumadeva.
He had donated a plot of his land west of the Jvāḥ Bāhāḥ for public use.
It is believed that the place is now known as Kusumabiyā Lāchi, as Kusumadeva had made such a donation (B. PradhānaVS 2064, p. 140).
However, it is unclear why and when he had relocated the Bāhāḥ.
The earliest inscription here at the Bāhāḥ is dated NS 754 (1634 CE).

Built in front of the Kālabhairava (KAT1770) shrine at Hanumandhoka Palace Square, the Koṭiliṅgeśvara Mahādeva temple is a stone structure that stands on three levels of plinths.
This carving of paired animals with composite heads was replicated from Licchavi art (G. Vajrācārya VS 2033, p.77).

Although historical records do not detail the temple's construction, later chronicles indicate that King Mahendra Malla (r. 1560-1574 CE) built the temple and adorned it with gold (D. Lamsāla 2023, p.57).
The year of its construction, however, remains unmentioned in the chronicles.

However, a manuscript preserved at the National Archives (reel no. D 25/25) records that the king constructed the Koṭiliṅgeśvara temple on the 13th of the dark fortnight of Pauṣa in 1566 CE (NS 687) and performed a fire ritual of 10 million oblations (koṭīhoma) on the 12th of the bright fortnight of Māgha (cf. M. Panta VS 2074, p.10).
While overseeing the temple's construction, he also presented the Rāmāyaṇa dance, a performance based on the epic Rāmāyaṇa.
Subsequently, Queen Bhuvanalakṣmī, the wife of King Bhūpālendra Malla (r. 1687-1700 CE), granted lands to the temple, leading to its designation as Bhuvaneśvara Mandira.
A record within the Guṭhī Saṃsthāna lists 39 ropanīs of land under the Bhuvaneśvara Guṭhī (lagata naṃ. śrī 5 sa. 24) (Guṭhī Saṃsthāna VS 2071, p.36).
A segment of the temple suffered damage in the 1934 CE earthquakes and underwent renovation in subsequent years (G. Vajrācārya VS 2033, p.78).
Adharmadhātujinālaya caityais established in the courtyard.
No documented evidence is so far traced out to date the Bahā’s initial construction.
A narration is circulated amongst the local residents that it was built by certain Śreṣṭhas (Cipālu).
The Bāhāḥ got destroyed due course of time and turned into ruins, which was then converted into a female toilet.
The Bāhāḥ’s remnants were found after the site was excavated and it was then rebuilt by Harṣa Bahādura Śākya, a resident of Oṃ Bāhāḥ in NS 1069 (1948 CE).
After it was restored, he provided this place for the nuns who practise Sthavīravāda (vernac. Therāvāda) Buddhism.

The north-facing, three-storied main building of thebāhāḥconsists of a carved main door flanked by two small lattice windows (tikijhyāḥ) on the ground floor, and an elongated window with a row of five small openings(pasūkājhyāḥ) on the first floor as a symbol of the Pañcabuddha.
The courtyard contains asikharopariviṃva caityaand ayajña kuṇḍaand is surrounded by residential buildings.
Only one building, which is attached to the monastic building to the east, is a historical one, with preserved carved windows.
The building at the northeast corner of the courtyard collapsed in the 2015 earthquake.
The condition of the roof and the base of theṭuḍālasshow that two of them have already collapsed.
The traditional roof has been replaced with corrugated galvanized iron sheets.
Akṣobhya Buddha is situated to the right of the main door which is unusal as generally, the main deity of a Buddhist monastery is installed in front of the main door.
The other four images seem to have been installed later and can be found between these Buddhas.
The Deypukhūsi Phalcā North-West, as evidenced by an old photograph, was reconstructed in 2018 CE (2075 VS).
According to the recollections of older community members, in the year 1950 CE, the phalcā had a damaged roof and was in a dilapidated state.
Due to this condition, the statue ofUmāmaheśvaraand aninscriptionwere moved to the sanctum of the nearby Nārāyaṇa Mandira (KIR0005).
Based on the photograph showing remnants of the Phalcā and the memories of the community's older members, the reconstruction of the Phalcā took place in 2015 CE (2075 VS).
During this reconstruction, one of the inscriptions that had been relocated to the nearby Nārāyaṇa temple was reinstalled in this Phalcā.
However, the other inscription and the Umāmaheśvara statue were not transferred.
The inscription transferred to the Phalcā dates back to 1889 CE (1009 NS) and records the restoration of the Phalcā by the son of Amitanārā (Amita Nārāyaṇa) and Mayajumunī.
It also mentions that Kvāṭhanāyaka Āsāmadu Bhāro initiated its construction.
Many Kvāṭha Nāyakas undertook the construction of temples, sattala, phalcās, and other structures in Kirtīpura during this period, along with making numerous offerings to Bāghbhairava (KIR0004).
The inscription also records the renovation of the dilapidated Phalcā by Ḍhuṇḍirāja Bhāro, akvāṭhanāyakasucceeding Āsāmāḍu, who also installed the Umāmaheśvara idol in 1716 CE (NS 836).

A guṭhī has been established, allocating land for conducting the anniversary ritual on the day of Bhīmā Ekādaśī (Māgha śukla ekādaśī, the day of renovation), as well as for the daily worship of the statue by Brāhmaṇa.
The current Pradhāna might be a descendant of the individual who carried out the renovation of the phalcā in 1889 CE (NS 1009).
The city of Bhaktapur, along with Patan and Kathmandu, was established within an imaginary protective circle guarded by theaṣṭamātṛkādeities (Eight Mother Goddesses).

For instance, historical accounts from theDevamālāvaṃśāvalī(p.106) reveal that Bhaktapur was established as a fortified city under the safeguard of theaṣṭamātṛkā-pīṭhasby King Ānandadeva in 1096 CE (Kaligata Era 4197).
However, it is likely that these statues were added later.
At present (as of January 2023 CE), a metal grille has been installed where the sanctum used to be open.
Much like otherpīṭhashrines, historical documentation on the initial construction of the Mahālakṣmī Pīṭha remains elusive.
A 1920 CE (NS 1080) inscription notes the installation of gilded coverings on the Pīṭha entrance andtoraṇasby Maṃgalalāla Bhomī of Yātāchẽ Ṭola.
During boys' initiation (vratabandha), an animal sacrifice is offered to the deity.
The Dakṣiṇa Vārāhī Temple, where inscriptions dating back to 1805 CE (NS 925) have been found, stands to the south of Śaṅkhadhar Chowk in Thimi.

In the traditional sacred geography of Thimi, the Aṣṭamātṛkās (Eight Mother Goddesses) were established in different directions for the protection of the town, and Vārāhī was installed in the southern direction; hence the epithet Dakṣiṇa Vārāhī.
Inside the sanctum, an aniconic stone is established as Vārāhī.
To the north of the temple lies a cremation ground where members of the Śreṣṭha, Vajrācārya, and Brāhmaṇa communities of Thimi are cremated (R. Tūbanjāḥ Śreṣṭha VS 2061, p. 30).
No historical record has yet been found concerning the original construction of the temple.
It is likely that the site existed earlier as apīṭhaand that a temple structure was built for it during the Malla period.
The earliest inscription related to the temple dates to 1805 CE (NS 925).
It states that Bhājudeva Bhāro, together with his wife Dhanalakṣmī and son Bhājukutu, commissioned an image of Vārāhī for use during the Biskā Jātrā.

Another inscription, a stone record dated 1812 CE (NS 932), notes that Deva Bhālo and Dhanalakṣmī, along with their sons Vidyāpati and Kṛttisiṃha and daughter Dayālakṣmī, endowed agricultural land asguṭhīfor the Dakṣiṇa Vārāhī Temple.
The income from this land was designated for the annual worship, including repairs to the temple if needed, the ritual sacrifice of a goat, proper worship, and a feast for the trustees of theguṭhī.
In 1887 CE (NS 1007), Bhānna­siṃ, Siṅgha Bhālo, his wife Budhi Thakuṃ, Jagatamāsiṃ, and others jointly offered a stonetoraṇato Dakṣiṇa Vārāhī.

In 1907 CE (NS 1027), Tulsīnārāyaṇa Galule of Thimi, together with his wife Kṛṣṇakumārī, sons Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa, Harṣanārāyaṇa, Beṣanārāyaṇa, Āsanārāyaṇa, and daughter Candramāyā, donated a gilded pinnacle to the temple.
The temple was damaged in the earthquake of 2015 CE (VS 2072) and was reconstructed in 2017 CE (VS 2074) by the Department of Archaeology at a cost of 6.3 million Nepalese rupees.
At the completion of the reconstruction, the installation of roof sheeting remained unfinished.

In August 2019 CE (Śrāvaṇa VS 2076), a brass roof was finally installed (oral testimony of the President of the Dakṣiṇa Vārāhī Mandira Parisara Sudhāra Evaṃ Vyavasthāpana Samiti from the Śreṣṭha caste, male, age 56).
Said to allegedly have been built by Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa Śāha as military headquarters for his invasion on Nuwakot, this arcaded platform was reconstructed after the 2015 earthquakes.
Situated at the Sāmarī Ṭola of Myagang Rural Municipality of Nuwakot, the Sāmarī Pauvā was named after the locality where it was built.
Sāmarī Pauvā has no deities installed, neither on ground nor upper floor.
ACaityaestablished by the Śākyas of Patan stands northwest of the arcaded platform.
According to locals, the monument was originally built in a courtyard style with the building spreading across four sides enclosing an open courtyard in the middle.
The western section has already collapsed, but a portion of the ground floor remains.
According to local residents, this arcaded platform was constructed by Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa Śāha as part of his endeavor to conquer Nuwakot.
He appointed a group of Khaḍkā Magars to maintain the building.

Aside from the fact that this claim lacks historical records to substantiate it, it also seems illogical that Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa Śāha would construct an arcaded platform for resting instead of a structure for military purposes.
It is more plausible that Sāmarī Pauvā was renovated and utilized by Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa Śāha for his military purposes.
There is no evidence of Śāha constructing the Sāmarī Pauvā.
They established acaityain Sāmarī (local resident, Śākya, male, age 83).
They probably constructed the Sāmarī Pauvā to provide accommodation for travelers using the Sāmarī route around the same time.
The 2015 earthquakes completely destroyed the rest house, which was already in a dilapidated condition.
The Department of Archaeology reconstructed the rest house and installed a colored metal sheet roof in place of the original tiled roof.
Despite the completion of the reconstruction, it has not been formally inaugurated yet (as of June 2024).
Currently, the local community uses the building for weddings, initiation of boys and girls, and other community feasts.
Every year on the full moon days of Vaiśākha and Phālguna, the Śākya community performs worship at thecaityalocated to the northwest of the building.
The shrine, facing west, is built in the classical śikhara style and is flanked by a pair of lions at the entrance.
Above this shrine, the sanctum (garbhagṛha) is constructed in an arched form, crowned with a carved woodentoraṇa.
Over time, additional metal elements have been added, enhancing the temple’s beauty and richness.

At the pinnacle of the shrine is a stone gajūra engraved with atriśūla(trident) and an inscription reading “Saṃvat 808a Kṛ3” 1688 CE (NS 808), indicating the shrine’s completion during the reign of King Yoganarendra Malla.
Several inscriptions—mainly from the Rāṇā period—document donations made for the metal embellishments and upkeep of the temple.
The temple is built in thelatina nāgaramode.

This Stone (Ḍhuṅge) Fountain (Dhārā), built between the 14th and 16th centuries on the western slope of the main Dullu hill, is now accessible via a motorable path that departs from Dullu's central area.
Water is dispensed through two stylized makara heads (only the right one was operational at the time the site was surveyed in 2022 CE).
