text: Given that a similar fountain found nearby was built in 1568 CE (DLK0370), it is possible to speculate that this Fountain was constructed between the 14th and 16th centuries, corresponding to the late period of the Khaśa Malla regime (12th-14th century) and the succeeding Rāskoṭi dynasty.
In September 2024, thesataḥ,located in the northwestern corner of the Kvalkhu crossing, adjacent to the Kvālkhu Gaṇeśa Mandira (LAL1120), was dismantled.
The three-storey building, a concrete frame structure, replaced a previoussataḥ, which was documented by Ganeshman Chitrakar in 1973.
The now dismantledsataḥfeatured cast concrete struts that were adorned with depictions of mythical animals and deities.

In 2018, the ground floorphalcāwas painted with graffiti during a street art festival (see social activities), which caused an ongoing dispute in the neighborhood concerning the impact of the graffiti on the building's "authenticity".
Facing west, the dome-shaped temple is entirely constructed of stone and features a stone finial.
A partially damaged Nandī bull sits in front of the temple, and a waterhole (kuṇḍa) is located to the northwest.
An inscription carved north of the temple's entrance indicates its construction in 1666 CE (NS 786).
Due to erosion, the inscription is difficult to read.
The mention of Vaṃśīdhara Nārāyaṇa suggests he might have been the temple's builder.
The term "pīṭha" signifies a sanctuary that hosts a protective goddess in an open space beyond the city's periphery, while her primary sanctuary, the god house, is constructed within the city itself.
Functioning as the consort (śakti) of Bhairava at the Taumadhī Ṭola, Tripurasundarī is also revered during Bhairava's worship at Taumadhī (P. Śreṣṭha VS 2058, p.34).
A metaltoraṇaadded atop the stone arch appears to be a later inclusion.
A two-storiedsataḥstands before the Pīṭha, containing inscriptions from 1732 CE (NS 852) and 1910 CE (NS 1030), unrelated to the Pīṭha.

TheDevamālāvaṃśāvalī, a chronicle, recounts the establishment of Bhaktapur as a significant city under the safeguard of the eightaṣṭamātṛkā-pīṭhaby King Ānandadeva in 1094 CE (Kaligata Era 4197) (Devamālāvaṃśālvalī2013, p.104). Ānandadeva also constructed and consecrated the capital, inclusive of Tripura—Tripurasundarī's abode (Gopālarājavaṃśāvalī, folio 25a).
The palace erected by King Ānandadeva came to be known as Tripura Palace, named in honour of the Tripurasundarī Pīṭha (P. Śreṣṭha VS 2058, p.17).

Nonetheless, the earliest available historical record at the Pīṭha dates back to 1897 CE (NS 1017), documenting Āsāmadu Karmācārya's offering of a bell (BKT0140-009) in memory of his deceased parents.
Presently (March 2023 CE), a lady from the Guluju caste fulfils the role of caretaker, benefiting from the offerings made by devotees, given the cessation of service by the Jogi community.
Theśivālaya(lit. Lord Śiva's abode), known as Ḍambaramukteśvara, was constructed in 1891 CE (VS 1947) in memory of Commander-in-Chief Raṇa Śamśera by his unnamed wife.
The temple, constructed of stone and consisting of three plinth levels, features a bell-shaped roof with a metallic finial.
Outside, a bell from 1938 CE (VS 1994) hangs from a bell stand to the south, while a Nandī figure guards the western entrance.
An inscription commemorating the temple’s construction is located on its plinth.

Commander-in-Chief Raṇa Śamśera's wife, only known as "Śrī Rānī" (lit. venerated queen) in the inscription, commissioned the Ḍambaramukteśvara temple in 1891 CE (VS 1947) in memory of her late husband.
In 1898 CE (VS 1954), she set up a trust by donating land parcels to ensure the temple's financial stability for the performance of various rituals.
Raṇa Śamśera, the third son of Dhīra Śamśera, became the commander-in-chief in early 1887 CE (VS 1943).
However, Raṇa died two months into this role in May 1887 due to alcoholism (Rāṇā VS 2059, pp. 284-285).

According to Michaels and Tandon (2017, p. 106), the temple was built by Ḍambara Śamśera, another son of Dhīra Śamśera, in 1897 CE (VS 1954). Ḍambara was involved in the assassination of Prime Minister Raṇa Uddīpa Siṃha in 1885 CE (VS 1942), which led to Vīra Śamśera becoming prime minister (Rāṇā VS 2059, p. 248).
The inscription at the temple, however, clearly credits Raṇa Śamśera's wife for its construction, resolving the confusion.
She built Ḍambaramukteśvara in 1891 CE (VS 1947) but set up a trust for the temple and installed the inscription only in 1898 CE (VS 1954).
The temple's bell, added in 1938 CE (VS 1994) by a state trust named “Śrī 3 Sarakāra Guṭhī,” is smaller than those of other nearbyśivālayas.
It is believed to have replaced a lost original bell.
As the temple collapsed in the 2015 earthquakes, it was rebuilt by the Pashupati Area Development Trust in 2019 CE (VS 2076).
A stone fountain from the medieval period and a Tibetan inscription from approximately 9th-12th century.
In the surrounding wall, a pillar (001) with an eroded inscription was recently inserted.
Another chamber is located above this one, and it contains a longitudinal slab with an eroded Tibetan inscription from the 9th-12th century (Andolfatto 2019).
The monument's idiosyncrasy and the lack of dated inscriptions complicate dating.
It could have been constructed during the mediaeval period.
This also indicates that the temple was previously constructed in a pagoda style.
It is possible that the temple was reconstructed in its present form after the 1934 earthquake.
The inscription on the Garuḍa statue displays is dated 1689 CE (NS 809).
However, this inscription does not clarify if the statue was installed when the temple was initially constructed or if (and this seems more likely) the temple already existed at that time.
Another inscription from 1910 CE (VS 1966) refers to the main deity of the temple as Ali Malla Keśava.
His rule took place around 1200 CE (seeRegmi1965, 196).
Jaṅga Bahādura demonstrated his political prowess by constructing a grand temple and a large rest house (sataḥ) at the cremation ground of Kālamocāna Ghāṭa.
This extensive Sataḥ made up of five sections was built to frame the Jaṅge Hiraṇya Hema Nārāyaṇa temple (KAT2800) from three sides, extending in all directions except for the north.
With Jaṅga Bahādura’s rise, the construction of large temples built in mixed styles and arcaded open shelters with tiled roofs (phalcās andsataḥs) around them began to flourish.
Under him, the colossal temple at Kālamocāna Ghāṭa was built in 1875 AD (VS 1931), named after himself and his two wives.
Bahadura also erected a statue of himself on an inscribed stone pillar, boasting his achievements.
A reason for the construction of such largesataḥs along with the temple at Kālamocāna Ghāṭa is that the area had been the need for shelter for different groups of ascetics, also from India.
A document from 1848 CE (VS 1905) reveals that ascetics of the Haṃsa, Ḍaṃḍī, Brahmacārī, Nāgā, and other fakirs used to live here.
Three separateakhaḍās (monasteries) were built close to this Sataḥ to host ascetics from India who had come for pilgrimages.

Saurabha (VS 2071, p. 6) has written that Jaṅga Bahādura and his brother Bama Bahādura used to regularly come to smoke marijuana at an ascetic who lived at Kālamocāna Ghāṭa and that the temple and the Sataḥ were built on request of the same ascetics.
In 1976 CE (VS 2033), the eastern section of this Sataḥ was largely destroyed.
Although it did not collapse in the 2015 earthquakes, it was deemed unsafe to live in and thus was completely demolished.

The reconstruction was carried out by the High-Powered Committee for Integrated Development of the Bagmati Civilization under the Ministry of Urban Development with the loan assistance of the Asian Development Bank.
The central office of the Guthi Corporation had already begun to operate from this Sataḥ during the Rāṇā period.
Thousands of Rāṇā-era documents related to religious trusts have been issued from this building.
Until today, a part of the Sataḥ is still occupied by the office of the Guthi Corporation.
The Guthi Corporation has been making arrangements for them to light bonfires, stay, and be fed.
Prime Minister Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā’s second son, Jītajaṅga Rāṇā, established the Lalitamukteśvara temple in 1874 CE (VS 1931).

Situated south of the Virupākṣa Mandira (PPK0210) at the cremation ground of the Ārya Ghāṭa on the eastern bank of the Bagmati river in the Paśupati area, this east-facing temple is constructed of brick and features a bell-shaped roof with a stone finial.
Two stone bulls, installed for the temple, are placed inside the sanctum.
Although there is no record of the temple's construction available at the site, Jītajaṅga Rāṇā is credited with its establishment.
He inscribed this achievement after completing the Jītajaṅgaprakāśeśvara Mandira (PPK0706) at the cremation ground of Rājarājeśvarī Ghāṭa (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2056, p. 578).

While the inscription does not mention the year of Lalitamukteśvara's construction, it is commonly believed to have been built in 1874 CE (VS 1931), the same year as the Jītajaṅgaprakāśeśvara Mandira (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p. 342; Michaels and Tandon 2017, p. 60).

text: He passed away in India in 1893 CE (VS 1950) (P. Rāja VS 2073, p. 119).
This Pond was commissioned in 1908 by Candra Śamśera, a Rana prime minister, in memory of his late wife Mahārāṇī Candrabhakta Lokarājyalakṣmī Devī.
The inscription mentions that the Queen had helped provide access to drinking water in Patan and passed away on 11 February 1905.

Thiscaityadisplays five layers of motifs (lotus, jewel, water, fireand thunderbolt) upon its upper part, and contains images of four Buddhas and four Tārās in the four cardinal directions and corners respectively.
These images are tied to iron rods to protect them against theft.
Statues of the 13 donors are located on the southern face ofvedikāalongside an inscription that records the construction date of thecaitya.
According to the locals, the Pukhū was constructed in the shape of a conch shell (śaṅkha) in the past with a statue of Lord Śiva enshrined in its centre.
There are no records to date the initial construction of the Pukhū.
As mentioned above, the Pukhūlāchi Ṭola is one of the eight majorṭolas of Sankhu that Jogadeva Vajrācārya established while founding the town of Sankhu in 1317 BC (Kaligata Era 1801).

A Buddhist scripture entitledMaṇiśailamahāvadānamentions that Jogadeva constructed a palace at the centre of the town along with the shrines ofaṣṭamātṛkā(Eight Mother Goddesses), ninebāhāḥs, and four gates in four directions while dividing the town into eightṭolas with a Gaṇeśa shrine at eachṭola(V. Vajrācārya1119, p. 32-33).
As the name Pukhūlāchi Ṭola comes from the Pukhū here, it is understood that the Pukhū was in existence before the establishment of Sankhu.
An image of Gaṇeśa with three heads and four arms is carved in the middle of thetoraṇaand an aniconic stone representing Gaṇeśa is consecrated in the sanctum.
There are twocaityasand a bell established in the temple premises.
There are no evidences to date the initial construction of the temple.
Pruscha(1975, K-103), without referring to any source, mentions that it was constructed by a certain Dharma Siṃha and others in 1789 CE.
In 1995 CE (VS 2052) the temple was renovated with the support from the Kathmandu Municipality and local community members.

While the Tripurasundarī temple was built by the Kumaoni king Udyot Chand around 1688, as a celebration of his double victory over Garhwal and Doti (Pandey 1997: 176-177), it is likely that the original Vaikuṇṭha image was brought from Kumaon (or Garhwal) on the occasion of the temple consecration.

In this context the two temple pinnacles can either be originating from 17th century structures built under Udyot Chand, or they can pre-date this period and would in this case indicate that Udyot Chand only expanded or renovated one or more already existing monuments.
An inscription published in S. Rājavaṃśī VS 2078, p. 69 documents the establishment of acaityain the courtyard in 1662 CE (NS 782).
This inscription has since been lost.

While a 1662 CE (NS 782) inscription cites “Jāgavaṇḍa Mahāvihāra,” leading to its common designation, alternative Sanskrit names, “Bhogacandra Mahāvihāra” (Pruscha 1975, K-234) and “Nāgacandra Mahāvihāra” (R. Vajrācārya & V. Vajrācārya NS 1103, p. 29), are also documented.
The 1934 earthquake completely devastated the monastery, fracturing the clay Akṣobhya's head and hands.
Subsequently, the monastery was rebuilt, and the Akṣobhya statue was restored and reinstalled.
Around 1981 CE (VS 2038), the clay Akṣobhya was stolen, prompting the creation and installation of a new copper statue.
Around 1989 CE (VS 2046), the monastery was demolished and replaced with a seven-story concrete-frame structure.
Steel shutters have been installed in front of the wood-carved door leading to the sanctum.
No reliable records pertaining to thebāhāḥ's construction have been found.
The first known mention, “Jyātha Bāhāra,” is in a 1454 CE (NS 574) palm-leaf document related to land sales, dated Āṣāḍha's bright fortnight, 8th day (M. Panta VS 2049, p. 82).
This is the earliest evidence for Jyā Bāhāḥ. “Jyātha Bāhāra” also appears in a 1545 CE (NS 665) palm-leaf document (M. Panta VS 2049, p. 82).
These documents establish thebāhāḥ's early medieval origins.

The oldest remaining evidence from within thebāhāḥitself is a 1662 CE (NS 782) inscription, which states Viṣṇusiṃha Bhāro of Asana Ṭola's Jhyālakochẽ built acaityaunder King Pratāpa Malla (S. Rājavaṃśī VS 2078, p. 69).
This inscription is now lost.
Another, from 1686 CE (NS 806), records Jiyūrāja's work during King Pārthivendra Malla's reign, but its damaged letters prevent deciphering (S. Rājavaṃśī VS 2078, p. 99).
This inscription is also missing.
Initially, a Vajrācārya from Lagaṃ Bāhāḥ conducted the rituals after the monastery's construction, later transferring this responsibility to a Vajrācārya from Iku Bāhāḥ.
Currently, with the exception of the sanctum, the building is occupied by a family of Citrakāra (painter) lineage.
They assert their prior status as Vajrācāryas, claiming the building as their private property.
A Tulādhara merchant commissioned the construction of Jyā Bāhāḥ and entrusted ritual duties to an Iku Bāhāḥ Vajrācārya.
Subsequently, a marital union with a Citrakāra woman resulted in the family's transition from Vajrācārya to Citrakāra (senior family member residing in the building, male, age 73).

Both statues are damaged; the upper body of the statue on the left-hand side is broken, and the statue on the right-hand side is in a state of deterioration, making it difficult to identify the weapons carried by the deity.
One of the inscriptions at the site (see below) informs us that (Jośī) Keśavarāja Bhāro constructed the Temple in 1682 CE.

Located in the Nugaḥ Ṭola in Patan’s eastern quarter, the temple is survived by only the originaljalaharībase with its lingam already lost, and now replaced with another smallśivaliṅgabearing its ownjalaharībase.
These structures are currently established out in the open on three tiers of brick-and-stone plinths.
Local elders have no memory of a temple atop the platform, indicating it likely collapsed before the 1934 earthquakes.
Two stone inscriptions are present on the platform.

One, dated 1695 CE (NS 816), is legible but unrelated to this temple, referencing a Kumāra temple in the area where Kṛṣṇamatī, granddaughter of King Śrīnivāsa Malla, installed an Umāmaheśvara statue and endowed land for a trust.
While this Kumāra temple later disappeared, its inscription appears to have been relocated here.
This inscription is from that missing temple.
The second inscription, also from the late Malla period, is too eroded to read but features a trident carving, suggesting a connection to this Śiva temple.
Situated on the western side of Dupāt Square, theDāphāBhajanaPhalcāis located to the north of the large five-storey building that also houses theKṛṣi UdayaPrimary School.

This was once a six-bayed Phalcā and was part ofdāphāguthichẽ(broken down, this means a house (=chẽ) of aguthithat supports the performance ofdāphāmusic) which has a tradition of displaying two Bhairāvas during the festival of Indrayātrā.
Dāphā Bhajana Phalcāwas dismantled in 2002 and then integrated into the five-storey concrete community building.
After 2004, the old Phalcā was dismantled and reconstructed in a new RCC structure with five storeys.

The rock bears an inscription from 1630 CE (NS 750), indicating Jagajyoti (text: Jayajyoti) Malla’s selection of stones for the construction of certain work of art.

Two inscriptions from the reign of King Viṣṇu Gupta, dated to the Mānadeva Era 64 and 65 (corresponding to 640 and 641 CE), detail the transportation of stone within the valley for sculpting statues (D. Vajrācārya VS 2030, pp. 446-448).

These records indicate that residents of Sunāguthi (a town southwest of Patan) and Dakṣiṇakolīgrāma (southern Kathmandu) were rewarded with the privilege of wearing jewelry for their service in transporting stones for the creation of Buḍhānīlakaṇṭha, the reclining Viṣṇu statue located north of Kathmandu.

Artistic creations crafted from this stone often proudly proclaimed their origin. Śrīnivāsa Malla, the king of Patan, generously provided Koṭakhā stone to Jitāmitra Malla, the king of Bhaktapur, at the latter's request to renovate the Kumārī Coka (Tevārī and others VS 2019, pp. 24-25).
Similarly, in 1691 CE (NS 811), Crown Prince Bhūpatindra Malla utilized Koṭakhā stone to restore a water spout in the Bhaktapur palace (Vaidya & Shrestha 2002, p. 207).
There is speculation that the stone procured by Viṣṇu Gupta for the Buḍhānīlakaṇṭha statue and the Koṭakhā stone originated from the same quarry (D. Vajrācārya VS 2030, p. 446).

The Bhaktapur kings and crown princes' proud proclamation that the stones used in their constructions were sourced from the kingdom of Patan's quarry reveals their sense of accomplishment in acquiring stones from a neighboring state.
These examples of rock inscriptions, therefore, appear to be an attempt to convey a message not to touch them, as they have been selected for certain purposes.
In addition to the selection of stones, short inscriptions were also found engraved on the stone surfaces to provide information about the completion of construction work.
Among some 20 inscriptions found at four locations in Nālāchāpa, this inscription of 1630 CE (NS 750) is the earliest.

By around 1993 CE (VS 2050), the temple had fallen into disrepair, prompting local residents to collect donations and undertake its reconstruction (R. Tūbanjāḥ Śreṣṭha, VS 2061, p. 42).
During this reconstruction, concrete flooring was used, replacing traditional construction methods.
That evening, a bonfire is lit outside the temple, and devotees keep vigil throughout the night.
The area surrounding thecaityais paved with black flagstone and has been encroached upon by building materials for the reconstruction of the Karuṇāmaya Mandira.
Thecaityawas built in 1962.
A special worship was organised in the courtyard for the welfare of the community three months before its construction began.
During the worship, donations were collected to fund its construction.
The Dhunighar is a two-storied, freestanding monument constructed with stone and mud masonry.
Adjacent to a small pit containing ashes from thedhunifire, there is a priest's seat adorned with medieval sculptures.
The southernmost room houses the sacreddhunifire.
In addition to its religious significance, the building also serves as a shelter for pilgrims.
According to local sources, the monument was originally constructed around 150 years ago, during the mid-19th century.
It underwent renovation in 2015.

Due to the unavailability of any inscriptive record and the discontinuation of socio-cultural activities associated with thecaitya, the year of its construction and the donor remain unclear.
A local resident was probably responsible for its construction sometime during the late medieval period.
Meanwhile, locals fail to recall when the disparaging renovation of the finial took place.

However, the Maitreya statue in the east has been lost, leaving the niche empty as of March 2024 CE.
The statues of the meditating Buddhas customarily placed above the Lokeśvaras are also missing from the four cardinal directions on the upper portion of thiscaitya, possibly due to theft.
The thirteen-tier spire (trayodaśabhuvana) on top has already been lost and is replaced with an unusually large cement finial probably belonging to some other temple.

Following the Śāha conquest of Nuwakot in 1744 CE, the political and economic measures adopted by the new ruler gradually transformed Nuwakot, a commercially vibrant city, into a village (see D. Vajrācārya and Ṭ. Śreṛṣṭha VS 2032, p. 81-83).

TheŚrīmadbhāgavatamahāpurāṇa(8.18) states that Viṣṇu descended as the Vāmana to restore the authority of Indra over the heavens, as it had been taken by the benevolent Asura King Mahābali.
Unable to fulfill his promise, Mahābali offered his head for the third, and so Vāmana placed his foot on Mahabali's head.
No inscription or any other historical document recording the initial construction of the temple could be uncovered.
Relying on the architecture of the temple as a dating method,Jośī(VS 2029, 58) assumes that this temple was constructed in the 18th century.
This Śikhara styled Śiva Mandira is entirely constructed in stone, from its plinth to its pinnacle.
A Śivaliṅga is consecrated in the sanctum, and a statue of Bhagavatī and Sūrya is also installed there.
There is a unique inscription inside the sanctum, alongside the Śivaliṅga.
Generally, inscriptions are inscribed on a single stone slab.
However, the same inscription is inscribed on four smaller stone slabs here.
Unfortunately, the part of the inscription where the construction date of these monuments was recorded, is damaged.
The inscription mentions a donor from Kirtipur who constructed the temple,hiti,and one of twophalcā.
It also records the establishment of aguṭhīand its social duties.
Kvāṭha NāyakaCaṇḍī Rāja Bhāro is mentioned in the inscription as one of theguṭhīmembers (Ś. ŚreṣṭhaVS 2057 182-183).
As the person in charge, there are severalKvāṭha Nāyakaswho constructedsataḥ, pāṭīs,temples, and alikein Kirtupur.
They also donated various objects to Bāghabhairava Mandira (KIR0004).

Even though the date of the initial construction of this temple cannot be deciphered from the inscription, mentioning of Caṇḍī Rāja Bhāro, the Kvāṭha Nāyaka, suggests that all the monuments of this temple complex were constructed simultaneously during the Late Malla Period.
Another inscription from 1854 CE (NS 975) on the stone slab supporting the statue of Nandī mentions the construction of adharmaśālā(phalcā).
The temple was severely damaged during the 2015 CE earthquakes and was reconstructed from the ground up in 2018 CE.
Tall buildings surround the courtyard in which the building is located.
The Bāhāḥ's carved door frames are its original ones, though the door leaves have been replaced with more simple framed metal shutters.
The façade of the two-storey building is completely covered with cement plaster and a simple band of cornice marks the separate floors.
Most of the original architecture of the building can no longer be found in this structure.
Pruscha(P-70) suggests that it was built some time around the 17th century.
In 1971, the Bāhāḥ was renovated and this was funded by selling a piece of its land. Śākyas are thesaṅghamembers of the Bāhāḥ; two families perform its daily ritual worships.
According toLocke(1985, 225) acaityaof thebāhāḥwas renovated in 805 NS, however, the inscription recording the event is missing.
During the reign of King Pṛthvī Vīra Vikrama Śāha in NS 1017, the Vajrācāryas performed worship in the Maṇiguphā and raining started (R. Vajrācārya1099, 88-89).
The renovation of the Hyuna Bāhāḥ is planned and the Lalitpur Metropolitan City has released a budget of Rs. 543,000.
As part of a protective network of Mātrikā shrines established around Lalitpur, her shrine was placed in the northwestern sector.

According to genealogical chronicles (vaṃśāvalī), during the reign of King Śivasimha Malla in Nepal Saṃvat 709 (1589 CE), the goddess announced to the people of Nandigrāma that she was about to be carried away by the Bagmatī River.
Before departing, she cursed the inhabitants of Nandigrāma and settled on the banks of the Bagmatī in Lalitpur (Yogī Naraharinātha VS 2013, p. 73).
Initially, only apīṭha(altar) was installed at the site; the temple was constructed later, though no historical record survives indicating the date or patron of its construction.
Originally, an unshaped stone served as her aniconic representation; this stone was later buried beneath the floor, and the current cast-metal image was installed above it.
The sanctum walls are lined with marble, and in front of the temple is a platform in the shape of the letter “T.”The oldest extant inscription at the site dates to Nepal Saṃvat 906 (1785 CE).
It records that Matsyendrasimha Bhāro of Dattalācheṃ (Dhālācheṃ) Ṭol built aphalca(resting pavilion) in the name of Lakṣmīramaṇa Upādhyāya and his three wives Dhanthakuṃ, Lakṣmī, and Pālulakṣmī.
He endowed three ropanis of land as guthi to fund annual worship of Dāmodara (Gaṇeśa), Sarasvatī, and Lakṣmī on 3rd of bright fortnight of Kārtika, followed byśrāddharituals.
Brahmins, Brahmaṇīs, Jyotiṣīs, and Karmācāryas were to be invited, and any surplus funds were to be spent on feasts for the guthi caretakers.
Matsyendrasimha Bhāro was also responsible for repairing the Bālakumāri Temple (LAL2000) after earthquake damage in Nepal Saṃvat 928 (1808 CE) (cf.LAL2000_I_20200922_08).
In 1918 CE (VS 1975), Jita Govinda Amātya of Daubāhā Ṭola and his sons Kīrtigovinda and Pūrṇagovinda constructed aghāṭaon the Bagmatī River at Dhantila.
Following the theft of the original image of Vārāhī, a new cast-metal image was installed in 2003 CE (VS 2059) by Kṛṣṇanātha Māske and his wife Śakuntalā Māske.

After the 2015 CE (VS 2072) earthquake caused structural damage, Balrām K.C. of Kopuṇḍol sponsored the temple’s restoration in 2019 CE (VS 2076) in memory of his late parents Kālugaṇḍe and Kāñchī K.C. and his late wife Bhagavatī K.C.

On the evening of Piśāca Caturdaśī, the metal image of the goddess is brought from the guthi house in a covered palanquin (ḍhakī) to the temple, worshipped in the sanctum for several hours, and then carried back to Kumbheśvar in procession.
The exact date of the temple's initial construction remains uncertain.

An inscription from another Śiva temple (KAT1550) of comparable size situated north of this monument records its reconstruction in 2018 CE (VS 2074), prompted by damage sustained during the 2015 CE earthquakes.
Although this inscription does not mention the southern temple, it is inferred that it was similarly reconstructed during that period.
In the course of restoration, some of the carved windows were replaced with new ones, while the struts were reused.
However, since around 2007 CE, priests of the Pāṇḍe caste have taken up the responsibility of worship (as confirmed by the priest, Pāṇḍe, a male aged 67).
Yangah Hiti takes its name from the locality known as "Yangah Tola." This historical monument houses various Licchavi-period artifacts and features three inscriptions from that era.
Similar to otherhitisin the Kathmandu Valley, Yangah Hiti was constructed near a crossroad.
However, contemporary developments have enclosed thehitiwith walls and private buildings, thus restricting access from the Yangah Tola crossroad.
Originally, a jaḥdhuṃprotruded from the northern wall, but it has since collapsed and become overgrown with bushes.
The presence of threesanadas from the Licchavi period in the form of inscriptions is another special feature at the Yaṅgāḥ Hiti.
Although these inscriptions are not related to thehiti, they appear to have been placed there ashitis are frequented by the locals in their daily lives.
The oldest of the three inscriptions dates back to the joint reign of King Bhīmārjunadeva and Jiṣṇugupta, circa 633 CE (D.Vajrācārya, VS 2030, p. 423).
However, due to erosion, the text of this inscription cannot be accurately dated.
Another inscription, dated Mānadeva Era 64 (640 CE), was installed during the joint reign of King Bhīmārjunadeva and Viṣṇugupta (D.Vajrācārya, VS 2030, p. 423 and p. 442).
The inscription reveals that the statue of the reclining Viṣṇu in Buḍhānīlakaṇṭha, was  constructed by Viṣṇugupta.

Another Licchavi inscription, dated Mānadeva Era 67 (643 CE), records the retention ofbirtālands by King Narendradeva in the name of Dakṣiṇakolīgrāma[1]draṅgathat was seized from the locals by Bhaumagupta (D.Vajrācārya, VS 2030, p. 463).see "Licchavi Kings according to three sources: https://asianart.com/articles/jaya/kings.htmlNo historical sources are available to provide a date for the initial construction of thehiti.
Thehitihas undergone numerous renovations over the years, but unfortunately, the sponsor and exact dates of these renovations are not documented.
The Department of Archaeology renovated thehitiin 2008-2009 CE (S. KhanālaVS 2068, p. 223).
Within the decade following the renovation, the northern section of thehiticollapsed, and the rubble is yet to be cleared.
At the time of documentation in 2021, thehitiwas overgrown by weeds, bushes, and partially submerged, thereby concealing numerous historically significant inscriptions and statues.
The rest of the buildings surrounding the courtyard are private houses.
However, the image of Nāmasaṅgīti has been stolen.
After the theft, an iron fence was installed in front of the entrance for protection.
Some years ago, the southern side of the worn roof was partially repaired with zinc sheets.
However, other parts of the roof are also badly damaged, with some tiles having fallen down.
It seems as though there was once a statue there but that it has perhaps been lost or stolen.

A stone inscription near to the entrance of the sanctum informs its readers that this monastic building was constructed by a member of Cikã Bahī Saṅgha in NS 991 (CE 1871) and that the founder had endowed the site withguṭhīlands to fund its ritual worship.
Theguṭhīmembers of the monastic buildings once performed the daily worship in turn, however this tradition no longer exists.
The Bahālukhā Maṭha, constructed during the late Malla period in Patan, belongs to the Girī lineage of the Daśanāmī tradition.
During the Malla period, numerous maṭhas were constructed in Bhaktapur and Patan, adorned with highly artistic windows and doors, making them appear as extensions of Malla palaces.
They consider Dattatreya as theirguruand believe that their tradition gradually spread to Nepal from India's Śṛṅgerī Maṭha for the purpose of religious propagation (Pande VS 2059, p. 2).
In the early medieval period, theDaśanāmīs first established manymaṭhas in Bhaktapur before expanding to Patan, with Bahālukhā Maṭha being one such example.
The ground floors of these buildings typically have open spaces supported by wooden columns and joists.
As of December 2024, the western section is entirely open, while a modern residential building occupies the southern section.
A photograph taken by Gutschow in 1992 CE (2011, p. 594) shows a traditional residential building in the southern section.
The maṭha suffered damage during the 1934 CE (1990 VS) earthquake (Pande VS 2059, p. 38).
However, it remains unclear whether the architectural modifications in the western and southern sections resulted from the earthquake or if they predate it, possibly originating in the Malla period.
Within the courtyard, a Śivaliṅga and a bell are installed.
Inscriptions from 1708 CE (NS 828) and 1713 CE (NS 833) (D. Vajācārya VS 2056, p. 362 & 391) suggest that the Gaṇeśa shrine was already in existence at that time.
Due to its proximity, the maṭha is also called "Triliṅgeśvara Maṭha" (Pande VS 2059, p. 38).
There is no inscription confirming its construction date.
An inscription from Licchavi King Vasantadeva, dated 513 CE (ŚS 435), is found in the Triliṅgeśvara Mahādeva Temple in front of the maṭha.
It states that the king granted 142mānikā kutaland (D. Vajrācārya BS 2030, p. 112).
The inscription has worn down over time, making it difficult to read.
If Vasantadeva donated land for this Mahādeva, it would make this one of the oldest Śivaliṅgas in Patan.
It seems that the Śaiva site with Triliṅgeśvara was chosen for the construction of the maṭha.
In 1743 CE (NS 863), sanyasī Amara Girī donated land for daily ritual of Śivaliṅga situated in front of the maṭha.
The inscription also states that the Śivaliṅga should be worshipped on various festivals throughout a year.
In 1760 CE (NS 880), Amara Girī donated his entire residence, and a piece of land with dilapidated house  in the name of Mahādeva (NHDP_0001_0010).
Thus, due to the Mahant’s great reverence, by donating lands from various places and his own residence, a distinct relationship was established between the nearby temple and the maṭha.
In 1811 CE (1868 VS), King Gīrvāṇayuddha granted 10 ropanī of land to Triliṅgeśvara.
The guṭhī income supported daily worship, ritual baths, Kṛṣṇa idol exhibitions on kṛṣṇāṣṭamī,rudrīrecitations, and the Śivarātrī fire ritual.
As the temple lost its endowed lands, many traditions declined.
A stone inscription attests to the temple's construction in 1662 CE, however, some of the inscriptions on the struts mention a date four years prior (1658 CE).
According to an inscription embedded in the courtyard wall, a new statue of Gaṇeśa was installed in 1787 CE.
The temple was severely damaged in the 2015 earthquakes but surprisingly did not collapse.
According to local informants, it has not yet been possible to raise the necessary funds for its restoration.

Smaller repairs have been carried out over the last few years, such as the installation of new cement-plastered shrines in the sanctum and the decorative cement plaster coverings of the ground floor walls.
The poorly maintained roofs are causing severe water damage to the timber structure, so that the temple is at a risk of collapsing.
The quadrangle is surrounded by residential houses on all sides but the south, where the main shrine building is located.
According to a local resident, the main shrine was rebuilt in 2004 and so is still in good condition.
During restoration work, most of the carved elements were reused.
The building has a two-way sloped roof with a small copper pinnacle on top.

The courtyard is surrounded by houses that have been able to preserve much of their original character: these buildings still retain their highly carved doors and windows, making this courtyard a place in Pātan well worth visiting.
However, the 2015 earthquake caused considerable damage to the buildings.
The building on the street is badly damaged; its veneer wall is separating from the plane, and it has taken major structural damage.
Its residents have erected raking shores to support the structure.

The building to the west of the courtyard has a colonnaded portico in its ground floor that opens up into the courtyard space, while the building to the east has a carved central door flanked by lattice windows.
The building to the north, which houses the main entry, has a five-baypāsuka jhyāabove its main entry door on the first floor.
Relying upon a copper plate inscription placed in the sanctum, Śākya (1994, 103) states that this Bāhāḥ was consecrated by Ruguju Śākya in NS 783.
Locke (1985, 108) corroborates this claim, however he reads the date as NS 782.
Unfortunately, this inscription is no longer available, and therefore the date could not be verified.
The Bāhāḥ was reconstructed by itssaṅgha-members in 1933, and in 2004 it was reconstructed by the Lalitpur Municipality.
Adjacent to the rest house is a water tank(jahdhum,NWK0670-001) which was built to provide refreshment alongside the resting place for travelers passing along this route.
The rest house was recently rebuilt in 2022 CE (VS 2079) through the joint efforts of the local community and the municipality.
Previously, the rest house stood in a different location before being shifted to its current site during the reconstruction.
Thejaḥdhuṃwater tank, however, is in a state of disrepair.
Records dating back to 1749 CE (NS 860) mention thisdyaḥchẽ, the residence of Chumā Gaṇeśa, whose temple (BKT0151) is situated west of thedyaḥchẽ.
This window area is where the Gaṇeśa statue, made of bronze (ḍhaloṭa), is established for the festival processions.
No historical evidence confirms the construction date of thedyaḥchẽ.
The earliest record, a copperplate from 1749 CE (NS 860), found in thedyaḥchẽ, is unrelated to it.

Recording the paving of the road in front of thedyaḥchẽ, likely with stones, by the local council members (pañca), the inscription addresses Chumā Gaṇeśa in the beginning, suggesting thedyaḥchẽexisted by then.
In 1742 CE (NS 862), craftsman Kvāche Śilpakāra and his son Ranharāma installed a pair of stone lions flanking the entrance (Y. Rāja VS 2057, p. 7).
Due to the structure’s age, Bhaktpur Municipality funded its reconstruction, with the foundation stone laid in 2023 CE (VS 2079).
As of April 2025, the reconstruction is nearly complete, but the Gaṇeśa statue, temporarily moved to Bhaṇḍārakhāla garden in Bhaktpur, has not yet been reinstated.
Guthi Chẽ 4 stands as a three-storied structure within the courtyard adjacent to the two front buildings opposite the Matsyendranātha Mandira (LAL0060) in Taḥ Bāhāḥ.
These two front buildings currently house the Patan Office of the Guṭhī Saṃsthāna.
Situated on the northern side of the courtyard, this building is the fourth in a series, all designated by the name Guthi Chẽ (building) followed by a sequential number for ease of documentation.
Similar to Guthi Chẽ 3 (LAL0064), Guthi Chẽ 4 serves as a storage facility for items associated with the procession of the Buṅgadyaḥ Chariot (LAL0001).
Facing towards the south, the building features a ground floor design reminiscent of aphalcā.
Historical records suggest that this building likely dates back to the Rāṇā period, having either been constructed or reconstructed during that era.
However, even prior to the earthquakes of 2015, the building was already showing signs of wear.
The space encompassing the courtyard in front of Guthi Chẽ 4 serves multiple purposes.

Additionally, this area accommodates the crafting of the finial seat (bāymvaḥ) for the chariot, the simmering of canes, and the preparation of wooden components required for the chariot's construction.
