text: This three-bayphalcāwas established in the early 18th century.
The temple was reconstructed after the 1934 earthquakein in śikhara-style.
The materials that were salvaged from the earthquake were used for its reconstruction.
No inscription or any other document related to the establishment of the temple or any other historical event is available.
This apparently assigns them and their family the duty of taking care of this temple and allows them to establish shops around the temple's plinths.
Thisbāhāḥcan be reached through the narrow underpass of a residential building.
Thebāhāḥcourtyard measures 13.75 m × 13.75 m and has a line ofdharmadhātujinālaya caitya,dharmadhātu maṇḍalaand avajrain front of the esoteric building (āgãchẽ), which faces north.
The main door of the building consists of carved wooden panels, stone doorjambs and a stone lintel head with a projecting base for thetoraṇa(tympanum).
The oldtoraṇawas dated NS 967 (1847 CE), however this was lost and a new cementtoraṇahas replaced it.
These windows were donated by Lokapati and Hirāmāyā.
The floors of the building are separated with a band of lime-plastered cornices and dentils.
On the rear side of the building, a dormer window with a circular opening can be found on the roof.

Gāḥ Bāhāḥ is neither considered to be a majorbāhāḥof Patan, nor is it a branch of anotherbāhāḥ.Śreṣṭha (VS 2044, 26) suggests that its name derives from the termgāḍaorgāḥ, which refers to a ditch or pit.
Although a palm-leaf manuscript dated NS 570 (1450 CE) mentions thisbāhāḥ(Śākya 1995, 161), no further historical records are available with which to date it more precisely.
Pruscha(1975, C/P-51) mentions that thebāhāḥwas constructed by a Brahmin named Yaśodhara.
Seven decades ago, the remnants of the damagedbāhāḥwere found lying on the ground.
They collected donations to construct abāhāḥbuilding and also formed a committee with seven members to conduct socio-religious activities there.
These days, a Vajrācārya priest from Nyākhācuka performs the monastic building's daily ritual worships.
Svakaraju Vajrācārya constructed the Ikhācva Bāhāḥ in 1654 CE (NS 774) on the site of acaityaestablished in 1619 CE (NS 739).
A two-story structure resembling a residential building, thebāhāḥfaces north.

The Ikhācva Bāhāḥ was built in 1654 CE (NS 774) on the site of a pre-existingcaityaestablished by Kīrtisiṃhadeva (text: Kitasiṃdeva) during the reign of King Siddhinarasiṃha Malla in 1619 CE (NS 739).
Thebāhāḥwas founded through a fire ritual and the installation of statues of Akṣobhya, Mahākāla, Cakrasamvara, and Vajravārāhī.
An inscription at thebāhāḥstates that Vīradeva and his mother Padmāvatī also took part in the fire oblation.
A Vajrācārya priest from Nyākhācuka, Patan, oversaw the establishment rituals.
Thebāhāḥwas renovated after the 1934 earthquakes by Devarāja Vajrācārya, who restored its traditional features usingjhĩgaṭītiles and atrikhājhyāḥwindow on the first floor (Pruscha 1975, Ca-3).
However, a subsequent renovation in the 1980s compromised its traditional appearance by adopting modern concrete architecture.
It was rebuilt in 2002 as a five-bayed Phalca with new columns and iron railings.
There is no inscriptive evidence about the construction of this Phalcā.
In VS 2057 (2000 CE) the derelict Phalcā was reconstructed with the support of the Lalitpur Municipality (they donated 153.000 rupees) and support from the local community.
An additional budget has been earmarked for further renovation and to replace the existing struts with ornately carved ones.
Thisphalcābears an inscription dating back to the reign of Yoganarendra Malla (r. 1684-1705 CE), suggesting that this rest house is the oldest in Chobhar.
Inscriptions from otherphalcās in Chobhar are only from post-Malla periods.
It was likely built to support religious and cultural activities associated with thecaitya.
Thephalcāhas an inscription related to its initial construction.
The inscription mentions that in 1696 CE (NS 816), a member of the Śākya clan named Kutuju led the construction of thephalcā.
A remark in the inscription suggests that Kutuju might have given up a part of his own residence to build thephalcā.
Although thephalcā, built during the later Malla period, may have undergone several renovations, no documentation is available to confirm this.
In c. 2012 CE (VS 2069), the Department of Archaeology carried out the restoration of thephalcā.
From the Licchavi period onward,caityas and Buddhist statues were continually added to this religiously significant square during the Malla and Śāha periods.
Later, Śākya clan member Kutuju added thephalcāto the square to facilitate cultural activities.
The inscription related to its construction also features a carvedcaitya, further confirming this.
One of these is the annual procession of Goddess Bhairavī, during which a ceremonial pole is erected.
The ground floor of the Lāma Pāṭī provides storage space for this pole, suggesting that its elongated design of the building was intended for this purpose.

Local folklore claims that the Lāma Pāṭī was once a palace belonging to the king of Patan, but there are no historical records to support this, nor is there any information on its original sponsor or construction date.

The wooden columns and capitals feature designs from different eras—some from the later medieval period and others from the Śāha-Rāṇā period—indicating that the pāṭī was likely built during the later medieval period and later reconstructed during the Śāha-Rāṇā era.
It remains unclear whether a new window was installed during the pāṭī’s reconstruction or if the entire upper floor was added afterward.
A painting by Dīrghamāna Citrakāra (1877–1951 CE) shows an additional small roof built in the middle of the existing roof.
In 1996 (VS 2053), part of the roof was damaged in a windstorm and subsequently renovated by the Department of Archaeology (local resident, Ḍaṃgola, male, age 62).
The veneer bricks on the outer walls were affected by the 2015 earthquake and have yet to be repaired.
Currently, the Lāma Pāṭī is undergoing renovation through a collaboration between the Department of Archaeology and the Chinese Academy of Cultural Heritage.
In the past, a local organization called “Sampadā Saṃrakṣaṇa” operated a museum within the Lāma Pāṭī, but it was relocated to Sātatale Durbar in 2011 CE (VS 2068).
The main sanctum is built with smalldacī apāin mud mortar.
No inscription or documents providing historical evidence about the establishment of this temple could be found.
Pruscha(2015: 134) assumes that the temple was constructed in the 16th century.
This temple was renovated in 1994 by the Department of Archaeology (DoA) with the help of the German government.
Some decades ago (the exact date is not known), the statue of Jagannātha was stolen.
Upon finding it, the DoA returned and reinstalled it inside the temple.
Thetoraṇaabove the main door was allegedly also stolen some years ago (again, the exact date is not known).
The photo of the temple shows that all theṭũḍālawere carved, but nowadays theyhave been replaced with plain wood, with the exception of those containing the images ofśārdūlason all sides.
The monuments were constructed on a flat terrain which may have hosted further built-forms, as indicative of the architectural remains foundin situ(KLK0190-003).
This built-environment reflects thesmārtaworship of Hindu gods.
The area surrounding the caitya is paved with black flagstones and has been encroached upon by some of the building materials used for the reconstruction of the Mandira.
This monument was constructed in 1983, and its anniversary worship is performed on the full moon day of Vaiśākha.
There are no historical sources to date the initial construction of the Shrine.
An inscription on one of its northern pillars records that the Shrine was renovated in 1692 CE (812 CE).
Facing south, the northern side of thisphalcāis directly attached to Bhaiṣajyabāhāḥ (LAL1650), a two-bay deep branch monastic building belonging to Cika Bahī (LAL1620) that was established in 1878.
As of January 2025, it has been rebuilt as a residential house, inhabited by a Kũvara family.

Although it has been completely destroyed and converted into a modern structure (January 2025), a photo showing its former shape was published in an inventory published by the Kathmandu Valley Town Development Plan in 1982 CE (VS 2039) (Inventory VS 2039, p. 166).
Sataḥ, temple and statues in front of it were established by Tejanārāṃ Bhāro, a resident of Kathmandu, and his mother Thakuṃmaiju.

Among the two inscriptions available here at the site, the first one from 1842 CE (NS 964) records the construction of theśivālayatogether with the statues of Lakṣminārāyaṇa, Bhavānīśaṅkara, Gaṇeśa, and Hanumān.
It also reveals that a “pālī” of seven bays was additonally constructed, a reference to the Sataḥ (KAT2630_I_003_20240603_02).
Another inscription (KAT2630_I_004_20240603_02) from 1850 CE (NS 970) mentions the same mother and son prescribing various rituals to be performed at the site.
This was probably the error of the inscriber, who mistakenly carved 1 instead of 7.

In 1850 CE (NS 970), mother and son endowed a sufficient amount of land to form a religious trust (guthi) to manage the regular operation of religious activities in the statues and the temple in front of the monument.
In front of the temple structure and at the center of the courtyard, one can find avajradhātu caityabuilt on a square plan of 386 cm.
A smalldharmadhātu maṇḍala(80 cm high) has been built between thecaityaand the temple structure.
The square courtyard measures 13.3 m x 13.3 m and is surrounded by residential buildings in all directions, with a small open space at the south-east corner.
However, this has been replaced by a stone statue of an eastern-facing Akṣobhya.
No inscription or other document providing any further information about the establishment of the Bāhāḥ could be uncovered.
Although he cannot find hard evidence to prove his theory,Pruscha(2015, 140) argues that this monument was constructed in the 16th century.
The Bāhāḥwas built by Śreṣṭhas, and Vajrācāryas from Bu Bāhāḥ used to perform the ritual worship in the shrine.
The inscription of the Caitya mentions that its construction was funded by Nararāja Pāneju in 1944 CE.
Nararāja also established aguṭhīto perform the daily and anniversary ritual worship of the Caitya.
However, his descendants sold their property and moved away from the locality, selling theguṭhīland and thus bringing an end to the daily worship.
An artistic gate made of bricks with a tiled roof is attached to thephalcāand marks the entry to the residential compound that surrounds the old monastic building.
Thephalcāused to be closed with latticed windows before it was reconstructed after 2015.
After the reconstruction, all bays have been opened again.
Until about 1950 CE, thephalcāwas one storey high.
In 1977 CE, theBālakumārīLibrary was opened on the ground floor.
The carving style of its columns suggesst that it was built in the 1870s.
On its northern side, thephalcāadjoins the compound wall of a private building.
In 2000, thephalcāwas partly dismantled and restored.
It is constructed on a relatively open space and this city quarter is named Cibhāḥkhyaḥ after thecaitya.
It has a three-level plinth, constructed with bricks, and plastered withbajramortar.
The local community members believe that this is one of the Aśoka Caityas and was constructed by King Aśoka himself.
It is believed that the place, where thecaityastands, was a pond of milk (durupukhū), Aśoka filled it, and constructed thecaitya.
Pruscha(1975, vol. II, p. 38) mentions that a person called Kelayel Tuladhar constructed thiscaitya.
Some of the local elders believe that the Śreṣṭhā family who runs the Hotel Ambassador at the Lazimpat Road, Kathmandu, constructed Chibhākhyaḥ Caitya.
Thecaityawas renovated in 1983 CE (VS 2040) after a tree, sprouting out of thecaitya’s upper part,trayodaśabhuvana, threatened to topple it.
It is believed to be initially built by a certain person called Guṇalakṣmī Varmā.
A statue of the Cakrasamvara is installed on its second floor as thebāhāḥ’s secret and sacred deity (āgaṃdyaḥ).
[3]TheNepālikabhūpavaṃśāvalī(19.3.18) mentions that thisbāhāḥwas constructed during the reign of King Siddhinarasiṃha Malla (r. 1620 – 1661).
However, other pieces of evidence (cf.H. ŚākyaVS 2036, 27-28 andLocke1985, 128) suggest that it must have been built before him.
Locke (1985, 128) assumes that thisbāhaḥwas initially built in front of the Kumbheśvara Temple and was later moved to its present place by Siddhinarasiṃha Malla.
None of the inscriptions so far traced out in thebāhāḥ’s premises is from his time.
Thedyaḥchẽwhich is currently (October 2020) under renovation was severely damaged during the 2015 CE earthquakes.

Bandhudatta Bāhāḥ, situated in the Te Bāhāḥ (KAT0630) premises is said to have been built by King Narendradeva, specifically for renowned priest Bandhudatta, who was instrumental in bringing Buṅgadyaḥ to the Kathmandu Valley.
However, there is no historical evidence that Narendradeva built it.
Two statues of Sūrya (established north of the Bāhāḥ) are said to have been erected during the reign of King Ratna Malla in 1520 CE (NS 640) (J. Vajrācārya VS 2053, p.12).
In 1462 CE (NS 583), a statue of Candra, the moon deity, was erected (see 'monument objects' and 'historical events').
Two Licchavi inscriptions and a few Licchavicaityasin the area indicate that it was a Licchavi settlement.
There is, however, no historical source relating to the construction of Bandhudatta Bāhāḥ.
Before Bandhudatta Bāhāḥ, another monastic building called Tīrtha Vihāra existed here, according to oral tradition (cf. J. Vajrācārya VS 2053, p.2).

Chronicles (for example,Nepālikabhūpavaṃśāvalī2016, 13.53) mentions that King Narendradeva, the sponsor and leader of the mission to bring Buṅgadyaḥ to the Valley, built avihārafor his priest Bandhudatta, who completed the mission using his tantric powers.
Despite the fact that Bandhudatta Bāhāḥ and Te Bāhāḥ are two separate monastic buildings, they share the same monastic association (saṃgha).
Tebaha (Te Bāhāḥ), as a place name, now refers to the whole of the large courtyard, which includes the Te Bāhāḥ monastic building.

However, there are two separate monastic buildings in the courtyard, which the locals claim that they are the same monastery, i.e., one Bāhāḥ with two buildings; both have the samesaṃghabut two separatekvāḥpāḥdyaḥsdue to the presence of two separate monastic buildings.
The Dyaḥchẽ is built in front of the passage that leads to Yatkhā Bāhāḥ (KAT1050) and it serves as the residence of Kaṅgaḥ Ajimā, the vernacular name of Cāmuṇḍā.

The first floor houses the sanctum, which contains a metal statue of Kaṅgaḥ Ajimā (Cāmuṇḍā) as well as statues of the remaining deities of theaṣṭamātṛkāgroup, Gaṇeśa, Bhairava, Siṃhinī, and Vyghriṇī (note that photographing the deities inside the sanctum was prohibited when we assessed the site in November 2022 CE).
citations: (note that photographing the deities inside the sanctum was prohibited when we assessed the site in November 2022 CE)

text: A stone statue of Siṃhanāda Lokeśvara is installed in the sanctum's western corner.
The Lokeśvara statue bears an inscription from NS 904, which corresponds to 1784 CE.
There are no historical records to date the initial construction of the Dyaḥchẽ.
In 724 CE (Kaligata Era 3825), King Guṇakāmadeva founded the city of Kathmandu in the shape of a sword (khaḍga) and established shrines to theaṣṭamātṛkādeities to protect the city.
When King Guṇakāmadeva founded the city in accordance with Mahālakṣmī's instructions, he may have also built the Kaṅgaḥ Ajimā Dyaḥchẽ.

The earliest record from the Dyaḥchẽ is an eroded inscription from 1633 CE? (NS 753?) that deals with something being renovated during the joint reign of King Lakṣmīnarasiṃha Malla and his son Pratāpa Malla.
Several other inscriptions in this area record various offerings such as the stone throne and metaltoraṇa.
The Dyaḥchẽ was reconstructed in 2013 CE (VS 2070) with the help of the Department of Archaeology and the Hanumandhoka Palace Conservation Program.
It was damaged by the 2015 CE earthquakes and was renovated in 2018 CE (VS 2075).
The second phase of renovation was completed in 2021 CE (VS 2077).
It is not a public building, but its worship is restricted to the members of a kin group, or guthi, and performed strictly according to the prevailing tradition.

monument_name: Hitigāḥcā (built during the late Malla Period)
text: Hitigāḥcā, built during the late Malla Period, is located to the northwest of the historic road leading to Thankot (Thānakoṭa) from Kirtipur.

monument_name: Hitigāḥcā (built during the late Malla Period)
text: An extremely damaged statue, embellished with atoraṇa,is placed above the spout, and a Bhagīratha statue is carved below the spout, which is a common feature of the mosthitisin the Kathmandu Valley.

monument_name: Hitigāḥcā (built during the late Malla Period)
text: An inscription in the adjacent Śiva Mandira (seeKIR0078) mentions the construction of Hitigāḥcā as well.

monument_name: Hitigāḥcā (built during the late Malla Period)
text: The part where the date is mentioned is damaged making it undecipherable.

monument_name: Hitigāḥcā (built during the late Malla Period)
text: It, however, mentions that a donor from Kirtipur constructed these structures (Hiṭigāḥcā, Śiva Mandira, and Phalcā) and established aguṭhī.

monument_name: Hitigāḥcā (built during the late Malla Period)
text: It is likely that all the monuments in this complex were constructed simultaneously during the late Malla Period.

monument_name: Hitigāḥcā (built during the late Malla Period)
text: The inscription details the duties to be carried out by theguṭhīin the mentioned monuments, such as worshipping in the temple, cleaning the premises among others.
The Phalcā's roof is covered withjhĩgaṭītiles and has been recently repaired by a Khaḍgī at his own cost.
Inside, one can find two inscriptions and a statue of Padmapāṇi Lokeśvara.

One of theinscriptions in this Phalcā mentions that it was constructed in 1704 CE (NS 824) by Narahari Bhāro and his wife Vasumuni, residents of Dhopogatra (present Dhaugala ṭola) during the reign of Yoganarendra Malla.
The same inscription mentions the construction of a stage platform (dabū), though this has since been removed.
The second inscription states that Siddhivajra Vajrācārya from Hiraṇyavarṇa Mahāvihāra recitedGuṇakāraṇyavyūhaat the chariot procession of Matsyendranātha in 1868 CE (NS 988).
The inscription does not mention whether the recitation took place inside the Phalcā or somewhere else.
The building was reconstructed one month after this recitation took place.
A representative of each of the four major Vihāras of Patan was involved in both the recitation and the reconstruction process.
The Bāhāḥ's main shrine building is on the southern wing.
The three-storey building is decorated with images of Buddhist deities on the cornice of the second floor and carved struts that support the overhanging metal roof.
The earliest reference to this Bāhāḥ is in a manuscript copy of theKriyāsaṅgrahapañjikā, copied in NS 373 (1252 CE).
An inscription on the plinth of the Nandī statue mentions that it was offered in the name of Śiva by a donor (name illegible due to erosion of text) from the Gaḥchẽ Ṭola in NS 838 (1718 CE).
Therefore, it is possible that theśivaliṅgawas already there before the installation of the Nandī statue.
Noguthirelated to this Temple exists now.
The present Temple structure for theśivaliṅgawas constructed only in the 1980s by local residents.
The Bāhāḥ's main building (kvāḥpāḥchẽordyaḥchẽ) is a simple one-story structure.
A woodentoraṇadated 1637 CE (NS 757) is placed atop thekvāḥpāḥchẽ's entrance.
The earliest historical record from the Bāhāḥ is an inscription on thetoraṇafrom 1637 CE (NS 757).
In 1968 CE (NS 1088), Śākyabhikṣu Cikadhi and his family from Hvakhā Bāhāḥ established adharmadhātujinālaya caitya(see monument objects below) at the Bāhāḥ premises.
The Bāhāḥ was renovated in 1995 CE (VS 2052) with donations from the locals.
During the renovation, thejhĩgaṭītile roof was replaced with concrete.

Situated within the Bishal Bazaar supermarket complex in Nhū Sataka (New Road), Kathmandu, the Bhagavatī temple is locally referred to as Janasevā Bhagavatī, a name associated with a cinema hall established on this site in 1949 CE (VS 2006) before the establishment of the supermarket.
Following a fire that ravaged the cinema hall in 1961 CE (VS 2018), the Bishal Bazaar supermarket was built on this spot in 1969 CE (VS 2026) (A. Ajīta VS 2064, p.40).
No historical sources provide information about the temple's original construction.
It is plausible that the site initially functioned as an open shrine, with the construction of a formal temple occurring during the Śāha era.
Following the earthquakes of 1934 CE, the temple underwent renovation (Pruscha 1975, K-146).
In 1973 CE (VS 2030), Rāmaprasāda Prajāpati sponsored the renovation of the temple's entrance, roof, and columns.
Before the earthquake of VS 2072, thephalcāwas in very poor condition.
After the earthquake, the upper part of thephalcāwas damaged and it remained in disrepair for nearly seven years.
In 2024 CE (VS 2081), Godavarī Municipality reconstructed thephalcāin its original form.
There is an inscription regarding its original construction, stating that Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa, a person living near thephalcāin Capāḥkva ṭola, built it in 1857 CE (NS 977).
He hoped that the merit from constructing thisphalcāwould allow his deceased ancestors and future generations to reach heaven after death.

However, after the land allocated to thephalcāwas lost, the tradition of distributingSamaybajiended, according to the family members of the concerned lineage (one of the clan members, Maharjana, male, age 83).
A somewhat hidden narrow door leads to thebāhāḥ’scourtyard, where a small shrine of Akṣobhya is attached to a six-storey building.
A stone inscription attached to the left wall of the shrine mentions the date of its initial construction.
A member of Bu Bāhāḥ(LAL0440)calledDevarāja Vajrācāryabuiltthisbāhāḥin 1902, one year after he constructed thedharmadhātujinālaya caityain the courtyard.
Established facing south, thispīṭhahouses an aniconic stone enshrined as Cāmuṇḍā.
A stone toraṇa has been installed over the stone worshipped as Cāmuṇḍā.
A stone maṇḍala has also been established in front of Cāmuṇḍā.
Other aniconic stones representing Mātṛkās have also been established within thepīṭha.
A pair of stone lions is also installed at thepīṭha.
No inscription regarding the establishment of thispīṭhahas been found.
According to chronicles, King Ratna Malla established a settlement by constructing a town of 300 houses in 1509-1510 CE (NS 629-630) (Yogī Naraharinātha VS 2013, p. 96).
The Cāmuṇḍā pīṭha may have been established at that time as part of the installation of Mātṛkās for the protection of the city.
In 2023 CE (VS 2080), a wall was built around thepīṭhaand an entrance gate was constructed with financial assistance from the Tarakeshwar Municipality (local resident, Śreṣṭha, male, age 51).
There, after theguṭhiyārasperform the main worship including the sacrifice of male goats and sheep, the deity is brought to Lāchi Ṭola in Ward No. 2 with a sindūra jātrā and installed.
Although a road currently separates thehitifrom the temple, its connection to the Nārāyaṇa Temple has preserved its name (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2077, p. 414).
The adjacent palace, constructed by Vīra Śamśera during the reign of Pṛthvī Vīra Vikrama, also came to be known as Narāyaṇa Hiti Durbar (R. Upādhyāya VS 2007, p. 55).
A Garuḍa Narāyaṇa image is installed on the central metal spout, whereas the side spouts feature Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa images.
Several Malla-period inscriptions are also affixed to the walls.
No inscription definitively records the original construction of thehiti.

According to theDevamālā Vamśāvali(Y. Naraharinātha VS 2013, p. 19), in Kalīgat Saṃvat 1911, King Vikrama Sena, in honor of King Dharmagat, commissioned a four-faced Narāyaṇa image west of the palace and constructed Narāyaṇa Hiti.
Numerous legends, however, associate thehitiwith Lichchhavi kings Dharmadeva and Mānadeva I, though no contemporary Licchavi inscriptions corroborate this.
Despite multiple attempts, the water could not be restored until an astrologer prescribed a tantric ritual requiring a human sacrifice possessing 32guṇas (perfections).
This episode is also documented in theDevamālā Vamśāvali(Y. Naraharinātha VS 2013, p. 19).
Four inscriptions are affixed to the upper part of thehiti.
The oldest dates to 1625 CE (NS 745), and another to 1786 CE (NS 907).

An inscription from the reign of Raṇabahādura Śāha records that a certain Movāsīlāla of Jahānāvāda, India, installed a rest-house (dharmaśālā) north of Narāyaṇa Hiti along with a Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇ image (KAT3270-010), which faces east, behind thehiti(G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2077, p. 416).
The remaining two inscriptions are badly eroded and unreadable.
According to a later inscription on the central spout, Garuḍa-Narāyaṇ was installed with a golden spout by Dhīra Śamśera Jaṅga Bahādura Rānā in 1884 CE (NS 1941).
Subsequently, in 1958 CE (NS 2015), King Mahendra restored thehiti, reactivating water flow through previously blocked spouts.
Since thisbāhāḥwas constructed by Vasundharā Vajrācārya, a member of Tarumūla Mahāvihāra, it came to be known as 'Vasundharākīrti Vihāra'.
The statue of Amitābha Buddha installed in thisbāhāḥwas established by a monk named Nityadhana in 1737 CE (NS 857).
Situated in a small courtyard on the western side of the Jhvaḥchẽ road, theDyaḥchẽof thisbāhāḥis constructed facing east.
On the ground floor of theDyaḥchẽ, Amitābha Buddha is established as the Kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ (principal deity).
Currently (January 2026 CE), an additional five-story structure has been constructed above the ground floor of theDyaḥchẽ.
The main door of thebāhāḥappears old and dilapidated, above which an artistic wooden toraṇa is installed.
An inscription from the reign of King Jayaprakāśa Malla, dated 1737 CE (NS 857), is affixed to the wall near the main door of thebāhāḥ.
According to the inscription, a monk named Nityadhana from Sikhamuḍi Ṭola established Amitābha Buddha here and donated land to conduct the annual worship of thebāhāḥ.
From this, it can be ascertained that thisbāhāḥwas established prior to 1737 CE (NS 857).

There is a popular saying that thisbāhāḥwas established by Vasundharā Vajrācārya, a member of Tarumūla Mahāvihāra, and hence it is called 'Vasundharākīrti Vihāra'; however, no written record of this is available.

Additionally, after thebāhāḥwas destroyed in the earthquake of 2015 CE (VS 2072), Buddharatna Śākya, a member of thisvihāra saṃgha, renovated it, and the additional structures were built above thebāhāḥ.
An inscription dated 1713 CE at the northern wall in the sanctum informs readers of donations made to the temple and the annual worships observed (VajrācāryaVS 2056, 391).
It can thus be assumed that the temple dates from 1713 CE or possibly earlier.
Thetoraṇaabove the entrance has been stolen.
Local people believe that their predecessors built the temple.

According to the inscription affixed to the Viṣṇu niche above the eastern (main) conduit, the water spout was built in 1911 CE (VS 1967) by Kājī Marīcamānasiṃha, fulfilling the wish of his deceased father Kājī Balavānasiṃha (text: Balavānsi).
The inscription names Balavānasiṃha's father as Munsī Gaurīdāsa.
While the inscription does not give their surname, the title ofmunsīwas exclusively held by the Pradhānas of Kathmandu during the Rāṇā period.

The pioneer among them was Lakṣmīdāsa Pradhāna, who was the head of themunsīs(mīra munsī) of the Munsīkhānā (lit. house ofmunsīs), the government office responsible for foreign affairs and correspondence during the rule of Bhīmasena Thāpā (term of office 1806-1837 CE) until the end of the Rāṇā period in 1951 CE.
As recorded in the inscription, Balavānasiṃha had intended to build a water spout at the Baṭāra Bazaar square but passed away before he could fulfil this vow.

His son Marīcamānasiṃha later carried out his father's wish by constructing this water spout, which aimed to address the "water woes of the residents of the area and those passing by." The inscription also notes that "the spout was built near a rest house built by Munsī Gaurīdāsa's ancestors."The water for the Baṭāra Bazaar water spout was sourced from Mulī, a distant location, through an intricate canal system.
However, modern construction disturbed this canal network, disrupting the water flow to the spout.
In 2018 CE (VS 2075), the government water corporation office in Bidur Municipality arranged for modern pipelines to restore the functionality of the spouts.

Locals report that the tradition of regularly cleaning water sources like wells and spouts on Sithi Nakhaḥ, the 6th of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, was previously practiced in the area but has ceased as of May 2024 CE (a local resident, Śreṣṭha, male, age 63).
The Phalcā was renovated in 1984.
This work saw the originaljhĩgaṭī-tiled roof replaced with a concrete slab.
In 1999, a Nāmasaṅgīti shrine was built on the eastern wall of the Phalcā.
A stone statue of Guru Lekhamāna Maharjana was erected on the right side of the shrine in 2009, and in 2014 the Phalcā was renovated, maintaining its traditional structure.
Hiku Hiti, constructed in the late medieval period for washermen (dhobī), was renovated in CE 1883 (NS 1004).
The Dhobī River is calledHijyā Khusiin Nepal Bhasa, meaning “the river for washing clothes” (K. Śreṣṭha VS 2044, p. 171).
Since Hiku Hiti was also built in a settlement of washermen who made their livelihood by washing clothes, its name must be associated with this occupation.
Thishiti, built facing west, contains three spouts.
Within thehiticourtyard, a Śivaliṅga is installed.
No historical evidence has been found regarding the original construction of thishiti.
The source of this hiti is a pond located inside the Jawalakhel Zoo (S. Khanāla VS 2068, p. 74).
That pond was built on the 3rd day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha in CE 1659 (NS 779) by King Siddhinarasiṃha Malla in the name of his mother Lālamatī (D. Lamsāla VS 2023, p. 65).
Therefore, thishitimust have been constructed in the late medieval period after CE 1659 (NS 779).
In CE 1883 (NS 1004), three individuals Budhimānsi (Buddhimānasiṃha) Rajaka, Rāmadāsa Rajaka, and Herā Rajaka together with their families, renovated the hiti.
After the renovation, they performed worship and consecration rituals (pratiṣṭhākarma) for thehiti.
Around CE 2005 (VS 2062), thehitiwas again renovated under the leadership of a local organization called the Dhobīdhārā Conservation Family, formed by local residents.
At that time, images of Gaṇeśa, Nārāyaṇa, and Umāmaheśvara were also installed (Local resident from a Rajaka caste, male, age 54).
The name Śvetakālī is also found in theDevamālāVaṃśāvalī, a later chronicle, and a copperplate inscription from 1802 CE (VS 1859).
An ornate archway (toraṇa), covered with gilded sheets and featuring Ṅatamaru Ajimā as its central figure, is installed over the central bay on the eastern side.

According to theDevamālāVaṃśāvalī, King Guṇakāmadeva established Śvetakālī by conducting tantric rituals after founding the city of Kathmandu in 724 CE (Kaligata Era 3825) following instructions from Goddess Mahālakṣmī in his dreams.
The earliest inscription from the temple dates back to NS 803, corresponding to 1683 CE, and refers to the goddess as "Ṅatamaru," indicating the name's popularity among locals already back then.
The uppermost tier was added by a high-ranking officer named Bhoṭu Pā̃ḍe, mostly known as akapardāra, a position described as the chief of the royal household.

He vowed to offer special worship and donations to Ṅatamaru Ajimā after being detained in China for some time while he was in a diplomatic mission in response to an offer of a treaty from the Chinese army that had already marched into a Nepalese territory named Ghaibung in 1792 CE (VS 1849) (D. Vajrācārya VS 2037, p.371).
Following his release, he added a gilded roof to the temple and donated over 150ropanīs of land in the name of the main deity.
The temple has shown resilience against major earthquakes, with no record of damage during the major earthquakes of 1833, 1934, or of 2015 CE.

Renovations were carried out during the reign of King Mahendra in 1958 CE (VS 2015) and further restoration was undertaken by King Virendra in 1999 CE (VS 2056), involving the dismantling and rebuilding of the upper tier.
The trust named the "Bhalabhala Aṣṭamī Guthi", was established by Bhoṭu Pā̃ḍe, and oversees periodic worships at the temple throughout the year.
A newly laid cement path leads to the monument, which is now part of a walled complex built by the village committee.
It is built on a large stone platform.
The Temple does not have anāmalakadisc installed.
From the 13th to the 15th centuries, suchśikharatemples were built throughout the Karnali Basin (Andolfatto 2019).
The rarity of inscriptions onśikharatemples (locally known asdevala) complicates dating of these monuments.
Given the Temple's proximity to three nearbyśikharatemples dating from the 13th to the 15th centuries, it is possible that this monument was built around the same time.
Established by the Śreṣṭhas who migrated from Banepa to Bālāgāũ, thiscaityareceives the annual worship on the full moon day of Āśvina.
Located in Bālāgāũ of Mātātīrtha, thecaitya, built on a brick platform, is in a dilapidated condition.
Anothercaitya(BLG0020-001) has been established on the ground to the east.
A stone inscription of 1716 CE (NS 836) rests against thiscaitya.
No records have so far been found that date the establishment of thiscaitya.
Judging by its style, it can be inferred that it was built during the late medieval period.
According to locals, thiscaityawas established by the Śreṣṭha community who migrated from Banepa to Bālāgāũ.
Thephalcāto the east of thecaitya(BLG0020-002) was built in 1716 CE (NS 836).
Mānasiṃha Bhāro of the Solaṃkī dynasty built thephalcāin the name of his deceased parents and installed a statue of Bhavānīśaṅkara.
He also established a trust for the worship of Bhavānīśaṅkara installed in thephalcā.
Two other stone inscriptions, dating back to 1717 CE (NS 837) and 1743 CE (864), are found a little distance from the site of thecaitya.
Both inscriptions mention the construction of aphalcā, but it is unclear which structures these inscriptions refer to.
Such shrines were commonly constructed during the Rana period forśivaliṅgasand other Hindu deities.
Locke further suggests that although constructed by a merchant donor, the daily ritual duties were probably assigned to the Vajrācāryas of Sikhomū Bāhāḥ (1986, p. 285).
The extant inscription of Bhavānīśaṅkara at the site helps clarify several of these earlier assumptions.
The inscription, dated 1746 CE (NS 866), explicitly records that Bhavānīśaṅkara installed the images of Akṣobhya, Śāriputra, and Maudgalyāyana of his own volition within his private residence.
The text, however, does not indicate whether this installation was originally conceived in terms of thebāhāḥinstitution.
Thus, the inscription simply confirms that a Buddhist triad was initially enshrined devotionally within a domestic space.

A comparable case of household installation is attested at Yatkha Ṭol, where, in 1862 CE (NS 982), Dhanasiṃha Tāmrākāra constructed abāhāḥwithin his residence and donated the house in the names of the Svayaṃbhucaityaand Vijeśvarī, along with a small monetary contribution to the Svayaṃbhu Caitya Guṭhī (H. Śākya NS 1099, 32–33; Locke 1985, 295).
In contrast, the Basantapur inscription contains no reference to the donation of the house itself.
Following the 1934 CE (VS 1990) earthquake, the surrounding houses were cleared to create the current open plaza.
During this process, domestic icons such as those installed by Bhavānīśaṅkara were relocated to their present positions and housed within simple brick shrines.

Some local accounts claim that up to fivebāhāḥonce existed in this vicinity and that these were displaced during the reconstruction campaign initiated by Prime Minister Juddha Śamśera after the 1934 earthquake (R. Bajrācārya NS 1136, 258–259).

Prior to installing the images of Akṣobhya, Śāriputra, and Maudgalyāyana, he and his family members established their own portrait images (KAT1850-010) in Lāykū Bahī on the nineth of bright fortnight of Kārtika of the same year, as confirmed by the inscription on the pedestal of the portrait (KAT1850_I_001).
Notably, the Basantapur inscription also records this act of portrait installation.

However, the name “Bhavānīśaṅkara” itself is typical of non-Buddhist usage, and the portrait inscription records family members whose names bear the suffixKṛṣṇa, suggesting a Hindu familial background.
At present, neither the lands allocated by the donor nor theguṭhīhe established can be traced.
The initial construction of the temple is not documented.
Three struts, supporting the temple’s upper roof bear the date 1702 CE (NS 822).
This date could refer to the initial construction of the temple, its renovation or possibly the addition of the upper roof.
An inscriptions records that a woodentoraṇawas offered to the temple in 1756 CE (NS 876) and in 1761 CE.
The Mallas of Bhīmasenasthāna, Kathmandu had commissioned the construction of this Phalcā.

Ratna Malla, the second son of Yakṣa Malla, got all the eightmahāpātras of the crucial sectors killed and took over the city of Kathmandu on the 11th of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha in 1484 CE (NS 604) (D. Śreṣṭha2059, p. 14-17).
The descendants of themahāpātras who ruled the Kvāḥ Bāhāḥ section of Kathmandu had got this Phalcā constructed.
The Mallas had got this Phalcā constructed and also formed aguthifor Mahādevasthāna Pukhū(SKH0011)while they looked after the local administration.
Although the sponsor of the Phalcā is known, the year of its construction is unclear.
It had collapsed and remained in ruins.
The Shankharapur Municipality had also planned for its reconstruction.
However, the Malla family at Bhīmasenasthāna, Kathmandu came forward to reconstruct the Phalcā that was sponsored by their ancestors.
In 2013 CE, the foundation of the Phalcā was laid.
The reconstruction was completed at a cost of NRs. 600,000 in 2014 CE.
Yogalakṣmī, the wife of the Late Pannāmānasiṃha Malla, had funded the reconstruction.
It possible that this depression was caused by the dismantling of the original pavilion (or another domed structure), down to the foundations.
The building's first floor has remarkably carved wooden windows.
The inscription recording the initial construction of the Phalcā disappeared from here after it was renovated following the 2015 earthquakes.
According toBasukala and Gutschow(2018), the inscription was from 1760 CE.
This could be the date of the Phalcā’s initial construction.
After this mask was stolen sometime between 1975-1985 CE, the tradition came to an end.
The small Lichhavicaityas established on the plinth of thiscaityaare of special significance as they attest the antiquity of Chobhar as a whole.
As Amitābha is the main Buddha here, adharmadhātu maṇḍalais also established in front of him.
There are no historical records that reveal the exact construction date of thiscaitya.
However, in 1696 CE (NS 816), aphalcā(CHO4080) was built in front of thecaitya.
Although the inscription on thephalcādoes not mention thecaitya, a carving of acaityais can be seen in the inscription.
It is, therefore, possible that thecaityaexisted before the construction of thephalcā.
Fragmented Lichhavicaityas can be seen established at the corners of thecaitya’s plinth.
This indicates that these two hills developed as distinct pilgrimage sites: Kirtipur as a Śaiva site and Chobhar as a Buddhist site (S. Śreṣṭha VS 2057, p. 5).
Due to the dilapidated state of thecaitya's plinth, it was renovated in 2024 CE (VS 2081) with the support of the Kirtipur Municipality (ward member, Maharjana, male, age 42).
For the protection of Lalitpur city, theDaśamahāvidyā(Ten Great Wisdom Goddesses) have been established in ten differentṭolas.
Thursday, the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, is considered the day of Mātaṅgī (J. Mānandhara VS 2046, p. 33).
There is a popular belief that worshipping Mātaṅgī by offering fruits on Thursdays and Fridays is beneficial for acquiring knowledge and wealth (M. Miśra NS 1127, p. 46).
The Mātaṅgī shrine is constructed facing westward.
It is established in an open space right beside the road.
Aniconic stones have been installed within the shrine, and the central stone among them is worshipped as Mātaṅgī.
It is said that the remaining half of thismandaḥpāḥis located inside the Mahālakṣmī temple in Thaḥchẽ, Lalitpur (M. Miśra NS 1127, p. 46).
No historical evidence regarding the date of the establishment of the Mātaṅgī shrine in Lalitpur has been found.
It is possible that Mātaṅgī was established when Lalitpur was being developed as an organized settlement, during the installation of theDaśamahāvidyāin various directions for the city's protection.
Bakhata Bāhādura repaired the shrine in 1946 CE (VS 2003).
Around 2022-2023 CE (VS 2079-2080) , a local individual offered the brass roof and pinnacle to the shrine (Local resident from a Lākhe caste, male, age 33).
An arrangement has been established wherein the specificṭolasin Lalitpur housing theDaśamahāvidyātake turns organizing the worship.
Built on the eastern side of the route connecting Bhaktapur and Nagarkot, the Lāncā Phalcā is a three-bayed rest house oriented towards the west.
However, due to road expansion that left insufficient space for the square Phalcā, a new Lāncā Phalcā was erected a few meters eastward, in 2022 CE (VS 2078).
Consequently, the Phalcā serves as a replacement for the erstwhile structure, differing in shape, size, and location.
The construction of Lāncā Phalcā was completed in a span of 10 months, with an expenditure of approximately NRs. 2.7 million.

While the exact date of the temple's initial construction cannot be determined from an inscription, later chronicles report that King Jayasthiti Malla established a relief of Gorakhanātha’s feet (pādukā).
It is aśikhara-style structure made of bricks, crowned with a gilded finial, and is one of the few temples in the Paśupati area built in this style.
No historical source has yet been recovered that relates to the initial construction of the temple.
Some place its origin in the medieval period (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p. 587), while others attribute it to a later construction by Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa Śāha (Hutt 1994, p. 192).

However, a later chronicle recounts King Jayasthiti Malla establishing the feet and the image of Gorakhanātha at Mṛgasthalī and reviving the ritual offerings according to thesiddhatradition (Nepālikabhūpavaṃśāvalī19.16).
Another chronicle, theDevamālāVaṃśāvalī(2013, p. 17), also credits Jayasthiti Malla with the establishment of the Gorakhanāthapādukā, which it reports to have taken place in NS 514, i.e., 1394 CE.
It further narrates the king consecrating thepādukā, founding the sect of Nātha ascetics, and forming a trust by donating land.
It is unclear from the chronicle whether King Jayasthiti Malla only established thepādukāout in the open or if he also built a temple for it.
Besides the formation of trusts, the donation of physical objects also continued within this period.
In 1901 CE (VS 1858), King Gīrvāṇayuddha and his mother Suvarṇaprabhādevī offered a bell (PPK1969-017) weighing 59dhārnīs (approx. 134 kgs) to the temple (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2056, p. 326).
In 1949 CE (VS 1906), Rakṣakumārī, the last wife of Jaṅga Bahādura’s father Bālanarasiṃha Kũvara, renovated the temple and offered a golden finial.
She also donated land to set up a trust for future renovations of the temple and the performance of various rituals (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, pp. 514-515).

In 1854 CE (VS 1951), Rakṣakumārī again endowed land parcels to form another trust for performing anniversary rituals at Gorakhanātha, along with worships at the Rakṣeśvara Śivālaya (PPK1937) and Raṇabāleśvaradevī (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2056, pp. 524-525).
Later, in 1894 CE (VS 1951), Prime Minister Vīra Śamśera installed a bell (PPK1969-013) weighing 85dhārnīs (approx. 193 kgs) at the temple (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2056, p. 610).
Likewise, Prime Minister Candra Śamśera offered a trident (triśula; PPK1969-020) at the temple (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2056, p. 645).
The temple was fortunate to not sustain any damage in the 1934 earthquakes (DevamālāVaṃśāvalī2013, p. 17).
During the reign of King Mahendra, the Gorakhanātha temple underwent renovations in 1958-59 CE (VS 2016) (J. Regmī VS 2033, p. 96).
On Sundays and Tuesdays, Gorakhanātha is offered his favorite sweet calledroṭa, a particular kind of sweet of flour prepared in the shape of the Diamonds playing card suit by deep frying in ghee.
A grand fire ritual is performed on this day at theyajñakuṇḍa(hollowed space designated for fire oblation) south of the temple.
OnŚivarātrī, Gorakhanātha and thepātradeities receive special worship along with fire rituals, and the banner at the temple is renewed on the occasion.
In 1977 CE (VS 2034), the building was renovated by the Bhaktapur Development Project.
After the Phalcā sustained minor damage in the 2015 earthquakes, locals renovated its roof and base plinth in 2021 CE (VS 2078).
The Phalcā does not contain any statue or inscription.
Due to the lack of historical sources, it is unclear when it was first constructed.
In 1851 CE (VS 1907), Prime Minister Bama Bahādura Kũvara erected Tīna Devala (KAT2670), a composite structure comprising three temples near the Bagmati River.
Indra Vadana, the last wife of Bama Bahādura, established the Indrabhakteśvara temple in 1862 CE (VS 1919), situated southwest of the Tīna Devala complex.
Fifteen years after the temple's construction, in 1877 CE (VS 1934), she organized daily, annual, and periodic rituals by establishing a trust endowed with land.
An inscription on a bell at the Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa temple (KAT2640) mentions its offering to the Indrabhakteśvara temple in 1864 CE (VS 1921).
Notably, the bell appears to have been relocated after the early 1970s photo published by Pruscha (1975, p.92).
P. Darnāla (VS 2061, p.36) mistakenly attributes the temple's construction to Indrabhakta in 1864 CE, the year the bell was installed.
A copperplate inscription in the adjacentsataḥlists endowed land plots and prescribed periodic rituals, although many activities have been discontinued.
The privatization of endowed lands has significantly reduced the temple's income, posing challenges for ritual observances.
As of July 2023 CE, the trust of the Bamavīravikaṭeśvara temple oversees the preservation of the Indrabhakteśvara temple and supports daily rituals performed by a Brahmin.
While the construction of this Śiva temple appears to have taken place during the Rāṇā period, the exact origin remains uncertain due to the absence of historical records.
Additionally, anotherśivaliṅga, likely transported from another location, is established to the east of the temple.
The absence of inscriptions at the site contributes to the mystery surrounding the donor's identity and the year of the temple's construction.
Nonetheless, the architectural characteristics of the temple suggest a construction date during the Rāṇā period (1846-1951 CE).

Jāiphala Adhikārī, a commander of a military company with the rank ofsubedāra, built the Hastikeśvara temple, the Kālikā shrine (object no. NWK0530-012), and the rest house in 1829 CE.
In 1810 CE (VS 1867), King Gīrvāṇayuddha granted 15ropanīsof land to Hastikā in recognition of her nursing services (K_0096_0048).
Additionally, a forest in Kahule was donated in 1812 CE (VS 1869) to support the maintenance of the rest house (RRC_0039_0922).

Known as Jāiphara in the temple's inscription, he also constructed the Jāiphala Pāṭī (rest house) in Nuwakot and the Jayarudreśvara Mandira (PPK1705) in Gaurīghāṭa, Paśupati area of Kathmandu, marking its completion with a lengthy inscription (G. Taṇḍana VS 2056, pp. 420-23).
He also renovated the Bāghabhairava temple (KIR0004) in Kirtipur and received numerous land grants from the state for his long service assubedāra.
Before the 2015 CE earthquakes, the Hastikeśvara temple was already in a deteriorating condition and was subsequently destroyed by the quakes.
The Department of Archaeology rebuilt the temple in 2023 CE (VS 2080).
Jāiphala Adhikārī endowed many land parcels to generate income for the temple’s trust, ensuring the performance of various rituals throughout the year.
A Brahmin from the Nepāla caste originally conducted daily rituals, but as of May 2024 CE, a Brahmin from the Rimāla caste has taken over these duties.
Jāiphala's descendants mention that all rituals have ceased due to non-payment of rent from tenants after the 2015 CE earthquakes (local resident, Adhikārī, male, age 52).
Located between the Sureśakānteśvara Mandira (PPK0523) and the Bhadreśvara Śivaliṅga (PPK0518), Prāṇamukteśvara is a brick-built temple with a dome design, facing south.
The superstructure is covered in traditional bajra plaster, while the substructure, serving as the temple's sanctum, is constructed with red bricks, devoid of any plaster.
Within the sanctum, there are 11 śivaliṅgas, giving the temple the appellation "Ekādaśarudra Mandira," the temple of 11 Śivas (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p.356).
Consequently, the temple is also referred to as the Vāṇaliṅgeśvara Mandira (J. Regmī VS 2033, p.252).
Vāṇaliṅgas are cylindrical stones found in the Narmada river in India, which are established as śivaliṅgas (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p.366).
Regrettably, a bell that was previously installed southeast of the temple has been lost.

In V.S. 1916 (CE 1859), Dīpakumārī Śāha initiated the construction of this temple to honor her late husband, Prāṇa Śāha who held prominent administrative positions as acautariyā, a royal appointee (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p. 356; Michaels and Tandon 2017, p. 70).

Given Dīpakumārī's association with a cautariyā, a position sometimes referred to ascautārā, she is addressed ascautārnīin the inscription documenting the temple's construction.
Following the 2015 CE earthquake, which caused damage to the temple, it was meticulously reconstructed in its original form in 2018 CE (VS 2075) (M. Thāpā VS 2077, p. 205).

The trust established by Dīpakumārī remains active, with records at the Guṭhī Saṃsthāna listing 25 ropanīs of land under the name of Prāṇamukteśvara, designated for providing alms to ascetics three times a day (Guṭhī Saṃsthāna VS 2071, p. 38).
The Jagannātha Mandira in Kathmandu was commissioned by King Mahindra Malla (r. 1560-1574 CE) in 1563 CE (NS 683).
This was followed by the erection of a parallel temple (LAL1320) in Patan in 1566 CE (NS 686), commissioned by Purandarasiṃha (G. Vajrācārya VS 2033, 66; D. Vajrācārya VS 2056, 23).

While theDevamālāvaṃśāvalīattributes the temple's construction to King Pratāpa Malla and the establishment of the Jagannātha triad (G. Vajrācārya VS 2033, p.66), an inscription from 1563 CE (NS 683) on the Caturvyūha statue contradicts this account, suggesting the temple's existence predates Pratāpa Malla's reign (r. 1641-1674 CE).

Another historical dimension lies in the temple's eastern plinths, which host substantial inverted stone tanks (jaḥdhuṃ) featuring five inscriptions of Pratāpa Malla from 1653 CE (NS 774) across 14 distinct scripts.

These inscriptions, devoted to various goddesses, carry Pratāpa Malla's assertion that genuine scholarship resides in the comprehension of verses, starkly contrasting those incapable of such understanding (Gutschow 2000, KVPT report, p.4-9).
The structural integrity of the temple sustained a setback in 1934 CE when a portion of its upper tier collapsed, as evidenced in the third photograph of Gutschow's 2000 KVPT report.

The year 2000 CE (VS 2057) marked a significant milestone with the Kathmandu Valley Preservation Trust embarking on a comprehensive restoration endeavour while simultaneously documenting the inscriptions within the edifice.
An integral ritual during this commemoration involves the installation of a repoussé brass cover upon the Caturvyūha Viṣṇu statue.
This beautiful tower, constructed with sixteen corners, was built by Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa Śāha in 1769 CE (VS 1826).
All four towers here are built in different styles.
This tower is constructed with sixteen corners, and the roof is also designed with many angles accordingly.
Artistic windows are installed in the upper part of the tower.

The inscriptions located on the northern and southern sides of the Nautale Durbar (KAT1640) indicate that Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa Śāha constructed the Nautale Durbar and the Lalitpur Burjā (KAT1650) in 1769 CE (Śaka era 1691).
However, these inscriptions do not mention both Bhaktapur and Kīrtipur towers.
From this, it can be inferred that Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa Śāha built additional towers at around the same time.
Pruscha (1975, p. 59) notes that the Bhaktapur Burjā was built by Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa Śāha in 1769 CE.
G. Vajrācārya (VS 2033, p. 129) states that all four towers of the Vasantapura Coka were constructed by Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa Śāha.
This implies that although Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa Śāha began the construction, it was finalized under Pratāpa Siṃha’s rule.
It is also recorded that the remaining construction work of the Vasantapura Coka was also completed by Pratāpa Siṃha in 1780 CE (VS 1837) (Gutschow 2011, p. 336).
The 1934 earthquakes had deteriorated this structure (J. Sanday 1978, p. 140).
With the cooperation of UNESCO, and in coordination with the Government of Nepal, this tower, along with three other towers, was restored in 1975 CE.
Likewise, the 2015 earthquakes damaged the Bhaktapur Burjā as well among many historical monuments in the Hanumandhoka Palace area.
Deteriorated by the earthquakes, the Bhaktapur Burjā and other structures, including the Nautale Durbar, were restored under a restoration project.
The project was completed in 2019 CE (VS 2076).
Before the 2015 earthquakes, visitors were permitted to explore the upper levels of the tower.
The Dyaḥchẽ of Cāmuṇḍā, revered as one of the guardian deities of Dharmasthalī, was constructed in 1838 CE (NS 958).
Built facing east, the Cāmuṇḍā Dyaḥchẽ is a two-story structure.
Additionally, gold-plated heads of six other deities, including Gaṇeśa, Kumāra, and Bhairava, are also installed.* The main entrance is located on the ground floor, flanked by a pair of stone lions.
Notoraṇais installed above the entrance.
ThisDyaḥchẽwas constructed in 1838 CE (NS 958) by a group of 14guṭhiyāras(trust members), including Punasiṃ, theThakālī(head) of the Cāmuṇḍā Guṭhī, and Kṛṣṇasiṃ, the secondThakālī.
As theDyaḥchẽsustained damage during the earthquake of 2015 CE (VS 2072), it was reconstructed in 2023 CE (VS 2080) with financial assistance from the Tarakeshwar Municipality.
While the structure previously had a roof ofjhiṃgaṭītiles, it was fitted with a copper roof following the reconstruction.
In 2025 CE (Māgha, VS 2081), all the statues of the deities housed in the Dyaḥchẽ were stolen (local resident, Śreṣṭha, male, age 51).
Following the theft of the original statues, new ones were crafted and are currently being worshipped.
As of October 2026 CE, the stolen statues have not been recovered.

Thisśivaliṅga, dating back to the Licchavi period, was consecrated by a trader named Ratnasaṅgha in 478 CE (ŚS 399).
It holds historical significance due to its Licchavi inscription, dating back to the rule of King Mānadeva (r. 464-505 CE).
In 1993 CE (VS 2050), the family erected a small room to safeguard theśivaliṅga.
During fieldwork, Dhanavajra Vajrācārya (VS 2036, p.55) discovered thisśivaliṅgabeneath a large tree in an open field, devoid of any surrounding structures.
Ratṇeśvara stands as one of the earliest Licchaviśivaliṅgas with an inscription.

As per the inscription on the base, Ratnasaṅgha, a prominent tradesman leader, consecrated theśivaliṅgain 478 CE (ŚS 399), naming it Ratneśvara after himself and endowing numerous land parcels in its honor (D. Vajrācārya VS 2030, pp.50-51).
Another inscription from 481 CE (ŚS 402) designates Ratnasaṅgha assārthavāha, a title bestowed upon the leader of a caravan of tradesmen (D. Vajrācārya VS 2030, p.55-56).
After being exposed to the elements, theśivaliṅgafound refuge inside a concrete room in 1993 CE (VS 2050), courtesy of the Rājabhaṇḍārī family.
In the year 2000 CE (VS 2057), an interesting discovery was made while digging the foundation for a private building located approximately 50 meters northeast of the Ratneśvara Śivaliṅga.

This newly foundśivaliṅgafeatured an inscription dating back to 486 CE (ŚS 407), documenting the donation of land parcels by Vimala Saṃgha, asārthavāha, for theśivaliṅgaestablished by an individual named Sutenātri (Ś. Rājavaṃśī VS 20, pp.43-56).
A statue of Bhagīratha is installed underneath the main spout (LAL0994-001) and a statue of Umāmaheśvara is placed above it.
The date of construction of thehitiis not recorded but it is assumed that it was built during the reign of Prime Minister Juddha Śamśera Rāṇā [r. 1932-1945] (Lalitpur Sub-Metropolitan City2007, 39).

A certain Jayarāja Śreṣṭha renovated thehitiin 1999 CE (VS 2056) and in 2011 CE (VS 2068) local residents, with the financial support from the Lalitpur Sub-metropolitan City, built a water storage and distribution system for the benefit of the local community.
A minor renovation of thehititook place in 2017 CE (VS 2074) when thehitisandphalcāsin the Ālko quarter were repaired with funds from the World Bank and the Lalitpur Municipality.
Unfortunately, little attention was paid to the use of authentic materials for the renovation.
The shrine adjacent to this tree was consecrated in care of tantric incantations and established to worship Buṅgadyaḥ’s mother.
The latest incident took place in 1995 CE (VS 2052).
There are no historical sources to date its initial construction.
The inscription on the pedestal of the Lokeśvara statue, most probably, records the date of the installation of the statue itself, but one of the three digits (8?8) is illegible.
The statue must have been installed no later than NS 8[9]8, i.e., 1778 CE.
The Ward Number 6 Office of the Shankharapur Municipality restored it in 2021 CE.
This non-existing rest house was constructed by a person named Dharaṇīdhara in 1694 CE (NS 814).
The statue of Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa faces west towards Umāmaheśvara Mandira (KIR0006) while the inscription recording the construction of the Phalcā is set on the rear wall of the shrine.
The inscription states that Dharaṇīdhara, who constructed the Phalcā in 1694 CE, was a resident of Kirtipur and held the post of the chief of the fort.
The donor also endowed sevenropanīs of land to form aguthifor performing various rituals throughout the year (Shokoohy and others2014, p. 94).
The Phalcā is due to be reconstructed in traditional architecture with funds from the US embassy.
The inscription also instructs concerned persons to organize thehāthuhāyketradition.
Constructed west of the Jyotirliṅgeśvara Mahādeva Mandira (SKH0010), this Pond (Mahādevasthā Pokharī) is locally known as Mahādyaḥ Pukhū.
There is no inscription that sheds light on the initial construction of the Pond.

It was renovated in the course of the renovation of the Jyotirliṅgeśvara Mandira and other monuments around it in 1997 CE with the funds provided by the local body and financial assistance from the Netherlands.
The Mahādyaḥ Pukhūcā Guthi is a community trust related to the Pond.
Six Śreṣṭhas of Sankhu are members of this Guthi.
The Thakū Jujus (mahāpātra) of the Kvaḥne area, the lower quarter of Kathmandu, had formed this Guthi.
The members of the Guthi clean the Pond onŚivarātrīand worship Jyotirliṅgeśvara.
During the annual festival of Vajrayoginī, the Guthi performs special worship at the deity’s temple in the morning of the 7th of the dark fortnight of Vaiśākha and hosts a feast in the same evening.
Despite the simplicity of its construction, it maintains a traditional appearance and proportion.
No inscription is available to indicate when it was originally built.
A Śikharakūṭacaityaconstructed in 1686 CE stands at the centre of the courtyard.
An image of acaityaabove the Phalcā's inscription suggests a relationship between thiscaityaand Chusikhānanī Phalcā.
Two historic pillars from the previous Phalcā have been placed at the back corners of the arcaded platform, and an additional wood pillar has been added below because of the extra height.
In 2012, Lalitpur Metropolitan City provided financial support for the renovation of the building.
The local community reconstructed it after dismantling the previous structure.
This is detailed further under the heading Damages & Threats (below).
Because of Gaṇeśa shrine there are two lions on the either side of the shrine ad a bell has been installed.
A Gaṇeśa seated in Lalitāsana is installed inside the shrine.
However, no medieval inscriptions were found here.
In the valley, there are many examples where locality (sthāna) Gaṇeśa stone statue are placed in the center, were later surrounded by temples and phalcās built around them.
This phalcā is also built in the same manner where Gaṇeśa stone statue is placed in the center.

It seems that the stone statue, which has been worshipped as a Gaṇeśa temple by the residents of GāḥBāhāḥ, Būbāhāḥ, Purṇacaṇḍī etc. was placed in the middle first, and only after the phalcā was added around it.

Since the phalcā was built exactly at the location where the chariot stops during the Gāḥ Bāhāḥ procession, it has been said that in the past, this phalcā may have been used by the Bungadyaḥ’s pāneju to spend the night (Shakya 2015, p. 14).
Bālakṛṣṇeśvara Mandira was established by Bālakṛṣṇa Bhāro in 1712.
The temple has suffered from vandalism; several stone sculptures are missing and the northern door's jamb has been removed.
Cement covers the three-tiered roof of the temple and further traces of cement plaster attest to a recent repair effort.
A stone inscription attached to the temple's wall, although badly damaged and missing its top part, records the temple's construction in 1712 CE (NS 832).
It was commissioned by Bālakṛṣṇa Bhāro, a resident of Bonde Ṭola.
The inscription names the temple area as Dakṣiṇa Bhairava Sthāna (the place of southern Bhairava) which refers to the famous Pacalī Bhaivara Temple (KAT2580).
The inscription also mentions that land was bestowed upon theguṭhīof the temple and indicates that acapāḥwas constructed.
A stoneśivaliṅgahas been erected at the center of the sanctum, and stone images of Sūrya, Bhagavatī, Garuḍa and their devotees have been placed at the corners of the room.
The south-west corner also houses a stone statue of the temple's consecrator Bālakṛṣṇa and his wife Arpūvāni.
The word'bāra(la)kṛṣṇa'is inscribed on the stone slab underneath the statues thus identifying them as the donors.
Constructed on one level of plinth, the temple's sole entrance faces north.
The statues carved on the walls were commissioned by local resident Tejabahādura (S. Amātya VS 2053, p. 9).
The earliest record of Bhāṭabhaṭenī can be found in thePadmagiriVaṃśāvalī, a chronicle written in the late Malla period (A. Dīkṣita VS 2059, p. 1).
TheBhāṣāvaṃśāvalī(VS 2022, p. 36) mentions that Bhāṭabhaṭenī came to Viśālanagara and established a city there.

During the Lichhavi period, Viśālanagara encompassed a vast area including Śaṅkhamūla, Deupāṭana, Paśupatinātha, Guhyeśvari, Mālīgāũ, Baneśvara, Jñāneśvara, Hā̃ḍīgāũ, and the entire Cābahila region (S. Amātya VS 2053, p. 18).

TheDevamālāvaṃśāvalī(VS 2013, pp. 64-65) recounts that when Vāṇāsura's son, Mahendra Damana, dammed the Bagmati River and transformed Kathmandu into a lake, Lord Kṛṣṇa vanquished all the demons and released the river, enabling the establishment of settlements.
Bhāṭabhaṭenī arrived in Viśālanagara and founded a kingdom with Svayaṃjata as its ruler.
When granted a boon, Bhāṭabhaṭenī yearned for a son who would be the very image of Viṣṇu.
Due to the absence of any inscriptions explicitly stating the establishment of the Bhāṭabhaṭenī statues and the construction of the temple, it is difficult to determine its exact age with certainty.

However, the fact that a temple dedicated to Bhaṭeni's mother, Ṭũḍāladevī, has an inscription dating back to 475 CE during the reign of Mānadeva suggests that the Bhāṭabhaṭenī temple may also belong to the Lichhavi period (A. Dīkṣita VS 2059, p. 15).
An inscription found on the eastern wall of a raised platform (maṇḍapa) southeast of the temple is the oldest inscription available in the temple complex.
It records Jayasiṃha Maharjana of the Thathu Ṭola renovating the oldmaṇḍapain 1790 CE (NS 910) due to its dilapidated condition.
He also established a tradition of annually observing the anniversary rituals on the 8th of the dark fortnight of Bhādra from income of the land endowed for a concerned trust.

Likewise, an inscription on the eaves board of the upper roof of the temple indicates that in 1841 CE (VS 1898), children of Kulānanda Jhā and Vidyālakṣmī from the Kilāgala Ṭola, covered the upper roof of the temple with copper sheets.
Later, in 1979 CE (VS 2016), King Mahendra and Queen Ratna had copper sheets placed on the lower roof of the temple.
This pillar was erected in 1941 by the people of Lalitpur in memory of the devastating 1934 earthquake and in honor of Prime Minister Juddha Śamśera and his assistance.
A similar kind of memorial was also established in the Bhugol Park of New Road, Kathmandu.
Inscriptions have been written on the south and west faces of the pillar.
One of these inscriptions records the destruction caused by the earthquake and the progress of the recovery work.
The inscription states that many people were helped by Juddha Śamśera, who donated 1 million 74 thousand and 913 rupees.
The Pā̃ḍe community reveres this Bhagavatī as their lineage deity, and Karavīra Pā̃ḍe established a guthi by donating land and funds to perform daily and anniversary rituals.
Statues of Dāmodara Pā̃ḍe and his wife Ayodhyādevī, the Guthi's donor's father, are placed beside the Bhagavatī statue.

The exact date of the temple's construction is unclear due to the lack of historical sources, but an inscription from 1839 CE (VS 1896) records the formation of theguthiand the establishment of a cash fund by Karavīra Pā̃ḍe, who may have built the temple.

In 1949 CE (VS 2006), Dravyalāla or dravyelålaŚreṣṭha, a resident of the Tyaḥra Ṭola, installed metal frills on the temple's roof, and in 1982 CE (VS 2039), a local group of devotional singers collected donations to renovate the temple.
Although the temple has gradually tilted to the west, it survived the 2015 earthquakes, and the Kathmandu Metropolitan City Office has allocated a budget for its reconstruction.

Ghana Bāhāḥ is a branch of Oku Bāhāḥ (Rudravarṇa Mahāvihāra,LAL2260), is a small area surrounded by a historic, private building to the north, the Mahākāla Phalcā to the east, the Vajradhara Phalcā to the west and small buildings and a boundary wall to the south.
Ghanānanda Śākya, a grandson of Amṛtānanda Vande (the man who taught Buddhism to Brian Hodgson), established thisbāhāḥand it is from him that it gets its name.
Parts of the base and the dome have been plastered with lime and white-washed, and the walls are built ofdaci apaand decorative bricks.
No historical document could be found to provide the exact date thebāhāḥwas constructed.
Ghanānanda is mentioned in an inscription dated NS 955 (Śākya1994, 55-56).
Furthermore, in NS 975 (1855 CE), on the first anniversary of his death, adharmadhātu maṇḍalawas established in front of the Mahābuddha Temple (LAL2340) in his honour (Śākya1988, 88-89) .
This suggests that thebāhāḥwas established before 1854 and very probably after 1835.
Harṣanārāyaṇa Dhaubhaḍela built this Śiva temple in 1879 CE (VS 1936) and donated 32ropanīs of farmland to sustain its rituals.
The Harṣamukteśvara Śiva temple complex is one of the two significant religious and historical landmarks in Bhaktapur’s Cupiṃghāṭa cremation ground built by the Dhaubhaḍela clan.
The other is Cupiṃghāṭa Śivālaya (BKT0480) established by the Gvaṃgaḥ clan.
Modeled after Paśupatināth, the south-facing Harṣamukteśvara temple follows a bell-shaped roof design with brick construction and a stone finial.
Statues of Harṣanārāyaṇa and his wives, Nhukṣe Thakuṃ and Hirā Thakuṃ, are also installed here.
Harṣanārāyaṇa, born in 1804 CE (VS 1861), was a prominent figure close to Dhīra Śamśera.
Beyond constructing this temple, he installed his statue at the Taumāḍhī Bhairava temple and managed religious endowments at Taleju (O. Dhaubhaḍela VS 2078, pp. 27-29).
In 1880 CE (VS 1937), Harṣanārāyaṇa added theaṣṭamātṛkāshrine and a rest house (saṭaḥ), followed by elevenśivaliṅgas in 1882 CE (VS 1939).
His son later donated a temple bell in 1883 CE (NS 1003).
Thesataḥhoused Siddhartha Boarding School and later Kathmandu University’s Music Department until the 2015 earthquake damaged it.

The temple’s anniversary rituals are observed on the 6th of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, featuring 84 varieties of dishes offered to Śiva, goat sacrifices to theaṣṭamātṛkāand Gaṇeśa (BKT0460-026), and round sweetmeats (laḍḍū) offerings to Hanumān (BKT0460-023).
On the 1st solar day of Vaiśākha, people bathe in the Hanumante river, believing it grants liberation (mokṣa).
Thebāhāḥ-courtyard is sunken and has an Aśoka Caitya at its center on the axis to the entrance and the mainbāhāḥbuilding.
The western wall of thebāhāḥis attached to a newly constructed five-storied building.
All are fixed on the walls of the residential buildings.
However, this was stolen some years ago.
No inscription or other documented evidence with any information about the establishment of thebāhāḥcould be found.
A legend suggests that this monastic building's statue of Akṣobhya is related to the Guji Bāhāḥ(LAL2490).
The Guji Bāhāḥ complex once caught fire, and the sandalwood statue of its main deity was brought here for its protection.
After the fire, in NS 1 (881 CE), a donor named Vaiśravarṇa reconstructed thebāhāḥ.
As such, the image becamesiddha(established) there, and so it was that thisbāhāḥgot the name 'Siddha Bāhāḥ'.
J. Locke(ibid.) mentions that a descendant of Abhayarāja (the man who constructed the Mahābuddha Temple (LAL2340)) built the Sikucā Bāhāḥ, though he does not provide any source.
Constructed east of the Mandaḥ Phalcā (SKH0140) in between the Kalaśanārāyaṇa Mandira (SKH0122) and Gāḥ Hiti (SKH0142), the Caitya stands on a level of the base plinth.
There are no historical sources to date the initial construction of the Sālkhā Caitya.

A Licchavi inscription from 616 CE (Mānadeva Era 40) installed in the Caitya premises contains references to a Tripura Vihāra and monastic association of the monks of the Mahāsāṅghika (lit. Great Congregation), a Buddhist school of thought, but it does not mention anycaityas.

[1]The inscription recording the construction of the Sālkhā Sataḥ (SKH0121) mentions that the Sataḥ was built at ‘Svayambhūcaityasthāna’ (lit. at the place of Svayambhū Caitya) of Śaṅkarapaṭṭana (Sankhu) in 1558 CE (NS 679).
As this is the only Caitya in the area, it is very likely that the Svayambhū Caitya mentioned in this inscription is the Sālkhā Caitya.
As mentioned above, the Caitya constructed before 1558 CE must have lost its original architectures during its renovation(s).
Local elderlies say that there is no specific ritual orguthiassociated with the Caitya.
Anyguthiformed during the initial construction of this Caitya probably ceased to exist long before its renovation back in the 1960s.
VajrācāryaVS 2030, p. 508 had published only a part of this inscription, as only one half of it was available.
Later in 2014 CE, the remaining half of the Inscription was also recovered while renovating thehitisouth of this Caitya.
It is built on a circular plan with four niches attached to the drum at each of the four cardinal directions.
A fire alter can be found in the courtyard in front of the shrine.
The images of Amitābha and Ratnasambhava seem to be have been added recently.
These four shrines have been topped withcaitya-shaped pinnacles, though the pinnacle of the northern niche is damaged.
The pinnacles of the north-western and south-eastern structures have been damaged; only theāmalakapart of the remains.
No inscription or any other documented evidence could be found to provide information about the establishment of thecaitya.
Since the Vairocana image on the south-westernkhaṭa-shapedcaityahas been dated to the 6th century, it can be assumed that the main Caitya was also constructed around that time.
