Built by Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa Śāha in 1769 CE (VS 1826), this tower, with its hemispherical metal roof, bears a look distinct from other adjacent towers.
Located in the northwestern corner of the Vasantapur Coka in the Hanumandhoka Palace complex, the Kirtipur Burjā is also referred to as "Baṅgalā" (G. Vajrācārya, VS 2033, p. 129).

The inscriptions affixed on the northern and southern sides of the Nautale Durbar (KAT1640) indicate that Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa Śāha constructed the Nautale Durbar and the Lalitpur Burjā (KAT1650) in 1769 CE (Śaka era 1691).
These inscriptions, however, remain silent on the construction of the Kirtipur and Bhaktapur towers that share the terrace with the other two towers.
Both G. Vajrācārya (VS 2033, p. 129) and Pruscha (1975, p. 59) state that all four towers of the Vasantapura Coka were constructed by Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa Śāha in 1769 CE.
This implies that although Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa Śāha began the construction, these two towers (Kirtipur and Bhaktapur towers) were probably finalized under Pratāpa Siṃha’s rule.
It is also noted that the remaining construction work of the Vasantapura Coka was completed by Pratāpa Siṃha in 1780 CE (VS 1837) (Gutschow 2011, p. 336).
The 1934 earthquakes had deteriorated this structure (J. Sanday 1978, p. 140).
With the cooperation of UNESCO, and in coordination with the Government of Nepal, this tower, along with three other towers, was restored in 1975 CE (VS 2032).
Likewise, the 2015 earthquakes damaged the Kirtipur Burjā as well among many historical monuments in the Hanumandhoka Palace area.
Deteriorated by the earthquakes, the Kirtipur Burjā and other structures, including the Nautale Durbar, were restored under a restoration project.
The project was completed in 2019 CE (VS 2076).
Before the 2015 earthquakes, visitors were permitted to explore the upper levels of the tower.
Inside the sanctum of this Temple, a two-armed stone statue of Karuṇāmaya (standing in thesamabhaṅgaposture), a popular name of Padmapāṇi Lokeśvara is consecrated.
The pedestal inscription of the statue states the statue was established in VS 2016 (1959 CE).
Bekhārāra, Dāna, Lana Bahādura, Bhima Bahādura, Bhuyucā Kaḥmi of Hāmanani Ṭola in Balambu established the statue in the memory of their parents Narasiṃ and Nānīmāyā.
Pūrṇa Maharjana renovated the temple in NS 1123 (2003 CE) in the memory of his father.
The originalvihārawas destroyed in the 1934 earthquake.
Before the 1934 earthquake, there was a  god house (dyaḥchẽ) here.
Levelled by the earthquake, however, the god house has not been reconstructed.
Herākājī Śākya, a local inhabitant, made this small shrine to replace it(Locke1985, 118).
One of thecaityasin the courtyard is dated as being from NS 782.
The classical name of thevihārais Dhanavajra Vihāra, which suggests that a person named Dhanavajra was the one to originally construct it.
This three-story building features a plain brick façade and vertically shuttered wooden windows.
The original tiled roof has been replaced with corrugated metal sheets.
This building is most likely a post-1934 earthquake reconstruction; the original monastery was destroyed in the 1934 earthquake.
Siddhi Bāhāḥ, built in 1938 CE by Siddhirāja Śākya, is a branch of Guji Bāhāḥ (LAL2490).
Acaityais established as the temple’s pinnacle (gajū), and a pair of guardian lionsare flanking at the main entrance of the sanctum (garbhagṛha).
A small statue of Akṣobhya is consecrated in the sanctum.
This statue was installed recently by the local residents after the original was stolen.
Thebāhāḥwas established by Siddhirāja Śākya, his wife, two sons, and three grandchildren in 1938 CE (NS 1058).
He installed a Dharmadhātu Maṇḍala around the same time in the courtyard.
The innovative decision to construct a residential palace in temple style represents a significant architectural experiment under King Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa Śāha (G. Vajrācārya VS 2033, p. 133).
For this reason, it is regarded as the first royal palace built in temple architectural form (S. Amātya VS 2045, p. 92).
Because the structure integrates both palace and fortification features, an inscription installed after its construction designates it as a “Durggaratna” (the jewel among forts).
The 2015 CE (VS 2072) earthquake caused substantial damage, and as of February 2026 CE restoration work remains ongoing.
The fifth storey, known as thekālakoṭharī, was built with low height and concealed externally; it functioned as a prison for traitors and war captives.
The first storey contains the treasury (ḍhukuṭī) in the east and rooms for the treasurers on the western side (G. Ṭaṇḍaṇa VS 2077, pp. 324–326).

Although uninscribed, priests and trustees ofguṭḥi(guṭhiyāras) of Nuwakot Bhagavatī at Hanumāna Ḍhokā identify them as Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa Śāha and his two queens, Indrakumārī Devī and Narendra Rājyalakṣmī.
In 2010 CE (VS 2067), during the tenure of Director General Viṣṇu Kārkī of the Department of Archaeology, they were transferred to the Sātatale Durbar.
As a result, Nuwakot flourished as apattana(urban center) (D. Vajrācārya & Ṭ. Śreṣṭha VS 2032, p. 23).

By the medieval period, structures such as the Nārāyaṇa Temple (NWK0170), the Raṅgamahal (NWK0140), the Śikharakūṭa Caitya (NWK0150), and the Viṣṇu Temple (NWK0190) had already been built at the site where the present palace complex now stands.

Recognizing its importance, Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa Śāha captured Nuwakot on October 1, 1744 CE (VS 1801, Āsvina 15) (M. Panta 2025, p. 33) and subsequently made it his capital (D. Vajrācārya & Ṭ. Śreṣṭha VS 2032, p. 70).
After consolidating control over the Tibetan trade route, he commissioned the Sātatale Durbar in April 1762 CE (Śaka 1684, Vaiśākha).
Although the inscription lacks a specific date, B. Ācārya (VS 2061, p. 272) calculates completion shortly after April 10, 1762.

In the inscription, he proudly proclaimed that he had broken the arrogance of the kings of Nepal (the Kathmandu Valley), captured King Trivikrama Sena of Tanahũ, and slain the Muslim customs officials stationed at the checkpoint upon his return from Kāśī.

The inscription boasts of his military achievements and emphasizes the palace’s fortified character, hence the epithet “Durgaratna.” Artisans were brought from Lalitpur for its construction (K. Tamoṭa VS 2029, p. 69).
Approximately three years later, under the supervision of Crown Prince Pratāpa Siṃha Śāha, the Serā Durbar (NWK0540) was built at Māḍī on the banks of the Ṭāḍī River.
After Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa Śāha’s death, repairs were undertaken.
In 1775 CE (VS 1832), King Pratāpa Siṃha Śāha allocated funds to purchase thatch for the roof, indicating its original roofing material (Ś. Rājavaṃśī VS 2026, p. 39).
The great earthquake of 1934 CE (VS 1990) caused major structural damage, reportedly collapsing the uppermost storey.
Prime Minister Juddha Śamśera subsequently restored it (S. Amātya VS 2045, p. 93).
A local tradition claims the palace originally had nine storeys, two of which collapsed in 1934, though this lacks historical verification.
In 1971 CE (VS 2028), Nuwakot’s administrative headquarters was relocated to Bidur, reducing activity around the palace complex.

The Department of Archaeology carried out restoration between 1975–1978 CE (VS 2032–2035), replacing corrugated roofing with brass sheets gilded with gold, repairing windows and balconies, and paving the courtyard.
In 2011 CE (VS 2068), the palace was converted into a museum displaying artifacts associated with Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa Śāha.
The 2015 CE (VS 2072) earthquake again caused severe damage.
In 2019 CE (VS 2076), Nepal and China signed an agreement for restoration, with the Chinese Academy of Cultural Heritage assigned responsibility.
Delays occurred due to the COVID-19 pandemic, but work resumed in 2024 CE (VS 2081).
Rituals such askṣamāpūjā(2024 CE, VS 2081) andbhūmipūjā(2025 CE, VS 2082) were performed prior to structural consolidation.
Restoration continues using modern technology while preserving the traditional form.
They are ceremonially adorned, worshipped, and animal sacrifices are offered.
There is no door to enter to thebāhāḥ;to reach the courtyard (8.8 x 10.2 m), one must walk through an underpass of a residential building.
It is located on the southern wing of the courtyard and is attached to residential buildings.
Corrugated metal sheets have replaced thejhĩgaṭītiles that once roofed the building, which also lacks a pinnacle.
No stone lions guard the sanctum, but iron fences have been installed to protect the deities from thieves.
Outside, abimba caitya(120 cm high), adharmadhātu maṇḍala(82 cm high) and apūrṇakalaśoparipadma caitya(135 cm high) are centrally lined up in the courtyard in front of the mainbāhāḥbuilding.
Naḥ Ṭola, the area where thisbāhāḥis located, seems to be a place that was removed from the main city of Patan in earlier times; this is suggested by the Newari word ‘naḥ’,meaning new.
It is unclear when the Temple was initially constructed.
A replica of Anantaliṅgeśvara was established here to allow the devotees from Sankhu to worship the deity without having to go to Bhaktapur (local resident, Śreṣṭha, male, age 61).
They were stolen in 1998 CE and were never replaced.
Although a privateguthirelated to the Temple existed in the past, all of its activities have now been discontinued.
Locals come together to carry out minor renovations of the Temple.
Locals set a bonfire at the Temple premises on the same evening and distribute dry-heated legumes (halamalaḥ) as the deity’s gift (prasāda).
Following its collapse in the 1934 earthquake the temple was reconstructed as a plain brick structure covered with a white-washed masonry dome.
Following the 2015 earthquakes two lion statues that used to be in front of the temple were moved to the front of the Court Building (LAL1222).
There are no inscriptions or any other historical documents mentioning the construction date of the temple.
The room was most likely built on the spot of a large śikhara temple, as indicated by the preserved stone door frame typical of this type of architecture.
The inner and outer walls of the building are made of white-washed roughly cut stones.
They are installed on a common base.
According to villagers the fountain KLK0130-006 was dismantled and moved to its current location following the widening of the road.
The area surrounding the Caitya is paved with black flagstones and has been encroached upon by some of the building materials for the reconstruction of the Karuṇāmaya Mandira.
The Caitya was constructed in 1964.
Historical sources at the temple in Cobhara reveal the involvement of the residents of Patan in building the temple and other structures at the premises.
The Dhanjvaḥ Phalcā appears to have been built to facilitate people from Patan while they visit the Jalavināyaka temple.

A small niche can be seen on top of thejaḥdhuṃ, which used to contain an inscription that mentioned that thephalcāwas built during the period of Candra Śamśera (local resident, Maharjana, male, age 69).
The bridge over the Bāgamatī river a few meters ahead was built by Candra Śamśera in 1903 CE (VS 1960).
Probably, thephalcāwas also built around the same time.
The Kũvara clan living nearby used to fill up thejaḥdhuṃtank with water from the waterhole but stopped doing so for the past five years or so (c. 2018 CE) (local resident, Maharjana, male, age 69).

The northern spout (object no. LAL1921-001) has a plain body without the usual carving of amakara(mythical water creature), bearing a damaged cover (hitipusā) carved with a fish motif and a Bhagīratha statue below.
Within thehitipremises lies a Licchavi-eracaitya(object no. LAL1921-004) dating 758 CE (Mānadeva Era 182).
Another Licchavicaitya, without an inscription, stands northeast of thehiti, along with aśivaliṅgaand a well dated 1718 CE (NS 838).

No historical records confirm thehiti’s construction date, but the presence of two Licchavicaityas, one inscribed with Mānadeva Era 182, which corresponds to 758 CE, and a lostjaḥdhuṃ(water trough) dated 763 CE (Mānadeva Era 187) (D. Vajrācārya VS 2030, p. 593) suggest it was built during the Licchavi period, with later medieval additions.
Thehitiwas renovated in 1965 CE (VS 2022) and its water source is in Bhinchẽ Bāhāḥ Ṭola (Lalitpur Sub-Metropolitan City 2007, p. 90).
There are numerous examples in the Kathmandu Valley where phalcās reconstructed in concrete were restored to their original forms after the earthquake of 2015 CE.
This phalcā, which extends in two directions, is one such example of restoration to its traditional form.
It seems that to facilitate these activities, the phalcā, extending in two directions with nine columns, was constructed.
There is no inscriptional evidence regarding the initial construction of the phalcā.
However, an inscription from 1789 CE (NS 901) was found here.
This early Śāha-period inscription mentions that the phalcā, which had fallen into disrepair, was reconstructed by the jyāpu and mālī communities.
Interestingly, the inscription lists the names of individuals from the Thāpā community who held positions such as pramāṇa, dvāre, and jeṭhābuḍhā.
The mention of reconstruction in the inscription confirms that the phalcā existed during the Malla period.
In the 1990s, the traditional phalcā was demolished and replaced with a concrete structure.
A photograph of the traditional phalcā before its reconstruction in concrete was published in a book by the Department of Archaeology (VS 2060, p. 34).
After the earthquake of 2015 CE, most of the heritage structures in the Kvaylāchi area were restored to their original forms.
This phalcā was also reconstructed in its traditional style (one of the ward members, Maharjana, male, age 32) ।.
Currently (November 2024), the reconstruction of the phalcā is underway with a budget of 6 million rupees allocated by Godāvarī Municipality.
Additionally, small wooden pillars are erected in front of the phalcā by private guṭhīs, on which Indra and Airāvata (Indra’s elephant) are displayed.
During the month of Kārtika, wooden pillars are erected in front of the phalcā, and an oil lamp (Ālaḥmata) is lit in honor of Brahmāyaṇī.
The Kirtipur Metropolitan City Office constructed this Phalcā in 2022 CE and named it Gāijātrā Phalcā (cf. Kirtipur Sandeśa VS 2072, p.3).
Prior to the construction of the Phalcā, it was a historical site with a remnant (plinth) of a traditionalphalcāthat was destroyed/removed for unknown reasons several decades ago.
The plinth was clearly visible until around 1983 CE (VS 2040), when it was covered by a table tennis court, according to local elders.
Local government representatives, as well as local nobles and commoners, attended the event (cf. Kirtipur Sandeśa VS 2072, p.3).
Two inscriptions set against the wall west of the main entrance of the Temple are already unreadable.
Pruscha(1975, p.19) mentions the Temple to be constructed in 1679 CE (VS 1622) without referring to any sources.
He probably got the information from one of the two unreadable inscriptions that perhaps were readable back then.
He also mentions that the Temple was renovated in 1939 CE (VS 1996), which is corroborated by the inscription on the eaves fascia of the lower roof.
Thebāhāḥis accessible after walking down a flight of fifteen staircases through the ground floor of a private residential building.
From the outside of this building, it is hard to assume that there is abāhāḥbehind it.
This could be the reason why KarlPruschawas not able to locate and include thisbāhāḥin his inventory (published in 1975 CE).
A stone statue of Akṣobhya is consecrated as thekvāpādyaḥ(bāhāḥ’s primary deity) inside thedyaḥchẽ’ssanctum.
There used to be a mural on the wall inside the sanctum, however, it is completely destroyed.
Cakrasaṃvara is consecrated in theāgaṃ(based on a personal conversation with a local resident, from a Vajrācārya caste, male, age 56).

A Śikharakūṭa Caitya is established in the middle of thebāhāḥcourtyard.
There is no evidence to date thebāhāḥ’s initial construction.
They believe that one of their ancestors constructed it.
These families moved to Kirtipur some generations back and the Vajrācāryas of the Cilancva Bāhāḥ gave them the permission to use Kusi Bāhāḥ for their initiation ceremonies (cf.Locke1985, 182).

Rājarājeśvarīdevī, the queen of Raṇa Bahādura Śāha, offered the door,toraṇa, and window to Vajrayoginī in 1799 CE (VS 1856) (D. Vajrācārya and Ṭ. Śreṣṭha2037, p. 306-307;D. Sharma and T. Shrestha2016, p. 431-432).

text: After the statue was stolen in 1985 CE, a smaller replica was installed, and a statue of Sarasvatī was also placed next to it.
After the statue was stolen in 1985 CE ((B. Shrestha2012, p. 419),), a smaller replica was installed, and a statue of Sarasvatī was also placed next to it.
Later, Jogadeva Vajrācārya, the 9th-generation descendant of Vācāsiddhi Vajrācārya, founded the town of Sankhu.

The Licchavi King Vṛṣadeva was also a pious devotee of Vajrayoginī and offered her food before eating himself (as mentioned in the (Nepālikabhūpavaṃśāvali12.38).No historic source is available that shed light on the initial construction of the temple. However, it is known that the tiered Temple of Vajrayoginī was previously aśikhara-style structure. It is unclear if the Temple was constructed in a different style before that. In 1655 CE (NS 775), King Pratāpa Malla commissioned the construction of a temple for Vajrayoginī and endowed lands for aguthito observe the daily rituals at the temple (D. Sharma and T. Shrestha2016, p. 408-412). The inscription that records this event does not clearly specify the style in which the temple was constructed. However, it does mention a practice of coating the temple with lime every year on the full moon day of Caitra. A tiered temple does not require lime coats. This suggests that the temple Pratāpa Malla got constructed was in theśikharastyle. A later-reconstruction of the temple in 1670 CE (NS 790) saw the installation of a finial (T. Siṃha1136, 4, folio 4B). It is not possible that a finial was installed 15 years after the construction of the Temple in 1655 CE.The Temple was probably rebuilt before the installation of a finial. Unfortunately, there are no historic sources that clarify this confusion. An entry in an annal mentions that thecakrainstalled on the northern side of theśikhara-style (granthakūṭa) Temple of Vajrayoginī fell off in 1683 CE (NS 803) (T. Siṃha1136, p. 12, folio 17B). This makes it clear that it was aśikhara-style Temple till at least 1683 CE. Later in 1712 CE (NS 832), Kathmandu's King Bhāṣkara Malla and his mother got theśikhara-style Temple dismantled and rebuilt it as a tiered structure (G. Vajrācārya2023, p. 33). The Temple was renovated by Friends of Sankhu, a local organization, with the funds from the Netherlands arranged by the efforts of Bālagopāla Śreṣṭha and the late Bert van den Hoek in 2002 CE. The Temple did not collapse in the 2015 earthquakes but was left with multiple cracks. Wooden supports were placed all around the Temple to prevent it from collapsing. The Department of Archaeology rebuilt both Vajrayoginī and Jogeśvara Temples at a total cost of NRs. 59.2 million.The priest of Jogeśvara Temple is responsible for performing daily rituals at the Vajrayoginī Temple. While four daily rituals are observed at the Jogeśvara Temple, only two are performed at the Vajrayoginī Temple. Daily worship takes place early in the morning, and an āratī is offered in the evening. Every year, the Vajrayoginī Jātrā is celebrated for eight days in Sankhu, beginning on the full moon day of Caitra. The Mhāsukhvāḥmāju Dyaḥchẽ (SKH0550) houses replicas of Vajrayoginī, Siṃhinī (the lion-faced deity), and Vyāghrinī (the tiger-faced deity). On the fourth day of the dark fortnight of Vaiśākha, a procession featuring the statues of Mhāsukhvāḥmāju, Siṃhinī, Vyāghrinī, Svayambhū Caitya, and Vasundharā takes place. On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Vaiśākha, the statues are brought back to the Dyaḥchẽ, marking the end of the Jātrā. Once every 12 years, the face of Vajrayoginī is repaired and repainted in a ritual known as lãpu chāygu. In case of any damages, such repair works are carried out even before the 12 years. It used to be carried out every year, but King Śivadeva arranged for the ritual painting to be performed every 12 years (Nepālikabhūpavaṃśāvali12.148). Vajrayoginī is revered as the lineage deity by caste groups such as Rāṇās, Thāpās, Basnyāts, etc., who frequently visit the temple to worship their lineage deity.[1]According toB. Bhattacharyya1958, p. 248-249, the deity enshrined at the sanctum is not Vajrayoginī. She is Ugratārādevī, who is also known as Mahācīnatārā. When East Bengal was defeated following the invasion of the Muslim army of Mohammedan, the Bengali priests from Ḍakkā (currently known as Dhaka, the capital of Bangladesh) came to Nepal with the statue of Ugratārā. This suggests that the statue of Ugratārā brought by the Bengalis is being worshipped as Vajrayoginī in Sankhu. Bhattacharyya does not give the source of this account.[2]The priests are reluctant to disclose the material the statue of Vajrayoginī is made of. They fear that disclosing it will strike them with the evil eyes of the deity.

This rest house, located in the Devapattana (Deopatan) area, is believed to have been constructed by a local Ayurveda physician using the gifts he received from the Lankan King Rāvaṇa as a token of gratitude for curing the king's ailment.
Situated west of Lũhiti (PPK1218) at Jayavāgīśvarī, thephalcā, unfortunately, lacks any inscriptions or statues, making its historical origin unclear.
However, locals maintain that the Rāvaṇa Phalcā was built by a Vaidya from the Navālī Ṭola, who utilized the gifts he received from King Rāvaṇa to construct the rest house.

An inscription from 645 CE (Mānadeva Era 69) records donations made during the reign of King Narendradeva to a hospital (ārogyaśālā) for treating ascetics residing in the Paśupati area (D. Vajrācārya 2030, p.472-473).

Similarly, another inscription from 679 CE (Mānadeva Era 103) at the Vajraghara in Paśupati specifies the charge of 100paṇafor extracting a fetus from a deceased mother's womb (D. Vajrācārya 2030, p.499-501).

Notable among them are manuscripts by Kṛṣṇadeva from the reign of King Śivasiṃhadeva in 1611 CE (NS 731) and Vaidya Vāsudeva from the reign of King Lakṣmīnarasiṃha Malla in 1630 CE (NS 750), both focusing on health and treatment (Vaidya and Kaṃsākāra NS 1111, p. 378, 380).
Presently, the Vaidyas of this Ṭola continue to serve as traditional physicians (ghāṭe vaidya) at the Paśupati cremation ground (M. Thāpā VS 2077, p.503).
With the gifts received from Rāvaṇa, the Vaidya constructed a two-storiedphalcāadorned with traditional tiles on its roof.

Additionally, he endowed over 200ropanīsof land in Kapana to establish a trust (guthi) in thephalcā's name, now renowned as the Rāvaṇa Phalcā (as recounted by a male resident from the Saṅghata caste, aged 76).

Nevertheless, his name was Melama Vaidya, and his descendants received a copper-plate inscription from Rāṇā Prime Minister Candra Śamśera, granting them the authorization to serve as Ayurveda physicians as long as the sun and the moon graced the sky (M. Thāpā VS 2077, p.503).
Unfortunately, the upper floor collapsed during the 2015 earthquakes, and its full renovation remains pending as of April 2023.
The water spout (tuṭī) is installed in a recessed pit below the present ground level.
No inscription is found on the water spout itself.
Above thetuṭīis installed a finely carved image of Gajalakṣmī (BKT0780-007), while below it is a depiction of Bhagīratha holding a conch shell (BKT0780-002).
Theja:dhūṃpositioned at the north-western corner (BKT0780-009) is particularly significant because it bears an inscription.
It was relocated to the present site approximately 10–12 years ago.
In addition, a damaged image of Garuḍa (BKT0780-011) is propped against the wall to the east of thehiti.
No inscription directly recording the construction of thehitiitself has been found within the precinct.

However, the inscription on theja:dhūṃ(BKT0780-009), brought from the Tripurasundarīdyaḥchẽand now placed at the north-western corner, records that Lakṣmīnārāṃ Mijā Bhāju, Mani Bhāju, and Rājana Narasiṃha of the Tulāchẽ neighborhood installed thisja:dhūṃin 1832 CE (NS 953).
Dhanavajra Vajrācārya has noted the existence of an earlier inscription from the reign of Yakṣa Malla at this site.
That inscription, however, is no longer extant as of June 2025.

According to Vajrācārya, the lost inscription recorded that in 1467 CE (NS 588) Yakṣa Malla installed a golden image of Nārāyaṇa equal to the height of his deceased son Jayarāja Malla, laid the foundation of a Viṣṇu temple, and erected adhvajāin his memory (D. Vajrācārya, VS 2068, pp. 357–359).
Thehitiunderwent restoration around 2008 CE (VS 2065) with support from the Guṭhī Saṃsthāna (local resident, Vaidya caste, male, age 75).
In addition, Bhaktapur Municipality has installed a drinking-water pipeline, through which water flows into thehititwice a week.
The houses on the west and north sides of the courtyard are built in traditional Newar style with colonnaded ground floors and carved triple-bay windows on their first and second floors.
The house on the east has been completely rebuilt in modern style.
A photo printed inLocke(1985, 213) shows that the house on the eastern side also had similar paintings and windows, however since its reconstruction it no longer has these features.
On the wall paintings are depictions of various deities, some from Jātaka tales,Locke(1985, 214) maintains that the Bāhāḥ was founded in NS 986 (1866 CE) without providing a source.
A stone inscription on thevediof the northern face of thedharmadhātu jinālaya caityamentions that Maṇiratna Vaidya enshrined the images of Triratnas in the sanctum in NS 998.
Three days afterwards, the naming ceremony of the monastic building took place, where it was given the name "Maṇikūṭa Vihāra".
The families affiliated with theguṭhīof the monastic building were professionalvaidyas (practitioners of Ayurvedic medicine); the monastic building is therefore also known as Vaidya Bāhāḥ.
Sālkhā Sataḥ was built in 1558 CE (NS 679).

An inscription records King Amṛta Malla commissioning the construction of asataḥat the Sālkhā Ṭola and donating many plots of land to feed ascetics from foreign lands at the Sataḥ (N. YogīVS 2012, p. 61-62).

[1]According to the inscription, the King built the Sataḥ in the name of his late wife Lakṣmīdevī and his late sons Abhayasiṃha and Kṛṣṇasiṃha, along with his daughters-in-law Jayatudevī, Phikudevī and Herādevī.
A line of this inscription refers to Śaṅkarapaṭṭana (Sankhu) as the capital city which is significant for the study of Sankhu’s political history.
Statues of Viṣṇu and Lakṣmī carved on a single stone is placed atop thejalaharīthat contains this Inscription.
The Statue also contains a one-line inscription that refers to the figure of Lakṣmī as Lakṣmīdevī, the wife of King Amṛta Malla, and Viṣṇu as the King’s son Abhayasiṃha.
It also reveals that there was a tradition of installing statues of deities based on their iconography but referring to them as one’s family members.
An inscription on the back of the Palm outlines the activities to be carried out by the respectiveguthiannually.
N. YogīVS 2012, p. 62 refers to this inscription asdātṛhastābhilekha(lit. the inscription on the donor’s palm).
After the Sataḥ collapsed in the 1934 earthquakes, it was never rebuilt in its former state.
N. YogīVS 2012, p. 62 writes that the Sataḥ was rebuilt at the behest of the locals in presence of the police although it was the responsibility of the Guṭhī Saṃsthāna to reconstruct it.
The reconstruction converted the Sataḥ into a plain building of one floor that provided space for the operation of a local library (local resident, Śreṣṭha, male, age 88).
Later in 1959 CE, the Chẽbhaḍela Office of Bhaktapur dismantled the Building and replaced it with a two-story concrete structure (local resident, Śreṣṭha, male, age 88).
For over six decades after the reconstruction, a local library named Ugra Pustakālaya operated from this Building.
After the 2015 earthquakes damaged the Building, all the books and furniture of Ugra Pustakālaya were shifted to another building.
As of January 2022, the Sataḥ is under construction with the fund provided by the Shankharapur Municipality.
The present reconstruction merges both structures into onesataḥof seven bays.
YogīVS 2012, p. 62, theguthiformed at the time of the construction of the Sataḥ was partially operational in 1959 CE.
The police station moved out of the Phalcā in 1980 CE, but the Post Office that provided its service from the nearby Vāphale Phalcā (SKH0103) moved in here.
The Post Office also moved out of the Phalcā after the 2015 earthquakes.
There is aguthiof a Śreṣṭha clan of Sankhu to observe this tradition.
[1]As of January 2022, the Sataḥ is being reconstructed and the inscription along with a statue at the Sataḥ are shifted to the nearby Mandaḥ Phalcā.
The historic Phale Sataḥ was dismantled following the 2015 CE earthquakes and all original materials were lost.
It was replaced with a crude brick and cement shack, covered with a corrugated metal roof.
The stone image is installed against a wall and oriented westward.
On the original stone image, both breasts and the right arm appear to have been deliberately damaged by blows from a sharp weapon.
The sculpture bears no inscription.
On the eastern wall of thedevasthala, a date—1689 CE (NS 809)—is carved without accompanying text.

This inscription is likely associated not with the image itself but with the construction of a stone retaining wall to stabilize the shrine, during which the date may have been recorded (Slusser 2005, pp. 98–99).
In 2019 CE (VS 2075), thedevasthalaunderwent repair and conservation through the financial support of Dhirjadās Rājakarṇikāra and his family, residents of Maru Tole, Kathmandu.
The restoration work was carried out through the coordinated efforts of the Rājakarṇikāra Śaraṇa Guṭhī and the Rājakarṇikāra Samāja.

To ensure the continuity of this ritual, the family of Dhirjadās Rājakarṇikāra established a perpetual endowment (akṣayakośa) of NPR 700,000 in his memory; the interest generated from this fund has been used to conduct thechāhāy-ke-guworship each year without interruption (President of the Rājakarṇikāra Śaraṇa Guṭhī, male, age 58).
The dilapidated Phalcā was dismantled and rebuilt in 2006 CE (Bāsukalā & Gutschow2019).
However, no documented evidence dating the initial construction of this Phālcā has so far been found.

Whether the Dvāre Ghara's unassuming appearance is a reflection of thedvāre's position from the outset or a result of successive renovations over time is a question that remains unanswered, due to a lack of definitive historical sources.
The house was reconstructed in 1988 CE (VS 2045) at the request of the then-dvāreby the Department of Archaeology (local resident, Śāhī, male, age 63).
In the aftermath of the 2015 earthquakes, the Dvāre Ghara's original roof of traditionaljhĩgaṭītiles was replaced with corrugated metal sheets.

In historical records, the title "dvāre" appears as early as the Licchavi period (c. 4th century onwards), with mentions of the position appearing in various Newar settlements during the medieval era as well (D. Vajrācārya VS 2030, p. 118).
Following the shifting of the capital city from Nuwakot to Kathmandu, Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa Śāha granted special privileges to thedvārehere.

Thedvārewas entrusted with the responsibility of leading the annual procession  of Bhairavī, which traditionally involved the participation of the king himself (D. Vajrācārya and Ṭ. Śreṣṭha VS 2032, p. 86).

text: Although known as abāhāḥ, Rāma Bāhāḥ neither has its main deity (kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ) nor does it have its monastic building (kvāḥpāḥchẽ).
Only a small ‘shrine’ (devasthala) is established here with acaityaplaced on top as its finial.
The Caitya was initially established on the Bāhāḥ’s ground in 1567 CE (NS 687) during the reign of King Mahendra Malla.
When the Shrine was renovated in 1937 CE (VS 1994), the Caitya established on the ground was moved to the top of the Shrine as its finial.
An empty niche with a stonetoraṇais installed inside the sanctum of the Shrine.
A statue of Akṣobhya is installed at the bottom of the Shrine which is flanked by a pair of lions.
There are no historical records to date the initial construction of the Bāhāḥ.
There is a mention of a ‘Lhāṃvihāra’ in two manuscripts of theAṣṭasāhasrikāPrajñāpāramitāfrom 1009 CE (NS 128) and 1015 CE (NS 135) (Petech1984, p.36).

An inscription from 1567 CE (NS 687) associated with the Bāhāḥ was recently published, which recorded the establishment of the above-mentioned Caitya (placed on top of the shrine at its finial) at ‘Raṃbāhāra’ by Jagatasiṃ and Paṃdu.
As the inscription names this monument as Raṃbāhāra, the name Rāma Bāhāḥ given byPruscha(K-7, p.12) seems to be incorrect.
The shrine sustained minor damages in the 1934 earthquakes and was renovated in 1937 CE (VS 1994).
Lo Gekar might be contemporaneous with the first monastery of Tibet, Samyé, which was founded in the late 8thcentury.
The complex is also used by villagers from Marang and Tsarang for special rituals. (see Luczanits: Seismic Strengthening and Restoration of Lo Gekhar, project proposal, 2020).

text: Two approach roads have been constructed recently on either side of the valley, the one on the side of Marang village considerably easier to maintain.
The monument as it stands today predominantly dates from the last decades of the 16thcentury onwards, a restoration of the complex being recorded at that time.
There is little information available regarding past restorations.
As legend informs the originally nine-story tall temple collapsed in an earthquake and was never rebuilt to its original size.

Sometimes in the late 1970s a lama from Lo Manthang moved to Lo Gekar and built a two-story structure in the courtyard; the lower room (L10) was used as a stable and the room above for his residence (U10-today called the “VIP room”).
It is not documented when the portico was added to the temple’s east facade and the new main entrance created.
The caretaker also reports that this lama was responsible for rebuilding the chörtens at the corners of Lo Gekar.
In 2003-2004 the northern half of the complex was restored under the guidance of John Sunday with funding from the American Himalayan Foundation.

Also recognized as Lokabhaktarājyalakṣmī, the first wife of Prime Minister Candra Śamśera Rāṇā, Lokabhaktalakṣmī oversaw the construction of thisśivālaya(lit. the dwelling of Lord Śiva) in 1903 CE (VS 1960) and later presented a bell to the temple a few months afterward.

Outside the temple, a Nandī figure, the sacred bull of Lord Śiva, guards the western entrance, while a bell from 1903 CE, suspended by a bell stand south of the temple, commemorates the construction of the temple.
Additionally, a statue of Kāmadeva is enshrined southeast of the temple, with a stone trident (triśūla) erected to the north.
Lokabhaktalakṣmī, the first wife of Rāṇā Prime Minister Candra Śamśera, commissioned the temple in 1903 CE (VS 1960) (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p. 347), in honor of herself and her husband.
A few months later, she presented a bell to the temple along with her sons (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2056, p. 620).
Candra Śamśera had five sons – Mohana, Babara, Keśara, Siṃha, and Kṛṣṇa Śamśera – and a daughter from Lokabhaktalakṣmī (P. Rāja VS 2070, p. 47).
She succumbed to tuberculosis on February 11, 1905 (P. Rāṇā VS 2080, p. 64).
A few years later, in 1908 CE (NS 1029), Candra Śamśera commissioned a small pond at the Patan Durbar Square and established a statue of his late queen there (R. Vajrācārya NS 1099, p. 104).
Many of the social-cultural activities related to Karuṇāmaya are organised in the locality, and thesephalcāswere constructed as sites within which to hold such activities.
This three-bayedphalcāis located on the ground floor of a three-storey building.
The roof of the building is supported by six carved struts and is covered with corrugated metal sheets.
The construction of thisphalcāwas facilitated by a Tāmrākāra family from Cāsukhela, Bhaktapur in 1868 CE.
Originally, the building was calledsatala.
Its founders had established aguṭhīfor its management.
However, the building collapsed in the 1934 earthquake and was reconstructed by the desecendents of the founders in 1942.
A historical photo taken around 1968 shows that the building once had ajhĩgaṭī-tiled roof and a traditional window (Bungamati1968, 21).
The Bāsimali Phalcā collapsed again in 2001 and in the same year Nārāyaṇadevī Tāmrākāra, another descendent of the founders, took on the task of renovating it.
Once the renovations were complete, she deposited a lump sum of money in the bank to allow for the continuation and management ofbhajanachanting in Bāsimali Phalcā.
Nārāyaṇadevī Tāmrākāra also donated musical instruments to abhajanagroup in 2001, and this group now performsbhajanaduring the months of Gũlā and Kārttika.
Situated at the Sun Ṭola, Sāṅgalā Dabū is one of two relatively recent elevated platforms of Sankhu constructed in 1996 CE (VS 2053).
The other one situated next to the Mahādeva Dhvākhā was constructed in 1998 CE (B. ŚreṣṭhaNS 1139, p. 66).
Therefore, Sāṅgāla Dabū was constructed with the presumption that adabūexisted here previously.
However,B. ŚreṣṭhaNS 1139, p. 66 mentions that a newdabūwas constructed at the place where no such platform existed previously.
Although adabūdid not exist here before 1996 CE, the tradition of displaying Hāthudyaḥ was observed every year at the same space where the new Dabū was constructed.
The Dabū was damaged in the 2015 earthquakes and reconstructed by the Shankharapur Municipality in 2021 CE.
A stone carving of aṣaṭkoṇa(lit. six angles), a six-pointed star, has now been installed at the center of the Dabū.
In the course of the renovation, a newhitiwas also installed west of the Dabū.

Although there is a lack of historical sources to prove thatdabūs already existed in the Licchavi period, a Licchavi inscription of Jayadeva II (713 CE-733 CE) from Nārāyaṇacaura, Kathmandu does mention terms likeponḍimaṇḍapikāandprekṣaṇamaṇḍapī(D. VajrācāryaVS 2030, p. 569).

Narmadeśvara Mandira, also known as Jaṅga Hiraṇya Hemeśvara Mandira, is said to be one of many temples built by Prime Minister Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā.
According to the priest (Koirālā, male, age 70), the temple was built by Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā, in 1847 CE, in memory of his wives Hiraṇyagarbha Kumārī Devī and Hema Kumārī.
The temple is in poor condition due to damages suffered in the 2015 earthquakes and the lack of proper maintenance.
Khaḍga Bahādura Kũvara is credited with constructing this Śiva temple in the year 1848 CE (VS 1905).

Positioned to the east of the Rakṣeśvara Mandira (PPK1937) on the eastern side of the primary path leading to the Gorakhanātha temple, thisśivālaya, or the abode of Śiva, is built from stone, crowned with a bell-shaped roof adorned with a metallic finial.
Unfortunately, a statue of Kāmadeva, enshrined southeast of the temple, has been stolen.
The Jagadīśvara temple was reportedly constructed in 1848 CE (VS 1905) (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p.349; Michaels and Tandon 2017, p.106).
citations: (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p.349; Michaels and Tandon 2017, p.106)

text: Despite G. Ṭaṇḍana (VS 2053, p.599) suggesting a different construction date of 1858 CE (VS 1915), this probably is a printing error.

The donor of the temple is a subject of confusion, with G. Ṭaṇḍana (VS 2053, p.349) claiming joint construction by Jayakṛṣṇa Kũvara and Khaḍga Bahādura Kũvara, while Michaels and Tandon (2017, p.106) attribute it solely to Jayakṛṣṇa Kũvara, the younger brother of Rāmakṛṣṇa Kũvara.

Both brothers were tasked with building an ammunition building in the midwestern district of Pyūṭhāna, where Rāmakṛṣṇa passed away in 1787 CE (VS 1844) (B. Bhaṇḍārī VS 2071, p.7) and Jayakṛṣṇa the following year (B. Bhaṇḍārī VS 2071, p.17).
Given Jayakṛṣṇa's demise 60 years prior to the temple's construction, it is likely that Khaḍga Bahādura Kũvara commissioned the temple's construction.
Khaḍga Bahādura, the son of Jaṅga Bahāura Rāṇā's uncle Balarāma Kũvara, enjoyed the trust of Jaṅga Bahādura (P. Rāṇā VS 2059, p.43).
A decade after the completion of the Jagadīśvara temple, in 1858 CE (VS 1915), Khaḍga Bahādura offered a bell to the temple along with another Śiva temple named Indreśvara (PPK1939).
Following the 2015 earthquakes, which left cracks on the temple walls, the Pashupati Area Development Trust undertook restoration efforts in 2021 CE (VS 2078).
This arcaded platform, known as Tīna Dhārā Pāṭī, was likely constructed in the 17th century CE to accommodate people visiting the Tīna Dhārā water spout for bathing and collecting water.
No statues are installed inside.
There are no clear historical records about when thepāṭīwas originally built.
According to a KVPT report (KVPT2000, 4), the original statue was stolen in 1980 CE and a new statue was enshrined in 2013 CE.
The inscription on the southern wall of the temple attributes its construction to Luṁgu Bhāro in 1576 CE (NS 696), mentioning his endowment ofguthiland for sustaining daily worship.
Unfortunately, theguthiis currently inactive, and the whereabouts of its land are untraceable.
Prior to the reconstruction by the Kathmandu Valley Preservation Trust in 2000 CE, the temple had suffered extensive damage.
The roofs of the top two tiers were completely lost and the lowest roof had partly collapsed.
The restoration effort integrated four of the original struts, while all other struts were carved anew (KVPT 2000: 53).

Unfortunately, the 2015 CE earthquakes again caused significant damage, requiring the temporary stabilization by means of wooden bracing. 6 years later, in 2021 CE, through the initiative of KVPT, all ground-level walls were reconstructedin situ, and the roof structure underwent repairs.
A newly discovered rock inscription in Nālāchāpa, a village northeast of Bhaktapur, has pushed back the history of rock inscriptions in the region.
Dating back to 1551 CE (NS 671), this inscription is the earliest yet found on the five massive natural rock formations that dot the landscape.
While four of these formations were previously known to bear inscriptions, the recent discovery at Ṭhulokholā brings the total to five.
This particular inscription, though recognized by locals for years, has only recently gained wider attention.
The previous earliest inscription, dating to 1636 CE (NS 756), mentioned the names of Bhaktapur and Kathmandu's kings.
A significant rock inscription has been unearthed on the banks of the Ṭhulokholā stream.
According to local resident Sudarśana Thāpā, 56, he recalls spending his childhood playing on this inscribed stone while herding cattle.
Over the years, the inscription became obscured by vegetation.
Thāpā made efforts to clear the overgrowth to reveal the inscription to the documentation team of this project.
The inscription mentions Inā Ṭola, likely referring to one of the two Inā Ṭolas (Inācva and Ināgāḥ) in present-day Bhaktapur.
It also records the names of two individuals, Tavadhīka and Harinārāyaṇa, who appear to have claimed the stone for a specific construction project.
This practice of marking stones to prevent their unauthorized use is evident in numerous rock inscriptions throughout the region.
By engraving short inscriptions, individuals sought to protect their chosen stones for future use.

Two inscriptions from the reign of King Viṣṇu Gupta, dated to the Mānadeva Era 64 and 65 (corresponding to 640 and 641 CE), detail the transportation of stone within the valley for sculpting statues (D. Vajrācārya VS 2030, pp. 446-448).

These records indicate that residents of Sunāguthi (a town southwest of Patan) and Dakṣiṇakolīgrāma (southern Kathmandu) were rewarded with the privilege of wearing jewelry for their service in transporting stones for the creation of Buḍhānīlakaṇṭha, the reclining Viṣṇu statue located north of Kathmandu.

Artistic creations crafted from this stone often proudly proclaimed their origin. Śrīnivāsa Malla, the king of Patan, generously provided Koṭakhā stone to Jitāmitra Malla, the king of Bhaktapur, at the latter's request to renovate the Kumārī Coka (Tevārī and others VS 2019, pp. 24-25).
Similarly, in 1691 CE (NS 811), Crown Prince Bhūpatindra Malla utilized Koṭakhā stone to restore a water spout in the Bhaktapur palace (Vaidya & Shrestha 2002, p. 207).
There is speculation that the stone procured by Viṣṇu Gupta for the Buḍhānīlakaṇṭha statue and the Koṭakhā stone originated from the same quarry (D. Vajrācārya VS 2030, p. 446).

The Bhaktapur kings and crown princes' proud proclamation that the stones used in their constructions were sourced from the kingdom of Patan's quarry reveals their sense of accomplishment in acquiring stones from a neighboring state.
The statues of Khāka and Kavã are an interesting addition to this Buddhist monastic building, as they are more commonly found in the Śākta temples of the Valley.
A stone statue of Akṣobhya is enshrined in its sanctum and an aniconic stone attached to the left wall of the building is worshipped as Bhairava.
Relying on an inscription,Locke(1985, 44) dates the Bāhāḥ to NS 779 (1659 CE).
A completely effaced stone inscription is attached to the wall of the building and is likely the one that Locke used for this.

monument_name: Rārā Temple and fountain (14th-15th cent. CE)
text: This type of construction was probably introduced from Uttarakhand (Chanchani 2019, 19).
Built on the banks of the Triśūlī river, Indrāyaṇī Pīṭha serves as a protective shrine for the Nuwakot settlement from the northwest.
On the southern wall, a statue of the goddess Bhagavatī has been installed, while to the north stands a trident (triśūla) donated by Brigadier Colonel Gaṅgābahādura Basneta Kṣetrī.
Located east of the shrine is a public rest house built by the Pā̃ḍe clan of Pakanajol, Kathmandu.
Despite being in a poor state of repair with a roof of corrugated metal sheets, it remains a significant structure in the area.

According to local accounts (B. Ācārya and Y. Naraharinātha VS 2070, p. 41), Śāha received divine guidance from Indrāyaṇī in a dream, advising him on the most auspicious time to launch an invasion of Nuwakot.
citations: (B. Ācārya and Y. Naraharinātha VS 2070, p. 41)

text: Following her instructions, he successfully conquered Nuwakot (B. Ācārya and Y. Naraharinātha VS 2070, p. 42).
citations: (B. Ācārya and Y. Naraharinātha VS 2070, p. 42)

text: The earliest documented evidence of the shrine dates to the later medieval period, with sacrificial rituals recorded here in 1638 CE (NS 758) and 1841 CE (VS 961) (cf. D. Vajrācārya and Ṭ. Śreṣṭha VS 2032, p. 129 and 133).
citations: (cf. D. Vajrācārya and Ṭ. Śreṣṭha VS 2032, p. 129 and 133)

text: In 1927 CE (VS 1983), Brigadier Colonel Gaṅgābahādura Basneta Kṣetrī commissioned renovations of thepīṭhaand installed the trident.
The ritual includes the sacrifice of a spotless black or white he-goat, with its head offered in a fire oblation.
Since their relocation from the area, the rest house remains unused.
From the Phalcā, one enters into an office that is located inside but otherwise disconnected from the building of the Capāḥ, which is dedicated to Nāsaḥdhyaḥ, the god of music and dance.
It was reconstructed in 2018 after being dismantled and rebuilt in 1992.
Its associated groups are the Nāsaḥ Guṭhī, the Cyāsaḥ Maṃkā Khalaḥ and the Yanyā Guthi of Byañjankārs of Nhukaṃchẽnani (Mahārānī Cukaḥ).
There are no records indicating whether thisśivaliṅgawas originally housed inside a temple or has always been under the open sky since its establishment.

The condition of thejalaharīand theśivaliṅgaatop it appears different, leading to speculation about possible damage or relocation over time: It is hard to say whether theśivaliṅgagot damaged at some point, resulting in a newliṅgabeing placed on this rectangularjalaharī, or if thejalaharīon which theliṅgawas resting got damaged, thus necessitating a newjalaharīor relocation for theliṅga.

On the occasion of Śivarātri, residents of Bhairavīsthāna and Brahmaṭola gather in front of the shrine, light a bonfire, and partake inprāsāda(leftover offerings to the deity), as reported by a local resident (Ḍaṅgola, male, age 36).
Constructed north of the main entrance to Thã Bahī (KAT0090) the two-tiered temple faces east.
Siṃhasārthavāhū is credited for building Thã Bahī after his return from Tibet.
Although it hard to date the first construction of the temple, it is considered to be as old as Thã Bahī.
A record in a medieval annal mentions the consecration of the ‘thrice venerablejātigāradevala’ in 1615 CE (NS 735) (MallakālikaAitihāsikaGhaṭanāvalī, folio 33).
In 2009 CE, Durgādevī and Gopāla Prasāda Pradhāna installed copper frills on the temple.
There is also a copperplate inscription listing the names of the donors without specifying their collective deed.
There used to be another copperplate inscription inside the temple but is no longer exists.
According to one interpretation, the term derives fromlaskara(“large assembly”), since Lokeśvara is venerated by great multitudes (H. Śākya NS 1089, p. 55).
Another view holds that “Laskaḥ Dyaḥ” is simply the Newar abbreviation ofLokeśvara(P. Śreṣṭha VS 2080, p. 545).
Beneath the middle roof, a carved woodentoraṇadepicting Amoghapāśa Lokeśvara has been installed, while metallic ritual vessels are fixed below it.
On either side of the temple staircase stand two brass and three stone lion figures, while in front of the shrine aDharmadhātu Maṇḍalaand smallcaityashave been installed.
No inscription directly recording the foundation of thebāhāḥhas been found.
According to a note preserved on palm-leaf manuscript, thebāhāḥwas established by King Varadeva, son of Bhaktapur’s King Narendra Deva.

When the attempt to install Buṅgadyah in Bhaktapur failed, Varadeva, to fulfill his father’s wish, constructed the Jētavarṇa Mahāvihāra and enshrined an image of Padmapāṇi Lokeśvara as Buṅgadyah’s replica in 600 CE (Kaligata 3701) (S. Śākya VS 2055, p. 7).
A copperplate inscription from 1993 CE (VS 2050) reiterates the same narrative but gives the date 500 CE (Kaligata 3601), further suggesting the account’s legendary nature (BKT0570_I_015).

Popular tradition adds that once the image of Buṅgadyah (Padmapāṇi Lokeśvara) was installed in Bhaktapur, agricultural fertility increased remarkably: the soil itself yielded abundant grain, even sprouting rice on the farmers’ hats.
Hence, this Lokeśvara became known as “Annapūrṇa Lokeśvara” (P. Śreṣṭha VS 2080, p. 549).

Despite the legendary Licchavi attribution, the earliest extant inscription from the site dates only to 1830 CE (NS 950), recording Tejaratna Siṃha’s donation of a pair of stone lions (BKT0570-005, 006) and a supportingṭuṇḍālainscribed with the nameMakuto, probably that of the donor.
In 1846 CE (NS 967), Bhimasimha Mānandra used profits from his Tibet trade to replace the uppermost roof tiles with gilded ones.
The same donor later offered, in 1885 CE (NS 1005), a goldentāyoornament adorned with a silvernāgamotif, as well as amohargarland, a bronze lamp, and a gilded amulet box (jantra) imported from Lhasa.
His daughters—Kumārī, Devamatī, Mayajumatī, and Māyā—endowed land asguthifor the deity’s upkeep.
In 1932 CE (VS 1989), Jagatlakṣmī Buddhācārya and her sons Dharmarāja and Herārāja donated brass and gilded coverings for the three ground-floor doors.
This tradition implies that the Lokeśvara of Laskaḥ Dyaḥ predates theNava Durgācult in Bhaktapur (P. Śreṣṭha VS 2080, p. 549).
Both practices have now ceased due to financial constraints, the lastnhvaṃbeing conducted in VS 2063 (2006 CE).

Each year during the month ofBhādra, devotees used to draw and worship aVasundharā maṇḍalain front of the temple, praying for agricultural prosperity and universal welfare (P. Śreṣṭha VS 2080, p. 549).

On 13th of dark fortnight ofŚrāvaṇa, the day ofPañcadāna, the Vajrācāryas of Nāla traditionally came to Bhaktapur to offer flowers and worship this Lokeśvara (B. Vajrācārya NS 1124, p. 77), though this custom has now lapsed.
The Shrine, therefore, is her seat (pīṭha) and the Phalcā appears to have been built to facilitate devotees who come to worship at the Shrine.
Due to the absence of an inscription at the Phalcā, it is unclear when it was initially built or when it was renovated over the years.
The 2015 earthquakes left massive cracks on the Phalcā.
It was dismantled later, as it was on the verge of collapse.
With the fund provided by the Shankharapur Municipality, the Phalcā was rebuilt in 2021 CE.
The Suntvāḥ Ṭola Sudhara Samiti, a local committee formed for the conservation of the area, also contributed some amount for the reconstruction (Samiti president, Śresṭha, male, age 46).
Noguthinor any donor family related to the Phalcā currently exists.
Positioned on the edge of a hill ridge to the west of Bhaṇḍārībādā, the shrine is built adjacent to a stūpa (JUM0030).
The monument bears typological similarities to the stūpa located directly south of it (JUM0030), suggesting that they were likely built simultaneously.
It resembles the stūpa at Kuchi Bihāra (ACH0010) and the one erected atop the Patharnauli reservoir (DLK0160).
Both of these monuments were constructed in 1354 CE (ŚS 1276) by Devavarmā, the Great Minister (mahāmātya) of King Pṛthvīmalla.
Therefore, it is plausible that both the stūpa and the shrine were built during the 14th century (Andolfatto 2019, pp. 96-97).

monument_name: Dugaṃ Bahī Gaṇeśa Mandira (built ca. 19th Cent.)
text: As the temple is constructed near Dugaṃ Bahī,Pursha(1975, p.27) named it Dugaṃ Bahī Gaṇeśa.

monument_name: Dugaṃ Bahī Gaṇeśa Mandira (built ca. 19th Cent.)
text: Thejhĩgaṭītiles laid on the roof were replaced by copper sheets in 1986 CE (VS 2043).

monument_name: Dugaṃ Bahī Gaṇeśa Mandira (built ca. 19th Cent.)
text: Aguthiof the Maharjanas from the area exhibits a metal statue of Gaṇeśa at the temple every year during thePāhāṃCaḥrhayfestival, the 14thof the dark fortnight of Caitra.

monument_name: Dugaṃ Bahī Gaṇeśa Mandira (built ca. 19th Cent.)
text: The Guthi used to assemble a heap ofsamaybajiin front of the temple on the 12thof the bright fortnight of Bhādra as part of theYẽnyāḥfestival.
To the east of the temple, a recently donated bell hangs on a stand.
There is no historical evidence detailing the construction of this temple.

The earliest inscription, dating back to 1798 CE (NS 918), mentions that individuals named Prajāpati Jeta, Amita, and Dhana, among others, collectively built aphalcarest house to the east of the temple for their lineage deity Viśvakarmā.
Likewise, in 1814 CE (NS 934), the Aṣṭamī Sevā Guthi, a religious trust of 28 people from the Jyāthā Ṭola, constructed another rest house (sataḥ) in front of the temple.
Later, in 1829 CE (NS 949), individuals including Beṣāsiṃha, Dhanaontasiṃha, and Dhanasiddhi built anotherphalcaand installed an inscription bearing their own figures.
Again, in 1846 CE (NS 966), a donor built aphalcain memory of his deceased father, Mahaṃtasī, his mother, wife, and son.

In 1853 CE (NS 973), Matyaṃsiṃ Prajāpati and his wife, Manamati, along with their sons and grandsons, replaced the old, worn-out statue of Viśvakarmā with a new one, wishing for the eternal peace of their deceased family members.
They also established a religious trust with land and money for the statue’s anniversary rituals.

In 1881 CE (NS 1001), the Digusivā Guthi, a religious trust responsible for serving the Prajāpati community's lineage deity, headed by Cidhisiṃha, renovated the dilapidated statue of Viśvakarmā and gilded it.
In 2011 CE (VS 2068), the Pañcadāna Guthi of the Prajāpatis in Jyāthā, with financial assistance from the Kathmandu Metropolitan City, renovated the dilapidated temple.
The king, it is said, married a commoner and granted their son 365ropanīs of land in various locations, allowing him to use oneropanīeach day (M. Prajāpati NS 1136, p. 59).
This endowment is believed to be the foundation of the financial stability of the Viśvakarmā Guthi, the religious trust of the Jyāthā Prajāpatis.
Rice for the alms-giving ceremony is cooked on the 12th of the same fortnight, and the alms are offered to Śākyas and Vajrācāryas the following day.
On the 14th, a feast calledmūbhvay(the main feast) was traditionally held for all trust members, but this has now been replaced with a meal ofsamaybaji, a traditional Newar food set.
Thepañcadānatrust is believed to have been established in 1830 CE (NS 950).
An inscription referring to the Gaṇeśa of Patan’s Jyāthā Ṭola as Viśvakarmā can be found in D. Vajrācārya VS 2056, p. 93, inscr. no. 50.
The upper roofs have been partly cut away due to encroachment of buildings to the north and east.
It has small blind windows on all four sides, however, the one on the eastern side is blocked by the encroachment of the adjacent building.
The top floor was heavily damaged by the 2015 earthquakes.
As of October 2024, the temple has been dismantled, leaving only the plinth, the bell stand and theśivaliṅgain place.
The Lalitpur Municipality is funding the reconstruction of the temple, while a local committee oversees project management and supervision.

monument_name: Bhājaṅgala Lvahaṃ Degaḥ East (built in 1684 CE)
text: The temple's construction dates back to 1684 CE (NS 804), an endeavour led by Rāmakṛṣṇa Bhāro and companions.

monument_name: Bhājaṅgala Lvahaṃ Degaḥ East (built in 1684 CE)
text: They also endowed tworopanīsof land to the temple at Namkhvāḥcā, a place south of the temple premises.

monument_name: Bhājaṅgala Lvahaṃ Degaḥ East (built in 1684 CE)
text: This land was allocated to facilitate the observance of the temple's anniversary rituals on the full moon day of Mārgaśīrṣa.

monument_name: Bhājaṅgala Lvahaṃ Degaḥ East (built in 1684 CE)
text: The Battle of Kirtipur in 1760 CE (NS 880) marked a historic chapter where Gorkha forces charged the town's hillock.

monument_name: Bhājaṅgala Lvahaṃ Degaḥ East (built in 1684 CE)
text: However, the temple, erected earlier in 1684 CE, predates this event.

monument_name: Bhājaṅgala Lvahaṃ Degaḥ East (built in 1684 CE)
text: An archival manuscript within the Āśā Archives (Reel No. 3480) preserves the account of Kālu Pā̃ḍe's heroic sacrifice during this battle (J. Maharjana NS 1134, p.56-57).

monument_name: Bhājaṅgala Lvahaṃ Degaḥ East (built in 1684 CE)
text: The Rājabhaṇḍārīs still reside in Kusikva Ṭola, the very location stated in the 1684 CE inscription as Rāmakṛṣṇa Bhāro's address (refer to 'historical events' below).

monument_name: Bhājaṅgala Lvahaṃ Degaḥ East (built in 1684 CE)
text: Although the inscription at the site mentions the establishment of Goddess Bhairavī as the donors’ patron deity, the temple itself lacks a physical statue.

monument_name: Bhājaṅgala Lvahaṃ Degaḥ East (built in 1684 CE)
text: Each year, on the 6th day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, the Rājabhaṇḍārī and Bisyaḥ families from Kirtipur's Bāghabhairava area assemble here to pay homage to their revered patron deity (P. Pradhāna NS 1141, p.171).
The courtyard is behind a row of residential buildings near theIkhālakhu Jahru.
A smallcaitya(70cm tall) can be found on the southern plinth attached to the building, and appears to be in a neglected state.
Bruce Owens notes that thekwāḥpāḥ dyaḥ,caitya, and other features are under threat as this space has been used to store lumber (and now detritus from the reconstruction) since at least 2008.

WhenLocke(1985, 140) studied this place, there was an image of Akṣobhya inside the middle shrine, an image of Prajñāpāramitā inside the shrine right to it and an image of Ṣaḍakṣarī Lokeśvara inside the left shrine, however these images have since been stolen.

In their place, statues of a doner in the act of praying have been installed inside the middle shrine, whilst the right-hand shirine now contains an image of Lakṣmī holding a lotus flower in her hand.
At the eastern corner of the courtyard is a bell that was donated in NS 1049, and at the southern corner one can find another smallcaitya.

There are no historical records to date the initial construction of the Temple.
The earliest record available at the site relates to a fairly recent event of 1954 CE (VS 2011) when a large bell was offered to the goddess.
The most recent renovation of the Temple took place in 1995 CE (VS 2052).
A lattice window with atoraṇahas been installed in the front facade of theāgãchẽ.
A Dharmadhātu Maṇḍala can also be found in the central axis of the main building.
It seems that most of the carved timber elements were reused during the reconstruction of this Bāhāḥ.
A small shrine containing an aniconic idol of Lord Gaṇeśa has been established between this Phalcā and the god house of the Bāhāḥ.
No inscription or any other document providing historical information regarding the Bāhāḥ could be found.
It is known that the Bāhāḥ was destroyed in the 1934 earthquake and reconstructed afterwards (Pruscha1975, 201).
The god house was reconstructed once again in 2012, however some of the work inside the sanctum is not yet finished.

TNakhu Mandaḥ Phalcā and its adjoiningjaḥdhuṃ(stone water spout) appear to have been constructed to provide shelter and drinking water for travelers moving along this traditional trade and pilgrimage route.
As of June 2025, the monument remains partially reconstructed, and the restoration process has come to a halt.

According to local informants, the recent reconstruction followed the design of the earlier structure, implying that Nakhu Mandaḥ Phalcā had already undergone prior rebuilding and modifications before the present effort.

The placement of Nakhu Mandaḥ Phalcā along the old Patan–Buṅgamatī–Bhīmaphedī route aligns with a broader pattern of rest houses featuringjaḥdhuṃs, constructed at intervals for the comfort of wayfarers.

Although no inscription has been found on Nakhu Mandaḥ Phalcā to clarify its exact date or patronage, the surviving pillars suggest a construction or renovation during the Rāṇā period, judging by their decorative patterns.
This points to either the original building or at least a major reconstruction during that era.
Local testimony indicates that thejaḥdhuṃ, now adjacent to the structure, previously stood a little farther east and was relocated during later reconstructions.
In the 2000s (ca. VS 2060), during the construction of the Sunrise Apartment housing project nearby, Nakhu Mandaḥ Phalcā was reportedly rebuilt as part of an urban development initiative.
After sustaining damage in the 2015 earthquakes, the Kathmandu Metropolitan City initiated another phase of reconstruction, which remains incomplete to date.

Oral accounts (local resident, Mānandhara, male, age 73) recall that during the 1980s (ca. VS 2040), when the Buṅgadyaḥ chariot required repairs midway at Nakhkhu Dobāṭo, the deity’s image was temporarily housed in Nakhu Mandaḥ Phalcā.
As at Nābhisthān (DLk0150 and DLK0151), this building and all those around it are of more or less recent construction.
During his visit to the site in 1967, Marc Gaborieau was able to photograph several sculptures that have now disappeared (stolen or kept secret for fear of theft).
According to the local residents, it was built by a Tulādhara family.

Local residents assume that a stone inscription is buried somewhere in this rubble.
One of the branch monasteries of Savala Bāhāḥ (KAT1430), Āḥju Bāhāḥ, exists in a restricted environment, confined to a narrow room on the ground floor of a nine-story commercial concrete building.
Thebāhāḥ-dyaḥchẽ(main building) has already lost its original structure and currently (as of January 2023 CE) features a metal door at the sanctuary, lacking atoraṇaabove the entrance.
Initially, thebāhāḥhoused a clay statue of Akṣobhya as its main deity, which was replaced with a stone statue in 1982 CE (NS 1102) after the original one was damaged.
In front of thebāhāḥ-dyaḥchẽ, threecaityas, including one from the Licchavi period, are established.
Historical records are not available to determine the initial construction date of thebāhāḥ.
According to accounts, a daughter of a member of Savala Bāhāḥ constructed thebāhāḥand gifted it to her guru from Taḥchẽ Bāhāḥ (KAT0470) (R. Vajrācārya & V. Vajrācārya 1103, p.116).
In 1982 CE (NS 1102), Dānamāyā Vajrācārya established a new stone statue of Akṣobhya after the previous clay one was damaged, as mentioned above.
A Licchavi caitya that was originally situated outside Savala Bāhāḥ was also relocated in front of Āḥju Bāhāḥ during that occasion (R. Vajrācārya & V. Vajrācārya 1103, p.116).
Until the mid-1970s, thebāhāḥmaintained its traditional architectural features, including a three-story main building with a tile roof and a small balconied tower (pula).
Additionally, a woodentoraṇaembellished with a statue of Dharmadhātuvāgīśvara was installed above the entrance to the sanctum (Locke 1985, p.296; R. Vajrācārya VS 2075, p.249).
Thebāhāḥalready resembled a residential structure prior to 1958 CE (Locke 1985, p.297).
Subsequently, around 2007 CE, thebāhāḥwas reconstructed in its current form.
However, due to their relocation from the area, the daily rituals are no longer conducted on a regular basis.
During the construction of the Ring Road in the vicinity of the shrine (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p. 533), the shrine ended up beneath the bridge.
Piṅgalāmāī is also known as Vajreśvarī and is locally revered as Mahālakṣmī (K. Koirālā VS 2051, p. 489).
Although the locals worship them as Vārāhī, Kālī, and Bhairava, the presence of large earrings suggests that these are female deities (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p. 473).
Previously, there used to be a reveredśivaliṅgaknown as Piṭhīgāreśvara Mahādeva, which was stolen (M. Thāpā VS 2077, p. 230).
Piṅgalāmāī is also recognized as apīṭhashrine that was established to honor a protective goddess.
While the exact historical origins of the shrine remain unclear, the three main statues within it are believed to date back to the 7th-8th century (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p. 473).
Located north of the main shrine, there is an inscription; however, all of its letters have eroded over time.
Apart from this, two copper-plate inscriptions from 1995 CE (VS 2052) and 2000 CE (VS 2057) are the only other inscriptions found at the site.

This special worship is conducted by representatives from the four social classes (varṇa) —thebrāhmaṇas,kṣetrīs,vaiśyas, andśūdras—from Deopatan, following both tantric and Vedic traditions, with the intention of promoting the welfare and prosperity of the nation (G. Ṭaṇḍana VS 2053, p. 524).

Before the Department of Archaeology reconstructed the Phalcā in 2008 CE under the supervision of Sukra Sagar Shrestha (Shokoohy and others2014, p. 162), only a square plinth along with theśivaliṅga and thejaḥdhuṃhad remained for decades (no other remnants of the Phalcā were found).
This suggest that the Phalcā had already ceased to exist before the 1934 earthquakes.
It probably collapsed in the previous great earthquakes and was never rebuilt.
An inscription recording the construction of the Sāḥgaḥ Mandaḥ Phalcā is installed inside a nearbyphalcā.
The inscription was probably relocated for security reasons after the Mandaḥ Phalcā collapsed.

It clearly mentions the initial construction of the Phalcā with ajaḥdhuṃand formation of aguthiby Bhāgīsiṃha Bhāro (Amātya) and his younger brother Siddhisiṃha from Dathu Ṭola (text: Dathu Tvāra) in memory of their father Manoharasiṃha.
Although the inscription also records the installation of statues of Trivikrama and Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa, they are no longer available at the site.
Since the inscription makes no reference to the saidśivaliṅga, the linga is probably a later addition.
Although the inscription mentions  the existence of aguthiand land endowment measuring sixropanīs, neither theguthinor land can be traced at present.

The inscription further records that the income of theguthishould be spent to observe the anniversary rituals of the Phalcā on the 7thof the dark fortnight of Māgha and donate various items on the new moon day of Caitra.

monument_name: Sera stone inscription of Ripu Malla (early 14th century)
text: The inscription dates from an early 14th century and is inscribed on the south façade of a stone boulder, located in a field of the hamlet of Sera.

text: This is an important historical record because it mentions Ripu Malla, a Khaśa Malla king who reigned between at least 1312 CE and 1316 CE (Andolfatto 2019).

It was constructed using a combination of mud and stone masonry.
Niels Gutschow studied similar dome temples in Far-West Nepal and observed that they were all built between the 1940s and 1980s (Gutschow 1992).
Although the exact construction date of this temple is unknown, it is reasonable to suggest that it was built during the latter half of the 20th century.
A few years ago, a suspension bridge was built thus making a visit to Gönpa Gang easily possible throughout the year.
Following the steep ascent to the monastery complex one enters a small courtyard with the residential building on the left and the monastery to the right.
A small, recently built entry room leads to the entrance hall which features murals depicting the Life of Sakyamuni, the Life of Padmasambhava and the Wheel of Life.
Unfortunately, caused by rising damp and severe water leaks from the damaged roof, many murals are damaged and some sections have been lost completely.
An extension to the south is a later addition built in stone.
Many details relating to the 12-year construction period can be found in the founder's biography.
The three medieval cities of the Kathmandu Valley were founded under the protection of theaṣṭamātṛkāpīṭha(abodes of the mother goddesses).
However, a proper statue of these deities is established at thedyaḥchẽwithin the city.
In the case of this Mahālakṣmī Temple (Pīṭha), the metal statue of Mahālakṣmī is kept and worshipped at the residence of thedyaḥpāḥlāḥfrom theMahālakṣmīGuthiof Thānakoṭa.
Although being the largest and most artistic Temple of the Thānakoṭa area, the date of the initial construction of the Mahālakṣmī Temple is unknown.
However, its wooden elements suggest that the Temple might have been built around the 17th-18th century.

The earliest inscription from the Temple, dated NS 788 (1668 CE), is seen inscribed on the image of a gatekeeper, but it not clear whether the gatekeeper figures were installed before or after the construction of the Temple.
Another inscription from the Temple, dated NS 804 (1684 CE), records about the installation of a statue of Umāmaheśvara by Rāmacandra Duvāra Bhāro and others.
Other medieval inscriptions found at the Temple are completely eroded.
The 2015 earthquakes badly damaged this Temple.

Although the locals carried out minor renovations, it was still being discussed whether to rebuild or only renovate the Temple at the time this survey was made (local knowledge, local resident, Nakarmī, age 30).
Variousguthis of Thānakoṭa perform their share of work to organize thejātrā.

An inscription informs that Jayānanda built the Caitya in 1801 CE (NS 921).
The Licchavi inscriptions mention this settlement as Lañjagvala (D. Vajrācārya 2030, p. 547).
They later founded a separatebahīat Lagana ṭola.
Thebahīwas founded by cutting down a bush of spear grasses.
Thebahīis a three-story building facing west that originally hadā̃ypātiles on its roof.
Corrugated sheets have now replaced theā̃ypātiles of the roof that has a stonecaityaas its finial.
Cidhi, Juju, and Muni, together with their mother Bhā Thakuṃ, had offered thistoraṇa.
There are no historical sources found yet that shed light on the initial construction of thisbahī.
The earliest inscription from thebahīis dated VS 1997 (1940 CE) found on the plinth of the stone lions guarding the main entrance.

The boys are taken to Naḥ Bahī for the ritual, as Cvākaṃ Bahī had moved out to Lagana ṭola from Naḥ Bahī.
Cvākaṃ Bahī is due to be reconstructed at the financial assistance of the Kathmandu Metropolis after its condition continued to deteriorate.
Kathmandu Metropolis has already allocated a budget of NRs. 15.4 million for the reconstruction.

Jagata Śamaśera, one of the brothers of Prime Minister Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā also built Jagatanārāyaṇa Mandira in 1855 CE (VS 1912) which is located to the east of Jagadīśvara Śivālaya (Regmī 2033, 249).
It is also said that eleven sages (ṛiṣi) came to this holy place and mediated for a long time; this is why the temple was built around the eleven śivaliṅgas on a single pedestal.
This temple has no source of income, so that its rituals are funded exclusively from donations made by devotees.
Above the spout, a shrine has been constructed, featuring a stone pinnacle adorned with a carved ritual sword (khaḍga).
This shrine, likely relocated from another site, houses a heavily eroded statue (object no. NWK0850-002), which is no longer identifiable due to extensive weathering.
The water spout was slightly moved from its original location to accommodate road widening efforts that took place in 2020 CE (VS 2077), as noted by a local resident, Khaḍkā Magar (male, age 62).
Adjacent to the spout is a resting place (cautāro), which bears an inscription dating the original construction of the site, to 1926 CE (VS 1982).

monument_name: Cilancva Phalcā South (built around the 19th cent.)
text: Built in front of Cilancva Caitya (KIR0001), the largest Buddhist monument in Kirtipur, Cilancva Phalcā (South) is one of two historicPhalcās.
The temple, which is constructed in a domed style, faces west.
A pair of Śārdūlas and lions, installed in 1660 CE (NS 780), flank the temple’s main entrance.
In addition to these statues, the stone statues of lions, placed in all four directions of the temple, were added around the same time.
A tall and standing Viṣṇu statue is consecrated in the sanctum (garbhagṛha).
Besides this, there are two Viṣnu statues, a statue of Umāmaheśvara, and three medieval inscriptions in the sanctum.
The inscription in the sanctum dating from 1660 CE (NS 780) records thatKvāṭhanāyakaJakerāja constructed the temple, however, it does not date the construction work.
A palm-leaf document related to Kirtipur from 1585 CE (NS 705) also mentions Jakerāja.
It can then be assumed that the temple was probably constructed around this time.
Initially, this temple should have been constructed in the pagoda style.
H. A. Oldfield has mentioned two or three damaged temples located to north of the Deypukhū in Kirtipur when he visited the place around 1855 CE (cf.Oldfield1980, 129).
Further, a royal decree issued in 1838 CE (VS 1894) suggests that the government should renovate this temple whenever necessary (cf.Ś. ŚreṣṭhaVS 2057, 52).

Thus, it can be largely assumed that the temple was renovated six years after the devastating earthquake in 1832 CE, and itsguṭhīland was brought under the jurisdiction of the government in order to finance its maintenance and renovation.
It is, however, puzzling that Oldfield did not see this temple during his visit to Kirtipur around 1855 CE which was renovated in 1838 CE.
It is also probable that the temple was destroyed a couple of years after the renovation.
A record in the Guṭhī Office dating from 1918 CE (VS 1975) mentions the ruinous state of this temple in 1912 CE (VS 1969) (cf.Ś. ŚreṣṭhaVS 2057, 512).
In 1920 CE, the temple was reconstructed by Kājimāna Pradhāna, one of the descendants of Jakerāja.
After its initial construction, Jakerāja must have established aguṭhī,and endowed land for its maintenance and for the performence of the daily and other rituals in the temple.
This suggests that there is a connection between these two monuments or that they were constructed at a same time.

Historically,dabūswere constructed near palaces, important temples, and the residences of influential courtiers in order to perform ritual dances and dramas during auspicious rituals or (royal) ceremonies and festivities (K. Tamot2013, p. 20).
While the temple's appearance is ordinary, the statue of Mahiṣāsuramardinī, established as the main deity, is a masterpiece.

An inscription in the sanctum records the establishment of the statue by Lakṣasiṃha and his brother (whose name is no longer legible), the sons of Śukrasiṃha Bhāro, in 1617 CE (NS 737) during the reign of King Śivasiṃhadeva (D. Vajrācārya and Ṭ. Śreṣṭha VS 2032, second part, p. 7).
